name: Maryland Matters
title: Analysts urge action on four years of projected gaps to get ahead of recession scenario
description: A key legislative fiscal committee is being encouraged to begin dealing with a series of projected budget deficits now in anticipation of an economic downturn that could add almost $1 billion to what is already expected to be a multibillion-dollar shortfall.
text:
House Speaker Joseline Peña-Melnyk (D-Prince George’s and Anne Arundel) talks with Senate President Bill Ferguson (D-Baltimore City) in January 2026. The legislative leaders are warning of touch economic decisions ahead in the 2027 session, and beyond. (Photo by Danielle J. Brown/Maryland Matters)A key legislative fiscal committee is being encouraged to begin dealing with a series of projected budget deficits now in anticipation of an economic downturn that could add almost $1 billion to what is already expected to be a multibillion-dollar shortfall.
At a briefing Wednesday of the joint Spending Affordability Committee, members were told that four years of tough budget decisions lie ahead, that includes budget gaps of more than $3 billion. That was before a recession stress test was added to the estimates..
“If you don’t act, facing a $4 billion or more problem would be extraordinarily challenging, especially during a recession,” said David Romans, the legislature’s top budget analyst.
Recessions are difficult to predict, and the analysis offered Wednesday was not presented as predictive. Still, the potential for a downturn is real. Some worry a bursting of an artificial intelligence bubble will spark a recession.
The National Bureau of Economic Research defines a recession as “a significant decline in economic activity that is spread across the economy, and that lasts more than a few months.”
State budget analysts warn that a moderate recession could add $1 billion to projected budget gaps over the next four years. (Department of Legislative Services)
The last recession lasted roughly two months in early 2020 during the COVID-19 pandemic. Before that was the 19-month Great Recession driven by the collapse of the housing bubble.
Gov. Wes Moore (D) and the General Assembly now face a series of budget challenges in the term that begins in January.
More than $700 million in projected deficiencies that must be resolved in the current year budget. Another projected structural gap of more than $2.5 billion looms for fiscal 2028.
The next three years do not get better.
Under the moderate recession scenario presented to the committee, the economic decline would begin in the current quarter.
Nationally, more than 4.5 million jobs would be lost. The unemployment rate would increase from 4.1% to 7.1% by the third quarter of 2027. The economy would not recover those jobs until the fourth quarter of 2028.
Maryland would follow those trends, losing about 79,000 jobs. The unemployment rate would rise from 4.2% to 5.8% in the third quarter of 2027.
Recovering those jobs in Maryland would lag behind the national trend, analysts said. The state would not fully recoup the jobs lost during the recession until mid-2029, according to the scenario presented.
Personal income along with wage and salary growth would be cut in half during that period.
The current projected shortfall “is about 55% greater than the shortfall we had in 2008 during the Great Recession in inflation adjusted dollars,” said Senate President Bill Ferguson (D-Baltimore City).
“I think sets the tone of the scope of the adjustments that we are going to have to make this upcoming year to provide predictability for Marylanders,” he said.
Chamber report calls for fixing budget woes with improved business climate

Moore, Ferguson and House Speaker Joseline Peña-Melnyk (D-Prince George’s and Anne Arundel) announced last week an agreement to craft a four-year plan to address the situation.
The agreement — if it holds — represents a change from the usual approach.
In September, Budget Secretary Yaakov “Jake” Weissmann said all budget options were on the table. Those include reductions in general fund spending. Some suggested the sales tax — an increase in the percentage or extending it to services — could be a likely place for a revenue increase, if lawmakers went in that direction.
A one-penny increase in the sales tax would generate about $1.2 billion in revenue. But sales taxes are often criticicizes as regressive for their outsized impact on low-income individuals.
Peña-Melnyk said Wednesday that work is already underway behind the scenes to prepare for the coming session.
“We know that the picture does not look pretty,” she said. “We knew that coming in, and we are doing the work.”

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: State, advocates aim to support and highlight work of unpaid caregivers
description: New Jersey launched an online hub to help unpaid caregivers, a workforce advocates are highlighting during November's National Family Caregivers Month.
text:
Wanda Flowers Peacock, a Voorhees caregiver, is shown in a portrait by Rutgers art student Beatryz Hornung. The portrait is one of ten arranged by AARP NJ and displayed in Atlantic City to mark November's National Family Caregivers Month. (Photo courtesy AARP NJ.)Wanda Flowers Peacock has been a caregiver most of her life, looking after younger children as a teen and later her son, who has complex health needs. Now the Voorhees woman is caring for her husband, Donald, who has cognitive issues and is recovering from a serious car crash. 
Flowers Peacock, who is in her 70s, considers herself lucky. She is healthy and financially stable. She and Donald are able to stay positive most of the time, she said, but caregiving takes an emotional toll on everybody. 
“People need to be aware of what caregivers do — because it’s so behind the scenes — and also be appreciative and acknowledge what they do,” Flowers Peacock told the New Jersey Monitor. 
National Family Caregivers Month, marked each November, aims to make the work done by people like Flowers Peacock more visible. Nationwide more than 63 million people provide free care for a loved one, including more than a million New Jersey residents, according to state officials. 
On Tuesday, New Jersey announced the launch of a new caregiver online resource hub, where families can connect to aging and disabilities programs, respite care, and hundreds of other services. The goal is to make it easier for this unseen workforce, many who are also working full time outside the home, to get the help and support they need. 
Kaylee McGuire, a deputy commissioner at the Human Services Department, which oversaw the hub’s creation based on 2022 recommendations from a caregiver task force, said the tool was designed with input from caregivers to help people navigate a complex social-service web. 
“New Jersey caregivers are incredibly resourceful, but too often they’re forced to spend precious time and energy searching for help while already balancing work, family, finances, and caregiving responsibilities,” McGuire said. “The reality is that many helpful programs and supports already exist, but finding the right information at the right time can feel overwhelming.”
New Jersey has 1.7 million residents 65 or older and that population is expected to double by 2050, state officials said, while the ratio of available caregivers is expected to fall. The state supports some 25,000 disabled adults, many of whom rely on families to advocate for them, coordinate programming, and provide transportation. 
Human Services Commissioner Stephen Cha called caregivers “the backbone of how we support older adults and people with disabilities in New Jersey, and often they do it quietly and alone.” 
Using the hub, families can find out if they are eligible for food aid or subsidized health insurance. There’s a search feature that uses plain-language program descriptions, a live hotline, a text chat feature, and an email address that officials said they will respond to within one business day. It has links to county offices, an Alzheimer’s day program, and connections to Archangles, a public benefit corporation founded to advocate for caregivers. 
Crystal McDonald, AARP New Jersey’s senior associate state director, praised the state’s work on the online hub. The elder care advocacy organization participated in the task force, she said, and caregivers told the group they struggled to navigate available services. 
“Programs and services often vary by county, by the needs of the person receiving care, and by a family’s specific circumstances. Creating a centralized hub was one of the Task Force’s key recommendations to help caregivers more easily find the support they need,” McDonald told the New Jersey Monitor in an email. 
“The Caregiver Hub is an important step toward helping caregivers connect with services more quickly and focus on what matters most: caring for their loved ones,” she wrote. 
Caregivers in New Jersey provide about 1.2 billion hours of unpaid care annually, valued at some $28 billion, AARP has calculated. On Wednesday, the organization unveiled an art exhibit in Atlantic City, where state and local government officials are attending an annual convention, to celebrate National Family Caregivers Month and caregivers in the Garden State. 
The exhibit features original portraits of 10 Garden State caregivers, created by artists from Rutgers University’s Mason Gross School of Arts. Beatryz Hornung captured a smiling Wanda Flowers Peacock in a pink-patterned shirt, seated on a blue couch below a portrait of Lady Justice. 
“Rather than a burden, I see it as a blessing that I have the health to be able to do this, and the desire to be able to do this,” Flowers Peacock said of caring for her husband, who is also in his 70s. 
Flowers Peacock said she feels lucky to have support from her children and Donald’s siblings, as well as help from AARP New Jersey, where she also volunteers, helping other seniors. 
“I’ve been doing this all my life and the more I feel I give back, the more I get back. And it helps me to expand my life, and gives me compassion and understanding about people’s circumstances,” she said.

name: Colorado Newsline
title: Commentary: Unfit federal judge’s confirmation a blow to justice in Colorado
description: One after another, President Donald Trump’s nominees for judgeships go before senators seeking confirmation and refuse to say who won the 2020 presidential election. Every person who participates in this mass act of abasement should be disqualified from holding office, especially judges, who are supposed to be models of integrity and independence. In this da[...]
text:
A view of the Byron White U.S. Courthouse, base of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 10th Circuit, in downtown Denver. (Google Maps)One after another, President Donald Trump’s nominees for judgeships go before senators seeking confirmation and refuse to say who won the 2020 presidential election.
Every person who participates in this mass act of abasement should be disqualified from holding office, especially judges, who are supposed to be models of integrity and independence.
In this dark period of corruption and cowardice, Republicans in the Senate keep confirming these dubious nominees, littering the federal bench with dozens of Trump-appeasing jurists. The latest is Daniel Domenico, a Denver-based U.S. district judge who on Monday was confirmed to the powerful federal appeals court based in Colorado. Domenico during his confirmation hearing in June refused to answer when asked directly who won the 2020 election, which Trump falsely insists to this day was stolen from him. That Joe Biden won is indisputable fact, like 2+2=4, and it turns the stomach to watch an adult go in front of cameras and choose abject dishonesty over simple truth, all to stroke the ego of an autocrat.
It should make every Coloradan queasy to know Domenico is now in a position to decide matters of justice at the 10th Circuit Court of Appeals. If we can’t trust him to tell a simple truth, how can we trust him on big ones?
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
This is fundamentally about principles, but it’s also about very real cases. In January, the 10th Circuit is scheduled to hear arguments in — you’d never guess — a 2020 election case. It involves one of Trump’s most loyal allies, Mike Lindell, the MyPillow guy, who did as much as anyone to spread the election-denial contagion across the country. After a federal jury in Denver found that he defamed former Dominion Voting Systems employee Eric Coomer and ordered Lindell to pay Coomer $2.3 million, Lindell appealed to the 10th Circuit.
It’s unlikely, given the process Domenico must undertake to fully join the court, that he’ll be assigned to that case. But it’s not out of the question, and his mere proximity to it proves the point — no one could trust him to handle it impartially.
It’s not just election cases that will be a problem. Given that Domenico was so willing to bargain away his good name in public, it will be hard for Coloradans to have confidence he can be neutral as he writes opinions behind closed doors. The 10th Circuit has near-final say on matters of great importance, such as constitutional rights and immigration, another topic Trump cares a lot about, and its jurisdiction extends beyond Colorado to include Oklahoma, Kansas, New Mexico, Wyoming and Utah.
In a further sign of Domenico’s unfitness, both of Colorado’s Democratic U.S. senators, neither of whom are given to performative partisanship, voted against his confirmation.
“At a time when the Trump Administration has spent years undermining the rule of law and eroding the independence of the federal courts, I cannot support elevating Judge Domenico to the Tenth Circuit,” said Bennet, who had voted to confirm Domenico to the district court in 2019.
Opposition to Domenico went well beyond his Trump sycophancy. As Michael Karlik at Colorado Politics has documented extensively, Domenico is a poor performer and ideological outlier. He is the only judge in Colorado to have agreed with the Trump administration on its policy of no-bond detention for people without authorization even when they’ve been present in the U.S. for a long time.
Domenico was confirmed as part of a rush in the Republican-controlled Senate to seat Trump-nominated judges before the GOP hands over the majority to Democrats in January. He’s part of a class of roughly 60 judges Trump has put on the federal bench during his second term. The group includes truly odious figures, such as Emil Bove, a former personal attorney for Trump who as acting deputy U.S. attorney general told government lawyers they might need to ignore court orders. But refusal to say who won the 2020 election is universal among them.
Don’t mistake regularity for harmlessness. The normalization of lies only underlines the putrefaction of politics in Trump’s America, where even the highest federal courts are increasingly tainted by toadies in robes. In Colorado, that’s Domenico.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Commentary: Hemp, CBD, and the bans we brought on ourselves
description: In the spring of 2025, my 15-year-old grandson was admitted to Kentucky Children’s Hospital at the University of Kentucky. He had experienced a psychotic break after ingesting Delta-8 THC he had ordered online from a website called OnlyGas.com. He scared his mother, his father, his little sister and me. He scared himself.  The Children’s Hospital […]
text:
A worker holds up unprocessed hemp at the Kentucky Heritage Hemp Company in Coxs Creek. (Kentucky Lantern photo by McKenna Horsley)In the spring of 2025, my 15-year-old grandson was admitted to Kentucky Children’s Hospital at the University of Kentucky. He had experienced a psychotic break after ingesting Delta-8 THC he had ordered online from a website called OnlyGas.com. He scared his mother, his father, his little sister and me. He scared himself.  The Children’s Hospital had a locked ward for cases like this – kids with drug overdoses. And my grandson was there.
I’m a grandmother and a well-known Kentucky farmer with a health-oriented national following. I was glad to bring hemp back to Kentucky fields and barns. Now, I say with regret: The hemp industry did this to itself. After years of warnings — including mine — the reckoning has arrived.
The glut that started it
The 2018 Farm Bill legalized hemp after Kentucky’s pilot program, of which we were a part, developed a research base for a crop which hadn’t been grown commercially since World War II. Farms like mine got on board quickly. We planted hemp for fiber, hemp for grain, and hemp for CBD.
But processors over-promised and farmers over-planted. In my own Clark County, two of the industry’s giants, Atalo and GenCanna – both headquartered in Winchester — went bankrupt in early 2020, owing farmers millions of dollars and leaving chaos and despair across central Kentucky. Together they had contracted with farmers to grow a crop that had no market. So they stiffed them. 
I saw this coming because I knew the arithmetic. In the spring of 2020, before COVID closed Washington, I lobbied my senator and congressman in person. I knew how many tons of hemp Kentucky had produced, and I knew how much it took Mt. Folly to make products which we sold locally and online at laurasmercantile.com. “There is nowhere for this crop to go,” I told them both. 
That hemp flower — distressed, dirt-cheap, sitting in barns and warehouses — became the feedstock for the Delta-8 boom. Chemists discovered they could take CBD from that surplus biomass and, using heat and acids like sulfuric or hydrochloric acid, rearrange its molecules into Delta-8 THC: compounds that get people high while technically meeting the letter of the law.
Then, in May 2022, the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals ruled in AK Futures v. Boyd Street Distro that these converted products fell within the Farm Bill’s definition of hemp. The court was candid: the statute “is silent with regard to delta-8 THC,” and if Congress did not intend to legalize psychoactive cannabinoids, “it is up to Congress to close the loophole.”
Congress did not. And an industry grew around that loophole like mold on a damp wall.
The industry did this to itself
After the court ruling, intoxicating gummies, vapes, and beverages appeared at gas stations, smoke shops, and on websites across the country.  Some companies went beyond Delta 8 – to Delta-10, HHC, THCP, and THCA flower, which becomes intoxicating the moment you light it.
Online, the website that sold to my grandson markets itself as “the #1 online dispensary,” promises “discreet delivery,” and bills credit cards under a bland name so parents can’t see what they paid for. Its own FAQ boasts that its flower “will get you high” while staying Farm Bill compliant because “the Farm Bill only measures Delta 9.”
In health-food stores and online, well-known legacy brands did a little math and took advantage of the 2018 farm bill’s “dry weight” rule: a heavy 6-gram gummy can hold 15 milligrams of THC — enough to make a kid or an adult stoned — and still “pass” at 0.25%, below the law’s limit. These brands market 5 and 10 mg THC gummies for calm and relaxation, deep sleep, powerful relaxation, and so forth. 
I am not anti-hemp. I have grown it since Kentucky’s pilot program in 2015. We have a line of dark chocolates made with hemp grain for protein, and only two of our products contain any THC at all. For example, one gummy or one dropper of Mt. Folly extract contains between 1 and 2 milligrams of THC alongside 25-50 milligrams of CBD — as close to the plant as we can keep it, so our customers can benefit from the entourage effect, a real thing. CBD has helped me personally recover from a horseback riding accident which left me with full-body pain.
But for years, I and others in the legitimate industry begged for rules that would separate us from the “gas-station weed” trade. Nobody in Washington did much, and the vacuum filled itself.
Bans without enforcement
States tried. Roughly 18 states banned Delta-8 and similar products outright. But a ban on paper is not a ban on a shelf. In Texas, the health department admitted it had the capacity to inspect stores roughly once every five years. In Washington, a court-era ban simply went unenforced. Texas outlawed THCA flower in March; an industry attorney there said plainly that enforcement “remains rare.” The FDA sent warning letters — dozens of them — but filed no criminal actions. The DEA declined to act. The result was a national gray market that could ship to any teenager with a credit card.
Now comes the federal hammer. On Nov. 12, cannabinoids the plant cannot make naturally — the Delta-8s, the HHCs, the lab-made THC look-alikes — lost their federal hemp status. On Dec. 11, the rest of the law takes hold: a “total THC” standard, and a cap of 0.4 milligrams of THC per container.
That cap will not just end the stoner products. It will also capture full-spectrum CBD products like mine — products that never spiked anything, that carry certificates of analysis, that stayed as close to the plant as the law allows. The compliant will be swept out with the corrupt.  
The industry that abused the Farm Bill’s silence are shedding crocodile tears about the crackdown. These companies should look in the mirror. My farmer neighbors in Clark County, and my grandson in that hospital bed, both paid for this industry’s choices. Congress is finally closing the loophole the courts told it to close — but a 0.4-milligram limit, applied without an FDA framework for the honest products, is a self-inflicted wound on an industry that spent a decade refusing to distinguish itself from snake oil. We can do better than a ban, and I hope eventually we do. But nobody should pretend we were not warned.

name: Maine Morning Star
title: A path to bring back parole in Maine emerges as a receptive governor steps in
description: A state commission teed up a plan on Wednesday to reinstate parole in Maine, a move the incoming governor is open to after opposition from the previous executive.   The majority of the commission recommended bringing back the conditional early release program and making both people incarcerated in the future and those already incarcerated eligible, under […]
text:
A state commission recommends people incarcerated at Maine State Prison in Warren and other facilities in Maine be eligible for parole under certain circumstances. (Photo by Evan Popp/ Maine Morning Star)A state commission teed up a plan on Wednesday to reinstate parole in Maine, a move the incoming governor is open to after opposition from the previous executive.  
The majority of the commission recommended bringing back the conditional early release program and making both people incarcerated in the future and those already incarcerated eligible, under specific circumstances. However, members disagreed on what those circumstances should be, punting a core question to the incoming Legislature which will settle the specifics.   
Maine was the first state to abolish parole 50 years ago and is one of 16 states that remain without it today. A proposal to reinstate the program last session failed to gain committee support, though opposition had less to do with the policy itself and more to do with how to implement such a change.
So lawmakers instead opted to examine the intersection of parole and current sentencing practices through a study commission, which held its final meeting on Wednesday, lasting eight hours, to set recommendations for the next Legislature. Rep. Nina Milliken (D-Blue Hill), who introduced the parole bill last session and sat on the commission, said she plans to pursue it again when session begins in January. 
Maine was the first state to abolish parole. Incarcerated Mainers, advocates hope to bring it back.

 
Previous efforts to reinstate parole were expected to fail, because outgoing Gov. Janet Mills, a former prosecutor and state attorney general, consistently opposed such a program. The next iteration will be considered by Gov.-elect Hannah Pingree, who told Maine Morning Star she supports reinstating parole, as long as it is established in a way that weighs evidence of rehabilitation alongside risk.
Parole is not automatic but a condition granted by a parole board for someone to serve the remainder of their sentence supervised in the community, while adhering to specific rules. 
“An effort to reinstate parole should focus on whether someone has demonstrated readiness to return to the community — through education, treatment, behavioral progress, and a clear plan for reentry — and ensure that decisions are made in a way that is fair, consistent, and proportionate to the individual’s circumstances,” Pingree said in a statement. 
She added that, “critically, this work cannot stop at the point of release. If we expect people to succeed when they return to the community, we must ensure that the conditions for success are in place: stable housing, access to health care, pathways to employment, and strong community connections.”
Who should be eligible?
One of the key questions the commission was asked to settle was whether parole should be applied only to people convicted after a parole law is passed or also to people currently incarcerated. 
Four members voted to recommend retroactive application for all crime types, with a higher evidentiary standard of rehabilitation for sexual assault and crimes against family and household members. Four members voted to recommend retroactive application with exclusions and/or a higher standard for retroactive application (leaving the specifics of both up to legislators). 
No members voted for an option to allow retroactive application for all crime types without exceptions, and one member voted to not allow retroactive application at all. One member abstained. 
“I want people to think that this is not just a question of whether the incarcerated person has done good work for themselves and are in a better place,” Francine Garland Stark from the Maine Coalition to End Domestic Violence told the commission on Wednesday. “I certainly hope that they are, but the harm that they have caused has not been rehabilitated. They may themselves be in a better place, but what has happened remains.” 
Garland Stark and other victims’ advocates, who did not have a seat on the commission, offered suggestions during the final meeting, overwhelmingly urging the group not to pursue reinstating parole retroactively specifically for cases that include elevated, aggravated assault, attempted murder, manslaughter, and murder cases. 
While people with violent offenses are eligible for parole in some other states, Maine would be an outlier if it included these types of sentences in parole retroactively. 
Pointing to the Maine Department of Corrections’ mission statement to rehabilitate and the low recidivism rate touted by the department, Sen. Rachel Talbot Ross (D-Cumberland) questioned why certain cases should be excluded, if the department and a parole board were to deem the incarcerated person rehabilitated and no longer a threat to society. 
Milliken added that putting such exclusions into statute doesn’t offer the nuance that exists among people who commit serious offenses. Victims’ advocates similarly emphasized during the meeting that victims are not a monolith. 
“What the challenge of retrospect application does is it upends what people currently working on that healing process thought was going to be the parameter of their span of peace,” Garland Stark said.
Pointing to Maine’s supervised community confinement program, Christopher Laliberte, a currently incarcerated person who sits on the commission, said early release through that program is not accounted for in a judgment, because “it’s not a guarantee — it’s an opportunity.”
Supervised community confinement allows people to serve the final few months of a sentence in the community supervised by the department through probation. It is available to people in the last 30 months of their sentence, up from 18 months after a change in 2021. 
“I view parole very much the same way,” Laliberte said. “It’s not taking away a judgment that a jury or a judge has given. It’s providing an opportunity for relief for someone who has done the work to prove that they have ‘rehabilitated’ themselves.”
But victims’ rights advocates said they discuss the implications of supervised community confinement with victims at length before and after sentencing, pointing out how that would not be possible if parole became retroactively eligible to people already serving sentences today. 
Other commission recommendations
A key point of confusion during debate of reinstating parole last session was what would happen if conflicts arose between the administration of parole and probation violations. 
The commission recommended on Wednesday that the probation violation take precedence if it falls under Maine’s split sentences statute.
The commission punted on the policy question of whether a judge should be able to issue a life sentence without parole, instead voting to recommend that a future parole bill not be passed without lawmakers addressing it. 
The majority of the commission also recommended parole not replace the supervised community confinement program. 
During consideration of the parole bill last session, the Maine Department of Corrections argued the current system was sufficient in part because of supervised community confinement. Long-timers in Maine State Prison told Maine Morning Star that the prospects of early release through that program are too far out to have a tangible impact on motivation. 
In 2026, 81 people eligible to apply for supervised community confinement did not, with 41% citing housing as a barrier and 58% reporting they weren’t interested, according to data the Department of Corrections provided the commission.
The overarching money question
Discussion of various aspects of reinstating parole made clear inadequacies in the current system, specifically when it comes to funding. 
“Victim notification in our state currently is woefully underfunded and under-resourced, and fails on the regular,” said Cara Cookson, director of victim services for the Maine Office of the Attorney General. 
Maine didn’t enact victim notification requirements until 1995, which continues to present challenges for DOC Victim Services getting contact information to notify people, Cookson added. The ability of victim witness advocates to do their work in a timely way also depends on prosecutors, and Maine has faced ongoing staffing shortages and heavy caseloads. 
The commission recommended on Wednesday that any parole system established include the financial and human resources necessary to have a robust victim notification system. 
Maine relies heavily on the federal Victims of Crime Act to fund victim services. That federal funding has declined in recent years and the state has tried to pick up the tab. 
“I think the Legislature has done a really insufficient job, and I think that’s being generous, in caring for the programs that you guys are all running,” Milliken said to victims’ services advocates during Wednesday’s meeting. “And frankly, that’s Democrats’ fault, and I’m going to say that on mic because we have been responsible for running the budget for the state for several years now and we have not done an adequate job to make sure that you guys can continue to provide the life saving services that you do for the state of Maine.”
Along with its specific recommendations regarding how to reinstate parole, the commission also agreed to include a statement in its final report recognizing that the success of the programs within a parole system would require financial investment by the legislature.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: Morales team vows to implement divestment ordinance despite legal concerns
description: The transition team for Providence Mayor-elect David Morales’ administration is preparing to implement — and defend in court, if necessary — a divestment ordinance that more than three-quarters of Providence voters approved in the general election earlier this month. “Providence voters overwhelmingly supported Question 7, and the Morales administration inten[...]
text:
A sign supporting Providence’s Question 7 divestment ordinance is seen off Broadway on Wednesday, Nov. 18, 2026. More than three-quarters of city voters approved the measure on Nov. 3. (Photo by Alexander Castro/Rhode Island Current)The transition team for Providence Mayor-elect David Morales’ administration is preparing to implement — and defend in court, if necessary — a divestment ordinance that more than three-quarters of Providence voters approved in the general election earlier this month.
“Providence voters overwhelmingly supported Question 7, and the Morales administration intends to honor that vote,” June Rose, executive director of Morales’ mayoral transition, said in an email Friday.
The measure instructs the city to divest from or restrict municipal investments tied to countries responsible for or companies complicit in severe human rights violations. Rose said that the city treasurer’s first report on municipal investments is due by the end of January 2027.
The measure does not single out Israel by name, but both organizers and opponents have identified the country as the target of the measure. Supporters cite Israeli military actions in Gaza as genocide, while opponents dispute that characterization. 
The incoming administration’s commitment to implementing the ordinance comes after a retired federal judge’s advisory opinion, requested by the outgoing Brett Smiley administration, concluded the measure could lead to numerous legal headaches for the city. 
The divestment measure appeared on the ballot following a successful citizen-led campaign. Rarely pursued in Providence’s electoral history, the citizen-led ballot process is outlined in the city charter and allows residents who obtain enough signatures to put a proposed ordinance before their fellow voters. 
Overall, organizers collected a little over 6,000 signatures that were later verified. The measure had a strong showing at the polls on Nov. 3 too, where it was Question 7 on the ballot and secured around 76% support from voters.
Morales’ transition team, announced earlier this month, includes 135 people across nine policy committees to figure out how his administration will lead the city.
“During the transition, we’re beginning conversations with the ordinance’s authors and investment professionals about the steps the city will need to take to put it into effect,” Rose said.
Following Morales’ January inauguration, Rose said, the new mayor’s staff will collaborate with the city treasurer, the city’s legal department and the Board of Investment Commissioners to review Providence’s investment portfolio and identify possible “priorities for divestment.” The treasurer has a Jan. 31, 2027, deadline to submit an initial report to the city clerk. 
Members of the Rhode Island Coalition for Israel, including board member and republican candidate for Providence Mayor Dave Talan, seen at right, rally outside Bell Street Chapel in Providence on Tuesday, Aug. 25, 2026, ahead of a mayoral forum. The group opposes Question 7, a divestment proposal that both opponents and proponents argue targets Israel, despite never being name in the ordinance. (Photo by Alexander Castro/Rhode Island Current)
Some people still have questions about the measure’s legality, however — including Dave Talan, Morales’ Republican opponent in the mayoral election who also sits on the board of the Rhode Island Coalition for Israel. 
Talan told Rhode Island Current Monday that he is certain the measure will face legal scrutiny in court. 
“We know that somebody is going to be suing regarding this Question 7,” Talan said, suggesting it could be a larger group like the Jewish Alliance of Greater Rhode Island, given that the Rhode Island Coalition for Israel has fewer legal resources, he said.
Rhode Island Current has asked the Jewish Alliance multiple times since the measure’s passage if it will engage in a legal battle over the ordinance. Alliance spokesperson Brian Sullivan initially pointed to a Nov. 4 statement from its president and CEO, Steven A. Baker.
“While we continue to believe that Question 7 was a divisive measure that may have adverse consequences for both the Jewish community and the City’s finances, our focus remains on bringing people together, strengthening understanding, confronting antisemitism, and working alongside partners across Rhode Island to build a state where every community can thrive,” Baker wrote.
Sullivan told Rhode Island Current Tuesday that the organization had nothing further to add.
Talan said was still unsure how the measure would work mechanically, and offered that the nature of pension funds — which often involve mutual funds — could make divestment difficult. 
“Since almost every major country has some sort of facility in Israel, it’s inconceivable they could find any kind of mutual fund that excludes Israel entirely,” Talan argued. “And if the pension fund was to invest in an individual company and that company went bankrupt, that would be really bad news as far as the retirees.”
The ordinance treats directly managed investments differently from pooled investments, such as mutual funds, and requires the city to ask fund managers to consider adopting its investment restrictions.
Thousands of signatures put a question on Providence’s November ballot. One country is the target.

Retired federal Judge William E. Smith, in his advisory opinion for Smiley’s administration, criticized the measure as poorly drafted and unlikely to be enforceable. 
“Unfortunately, when laws are poorly drafted as this one is, litigation is almost inevitable,” Smith wrote.
Smith argued that the ordinance likely goes beyond what the citizen initiative process actually allows. The city charter does not allow such initiatives to affect select financial matters in the city, such as city employees’ salaries and benefits.
In August, Salar Ghahramani, a Penn State professor whose research includes investment law and fiduciary responsibilities, told Rhode Island Current he thought the measure was “expertly written.”
Ghahramani was unavailable for additional comment Wednesday, but previously noted that the draft bases its legal applicability from reliance on international treaties to which the U.S. is a party, as well as a broader definition of “complicity” that is not directed at one country. 
However, Smith’s opinion suggests this flexibility might create more problems. He argued the ordinance “lacks the precision” to effectively define the human rights violations at its core. He noted that even a restrictive interpretation could implicate multiple countries, citing findings — sometimes conflicting ones — by U.S. and international authorities concerning China, Myanmar and Israel.
“Even a narrow reading, in other words, would require the [city’s] Investment Commission to make contested judgments about which of these findings count,” Smith wrote.
Smith also wrote the measure could violate the city’s fiduciary obligations to its pensioners. While the ordinance exempts investments from its restrictions if divestment would violate those obligations, Smith didn’t think it would dispel any and all disputes, as legal arguments could still arise from differing interpretations of these responsibilities.
Andrew Spacone, a Roger Williams University law professor who teaches fiduciary duties and securities regulation in his courses, said in a phone call Wednesday that, while he’s not an expert in Providence’s municipal law, he agreed with much of Smith’s legal assessment and thought there were possible financial impacts beyond even what the judge described.
“You just don’t go and unload investments without suffering losses,” Spacone said of the actual divestment strategy, citing similar initiatives undertaken by financial institutions in recent years to invest more of their portfolios in eco-friendly companies — a strategy which he said some institutions now see as not a maximal return on investment. 
“So, many of these financial institutions have pulled back,” Spacone said. 
Potential litigation, Spacone said, represents another venue by which the ordinance could cost the city money. Laws surrounding pension fund management are intricate and complex, Spacone noted, and litigation involving fund managers could possibly deplete pension assets, depending on how legal expenses are paid, he said.
The ordinance’s inclusion of a safeguard that would stop the city’s investment officials from violating their fiduciary duties, Spacone acknowledged, was clever. 
“Whoever put that in there was pretty smart,” he said, but remained skeptical that it would tangibly prevent legal disputes.
Spacone, who called the measure’s avoidance of naming Israel a case of “artful drafting to cover up what really is going on here,” was curious how the ordinance might play out in the state courts.
A box of Spanish-language flyers urging Providence voters to approve Question 7 is shown at an Election Night party for divestment campaign supporters at Salon on Eddy Street. (Photo by Christopher Shea/Rhode Island Current)
“It would be very interesting to see if any of the state or federal courts would have the moxie, if you will, in this current political climate, to declare it illegal for whatever reason,” Spacone said, adding that he feels state and federal judges generally “try and do the right thing and they try to set aside their biases.” 
The commission for Smith’s legal opinion cost the city $15,647.63, according to Carl Austin Miller Grondin, press secretary for the Smiley administration.
“As written, the City’s legal department has determined that this ordinance is both unenforceable and likely in violation of existing state law,” Miller Grondin said. “This proposal will undoubtedly harm our city’s finances and our already severely underfunded pension system.”
Said Rose of any eventual legal challenges: “If the ordinance is challenged, the city will be prepared to defend it, just as it would any other city ordinance.”
The organizers behind the divestment campaign are also confident about the ordinance’s future, while also acknowledging the remaining path to its full realization. Zack Kligler, an organizer with the Providence for Palestine coalition, said in an email Monday that the ordinance was approved by Providence voters as “a resounding mandate.”
“Divestment will be an ongoing process over the coming years, and we will work to continue informing the public about next steps and the roadmap moving forward,” Kligler said. “The will of the voters is clear, and we are confident that divestment will be enforced.”

name: Virginia Mercury
title: Virginia parents weigh screen-time limits as schools expand classroom technology
description: Jasmine Bai wants to limit her rising kindergartener’s screen time on electronic devices at home and school. But with pressure to make sure her daughter is prepared for the future, as children learn to write code and prompts, she’s at a critical decision point in the digital age. “(It) gives me sort of an anxiety […]
text:
A view from the Tech in Schools Town Hall in Chesterfield County on Nov. 17, 2026. (Photo by Nathaniel Cline/Virginia Mercury)Jasmine Bai wants to limit her rising kindergartener’s screen time on electronic devices at home and school.
But with pressure to make sure her daughter is prepared for the future, as children learn to write code and prompts, she’s at a critical decision point in the digital age.
“(It) gives me sort of an anxiety of being left behind,” said Bai, of Chesterfield. “I’m not sure when or how I should introduce tech to my young kid, and what might be a better age or time for me to do that, and how I can balance teaching them the right skills versus keeping them mentally developed very well.” 
Bai is not the only parent between a firewall and a hard drive. On Tuesday, she joined other parents seeking answers on how to curb their children’s use of technology, including from medical experts and policy leaders, some of whom recently discussed the intentional and balanced integration of technology in Virginia’s K-12 classrooms.
 Balance, balance, balance

Hosted by the Balance Project and moderated by Amber Rhodes, Central Virginia community lead, the “Tech in Schools” discussion on Tuesday in Chesterfield County focused on building a purposeful, balanced, and developmentally appropriate approach to educational technology.
The discussion invited parents to share their perspectives and hear from local leaders, educators, and technology and health experts, including W. Monty Jones, VCU professor of education, and Angela Petry, a counselor and owner of Phoenix Behavioral Health LLC in Midlothian. 
Petry compared giving young children extended screen time to handing a toddler a butcher’s knife, arguing that technology use should be limited according to a child’s age and developmental needs.
“What’s happening is that child is not learning patience. They’re not learning emotional regulation,” Petry said, warning that screens can replace important developmental experiences.
She acknowledged that screens can make it easier for parents to keep young children occupied, but said children should not be left using devices independently for hours at a time.
“Scaling down that amount of time is hugely important, and parental and/or teacher guidance is also hugely important,” Petry said.
Technology use by students and teachers in the classroom increased during the pandemic as learning shifted from in-person to remote learning using computers and tablets. Schools have also shifted from pen and paper to electronic devices, raising concerns for teachers and parents about what students use them for and how it affects their development.
Those concerns have also linked students’ behavior and mental health to their use of mobile devices, prompting action by school leaders and lawmakers.
A view from outside the Tech in Schools Town Hall in Chesterfield County. (Photo by Nathaniel Cline/Virginia Mercury)Pictured at the center is pediatrician Kate Bowers at the Tech in Schools Town Hall in Chesterfield County. (Photo by Nathaniel Cline/Virginia Mercury)Pictured is Amber Rhodes, Central Virginia Community Lead for The Balance Project, at the Tech in Schools Town Hall in Chesterfield County. (Photo by Nathaniel Cline/Virginia Mercury)Pictured is Madison Irving, Henrico School Board chair and Chesterfield County teacher, at the Tech in Schools Town Hall in Chesterfield County. (Photo by Nathaniel Cline/Virginia Mercury)Pictured is W. Monty Jones, VCU professor of education with a Ph.D. in instructional technology, at the Tech in Schools Town Hall in Chesterfield County. (Photo by Nathaniel Cline/Virginia Mercury)
Building on those concerns, the panel and guests discussed using educational tools effectively while maintaining teacher-led, safe instruction.
They also discussed explicitly teaching digital literacy and responsible technology use across grade levels while minimizing distractions through engaging instruction, website restrictions, and clear classroom expectations.
On educational technology expectations and assessments, the group discussed required educational software and setting minimum usage expectations for purchased educational programs while allowing teachers flexibility in how they integrate them.
Parents urged leaders also to consider determining whether students need regular digital testing practice and whether paper-based testing should remain an option.
Experts and parents also discussed when and how to introduce screens and AI while balancing educational benefits, developmental needs, and appropriate screen time.
Kate Bowers, pediatrician and founder of Firefly Pediatrics in Midlothian, raised concerns that screens may affect children’s social-emotional regulation, focus, and persistence, while echoing the need for more research and careful interpretation of the evidence.
“If every activity we do with kids involves flashing lights and lasers, then you’re going to get kids who can’t pay attention when it’s paper,” Bowers said.
The group also raised awareness of parent-school communication, with parents expressing interest in improving family access to course materials, better understanding classroom teaching methods, and schools helping support learning and homework at home.
 Legislation ahead

Last week, Virginia Democrats announced plans to prioritize screen-time limits, teacher-led instruction, and classroom technology oversight as part of their legislative package for the 2027 General Assembly session.
Madison Irving, Henrico School Board chair and Chesterfield County teacher, said after his panel discussion with parents that he welcomes Gov. Abigail Spanberger and the state legislature’s involvement in addressing technology use in schools. 
He also highlighted Henrico County’s leadership in developing guidance for balanced technology use in schools, emphasizing that the division has taken a proactive, not reactive, approach.
“I think (the discussion) just reiterates to me that the parents care, and I think this is a microcosm of a larger societal shift that we’re going through in our evaluation of our technology,” Irving said. “Even as adults, we look at it and say we’re probably doing this a bit too much. And I think that we look at our kids and say, how do I prevent them from going down a similar path?”
Virginia state Sen. Schuyler VanValkenburg, D-Henrico, fields questions about tax proposals filed by Democrats at a news conference at the state Capitol in Richmond on Feb. 3, 2026. (Photo by Markus Schmidt/Virginia Mercury)
Sen. Schuyler VanValkenburg, D-Henrico, who was also on the panel, said the General Assembly passed legislation limiting minors’ time on social media. However, the law was challenged and cannot currently be enforced. 
The case is now before the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit, awaiting its decision.
VanValkenburg said he is also working on proposals concerning social-media defaults for minors and online fraud, students returning to printed textbooks — a state mandate that would require funding and school-district interest — and turning off infinite algorithmic feeds by default for minors, requiring someone to turn them on.
Legislation that could also be discussed this session includes screen-time limits for K-2 students and a proposal requiring localities to create policies for purposeful technology use, with legislative guardrails and a state model policy available to localities. Lawmakers on the Joint Commission on Technology and Science are also planning to roll out a package related to artificial intelligence.
Lawmakers will begin discussing legislation in Richmond on Jan. 13.
Bai said she would like to see more options and guidance for parents when asked about policy ideas following Tuesday’s meeting. 
She said, “If they can provide some options, resources for those who are interested, and while they’re providing these resources, if they can provide some guidance as well… that would be really great.”

name: Virginia Mercury
title: Rural advocacy groups band together to oppose data centers, related energy projects
description: Across rural swaths of Virginia, grassroots groups have joined the growing resistance to data centers, transmission lines, and the energy generation projects that are proposed to power them. From Buckingham to Henrico, the groups have banded together to amplify their fight against the mega corporations bringing the projects to the commonwealth. “Rural areas [...]
text:
Rural advocacy groups rally to oppose data centers and related energy infrastructure in Henrico on Nov. 18, 2026. (Photo by Shannon Heckt/Virginia Mercury)Across rural swaths of Virginia, grassroots groups have joined the growing resistance to data centers, transmission lines, and the energy generation projects that are proposed to power them. From Buckingham to Henrico, the groups have banded together to amplify their fight against the mega corporations bringing the projects to the commonwealth.
“Rural areas are becoming sacrifices for profit-driven businesses, and we can’t sit by and just let it happen,” Katie Hoffman, founder of Protect Cumberland, said at a demonstration Wednesday morning.
Standing on the banks of the James River in eastern Henrico, organizers from Hanover, Henrico, Buckingham, Goochland, Dinwiddie, and Cumberland counties highlighted their concerns about data center power and water use, the proposed gas fired power plants and the resources they require, and the land use challenges for the Valley Link Transmission line that is slated to bring more power to Northern Virginia. 
“Data centers is the hot button topic that we see in the news, but this is about the gas plants, this is about the transmission lines. It’s all connected,” said Jennifer Corpus with Friends of Hanover.
At the center of their concerns about the buildout of the tech and energy projects is a resource that their communities and the corporations depend on: water.
Hoffman strongly opposes the Cumberland Energy Center proposed by Dominion Energy, which would be the second largest gas plant in the nation at 3,000 megawatts. 
The advocates said that the Cumberland gas plant is meant to bring more power not to their communities but to far-flung Northern Virginia, where data centers are prolific and driving up the power demands statewide.
The plant would use too much water and possibly pollute other natural resources the advocates said. 
“It’s our air. It’s our soil. It’s a shared resource, and we can’t live without it,” Hoffman said Wednesday.
The Cumberland Board of Supervisors promised Dominion two million gallons of water a day for the gas plant that would be drawn from Cobbs Creek Reservoir. But Cumberland doesn’t own that water, Henrico does – and the county hasn’t given the green light for Cumberland to have the water either. 
“Cumberland didn’t and still does not have access to a drop of that water,” said Steve Haring, a resident who lives near the proposed plant.
Talks between the counties have reportedly been on-going but no there is no deal yet on the 17 million gallons per day increase that could be sold to Henrico’s partners, Powhatan County and Cumberland.
“Henrico leaders, you’ve said you’ve heard the public on data centers. Well, hear us now. Do not sell water to fuel data centers and gas plants,” Corpus said.
Dominion did not respond in time for publication of this story.
In addition to the water use, residents shared their worries about particulate matter that would be emitted from the plant when it is operational. 
While the companies emphasize they follow the law and only emit what they are permitted to by the Department of Environmental Quality, advocates state that no level of exposure is safe. Some of these particulates have adverse effects on human health. 
Near the proposed plant across the border in Buckingham County, Dominion already operates the 628 MW Bear Garden gas fired plant. Just up the highway in Fluvanna County, supervisors approved Nebraska-based Tenaska constructing a 1540 MW gas plant. 
The communities in between the projects united to present a stronger front against the developments, some attendees of Wednesday’s rally said.
“We’re done fighting data centers and their implications one county at a time. We see this for what it is: a gas plant in Cumberland, transmission lines like Valley Link, the data centers in Hanover, in Henrico, in Dinwiddie, in Goochland,” Corpus said. “These are not multiple fights. It is one fight, stemming from the same cause. Data centers are taking over Virginia.”
The groups also collectively called for the state to implement a data center moratorium. Last week, nearly a dozen environmental groups announced their push for similar action, to allow new regulations and protections to be put in place for data center development and operations.
Speakers at Wednesday’s rally said they will continue fighting to protect local water and natural resources.
“The James River connects all of us, and we’re going to protect it together,” Corpus said.

name: Honolulu Civil Beat
title: Lawsuit Against DHHL Is Not Just About Housing
description: Much of the public commentary surrounding the Ryan v. Watson lawsuit filed this year has focused on the 50% blood quantum requirement for Hawaiian Home Lands. For our community, this debate touches identity, family histories, and the urgent need to hold the state of Hawaiʻi and the Department of Hawaiian Home Lands accountable to their […]
text:
Much of the public commentary surrounding the Ryan v. Watson lawsuit filed this year has focused on the 50% blood quantum requirement for Hawaiian Home Lands. For our community, this debate touches identity, family histories, and the urgent need to hold the state of Hawaiʻi and the Department of Hawaiian Home Lands accountable to their trust mandates.
Yet the lawsuit raises questions far beyond Hawaiian Home Lands. Brought by Eric Ryan, president of the Hawaii Republican Assembly, and represented by the Pacific Legal Foundation, a national public-interest law firm, it challenges the distinction between Indigenous political and racial classifications.
When the foundational trust instruments of the Native Hawaiian people are treated as mere equal-protection hurdles rather than solemn compacts, we are not just debating real estate — we risk the legal erasure of our standing as a people and the rights secured for future generations.



Ideas showcases stories, opinion and analysis about Hawaiʻi, from the state’s sharpest thinkers, to stretch our collective thinking about a problem or an issue. Email news@civilbeat.org to submit an idea or an essay.


Read More

The Trojan Horse Of “Equal Protection”
In his First Amended complaint, filed Oct. 23, 2026, plaintiff Eric Ryan continues his constitutional challenge to the Hawaiian Homes Commission Act. He invokes the Fourteenth Amendment’s equal protection clause against the State and the equal-protection component of the Fifth Amendment’s Due Process Clause against the federal government, arguing that the HHCA’s ancestry-based eligibility requirements constitute an impermissible racial classification.
The HHCA should not be reduced to a racial preference. It is a federally established remedial trust intended to rehabilitate an Indigenous population that suffered catastrophic demographic decline, widespread land dispossession, and the loss of its independent government.
The Legal Reality
Three legal considerations are central:

The Political Classification: In Morton v. Mancari (1974), the Supreme Court recognized a classification grounded in tribal political status and self-government as political, not racial. In Rice v. Cayetano (2000), the Court struck down ancestry restrictions in state-administered OHA elections under the Fifteenth Amendment but declined to decide whether Mancari applies to Native Hawaiians. The HHCA presents a distinct question involving a federal trust enactment incorporated into Hawaiʻi’s statehood compact.
The Statehood Compact: Section 4 of the 1959 Admission Act required Hawaiʻi to incorporate the HHCA into its Constitution and restricts changes to beneficiary qualifications without federal consent. This binding federal-state compact is central to understanding the HHCA, rather than treating it as an ordinary state housing preference.
Federal Trust Responsibilities: On Jan. 16, 2025, the Department of the Interior issued Solicitor’s Opinion M-37083 addressing federal trust responsibilities concerning Native Hawaiians and Hawaiian Home Lands. Suspended for review on February 28, 2025, it remains a record of legal analysis, not currently operative guidance.

Ryan nevertheless seeks to subject HHCA eligibility requirements to strict scrutiny as a racial classification, notwithstanding the trust’s distinct federal statutory foundation.
The Domino Effect
The constitutional reasoning advanced against the HHCA could have implications beyond Hawaiian Home Lands if courts or future litigants attempt to apply it to other Native Hawaiian institutions.
Consider Princess Bernice Pauahi Bishop, the last direct descendant of the Kamehameha royal line. Her will established a private charitable trust providing for Kamehameha Schools, directing trustees to give “the preference to Hawaiians of pure or part aboriginal blood” in educational support for orphans and others in need.
Pauahi’s bequest reflects her enduring commitment to her people’s future. Although the Bishop Estate rests on a legal foundation distinct from the HHCA, broader arguments concerning ancestry-based protections warrant vigilance. We must safeguard these institutions while recognizing the distinct legal foundations upon which each stands.
The Broader Constitutional Stakes For Water Rights
Ryan v. Watson does not directly challenge water rights, but its legal theories offer a cautionary lesson. Traditional and customary practices, including water uses, are protected under Article XII, Section 7, of Hawaiʻi’s Constitution, subject to state regulatory authority. Article XI, Sections 1 and 7, establish public-trust duties concerning natural resources and water.
The Waiāhole Ditch decisions affirm those duties, including protection of water for traditional uses. Rights involving kalo cultivation, gathering, and cultural practices have independent constitutional and public-trust foundations. We must remain alert to arguments that could undermine them.
A Call For Unity And Action
Prince Jonah Kūhiō Kalanianaʻole initially advocated a 1/32 eligibility threshold to include as many beneficiaries as possible. The 50% requirement emerged from political compromises with powerful sugar and ranching interests.
These interests operated within a plantation-dominated political economy with deep ties to missionary-descended families and business leaders, some of whom participated in the 1893 overthrow of the Hawaiian Kingdom. Kūhiō’s struggle to secure homelands unfolded within that legacy of land dispossession and concentrated political power.
The Department of Hawaiian Home Lands is under legal threat. DHHL
We cannot allow external legal challenges to exploit internal debates over eligibility to dismantle the trust itself. Those seeking reform and those defending the trust share the same objective: preserving Kūhiō’s legacy of rehabilitating our people on ancestral land.
As litigation proceeds, the Native Hawaiian community must remain informed, engaged, and prepared to defend its rights. We must exercise our political agency to safeguard our inheritance for generations yet unborn. We must do more than defend what earlier generations secured; we must strengthen our political institutions, advance our constitutional development, and protect our vested rights and the international standing of the Hawaiian nation.
Prince Kūhiō did not fight to secure a permanent foundation on ancestral soil only to see that legacy threatened by legal arguments that reduce our political and trust rights to matters of race alone.
E kū paʻa i ka ʻāina — stand firm on the land. It is now up to us to protect that heritage. This is our ʻāina, our wai, and our future. We cannot afford to wait for someone else to defend them.

name: Georgia Recorder
title: Commentary: Bookman: Welcome to Bleorgia
description: Is Georgia now blue? With every statewide office in the hands of Democrats, you’d probably have to say yes. And while the abruptness of the transformation has been stunning, it’s also true that it has been coming for a long time. The signs were there. For example, you now have to go back an entire […]
text:
Georgia U.S. Sens. Jon Ossoff and Raphael Warnock appeared at a rally for Vice President Kamala Harris in 2024. Both senators have now been reelected since originally winning the seats in 2020, with Ossoff winning this month by 18 percentage points. Ross Williams/Georgia RecorderIs Georgia now blue?
With every statewide office in the hands of Democrats, you’d probably have to say yes. And while the abruptness of the transformation has been stunning, it’s also true that it has been coming for a long time. The signs were there.
For example, you now have to go back an entire decade, to 2016, to find the last time a Republican won a U.S. Senate race in Georgia. Since then, Democrats have won four consecutive Senate races, two by Raphael Warnock and two by Jon Ossoff. The first two were extremely close, but the margins grew in the more recent two, with Ossoff putting a cherry on top by winning his re-election race by 18 percentage points. 
As they say in the sports world, you are what your record says you are. And the record says we’re blue.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
You also have to consider that Joe Biden carried the state in 2020, and while Donald Trump won it narrowly in 2024, I doubt even the most optimistic Georgia Republican would put big money on winning the state’s 16 electoral votes in 2028. It’s just hard to imagine the trend line reversing so quickly.
So for the state Republican Party, it’s time to stare into a mirror and be honest about what you see. How did you get here, and what do you do next? If your spouse has left you, your kids won’t talk to you, you lost your job and the mortgage is past due, what now? 
Do you keep doing what got you in this situation, or do you alter course?
They got in this predicament because the state of Georgia and the state Republican Party have both changed significantly in the last decade, but they’ve changed in different directions. 
While the state has grown more diverse and less conservative, the state GOP has done the opposite. Instead of making peace with that diversity, instead of embracing it and adapting to it, Georgia Republicans have used it to fuel a backlash against such changes. 
That strategy worked, for a while, and in large parts of the state it still does. Those GOP state legislators who survived the midterm debacle did so because they represent districts that remain deep red to this day, so they may not feel pressured to alter course. 
But in statewide races such as a U.S. Senate campaign, that strategy does not work and never will again. The demographic changes have simply become too profound to overcome: Every voter they win by advocating an aggressive anti-immigrant platform, for example, is offset by two voters who they drive away with that policy.
Look at the Mike Collins campaign for Senate. He took a hardcore, juice-the-base MAGA strategy that ought to work well in his deep-red home congressional district – a district that Trump won by 21 points – then used it as a blueprint from which to run a statewide campaign. 
He lost by more than 700,000 votes. 
The details are even more damning. Even though Collins sat at the top of the ballot, he got 200,000 fewer votes than the Republican candidate for agriculture commissioner. That means even Republican voters went out of their way to reject him and his message. His performance was so bad that he won his own deep-red 10th District by less than a percentage point. Two years ago, he had won re-election in that district by 26 points.
So blue state or not, Georgia is not a MAGA state. In fact, you could even argue that it never was. Our last Republican senator, the one we elected a decade ago, was the late Johnny Isakson, a moderate who today’s GOP base would run off as a RINO. Our three most recent Republican governors, Sonny Perdue, Nathan Deal and Brian Kemp, were all conservative, and were all re-elected to second terms, but none of them governed in the MAGA fashion.
If Republicans fear that Democrats are going to do real harm to the state, they need to become competitive again as quickly as possible. That process begins by understanding that the Georgia they once knew no longer exists, because the people of this state have decided it shouldn’t.

name: Michigan Advance
title: Michigan Court of Appeals affirms unconstitutionality of abortion limitations
description: In a ruling issued Tuesday, a panel of judges on the Michigan Court of Appeals unanimously ruled that limitations on abortion procedures within Michigan’s public health code are unconstitutional, a decision that was celebrated by reproductive rights advocates. The specific mandated limitations in question are a 24-hour mandatory waiting period, uniform infor[...]
text:
A sign at the Michigan Pride rally in Lansing on June 26, 2022. (Photo by Laina G. Stebbins/Michigan Advance)In a ruling issued Tuesday, a panel of judges on the Michigan Court of Appeals unanimously ruled that limitations on abortion procedures within Michigan’s public health code are unconstitutional, a decision that was celebrated by reproductive rights advocates.
The specific mandated limitations in question are a 24-hour mandatory waiting period, uniform informed consent requirements, a physician participation mandate and mandatory screening for coercion.
The suit, which was first heard in the Court of Claims, was brought by the Northland Family Planning Center, alleged that these provisions in the law “unconstitutionally burdened the right to abortion without serving the limited compelling purpose of protecting the health of an individual seeking care, that each provision was inconsistent with accepted clinical standards of practice and evidence-based medicine, that the provisions imposed requirements that intruded on the autonomous decision making of patients, and that the provisions discriminated in the protection and enforcement of the right to reproductive freedom.”
In the decision from the Court of Claims, which was issued in May 2025, the court decided that the mandatory 24-hour waiting period, the uniform mandatory consent requirement and the physician mandate were unconstitutional and issued a permanent injunction enjoining enforcement of those provisions.
Planned Parenthood of Michigan to close three clinics after funding cuts

However, the lower court did not rule that the mandatory screening for coercion was unconstitutional, arguing that it is neutral on the face of the law. The Court of Appeals, on the other hand, ruled that because the statute prohibits only coercion to abort, not coercion to become pregnant or continue a pregnancy, it “risks operating in a manner that discriminates against individuals who seek to exercise the full range of reproductive choices guaranteed by our Constitution.”
The decision goes on to say that the Court of Claims did not fully interrogate the question at hand, “namely, whether the law, as applied, impermissibly discriminates in the enforcement of reproductive rights by creating a disparate impact on those who do not wish to continue a pregnancy, or who are coerced to become pregnant. The absence of such analysis renders the lower court’s decision incomplete with respect to the constitutional issues presented.”
As such the court remanded the decision to the Court of Claims, which “must determine whether the statutory framework, both in its language and in its application, comports with the constitutional mandate of equal protection in the enforcement of the right to reproductive freedom” and must complete “a searching examination not only of the statutory text, but also of the real-world consequences of its enforcement.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Reproductive rights advocates, including Planned Parenthood of Michigan President and CEO Paula Thornton Greear, welcomed the decision. 
“Michigan voters decided that decisions about pregnancy belong to the person who is pregnant, and this ruling holds the state to that,” Thornton Greear said in a press release issued Wednesday. “These laws had nothing to do with patient health, because they delayed care, forced people to read state-written material no clinician would hand a patient for any other kind of care, and limited who could provide that care — and now the courts have said so twice.”
Thornton Greear also encouraged the incoming Democratic-controlled Legislature, which will convene in January, to update the laws in statute, instead of relying on court decisions to prevent the enforcement of the limitations — a priority that she has previously called on legislators to take up in the new legislative session.
