name: California
title: Newsom touts an AI kill switch to halt dangerous OpenAI, Anthropic releases
description: California’s governor unveiled sweeping recommendations from a panel of experts on how to make AI systems safer.
text:
In summary
California’s governor unveiled sweeping recommendations from a panel of experts on how to make AI systems safer.


Gov. Gavin Newsom today released a wide-ranging set of policy recommendations to mitigate risks from artificial intelligence, including by letting state officials order an immediate emergency shutdown of AI systems they deem dangerous.
Other recommendations would mandate that independent auditors test AI models and establish safety and security standards.
The shutdown power, popularly known as a “kill switch,” would apply when companies like ChatGPT maker OpenAI and Claude maker Anthropic refuse to take action to contain systems that go awry.
The recommendations were drawn up by a panel of experts brought together by Newsom earlier this fall, following high-profile cyberattacks by AI agents on governments, banks, and private companies.
The governor touted them as a blueprint for state legislation during a recent visit to Washington, according to a report in Politico. Newsom, who is widely expected to mount a presidential run, said the state is filling a vacuum left by a lack of AI rules at the federal level. “Instead of protecting the public, Donald Trump shrugs his shoulders and leaves AI regulation up to the companies themselves,” he said in a press release announcing the recommendations. 
California is home to some of the largest AI companies in the world, and the California Legislature has passed more bills to regulate AI than any other state in the country. Newsom signed dozens of bills passed by the California Legislature into law in September to do things like protect kids, workers, and people living near data centers from AI and related impacts. He also accelerated implementation of laws to create an AI auditor registry and set standards for auditors. Legislators can propose new bills when they return to Sacramento on December 7.
The recommendations come the same week as a lawsuit by Attorney General Rob Bonta against OpenAI in an attempt to hold the company legally responsible for cybersecurity attacks carried out by agents made by the company.
The group also recommends the state of California:

License auditors — known as independent verification organizations — and have the power to revoke the licenses of those who fail to maintain sufficient independence or technical expertise. Auditors are “under soft pressure to maintain good relationships with the [AI] labs so that they want to continue to work with us,” a staffer at auditing nonprofit METR, Rif Saurous, said during a California Senate hearing last month. 
Consider having state officials assign evaluations to auditors instead of AI companies hiring auditors  in order to maintain independence. 
Fund CalCompute, a public cloud initiative intended to provide equitable access to AI, with a surcharge on fees AI companies pay to auditors. Governor-elect Xavier Becerra supported CalCompute funding during his campaign.
Expand existing protections for AI whistleblowers to include contractors and former employees.
Expand reporting of AI safety incidents to government agencies and shorten the window to report critical safety incidents to 48 hours from 15 days.
Allow government limits on the use of AI to design AI, since some experts believe this practice makes systems more dangerous.
Require developers to disclose the amount of computing resources they’re using to automate AI development.
Require developers of large AI systems to demonstrate the ability to shut down models in emergencies.
Establish state standards for safety, security, and transparency while referring to national and international standards.

The four-person panel of experts includes Alondra Nelson, who ran the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy during the Biden administration; Stanford University professor Rob Reich, who studies the governance of science and technology; ; former Google and Twitter executive Jason Goldman, who was the first White House Chief Digital Officer; and Gillian Hadfield, a John Hopkins professor who studies various issues related to AI. 
Becerra said in a written statement that he will move quickly with the Legislature to put “full incident reporting and real shutdown authority into law.” 
Anthropic, which makes the Claude AI system, is encouraged to see the report move the conversation forward on issues like the independent evaluation of AI models, according to the company’s chief global affairs officer, Tino Cuéllar.
“We will continue working with leaders in California and throughout the world to make sure we keep making progress on these issues at a critical time,” he wrote.
The recommendations by the governor’s panel and by auditors in recent weeks provide fodder to an incoming class of lawmakers in the California Legislature and Congress.
State Senator Scott Wiener, who wrote a state law to mitigate catastrophic AI dangers and was recently elected to take Nancy Pelosi’s seat in Congress, has pledged to introduce AI safety regulation after he’s sworn in.
State law currently defines catastrophic risk as a single event capable of killing more than 50 people or $1 billion in theft or property damage through a cyber attack or activity of an autonomous system. The report out today focuses only on catastrophic risk and does not explore ways to protect people from other AI harms, such as automated discrimination, job loss, or threats to the safety or mental health of children. Coauthors of the recommendations argue that building a system for credentialed auditors to test models for catastrophic risk will make it easier to evaluate models for other forms of harm.
Recommendations released today are the latest ordered by Newsom since the start of the age of generative AI. A late 2023 executive order required the state compile and assessment of the opportunities and risks associated with government use of generative AI. A subsequent state report assessed the impact of generative AI on vulnerable and marginalized communities. A June 2025 expert panel report also concluded that in order to balance innovation and safety, the AI industry needs evaluations by an independent, outside party.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Nebraska federal court nominee Eric Hamilton faces criticism and support during hearing
description: LINCOLN — A former Nebraska solicitor general who is President Donald Trump’s pick to fill a federal judgeship faced questions Wednesday during a confirmation hearing before a Senate committee. Nebraska’s two U.S. senators appeared in support of Eric Hamilton’s nomination to the U.S. District Court of Nebraska — offering a starkly different picture from an [[...]
text:
The Senate Judiciary Committee held a hearing with Trump judicial nominees, including Eric Hamilton, who is up for a lifetime appointment to the U.S. District Court of Nebraska. (Photo courtesy of David Talukdar/Getty Images)LINCOLN — A former Nebraska solicitor general who is President Donald Trump’s pick to fill a federal judgeship faced questions Wednesday during a confirmation hearing before a Senate committee.
Eric Hamilton, 38 and raised in Omaha, appeared at a judicial nomination hearing before a Senate Judiciary Committee Wednesday on Capitol Hill. (Photo courtesy of U.S. Department of Justice)
Nebraska’s two U.S. senators appeared in support of Eric Hamilton’s nomination to the U.S. District Court of Nebraska — offering a starkly different picture from an opposition letter by a coalition of civil rights, economic justice and numerous other advocacy groups.
The Judiciary Committee took no immediate action. If approved, the nomination will go to the Senate floor for a vote. 
Hamilton, 38, is a sixth-generation Nebraskan who served as an associate counsel to the president during Trump’s first administration. He responded to lawmaker questions during a group interview involving a half-dozen Trump nominees also up for a lifetime judicial appointment. Others represented Texas, Indiana, North Carolina and South Carolina.
‘What a legacy’
Sen. Richard Durbin, an Illinois Democrat and ranking member of the committee, voiced concern about Hamilton, recounting a federal judge’s 2025 rebuke of a federal defense team he oversaw during a case involving the attempted dismantling of the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau. 
Durbin cited the judge’s written doubts whether the defense could be “trusted to tell the truth about anything.”
“What a legacy,” Durbin said. 
Hamilton would replace Judge Robert Rossiter, an Obama appointee who is taking senior status on the federal bench. In remarks to the committee, Hamilton thanked Trump and Nebraska U.S. Sens. Deb Fischer and Pete Ricketts, both Republicans, for putting forth his name.
He told the committee chaired by Sen. Charles Grassley, R-Iowa, that his greatest gift was being born to his parents. His dad died earlier this year and, he said, his mom was watching virtually from Omaha.
President Donald Trump points into the crowd after headlining a midterms rally in Grand Island, Nebraska, on Oct. 5, 2026. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
If appointed, Hamilton said, he would follow the example of his first legal mentor, Judge Thomas Hardiman of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 3rd Circuit, whom he clerked for after graduating from Stanford Law School in 2013.
Sen. Richard Blumenthal, a Connecticut Democrat on the Judiciary Committee, peppered Hamilton and the other nominees about who won the 2020 popular vote and whether there was an “attack” on the U.S. Capitol on Jan. 6, 2021.
He said he was testing their judicial independence and objectivity over “political loyalty.” 




Quotation







Is there anyone on this panel who is willing to say the Capitol was attacked on Jan. 6, 2021? ... Nobody? It’s a sad day.


– U.S. Sen. Richard Blumenthal at a Senate Judiciary Committee hearing



Hamilton generally agreed with other nominees who answered before him. “Joe Biden was certified as the winner of the 2020 election when the electoral votes were tabulated,” he said.
Asked by Blumenthal about the Jan. 6  “attack” on the Capitol, two nominees instead used what they said was the Supreme Court’s description: a “breach of the Capitol.” Following two who spoke before him, Hamilton said he agreed with their description. They also said that they condemn that day’s violence.
The echo of responses spurred Blumenthal to ask, “Is there anyone on this panel who is willing to say the Capitol was attacked on Jan. 6, 2021?”
“Nobody? It’s a sad day.”
Letters of support
Raised in Omaha, Hamilton since 2025 has served as deputy assistant attorney general for the Federal Programs Branch of the Justice Department’s Civil Division, which defends the federal government in litigation.
The committee received multiple letters of support for Hamilton from organizations including former Department of Justice officials, former Hardiman law clerks and the staff of Nebraska Attorney General Mike Hilgers, where Hamilton once worked.
The coalition that outlined objections to Hamilton’s lifetime seat comprised 13 organizations including the Alliance for Justice, National Women’s Law Center, Leadership Conference on Civil and Human Rights and Lawyers for Good Government.  
In the statement, the coalition noted that Hamilton faced bar misconduct complaints in three jurisdictions, with two of those still pending, including before Nebraska’s highest court.
U.S. Sen. Deb Fischer, R-Neb. June 6, 2025. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
It said people of color in Nebraska are disproportionately affected by the fair administration of justice in federal courts and would be “harmed” by Hamilton’s confirmation prior to resolution of the ethics charges.
“We believe he does not possess the moral character and fitness necessary to serve as a federal judge,” the group stated in a two-page letter. 
“Hamilton has chosen to side with the Trump administration above all else — even when that loyalty required misconduct to further the continued dismantling of the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau,” the coalition wrote.
 Fischer, on the other side, said Hamilton “has shown himself to be a capable, sober minded legal professional in many capacities” and in “high stakes” litigation. 
She told the committee she was struck by a recent conversation in which Hamilton displayed legal knowledge and “enthusiasm for upholding the law.”
Ricketts said he has known Hamilton — a graduate of Millard West High School and the University of Nebraska-Lincoln — since Hamilton was 18 years old and both were getting involved in politics.
U.S. Sen. Pete Ricketts, Sept. 1, 2026. (Erin Bamer/Nebraska Examiner)
The recently reelected Ricketts told the committee that Nebraska’s motto is “the Good Life,” and that he believes Hamilton “will continue to represent and protect the good life in my state.”
He said that Hamilton defended bills passed by the state Legislature, including a law to “protect preborn babies after 12 weeks.”
Hamilton also served as an assistant solicitor general for Texas.
In announcing his nomination on Truth Social in October, Trump said Hamilton has done a “phenomenal job as the Deputy Assistant Attorney General for the Federal Programs Branch, defending our Administration’s most important Policies in Court.”
Judge’s scolding
The Hamilton critics took particular aim at his actions as a senior federal government lawyer defending Russell Vought in Vought’s efforts to shutter the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, one of the government’s key consumer protection agencies. Vought was CFPD acting director during the  lawsuit filed by employee unions.
The coalition noted federal Judge Amy Berman Jackson’s comments regarding Hamilton’s team. She described its account as “highly misleading, if not intentionally false” and wrote that she was left with little confidence the defense “can be trusted to tell the truth about anything.”
A legal watchdog group, the Legal Accountability Center, last year filed complaints with grievance committees of bar associations, saying that Hamilton and two associates made false statements in the case.

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Arkansas justice nominated for federal appeals post questioned on 2020 presidential election
description: Arkansas Supreme Court Justice Cody Hiland declined to say Wednesday who won the popular vote in the 2020 presidential election as he appeared before a U.S. Senate committee considering his nomination for a federal appeals court seat. Hiland, who President Donald Trump nominated for a post on the 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals, faced […]
text:
Arkansas Supreme Court Justice Cody Hiland speaks to the U.S. Senate Judiciary Committee about his nomination to a federal appeals court seat on Wednesday, Nov. 18, 2026 in Washington (Screenshot from Senate Judiciary Committee livestream)Arkansas Supreme Court Justice Cody Hiland declined to say Wednesday who won the popular vote in the 2020 presidential election as he appeared before a U.S. Senate committee considering his nomination for a federal appeals court seat.
Hiland, who President Donald Trump nominated for a post on the 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals, faced questions about the election, an investigation into state bar exam results and his interest in the judgeship during his hearing with the Senate Judiciary Committee.
Hiland, a former federal and state prosecutor, was nominated to the appeals court post last week. Trump withdrew his previous nomination of U.S. District Court Judge Lee Rudofsky, another Arkansas-based judge.
“My goal is for people to say Judge Hiland brought honor to the title of 8th circuit judge,” Hiland said in his opening remarks.
Democratic Sen. Richard Blumenthal asked Hiland who won the 2020 presidential election, a question Democrats have repeatedly asked of Trump’s judicial nominees. 
Hiland, a former chairman of the state Republican Party, said Joe Biden was certified the winner but declined to say who won the popular vote. 
“Senator, the popular vote is not what’s important,” Hiland said. “Respectfully, it’s the Electoral College and Joe Biden received those votes.”
When pressed further by Blumenthal about the popular vote, Hiland declined to say.
“I think it’s going down a political track on an issue that happened six years ago and I don’t want to come close to a potential ethical violation,” Hiland said.
Sen. Dick Durbin, the top Democrat on the committee, asked Hiland about the recent arrest of the former executive director of the Arkansas Supreme Court’s Office of Professional Programs on charges of tampering with bar exam scores between 2020 and 2025.
Hiland, who has served on the court since 2023, said he was first made aware of the investigation in May. Hiland said he played no role in the alleged tampering and that officials are trying to get a sense of the full extent of the alterations.
“We’re trying to get our hands around exactly what the universe of the problem is,” he said.
Hiland also walked back remarks he made to law students in August that he was “belligerent” when he told the White House he wasn’t interested in a federal district court seat rather than the appellate bench. 
“This was a 10-minute, extemporaneous speech to first year law students. When we speak extemporaneously, sometimes we use words we shouldn’t,” Hiland said. “The proper word was probably resolute as it relates to being an appellate court judge versus the other.”
White House faces unusual obstacle on confirming Trump judges: other Republicans

Arkansas’ two Republican senators both praised Hiland as he appeared before the committee.
“Justice Hiland’s legal experience, his track record from both the bench and the lawyer’s table, and his unwavering respect for the rule of law make him an ideal candidate for this position,” Sen. Tom Cotton said in remarks introducing Hiland.
Sen. John Boozman hailed Hiland’s legal experience and temperament for the bench.
“Cody Hiland has all the qualities we want in a federal judge,” Boozman said. “Extensive legal experience, sound judgement and a commitment to upholding the law rather than legislating from the bench.”
Durbin said he had “deep concerns” about Hiland and cited his background leading the state GOP and the state Supreme Court’s ruling last year that the Legislature can change voter-approved constitutional amendments.
The Democrat accused Republicans of breaking longstanding norms to rush through judicial nominees before they lose control of the Senate in January.
“Just eight days after the committee’s last nominations hearing, we’re back again because Senate Republicans are determined to confirm as many nominees as possible before control of the Senate shifts in six weeks,” Durbin said in a statement.
The 8th Circuit covers Arkansas, Iowa, Minnesota, Missouri, Nebraska, North Dakota and South Dakota.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Susan Hamilton to leave embattled DCF in early 2027
description: The Lamont administration is launching a nationwide search for a successor, following three commissioners who came up in DCF's ranks.
text:
Gov. Ned Lamont announced Wednesday that the Department of Children and Families will see its third commissioner leave the agency since 2024. Susan Hamilton, who was confirmed as the embattled agency’s leader in April, will retire less than a year later on Feb. 1. This was Hamilton’s second turn as DCF commissioner, having led the agency before from 2007 to 2011.
The Lamont administration is launching a nationwide search for her successor, following three consecutive commissioners — Hamilton, Jodi Hill-Lilly and Vannessa Dorantes — who came up in its ranks. Some say it’s a chance for DCF to look for a fresh perspective on an agency that has faced numerous challenges over the past year, from recruitment and retention to questions about its handling of cases that led to tragic deaths of children who had contact with the agency before they died. Lawmakers passed a bill in 2026 packed with reforms for the agency, including the creation of a new oversight committee.
Whoever is selected to fill the role will almost certainly take charge of the agency after the Lamont administration has already proposed its biennium budget, which normally happens in February. This means the timing of the appointment could leave the new commissioner pursuing reforms at the agency based on numbers that reflect the priorities of current leadership.
“Throughout her career, Susan has shown dedication and commitment to safeguarding the most vulnerable youths in Connecticut,” Lamont said in a press release. “I thank her for her service to our state, and I wish her nothing but the very best on this well-earned retirement.”
Lamont indicated that he’d known Hamilton’s tenure as commissioner would be short, noting that when she took on the role of interim commissioner in 2025, he knew she planned to retire. Hamilton took on the job to head the agency during a difficult time, and heading into an election year: “Her extensive experience and leadership has been immensely valuable during this period,” Lamont said. 
Hamilton said in the press release that it had been her “distinct honor and privilege to serve Connecticut’s children and families over the last 33 years in the fields of youth justice and child welfare.” 
“I deeply appreciate Governor Lamont’s trust in me and his steadfast commitment to improving outcomes for the people we serve. I am sincerely grateful to our DCF staff for their unwavering dedication to our critical mission, often under very difficult circumstances,” she said. “We carry out that work in partnership with an incredible network of lived experts, communities, private providers, sister state agencies, the legislature, the courts, advocates and, most importantly, the children and families we serve.”
Sen. Ceci Maher, co-chair of the legislature’s Committee on Children, said Wednesday that Hamilton’s departure represents a chance for the agency to go in a different direction.
“We’ve had in the past four years three commissioners, all of whom came up through the Connecticut DCF system and while that has been tremendously beneficial in some ways, it has not allowed Connecticut to draw on a national perspective of leadership that comes from a different area and perhaps brings a new way of looking at the problems with new solutions,” she told The Connecticut Mirror. 
Maher said she was hopeful that Lamont would find a candidate outside of Connecticut who could “look at our DCF system through a new lens.”
Like her predecessors, Hamilton spent many years at DCF. She was a social worker and social work supervisor in the 1990s, then directed DCF’s legal division and was appointed commissioner in 2007 under Gov. Jodi M. Rell.
During her first appointment as commissioner, the agency saw some slippage in progress toward meeting children’s basic service needs, according to reports. Hamilton’s initial tenure as DCF commissioner took place while the agency was under the supervision of a court monitor, assigned as part of a 1989 federal civil rights lawsuit on behalf of “Juan F.,” an anonymous 10-year-old boy representative of a class of children whose needs were unmet by an agency run with poor resources and guided by outdated policies.
The court monitor issued regular reports on the agency’s progress toward reform until DCF was released from the order in 2022.
A 2009 report from the monitor reported on by Children’s Rights, Inc. found that nearly half of the children in DCF care weren’t having their basic service needs met, and that the state was losing ground in its court-assigned reforms. 
The agency saw a drop in the percentage of children who were reunified with their parents from about 72% of cases studied to 56%, reported Children’s Rights, Inc. The group noted that DCF was meeting 15 of the 22 indicators for success, after previously meeting 17 of 22, marking “the state’s worst performance since Susan Hamilton was appointed commissioner of DCF in June 2007.”
Hamilton ended her first stint as commissioner in 2011 and operated her own private law firm until 2014. Then she served as a public defender for nearly a decade before returning to DCF in 2023 as the agency’s general counsel. She was announced as interim commissioner by Lamont in September 2025 and then confirmed as commissioner by the legislature in April of this year.
During her confirmation process, Hamilton faced tough questioning and criticism, including from Maher. Maher, who announced her own retirement from the legislature earlier this year, asked Hamilton why she wasn’t advocating more forcefully for the agency.
“I’m not seeing the passion or the vision for what you see the future could be. And that to me is very, very concerning,” Maher said.
A statement from Hamilton that she understood the budget process and the “importance of data-driven allocation decisions,” alarmed Maher as wonky, insider-speak. “I would say that understanding them [budgetary decisions] often is tantamount to accepting them as opposed to pushing for what you might need from the governor’s budget, from the legislature,” Maher said at the time.
Recently, the agency has been questioned for its effectiveness in addressing a key part of its mission: administering services for youth mental health. Workers at Solnit South, a psychiatric facility for youth in Middletown, protested conditions there this summer after the facility’s hospital was taken over by UConn John Dempsey Hospital.
Child Advocate Christina Ghio said in a statement that the churn of commissioners at DCF has been a challenge in the quest to make system-wide improvements. She too said she was cheered to hear that Lamont would be searching nationwide. 
“We need a Commissioner who is committed to staying on long term,” she wrote, “who understand DCF’s role as both the state’s child protection agency and mental health agency, and who has experience managing a large agency with a need for systemic improvement.”
“I urge the Governor to bring in a candidate who will focus on improving support for both child protective services and child behavioral health,” Maher said. 
Former Child Advocate Sarah Eagan, now executive director of the Center for Children’s Advocacy, called Hamilton a “consummate professional,” who has spent her career committed to making a difference for children and families.
“Moving ahead the next commissioner will need to steer DCF through very turbulent waters as Connecticut children and families dependent on DCF are struggling profoundly without adequate community supports, foster homes, and services,” Eagan added in a statement. “In the months ahead CCA hopes to work with policymakers, state agency leaders, and families to ensure meaningful investment and innovation that will support the safety and support of the most vulnerable children in our community.”

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Will we preserve a Cape Cod where working families can thrive?
description: The year-round working family on the Cape, composed of parents who hold vital jobs in health care, hospitality, or as public safety workers and children enrolled in public schools, is headed for extinction.
text:
THE STORY IN in the Sunday sports section said it all: High school football teams on Cape Cod are at risk of folding because they can’t get enough students to participate. 
Football programs are challenged everywhere because of concerns around head injuries, but on the Cape the issue is different. Schools are having trouble fielding full teams because the year-round population here is dwindling. Families are being crowded out of housing as vacation homes and seasonal rentals continue to surge in a post-pandemic trend that has not ebbed almost seven years on. 
Even more telling is that the team referenced in the story is Dennis-Yarmouth Regional High School. While Outer Cape communities such as Provincetown or Lower Cape communities like Chatham have had trouble fielding sports teams of all types for years, Dennis and Yarmouth are Mid-Cape communities that have always had a steady year-round population.  
The year-round working family on the Cape, composed of parents who hold vital jobs in health care, hospitality, or as public safety workers and children enrolled in public schools, is headed for extinction. They are being replaced by affluent individuals who buy seasonal homes on the Cape to use for a few months of the year and investors who can make six figures placing their homes on short-term rental platforms. 
Evidence of the affluent buyer and investor trends is easy to spot: In August, 40 percent of all Cape real estate transactions involved a cash buyer. Nationally, the figure is less than 30 percent. The inventory of available homes is shrinking, too. Between 2025 and 2026, according to August data, 6 percent fewer single-family homes were listed. 
To really get a picture of what the future looks like, all one needs to do is look across Nantucket Sound. The Nantucket Public Schools just hit its lowest enrollment numbers in a decade.  Meanwhile, between 2016 and 2025, the average sale price of a home grew from $1.47 million to $3.45 million. Homes selling for less than $1 million no longer come on the market, and homes under $2 million list very infrequently. Nantucket is Cape Cod’s canary in the coal mine. 
In just 10 years, Wellfleet’s elementary school enrollment will fall by 6 percent. A recent study raised the possibility of closing the town’s sole elementary school and sending young learners to neighboring communities. It would be the first town on the Cape to have no elementary school. 
Up the road in Harwich, in what was once one of the Cape’s more affordable communities for year-round workers, the town was just named the “hottest zip code” in Massachusetts for real estate sales and the third hottest zip code in the nation. The average sale price is now $1.4 million. 
The latest Cape housing data should serve as a clarion call. Action is urgently needed before we lose something special that we can never truly get back. 
There is no single solution to this problem. Rather, an array of incremental but targeted steps can create new positive momentum. 
New regional revenue sources need to be considered to stabilize the market in seasonal communities and give local families a fairer shot at affording a home. 
A comprehensive review of zoning on the Cape, including the minimum lot size to build a home, is essential. While Question 7, which would have allowed starter homes on lots of 5,000 square feet or more, was narrowly defeated this month by voters statewide, it was supported by voters in three Outer Cape towns that have seen major losses in year-round inventory.   
The economic development bill being hammered out by a legislative conference committee includes a provision in the House version – Yes, In God’s Back Yard – that would allow housing development on the property of faith-based organizations. With an abundance of churches across the Cape, and congregations that are shrinking, this is a practical solution that can make the best use of spare land.  
The conference committee is also considering a Senate provision allowing duplexes as of right, so that communities could no longer mandate single-family zoning. This would specifically allow families living and working on the Cape to convert their home to a duplex and allow the next generation to put down roots on the very same parcel. 
The Cape is at a crossroads. Nobody truly benefits from a seasonal playground where working families can’t thrive and schools can’t field an athletic team. We can and must do better. Our future depends on it. 
Alisa Magnotta is the CEO of Housing Assistance on Cape Cod.

name: Michigan Advance
title: Federal judge considers rare review of grand jury proceedings in U-M protest case
description: ANN ARBOR — A federal judge in Michigan may take the rare step of opening secretive grand jury testimony to determine if the panel was given the full and accurate account of a raid on a home that led to additional charges being filed against Zainab Hakim, one of 12 current and former University of […]
text:
Zainab Hakim, left, and her attorney, Amanda Bashi, exit the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Michigan on Wednesday, Nov. 18, 2026 in downtown Ann Arbor, Mich. Hakim was in court for a revocation of bail hearing. (Photo by Ben Solis/Michigan Advance)ANN ARBOR — A federal judge in Michigan may take the rare step of opening secretive grand jury testimony to determine if the panel was given the full and accurate account of a raid on a home that led to additional charges being filed against Zainab Hakim, one of 12 current and former University of Michigan students charged with crimes related to pro-Palestinian protests over the last several years.
Hakim, along with 11 others, has been charged in federal court on allegations of protests, graffiti and property damage at the offices and homes of weapons developers, political organizations and U-M officials related to actions in support of Palestine. She appeared in court on Wednesday for a hearing to determine if she would be jailed before her trial in the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Michigan due to new charges of evidence tampering, which her defense denies took place.
Hakim was not taken into custody on Wednesday and will be back in court on Dec. 2 as there were questions of whether the grand jury that brought the new charges — and made up the basis for the government to revoke her initial bond — was given the full scope of evidence on the raid that led to the request to revoke bail.
Supporters of Zainab Hakim and the “Michigan 12” hold a demonstration and solidarity rally on Wednesday, Nov. 18, 2026 outside of the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Michigan in downtown Ann Arbor, Mich. (Photo by Ben Solis/Michigan Advance)
Hakim’s defense believed that the grand jury was not given an accurate picture of the raid, or the evidence of alleged tampering, and is asking U.S. District Judge Judith Levy to review the grand jury testimony to determine if prosecutors had presented misleading testimony or whether irregularities in the proceeding undermined the grand jury’s decision to bring the charges.
Levy entertained that idea and adjourned the bail hearing to do her own research on whether she had authority to do so. Levy also asked the government and Hakim’s defense attorney, Amanda Bashi, to file additional briefing on the issue.
Levy was clear, however, that there was limited precedent allowing judges to unseal grand jury proceedings, and Bashi only read off a handful of cases that helped her position.
State charges against the group were dropped last year, but the federal government pursued the case and charged Hakim and others for allegedly terrorizing various individuals who they deemed connected to or supporting Israel’s war in Gaza against Hamas.
The federal government has alleged that the group did so outside the bounds of the First Amendment and constituted criminal acts in support of Hamas.
In October, the FBI arrested  Henry David Mackeen-Shapiro, one of the co-defendants, and then raided the home where Hakim and Mackeen-Shapiro live to execute an additional search warrant. In that raid, agents uncovered a laptop that they believed was dumped into a bath of either salt water or fresh water, in an alleged attempt to tamper with or destroy evidence. However, the complaint didn’t specify if it had been dumped in water or just kept in a wet bag. The government has claimed that the laptop was found in Hakim’s bedroom, and not in the room of its owner, Mackeen-Shapiro.
Zainab Hakim, one of 12 facing federal terrorism charges for their involvement in pro-Palestinian activism, is presented with a birthday cake outside the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Michigan on Wednesday, Nov. 18, 2026 in downtown Ann Arbor, Mich. Hakim was in court for a revocation of bail hearing. (Photo by Ben Solis/Michigan Advance)
In court on Wednesday, Bashi said the public complaint filed with the court, in her view, contained so many inconsistencies that it appeared as there were two diametrically opposed accounts of what happened during the raid, and that the government’s account amounted to a misrepresentation to the court. During the bond hearing,  federal prosecutors had to correct themselves multiple times before Levy as to the veracity of the statements in the complaint.
That led Bashi to believe that, potentially, the grand jury which brought additional evidence tampering charges against Hakim hadn’t been told the whole story, or an incorrect version of events.
A timeline of the raid, along with body-worn camera images, showed that Hakim and others appeared to have cooperated with FBI agents and made themselves present at their front door. It also indicated agents had not congregated inside the home. Statements from defense witnesses also showed that agents had commended the home’s residents, including Hakim, who had cooperated with agents during the raid.
The federal government said it is still actively restoring the laptop in question, and that it had not been chemically tested prior to the grand jury presentation to show whether it had been dumped in salt water or fresh water in an attempt to destroy it.
Federal prosecutors, however, did not quarrel with Bashi’s alleged timeline of the events.
Bashi noted that neither the laptop’s surroundings nor Hakim were wet when agents obtained the laptop, and that earlier insinuations that the laptop was found in a bag of wet clothes — as a way to destroy it — were inaccurate; the wet bag had been found on top of the laptop during the raid.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The laptop belonging to Mackeen-Shapiro, Bashi added, was in poor condition that showed it was heavily used and possibly damaged by Mackeen-Shapiro well before the raid and the alleged attempt to destroy it.
Bashi posited that it was more likely that Mackeen-Shapiro “was a slob” and failed to take care of the laptop, leading to its dilapidated condition, which was not evidence of material destruction.
Federal prosecutors characterized Bashi’s attempts to poke holes in the grand jury testimony as a delay tactic, but Levy was open to the idea of at least peeking behind the curtain — if she was allowed to do so under legal precedent — to gauge the official account of the raid to what was presented to the grand jury.
Briefs on the matter are due next week from both Bashi and federal prosecutors while Levy researches the matter.
Meanwhile, Hakim was able to walk free on Wednesday. She had a crowd of supporters with her, including her parents, in the courtroom, as well as another group holding a small solidarity rally for her outside.
It was also Hakim’s birthday and her friends and allies presented her with a cake and sang to her on the courthouse steps following the proceedings.

name: Source New Mexico
title: Federal appeals court overturns New Mexico ruling granting emotional harm payments to fire victims
description: The U.S. 10th Circuit Court of Appeals on Tuesday overturned a lower court’s ruling that required the Federal Emergency Management Agency to compensate northern New Mexico residents for the emotional toll of the state’s largest-ever wildfire.
text:
The U.S. 10th Circuit Court of Appeals on Nov. 17, 2026, overturned a New Mexico district court judge’s ruling that Hermits Peak-Calf Canyon Fire victims were allowed noneconomic payments for the damage the 2022 wildfire caused. (Photo by Patrick Lohmann/Source NM)The U.S. 10th Circuit Court of Appeals on Tuesday overturned a lower court’s ruling that required the Federal Emergency Management Agency to compensate northern New Mexico residents for the emotional toll of the state’s largest-ever wildfire. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Two judges on the three-member panel determined that legislation Congress enacted to compensate victims of the Hermits Peak-Calf Canyon Fire in 2022 did not clearly direct FEMA to pay fire victims for emotional distress they suffered as a result of the fire. 
The roughly 534-square-mile wildfire in northern New Mexico resulted from two botched prescribed burns on federal land in 2022. Congress later that year passed the Hermits Peak Fire Assistance Act that directed FEMA to oversee a $5.45 billion compensation fund for fire victims.
But FEMA officials determined shortly after they launched the wildfire claims process that the new funding could not go toward noneconomic damages. 
Attorneys representing more than 1,000 fire victims sued FEMA in federal court in 2023, arguing that the law Congress enacted intended FEMA to pay victims for both economic damages, such as burned homes, and noneconomic damages, akin to pain and suffering.
Noneconomic damage compensation is particularly important for low-income fire victims, their lawyers contend, because they often stand to gain little from the compensation program otherwise. 
In the scar of New Mexico’s largest wildfire, a legal battle is brewing over the cost of suffering

New Mexico U.S. District Court Judge James Browning, who has since retired, twice ruled in fire victims’ favor, most recently in a 142-page ruling in July 2025. He urged FEMA to quickly allow noneconomic damage payments, citing the years-long delay some victims had already experienced awaiting compensation.
But attorneys for FEMA appealed the ruling to the 10th Circuit of the U.S. Court of Appeals in September 2025.
In the majority’s ruling issued Tuesday, U.S. Circuit Judge David Ebel wrote that Browning applied too lax a standard in his determination that Congress intended for fire victims to receive noneconomic damages. 
The legislation does not contain “clear and unequivocal” language allowing such payments, he wrote. He also determined that Congress could not have intended noneconomic damages to be paid through a claims process designed to quickly compensate victims by establishing a 180-day deadline for FEMA to make payment offers. 
In her dissent, U.S. Circuit Judge Carolyn McHugh argued that the law is written “in expansive, inclusive terms” allowing for noneconomic damages, and that calculating such harms is no more difficult than assessing damage to acequia systems or calculating payments for lost subsistence from hunting or fishing. 
Attorney Antonia Roybal-Mack, one of the victims’ lawyers, said in a phone interview Tuesday that she believes the majority judges misunderstood key aspects of the claims process and that victims’ attorneys will file a “motion to reconsider” before potentially appealing to the U.S. Supreme Court.
Plaintiffs’ lawyers also intend to request that New Mexico’s congressional delegation amend the law to make clear that noneconomic damage payments are allowable. Doing so would require approval from both chambers of Congress and President Donald Trump, Roybal-Mack said, but would be a “very simple fix.”
Earlier this week, community advocates for fire victims sent the state’s congressional delegation a letter with 165 signatures that makes a similar request. 
Hermits Peak-Calf Canyon Fire victims still wait on FEMA’s decision to appeal judge’s ruling

“The federal government should not be spending taxpayer dollars to litigate against New Mexico families over what it means to be made ‘whole,’” the letter reads.
U.S. Sen. Ben Ray Luján (D-N.M.), one of the legislation’s main sponsors, did not address in a Wednesday statement to Source NM whether he would consider amending the law. But he said he “remains focused on ensuring FEMA fulfills its responsibility to New Mexico fire victims, expedites outstanding total loss claims, and gets money out the door without further delay.”
The law’s other sponsor, U.S. Rep. Teresa Leger Fernández (D-N.M.), did not respond to Source NM’s request for comment. 
Officials from FEMA also did not respond to Source NM’s request for comment about the ruling. 
Brian Colón, whose firm Singleton Schreiber also sued FEMA, said he will continue to fight for equitable distribution of the compensation fund in line with what he believes the legislation allows.
“We are going to appeal this decision. We are going to work with Congress, and we’re going to make sure our clients get that full compensation,” he said. “We’re not stopping until they do.”

name: VTDigger
title: For 100 years, a nonprofit has provided free services for visually impaired Vermonters. Now it’s looking to scale up.
description:
Vermont has about 15,000 significantly visually impaired residents, and could have as many as 25,000 by 2030.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  For 100 years, a nonprofit has provided free services for visually impaired Vermonters. Now it’s looking to scale up..
text:
The Vermont Association for the Blind and Visually Impaired in South Burlington held a ceremony to mark the organization’s 100th anniversary with the burial of a time capsule on Tuesday, November 17, 2026. Performing the ceremonial shoveling are, from left, VTABVI director Dan Norris, and Demi Selzer, mother of Luca and Milo. Both boys are clients of VTABVI. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger
SOUTH BURLINGTON — When Demi Selzer moved to Vermont in 2019 and searched online for services to support her infant son, she immediately found the Vermont Association for the Blind and Visually Impaired.
Coming from New York City, where dealing with large scale services is often overwhelming, Selzer said she was surprised it took one phone call and a fairly simple intake to connect her son, Milo Carr, to people who immediately leaped in to help.
What started with home visits and tips — such as using colored plates for his meals and putting down colored tape in areas around the house — has expanded to a teacher supporting Milo in his first grade classroom in Middlebury weekly with tools and tech to help him learn at the same pace as his sighted peers.
In its 100 years of operation, VABVI has aided many Vermonters with vision loss. It has provided licensed teachers to support students in school, helped seniors use built-in accessibility features on smartphones and tablets, and connected adults to community resources via peer support groups across the state. As Vermont’s population ages, its leaders have launched a capital campaign to expand its endowment to better meet growing needs “from the cradle to the cane.”
On Tuesday, Milo, 6, was one of the speakers at the organization’s centennial celebration, which drew a crowd of more than a dozen to its Kimball Street office. He demonstrated use of some of the assistive devices displayed, such as Jupiter, a portable monitor that helps magnify text from books on the desk to blackboards in the classroom.
With help from Executive Director Daniel Norris, Milo also buried the key to a time capsule in the center of a green patch that is slated to become a sensory garden in six months. The organization plans to feature fragrances, textures, rain drums and wind chimes, allowing visitors to explore by touch, sound and smell. The organization also plans to paint the flagpole there to resemble a giant cane in what will become VABVI’s Independence Square.
Prepared with items Norris said could become relics in 25 years, the time capsule, stored in the office building, will contain various adaptive aids including AI-assisted Meta glasses, an electronic refreshable braille display, a digital book player, a cellphone, a monocular, a newspaper and a letter from Milo on the adaptive technology he uses today and his wish to become a police officer.

Dan Norris, director of the Vermont Association for the Blind and Visually Impaired, speaks during a ceremony marking the organization’s 100th anniversary in South Burlington on Tuesday, November 17, 2026. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger

Critical services
The organization’s 46 staff members and additional volunteers help visually impaired and blind residents with everything they need to live independently in their homes. That can range from help with cooking and cleaning to learning braille to finding a guide dog, said Stephanie Bissonett, director of children services, who has been working with VABVI for 41 years.
“Whatever their challenge might be with their visual impairment, we help them to reach the goals that they want to strive for,” Norris said. “If that’s a grandmother that wants to do social media with her grandkids, we’ll help her do that. If it’s a student who wants to go to college and needs to access technology to get to college, we’ll teach them how to do that.”
The nonprofit helps about 1,500 Vermonters a year across all 14 counties, but that’s only 10% of the 15,000 significantly visually impaired people who live in Vermont, according to Norris. That number is expected to keep growing given that a large proportion of the state’s population is older.
“By 2030, we anticipate that that number is going to be closer to 25,000,” Norris said. “So we know there’s a lot more people out there that we’re not serving that we need to reach.”
Norris, who carries a white cane, told VTDigger he was in the second grade when his visual impairment developed. He was legally blind by age 8. 
“I had a teacher for the visually impaired who back then taught me the latest technology, which was a typewriter,” he said with a laugh. 

Luca Selzer, left, interrupts his brother Milo with an offer of a donut bite as Milo speaks during a ceremony marking the 100th anniversary of the Vermont Association for the Blind and Visually Impaired in South Burlington on Tuesday, November 17, 2026. Both boys are clients of VTABVI. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger

Leaders of the organization that tends to fly under the radar cited a long-term unique partnership with the state since 1927. Taya Tarr, director of the Vermont Division for the Blind and Visually Impaired (DVBI celebrates its 100th next year), who attended the event, commended VABVI for the critical services and care it provides. 
The somewhat hidden main office, one of four VABVI locations in Vermont, has classroom space, a library and offices housing toys, such as a large blue lobster made on a 3D printer for a child who was scared of encountering one on the beach. There are large print tactile books and maps for children, diabetes management tools, and a long shelf featuring 30 volumes that comprise the braille dictionary.
Unlike regular print, you can’t change the font size for braille, Norris said. So one typical page of print is three pages in braille.
Luna, a gentle 2 ½-year-old black lab who belongs to a staff member, greeted visitors in the lobby. Milo petted her and said he is excited to have his own dog, perhaps next year. 
Milo has been approved to get a companion dog (a trained guide dog who did not qualify to be one but can still be a pet for someone like Milo), said Emily Algranati, director of adult services and a guide dog mobility instructor.
A continued legacy
The organization’s roots date back to 1912 when the Vermont Association for the Blind was founded in the Edmunds school in Burlington, said John Thomas, a historian and development director of the Vermont Association for the Blind and Visually Impaired.
The early organization went dormant during World War I. It was reorganized as VABVI in 1926 by a pioneering blind woman and teacher, Anne Connelly, who came to Burlington with a stamp of approval from Helen Keller, Thomas said.
Connelly created a stir at a time when the general public hadn’t seen an independent blind person navigating daily life. She advocated for blind people, wrote essays and editorials, and secured state support for the organization. She died in 1939 and was forgotten until Thomas’ research wrote her into the record of the organization and Vermont’s history as part of the centennial celebration.
When Connelly brought Vermont’s first guide dog to Burlington in 1930, there are accounts of a large crowd following her and her German Shepherd Betty from her Pearl Street home to her work at City Hall, Thomas said. The next year, she introduced the first white cane in Vermont. Trained guide dogs and white canes were cutting edge assistive technology then, and paved the way for the landmark 1949 Vermont White Cane Act, which legally recognized white canes and guide dogs as mobility aids in the state.

 
Milo placing the time capsule into the ground during a ceremony held to mark the 100th anniversary of the Vermont Association for the Blind and Visually Impaired in South Burlington on Tuesday, November 17, 2026. Video by Auditi Guha/VTDigger

Last month, Burlington honored the blind pioneer by recreating that famous walk, dedicating a plaque to her trail-blazing efforts, and declaring Oct. 16 Anne Connelly and Betty the Guide Dog Recognition Day.
A century later, VABVI honors Connelly’s legacy by continuing to expand support and services to a wide range of Vermonters across the state — from infants to the elderly.
Selzer said she can’t imagine how she would manage without it.
Two of Selzer’s three sons have ocular albinism — a genetic condition that severely affects their vision — and they both receive services from VABVI, which is the only nonprofit in the state to offer rehabilitation services to the blind and visually impaired.
“It’s just been such a great resource in all aspects,” she said. “If it weren’t for them, Milo’s day-to-day with school would be more of a struggle… I think he would be lost in the crowd a little bit if he didn’t have a (VABVI) machine there supporting him and advocating for him.”

name: Washington State Standard
title: WA commission votes down plan for golf course at coastal state park
description: The controversial plan for a Scottish links-style golf course at an oceanfront Washington state park is stuck in the rough. The state’s Parks and Recreation Commission voted Wednesday not to move forward with the proposal at Westport Light State Park, arguing the long-in-the-works development would be harmful to wetlands and noting the Department of Ecology’[...]
text:
Project developers pledged to maintain, or even improve, ocean beach access if allowed to build a golf resort within Westport Light State Park. But beachgoers submitted comments opposing what they viewed as over-commercialization of a beloved state park. (Photo by Tom Banse)The controversial plan for a Scottish links-style golf course at an oceanfront Washington state park is stuck in the rough.
The state’s Parks and Recreation Commission voted Wednesday not to move forward with the proposal at Westport Light State Park, arguing the long-in-the-works development would be harmful to wetlands and noting the Department of Ecology’s guidance that it likely wouldn’t be permitted as designed. 
“Our responsibility is to the public and to the care of these public lands, not to the momentum of a long process,” said commission Chair Holly Williams. “I do not see how this proposal, as it stands, meets the state’s mission, vision or policies.”
“Due to the issues with the proposal, the inconsistencies, misinformation, and lack of faith, integrity, and in the integrity of this partnership, I do not support this proposal and oppose state park staff spending any additional resources on it,” Williams continued.
The idea divided the Westport community. 
Last month, a parks commission hearing in Aberdeen was packed with locals sharing their opinions about the proposal. Supporters felt it would be an economic boon for the community. Opponents saw it as disruptive to the environment. 
The 18-hole public course, compared to the famous Bandon Dunes in Oregon, would have come with a short course, clubhouse, lodge with dozens of rooms, driving range and food options. By the mid-2030s, the project would’ve brought in between $15 million and $18 million in estimated revenue per year, according to the developers, Westport Golf Links, which is led by homebuilder Ryann Day. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The company expected 26,000 visits in its first year of operation, a figure that would grow over time and help local restaurants, hotels and shops. The revenue would’ve been shared with the state, with some going toward caring for parks across Washington. 
The developers would also have established miles of new and improved trails and leave open the beach, which is popular among surfers. Day argued the links-style course would be less disruptive to the habitat and use less water and fertilizer than traditional courses. His company committed to restoring or creating wetlands to make up for what building the course would do. 
But the state Department of Ecology said Westport Golf Links leadership was underestimating the negative impacts its development would have on wetlands, with impacts to over 30 acres’ worth. The Quinault Indian Nation was concerned about risks to nearby fish habitat from the proposal, as well.
Commissioner Laurie Connelly said she has “lost faith in the proponent’s ability to work productively with Parks to bring this project to fruition.”
“The proponent has downplayed issues,” Connelly added. “It has accused staff as being uncooperative when they have pointed out the issues based on the studies that have been performed, and then has responded with pressure on the commission to approve the project when we have expressed our concerns about the environmental issues.”
Day didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.
Scott Merriman, the commission’s vice chair, said it’s also a financial decision, as the state faces a $4 billion budget shortfall that led Gov. Bob Ferguson this week to push agencies, including Washington State Parks, to cut more spending.
“There’s going to be some difficult choices put on the table moving forward that’s going to dramatically affect the agency,” Merriman said. “I don’t know how we can continue to spend money on this project as it currently sits.”
The project had been in the works for years. A previous golf course plan at Westport Light State Park fell through in the early 2000s. Williams said she wants commission staff to now look at other options for the park.

description: Embattled Idaho Fish and Game Commissioner Brody Harshbarger has resigned from the commission after agreeing to plead guilty to misdemeanor hunting charges, state records show.  On Wednesday, Gov. Brad Little’s Chief of Staff Zach Hauge wrote Harshbarger to tell him that Little had accepted Harshbarger’s resignation.  “Accordingly, your service on the commis[...]
text:
The Idaho Fish and Game Commission was established in 1938 through a ballot initiative by voters. (Photo courtesy of the Idaho Department of Fish and Game)Embattled Idaho Fish and Game Commissioner Brody Harshbarger has resigned from the commission after agreeing to plead guilty to misdemeanor hunting charges, state records show. 
Idaho Fish and Game commissioner Brody Harshbarger (Photo courtesy of the Idaho Fish and Game website)
On Wednesday, Gov. Brad Little’s Chief of Staff Zach Hauge wrote Harshbarger to tell him that Little had accepted Harshbarger’s resignation. 
“Accordingly, your service on the commission is concluded, effective immediately,” Hauge wrote. 
On Wednesday afternoon, Little’s spokeswoman Emily Callihan said the governor’s office is actively looking to recruit a qualified individual to fill the vacancy on the Idaho Fish and Game commission. 
“Maintaining the integrity, credibility and effective operation of the Idaho Fish and Game Commission remains a top priority for Gov. Little,” Callihan wrote. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
 Why did an Idaho Fish and Game commissioner facing criminal hunting charges?

Earlier this month, Harshbarger signed a written plea agreement agreeing to plead guilty to misdemeanor charges of hunting without a valid tag and shooting from or across a public highway, the Idaho Capital Sun previously reported. 
In exchange, prosecutors agreed to drop five other poaching and trespassing charges Harshbarger was facing. 
Members of the Idaho Fish and Game Commission are appointed by the governor and responsible for overseeing the Idaho Department of Fish and Game and regulating hunting, fishing and trapping in the state. 



Need to get in touch?
Have a news tip?


CONTACT US



The charges stem from a Dec. 20, 2025, Citizens Against Poaching hotline complaint about individuals hunting elk near Spring Hollow boat ramp in eastern Idaho’s Fremont County. 
According to sworn probable cause statements, an Idaho Fish and Game law enforcement officer determined that Harshbarger and another man, Eric Murphy, both fired shots across Spring Hollow Road and Harshbarger fired from the driver’s seat of his vehicle. 
The probable cause report states that during the incident, a six-point bull elk was illegally killed on private property and an antlerless bull elk was illegally killed on Bureau of Reclamation property. 
“Neither Brody Harshbarger nor Eric Murphy called the landowners to request permission to retrieve the six-point bull and did not make a reasonable effort to retrieve the six-point bull elk …,” the probable cause statement reads. 
“Neither individual had permission to be shooting onto the private property, in violation of Idaho Code,” the report continued. 
As part of the plea agreement, prosecutors agreed to drop these fives charges against Harshbarger:

Two charges of unlawfully taking or killing a big game animal.
One charge of hunting with the aid of a motorized vehicle.
One charge of failure to make a reasonable effort to retrieve a six-point bull elk that was killed.
One charge of trespassing to hunt or fish.

Harshbarger did not immediately step down after signing his plea agreement Nov. 5. 
On Monday afternoon, Little’s spokeswoman said Harshbarger remained a member of the Idaho Fish and Game Commission and that Little had not requested Harshbarger’s resignation
On Wednesday, state Rep. David Leavitt, R-Twin Falls, posted on Facebook that he wrote a letter asking Little to remove Harshbarger from the Idaho Fish and Game Commission. 
“Government officials, whether elected or appointed, take an oath to uphold the law,” Leavitt wrote. 
“Idaho’s hunters and sportsmen are expected to follow the laws and regulations established by the Fish and Game Commission,” Leavitt added. “They should reasonably expect those serving on that commission to demonstrate the same respect for those laws.”
Efforts to reach Leavitt were not immediately successful Wednesday.

title: North Dakota Ethics Commission sues Attorney General Wrigley over ‘void’ advisory opinion
description: The North Dakota Ethics Commission is challenging Attorney General Drew Wrigley’s authority to void a commission advisory opinion last year. The five-member ethics panel voted unanimously Wednesday to file a lawsuit in state district court in Burleigh County. The commission is asking the court to clarify that the judicial branch is the only state entity […]
text:
Ethics Commissioners Jared Huibregtse, left, and Mark Western, center, listen to Ethics Commission Chair Pam Sharp announce a lawsuit against North Dakota Attorney General Drew Wrigley on Nov. 18, 2026. (Photo by Jack Dura/North Dakota Monitor)The North Dakota Ethics Commission is challenging Attorney General Drew Wrigley’s authority to void a commission advisory opinion last year.
The five-member ethics panel voted unanimously Wednesday to file a lawsuit in state district court in Burleigh County. The commission is asking the court to clarify that the judicial branch is the only state entity with authority to declare the action of another state entity void, Chair Pam Sharp said.
“The law demands clarity when one government entity seeks to void the decisions of another government entity,” Sharp said. “Our system of constitutional government requires the courts to provide that clarity.”
The lawsuit appeared online Wednesday.
North Dakota attorney general voids ethics opinion, says agency lacked authority

In a text message Wednesday, Wrigley said his office had not been served with the lawsuit. He released a critical opinion about the ethics panel nearly a year ago, which he said “calls into question the timing of the Commission’s lawsuit.” 
“One could reasonably conclude that this lawsuit is retaliatory in nature, extending a pattern of conduct across recent years, a pattern that raises significant ethical issues with regard to the conduct of individuals associated with the Commission,” Wrigley said. 
North Dakota voters in 2018 created the Ethics Commission, whose members are appointed by the governor and Senate majority and minority leaders. The attorney general is an elected position. Wrigley won reelection earlier this month.
The lawsuit concerns a June 2025 advisory opinion the ethics panel issued to then-Sen. Josh Boschee, D-Fargo, who had asked about whether a candidate can use campaign funds to pay for caregiving or security expenses. The commission said each is permissible in some instances. 
The ethics panel issues advisory panels to requestors, such as lawmakers, for guidance on prospective, ethics-related actions.
Secretary of State Michael Howe subsequently asked the attorney general for an opinion on the panel’s related authority, saying the ethics panel’s opinion “raises significant concerns regarding the legal and administrative boundaries between our offices.” Gov. Kelly Armstrong also has questioned the range of the Ethics Commission’s authority on advisory opinions.
Governor questions scope of Ethics Commission authority

In December, Wrigley issued his opinion to Howe saying the Ethics Commission “made unauthorized and expansive legal conclusions” in its opinion “without legal authority to do so.” He also said the ethics panel’s advisory opinion is “void” and “has no legal effect.”
Ethics Commissioner Mark Western said Wednesday, “We believe the law provides that an attorney general may not void the acts of another entity of state government. Only a district judge may do so.”
The commission wrote three times to the attorney general’s office in April and May seeking clarification on Wrigley’s opinion, with no responses, Western said. In a text message screen shot included in court papers, Wrigley sent an image of a Google result for the definition of the word “nullity” to Sharp in May. 
Western said the dispute isn’t about personalities but seeks “judicial clarification about where the attorney general’s office authority ends and the Ethics Commission authority ends.” 
The lawsuit asks the court, in part, to declare the AG lacks legal authority to nullify or void an action of the Ethics Commission, not just advisory opinions.
Sharp called advisory opinions “a strong tool to provide proactive and clear guidance when ethics requirements, statute and commission rules are not straightforward.” The panel discussed one request Wednesday from Rep. Mike Motschenbacher, R-Bismarck, related to his roles as a lawmaker and executive director of the North Dakota Gaming Alliance.
Attorney General Drew Wrigley listens during a North Dakota Industrial Commission meeting on Oct. 30, 2026. (Photo by Jacob Orledge/North Dakota Monitor)
Wrigley issued his opinion on the Ethics Commission nearly a year ago. The commission filed the lawsuit now because of its attempts earlier this year to communicate with Wrigley’s office and did not want to do anything before the November general election, Sharp said.
Sharp read a statement announcing the lawsuit near the end of the commission’s meeting and took reporters’ questions. The meeting earlier dealt with routine updates and three executive sessions closed to the public related to Wrigley’s opinion, various complaints and an inquiry into the North Dakota Development Fund.
Reporter Michael Achterling contributed to this report.
Reach North Dakota Monitor reporter Jack Dura at jdura@northdakotamonitor.com.

name: VTDigger
title: Vermont officials take police dispatch and records system offline following ‘potential security threat’
description:
“We haven’t seen evidence that this event is related to other recent incidents,” the Agency of Digital Services chief information officer said.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Vermont officials take police dispatch and records system offline following ‘potential security threat’.
text:
Vermont Department of Public Safety headquarters in Waterbury on Wednesday, July 10, 2024. File photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger
Vermont’s law enforcement records management and dispatch system, Valcour, is offline following a potential security threat, according to a joint statement from the Agency of Digital Services and the Department of Public Safety. 
“We haven’t seen evidence that this event is related to other recent incidents,” Agency of Digital Services Chief Information Officer Andrea DeLaBruere told VTDigger.
Officials took Valcour offline Monday night. The computer-aided dispatch and records management system is used by most Vermont law enforcement and other public safety agencies to track reported incidents from the initial call to resolution. 
Valcour’s vendor, CrossWinds, notified the state of the potential threat, and has been working with the Agency of Digital Services to investigate the “nature and scope of the incident,” according to a Tuesday joint statement by DeLaBruere and Public Safety Commissioner Jennifer Morrison. 
Emergency services and 911 are not impacted by the incident, they said. 
Issues with Valcour come amid a series of other digital disruptions across the country this week, including cases in New England. 
Suspected cyberattacks in New Hampshire and Maine have left small towns without vital services. Some hospital functions remain offline or not working at a community hospital in Peterborough, N.H., following a Nov. 9 cyber incident. City operations in South Portland, Maine, shut down Monday due to a suspected cyberattack. 
Globally, a platform for digital tools used by IKEA, Zoom and several other companies was hacked Monday as a third party “insert(ed) malicious JavaScript” into customer accounts through the server, forcing the companies to disable certain functions. 
Technological error has also impacted several large industries across the country this week. Officials say the errors are not connected. 
On Friday, all flights, including those at Patrick Leahy Burlington International Airport, were grounded by the Federal Aviation Association after a telecommunications issue. 
Several other recent digital disruptions have had both national and local impact. Microsoft platforms suffered an outage Nov. 12 – Nov. 14. The company, which said in January it had more than 450 million commercial subscriptions, according to the Associated Press, wrote on social media that the outage was not the result of malicious cyberactivity, but “introduced by an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade that surfaced.” 
Widespread banking issues began Monday, too, as a technical issue at JPMorgan Chase caused ripple effects through the national financial systems. Monday also saw a 1.5-hour United Airlines system outage. 
The National Security Agency’s internal communications network went offline Tuesday, during “routine maintenance.” Tech giant Apple also suffered a system outage Tuesday caused by a routine update. 

READ MORE

Potential threats within Vermont’s Valcour system remain under investigation, according to the Digital Services and Public Safety joint statement Wednesday afternoon. 
“The Valcour system will remain unavailable until the completion of our investigation and any necessary remediation,” they wrote. “We do not anticipate the system will be back online today.”
Inquiries to the Agency of Public Services were directed to Adam Silverman, Vermont State Police’s public information officer. Silverman declined to provide additional information and directed a reporter to the joint statements.
