name: California
title: ¿Los últimos reclutas del Departamento de bomberos del condado de San Diego? Cientos de cabras hambrientas
description: Un rebaño de cabras pasta en un parque de San Diego, como parte del plan de prevención de incendios forestales del condado: "Son como un perro con cuernos, pero tan listos como un gato".
text:
This article is also available in English. Read it here.
Este mes, más de 500 nuevos miembros del cuerpo de bomberos trabajaron arduamente en Star Valley Park, en el condado de San Diego, limpiando la maleza y la hierba hasta dejar solo los rastrojos.
Al terminar, corrieron hacia el campo contiguo, empujándose unos a otros, saltando por encima de un perro pastor y mordisqueando la vegetación crecida.
 El proyecto, en la comunidad de Valley Center, es un programa piloto que emplea rebaños de cabras para eliminar la vegetación y reducir el riesgo de incendios forestales.
 “Es de gran ayuda para las agencias locales utilizar estas cabras, utilizar estos segadores vivientes aquí, para hacer que este lugar sea seguro”, dijo Jake Enriquez, gerente regional del Departamento de Parques y Recreación del Condado de San Diego.
Mientras los animales se agolpaban en el prado sin tratar, las madres guiaban a sus crías hacia los parches de hierba, y los animales más grandes se apoyaban contra un roble para comerse las hojas. Cinco perros blancos y mullidos —una mezcla de pastor de Anatolia y gran pirineo— patrullaban el rebaño. Varias cabras se acercaron para inspeccionar a los visitantes y que les rascaran la cabeza.
 “Son como un perro con cuernos, pero tan listos como un gato”, dijo Enriquez. “Son animales muy inteligentes, y se puede ver cómo interactúan, cómo siguen al perro”.
 Las cabras forman parte de la estrategia del condado para reducir el riesgo de incendios forestales en terrenos públicos, mediante la limpieza de la vegetación alrededor de las viviendas, a lo largo de las carreteras principales y en áreas que puedan ser necesarias como lugares de evacuación.
 Los devastadores incendios forestales que azotaron las zonas rurales de San Diego a principios de este siglo obligaron al condado a reformular su estrategia de lucha contra incendios.
Con viviendas dispersas entre la densa maleza en la zona rural, el incendio de Cedar en 2003 arrasó más de un cuarto de millón de acres, destruyó 2,820 edificios y causó la muerte de 15 personas.
En 2007, los cables de alta tensión azotados por el viento provocaron el incendio de Witch Creek, mientras que otros dos incendios de gran magnitud comenzaron el mismo día. En conjunto, arrasaron casi 300,000 acres, destruyeron 1,650 edificios, obligaron a la evacuación de medio millón de personas y causaron 7 muertes.
El fuego avanza hacia las casas en Scripps Ranch a lo largo de Pomerado Road durante el incendio Cedar en San Diego, el 26 de octubre de 2003. Foto de John Gibbins, The San Diego Union-Tribune vía Getty Images.
 Tras esos desastres, el condado de San Diego mejoró su capacidad de extinción de incendios desde el aire mediante la creación de una base Helitack de CalFire en la comunidad de Ramona, al este del condado, la incorporación de un avión cisterna C-130 Hercules de CalFire y un helicóptero Sikorsky S-70 CalFire Hawk, y la mejora de los sistemas de comunicaciones de emergencia.
Pero la prevención de incendios comienza en tierra. El condado limpia la maleza a lo largo de 1287 kilómetros de carreteras al año para garantizar rutas de evacuación seguras y realizó inspecciones de seguridad contra incendios en 15,000 viviendas el año pasado, según declaró Jeff Collins, director del Departamento de Bomberos del Condado de San Diego. Ahora, está incorporando cabras a su equipo de extinción de incendios.
Los funcionarios utilizaron fondos iniciales del condado para poner en marcha el proyecto piloto en Star Valley Park, y acaban de recibir una subvención estatal de 300,000 dólares para llevar el programa de pastoreo a otras zonas con alto riesgo de incendios.
 “Es una herramienta más en el conjunto de herramientas para intentar reducir el riesgo, tanto en incendios pequeños como en incendios a gran escala”, dijo Collins.
 Recientemente, las cabras se han unido a los equipos de bomberos en otras partes del estado y del condado. San Diego Gas & Electric utiliza cabras para la prevención de incendios , que se encargan de desbrozar la maleza cerca de las líneas eléctricas. En septiembre, la Estación Aérea del Cuerpo de Marines de Miramar lanzó la “Operación Cuerda de Cabra” para reducir el riesgo de incendios forestales en terrenos accidentados dentro de la base, en lo que, según los oficiales del Cuerpo de Marines, es la primera campaña de este tipo con cabras en una instalación militar estadounidense.
 Hace unos años, los bomberos de Glendale, California, trajeron cabras para limpiar la maleza seca de los barrios residenciales del condado de Los Ángeles. Asimismo, investigadores de Cal Poly, San Luis Obispo, desplegaron cerca de 1000 de estos animales para devorar la maleza y las plantas invasoras en la estación de investigación de la universidad en Swanton Pacific Ranch, en el condado de Santa Cruz, que fue arrasada por incendios forestales en 2020.
 Chad Hanson, experto en ecología del fuego y director del Proyecto John Muir, afirmó que las cabras pueden ser útiles, siempre y cuando se utilicen en los lugares adecuados. Advirtió que cualquier método de eliminación de vegetación en bosques y arboledas puede tener un efecto contraproducente al convertir esas áreas en pastizales más inflamables. En cambio, los administradores de tierras deberían centrarse en despejar el espacio alrededor de las viviendas y la infraestructura clave.
 “Lo que defiendo es centrar nuestros recursos y atención en crear comunidades seguras contra incendios, reforzar las viviendas y eliminar la vegetación que las rodea”, dijo Hanson.
 Star Valley Park es un antiguo rancho de aproximadamente 16 hectáreas ubicado en la comunidad rural de Valley Center, al norte del condado de San Diego, rodeado de casas y caminos públicos. Se encuentra mayormente sin desarrollar, y el condado está explorando ideas para nuevas instalaciones, pero mientras tanto, el parque es un centro para actividades ecuestres. Los vaqueros de Valley Center se reúnen allí para entrenamientos y eventos ecuestres, y el Valley Center Stampede celebra un rodeo anual en el lugar.
 “El Departamento de Bomberos del Condado se puso en contacto con nosotros y nos preguntó: ‘¿Tienen alguna propiedad en esta zona del Condado de San Diego donde realicen un manejo continuo de la vegetación?’”, dijo Enriquez. “Star Valley nos brindó una excelente oportunidad para poner a prueba este programa”. 
 Aproximadamente 525 cabras pastan en el Parque Star Valley en Valley Center como parte de un programa piloto para eliminar plantas que pueden alimentar incendios forestales. Foto cortesía del Condado de San Diego.
 Seleccionaron el parque como sitio piloto para el pastoreo de cabras debido a la combinación de riesgos y beneficios que presenta. Está rodeado de viviendas al norte, este y oeste, y de carreteras al norte y sur, todas las cuales serían vulnerables en caso de incendio.
Mientras tanto, la presencia de camiones y remolques en los eventos ecuestres representa un riesgo de ignición en época seca, dijo Johnny Gonzalez, gerente de operaciones de campo de Environmental Land Management, la empresa contratista del condado.
 Pero una vez despejado de maleza, el parque podría servir como lugar de evacuación para el vecindario en caso de incendio forestal, y como punto de concentración para equipos de bomberos, helicópteros, camiones cisterna, camiones de agua y otros equipos.
 “Tener una franja de vegetación aquí es muy ventajoso para los bomberos”, dijo Enriquez. “Les proporciona un espacio seguro desde donde trabajar… Hay muchas ventajas en tener un terreno limpio y bien mantenido, y estas cabras hacen un trabajo fantástico”.
 Según Collins, los bomberos del condado también utilizan segadoras, motosierras o quemas controladas para despejar la maleza y los arbustos crecidos en exceso. Sin embargo, las cabras pueden acceder a espacios reducidos y transitar por terrenos escarpados y rocosos. Además, mastican la vegetación hasta una altura mayor que la que alcanza la cuchilla de una segadora, por lo que el mantenimiento es más sencillo una vez que terminan su trabajo, explicó Enriquez.
 Según González, la naturaleza desnuda de los terrenos donde pastan las cabras permite que la tierra actúe como cortafuegos, en lugar de como fuente de combustible: “Esto es lo segundo mejor después de la tierra mineral, porque la tierra absorbe las brasas cuando estas se incendian en el campo”.
 Las cabras también ayudan a podar plantas invasoras como la mostaza, el cardo y la hierba rodadora, que les resultan más sabrosas que la vegetación autóctona, que es más alcalina.
 El uso de estos animales reduce el polvo y los gases de escape producidos por las motosierras y las cortadoras de césped, lo que resulta más respetuoso con el medio ambiente del vecindario. Además de sus balidos, las cabras hacen menos ruido que la maquinaria pesada.
 “Aquí, están gestionando la vegetación con discreción”, dijo Enriquez. “Se puede ver lo bien podada que la han dejado y lo limpio que está alrededor de los árboles. Como administradores de tierras, nos entusiasma mucho esto porque se necesita mucho tiempo, energía y trabajo para mantener una propiedad segura y limpia”.

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: An eighth person has died with measles in Pennsylvania, Health Department says
description: An unvaccinated person died with measles in Clinton County, marking the eighth measles-associated death in the state this year, according to the state Department of Health.
text:
Children can receive their first dose of the MMR vaccine, above, after 12 months of age. The United States lost its measles elimination status in mid-November 2026 after more than 25 years. (Photo by Joshua Haiar/South Dakota Searchlight)An unvaccinated person died with measles in Clinton County, marking the eighth measles-associated death in the state this year, according to the state Department of Health.
Few additional details were provided, including information about the person’s age, potential comorbidities or whether measles was recorded as the underlying cause of death. The department said the lack of information was to protect the privacy of the person and their family.
The Health Department defines a “measles-associated death” as a death that occurs within 30 days of confirmed measles symptoms onset and not due to unrelated causes, like a car accident.
The number of confirmed measles cases in Pennsylvania this year has also risen to 1,589, as of Wednesday. The state has recorded more measles cases and related deaths than any other in the country this year.
Of the nearly 1,600 people who have contracted measles in the commonwealth this year, less than 1% were fully vaccinated, and the ongoing outbreak has led to 315 hospitalizations, according to the state Department of health.
It’s official: Measles is endemic again in the US

Roughly one in five people who contract measles require hospitalization, with children, pregnant women, the immunocompromised and unvaccinated people at the highest risk. About one to three out of every 1,000 people who contract measles will die.
The best way to prevent measles infections is by being vaccinated. The MMR and MMRV vaccines are safe, and 97% effective at preventing measles with two doses.
Measles vaccines are widely available at Pennsylvania’s 59 state health centers, which provide them for free to uninsured and under-insured Pennsylvanians. Many county or municipal health centers are providing them as well. Those who are unvaccinated or unsure of their vaccination status are urged to talk to their doctors or visit these centers.
“We are saddened to hear of another death in Pennsylvania,” said Emily Hilliard, a spokesperson for the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services.  “[The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention] deployed additional support to Pennsylvania to work alongside state and local health officials to investigate the outbreak, strengthen response efforts, and prevent further spread.”
She said the agency has provided the state nearly $4 million in one-time emerging funding to support measles response efforts in 2027.
As it stands, the CDC has not confirmed all eight reported measles deaths in Pennsylvania. While the agency has historically relied on states to collect the data, they changed their policy in September, shortly after U.S. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. accused Gov. Josh Shapiro’s office of having possibly “fabricated” two measles-associated deaths in Pennsylvania.
The agency now relies on data from the National Center for Health Statistics, counting cases where measles was confirmed as the underlying cause of death. The CDC has said it is working with the Council of State and Territorial Epidemiologists to develop a new standard definition for measles deaths.

name: VTDigger
title: Franklin County man admits to sexually assaulting and killing woman, faces at least 27 years in prison
description:
Darren Martell Jr. entered guilty pleas Wednesday as part of an agreement with prosecutors to three charges, including second-degree murder in the death of 82-year-old Roberta Martin in Enosburgh in July 2024.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Franklin County man admits to sexually assaulting and killing woman, faces at least 27 years in prison.
text:
Judge Mary Morrissey presides over a change of plea hearing for Darren Martell Jr. Wednesday, Nov. 18, 2026 in Franklin Superior criminal court in St. Albans. Court screenshot by Nora Doyle-Burr/VTDigger

A Franklin County man charged with sexually assaulting and killing an 82-year-old Enosburgh woman more than two years ago has reached a plea deal that calls for a sentence of at least 27 years in prison.
Darren Martell Jr., 25, pleaded guilty Wednesday in Franklin Superior criminal court in St. Albans to a charge of second-degree murder in the death of Roberta Martin in July 2024. He also pleaded guilty to charges of sexual assault and obstruction of justice.
As part of the plea deal with prosecutors, Martell faces a sentence of 35 years to life in prison, all suspended except 27 years to serve. 
In addition, according to the plea agreement, Martell would be on probation for life after his release and be required to register as a sex offender. 
“The court is inclined to accept the agreement, recognizing that it has been negotiated in good faith by the parties in recognition of trial risk on both sides,” Judge Mary Morrissey said, setting a formal sentencing hearing for Jan. 13.
“There has been an attempt,” Morrissey added, “to balance public safety along with punishment for the offenses that have been charged here, as well as the fact that the family, understandably, reluctantly supports the agreement.”
Martell had initially faced a charge of aggravated murder, the most serious charge in Vermont, which carries a sentence of life in prison without the possibility of parole. 
The plea deal heads off a trial that had been set for next month.
According to charging documents, Martell broke into Martin’s residence on Butternut Hollow Road early on July 17, 2024. Martell had been living at the time in a trailer on a property adjacent to Martin’s residence.
Martell also sexually assaulted and killed Martin, the documents stated. He removed Martin’s body from the home and took the remains to a wooded area where he grew marijuana plants about three-quarters of a mile away from Martin’s home and burned Martin’s body, the documents stated.
Alerted by Martin’s daughter who had not heard from her mother, neighbors arrived at the Butternut Hollow Road home later on July 17 to check on Martin but saw no signs of her. Inside the residence, court filings stated, they saw an unmade bed and a dresser drawer left open, the filing added.
“They advised this was very abnormal for Roberta because she was a very tidy and regimented individual who typically kept to the same schedule every day,” an investigator wrote in charging documents.Police also discovered duct tape on the floor of the bedroom and “dolly cart” tracks leading from the house to a neighboring property, the investigator added. 
Police searching for Martin found her remains about a week later. Martell was arrested soon after, and his DNA was reportedly located on Martin’s body, according to authorities.

READ MORE

Martell was listed Wednesday afternoon as incarcerated at the Northwest State Correctional Facility in St. Albans. 
Assistant Attorney General Franklin Paulino, a prosecutor, told the judge that Martin’s family was aware of the terms of the plea deal. 
“The family reluctantly supports this resolution,” Paulino said, adding, “The family seeks comfort in knowing what will happen, which is the plea agreement that’s stated.”
Paulino told the judge several of Martin’s family members are expected to give statements at the sentencing hearing. 
Jessica Burke, Martell’s attorney, also spoke in court in support of the plea deal.
“We think that this accurately balances the risks to both sides and is sufficient but not greater than necessary to ensure public safety moving forward,” Burke told the judge.
The judge detailed the terms of the plea deal to Martell during Wednesday’s hearing. 
“Yes,” Martell repeatedly replied when asked by Morrissey if he understood each provision of the agreement. 
Morrissey, the judge, ordered the state Department of Corrections to complete a presentence investigation ahead of that proceeding. The investigation leads to a report by a probation officer detailing several factors, including a defendant’s criminal history, to assist the judge in sentencing. 
The judge said at the close of the hearing Wednesday that unless that report comes back with information that “causes concerns about the plea agreement,” the proposed sentence would be imposed.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: School funding reform could prompt NJ constitutional convention
description: New Jersey should call a constitutional convention to include voters in the approval of a new school funding formula once a proposal is finalized, Assembly Majority Leader Lou Greenwald (D-Camden) said. Though legislators and Gov. Mikie Sherrill in August began soliciting input for changes to the state’s funding formula, officials have said little about how [...]
text:
NJ Assembly Majority Leader Louis Greenwald (D-Camden), shown at a news conference earlier this year in Trenton, says the state needs to hold a constitutional convention to approve a new school funding formula. He was speaking at a New Jersey League of Municipalities conference Wednesday, Nov. 18, 2026. (Photo by Dana DiFilippo / New Jersey Monitor)New Jersey should call a constitutional convention to include voters in the approval of a new school funding formula once a proposal is finalized, Assembly Majority Leader Lou Greenwald (D-Camden) said.
Though legislators and Gov. Mikie Sherrill in August began soliciting input for changes to the state’s funding formula, officials have said little about how their eventual proposal would differ from the funding formula enacted in 2008, and it’s not clear whether or how a formula enshrined in the state’s constitution would affect court precedent that demands New Jersey students receive a thorough and efficient education.
“I think ultimately this is going to need to lead to a constitutional convention and then a question that will include the voters as part of the solution because I think, ultimately at the end of the day, this is an issue that New Jersey has struggled with for generations,” Greenwald said Wednesday during a panel discussion at the New Jersey League of Municipalities annual conference.
In New Jersey, the state calculates how much each municipality must spend to provide their students a constitutionally sound education and how much those districts can raise on their own based on their residents’ incomes and property values.
State aid fills the rest, though not all districts raise enough revenue to meet the local spending — called a local fair share — needed to fully fund schools after state aid is added.
Some cannot raise enough revenue locally because of the state’s 2% cap on annual property tax levies, and others have been hammered by steep swings in state aid as the state in 2018 moved to begin phasing out aid meant to keep districts whole after the enactment of the 2008 funding formula.
At present, local governments in New Jersey look to property taxes to fund their share of school expenses, and Greenwald suggested that could change as a result of the yet-to-be-determined reforms.
“We need to understand that we are fixing a fundamentally broken tax system that dates back to the origins of this state as one of the founding states of this country,” Greenwald said.
New Jersey in 2024 tied with Illinois for the highest property tax rate in the nation, according to the Tax Foundation, and the average property tax bill in the state rose to a record high $10,570 last year.
It’s unclear what changes to the state’s funding formula lawmakers will eventually propose. The Department of Education last week said it would continue soliciting feedback from stakeholders at least through December.
Senate Majority Leader Teresa Ruiz (D-Essex) earlier told the Monitor she does not expect a proposal to be ready before the end of the current July-to-June fiscal year.
Among some other things, the reforms aim to better fund school transportation and extraordinary special education.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Maximus closing Hattiesburg location, affecting hundreds of employees
description: Maximus call center employs several hundred people at the Hattiesburg location it plans to close in April 2027.
text:
HATTIESBURG – Multiple sources have now confirmed that Maximus Federal Services, Inc., will permanently close its Hattiesburg location at the old Cloverleaf Mall, potentially affecting hundreds of employees.  
Mississippi State Sen. Johnny Dupree, a Hattiesburg Democrat, confirmed the news on Tuesday and called a meeting of relevant state and local officials to begin discussing plans to help affected employees. He did not confirm any additional details at that time.  
The original claim said the closure would take place before the Christmas holidays, but Maximus did not file a Worker Adjustment and Retraining Notification Act notice in time for a winter closure. By federal law, companies with more than 100 employees must file a WARN at least 60 days before a covered closure or layoff. 
According to an email obtained from a union organizer, Maximus sent a WARN notice to employees on Nov. 12. The notice stated that the closure will begin to take effect on April 3, 2027.  
RHCJC reporters have requested a copy of the WARN filed with the Mississippi Department of Employment Security. The MDES Rapid Response office responded with the following:  
Pictured is an email obtained from a union organizer that was allegedly sent from Maximus Human Resources to employees of the Hattiesburg call center.  Credit: RHCJC NEWS
“In accordance with agency policy and confidentiality requirements, all WARN information is released only through our official website and only within 30 days following the end of each quarter. No additional WARN information can be provided outside of these public postings.” 
The original claim also stated that over 400 employees would be laid off. While there is no public listing of current employment size, the Hattiesburg location held a government contract in 2024 and 2022 to employ between 600-900 people.  
RHCJC reached out to both the local Maximus office and Cecilia Montalvo-Silburn, the director of human resources for Maximus Federal, for comment. As of Tuesday, neither has responded to confirm or comment on the closure.

The RHCJC “What Is True?” team of graduate investigators examines everything from viral online posts to local community rumors. If you have a question, submit it to the “What Is True?” inquiry form on the RHCJC website or call 855-IS-IT-TRU (855-474-8878).

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: Regulators keep SLECA plugged into coastal camps in Lafourche, Terrebonne
description: The Louisiana Public Service Commission has denied a South Louisiana electric utility’s wish to permanently cut off portions of its service area in Lafourche and Terrebonne parishes that Hurricane Ida damaged five years ago, with the areas still reliant on generators.
text:
Power lines in Houma swayed following Hurricane Ida in 2021. The Louisiana Public Service Commission has denied a South Louisiana Electric Cooperative Association wish to permanently cut off portions of its service area in Lafourche and Terrebonne, damaged by Hurricane Ida five years ago. The properties are still reliant on generators. (Photo by JC Canicosa/Louisiana Illuminator)The Louisiana Public Service Commission has denied a South Louisiana electric utility’s wish to permanently cut off portions of its service area in Lafourche and Terrebonne parishes that Hurricane Ida damaged five years ago, with the areas still reliant on generators.
Commissioners rejected a request Wednesday from the South Louisiana Electric Cooperative Association for a new hearing over whether it can abandon infrastructure in Lake Fields, Four Point Island and Grand Pass. The Public Service Commission voted in September to allow SLECA to walk away from customers it served in Lake DeCade, one of four areas it sought to leave, but it kept the other three in its network.  
The four areas SLECA wanted to abandon would have left 282 properties that had electricity before the hurricane without power, according to its filings with the commission. These customers are mostly fishing and hunting camps in the coastal marshes.
A heated discussion between SLECA’s lawyers and Public Service Commission members at Wednesday’s meeting reflected many months of frustration over the matter. 
Commissioner Eric Skrmetta, R-Metairie, said the co-op was making a business decision that was unfair to the affected camp owners. 
“SLECA is given a license, effectively, from the commission to provide service to all people in that region who seek service,” Skrmetta said. “They are not given a license to deny service to people in that area.” 
“What if this was a neighborhood, a concentrated neighborhood that had lost power? … They would have repaired their service and sent you the additional bill associated with repairing,” he added. 
SLECA has said restoring power to the four areas would cost upwards of $140 million, with another $11 million to $23 million for environmental permitting and right-of-way acquisition. Though the Federal Emergency Management Agency will cover 90% of the restoration, the co-op said it would have to bill customers another $13 to $24 a month to cover its expenses.  
Commissioner Davante Lewis, D-Baton Rouge, told SLECA’s lawyers the matter was settled and did not deserve a re-hearing. 
“I think it is very disingenuous to constantly throw the cost out there as a consideration of understanding why you didn’t comply with (the September decision),” Lewis said.
Camp owners from the storm-damaged areas also spoke at the meeting in opposition to SLECA’s rehearing request. They have previously said the co-op has taken down power lines without the Public Service Commission’s approval.
“I understand the whole co-op would have to pay for us, but I’m part of that co-op,” Houma resident and camp owner Brent Story said. “I’ll be paying my share, as I have in the past when it wasn’t me that was being restored.” 
Discussion before Wednesday’s vote turned to SLECA possibly paying settlements to the abandoned customers to cover the cost of generators, but ratepayers were unswayed.
“What would it take to make you happy?” Commissioner Foster Campbell, D-Shreveport, asked the property owners in attendance, looking for a dollar amount. 
“Put my power back,” said Sara Boudreaux, one of the camp owners. “Money is not equitable.” 
Skrmetta agreed, making the point that operating a generator would be a continuing expense.
“Yeah, they can give you some money, you might be able to get a generator, you might get some fuel,” he said. “Generators are mechanical. They don’t last forever. Fuel is an ongoing expense.” 
Along with the high restoration costs, SLECA has said it wanted to abandon service to the areas because of safety concerns and difficulty in accessing the marshy areas in the event of an emergency. 
The co-op’s leaders have argued that when the lines were originally installed in the 1960s, the land was more stable and able to support infrastructure and access. But because of “continuing coastal erosion and subsidence,” as well as repeated damage from storms, it’s a more vulnerable area than ever before and no longer in the interest of the co-op or its members to service. 
The Alliance for Affordable Energy, a consumer advocacy group, has said SLECA’s quoted costs for restoration are based on the most expensive option available, and they reflect replacing infrastructure the co-op chose prematurely to remove — including lines that were hardly damaged.

name: California
title: Aumentan los bonos en los fondos de pensiones de California; tres ejecutivos recibieron más de un millón de dólares en incentivos
description: Los mayores fondos de pensiones de California, CalPERS y CalSTRS, otorgan bonificaciones cada otoño. Los incentivos por rendimiento aumentaron a medida que se mantenía una racha de buenos rendimientos de las inversiones.
text:
This article is also available in English. Read it here.
Según los resúmenes sobre la remuneración adicional publicados recientemente, el personal de inversiones de los dos mayores fondos de pensiones públicos de California recibió este año mayores incentivos por rendimiento, y tres ejecutivos obtuvieron bonificaciones de siete cifras.
 Ambos fondos superaron sus objetivos de inversión durante los últimos tres años, lo que explica parte del pago de bonificaciones.
A principios de este mes, el Sistema de Jubilación de Maestros del Estado de California reveló que pagó 21.8 millones de dólares en incentivos al personal de inversiones, frente a los 20.3 millones del año pasado.
El director de inversiones de CalSTRS, Scott Chan, recibió una bonificación de 1 millón de dólares además de su salario de 576,000 dólares; la directora ejecutiva de CalSTRS, Cassandra Lichnock, obtuvo un incentivo de 750,000 dólares además de su salario de 500,000 dólares.
La bonificación de Chan el año anterior fue de 881,000 dólares, mientras que la de Lichnock fue de 675,000 dólares.
El Sistema de Jubilación de Empleados Públicos de California reveló esta semana que distribuyó 37.9 millones de dólares en bonificaciones a su personal, un ligero aumento con respecto a los 37.7 millones de dólares en incentivos del año pasado.
Tal y como ya informó CalMatters, las mayores bonificaciones fueron para la directora ejecutiva, Marcie Frost, con 1.1 millones de dólares, y para el director de inversiones, Stephen Gilmore, con 1.7 millones de dólares. El año anterior, Frost recibió un incentivo por desempeño de 766,000 dólares y Gilmore se llevó una bonificación de 1.5 millones de dólares.
 Ambos fondos consideran que las bonificaciones son esenciales para la captación y retención de personal de inversión. Asimismo, son conscientes de que dichas bonificaciones son excesivas.
 En los informes presentados a sus juntas directivas, cada sistema describía los incentivos como una pequeña fracción de las ganancias de los fondos.
 CalPERS incluyó un gráfico generado por inteligencia artificial que mostraba los incentivos como el equivalente a 6 centavos por cada 1000 dólares que el fondo mantenía en su cartera al 1 de julio, cuando sus activos estaban valorados en 637 mil millones de dólares. Proporciona planes de jubilación a aproximadamente 2 millones de personas.
 Hasta el mes pasado, CalSTRS contaba con una cartera valorada en 415 mil millones de dólares. Proporciona planes de pensiones a aproximadamente 1 millón de personas.

title: Delaware blocks ChristianaCare’s Georgetown hospital. What would more competition be worth?
description: The proposed Sussex County campus would have added emergency, inpatient, and outpatient care. The 8-1 vote leaves open how the county will expand access. GEORGETOWN, Del. — The Delaware Health Resources Board voted 8-1 Tuesday, Nov. 17, to reject ChristianaCare’s proposed $65.1 million health campus in Georgetown after board members questioned the system’s d[...]
text:
The Delaware Health Resources Board voted 8-1 Tuesday, Nov. 17, to reject ChristianaCare’s proposed $65.1 million health campus in Georgetown after board members questioned the system’s data and plans for transferring patients who would need a higher level of care. image created on 11/18 using AI
The proposed Sussex County campus would have added emergency, inpatient, and outpatient care. The 8-1 vote leaves open how the county will expand access.
GEORGETOWN, Del. — The Delaware Health Resources Board voted 8-1 Tuesday, Nov. 17, to reject ChristianaCare’s proposed $65.1 million health campus in Georgetown after board members questioned the system’s data and plans for transferring patients who would need a higher level of care.
The 42,000-square-foot campus would have been built near U.S. 113 and Ennis Street, across from Delaware Technical Community College. It would have included eight emergency department beds, eight inpatient beds and offices offering primary, specialty and behavioral health care.
In a separate 8-1 vote, the board rejected a $58.1 million ChristianaCare campus in Camden in Kent County, Spotlight Delaware reported. ChristianaCare told the board it planned to move forward only if both applications were approved. President and CEO Jenn Schwartz said after the vote that the health system would review the decision and consider its options.
Bayhealth, Beebe Healthcare and TidalHealth opposed the proposals. At an October hearing, Bayhealth argued that another emergency department would add expensive services in an area already served by existing hospitals. Beebe questioned how transfers would work for patients who needed services the facility could not provide. ChristianaCare said its small hospitals would treat patients with less severe emergencies and transfer those who needed more advanced care to an appropriate hospital, WHYY reported.
Delaware law requires projects such as these to obtain a Certificate of Public Review. The board considers community need, available alternatives and effects on costs and quality. As of Nov. 18, its public website did not list written decisions for the two projects. delcode.delaware.gov
ChristianaCare said the Georgetown campus would bring care closer to a growing and aging population. Delaware’s rural health plan identifies a primary care shortage in Sussex County, citing about 130 active primary care physicians for roughly 271,000 residents. Deciding whether Georgetown also needs another emergency department requires looking at travel times, how patients use existing emergency departments and what kinds of cases a small hospital could handle.
Analysis from Two Perspectives
The pro-market case
From a pro-market perspective, the denial could hurt families by keeping another hospital system from competing for their care. A Georgetown campus could mean shorter trips, more appointment options and another provider for insurers to contract with. Where services overlap, and insurers can direct patients to another hospital, competition can give insurers leverage when negotiating rates. Federal antitrust officials have warned that advance approval laws can give established providers a way to delay or block competitors. Health Care Cost Institute
The benefit depends on what ChristianaCare could deliver. Eight inpatient beds would give insurers limited leverage if they still need the larger hospitals in their networks for most services. If the campus hired mainly from nearby practices, it could shift appointments from one location to another with little increase in availability. The strongest case for approval would show how many clinicians the campus could bring to Sussex, which insurance plans it could accept, and how many patients it could treat closer to home.
The single-payer case
Under a single-payer approach, one public plan would finance covered care. It could use its purchasing power to set payment rates and direct funding to underserved areas. If a staffed primary care clinic, more behavioral health appointments and better emergency transport could meet more of Sussex County’s needs, declining the hospital portion could make sense. A public plan could also fund a small hospital if evidence showed that long trips for emergency care were putting patients at risk. Congressional Budget Office
That case depends on the public plan actually financing and staffing the services it identifies. Broader coverage and lower out-of-pocket costs can help people get care, but demand can grow faster than the supply of clinicians. The Congressional Budget Office found that the single-payer designs it studied could lead to both more people receiving care and longer waits. For Sussex families, the case for turning down the hospital depends on whether another plan delivers timely care closer to home.
What the vote means for patients
The vote halted a specific plan to add care in Georgetown. Whether the decision serves Sussex County families will depend on what care becomes available, where and when. Under either approach, patients can judge the result by how long it takes to get an appointment, how far they travel for emergency care, how often they need a transfer and what they pay for treatment.
To Go Box

See the project presentation on the Delaware Health Resources Board website. Under Title 16, Chapter 93 of the Delaware Code, anyone can request the board’s written decision and the reasons for it.

name: California
title: Cinco elecciones clave que cambiaron la composición de la delegación de California en el Congreso
description: La ola azul demócrata que arrasó el país en las elecciones de mitad de mandato eliminó a cinco republicanos de California, dejándolos con su menor representación en el Congreso en 90 años.
text:
This article is also available in English. Read it here.
Finalmente, ya está definida la composición del Congreso de California: 48 demócratas y solo cuatro republicanos, lo que supone una pérdida neta de cinco escaños para el Partido Republicano.
 Las elecciones de mitad de mandato de 2026 fueron una derrota histórica para los republicanos de California, en gran parte debido a la Proposición 50 , el plan del gobernador demócrata Gavin Newsom para combatir las maniobras, finalmente infructuosas, del Partido Republicano para manipular los distritos electorales en los estados tradicionalmente republicanos.
 La agencia Associated Press anunció el lunes por la noche el resultado de la última contienda congresional del estado: una victoria inesperadamente ajustada para el actual representante Jay Obernolte, de Big Bear Lake, uno de los pocos republicanos que quedan en el estado. Regresará a Washington, D.C. junto con otros representantes republicanos que también resultaron reelegidos: Tom McClintock, de Elk Grove; Ken Calvert, de Corona; y Vince Fong, de Bakersfield.
 En cuanto al Partido Demócrata, se enfrentó a su propia lucha interna de poder en las elecciones de mitad de mandato entre progresistas y moderados, y los resultados fueron claramente dispares. Algunos candidatos progresistas superaron las expectativas y derrotaron a los titulares del establishment por amplios márgenes, pero en otros distritos, los moderados se impusieron.
 A continuación, un repaso a cinco elecciones clave que contribuyeron a remodelar la delegación de California en el Congreso. 
 Bakersfield y el Valle Central: Villegas contra Valadao
 Ningún resultado fue más sorprendente que la contundente victoria del demócrata Randy Villegas, de Bakersfield, sobre el congresista republicano David Valadao, un agricultor de Hanford. Salvo una derrota en las elecciones de mitad de mandato de 2018, tras los dos primeros años de la presidencia de Donald Trump, Valdao había evitado sistemáticamente los intentos de destituirlo presentándose como un moderado y un pensador independiente.
 Pero Villegas, un recién llegado progresista respaldado por el senador Bernie Sanders y la representante Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, derrotó a Valadao por más de 35 puntos porcentuales en el distrito, de gran mayoría latina, que se extiende por el valle de San Joaquín desde Fresno hasta Bakersfield. 
 Los Ángeles: González-Torres vs. Gómez
 También fue destacable para la izquierda la victoria de Angela Gonzalez-Torres, miembro de los Socialistas Democráticos de América, quien derrotó al representante demócrata Jimmy Gomez por un margen de más del 24%. Ahora representará al distrito de Los Ángeles que se extiende desde Koreatown, pasando por Boyle Heights, hasta el este de Los Ángeles. 
 Sacramento: Matsui contra Vang
 La derrota más decepcionante para los progresistas se produjo en la histórica contienda demócrata del área de Sacramento entre la concejala Mai Vang, de 41 años, y la representante Doris Matsui, de 82. Matsui salió victoriosa tras enfrentarse por primera vez a una funcionaria pública en ejercicio que contaba con los recursos necesarios para una campaña bien financiada. Matsui prestó a su campaña 7 millones de dólares y derrotó a Vang con el apoyo de votantes republicanos e independientes. 
 Napa y Sonoma: Jones contra Thompson
 En otra contienda entre demócratas en el norte de California , el novato político Eric Jones financió en gran medida con sus propios recursos su campaña multimillonaria para desbancar al congresista en funciones Mike Thompson, un veterano con casi 30 años de servicio en el Congreso. Jones, quien amasó su fortuna con una firma de capital de riesgo que cofundó llamada Dragoneer Investment Group, avanzó desde las primarias presentándose como un candidato progresista, a la izquierda de Thompson, con el respaldo del grupo liberal Justice Democrats, afín a Sanders.
 Pero Jones ganó las elecciones generales al virar hacia el centro y, con el apoyo de un super PAC financiado principalmente por inversores y socios de Dragoneer, convenció a algunos republicanos y votantes independientes para que le dieran una oportunidad. Varios de los anuncios financiados por el super PAC, conocido como New Leadership Now, emplearon una retórica antiinmigrante incendiaria para atacar a Thompson, tildándolo de “indulgente con los delincuentes ilegales” y “un demócrata liberal” que “apoya las ciudades santuario”. 
 San Francisco: Wiener contra Chan
En San Francisco, el senador estatal Scott Wiener sucederá a la expresidenta de la Cámara de Representantes, Nancy Pelosi, tras derrotar a su candidata predilecta, la supervisora de San Francisco, Connie Chan. Si bien Wiener es uno de los miembros más progresistas de la Legislatura, los progresistas ultraliberales de San Francisco lo retrataron como un moderado , especialmente después de que la gigante de la inteligencia artificial Anthropic canalizara fondos para anuncios a su favor. Wiener lideró las encuestas de forma constante desde las primarias de junio, a pesar del intento de Pelosi de movilizar a su dinastía política en su contra.
 Wiener derrotó fácilmente al millonario tecnológico progresista Saikat Chakrabarti en las primarias. Chakrabarti no logró avanzar tras una campaña autofinanciada impregnada de la misma energía rebelde que han promovido los progresistas a nivel nacional.
 Los cuatro congresistas republicanos de California regresarán a Washington el próximo año en lo que parece ser la delegación republicana más pequeña del estado desde 1937, cuando el partido también contaba con solo cuatro escaños en la Cámara de Representantes de Estados Unidos. Sin embargo, hace 90 años, California solo tenía 20 escaños en la Cámara de Representantes.

name: VTDigger
title: Vermont Conversation: Former GOP strategist Stuart Stevens says Republican Party has become an ‘extremist movement’ that must be held accountable
description:
This dynamic, Stevens argued, is driving away talented candidates and creating what he sees as a widening gap in candidate quality between the two parties.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Vermont Conversation: Former GOP strategist Stuart Stevens says Republican Party has become an ‘extremist movement’ that must be held accountable.
text:
The Vermont Conversation with David Goodman is a VTDigger podcast that features in-depth interviews on local and national issues. Listen and subscribe for free on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, YouTube or wherever you get podcasts.
Stuart Stevens at home in Morristown on Tuesday, Feb. 12, 2019.  Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger
Stuart Stevens helped make the Republican Party an electoral powerhouse. Now he is trying to kill the monster that he did much to create.
The former advisor to five Republican presidential candidates said on The Vermont Conversation that “the Republican Party isn’t a traditional American political party anymore. It’s an extremist movement, and it’s performing in a way that extremist movements perform. They only become more extreme.”
“It wasn’t a moderate element of the Red Guard that emerged and (said), ‘OK, too much,” he said, referring to Mao Zedong’s brutal paramilitary youth organization in China in the 1960s. “They just had to burn themselves out.”
Stevens pointed to Republican leaders continuing to embrace former President Donald Trump’s false claims about the 2020 election and, in some cases, defending neo-Nazi activists and positions in pursuit of political advancement.
“The threshold of entry to the Republican Party… is to say what fifth graders know not to be true, that Donald Trump won the 2020 election,” he said.
Stevens argued that this dynamic is driving away talented candidates and creating what he sees as a widening gap in candidate quality between the two parties.
“Who wants to join something where you have to go out and humiliate yourself and say something that fifth graders know is not true?” he asked.
Stevens is among the most successful campaign consultants in the country. He was a top adviser to Mitt Romney, George W. Bush and John McCain, and he has been a consultant on dozens of GOP campaigns for governor, Congress and the U.S. Senate.
In 2016, Stevens abandoned the Republican Party. He has written several bestselling books about his political conversion, including, “The Conspiracy to End America: Five Ways My Old Party is Driving Our Democracy To Autocracy,” and “It Was All a Lie: How the Republican Party Became Donald Trump.”
Stevens is now a senior adviser to the Lincoln Project, which works to oppose Trump and other MAGA candidates. He grew up in Mississippi but has lived for many years in Stowe.
Stevens rejected the notion that a meaningful distinction remains between traditional Republicans and the party’s Trump-aligned faction.

READ MORE

“MAGA is Republican,” he said. “There is no distinction.”
While Stevens sees growing voter resistance to MAGA candidates, particularly among independents, he warned Democrats not to mistake electoral victories for a fundamental change in Republican politics.
“These people couldn’t care less about the Democratic Party,” he said. “They just want stuff done.”
According to Stevens, the growing bloc of self-described independents represents the future of American politics. Younger voters, he noted, increasingly reject formal party identities altogether.
“They don’t feel particular allegiance to a party, and they are the future of American politics,” he said. “This is what is going to decide American politics.”
While candidates varied widely by region and ideology, Stevens said many shared a common appeal rooted in integrity and public service rather than partisan loyalty.
“I would posit that they had a focus on integrity. They had a focus on service,” he said. “They have a value system that seems not transactional.”
That anti-transactional politics, Stevens argued, stands in stark contrast to former President Donald Trump, whom he called “the ultimate transactional politician.”
Stevens has some advice for Democrats. “The greatest challenge for Democrats is to understand that they do not have a governing partner in Republicans,” Stevens said. “They don’t. It doesn’t exist.”
Instead of seeking bipartisan compromise, Stevens argued that Democrats should pursue sweeping reforms and aggressively investigate corruption and abuses of power during the Trump era by officials including Stephen Miller and Kristi Noem, the architect and enforcer, respectively, of Trump’s immigration crackdown.
The former Republican strategist called for congressional investigations, stronger ethics laws, financial transparency requirements, and coordinated legal action by state attorneys general. He also advocated ending the Senate filibuster and exposing the identities of ICE agents. 
Stevens criticized Democrats for what he sees as a failure to adequately pursue accountability during President Joe Biden’s administration.
“The problem in the Biden years is not that they tried to prosecute Trump,” he said. “It’s that they failed to prosecute Trump.”
He argued that future investigations should move beyond hearings and political rhetoric.
“We need trials,” Stevens said. “Who puts people on trial? State attorneys general do.”
For Stevens, the stakes extend far beyond partisan competition. The struggle, he argued, is about whether American democracy is willing to defend itself against anti-democratic forces operating within one of the country’s two major political parties.
“The fastest way to restore faith in the system is to hold people accountable,” he insisted.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Vermont Conversation: Former GOP strategist Stuart Stevens says Republican Party has become an ‘extremist movement’ that must be held accountable.

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Poll: Arkansas voters want lawmakers to work on improving maternal health
description: Improving Arkansas’ maternal health landscape should be one of the Legislature’s top priorities in the 2027 session, according to a large majority of 500 likely voters surveyed before this month’s election. More than 90% of the Arkansans surveyed want the state to increase its investment in maternal and infant healthcare, the highest rate of support […]
text:
(Photo by Joe Raedle/Getty Images)Improving Arkansas’ maternal health landscape should be one of the Legislature’s top priorities in the 2027 session, according to a large majority of 500 likely voters surveyed before this month’s election.
More than 90% of the Arkansans surveyed want the state to increase its investment in maternal and infant healthcare, the highest rate of support among the 10 states studied by Heartland Forward, a Bentonville-based research organization focused on economic growth in middle America.
Majorities of both Democrats and Republicans supported greater investment and resources, such as follow-up visits for new mothers to screen for mental and physical health issues within two weeks of giving birth.
“When nine in ten likely voters agree on something, regardless of party, that is a real opportunity for Arkansas to lead the heartland in building a stronger system of care,” Heartland Forward President Angie Cooper said in a Wednesday news release.

AR-Zogby-2-Pager 
The interactive poll of 500 likely voters in Arkansas was conducted by John Zogby Strategies, and had a margin of error of plus or minus 4.5 percentage points.
The other nine states surveyed were Missouri, Louisiana, Mississippi, Oklahoma, Kansas, Tennessee, Kentucky, Indiana and Minnesota.
Arkansas has the nation’s fourth-highest rate of maternal mortality, with 38 maternal deaths per 1,000 live births between 2018 and 2022, according to the independent health research center KFF.
The state also has the nation’s fourth-highest premature birth rate at nearly 12% in 2025, according to a March of Dimes report released Tuesday.
Arkansas is the only state that has not taken the federal option to extend postpartum Medicaid coverage from 60 days to 12 months after birth.
A bill to create this policy did not advance in the Legislature in 2023. The same bill passed the House in 2025 and then failed in a Senate committee. The Legislature is set to begin its 2027 session on Jan. 11.
Roughly four of every five voters surveyed said they were concerned about Arkansas hospitals closing their labor and delivery units and about access to specialized care in rural areas.
Eight labor and delivery units have closed in Arkansas since 2020, including two this year. Only 22 of Arkansas’ 75 counties now have labor and delivery units.
Several labor and delivery unit closures have been in south Arkansas, including Ouachita County, where the hospital closed its maternity ward in January. The Heartland Forward survey found that 62% of south Arkansans surveyed “strongly support” increased investment in maternal healthcare.
Drive time to Arkansas hospitals for labor and delivery getting longer, report shows

Arkansas hospital administrators have said low insurance reimbursement rates have forced them to cut services, including labor and delivery.
The longer it takes to get to a delivering hospital, the higher the risk of health problems for mothers and newborns, according to a 2022 study from the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists. Paramedics in rural areas have seen an uptick in the number of deliveries being performed in ambulances.
Maternal healthcare has been a bipartisan priority among Arkansas’ elected officials in the past few years. Republican Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders signed the Healthy Moms, Healthy Babies Act last year. The law fast-tracks pregnant Arkansans’ Medicaid applications and provides them coverage until it’s proven they’re not eligible.
The same law established Medicaid coverage for certain kinds of pregnancy-related care and allows doulas and community health workers to be reimbursed by the state. Medicaid coverage for doula care went into effect Sept. 1.

name: Colorado Newsline
title: Colorado environmental groups call on lawmakers to oppose permitting overhaul
description: Colorado environmental advocates spoke in downtown Denver Wednesday to urge Congress to reject a sweeping overhaul of federal permitting laws that has split Democrats and left-leaning interest groups. The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, or BAAJA, has emerged as a top legislative priority for the lame-duck Republican Congress, following years [...]
text:
Gas wells operate near Interstate 70 and the Union Pacific railroad in Garfield County near Parachute, June 9, 2023. (William Woody for Colorado Newsline)Colorado environmental advocates spoke in downtown Denver Wednesday to urge Congress to reject a sweeping overhaul of federal permitting laws that has split Democrats and left-leaning interest groups.
The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, or BAAJA, has emerged as a top legislative priority for the lame-duck Republican Congress, following years of failed negotiations in Washington over how to speed up approval processes that developers say can bog down major energy and infrastructure projects in years of study and litigation.
Trade groups representing fossil fuel and pipeline companies have lobbied aggressively for the bill. But it also has the support of some influential climate and clean energy advocates, who argue it will accelerate the buildout of large renewables projects and transmission lines necessary for the energy transition.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
In a press conference at Denver’s Confluence Park, however, Ellie Andrews of Environment Colorado called the bill “a Trojan horse” that would undermine “bedrock environmental laws that have protected our land, air and water for over 50 years.”
Bipartisan permitting bill in Congress could speed energy projects, but draws green critics

“BAAJA would send us backwards,” Andrews said. “It may help some renewable energy projects move forward, but it accelerates mining, it accelerates drilling, it will accelerate building pipelines.”
The bill was negotiated by two Republicans, Sen. Shelley Moore Capito of West Virginia, chair of the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, and Mike Lee of Utah, chair of the Energy Committee, along with two Democrats, Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island and Sen. Martin Heinrich of New Mexico, who serve as the ranking members on those committees.
The bill has split Democrats, including Colorado’s Senate delegation. Sen. John Hickenlooper has cast multiple votes in favor of advancing the measure this month, while Sen. Michael Bennet has remained opposed, saying in a Nov. 9 statement that he was “concerned that not all perspectives were sufficiently heard during the drafting of this far-reaching piece of legislation.”
“This bill is not the way forward to a clean energy future. It’s a destructive path that will cause irreversible harm to our public lands and the communities that depend on them,” said Taylor Luneau, Colorado conservation manager for The Wilderness Society. “We’re grateful to Sen. Bennet for opposing this bill, and we urge Sen. Hickenlooper to do the same.”
‘Locking in’ fossil fuels?
Among opponents’ top concerns are provisions in the bill relating to “project certainty,” which would curtail the power of federal agencies and courts to revoke or modify project approvals after they have been granted. Supporters frame the changes as ensuring stability across changes in administration, preventing a repeat of former President Joe Biden’s cancellation of the Keystone XL pipeline in 2021, or President Donald Trump’s cancellation of offshore wind projects.
In the view of many environmental groups — for whom the arcane regulatory and legal procedures under laws like the National Environmental Policy Act, the Clean Water Act and the Endangered Species Act have become their bread and butter since their passage in the 1970s — the changes go too far, and could “lock in” major fossil fuel projects at a time when climate scientists are urging policymakers to do just the opposite.
“To stop (a project) because somebody discovered something, that no doubt is frustrating,” Andrews said. “But the things that get discovered matter, and there’s a process for that, and it’s been hammered out over 50-odd years.”



Quotation







This bill is not the way forward to a clean energy future. It’s a destructive path that will cause irreversible harm to our public lands and the communities that depend on them.


– Taylor Luneau, of The Wilderness Society


Other criticisms leveled at the bill include the charge that it would accelerate data center development, including on public lands, and further enable the rapid expansion of Immigrations and Customs Enforcement detention capacity envisioned by architects of Trump’s mass-deportation program. Tribal groups have also faulted the bill’s narrowing of tribal consultation requirements and protections for sacred and cultural sites.
The measure cleared several more procedural votes on Wednesday, with a group of about 15 to 20 Democrats, including Hickenlooper, continuing to vote in favor. It could be amended further before its final passage in the Senate sometime this week. The bill would then need to be approved by the House of Representatives before heading to Trump’s desk for a signature.
In the wake of the “blue tsunami” in the midterm elections, some of the bill’s Democratic supporters cast it as a way for the party to deliver on the affordability message that drew many swing voters to their side. Proponents also cast doubt on the possibility of a future compromise that could win support from the next Congress’ Democratic majorities while still passing muster with Trump and the handful of Senate Republicans needed to break the filibuster.
“This bill isn’t perfect. No bill is. We should continue working with Tribal Nations and environmental groups to strengthen it as it moves through the legislative process,” Hickenlooper said in a statement earlier this month. “But we have a golden opportunity to make good on our promise to voters to make energy more affordable. We cannot afford to let it slip away.”
Opponents, meanwhile, argue that Democrats’ historic victories in the midterms should leave them emboldened to take up the issue again in January, rather fast-tracking a bill through Congress in the final weeks of GOP control.
“The midterms sent a pretty clear message,” Andrews said. “I think there is definitely hope in the future for a stronger political coalition that can keep more of those voices at the table.”

title: Voters in two more South Dakota counties reject implementing a sales tax to reduce property taxes
description: Voters in two more South Dakota counties rejected proposals Tuesday to impose sales taxes for homeowner property tax relief, making the new option 0-for-4 when it’s submitted to county voters. At least seven other counties have adopted a sales tax without putting it to voters or being subjected to a referendum. There are 66 counties […]
text:
The Charles Mix County Courthouse in Lake Andes, South Dakota. (Photo by John Hult/South Dakota Searchlight)Voters in two more South Dakota counties rejected proposals Tuesday to impose sales taxes for homeowner property tax relief, making the new option 0-for-4 when it’s submitted to county voters.
At least seven other counties have adopted a sales tax without putting it to voters or being subjected to a referendum. There are 66 counties in the state.
The latest votes were in Clay and Charles Mix counties. Voters in Brown and Codington counties rejected sales taxes during the Nov. 3 general election.
State lawmakers and Gov. Larry Rhoden gave counties the authority during this year’s legislative session to implement their own sales taxes for the first time in state history, with proceeds going toward lowering homeowners’ property taxes. Counties are limited to a half-percent sales tax. Lawmakers and the governor also decided to use proceeds from next year’s increase in the state sales tax rate, from 4.2% to 4.5%, to reduce property taxes for homeowners statewide.
Voters in two South Dakota counties reject local sales taxes for property tax reductions

In Clay County, which has Vermillion as its county seat, nearly 58% of voters opposed the tax, while 50.2% opposed the tax in Charles Mix County, where the county seat is Lake Andes. The counties’ auditors reported 27.5% and 22.5% voter turnout, respectively. The elections were this week instead of Nov. 3 because general election ballots were already printed when petitioners turned in signatures to force the referendums.
The Charles Mix County unofficial returns were 656 votes against the sales tax and 649 in favor, a margin of seven votes.
Charles Mix County commissioners are scheduled to canvass the election results at their Thursday meeting. The county auditor did not immediately return a message from South Dakota Searchlight seeking information about the potential for a recount.
Rhoden sent a statement to South Dakota Searchlight after the two county sales tax rejections on Nov. 3.
“My plan to cut property taxes empowers South Dakotans to choose what works best for their county,” Rhoden said. “And people in different counties will make different choices — that’s why we left all options open to refer and initiate these measures.”
Counties that have adopted sales taxes without sending the issue to voters or being subjected to a referendum include Custer, Hughes, Lawrence, Lincoln, Meade, Pennington and Fall River.

title: New Mexico, federal experts emphasize postnatal care to address maternal mental health
description: Mental health conditions are the leading cause of maternal mortality in New Mexico and nationwide, which is why a panel of state and federal experts this week stressed the need for expanded community-based screening through the first year after birth.
text:
Mental health conditions are the leading cause of maternal mortality in New Mexico and nationwide, which is why a panel of state and federal experts at the Nov. 16-17, 2026, Western Governors' Association meeting in Santa Fe on mental health stressed the need for expanded community-based screening through the first year after birth. (Photo by onebluelight via Getty Images)Mental health conditions are the leading cause of maternal mortality in New Mexico and nationwide, which is why a panel of state and federal experts this week stressed the need for expanded community-based screening through the first year after birth. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
This presents particular challenges in New Mexico, however, due to ongoing workforce shortages, one local expert noted.
The panel, part of a two-day Western Governors’ Association workshop on mental health held in Santa Fe, included U.S. Department of Health and Human Services Director of Strategic Partnerships Caryn Marks, who noted that the birth of a baby is a time of significant transition for the entire family, but particularly for the mother who is experiencing both physical and mental changes. She said one in five women experience maternal mental health conditions, and that number is “very underreported,” but maternal mortality is also generally “90% preventable.”
“For mom, she’s recovering physically, there’s the adjustment for the emotions that she’s feeling. She’s caring for a newborn, and right at that time, it’s also when the clinical support decreases quite a bit, and it’s a lot,” Marks said during the panel discussion. “It’s a lot for moms that have support; it’s a lot for moms that don’t have support, and it’s stressful. It’s joyous. Let’s not forget it’s joyous, but it’s also emotionally and financially a taxing period.”
Jade Woodard, President and CEO of Family Connects — an international organization that connects families with in-home nurse checks and community resources — said most families have a six-week postpartum check up with their health care provider, but only about 60% of families attend the visit, where mental health screening can happen. 
“That means we have about 40% of families that get no care after their discharge from the hospital, and this is all about how our postpartum care is structured,” Woodard said. She said the Family Connects model, which in New Mexico  is offered through the state’s Early Childhood Education and Care Department — works to have a nurse visit families in-home within three weeks of birth to help them identify what supports they need.
UnitedHealth Group’s Senior Vice President of Health Optimization Catherine Anderson added that doulas and lactation coaches can be beneficial community-based providers who support mothers postpartum and help identify possible mental health conditions and refer them for assistance. 
“These are things that we’ve proven and have seen incredible results in and they have remarkably reduced the terrible consequences, particularly from a postpartum perspective,” she said. 
However, such support requires an expanded health care workforce to fill gaps, and New Mexico is faced with a shortage of providers across the health care spectrum, according to University of New Mexico Health Science Center Assistant Professor Trevor Quiner, who works in the Department of Obstetrics and Gynecology’s Division of Maternal and Fetal Medicine. 
“We don’t have enough workforce for any one group of providers to be doing everything that’s necessary,” Quiner said. “We don’t have enough OB/GYNs, family medicine doctors, or midwives. We don’t have enough doulas, we don’t have enough psychologists, we don’t have enough psychiatrists. It really does require all of us, including these clinician extenders roles to be able to do so. And not just to have these roles, but to build a system that allows for collaboration, a community of practice.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: RI attorney general moves to defend law allowing child sex abuse lawsuits
description: Rhode Island Attorney General Peter Neronha is seeking to defend the constitutionality of the 2026 state law that allows survivors of childhood sexual abuse to sue institutions that enabled their abuse, including the Diocese of Providence. Neronha’s office filed a motion Nov. 13 seeking to intervene in the nearly 200 Superior Court cases, as the […]
text:
The offices of the Roman Catholic Diocese of Providence are shown on March 4, 2026. (Photo by Christopher Shea/Rhode Island Current.)Rhode Island Attorney General Peter Neronha is seeking to defend the constitutionality of the 2026 state law that allows survivors of childhood sexual abuse to sue institutions that enabled their abuse, including the Diocese of Providence.
Neronha’s office filed a motion Nov. 13 seeking to intervene in the nearly 200 Superior Court cases, as the Diocese prepares to challenge the law’s constitutionality before the Rhode Island Supreme Court. 
The constitutional question has also surfaced in a separate federal lawsuit filed in July against the Diocese of Providence and St. Matthew’s Church in Central Falls. The parties jointly asked a federal judge Nov. 11 to have the Rhode Island Supreme Court decide whether the law can revive claims that had already expired.
Neronha’s position: The law signed by Gov. Dan McKee on June 11 is constitutional.
“The pain that survivors suffer knows no statute of limitations, and they deserve to seek accountability from the people and institutions that enabled these crimes,” Neronha said in a statement Tuesday. “I look forward to continuing to advocate for this important legislative reform in court.”
A spokesperson for the Diocese of Providence did not immediately respond to request for comment Wednesday.
Superior Court rules require anyone challenging a state law’s constitutionality to notify the attorney general, giving the office a chance to join the case.
The General Assembly passed landmark legislation in June amending the state’s statute of limitations after the long-awaited release of a 282-page report by the AG’s office in March that detailed decades of abuse by clergy and a cover up by the Diocese of Providence. A total of 72 deacons and priests faced credible accusations of abuse dating as far back as the 1950s, according to the report. 
The law opened a two-year window on July 1, 2026, allowing survivors to file claims that had previously been barred by the statute of limitations. The window closes June 30, 2028. Previously, victims had 35 years after turning 18 to sue individual priests, teachers, coaches and others who molested them, or up until they turned 53.
More than 190 abuse cases were pending in Superior Court as of Nov. 11, according to the joint motion for certification in the federal case.
Neronha’s motion states Superior Court Judge Richard Licht, who is overseeing many of the cases, met with attorneys in September to discuss whether to ask the Rhode Island Supreme Court to take up the law’s constitutionality. Licht indicated he was exploring that option, according to the motion, which cites a September court filing in a separate federal case.
A spokesperson for the Rhode Island Judiciary did not immediately respond to request for comment.
The AG’s office argues that it would be premature for the Superior Court to send the question to the Supreme Court before the defendants have laid out their legal arguments.
“The revival window is entitled to a presumption of constitutionality, and the burden is on the defendants in these cases to prove otherwise,” Neronha said.
Rep. Carol Hagan McEntee, a South Kingstown Democrat who sponsored the House version of the bill, also objected to sending the constitutional question to the Supreme Court before Superior Court judges have heard the underlying cases.
“Let’s finally give some of these cases the opportunity to be heard,” McEntee said in an interview Wednesday. 
The question of whether the law could withstand a constitutional challenge was raised even before lawmakers passed it. Sen. Matthew LaMountain, a Warwick Democrat who chairs the Senate Committee on Judiciary, proposed a resolution during the legislative debate that would have referred the matter to the Rhode Island Supreme Court for an advisory opinion.
Neronha and retired federal Judge William E. Smith argued during the resolution’s initial hearing on May 14 that the legislature should set policy and urged the committee to pass the bill without waiting for advice from the court. Neronha said his office was qualified to make the call on whether the bill would pass constitutional muster.
Senate leaders ultimately reached a deal to move the bill forward without seeking an advisory opinion, amending the legislation to preserve prior court judgments, clarify exemptions from prejudgment interest for state and local governments, reaffirm the $100,000 cap on state liability and change how interest is calculated on revived claims.
“These amendments are constitutional and necessary to vindicate the rights of survivors,” Neronha said Tuesday.
Neronha, who is term-limited, leaves office in early January. Attorney General-elect Kim Ahern supports holding the institutions that enabled abuse accountable, spokesperson Josh Block said, adding that she plans to learn more about the cases and legal issues during the transition.
