name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Luke Bronin sees congressional stock trading ban as Day 1 priority
description: Bronin wants to see the House adopt a rule to ban stock trading by congresspeople and spouses before pushing for a comprehensive bill.
text:
When Luke Bronin gets sworn into Congress next year, the Connecticut Democrat wants to immediately ban stock trading by members of Congress and place such a prohibition into the House rules.
In the longer term, Bronin hopes Congress can pass legislation that would enshrine such rules into law — and go even further on his party’s goals of campaign finance reform and anti-corruption measures.
Bronin has been in Washington since last week as part of the new member orientation to get acclimated with the responsibilities and quirks of Congress. Between trainings and the longstanding tradition of the House office lottery, the member-elect is staking out some early policy positions he believes Democrats can tackle as early as Day 1.
He’s part of a group of 50 incoming Democrats urging leadership to prohibit members and their spouses from “owning or trading stocks, commodities, futures, derivatives, and other related securities” with the exception of diversified mutual funds or investments in a qualified blind trust. 
“We have to hold this president accountable for that corruption. But if we’re going to be serious about reform, then we have to make those changes that bind us too,” Bronin said at a Tuesday press conference outside of the U.S. Capitol. “And it is long overdue for Congress to say that anybody who has the honor of doing the people’s business in this capital should not be spending a minute focused on their own private gain.”
The members at Tuesday’s press conference reflected the ideological diversity behind the effort: sitting lawmakers and moderate and progressive candidates who flipped GOP-held seats or defeated incumbents in primaries. While the focus was largely on stock trading, each member named other priorities in that vein: limiting super PACs and corporate PAC money in elections, banning former members from becoming lobbyists, and seeking to overturn Citizens United.
They were also among the signers of the Political Integrity Project’s pledge. Along with Bronin, U.S. Sen. Chris Murphy is the other member from Connecticut to sign it, according to its website. The pledge names many of the priorities listed by the sitting and newly elected members, including “to not hold or trade any individual stocks” while advocating for a congressional stock trading ban.
While running as a candidate for office this year, Bronin filed a financial disclosure report over the summer, a requirement that shows any earned income, assets and liabilities. Between the filing period that covered January through mid-May, he reported owning a few individual stocks, but he confirmed he no longer holds those.
There have been previous legislative attempts to limit or outright ban stock trading in Congress. Polling from a few months earlier indicates a large majority of Americans believe it should be illegal for elected officials to buy or sell individual stocks.
Democrats have knocked a GOP-led bill, the “Stop Insider Trading Act,” which passed the House in July with support from only about a dozen Democrats, none from Connecticut. The bill failed to a clear a filibuster in the Senate, with no Democratic votes. They argue the bill didn’t go far enough — prohibiting members, spouses and dependent children from buying new stocks related to publicly traded companies but allowing them to still own and sell — and attached a voter ID measure.
Some of the incumbent members, like Jason Crow of Colorado and Pramila Jayapal of Washington, said they’ve been working on the issue for years. They feel like next year is their best shot to getting it done and making progress on money-in-politics issues. Jayapal has introduced the bipartisan “Restore Trust in Congress Act.”
Bronin said he wants to learn about the various legislative proposals that are already out there. “And if the proposals that are out there aren’t sufficient, then [I’m] eager to work with my colleagues to put one together that’s strong,” he added.
Bronin and the rest of the members of the 120th Congress will get sworn in on Jan. 3. He defeated longtime U.S. Rep. John Larson during the four-way Democratic primary in August and easily won a first term to the Hartford-based seat earlier this month.
Campaign finance became a major sticking point during the Democratic primary for Connecticut’s 1st Congressional District, with Larson and Bronin sparring over the sources of their fundraising.
Bronin, who led the Democratic field in fundraising, said he wouldn’t accept campaign donations from corporate political action committees then or in the future. He criticized Larson’s fundraising haul, half of which had come from PACs, including some that represent corporations and unions.
Larson hit back that Bronin’s financing depended heavily on a network of billionaires and executives associated with large firms. Bronin’s campaign also pointed to the wealthy donors who were making individual contributions to Larson.
Two other Democratic challengers, Ruth Fortune and Jillian Gilchrest, bemoaned the torrent of fundraising and spending coming from both Bronin and Larson’s campaigns. Gilchrest and Fortune, who lagged far behind in fundraising throughout the campaign, had described a “broken” political system where big money and special interests uplift candidates with the expectation they’ll benefit if they get into office.
Even with the vast fundraising and outside spending in Connecticut’s primary, all four Democrats campaigned on the need for campaign finance reform, including Bronin.
In the new Congress, Bronin said, he wants to see a constitutional amendment to overturn Citizens United, the U.S. Supreme Court ruling in 2010 that paved the way for unlimited political spending by special interests such as corporations and unions. He made similar comments regarding Citizens United throughout his campaign.
He also named other priorities around reducing money in politics and establishing ethics codes for the various branches of the federal government. That includes a binding code of conduct for U.S. Supreme Court justices. (Murphy and U.S. Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., pushed for a similar code of ethics following scrutiny of Supreme Court Justice Clarence Thomas’ undisclosed gifts and deals in 2023.)
“I want us to be pushing an aggressive, comprehensive ethics reform and anti-corruption package and that includes everything from banning stock trading by members of Congress to ethics laws that actually constrain an out-of-control president and bind the Supreme Court too,” Bronin said in an interview. “And I want to see us make a serious push to overturn Citizens United with a constitutional amendment.”
There have been past policy pushes to ban stock trading in Congress that went nowhere. Lawmakers in support of such a ban argue congresspeople who are privy to certain information through their committees and overall jobs shouldn’t get to benefit financially from inside information.
“Members of Congress should not be allowed to enrich themselves by trading stocks,”  U.S. Rep. Adelita Grijalva, D-Ariz., said Tuesday. “As part of our job, many of us have access to information the rest of the world does not. Using that information for profit is called insider trading, and for any other person, it would be illegal. Members of Congress should not get to play by different rules.”
Democrats’ legislative dreams in the House could run into a wall in the Senate. Even though the party will hold a majority that grew to 56 seats, Democrats will still be short of clearing the 60-vote threshold in the Senate needed to avoid a filibuster. Next year, advancing most legislation will take support from all Democratic members along with the votes of at least four Republican senators.
But Bronin remains hopeful that they’ll have the numbers and momentum to make progress on an elusive issue that’s had bipartisan support in the past.
“This was specifically about a stock trading ban, because that’s something we can do on Day 1 as a good-faith effort to the people who sent us here,” Bronin said. “I think there are a whole lot of Democrats who have been here already, who are eager to make change, but I also think there’s no question that this huge new freshman class is bringing a strong new energy to this work.”

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: US House approves South Dakota Rep. Johnson’s bill to fund water pipeline project studies
description: The U.S. House passed legislation Tuesday sponsored by Republican Rep. Dusty Johnson of South Dakota to fund studies for three proposed Missouri River water pipeline projects. Similar legislation sponsored by South Dakota Republican Sens. John Thune and Mike Rounds has received committee approval and awaits action by the full Senate. Johnson’s bill is called[...]
text:
U.S. Rep. Dusty Johnson participates in a Republican gubernatorial primary debate on April 13, 2026, at the South Dakota Public Broadcasting studio in Sioux Falls. (Photo by Joshua Haiar/South Dakota Searchlight)The U.S. House passed legislation Tuesday sponsored by Republican Rep. Dusty Johnson of South Dakota to fund studies for three proposed Missouri River water pipeline projects.
Similar legislation sponsored by South Dakota Republican Sens. John Thune and Mike Rounds has received committee approval and awaits action by the full Senate.
Johnson’s bill is called the South Dakota Water Feasibility Studies Act. It would direct the U.S. Department of the Interior to evaluate whether the three proposed projects are viable before moving forward with construction, and allocate up to $30 million toward the studies —$10 million for each project. 
“Water is an essential resource, and as South Dakota continues to grow, we will need more of it,” Johnson said in a press release.
The Lewis and Clark Regional Water System project proposal is an expansion of its existing Missouri River drinking water system that serves communities in southeastern South Dakota, northwestern Iowa and southwestern Minnesota. The expansion would supply water to about 350,000 people.
The Dakota Mainstem Regional Water System would be a new Missouri River water supply. It would serve nearly 60 water providers in South Dakota, Iowa, Minnesota and Nebraska, with a capacity of 195 million gallons per day. 
The Western Dakota Regional Water System would be another new Missouri River water supply. The proposed pipeline would bring Missouri River water to western South Dakota, including the Rapid City area, reducing reliance on groundwater.
Johnson, who ran unsuccessfully for the Republican nomination for governor in June rather than for reelection to the House, will leave office in January.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Nebraska doubles down on adopting Medicaid changes early
authors: Noelle Annonen, Nebraska Public Media News
description: The federal government is giving states across the country an extended deadline to roll out changes to Medicaid work requirements. The delay is intended to give staff enough time to ensure all Medicaid recipients are receiving the right benefits for their specific eligibility for services. Nebraska will not participate. The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid […[...]
text:
The Nebraska State Capitol Building in Lincoln. (Rebecca S. Gratz for the Nebraska Examiner)
The federal government is giving states across the country an extended deadline to roll out changes to Medicaid work requirements. The delay is intended to give staff enough time to ensure all Medicaid recipients are receiving the right benefits for their specific eligibility for services.

Nebraska will not participate.

The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services announced a six-month “hold harmless” period on Friday. The extra six months is intended to give state staff time to assess whether patients meet certain requirements or exclusions and how they need to proceed to get coverage as a result. This impacts people who may be required to work a certain number of hours each month while receiving Medicaid. The original deadline to implement changes was Jan. 1.

Nebraska, meanwhile, adopted the changes to Medicaid early, opting in on May 1 and becoming the first state to do so. Jeffrey Powell, director of communications for the Nebraska Department of Health and Human Services, which oversees Medicaid implementation in the state, said in a Tuesday statement that the state managed the transition to new requirements effectively for eligible individuals.

“Our implementation has been successful and serves as a model for other states,” Powell wrote. “Given Nebraska’s strong implementation and the progress we have made, there is no need for the state to participate in the hold-harmless period. We are confident in our approach and remain committed to ensuring the federal requirements are implemented effectively.”

Not every Nebraskan shares his confidence.

Nebraska Appleseed, a justice-focused advocacy organization, reports that the latest data available, though two months old, shows more than 1,000 Nebraskans have been denied care or have lost coverage since May. Appleseed’s Healthcare Access Program Director Sarah Maresh said the changes are confusing and deter eligible patients from even applying for coverage.

“It’s going to cause people to be sicker and more disabled,” Maresh said at a Nov. 9 Omaha town hall  revisiting the changes.

Most of the changes to Medicaid, passed under the One Big Beautiful Bill last year, apply to the Medicaid expansion group. New work requirements apply to able-bodied enrollees who now have to log at least 80 hours a month of employment, work program attendance, volunteering or schoolwork.

These restrictions apply to Medicaid members between the ages of 19 and 64 who are not pregnant, do not have a disability, are U.S. citizens or meet immigration rules and make less than 138% of the federal poverty level. In Nebraska, that’s about $22,025 per year for one person and $45,540 for a family of four, according to the Department of Health and Human Services.

Critics of the program argue that cancer patients, pregnant people and other patients who should not have to work are falling through the cracks due to Nebraska’s expedited adoption of the requirements. People who spoke at the town hall said some Medicaid recipients have spent hours on the phone with DHHS and often are disconnected before they can reach the help they need to explore what they are eligible for. Maresh said this is because the state does not have enough staff to handle the changes.

title: Democrats seek special election in GOP Indiana Senate leader’s disputed race
description: Democrats have asked for a special election to be held as they dispute the vote count in state Senate President Pro Tem Chris Garten’s apparent narrow election victory. text:
Republican state Sen. Chris Garten, left, and Democratic challenger Nick Marshall. (Photos by Leslie Bonilla Muñiz/Indiana Capital Chronicle and Marshall campaign's Facebook page)Democrats have asked for a special election to be held as they dispute the vote count in state Senate President Pro Tem Chris Garten’s apparent narrow election victory.
The Clark County Democratic chair filed a petition Wednesday for a recount and election contest of the outcome for the Senate District 45 race.
Garten was installed Tuesday as leader of the Republican-dominated Senate, shortly after the Indiana Supreme Court lifted a county judge’s order blocking him from taking the oath of office for a new four-year term. A hearing in a separate court case was canceled as the judge recused himself.
Democrats maintain that the Clark County Election Board failed to adequately investigate Election Day voting equipment problems before moving forward with the election results.
Garten sworn in as Indiana Senate leader after court intervention, calls for recount of own election

The reported totals for the Senate district, which includes all of Clark County and part of Floyd County, show Garten ahead of Democrat Nick Marshall by 297 votes, or about two-thirds of a percentage point.
Garten on Tuesday denounced the Democratic efforts against him as “lawfare” and submitted a petition for a recount of four Jeffersonville precincts.
The petition from Clark County Democratic Chair Miguel Hampton seeks a recount of all 86 precincts in the Senate district. 
Hampton’s petition cites equipment troubles at multiple polling sites that it says “potentially make it impossible to audit and confirm who voted, whether each voter was registered, and whether each voter voted in the appropriate precinct.”
It asks the Indiana Recount Commission to conduct the ballot review and take the rare step of ordering a special election for the Senate district.

name: Maine Morning Star
title: Government oversight committee questions Lewiston victims fund spending
description: The Maine Legislature’s government oversight committee Wednesday asked the nonprofit responsible for disbursing funds raised after the 2023 Lewiston shooting to apologize for failing to communicate clearly with victims’ families and survivors about how the money would be distributed. The Maine Community Foundation established the Lewiston-Auburn Area Respons[...]
text:
Pumpkins carved to honor the victims of the Lewiston mass shooting. (AnnMarie Hilton/Maine Morning Star)The Maine Legislature’s government oversight committee Wednesday asked the nonprofit responsible for disbursing funds raised after the 2023 Lewiston shooting to apologize for failing to communicate clearly with victims’ families and survivors about how the money would be distributed.
The Maine Community Foundation established the Lewiston-Auburn Area Response Fund in the aftermath of the shooting, which raised about $6.6 million. Two separate funds were within the larger umbrella: The Victims and Families fund which distributed $4.2 million to 162 victims, families and survivors and the Broad Recovery Efforts and Organizations Fund which distributed $1.9 million to 29 local organizations. Donors could either choose one fund or split their contributions into both.
But victims’ families and survivors of the deadliest mass shooting in Maine history have raised issues with how the money was handled, claiming that they were originally told all funds would go to them. In a press conference last month, some of them resurfaced the issue, objecting to the fact that $1.9 million was given to local nonprofits. Some of these nonprofits, they said, did not spend the money they received to help survivors.
Maine Community Foundation President and CEO Deborah Ellwood defended her organization for more than an hour at the oversight committee meeting, repeating that she was proud of the nonprofit’s work and fundraising. After prompting from several members of the bipartisan committee, she eventually admitted that communication to victims and survivors about how the funds would be distributed could have been clearer.
Much of the committee’s questioning focused on one specific document the foundation sent to victims: a flyer with a QR code advertising the general Lewiston-Auburn Area Response Fund, saying it would “distribute 100% of donations as gifts to victims and survivors.”  
“I read this document from the perspective of many victims and survivors who have told me their frustrations with this document, and it’s hard for me to say that there’s not merit in those frustrations,” Rep. Adam Lee (D-Auburn) said to Ellwood.
“I just wish there was an apology, essentially, for perhaps misleading those victims and survivors with respect to the ultimate distribution of the funds.”
Ellwood responded with “I’m very proud of the work we did.
“We served as an important conduit for charitably minded people across the world who wanted to help, and they had the choice to give between the victims fund and the broad recovery fund.” she added.
Several other legislators chimed in, taking issue with the foundation’s stance. Sen. Brad Farrin (R-Somerset) pointed out that nonprofits received about an average of $65,000, while the victims received about $29,000.  
Rep. Michael Lemelin added, “I see a form of deception here — and I’m not saying that either one of you did this with malice — but regardless, the deception’s there.”
And Sen. Jill Duson took issue with Ellwood adhering to her statement that the foundation followed national best practices to set up separate funds and communicate what they each were for.
“A key piece that I still don’t hear you saying … is that as much attention was paid to assuring that donors knew where their money was going, that much attention and perhaps more should have been paid to make sure the victims and family knew where and how the money would be distributed,” she said.
Ellwood eventually acknowledged that the foundation could have been more transparent with victims. 
“I’m sorry that they felt confused by this particular piece of documentation. That was not our intention,” she said. “Our intention was to provide as much information as possible for victims to be able to get the contributions that were provided.”
Amy Sussman, whose nephew was killed in the shootings, has been leading advocacy on behalf of victims who took issue with the foundation. When asked by committee members Wednesday about Ellwood’s apology, she said it was insufficient. 
“When an apology is couched with ‘I’m sorry, they misunderstood.’ That is not truly an apology,” Sussman said. “‘I’m sorry you misunderstood what I said’ is not ‘I said it wrong, and I’m sorry I said it wrong.’ That would be admitting the error on their part, and it appears they are unwilling to do that.”
Maine Attorney General Aaron Frey told the committee in September that the Office of Program Evaluation and Government Accountability, or OPEGA, lacks the authority to investigate how the funds were distributed. OPEGA is an independent legislative office that often conducts probes and reports back to the committee. Frey’s office could investigate potential misuse of charitable donations, although a previous investigation conducted in 2024 did not reveal legal concerns.

title: Morgantown Democrats vow bill on medical child abuse after minor allegedy receives unneeded surgery
description: A bill to create a criminal offense for medical child abuse, commonly known as Munchausen syndrome by proxy, is expected in upcoming legislative session.
text:
Democrats Del. John Williams (left) and Delegate-elect Olivia Miller plan to introduce a bill following a local child abuse investigation into allegations of medical child abuse and neglect involving two children. (West Virginia Legislative Photography and courtesy photo)A bill to create a criminal offense for medical child abuse, commonly known as Munchausen syndrome by proxy, is expected in upcoming legislative session.
Del. John Williams, D-Monongalia, and Delegate-elect Olivia Miller, a Democrat from Morgantown, plan to introduce the bill following a local child abuse investigation into allegations of medical child abuse and neglect involving two children.
“When kids in West Virginia are abused, we have to step up and be there for them. Medical child abuse is far more common than people realize, and we need a clear statute that will allow us to go after those who do harm to our kids,” said Williams, who will move to the Senate in 2027 after winning his November election. 
Three adults were arrested Monday for the alleged child abuse after a lengthy investigation, MetroNews reported on Tuesday. All three live in Monongalia County.
Detectives with the Monongalia County Sheriff’s Office allege Emilee Guzman repeatedly provided inaccurate and misleading information to medical professionals concerning one of the children’s medical conditions and nutritional needs. The misrepresentations about a child’s medical condition contributed to the minor undergoing an invasive surgical procedure that detectives allege was medically unnecessary.
The investigation ultimately resulted in a diagnosis of medical child abuse, commonly known as Munchausen syndrome by proxy, by a child abuse pediatrician at WVU Medicine Children’s Hospital.
Munchausen syndrome by proxy, a psychological disorder in which parents or caregivers seek sympathy through the exaggerated or made-up illnesses of their children.
The medical condition was central in the well-known case of Gypsy Rose Blanchard and her mother, Clauddine “Dee Dee” Blanchard, who suffered from Munchausen syndrome by proxy. The mother falsely convinced doctors, family and the public that Gypsy suffered from severe conditions like leukemia, muscular dystrophy and needed to use a wheelchair and feeding tubes. Gypsy Blanchard spent time in prison for her role in her mother’s 2015 murder. 
Williams and Miller said on Tuesday that their proposed measure followed the Monongalia County Sheriff’s Office alleging that misleading information provided to medical professionals contributed to a local child undergoing an unnecessary invasive surgery.
Their legislation would address a gap in West Virginia code by expressly criminalizing the knowing fabrication or concealment of medical information that leads to unnecessary medical interventions or a medically substantiated risk of harm. 
“We will protect West Virginia’s children and hold those who abuse them accountable,” said Miller, who won a Nov. 3 election for the District 80 House seat currently held by Williams. “Our goal is to close this gap in the law while providing safeguards for medical professionals acting in good faith. We have a strong team here in Monongalia County, and we will work with the sheriff’s office, local experts and colleagues across the aisle to get this done.”
The legislation would include safeguards for good-faith reporting, legitimate family advocacy, disagreements with physicians and medically appropriate care.
The 2027 legislative session is set to begin Jan. 13.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Meet the new bosses, same as the old bosses: Senate reelects leaders for next session
description: Despite a relatively high number of new faces in the Senate next year, Democratic and GOP senators voted to stick with their previous leaders in the coming General Assembly, but leaders shuffled committee assignments to make room for eight newcomers.
text:
Senate President Pro Tem Malcom Augustine (D-Prince George's), left, and Senate President Bill Ferguson (D-Baltimore City), in a 2024 photo, were reelected to their leadership positions Tuesday, as were Senate Minority Leader Steve Hershey (R-Upper Shore) and Minority Whip Justin Ready(R-Carroll and Frederick). (Photo by Bryan P. Sears/Maryland Matters)Despite a relatively high number of new faces in the Senate next year, Democratic and Republican senators voted to stick with their previous leaders in the coming General Assembly.
Senate leaders also confirmed committee assignments for the 2027 General Assembly, cementing previously reported proposals that will more evenly spread the geographic and demographic diversity of committee chairmanships and vice chairmanships.
Senate President Bill Ferguson (D-Baltimore City) and Senate President Pro Tem Malcolm Augustine (D-Prince George’s) were unanimously reelected Tuesday by members of the Democratic Caucus to the leadership positions they have held since 2020 and 2023, respectively, according to a statement from Ferguson’s office.
“We have a clear agenda: diversify our economy, close the budget shortfall while improving affordability, and ensure emerging technologies benefit our communities,” Ferguson said in the statement. “We are ready to get to work and are positioned to deliver meaningful results.”
On the Republican side Tuesday, the caucus again tapped Senate Minority Leader Stephen Hershey (R-Upper Shore) and Minority Whip Justin Ready (R-Frederick and Carroll).
Hayes takes over Finance as Ferguson announces early changes to leadership

Hershey, who has been leader since 2023, and Ready, who has been whip since 2021, acknowledged that the minority faces an even more challenging task than usual in Annapolis, as Democratic victories in this fall’s elections cost them a seat in the Senate. The 12 GOP senators face off against 35 Democrats, the biggest majority in 16 years.
“This was a tough year for Republicans across the country, and Maryland was no exception,” Ready said in a statement from the Senate Republican Caucus. “Democrats will have a bigger majority in January, but a bigger majority is not a blank check. Our members will be ready on every bill, every amendment, and every floor vote, and Marylanders will know exactly where their senators stood.”
Hershey said Republicans plan to hold Democrats to the campaign pledges Ferguson cited, to address affordability and improve the budget situation.
“Voters have made it clear that affordability and the rising cost of living are their top concerns. While Democrats have a poor track record of fiscal responsibility, they campaigned on promises to lower taxes, reduce costs, and address soaring utility bills,” Hershey said in the caucus statement. “Senate Republicans intend to hold them accountable to those promises.”
The loss of a GOP senator — Sen. Bill Folden (R-Frederick) was unseated by Democrat Lara Westdorp in the 4th District — means Republicans lost the fourth seat they held on the Budget and Taxation Committee. Each of the four standing committees will now have three Republican senators.
With eight new senators, there was bound to be a shakeup on committee assignments. But the biggest changes may have come among the chairs and vice chairs, as Ferguson worked to spread the wealth a little more evenly.
The biggest change was on the Education, Energy and the Environment Committee, were the chair and vice chair, Sens. Brian Feldman and Cheryl Kagan, both Montgomery County Democrats, will be replaced by Sen. Dawn Gile (D-Anne Arundel) as chair and Sen. Benjamin Brooks (D-Baltimore County) as vice chair. In moves announced last month, Kagan is set to become the Senate’s liaison for national legislative affairs, which Feldman will serve as Senate Majority Leader and in the new role of chief of policy, with and ex officio seat on every committee.
On the Finance Committee, Sen. Antonio Hayes (D-Baltimore City) will move from vice chair to chair, filling the seat left by the retirement of Sen. Pam Beidle (D-Anne Arundel). Sen. Katie Fry Hester (D-Howard and Montgomery) becomes the vice chair. On the Budget and Taxation Committee, longtime Sen. Jim Rosapepe (D-Prince George’s) will be replaced as vice chairman by Sen. Cory McCray (D-Baltimore City).
Sen,-elect C.T. Wilson (D-Charles), who had been chair of the House Economic Matters Committee from 2021-2025, was assigned to the Senate Finance Committee. Three freshmen, all Democrats, were assigned to Education, Energy and the Environment, or triple-E Committee: Mark Chang of Anne Arundel County, Tiffany Alston of Prince George’s County and Malcolm Ruff of Baltimore City.
Four incoming freshmen landed on Judicial Proceedings, Democrats Westdorp, Kevin Ford of Prince George’s and Amar Mukunda of Montgomery County and Republican Nic Kipke of Anne Arundel County.
Among returning members, Sen. Mary Washington (D-Baltimore City) moves from triple-E to Finance and Sen. Mike McKay (R-Western Maryland) moves from Judicial Proceedings to triple-E. Sen. Johnny Ray Salling (R-Baltimore County) will move from Budget and Taxation to Judicial Proceedings.
Budget and Taxation, meanwhile, will pick up Sen. Shaneka Henson (D-Anne Arundel) and Sen, Sara Love (D-Montgomery County) from Judicial Proceedings and Sen. Ron Watson (D-Prince George’s) from Education, Energy and the Environment.
More appointments, including a full listing of subcommittee, are expected to be announced in the coming weeks.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: U.S. Army is scheduled to detonate lead azide near Middletown, elevating risk for lead in air
description: Iowans have expressed concern about the potential effects from the detonation of lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant that is scheduled for Friday, but officials say the intentional detonation is the best way to manage the concerns.  Iowa Army Ammunition Plant informed residents of Middletown and surrounding areas that on Friday, around noon, […]
text:
Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown. (Photo via Google Earth) Iowans have expressed concern about the potential effects from the detonation of lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant that is scheduled for Friday, but officials say the intentional detonation is the best way to manage the concerns. 
Iowa Army Ammunition Plant informed residents of Middletown and surrounding areas that on Friday, around noon, the U.S. Army will intentionally detonate 68 drums of deteriorated lead azide — an explosive — on site, causing a plume of air “with some lead-containing particles” which could spread close to 100 miles from the site and leave lead-particle-containing dust in a 40-mile range. 
Justine Barati, a public and congressional affairs specialist with the Army Sustainment Command, said the decision to detonate the materials in the controlled and scheduled matter, comes from an “abundance of caution.” 
The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, which approved an emergency permit for the detonation, said the “explosion risk” of the degraded lead azide presented an “imminent and substantial threat to human health and the environment.” 
The intentional detonation instead allows the Army to plan based on best conditions, inform the public ahead of time and work to contain as much of the heavy metals as possible. 
Barati said the Friday detonation will be surrounded by large sand piles and that technicians will be spraying the area and surrounding soil with water to “minimize the amount of lead that’s going to be dispersed.” 
Barati said this detonation is an “extra-ordinary event.”
“This is an emergency operation to get rid of a chemical that could detonate on its own,” Barati said. 
Potential risks and precautions
Iowa Army Ammunition Plant held an open house in mid October for Middletown residents and provided information about the developing plans to detonate the material. 
One neighborhood of Middletown, is being asked to temporarily vacate the area from 8 a.m. to 2 p.m. on Friday. Barati said this request is “out of an abundance of caution” in case the detonation causes old, or large format windows to shatter. The Armed Forces Reserve Center in Middletown is open to residents who need a place to go during the detonation. 
The lead dust is anticipated to “linger for no more than an hour” according to public documents from IAAP.  The army has released modeling, and plans to update the maps frequently leading up to detonation, of areas that will potentially be exposed to “toxic lead dust” through air dispersion and surface deposition. 
Most recent modeling, which changes depending on wind and weather conditions, shows the dust could spread through the air about 100 miles northeast of the detonation site, traveling up past Muscatine and toward Maquoketa. Lead dust could settle on surfaces in areas northeast of the detonation site for about 40 miles, according to the map which shows areas outside of Wapello and New Boston, Illinois in the potential exposure area. Updated maps will be available online.
According to the EPA, lead is toxic to humans and animals and there is “no safe level of lead in children that has been identified.” Barati said pregnant women and children under 10-years old are most at risk in this instance. 
The issue has gained significant attention on social media, with influential content creators outside of Iowa expressing concern for the health impacts of the detonation and lead particles in the air. 
According to information released by the Army, folks in the area for potential air dispersion should avoid being outdoors during the detonation time Friday, switch their heating and cooling systems to recirculate, and keep windows and doors closed. Additionally, the army says impacted residents should “consider cleaning indoor and outdoor surfaces such as play surfaces for children and windowsills” after the air exposure period has ended. 
“What we’re asking people to do if they’re concerned is to hose down the area around their house that they’re concerned about, and if they hose it off, it should be safe,” Barati said. 
EPA granted the Army an emergency permit, on Nov. 13, for the treatment and storage of lead azide for the operation. The permit requires public notifications before and after the detonation, a cleanup process and certain reporting, including samples taken before, during and after the detonation. 
Kellen Ashford, a press officer for EPA Region 7, said in an email: “Treatment of the lead azide under the Emergency Permit helps ensure maximal control of the conditions leading up to the detonation, including prior public notification of exposure risks that may result from this treatment activity.” 
Ashford said the Army had previously provided EPA with documentation of the recrystallization of the stored lead azide which “created a risk of spontaneous explosion due to the material’s sensitivity to friction and shock.” 
“The Army, which has unparalleled expertise in matters concerning explosives safety, concluded that this material cannot safely be handled or moved and therefore, cannot be treated by any method other than in-place detonation,” Ashford wrote. 
EPA has created a webpage that Ashford said will be updated with additional information on the site. 
An FAQ document from the Army to residents explained that the heat of the explosion, when done properly, “incinerates” the lead azide. Active air monitoring and post-detonation sampling will be conducted to “identify material that may need to be cleaned up.”
The document also notes that residents concerned about environmental impacts on their property should sign up for voluntary sampling.  Additionally, the Army is responsible for cleaning up potential lead found in the soil if it “exceeds regulatory thresholds.” 
On Tuesday, Iowa Environmental Council expressed concern about the detonation and its potential impacts on human and environmental health. The group called on federal and state leaders to “provide more transparency” on the situation. 
“Coordination and leadership are critical at this moment for local officials trying to make well-informed emergency response and public health decisions, such as keeping schools open, evacuating communities, and providing assistance to vulnerable populations including pregnant women, seniors with mobility issues, and children,” Iowa Environmental Council wrote in a news release. 
Several local school districts have decided to close on Friday because of the detonation, including West Burlington Independent, and Mediapolis Community. 
Barati, when asked if the Army was working with state or local partners, said “we’re notifying the states about what the issues are and the concerns.” 
A spokesperson with the Office of the Governor said the state became aware of the IAAP’s plans to detonate the lead azide “on Monday after a public advisory was issued by the U.S. Army.”
“Members of the governor’s staff and state agencies contacted both organizations and have since been meeting about the situation,” the spokesperson said in an email. “All planning and permitting for this event have been managed at the federal level by the Army with the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency. The Army engaged local public health and emergency management officials to assist with community awareness efforts.”

name: West Virginia Watch
title: West Virginia Public Service Commission approves Mon Power plant, raises electric bills
description: The West Virginia Public Service Commission approved Tuesday a $2.48 billion gas plant in Monongalia County, and another $182 million in solar projects for Potomac Edison, to accommodate projected increases in power from the regional grid being driven by data center development.
text:
Public Service Commission Chair Charlotte Lane speaks to members of the West VIrginia Senate in Charleston, West Virginia in March 2026. (Photo by Will Price/West Virginia Legislative Photography)The West Virginia Public Service Commission approved Tuesday a $2.48 billion gas plant in Monongalia County, and another $182 million in solar projects for Potomac Edison, to accommodate projected increases in power from the regional grid being driven by data center development.
Mon Power/Potomac Edison customers are estimated to be charged $1.18 per month to pay for the projects, according to company projections submitted to the commission. Raises to power bills won’t be determined until January 2027 and will not go in effect until March 2027.
The gas powered station added to the existing Fort Martin plant will generate 1,200 megawatts, while solar projects scattered around Davis, Albright and Weirton would generate 70 megawatts.
Consumer advocates and environmental groups like the Citizens Action Group and the Sierra Club raised concerns that the additional power wouldn’t be necessary if data centers don’t hook up to the grid.
However, staff at the PSC determined that even if data centers aren’t built, there would still be shortfalls in power being supplied to the grid in the 2030s and 2040s.
Emmett Pepper, policy director for Energy Efficient West Virginia, released a statement deriding the approval, calling it “bad for ratepayers.”
“Let’s be clear: a power plant of this size is not needed for existing ratepayers. But it is getting built nonetheless, with current ratepayers on the hook for it,” he said. “This plant is being built for data centers, and there is no requirement that those data centers cover the costs.”
Pepper called for a special session to address power rates, noting that Gov. Patrick Morrisey’s announcement last week for American Electric Power to build three gas plants throughout the state at a cost of $17 billion could potentially cost customers as well.
“AEP customers can’t afford to bear the brunt of $17 billion in data center costs, and they should not have to,” he said.
Both sides of the aisle have an appetite for addressing rising power costs.
Del. Evan Hansen, D-Monogalia, said he is going to reintroduce a bill shot down last year to make the PSC define what the “public interest” is when the PSC makes a determination, along with an ethics reform package.
With 21 Democrats in the House following the midterm elections, Hansen said he hopes it’ll gain traction.
“I think there’s still a wide difference of opinion in the Legislature about why our electric bills have gone up so significantly over the past 10 or 15 years, so a different understanding of the problem might lead to different types of solutions,” Hansen said. “But it’s my hope that that energy, that electric bills, are a focus of the next legislative session.”
Hansen also noted that another Democrat-backed a bill to make the PSC commissioners an elective position.
“That should make commissioners more responsive to the public if they have to face the voters,” he said.
State Sen. Laura Chapman, R-Ohio, introduced a bill last year to freeze rates for one year in order to give the PSC time to figure out a solution to rising power costs. She said she will be doing so again in the upcoming session.
“We need to figure out why it keeps going up when we have more energy under our feet than any other state,” Chapman said. “ I’m not going to say projects are good or bad, but I think there needs to be a little bit more scrutiny when it comes to improvements or new builds.”
In today’s economy, Chapman said everything helps.
“Everybody’s being crushed right now with inflation,” she said. “You know, making the tough decision about putting food on their table, life-saving medication, or their energy bills, and especially for our seniors, it’s a real problem.”

text:
Rhode Island Department of Labor and Training Director Matt Weldon will leave his cabinet position in January to take a job as chief of staff for Attorney General Kim Ahern. (Courtesy of Ahern transition team)Another state cabinet member is stepping down as the new administration takes over.
Rhode Island Department of Labor and Training (DLT) Director Matt Weldon is taking a job as chief of staff for Attorney General-elect Kim Ahern, Ahern’s transition team announced on Wednesday. Ahern succeeds Attorney General Peter Neronha, who is term-limited.
Weldon’s Jan. 5 departure from his $200,000-a-year cabinet job concludes 15 years with the state workforce agency, including more than five years as its director, according to his resume.
Ahern praised Weldon for his experience and commitment to working families in a statement announcing the hire.
“Matt is a tireless advocate for workers,” she said. “He is deeply passionate about Rhode Island. And he knows how to get things done. He brings a wealth of experience, strong relationships, and a deep understanding of state government that will allow him to hit the ground running on day one.”
Weldon’s ascension to DLT director was one of the final staffing changes made by former Gov. Gina Raimondo before she stepped down in early 2021 to take a job with the Biden administration. He was reappointed by Gov. Dan McKee in 2023.
A graduate of the University of Rhode Island, Weldon previously served as the department’s chief of program development and assistant director for administrative services. He has also worked for the Rhode Island Senate president’s office, and as manager of the Superior Court’s adult drug court program, according to his resume.
As head of the DLT in the aftermath of the pandemic, Weldon led the temporary expansion of unemployment benefits, new workforce and job training programs, and enhanced anti-fraud protections.
A frequent guest on local broadcast networks to explain agency services and initiatives, Weldon is one of the more public-facing cabinet directors, easily identified by his signature, full beard.
His departure leaves another vacancy for Gov.-elect Helena Buonanno Foulkes to fill when she takes office. Foulkes previously said that she was open to keeping some existing cabinet directors from McKee’s administration, though she did not name specific people or departments. She has also solicited expressions of interest from people who want a job in her administration through her transition website. 
More than 745 people have submitted online forms to work for her or serve as a volunteer board member, said Jon Carvalho, a spokesperson for Foulkes’ transition team. 
Brian Daniels, director of the Office of Management and Budget, has already submitted his resignation, effective Dec. 11. Former Health and Human Services Secretary Richard Charest left state government on Oct. 31.

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: All aboard! Government leaders welcome second Amtrak train connecting Pittsburgh and New York City
description: There will now be a second daily train connecting Pittsburgh to New York City via Philadelphia for the first time in decades.
text:
Passengers board an Amtrak train at Harrisburg's station. (Capital-Star/Peter Hall)Before his military career, stint as a Secretary of the Commonwealth and time as the state chair of the Republican Party, Robert Gleason was a Johnstown college student who rode the train to attend the University of Pennsylvania in Philadelphia. 
At the time, he had several options for rail lines that made daily stops at his hometown and final destination. Over the years, those choices dwindled. Since 1981, just one line has made the daily trek between Pittsburgh and New York City — until now. 
“Unfortunately, over the years, passenger rail disappeared. Not only in Pennsylvania, but across the country,” said Gleason, now the Amtrak board director. “Unbelievably, it has taken 45 years to get a second Pennsylvanian. Gov. (Josh Shapiro), I hope we don’t have to wait that long for a third one.”
Robert Gleason, former chair of the state Republican Party and current Amtrak board director, says better train service can bring economic development to western Pennsylvania. (Screenshot from livestream)
The second daily passenger train on the Pennsylvanian line had its first Pittsburgh departure Wednesday, the result of more than $224 million in state and federal funding that took years of planning and railroad upgrades.
Between Harrisburg and Pittsburgh, the railroad is owned by Norfolk Southern, which concluded in 2021 that a second train would create unacceptable delays with improvements to reduce congestion. In contrast, Amtrak owns the rails between Harrisburg and New York City, and it makes a round-trip loop through Philadelphia multiple times per day. 
Stakeholders hope the additional Amtrak service will bring economic development to the dozen-plus Pennsylvania stops along the route, strengthening community ties along the state’s southern border.
“For our region, it’s another way to bring visitors, jobs and investment — and that’s what I care about at the Pittsburgh Regional Alliance,” added Stefani Pashman, CEO of the Pittsburgh Regional Alliance. “Doubling daily service on the Pennsylvanian makes it significantly easier for businesses to operate across a seamless border. Travel time can turn into productive work time without fighting highway congestion or airport bottlenecks.”
That includes the smaller cities, boroughs and townships along the route like Gleason’s hometown in Cambria County that “have suffered for many years” and could use the boost.
“This train is going to make an economic difference,” he said.
 More rail investment ahead?

Speaking after Gleason, Shapiro, a Democrat, remarked that “trains bring people together” across party lines.
“This is obviously a big day for western Pennsylvania. It’s going to mean more ways for our neighbors to travel around, and it’s going to mean more opportunities to visit our great commonwealth,” Shapiro said. 
Pennsylvania has the most operating railroads in the state, and ridership increased by more than 8% last year, he continued. The number of passengers is expected to increase with the new service, which is already sold out for the weekend after Thanksgiving. 
Shapiro, who won a decisive reelection victory earlier this month, will helm a Democratic trifecta next year in Harrisburg, an arrangement that he said will allow for more transportation investment. 
Gov. Josh Shapiro said Pennsylvania’s railroad history, fueled by the state’s coal mines and steel mills, is a point of pride. (Screenshot from livestream)
“Come next year, we will finally deliver sustainable transit system funding that Pennsylvanians deserve and need,” Shapiro added. 
“Railroad is a key part of our transportation agenda and a key focus of that GSD attitude,” he continued, invoking a shorthand for his “Get Stuff Done” motto.
The state contributed $80 million in funding alongside $143 million from the Federal Railroad Administration for infrastructure upgrades. FRA Administrator David Fink called the funds “emblematic” of the types of projects his agency pursues. 
“This is just the beginning, as we are making similar investments in the future of passenger rail across the country,” said Fink, a Harrisburg native.
The state is using other FRA grants to study passenger rail revival options between Scranton and New York as well as Reading and Philadelphia.

name: Michigan Advance
title: Advocates, state representative criticize ‘bad faith’ appointment to sentencing commission
description: State Rep. Kara Hope (D-Holt) joined criminal justice advocates Wednesday to criticize the appointment of former state Sen. Rick Jones to the Michigan Sentencing Commission, which was established in 2024 to examine the state’s sentencing laws and procedures.  Jones was appointed not because of his previous legislative experience or his time as Eaton County S[...]
text:
State Rep. Kara Hope (D-Holt) speaks at a press conference criticizing the appointment of former state Sen. Rick Jones to the Michigan Sentencing Commission in a seat reserved for formerly incarcerated individuals. Nov. 18, 2026. (Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance)State Rep. Kara Hope (D-Holt) joined criminal justice advocates Wednesday to criticize the appointment of former state Sen. Rick Jones to the Michigan Sentencing Commission, which was established in 2024 to examine the state’s sentencing laws and procedures. 
Jones was appointed not because of his previous legislative experience or his time as Eaton County Sheriff — but instead to fill a seat designed for a previously incarcerated person, based on a single night spent in jail after being arrested for drunk driving in February.
“Power can sometimes be misused, and I think that’s what we saw here,” Hope said. “Misused to shut out the very people that we met to give a seat at the table, and that’s why I’m here. That’s why we’re all here, to demand that it never happens again.”
Jones was appointed to the commission, which held its first meeting in May, by outgoing Senate Minority Leader Aric Nesbitt (R-Porter Township).
Ken Nixon, director of outreach and community partnerships for Safe and Just Michigan, likened the appointment to filling a seat intended for a judge with “someone who once sat in a courtroom.”
“When the Legislature built this commission, it made a choice. It said judges get a voice, prosecutors get a voice, law enforcement gets a voice, and people who have actually lived under these sentences get a voice too,” Nixon said. “That seat was a promise, and right now that promise isn’t being kept. One night in the county jail is a bad weekend. Five years in prison changes your life. It changes your family. It changes whether your kids know you. It changes whether you can find a job or a place to live when you come home. Those are consequences this commission is supposed to weigh, and the people who carry them are the experts nobody has been asking.”
Ken Nixon, the director of outreach and community partnerships for Safe and Just Michigan, speaks at a press conference criticizing the appointment of former state Sen. Rick Jones to the Michigan Sentencing Commission in a seat reserved for formerly incarcerated individuals. Nov. 18, 2026. (Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance)José Burgos, a policy advocate for the Campaign for the Fair Sentencing of Youth, speaks at a press conference criticizing the appointment of former state Sen. Rick Jones to the Michigan Sentencing Commission in a seat reserved for formerly incarcerated individuals. Nov. 18, 2026. (Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance)Edward Sanders, the founder and CEO of Alternative Sentencing and Reentry Solutions, speaks at a press conference criticizing the appointment of former state Sen. Rick Jones to the Michigan Sentencing Commission in a seat reserved for formerly incarcerated individuals. Nov. 18, 2026. (Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance)
A request for comment was made to both Jones and the commission. This story will be updated when a response is received.
Edward Sanders, the founder and CEO of Alternative Sentencing and Reentry Solutions, who was incarcerated in a Michigan prison for over 40 years, similarly said that a person with Jones’ experience could not personally speak to the impacts on education, employment, or emotional and physical development of someone who has spent significant time in custody — especially someone who was first incarcerated as a minor, as Sanders was. 
“It’s more likely that that child would die a premature death. It’s more likely that that child’s employment outcome would look different after that experience. It’s more likely that that child’s mental state would deteriorate,” he said. “A person that has spent a day in jail cannot share that with you. Not one day could that person take and explain to you what that meant or will mean for that child.”
Hope emphasized throughout the press conference that her problem is not with Jones specifically, but instead with the fact that he was appointed in what she called bad faith to a seat intended for someone with significant experience in Michigan’s carceral system.
“This isn’t about him personally,” she said. “It’s about reading the statute in bad faith and doing something that’s completely contrary to the intent of the drafters and all the advocates who worked so hard on this.”
Nixon, who was previously incarcerated himself, also emphasized that his criticisms were not about Jones as an individual, but that it was “heartbreaking” to have a member on the commission in that seat who “can’t speak to any of the things that we’ve been through or we’ve seen or the struggles of reentry, the struggles of trying to fight your way back into society after that.”SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Hope introduced a bill in the state House on Nov. 5 to alter the language that dictates the commission’s membership. The law, as currently written, states that the commission’s membership will include “One individual who was previously incarcerated,” and that member will serve for a term of three years.
Hope’s bill would amend that section of the law to specify that seat for an “individual who was convicted of a felony in this state and served a sentence of not less than 5 years in a department of corrections facility.”
“We can’t undo the commission that we have now,” Hope said. “That’s not what this bill is intended to do, but it is intended to cut the reader in bad faith, or the legislator in bad faith, off at the knees if they try to apply it in a way that’s totally contrary to what was ever intended.”
She noted during the press conference that she does not expect her bill to pass during the lame duck session that will run through the end of the calendar year. Although Hope herself decided not to seek re-election in 2026 and will be leaving the Legislature at the end of the term, she said that she has spoken with leaders of the incoming Democratic House majority, including caucus chair Rep. Stephanie Young (D-Detroit), who have committed to take up the issue next term.
José Burgos, a policy advocate for the Campaign for the Fair Sentencing of Youth who spent 27 years incarcerated in Michigan, expressed hope that the changes would eventually lead to better representation on the commission.
“I am very hopeful, very optimistic that at some point the seat that was promised to us will eventually be for somebody with that lived experience to inform that committee on the impact that those sentencing guidelines have on Michigan residents,” he said.

title: Commentary: New Hampshire has an awful lot of real problems to solve
description: New Hampshire has a dam problem. It also has a bridge problem, as well as hazardous waste, drinking water and wastewater problems. That’s according to the most recent American Society of Civil Engineers’ infrastructure report card, which after the examination of a dozen categories delivers the state an overall grade of C. Vermont, Maine and […]
text:
"It’s long past time that the people of New Hampshire are shown what it looks like when lawmakers shift the state’s values toward actions and investments that elevate people, infrastructure and public services." (Photo by Dana Wormald/New Hampshire Bulletin)New Hampshire has a dam problem. It also has a bridge problem, as well as hazardous waste, drinking water and wastewater problems.
That’s according to the most recent American Society of Civil Engineers’ infrastructure report card, which after the examination of a dozen categories delivers the state an overall grade of C. Vermont, Maine and Connecticut also received Cs, while Rhode Island and Massachusetts fared worse, with a C-minus and D-plus, respectively. Beyond New England, the national picture looks very much the same.
All the evidence, everything from the prevalence of potholes on American roads to last Friday’s aviation ground stop, points to a conclusion both unsurprising and of bipartisan concern: The richest nation in the world is not properly investing in its people or its structural foundations — and it hasn’t for a very long time.
So while New Hampshire may not be an outlier when it comes to the status of its physical infrastructure, the challenges outlined in the report are very real and they are daunting.
“New Hampshire’s dams average more than 100 years old.”
“Of its bridges, 8.4% are on the ‘Red List.’”
“Many drinking water systems are exceeding their intended service life.”
“Much of the wastewater collection infrastructure, with some systems dating to the 1870s, is in poor or failing condition.”
“The state has approximately 2,200 active hazardous waste generators producing 12 million pounds of hazardous waste annually.”
The report notes that the state has made progress in recent years, but that is largely owed to one-time federal investments through the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act and the American Rescue Plan Act.



Quotation







That means no more telling the people what they should want instead of listening to what they need, and no more instigating fear among the citizens just so that fear can be used as justification for reactionary policies that deliver only harm.


“Dedicated, predictable funding is needed for bridges, roads, dams, ports, rail, and aviation,” the report states, “and existing dedicated funds, including the Renewable Energy Fund and the state’s hazardous waste, petroleum, and drinking water funds, should be protected from diversion to unrelated purposes.”
“Dedicated, predictable funding” is not New Hampshire’s strong suit, however. Nor is protecting from “diversion to unrelated purposes,” as we’ve seen not only with the Renewable Energy Fund but also the rooms and meals tax and tobacco settlement payments.
“During the last ten years, the State has actively reduced the amount of revenue it has collected,” writes Phil Sletten in a new brief for the New Hampshire Fiscal Policy Institute. “Among other changes, the State lowered the rates of its two primary business taxes, including the State government’s largest tax revenue source, iteratively since 2015. The State also … repealed the 102-year-old Interest and Dividends Tax. … Together, those choices reduced State revenue by an estimated $500 million to $800 million during the current budget cycle.”
Along with tax cuts and repeals, here’s a partial list of where else lawmakers in the Republican legislative majority have focused their attention: 

A universal school voucher program that will cost the state $68 million this school year.
A ban on teaching subjects deemed “divisive” by conservative non-educators, especially on matters of race and gender identity.
A “parental bill of rights” that, again, exhibited Republicans’ fixation on how teachers handle gender dysphoria among their students.
Assisting the Trump administration’s violent anti-immigrant agenda.
A purge, akin to the “Red Scare” of the 1950s, of any and all diversity, equity and inclusion language in state government and education.
A perpetual rollback of state voting rights under the guise of rooting out voter fraud, despite such fraud being virtually nonexistent.
Annual attacks on vaccine requirements, even as evidence of the harm caused by anti-vaccination efforts mounts.
The gutting of the Office of the Child Advocate amid case after case exhibiting how youth-focused systems have failed one of the state’s most vulnerable populations.
And a step backward on greenhouse gas emissions, solely to free New Hampshire drivers from the supposed tyranny of their “check engine” lights.

There is a lot of damage in there that New Hampshire’s new Democratic legislative majorities could work to undo, but the undoing must only be the start of it. It’s long past time that the people of New Hampshire are shown what it looks like when lawmakers shift the state’s values toward actions and investments that elevate people, infrastructure and public services. The era of policy whisperers dictating which ideological box lawmakers should check off next must come to an end, and permanently.
That means no more telling the people what they should want instead of listening to what they need, and no more instigating fear among the citizens just so that fear can be used as justification for reactionary policies that deliver only harm. 
How do you rationalize tens of millions of dollars on a school voucher program when New Hampshire is one of only five states without state-funded preschool and is dead last in the nation when it comes to state investments in public K-12 and public higher education? How do you rationalize spending so much time and effort fighting for a DEI purge, voting rights rollbacks and a “parental rights” omnibus bill when more than half of the state’s “high hazard” dams and more than 300 bridges are in poor condition, when many of the state’s 2,500 public water systems are under strain? How do you rationalize ignoring real problems in favor of doing battle with invented ones?
If there is one clear message to be found in the results of this month’s elections, it’s this: After too many years of elected officials conjuring and hunting down boogeymen, maybe it’s time to start fixing things that are actually broken.

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico emergency management agency seeks 50% more state funding amid federal ‘uncertainty’
description: The New Mexico Department of Homeland Security and Emergency Management is seeking a significant state funding boost next year due to “uncertainty” in federal grants the department usually relies on for most of its funding.
text:
Leaders of the New Mexico Department of Homeland Security and Emergency Management on Nov. 17, 2026, detailed a funding request for the upcoming fiscal year that includes more state funding amid a reduction in federal grants alongside an increase in natural disasters, including flooding in Bloomfield in October 2026 above. (Photo courtesy Elmer Ignacio)The New Mexico Department of Homeland Security and Emergency Management is seeking a significant state funding boost next year due to “uncertainty” in federal grants the department usually relies on for most of its funding.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The department intends to ask for more than $8 million in state funds in the upcoming legislative session to pay staff and maintain “essential” agency operations, according to a presentation from Miguel Aguilar, the adjutant general of the New Mexico National Guard and DHSEM cabinet secretary. 
The amount marks a more than 50% increase in state funding over what the department currently relies on. But the increase is necessary, Aguilar said, because the department can no longer rely on federal grant funding to pay the bulk of personnel costs like it has in previous years. 
“There was a time when this agency was getting a significant amount of funding in those grants, and every year it just seems to diminish more and more,” Aguilar told lawmakers on the Legislative Finance Committee during a presentation Tuesday.
According to the secretary’s presentation, funding from two federal programs — the Emergency Management Performance Grant and Homeland Security Grant Program — has fallen sharply in recent years, from approximately $3 million in both the 2024 and 2025 fiscal years to less than $1 million in the 2026 fiscal year. 
The reduction in federal funds and uncertainty over their future availability means the department needs state funding to pay approximately 80 employees tasked with coordinating the state’s response to increasing natural disasters and other emergencies, Aguilar said. 
The department in 2026 has responded to severe wildfires and floods across the state, most recently in northern New Mexico communities like Bloomfield and Chama. Officials are currently conducting additional damage assessments across the flood-damaged areas in hopes of securing additional disaster funding from the Federal Emergency Management Agency. 
State Rep. Harlan Vincent (R-Ruidoso), whose district has repeatedly been struck by post-fire flooding, told Aguilar, “I’d write you a check today, if it’s up to me, and get you funded.”
But lawmakers also noted that the rising cost and frequency of natural disasters means they need to find a broader solution to both funding the state agency and providing direct assistance to individual homeowners. 
New Mexico Gov. Lujan Grisham criticizes Trump for not approving flood cost reimbursement

The state currently is limited in its ability to pay individual assistance to families after disasters because the anti-donation clause prohibits it, DHSEM State Director Ali Rye said Tuesday. The anti-donation clause prohibits public funds from going to private benefits, but some exceptions exist for affordable housing, indigent healthcare and scholarships for veterans, among others.  
As a result, the state generally relies on the federal government, which is not bound by the state’s anti-donation clause, to provide individual assistance, Rye said. That process is also lengthy and uncertain, she said. 
Senate Majority Leader Sen. Linda Trujillo (D-Albuquerque) said the Legislature should consider another exemption to the anti-donation clause in order to allow the state to directly assist families immediately after a disaster. 
Doing so would require a state constitutional amendment, but Trujillo said one is necessary “so that we can help out in these instances.”
“It’s heartbreaking to hear what’s happening in your communities, and I know it doesn’t seem like much, but our thoughts and prayers go to all of the families in those communities,” she said.

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Bayh adds secretary of state campaign rival to transition team
description: Democratic Secretary of State-elect Beau Bayh is including Greg Ballard — one of the candidates he defeated in this fall’s election — among his transition advisers as he prepares to take over the office.
text:
Indiana Secretary of State-elect Beau Bayh speaks with reporters at the state Election Division offices on Wednesday, Nov. 18, 2026. (Photo by Tom Davies/Indiana Capital Chronicle)Democratic Secretary of State-elect Beau Bayh is including Greg Ballard — one of the candidates he defeated in this fall’s election — among his transition advisers as he prepares to take over the office.
Bayh released the list of 17 advisers Wednesday and told reporters he had a productive meeting last week with current Republican Secretary of State Diego Morales about the office handover ahead of Bayh’s term beginning Jan. 1.
While Bayh and Comptroller-elect Jessica Bailey are the first Democrats to win statewide offices since 2012, Bayh said he’s felt welcomed by Statehouse Republicans so far.
Bayh says he’s aiming for nonpartisan transition
Bayh’s announcement of his transition advisers follows his naming this week of Peter Hanscom, who was a top staffer to former U.S. Sen. Joe Donnelly, as transition director and incoming chief of staff.
Bayh said he sought a wide group of advisers with experience regarding elections and the business services that the office oversees.
“I wanted to make clear that this office will not be run in a partisan manner,” he said.
Ballard, a former Republican mayor of Indianapolis, ran as the Lincoln Party candidate for secretary of state and received about 4% of the vote.
Ballard joined Bayh in many criticisms of Morales’ tenure as secretary of state and called for a revamping of the Indiana Election Commission — made up of two Republicans and two Democrats — as it did not take up campaign finance complaints against Bayh and Republican candidate Max Engling ahead of Election Day.
Bayh said Wednesday that he asked Ballard to help with the transition after getting to know him during the election campaign.
“A lot of the things that he was talking about, I was also talking about — taking some of the partisanship out of this office, cleaning up some of the corruption and the insider dealing,” Bayh said. “He’s had a lot of experience leading the city of Indianapolis and we’re both Marines, and so that’s why I brought him in.”
Other prominent members of Bayh’s transition group are:

John Gregg, a former Indiana House speaker who was the Democratic nominee for governor in 2012 and 2016.
David Shelton, the Republican Knox County clerk who finished second to Engling at the state GOP convention for the party’s secretary of state nomination.
Brett Voorhies, president of the Indiana AFL-CIO.
Miriam Dant, a Statehouse lobbyist who was a staffer in the 1990s to then-Gov. Evan Bayh, who is Beau Bayh’s father.
Bill Moreau, publisher of the Indiana Citizen news site who was a governor’s office chief of staff for Evan Bayh.

Morales “cooperative to date”
Morales issued a statement the day after Election Day congratulating Bayh on his victory and pledging “a smooth and successful transition.”
Bayh said Wednesday that he had “a great meeting last week” with Morales.
Secretary of State Diego Morales prepares to preside over the House on Nov. 16, 2026. (Photo by Niki Kelly/Indiana Capital Chronicle)
“He’s been cooperative to date, and he was very kind to us,” Bayh said. “Now, one of my central campaign promises has been to conduct an independent audit of the office. So we look forward to, hopefully, his cooperation with that effort as well. It’s been good so far.”
Morales’ office did not immediately reply Wednesday to a message from the Capital Chronicle seeking additional comment.
Bayh said he planned to put out a request for proposals from potential auditors soon after taking office in January and expected that work would begin within the first few months of 2027.
“I don’t want to rush this because it’s an important effort, and it’s not some political witch hunt,” he said. “We really want to get to the bottom of what has happened here, uncover the extent of what’s gone wrong, the wasteful spending, the insider dealing, and hold people accountable.”
New political committee paying transition costs
The costs of the transition work will be paid for by the Beau Bayh Transition political action committee that was formally created Wednesday with a filing to the Indiana Election Division.
Bayh said that PAC was being funded by a transfer of money from this campaign committee. He contrasted his plan with the use of nonprofits groups that don’t have to disclose their donors that have been used by Gov. Mike Braun and others for transition spending.
“I think, as the person overseeing our campaign finance transparency portal, it’s incumbent on me to make sure that our donations are public and that we can hold true to some of the pledges that I’ve made during this campaign,” he said. “That no donor to our campaign will be awarded a secretary of state contract.”
Bayh’s campaign was boosted by at least $2.4 million that was transferred from his father’s dormant U.S. Senate campaign fund to the state Democratic Party — along with a direct $700,000 contribution by Evan Bayh a week before Election Day, according to state campaign finance filings.
Since winning the election, Bayh said he has had a phone conversation with Braun and is setting up meetings with legislative leaders and state Treasurer Daniel Elliott, who was the sole Republican statewide winner.
“There is a spirit of bipartisanship for the time being,” he said. “Hopefully, that can last throughout the (legislative) session and onward because it’s central to my philosophy in terms of governing.”

title: Cornell College selects new president to join campus next summer
description: Cornell College will welcome its 16th president to campus this upcoming summer after a six-month national search to replace Jonathan Brand ahead of his departure next June. The Mount Vernon private college announced in a news release it has named Jeff Gingerich, current president of St. Bonaventure University in New York, as its next president, […]
text:
Cornell College has selected its 16th president. (Photo courtesy of Cornell College)Cornell College will welcome its 16th president to campus this upcoming summer after a six-month national search to replace Jonathan Brand ahead of his departure next June.
The Mount Vernon private college announced in a news release it has named Jeff Gingerich, current president of St. Bonaventure University in New York, as its next president, with a start date of July 1, 2027.
Brand announced his plans in February to leave Cornell at the end of his contract, ending a 16-year tenure at the institution. The national search for his successor began in June with the goal of selecting a new president by the end of the fall semester.
“Joining Cornell College feels like a homecoming, both because I am returning to my home state of Iowa, and because of the warmth and sense of belonging I experienced throughout the search process,” Gingerich said in the release. “I am excited to become part of a community so deeply committed to its students and to the transformative possibilities of a liberal arts education.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
According to the release, Gingerich is a Parnell, Ia. native who has held leadership roles in higher education at St. Bonaventure, the University of Scranton and Cabrini University. Bonaventure saw the highest total enrollment in its history and four record-breaking incoming undergraduate classes under Gingerich’s presidency, and he helped lead the university’s largest fundraising campaign to surpass its goal and grew the university’s endowment by 56%.
Jeff Gingerich and his wife, Betsy. (Photo courtesy of Cornell College)
Cornell College Board Chair Jan Thomas said in the release Cornell has seen plenty of growth itself over the past 15 years, including raising $200 million for student, academic program and facility support and renovating buildings and athletics fields across campus. Gingerich is now “part of this momentum,” Thomas said.
The college has also cut programs and positions amid evolving higher education needs and a $2-million budget deficit, one Brand said in December 2025 would be gone within three years.
“I am confident that we have found in Dr. Gingerich the right combination of leadership, expertise, and vision to meet the challenges of today’s higher education landscape,” Thomas said in the release. “The Board of Trustees welcomes Dr. Gingerich to the Cornell community and looks forward to collaborating with him to further Cornell’s mission.”
