name: Florida Phoenix
title: Florida is scheduled to carry out a record 20th execution on Thursday
description: Death row inmate Thomas M. Overton is scheduled to be executed at 6 p.m. Thursday at Florida State Prison. His would be the 20th conducted by the state this year, breaking the record 19 that took place in 2025. More are coming: Gov. Ron DeSantis has signed death warrants for Ricardo Gonzalez and that execution […]
text:
The execution chamber at Florida State Prison. (Via Florida Department of Corrections)Death row inmate Thomas M. Overton is scheduled to be executed at 6 p.m. Thursday at Florida State Prison. His would be the 20th conducted by the state this year, breaking the record 19 that took place in 2025.
More are coming: Gov. Ron DeSantis has signed death warrants for Ricardo Gonzalez and that execution is set Dec. 1, and for Willie Seth Crain Jr. for Dec. 10.
Overton was sentenced in 1999 for the 1991 murders of a Monroe County couple and their unborn child. At the time of her death, the woman was eight months pregnant, and Overton was also convicted in the death of their unborn son.
Overton has always maintained that he is innocent.
“Executing Overton would violate his right to Due Process and be a manifest injustice because there remains a great deal of untested evidence and inconclusive evidence that must be retested,” his attorneys claimed in a motion to vacate his conviction and death sentence filed in the circuit court in Monroe County on Oct. 28. “Further, there remains information that was never disclosed to Overton regarding potential third-party guilt. This evidence would independently support Overton’s actual innocence claim.”
The group Floridians for Alternatives to the Death Penalty says the new motion documents “extraordinary failures” in the original investigation of the murders.
“Thomas Overton’s case sounds outrageous, but the reality is that Florida routinely sends people to death row based on unreliable evidence and deeply flawed investigation,’ said Grace Hanna, executive director of the organization.
Overton’s attorneys have also filed for a stay of execution with the U.S. Supreme Court. They contend DeSantis’ refusal to grant clemency to anyone convicted of murder violates the due process rights of those on death row seeking a final act of mercy.
More than half of all the public executions in the United States have taken place in Florida this year. If Overton’s execution takes place as scheduled, it would be the 38th in the country in 2026. It would also be the 39th execution to take place in Florida in the past two years.
 The death penalty is legal in 27 states, but only 14 states have executed anyone since the start of 2019, according to the State Court Report.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Private equity-owned Minnesota Power wants customers to pay an extra $288 per year
description: One day after fulfilling a one-year pledge to freeze rates and two weeks after a larger in-state rival proposed freezing rates for two years, BlackRock-owned Minnesota Power asked state regulators for permission to raise its average residential customer’s electric bill by about $288 per year. “Minnesota Power has a responsibility to balance affordability wit[...]
text:
Company headquarters in New York City. (Photo by Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images)One day after fulfilling a one-year pledge to freeze rates and two weeks after a larger in-state rival proposed freezing rates for two years, BlackRock-owned Minnesota Power asked state regulators for permission to raise its average residential customer’s electric bill by about $288 per year.
“Minnesota Power has a responsibility to balance affordability with the investments needed to keep service dependable and costs manageable over the long term,” Jennifer Cady, the utility’s vice president of public policy and external affairs, said on Nov. 2.
The rate hike is not a done deal, but if the Minnesota Public Utilities Commission grants the northeastern Minnesota utility’s request, its customers’ bills would rise by an average of nearly 18%. 
Residential customers’ bills would rise by more than 19%. 
Attorney General Keith Ellison called the utility’s move a predictable consequence of its takeover last year by a profit-motivated partnership led by BlackRock, a private equity firm with investments worth more than $15 trillion. Ellison’s office staunchly opposed the $6.2 billion deal even after the Minnesota Department of Commerce dropped its opposition as part of a far-reaching July 2025 settlement with Minnesota Power’s parent company and its buyers.
“We worried that the buyers would want to recoup their money quickly, and that they would want to recoup it from Minnesota Power’s captive ratepayers,” despite the utility’s assurances otherwise, Ellison wrote in a blog post Tuesday.
“Now, barely a year later, the bill we warned about has arrived,” he wrote.
Minnesota Power cited a litany of financial pressures behind the request, including higher operations and maintenance costs for a delivery system covering roughly a quarter of Minnesota’s land area; ongoing investments to harden its grid and deploy more renewable energy; and “inflationary increases that affect everything from materials to equipment to insurance.”
The utility also cited its disproportionate dependence on large industrial customers in the beleaguered mining and paper industries. Two of Minnesota’s six active iron mines have fully or partially idled since early 2025, depriving Minnesota Power of significant revenue without changing “the cost of operating, maintaining and repairing the electric grid that is shared among all customer classes,” it said.
Minnesota Power did not say how the state’s first new iron mine in 50 years would impact its revenues. Mesabi Metallics is in the final stages of construction on a sprawling pit mine and pellet-production complex near Nashwauk that could account for nearly 10% of the utility’s total peak power demand once it’s fully operational.
The utility did deny any connection between the requested increase and the proposed Google data center near Duluth. The Hermantown City Council approved Google’s development agreement and other key permits for the facility last month, but state regulators must still approve the tech giant’s electric service agreement with Minnesota Power before it moves forward.
“Once the proposed data center is operational, Minnesota Power expects all its customers to benefit from the addition of a new 24-7 large customer that is required by Minnesota state law to fully pay for the cost of its electric service,” the utility said.
Ellison acknowledged that the July settlement and additional conditions placed on the merger in September offer some protection for Minnesota Power customers. Among more than $200 million in “quantifiable savings, protections and benefits” announced by the Minnesota Public Utilities Commission last year are $50 million in customer bill credits over seven years, a $20 monthly discount and $3.5 million in total arrearage forgiveness for eligible low-income customers, and a hard cap on the utility’s regulator-approved profit margin until 2031.
Unlike most private businesses, for-profit energy utilities like Minnesota Power and Xcel Energy can’t raise rates or juice profit margins whenever they feel like it. They must ask the Public Utilities Commission for permission to do so — and convince them that the request is justified — in a quasi-judicial process known as a rate case. 
Ratepayer advocates, major utility customers and other outside organizations can formally intervene in utility rate cases, which can take a year or longer to resolve. The commission typically allows the utility to temporarily raise rates as the case unfolds, on the understanding that the utility will refund customers with interest if the interim increase ends up exceeding the final approved increase. 
In this case, Minnesota Power asked for a 15% interim increase, or $15 per month for the average residential customer, to begin in January. Previously authorized bill credits set for the first quarter of 2027 will offset about 70% of the interim increase next year, the utility said.
Minnesota Power’s previous rate case ended in 2024 when the Public Utilities Commission approved a 4.9% hike for residential customers and a 4.4% increase for larger power consumers, down from an initial ask of 12% for all customers. 
The current rate case could also end with the commission approving less than the full request.
Still, Minnesota Power’s bid suggests its new ownership is not outwardly concerned about the optics of energy-price inflation, a key issue in this month’s midterm election. Several Minnesota Power peers have proposed freezing rates this year, including Xcel Energy, the state’s biggest for-profit electric utility.
A representative for the Private Equity Stakeholder Project, a watchdog group that opposed the BlackRock takeover, said the situation deserves notice from regulators weighing private equity deals for utilities in other states. 
“The warning signs were there from the beginning. Regulators reviewing other private equity utility takeovers should be asking whether temporary promises to protect customers mean much once the deal is done,” said Nichole Heil, the group’s senior research and campaign coordinator. 
On Tuesday, the federal regulator that oversees interstate energy issues approved a BlackRock-led consortium’s $10.7 billion bid to buy AES Corporation, which operates utilities in Indiana and Ohio, despite pushback from Democratic U.S. Sen. Elizabeth Warren and other lawmakers.
New Mexico regulators, meanwhile, are closely scrutinizing Blackstone Infrastructure’s $11.5 billion bid to buy TXNM Power, the state’s biggest electric utility. 
“Minnesota should be a warning for Indiana, Ohio and New Mexico. Private equity firms are looking to generate big profits, and Americans can’t just shop around for another electricity provider,” Heil said.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: NC Republicans eye 2028 comeback as two US House races move to recount
description: Democrats appear to have flipped seven seats in North Carolina’s congressional delegation, ousting half a dozen incumbents.
text:
The U.S. Capitol on the evening of Sept. 30, 2025. (Photo by Ashley Murray/States Newsroom)As two of North Carolina’s congressional races head to a recount, state Republican leaders are confident about their chances to win back seats in 2028.
In the blue tsunami that swept the nation, Democrats appear to have flipped seven seats in North Carolina’s congressional delegation, ousting half a dozen incumbents. If results hold, the Tar Heel State will send 11 Democrats and three Republicans to Washington in January. 
However, two trailing candidates have requested recounts: longtime GOP U.S. Rep. Virginia Foxx and Democratic challenger Ashley Bell.
The recount process
Foxx has represented North Carolina’s 5th Congressional District since 2005. She chairs the House Rules Committee, a position of seniority and influence. 
The incumbent requested a recount Tuesday. She trails Democrat Chuck Hubbard by 331 votes after provisional, absentee and overseas ballots were counted, according to unofficial results from the State Board of Elections. That’s a margin of 0.1% out of more than 286,000 votes cast.
“We certainly are willing to go through the process as laid out by law, and that won’t really change anything,” Hubbard told NC Newsline. 
U.S. Reps.-elect Chuck Hubbard, Jamie Ager, and Richard Ojeda at freshman orientation in Washington on Nov. 8, 2026. (Photo courtesy of Richard Ojeda)
On election night, the pair alternated taking the lead as votes trickled in from across the district. There was a precinct in Greensboro that took a while to publish results, and Hubbard said he wondered why.
“Turns out it was N.C. A&T and UNCG students who were basically wrapped around the building trying to cast their votes,” said Hubbard, a former journalist and publisher. 
As the night went on, Hubbard and his wife decided to head home from their watch party and go to bed. The results from that final precinct came in as they were in the parking lot. 
“The place where we were having the watch party just exploded,” Hubbard said. “People came running out the door and said, ‘It’s over. You’re up by 99 votes.’”
The next day, Foxx said the counting process wasn’t over. She claimed overseas and provisional ballots could play in her favor. But Hubbard’s lead increased after those votes were counted.
In the 10th District, freshman Republican U.S. Rep. Pat Harrigan leads by 2,510 votes or 0.85 points, according to unofficial results. Bell, a physician associate, requested a recount on Friday. 
Under North Carolina law, candidates can request a recount if the difference between the top candidates is less than 1% of total votes cast. 
“The first thing to do would be to see if the machines retabulating the votes produce the same or very close to the same results,” said Adam Newmark, a political science professor at Appalachian State University. “That might produce a couple votes difference here and there. Maybe two ballots got stuck together or something, little things like that.”
However, Newmark says, a recount is unlikely to change a margin of a few thousand votes — or even a few hundred, like in the 5th District.
Another gerrymander that backfired
North Carolina’s 5th District covers the northwestern part of the state. It stretches from Caldwell and Watauga counties in the west to Rockingham and Guilford counties in the east.
U.S. Rep. Virginia Foxx (R-NC) (Photo by Alex Wong/Getty Images)
Over her two decades of U.S. House elections, Foxx typically received about 55 to 65 percent of the vote. 
North Carolina Republican lawmakers redrew the congressional districts in 2023 to elect more Republicans by splitting up or “cracking” Democrat-held seats in the Triad and Triangle. Under the new map, the Tar Heel State sent 10 Republicans and four Democrats to Washington in the 2024 cycle. 
Foxx held on in 2024, when President Donald Trump’s name was on the ballot to draw Republican voters, but 2026 appears to have been a different story.
“The only way Republicans could grab another district was to take away some of those Republican voters, and in doing so, you made Virginia Foxx a lot more vulnerable,” Newmark said. “If you gerrymander too much, you’ve created a thinner advantage, and in a lopsided Democratic victory, that was too much for her to retain the majority in that district.”
Democratic wave in NC flips another Congressional seat as counting wraps up

Following Trump’s call, GOP legislators implemented yet another map in 2025. This time, they targeted U.S. Rep. Don Davis in the 1st Congressional District, spanning eastern North Carolina.
To make the 1st District more friendly to a Republican, GOP lawmakers drew in more Republican voters from the neighboring 3rd District. That made 3rd District Republican incumbent U.S. Rep. Greg Murphy slightly more vulnerable. 
The move backfired in what is often called a “dummymander”: Davis still won reelection, while Murphy was ousted. The incumbent initially held a slim lead, but conceded after provisional and absentee ballots placed Democratic challenger and former state lawmaker Raymond Smith ahead.
“Be careful what you wish for, because you might just get it,” North Carolina Senate Democratic Leader Sydney Batch of Wake County told reporters Tuesday. “They wanted an 11-3 map. We got exactly that. It just didn’t go in their favor.”
The road to 2028
This year, Democrats benefitted from Trump’s unpopularity and voters’ concerns about rising costs. Now they face the challenge of holding gerrymandered seats when that may not be the case.
Batch, whose caucus picked up four seats Nov. 3, said she wants to focus on issues rather than politics. 
“If we continue to keep an eye on affordability and also on the voters, and we pass legislation that is bipartisan and helps the many rather than the few, then I’m not worried about our chances in 2028,” she said. 
North Carolina Speaker of the House Tim Moore presides over the House chamber on Sept. 11, 2024. (Photo by Galen Bacharier/NC Newsline)
Republicans are looking at the next cycle as well. Foxx told supporters in a fundraising email that she’s planning to file for the 2028 election. 
“Regardless of the outcome of this race, I’m not going away,” Foxx said. “It’s going to be the toughest fight of my life.”
U.S. Rep. Tim Moore led the North Carolina General Assembly’s redistricting efforts in 2023, when he served as Speaker of the House. He drew the 14th District for himself, won it in 2024, and lost this year to Democrat LaKesha Womack.
Moore intends to make another congressional bid in 2028, according to Politico. 
North Carolina House Speaker Destin Hall, a Republican from Caldwell County, said he doesn’t see the legislature taking up redistricting again. 
“The reality is with the wave election that we just saw, the maps are almost beside the point,” Hall told reporters Tuesday. “I’m confident that my party will be able to get back all those congressional seats they lost this time around in the upcoming election.”

name: New Hampshire Bulletin
title: Wildfire in the White Mountains ‘moderated’ but still burning
description: A wildfire that surged to nearly 1,000 acres in the White Mountain National Forest earlier this month is increasingly under control as it enters its third week, according to the U.S. Forest Service. “Recent rainfall and cooler temperatures have significantly moderated fire behavior allowing firefighters to strengthen containment lines, and make steady progre[...]
text:
Fire smolders inside a log in the White Mountain National Forest in this image dated Nov. 9. (Photo courtesy U.S. Forest Service)A wildfire that surged to nearly 1,000 acres in the White Mountain National Forest earlier this month is increasingly under control as it enters its third week, according to the U.S. Forest Service.
“Recent rainfall and cooler temperatures have significantly moderated fire behavior allowing firefighters to strengthen containment lines, and make steady progress toward containment,” Forest Service Public Affairs and Partnership Staff Officer Colleen Mainville said in an email Wednesday. 
But the human-caused fire, which began on Sunday, Nov. 1, is not yet over, and the fire may continue to smolder for some time. It will likely take a “season ending” rain or snowfall event to quench the blaze, Mainville said. That would entail “multiple inches” of rain or a blanket of snow, Ryan Hughes, incident commander with the Forest Service, said during a community meeting in Shelburne Nov. 5.
As of Tuesday, Nov. 18, the fire was about 59% contained and 817 acres in size, down from a peak that approached 1,000 acres early this month, according to a release shared by the Forest Service on Tuesday. Twenty-two firefighters were assigned to the blaze, a number also reduced from the approximately 140 personnel that were active on the scene as of the Nov. 5 meeting.
“Fire behavior is minimal,” Tuesday’s release said. While investigators have said the blaze appears to have been human-caused, Mainville said there was no more information available as of Nov. 18 about what that cause may have been. 
The scale of the blaze is unusual for New England and the White Mountain National Forest, where large wildfires have not been prevalent since massive timber harvests created fire-prone conditions in the late 1800s. At their peak, fed by destructive logging practices, human-sparked wildfires in the disturbed forests occurred hundreds of times a year. Within the last century, however, fires have not been widespread in the national forest, making the Wild River blaze historic.
Scientists have cautioned that the changes happening in the Northeast as a result of global climate change are creating fire-prone conditions in the region. That includes more frequent and prolonged droughts, like the ones within the last few years that helped seed conditions for the Wild River blaze. 
The fire spread quickly, and has been difficult to extinguish, because of the effects of deep and prolonged drought on the forest, firefighters said. Materials like fallen oak leaves and the first few layers of soil on the forest floor are drier than normal, he said, making them extra flammable.

name: Maine Morning Star
title: Regulators approve standard offer rates, Mainers will see electric bills increase in January
description: Maine households enrolled in  standard offer rate for electricity will see their bills increase in January, though by less than previous rate hikes.  The Maine Public Utilities Commission met twice this week to confirm the final bids for residential standard offer rates.  A power bill has two primary components: the cost of the energy being […]
text:
The Maine Public Utilities Commission in Hallowell. Feb. 25, 2025. Photo: Jim NeugerMaine households enrolled in  standard offer rate for electricity will see their bills increase in January, though by less than previous rate hikes. 
The Maine Public Utilities Commission met twice this week to confirm the final bids for residential standard offer rates. 
A power bill has two primary components: the cost of the energy being supplied and the cost of the infrastructure to deliver it. Private utilities are responsible for delivering power. They also serve as intermediaries with energy suppliers, which are selected through a competitive bidding process overseen by the commission. This chosen supplier is known as the “standard offer,” since households are also entitled to seek an alternative “competitive electricity supplier.” 
For Central Maine Power customers, the standard offer rate for 2027 will be 13.63 cents per kilowatt hour, up from 12.72 this year. For an average customer using 550 kWh a month, that will mean an increase of roughly $4.99 on their monthly bill. 
Versant Power customers are split into two districts with different rates: the Maine Public District which covers northern Aroostook County, and the Bangor Hydro District. 
For Versant customers in the Maine Public District, the 2027 standard offer rate will be 15.34 cents per kWh, compared to 14.88 in 2026. That comes out to a monthly increase of $2.30 for an average customer using around 500 kWh of electricity.
In the Bangor Hydro District, the 2027 rate will be 13.55 cents per kWh, up from 12.95 now. For the average customer that will be an increase of about $2.99 a month. 
“It’s unfortunate that we’re seeing an increase in residential customer standard offer prices for 2027 — not as great an increase as we’ve seen in recent years, but an increase nonetheless,” Acting Commission Chair Patrick Scully said Wednesday. 
Electricity supply prices in Maine are largely driven by the price of natural gas, which has increased in recent years amid the war in Ukraine and now in Iran.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Eversource, UI announce increases to winter supply rates
description: CT's electricity rates could increase by double digits this winter as part of the latest energy cost-crunch prompted by the war in Iran.
text:
Connecticut’s electricity rates are on track to increase by double digits this winter as part of the latest energy cost-crunch prompted by the war in Iran, the state’s two largest utilities revealed in new filings Tuesday.
In paperwork submitted to the Public Utilities Regulatory Authority, Eversource asked to increase its standard service charge from 11.58 cents per kilowatt hour to 14.93 cents starting on Jan. 1 and lasting through June 30. United Illuminating requested an increase from from 11.94 cents/kWh to 15.69 cents for the same period.
Those increases equate to roughly $23 a month for the typical Eversource residential customer and $26 a month for UI customers, or roughly 13% for both utilities, according to the filings. Separately, Eversource is also requesting a December adjustment in the public benefits charge that will cost the average customer around $6 a month, according to the company’s filings. Actual bill impacts will vary depending on customer class and usage.
While regulators must review and approve any rate increases, they have relatively little control over supply charges — which by law must be passed along to customers without any markup or profit margins. “We recognize that any increase in energy costs matters to our customers,” UI President and CEO Frank Reynolds said in a statement Wednesday. “Standard Service supply costs are determined through Connecticut’s regulated procurement process and reflect the market cost of electricity purchased on customers’ behalf.”
Supply rates typically go up during winter, when the natural gas that’s used to fuel the majority of New England’s power plants becomes constrained by home heating demands.
This year, that increase has been exacerbated by elevated fuel prices linked to the Iran War, according to experts and utility officials.
In addition to natural gas that is transported via pipeline, New England relies on shipments of liquefied natural gas from the Middle East, where the war has damaged critical infrastructure. During cold snaps, some regional power plants are also designed to run on oil, which has similarly experienced rising prices.
“As is usually the case, significant energy market volatility and the region’s constrained supply continue to have the biggest impact on electric supply prices and bills overall,” Eversource spokeswoman Jamie Ratliff said in a statement. “This volatility is due to several factors, including global events — such as the conflict in Iran — disrupting the energy market and causing costs to surge.”
Within Connecticut’s deregulated energy market, customers do have the option of purchasing power from one of several third-party suppliers, instead of relying on the standard service rates charged by their utility.
But rising energy costs from the war have hit those suppliers as well, reducing the prospect of finding good deals. As of Wednesday, the cheapest third-party offering on Connecticut’s competitive supply marketplace was a 13.49 cents per kilowatt hour — a discount from the proposed winter increases but still more than the current supply rates charged by Eversource and UI.
“As we go into this coming winter, it is the unfortunate reality that those global fuel costs are going to translate into higher electricity prices,” said Dan Dolan, the president of the New England Power Generators Association. 
Dolan said that there is likely to be some relief this winter in the form of two large offshore wind farms — Revolution Wind and Vineyard Wind — that have come online in recent months.
Those projects are expected to perform best during the cold, blustery winter months when demand for power is near its peak, offsetting some of the need for additional fuel imports, Dolan said. 
Additionally, forecasters are predicting a more mild winter compared to last year, which was one of the coldest in recent history for much of New England. 
“To the degree that this winter is more mild, that could provide significant consumer relief,” Dolan said.
The expected increase in supply rates is separate from Eversource’s request for a 18%, $727 million hike in base distribution rates starting next summer. That request, which remains pending before PURA, reflects the cost of building and maintaining the local grid network from which the utility derives the bulk of its profits.

name: WyoFile
title: Sublette County attorney warned commissioners that targeting billionaire Ricketts’ resort is legally ‘dangerous’
description:
Weeks before commissioners invalidated a building permit, Clayton Melinkovich told them “full stop” that singling out Ricketts could cost the county credibility.
The post Sublette County attorney warned commissioners that targeting billionaire Ricketts’ resort is legally ‘dangerous’ appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
After being told by their attorney that singling out billionaire Joe Ricketts puts them on legally shaky footing, Sublette County commissioners are moving ahead with plans to block the native Nebraskan’s effort to transform the Bondurant area by building a grocery store-sized luxury resort. 
Meeting in Pinedale on Tuesday, commissioners decided in a 3-2 vote to invalidate a building permit that flew under the radar and was approved by Sublette County planners in September. The five-person board of commissioners also scheduled a Feb. 9 hearing in pursuit of undoing current resort zoning on the TD Ameritrade founder’s ranchland along Upper Hoback River Road.
Weeks before, Sublette County Attorney Clayton Melinkovich warned commissioners in an email that they were violating a “foundational” tenet of governance to “treat similarly situated people the same.” He quoted from the Declaration of Independence, 5th and 14th Amendments of the U. S. Constitution and from the Wyoming Constitution in support of his point.  
“I witnessed two instances yesterday where Sublette County, through its [board of commissioners], made decisions that treated similarly situated people differently,” Melinkovich wrote to commissioners in an Oct. 7 email acquired by WyoFile. 
Sublette County Attorney Clayton Melinkovich stands outside the Sublette County Justice Building on August 21, 2025 in Pinedale, Wyoming. (Erin Burk/WyoFile)
In one example, Melinkovich pointed toward the commissioners’ action to rezone Ricketts’ ranch. Commissioners reasoned that two years had lapsed since his resort was approved without “substantial development” — a condition in the county’s zoning and development regulations that is supposed to invalidate the zoning. 
Melinkovich highlighted commissioners’ inconsistent treatment: “Sublette County has deliberately chosen to not initiate termination proceedings regarding two zone changes where the two-years’ time requirement had [also] lapsed,” he wrote, citing the Mountain Meadow and Moyes family subdivisions. 
Melinkovich’s email to commissioners would normally be a non-public document because of attorney-client privilege — there’s a disclaimer at the bottom saying so. But because they forwarded it to each other, it was acquired by a citizen through a Wyoming Public Records Act request, and then shared with a representative for Ricketts and in turn WyoFile. 

TD Ameritrade founder Joe Ricketts addresses Sublette County residents in May 2023. (Mike Koshmrl/WyoFile)

Melinkovich declined to comment on the email. In it, he told commissioners “in my legal opinion” that Sublette County walks “a very dangerous path when you step outside of your authority and disregard the foundational law of the land.” 
He also told commissioners he has their back. 
“Can the County succeed in terminat[ing] the zone change? Yes, it is possible,” he wrote. “Will my office vigorously defend your decision in the event that the [commission] terminates the zone? Yes, we certainly will. Does the County lose its credibility when it treats similarly situated individuals differently? Yes, full stop.” 
Ricketts, whose family owns the Chicago Cubs, has been trying for more than five years to develop picturesque Bondurant, home to roughly 100 people in the Hoback Basin half way between Jackson and Pinedale. Although his efforts to overhaul Upper Hoback River Road have so far fallen short, nearby he’s been on a development tear. 
North of Bondurant, Ricketts purchased in 2024 the 33-acre Safari Club International property along Granite Creek, where he plans to expand and open a guest ranch, dubbed The Hawken. The billionaire also purchased the Timberline Ranch near Merna, formerly occupied by hunting influencers brought down for poaching. And he bought the embattled Renegade subdivision up Greys River Road, an inholding he tried and failed to trade to the Forest Service. The property is now subject of a civil lawsuit alleging he was defrauded out of tens of millions of dollars.
In Sublette County, Lynn Bernard, Dave Stephens and Doug Vickrey have been the three commissioners voting to terminate Ricketts’ resort zoning. Bernard could not be reached immediately, and Stephens declined an interview. Vickrey told WyoFile that he’s doing the best he can to represent the community. 

Sublette County Commissioner Doug Vickrey at an October 2022 meeting. (Mike Koshmrl/WyoFile)

“I looked around yesterday, and I saw a house full of folks concerned about what’s happening,” Vickrey said Wednesday morning. “I didn’t see many supporters for Mr. Ricketts. Mr. Ricketts’ entourage consisted of his lawyers.” 
“Mr. Ricketts could have been a wonderful addition to the Bondurant community,” he added. “He chose not to do so, and why? I have no idea.”
A commercial building permit for a resort Ricketts dubbed “the Confluence” spurred the current dustup. A larger resort was under construction in 2024, but Ricketts halted the project after commissioners declined to waive wildlife-friendly construction stipulations that drove up the price tag. 
Commissioners invalidated the permit for the Confluence on Tuesday in response to an appeal from neighbors Dan and Yvonne Bailey, Pat Burroughs, Marilyn Filkins, Tom Filkins, DJ Kominsky, Lisi Krall and Mark Prus. The now-stymied development was for a three-level, 47,000-square-foot resort that included lodging, a restaurant and spa, with an additional 47,000-square-foot underground parking garage. 
During the meeting, Jackson attorney John Graham argued that Ricketts had achieved “substantial development” during his first attempt at building the resort, and he pointed toward millions of dollars in related investments. A motion to intervene in the neighbors’ appeal included a June 2023 letter from former Sublette County Planner Dennis Fornstrom that served as “documentation of substantial development.” 




A detail showing the footprint of a 20-room guest lodge as part of a landscape plan submitted July 20, 2026, to Sublette County Planning and Zoning for a new development on Joe Ricketts’ property along the Upper Hoback River Road in Bondurant. (Courtesy)
“Jackson Fork [Ranch] relied on that representation,” Graham told commissioners. “Every step of the way, we were relying on Sublette County’s word, and Sublette County’s word is consistent with the regulations. Regulations don’t require vertical building; they require investment.”
Jackson attorney Leah Schwartz, representing the neighbors, encouraged commissioners Tuesday to reverse the resort zoning in addition to invalidating the building permit. They declined, instead setting a contested case hearing for Feb. 9, 2027. Another Jackson attorney, Justin Daraie, will preside over that hearing. 
By that time, there will be changes in the composition of the Sublette County Board of Commissioners. Newcomers Andy Nelson and Robin Schamber unseated Vickrey and Commissioner Mack Bradley in the August primary election. Vickrey told WyoFile he has no inclinations as to how the new commission will decide the rezoning dispute. 
“They’ll look at the information that’s there, and they’ll do the best they can to make the decision they feel is just,” Vickrey said. “It’s going to be an interesting ending to this saga.”

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Former rural Kansas prosecutor gets 60 days in jail for lying under oath
description: TOPEKA — A senior judge ordered former Neosho County prosecutor Linus Thuston to serve 60 days in jail for his conviction in August of lying under oath about why he met a woman alone at night at a softball field after they exchanged explicit photos. At a sentencing hearing Tuesday in Erie, senior judge Gunnar […]
text:
Linus Thuston, right, is led from the Neosho County courtroom in Erie on Sept. 4, 2024, after being sentenced to jail time for misdemeanor financial crimes. (Sherman Smith/Kansas Reflector)TOPEKA — A senior judge ordered former Neosho County prosecutor Linus Thuston to serve 60 days in jail for his conviction in August of lying under oath about why he met a woman alone at night at a softball field after they exchanged explicit photos.
At a sentencing hearing Tuesday in Erie, senior judge Gunnar Sundby denied a special prosecutor’s request to depart from guidelines and sentence Thuston to more time behind bars. The judge also denied Thuston’s request for a new trial.
Sundby instead sentenced Thuston to a year of probation and ordered him to spend 60 days in jail, starting in January. If Thuston were to violate his probation, he would have to spend six months in prison.
“The judge stated that he believes the defendant is a fraud,” said Sheryl Bussell, who has Thuston’s old job as county prosecutor. “I am hopeful that the community perhaps can move on now that the case is complete, even if an appeal is taken.”
The conviction caps a yearslong struggle between Thuston and the current and former county sheriffs who accused Thuston of serious financial crimes, as well as the extortion of about 50 women who sent him nude photos in exchange for legal services. The sheriffs said justice was for sale in the form of diversion agreements, including in child sex abuse cases, in which Thuston agreed to drop charges for cash.
Thuston served as prosecutor, an elected position, for 12 years in the rural southeast Kansas county with about 15,000 people. In 2024, Attorney General Kris Kobach’s office allowed Thuston to retire with full benefits before offering him a plea deal: Thuston agreed to plead guilty to two misdemeanor financial crimes, and the Attorney General’s office agreed never to pursue charges for the more serious crimes.
Thuston was ordered to serve 120 days in jail after pleading guilty in 2024.
Thuston also testified that year in a case where police accused him of leaking information to drug dealers about houses that were under surveillance by law enforcement. Thuston explained his late-night rendezvous with a woman at the community college softball field by claiming she was an off-the-books confidential informant, rather than someone he hoped to barter with.
When pressed, Thuston named other informal confidential informants who later denied they had ever given him information.
Special prosecutor Branden Bell, an attorney from the Kansas City area, initially charged Thuston with three counts of felony perjury and three counts of misdemeanor intimidation of witnesses. A jury in December 2025 failed to reach a verdict.
Bell and Bussell tried Thuston again in August on two counts of felony perjury. The jury convicted him on one count.
“Justice is no longer for sale in Neosho County,” Bell told Kansas Reflector after Tuesday’s sentencing hearing.
The judge’s order allows Thuston to delay serving 60 days in jail if he posts a $100,000 bond while his case is being appealed.

name: Virginia Mercury
title: Spanberger, lawmakers reveal proposals to preserve and build affordable housing in Virginia
description: On Wednesday morning outside a redeveloped apartment community in Woodbridge, Gov. Abigail Spanberger unveiled several housing proposals alongside the lawmakers who will sponsor them in the upcoming legislative session, driving home her administration’s goal to preserve and create more affordable housing amid a housing shortage statewide.  “This year’s slate[...]
text:
Apartments under construction in Richmond, Va. on May 15, 2026. (Photo by Charlotte Rene Woods/Virginia Mercury)On Wednesday morning outside a redeveloped apartment community in Woodbridge, Gov. Abigail Spanberger unveiled several housing proposals alongside the lawmakers who will sponsor them in the upcoming legislative session, driving home her administration’s goal to preserve and create more affordable housing amid a housing shortage statewide. 
“This year’s slate of housing bills makes sure more Virginians can find a home they can afford and keep the one they already have,” Spanberger said. 
Transit-oriented development, housing built near public bus lines, trains and Metro stops, will be a key initiative, with the goal of reducing transit costs for families who live there.
Spanberger said a forthcoming bill will “create transit-oriented development zones that will get priority for funding and incentives.” 
Sen. Saddam Salim, D-Fairfax, spoke from personal experience about how essential proximity to public transit is for many Virginians. 
“When we came to this country, we were living in a basement and we could not afford a second car. My mother walked one block to a bus stop and took that bus to work. That bus is how both of my parents could go to work, support a family and raise three children in Northern Virginia.” 
Another measure will require the state to use surplus land it owns for housing and transit-oriented development.
A proposal to create an affordable housing preservation fund would help localities and nonprofits buy properties when their affordability protections are nearing expiration, preserving home prices in an affordable range.
A bill to create an heirs property assistance program would help families navigate difficulties when they inherit land or a home without a will. The program would connect families with legal experts to help them keep their properties.
The state will take a survey to pinpoint areas with zoning policies that allow more affordable housing to be built and “support localities that want to do more but don’t know what may work,” Spanberger said of another bill.
A proposed update to state code regulating manufactured homes is on the horizon, the governor said, to no longer require they include a permanent steel chassis or frame designed to move these types of homes. This will allow these homes to be treated as permanent structures, just like other single-family homes. 
Del. Stacey Carroll, D-Stafford, said her district, the 64th, includes “beautiful” manufactured home communities, describing them as a viable option for people who want to purchase an affordable home. 
“We know manufactured homes are often half the cost of a regular single-family home or townhome. And as people desire to chase the dream of homeownership, the commonwealth of Virginia is going to stand and remove any particular policy that’s in the way or inhibit that, we’re going to directly decrease those costs.”
Spanberger took questions from the press at the end of the conference, including one about whether a newly-filed bill to repeal right-to-work by Sen. Jennifer Carroll Foy, D-Prince William, should get a committee hearing when lawmakers return to Richmond. 
Another labor question pointed out that a public sector collective bargaining bill was not part of Spanberger’s legislative priorities agenda unveiled last week, and asked if she would sign such legislation this session.
On Carroll Foy’s right to work repeal bill, Spanberger said she would not sign it, but “that is not saying that it should preclude any conversation related to the issue.”
Concerning collective bargaining, Spanberger said “there was a bill last year I would have signed, (but) we didn’t get there.”
Spanberger vetoes bills allowing public employees to collectively bargain working conditions, wages

Unions and labor advocates characterized her veto of last year’s bill as a “betrayal,” and it is poised to be one of the top debates in the legislature next year. Spanberger didn’t rule out approving a collective bargaining bill but said it needs to be crafted carefully and correctly. 
“My goal is to make sure that the bill … I ultimately sign, is one that works for Virginia, that is implementable, that is set up for success on the implementation side, the regulatory side,” she said. “And that it ultimately serves the primary goal, that anyone who devotes themselves to public service … (has) the option … to leverage their voice in a collective manner. That continues to be a priority.”
The 2027 General Assembly session will kick off in Richmond on Jan. 13.

name: National
title: Lawsuit challenges SNAP restrictions on sugary drinks, food in 18 states
description: A lawsuit filed Wednesday seeks to block more states from restricting what kind of items food stamp recipients can buy.   Led by the National Center for Law and Economic Justice, the class action lawsuit seeks to strike down restrictions on products such as candy and soda in 18 states for recipients of the Supplemental Nutrition […]
text:
Sodas and chips are displayed at a convenience store in New York City. A new lawsuit targets restrictions on sugary drinks and foods for food stamp recipients across 18 states. (Photo by Shalina Chatlani/Stateline)
A lawsuit filed Wednesday seeks to block more states from restricting what kind of items food stamp recipients can buy.  
Led by the National Center for Law and Economic Justice, the class action lawsuit seeks to strike down restrictions on products such as candy and soda in 18 states for recipients of the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, or SNAP. 
It targets Arkansas, Florida, Hawaii, Idaho, Indiana, Kansas, Louisiana, Missouri, Montana, Nevada, North Dakota, Ohio, Oklahoma, South Carolina, Texas, Utah, Virginia and Wyoming.
In previous litigation, a judge already blocked state and federal efforts to use waivers to restrict SNAP purchases in Colorado, Iowa, Nebraska, Tennessee and West Virginia.
“These unlawful waivers serve as a backdoor method to restrict access to SNAP,” Katharine Deabler-Meadows, senior attorney at the national center, said in a Wednesday news release. “Our lawsuit seeks to hold the Trump administration accountable for violating the law and causing unprecedented chaos for SNAP recipients and retailers alike.”
The Trump administration has encouraged states to seek federal waivers restricting what kinds of purchases can be made with SNAP, which has traditionally allowed recipients broad autonomy to select their own groceries. 
Those waivers have targeted a variety of products but generally focus on sugary beverages and candies. 
Hawaii’s waiver restricts only the purchases of soft drinks, according to the U.S. Department of Agriculture. But Florida’s waiver restricts purchases of soda, energy drinks, candy and prepared desserts.
More Americans lose SNAP as Congress weighs food stamps’ future

The federal government argues those restrictions divert taxpayer dollars away from food purchases that fuel the nation’s epidemics of diabetes and other chronic diseases. 
“These waivers help put real food back at the center of the program and empower states to lead the charge in protecting public health,” U.S. Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. said in a statement last year. 
Critics say the changes could harm people in food deserts, where healthy options are limited, and take away recipients’ power to make their own food choices. In the lawsuit, plaintiffs argue that the changes have harmed their health.
One Idaho plaintiff said she had multiple chronic health conditions including autoimmune conditions that make it difficult for her to regulate her blood pressure, heart rate and blood sugar levels. She relies on electrolyte-infused drinks and easy-to-eat foods, such as nutrition and granola bars that are now restricted in Idaho.
“Since the waiver was implemented, she has frequently been dehydrated, and her kidney function, digestion, and autonomic function, which affect her heart and ability to remain upright, have worsened,” the lawsuit said.
Another plaintiff in Oklahoma said she relied on easy-to-prepare foods as she lives in an extended-stay hotel without a kitchen. With upper gastrointestinal issues that cause discomfort, she drinks soda to relieve gas that gets trapped in her esophagus. But those beverages are now restricted under Oklahoma’s waiver.
The lawsuit, filed in federal court in the District of Columbia, argues that USDA lacks the legal authority to use waivers to undertake such large-scale change to SNAP’s structure.
Stateline reporter Kevin Hardy can be reached at khardy@stateline.org.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: New Haven’s ConnCORP announces new name and leadership
description: The Connecticut Community Outreach Revitalization Program, or ConnCORP, is being renamed to the First Haven Group.
text:
An organization focused on economic empowerment and growth in New Haven’s historically Black communities is entering a new chapter, announcing new leadership, a new name and a broader mission Wednesday.  
The Connecticut Community Outreach Revitalization Program, or ConnCORP, is being renamed to the First Haven Group. The renamed organization will be led by former ConnCORP Chief Operating Officer Paul McCraven, who took up his new position in October.
In addition to McCraven, who will serve as the First Haven Group’s CEO, the organization’s board will now be led by Anna Blanding, ConnCORP’s previous chief investment officer. Blanding was appointed to the leadership position in September. 
The announcement comes after a series of shakeups at the top of the organization in recent months. Carlton Highsmith, who served as founder and board chair of both ConnCORP and its sister organization, the Connecticut Center for Arts and Technology, ConnCAT, had previously announced he would leave his positions by the end of the year.
And Erik Clemons, the founding CEO and longtime leader of both ConnCORP and ConnCAT, announced earlier this year that he would leave ConnCAT, later confirming that he would also leave his position at ConnCORP to focus on new opportunities.
Both organizations, Clemons told the Connecticut Mirror in September, have helped “create an ecosystem of service to the people.”
“It is most important for me to demonstrate what could be possible for communities who look like me,” he added.  
ConnCAT and ConnCORP board chairman Carlton Highsmith (second from left) and then-CEO Erik Clemons (center left) celebrate after the ribbon cutting for the new ConnCAT headquarters on June 19, 2026. Credit: Courtesy of ConnCORP/The Narrative Project
Founded in the early 2010s, ConnCAT has used job training and workforce development programming to build self-reliance in New Haven’s Dixwell and Newhallville communities. ConnCORP, meanwhile, focuses on economic development and promotes community-driven investments in real estate and minority-owned businesses. 
The new leaders said the groups’ work in the city’s historically-Black neighborhoods will continue, with an expanded focus on supporting community growth and local development in areas like affordable housing, access to groceries and childcare. 
“ConnCAT and ConnCORP laid the foundation in education and entrepreneurship,” McCraven said in a statement. “Our goal is to bring resources and investment into the community so residents can build their futures here.”
And as the organization moves forward, the First Haven Group says that they will work to transform the Dixwell and Newhallville neighborhoods into national examples of the power of self-determination and community investment in neighborhoods that have historically been underinvested in. 
“Our ambition is not simply to develop buildings or attract investment,” said Blanding. “It is to build an ecosystem where families can create wealth, businesses can thrive, and future generations have opportunities that did not exist before.” 
Rebuilding Black New Haven
Founded with a focus on economic development and business investments, ConnCORP has long aimed to promote a strong impact investing ecosystem in New Haven centered on the city’s Black communities. 
The organization tackled some of the biggest challenges facing Black communities in Connecticut, including entrepreneurship support for small business owners, assessing the state of Connecticut’s Black businesses and creating new programs for financial literacy and generational wealth building. 
The First Haven Group will continue that work, expanding it to include additional community investments and supports. 
“Our work is critical because families in neighborhoods that have experienced long-term disinvestment face connected challenges: finding quality housing, earning a livable wage, affording groceries, and raising their children,” McCraven said in emailed comments provided before the announcement. “We’re addressing those needs together.” 
The organization will also continue its leadership of First Haven in Dixwell, a nearly eight-acre redevelopment project in the heart of the Dixwell neighborhood. When completed, the roughly $200 million project will include a mixed-use development with retail and grocery space, apartments, a performing arts center and a workforce development hub. Initial projections from the group suggest that the project could generate upwards of $1 billion in statewide economic activity and more than 500 jobs, much of that within the local community. 
A rendering shows what the completed First Haven in Dixwell redevelopment could look like. Credit: Peter Cook / HGA
The first phase of the redevelopment project was finished over the summer with the opening of a new headquarters for ConnCAT. The $65 million, 65,000-square-foot facility houses workforce development and youth programming efforts, as well as additional space for a health clinic and a childcare center. 
The project has been driven by the community, with numerous listening sessions and forums taking place to ensure that the reimagined Dixwell development reflected local needs. 
“We said that if we’re going to make a real impact that’s transformative and powerful, we should start with the Dixwell Plaza,” McCraven said in a June interview at the new ConnCAT building. “We wanted to create something that’s going to be restorative within the Black community.” 
The newly constructed ConnCAT building on Dixwell Avenue in New Haven, June 18, 2026.  Credit: Julia Levine / CT Mirror
The First Haven Group said that this community engagement work is ongoing as the project moves into its next phase, which includes the creation of a roughly 180-unit mixed-income housing development in Dixwell. Site work is expected to begin early next year. 
“We’re moving forward with urgency, and we’re not going to skip a beat because of the leadership transition,” McCraven said. 
A local project with national impact
The work of ConnCAT and ConnCORP have turned the organizations into vital community engines, bringing jobs, knowledge, and opportunity to New Haven. 
But the organization is also looking to expand its national footprint, arguing that the community-driven work being done in Connecticut can serve as a national model of how to uplift Black communities and promote intergenerational wealth and economic power.  
They point to community–led revitalization efforts unfolding across the country in cities like Atlanta, Chicago and Oakland. At a time where the wealth of Black households continues to pale in comparison to other groups, and as research shows that broad investment in communities and neighborhoods could be a more effective solution than individual programs, the First Haven Group says that it is looking to move to the forefront of efforts to rebuild Black communities. 
A number of elected officials and state leaders participated in the ConnCAT ribbon cutting ceremony on June 19, 2026.  Credit: Courtesy of ConnCORP/The Narrative Project
“New Haven’s size, population mix, and major institutions — including Yale, its work in biotech, quantum, and the hospitals — create an opportunity to help surrounding neighborhoods benefit from growing industries,” McCraven said. “We’re rooted in this community and committed for the long term, and we hope the way this coalition works together can become a model.”
In the coming years, the First Haven Group leaders say that the final verdict on their effectiveness will be made by the people at the center of everything the group does:  the local community.
“The true measure of our success will be whether five or ten years from now, the people of Dixwell and Newhallville can point to greater economic opportunity, stronger neighborhoods, and a more prosperous future for their children,” Blanding said. “That is what it means to invest with purpose.”

name: Mississippi Today
title: Mississippi’s John Palmer, technology pioneer, former ambassador to Portugal, dies at 92
description: Former Ambassador John Palmer speaks at the dedication of the new $10 million Gertrude C. Ford MIND Research Center at UMMC.
text:
Businessman, philanthropist, community leader and former U.S. Ambassadorto Portugal John Palmer died on Monday in Jackson. He was 92.
A native of Corinth, Palmer attended the University of Mississippi on a basketball scholarship, graduating with a bachelor’s degree in accounting. After serving two years in the Army, he returned to Ole Miss and earned his MBA. 
While he started his career as an accountant, Palmer began an answering service in Jackson that grew into Mobile Communications Corporation of America. Under his leadership, Mobile Communications became one of the country’s largest paging companies.
John Palmer
He later sold the business to BellSouth Corporation, and spun off Mobile Communications’ mobile paging feature into SkyTel Communications, which the New York Times described in 1993 as “a pioneer in advanced paging technology.”
Among his numerous other business accomplishments, he founded GulfSouth Capital, an investment firm; served on the President’s Export Council and was a board member of AmSouth Bancorporation, EastGroup and Entergy Corporation.
A community leader and philanthropist, Palmer served as chairman of the National Trustees of the National Symphony Orchestra based at the Kennedy Center in Washington, D.C., and on the boards of the Foundation for the Mid-South, Millsaps College, the University of Mississippi Foundation and more. 
Inspired by his family’s personal experience with Alzheimer’s, he helped to establish the MIND Center at the University of Mississippi Medical Center, which is a leader in dementia and Alzheimer’s research, and he led its advisory group for many years.
“Ambassador Palmer was a true friend to The MIND Center, supporting our efforts philanthropically and as a strident advocate,” said Meredith Aldridge, UMMC’s chief development officer, “his legacy is one of service to our country, his family, and all Mississippians, and we are grateful that his work will continue through the programs he loved at the Medical Center.”
In 2001, President George W. Bush appointed Palmer as Ambassador to Portugal, a role in which he served until 2004. 
A funeral service will be held at 2 p.m. on Nov. 23 at Northminster Baptist in Jackson, with visitation beginning at the church at noon. 
Editor’s note: John Palmer was a donor to Mississippi Today, as is his wife, Carol.

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: Louisiana continues to rank poorly for maternal and infant health
description: The percent of live births classified as preterm in Louisiana was 13.7% in 2025, higher than in every other state except Mississippi (14%), according to the March of Dimes.
text:
Louisiana continues to receive low ratings for infant and maternal mortality from the March of Dimes, a national nonprofit that works to improve the health of women and babies. (Stock photo via Getty Images)Louisiana continues to receive a failing grade for its infant and maternal healthcare outcomes, according to the March of Dimes, a national nonprofit that works on improving the health of mothers and babies. 

The state was one of seven to receive an “F” on its report card from the organization when it comes to the percentage of preterm babies, those born before 37 weeks of gestation. The March of Dimes considers it a significant health indicator for birthing parents and children. 

“Later in life, babies who are born early have the highest risk of having developmental delays and they are more likely to have medical complications,” said Dr. Veronica Gillispie-Bell, a New Orleans-area obstetrician and national expert on maternal health. She was not involved in the March of Dimes analysis. 

The percent of live births classified as preterm in Louisiana was 13.7% in 2025, higher than in every other state except Mississippi (14%), according to the March of Dimes. The national rate  was 10.4%.
Louisiana’s infant mortality rate, at 7.6 deaths per 100,000 births in 2024, was also worse than every other state except Mississippi (8.6) and Arkansas (8.3). 
The state also continues to have a high rate of maternal mortality, at 39.4 women per 100,000 births compared with the national rate of 23.1. 

Dr. Rebekah Gee, an obstetrician who was secretary of the Louisiana Department of Health under Gov. John Bel Edwards, said the state struggles with maternal and infant health outcomes because its population is generally less healthy. Obesity, diabetes and hypertension rates are high in Louisiana, which can create complications during pregnancies and births, Gee said. 

“You have to have healthy women to have healthy babies,” she said. “Pregnancy is the absolute worst time to try to get yourself healthy.”
Louisiana has one of the highest poverty rates in the country, and the cost of 58% of all Louisiana births is paid for by Medicaid, which provides health insurance to low-income residents. Medicaid births are more likely to be preterm when compared to those covered by private insurance, at 15% and 11.6%, respectively, according to the March of Dimes report. 

Gee said people who are poor have access to less preventative health care before they become pregnant, putting them more at risk for complications. 

“If you were to fix poverty, we would fix our birth outcomes,” she said. 
Gillispie-Bell said there are a few positive signs in recent state data. 
While March of Dimes said it wasn’t statistically significant, Louisiana’s preterm birth rate dropped slightly from 2024 to 2025, from 14% to 13.7%. Also, the rate of doctor visits during the first trimester of a pregnancy ticked up, from 71.2% to 72.1%, and low-risk Cesarean births for first-time mothers went down, from 28.9% to 28.6%, from 2024 to 2025.

In Louisiana, there is an effort to reduce the number of people who undergo Cesarean births because of the increased risks, according to Gillispie-Bell.
“We still have a lot of work to do for sure but I think we have made a lot of advances,” she said.
Preterm births
Louisiana’s preterm birth rate for every racial and ethnic group is higher than the national average, according to the March of Dimes report. The state’s rate for white women is 10.5%, compared with 9.5% nationally. For Black women in Louisiana, the preterm rate is 17.9%, while it stands at 14.8% across the country.   
Hispanic women have the state’s lowest preterm birth rate at 10.5%, while Black women, at nearly 18%, were most likely to have a preterm birth in Louisiana. 
Gillispie-Bell, who is Black, said Black women typically have less access to medical care and healthy foods, and they are more likely to experience economic instability — factors detrimental to their overall health. 
Black women are also more likely to experience discrimination in hospitals and other health care settings, according to Gillispie-Bell and Gee, who is white. 

“Even Wimbledon winners have complained of pain and been ignored,” Gee said, referring to tennis star Serena Williams, who was initially ignored when she said she was having trouble breathing after giving birth to her daughter via Cesarean section. Williams said scans later showed she had several small blood clots in her lungs that were life-threatening and required emergency treatment. 
Infant mortality 
Racism is also a factor in infant deaths, experts say. 

In 2024, 404 babies in Louisiana died before their first birthday, according to the March of Dimes. Children born to Black mothers were much more likely to die than those born to white, Asian or Hispanic mothers. 
The mortality rate of babies born to Black moms in Louisiana was 1.5 times the state’s general rate from 2022-24.  At 11.5%, it was also twice as high as the mortality rate of infants born to white, Asian and Hispanic moms during the same period. 

Gillespie-Bell said she believes having more medical providers who are people of color would combat the implicit bias when it comes to providing health care to Black people and other minority communities. 

That is why she is helping to start the Xavier Ochsner College of Medicine, a medical school that will open in 2027 on the campus of the historically Black Catholic university in New Orleans. Gillispie-Bell said the school has received almost 700 applications for its medical school since its submission period started less than two weeks ago. 

“It creates an automatic level of trust when people see themselves represented in their health care team,” she said. 

She also said it is helpful to have doulas, trained professionals who provide support to pregnant people, present during births. The doula can advocate for a patient to receive better medical care when they might not be able to do so while giving birth, Gillispie-Bell said. 

Louisiana’s Medicaid program started covering doula services for births in early 2026.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.

text:
Bush Elementary student Ryker Asher won Kentucky's "I Voted" sticker contest for 2026. (Photo courtesy Secretary of State's office)Fresh off winning reelection earlier this month, two House members have announced they are joining a growing field of candidates hoping to succeed Kentucky Republican Secretary of State Michael Adams in office. 
Democratic Rep. Adam Moore, of Lexington, and Republican Rep. Nick Wilson, of Williamsburg, launched their respective campaigns Wednesday. Moore defeated former state Rep. Killian Timoney in a Central Kentucky House seat for another term in the General Assembly, while Wilson ran unopposed this year. 
Moore is the first Democrat to announce a run for the office, while other Republicans have already put their hats in the ring. They are former State Auditor Mike Harmon, attorney and veteran Jack Whitfield and Brad Holsclaw, the son of late Jefferson County Clerk Bobbi Holsclaw. 
Adams is term-limited in his role and once mulled a run for governor next year, but opted at the Fancy Farm Picnic to endorse U.S. Rep. James Comer for the role instead. Adams has had broad support among voters and was the top-voter getter of all 2023 constitutional officer candidates and won all but two of Kentucky’s 120 counties. 
In addition to governor and secretary of state, Kentucky’s other statewide offices are on the ballot next year. The filing deadline for candidates to join the race is Friday, Jan. 8.

name: VTDigger
title: Around Vermont this week: Nov. 18-25
description:
Seven Days’ Magnificent 7 highlights seven events in and around Vermont this week, including the “Hug Your Farmer: The Last Waltz Revisited” concert at the Flynn Main Stage in Burlington.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Around Vermont this week: Nov. 18-25.
text:
Dwight + Nicole Credit: Courtesy of Josh Steele
This story was first published in Seven Days on Nov. 16, 2026. 
VTDigger is teaming up with Seven Days. Each week, we’ll share their Magnificent 7, a hand-picked roundup of must-see, must-do events happening around the state. This is a new experiment, so please take our quick survey at the bottom of the page and tell us what you think.
Carry the Weight 
Friday, Nov. 20
The Band plays on at “Hug Your Farmer: The Last Waltz Revisited” at the Flynn Main Stage in Burlington. The annual concert benefiting local agriculture initiatives boasts an impressive roster of Vermont music stalwarts — including Bob Wagner, Clint Bierman, and Dwight + Nicole (pictured) — in a tribute to the Band’s landmark 1976 farewell concert at the Winterland Ballroom in San Francisco.
#Twinning 
Sunday, Nov. 22
The Brother Brothers Credit: Courtesy of Alex Nefarias
At Burnham Hall in Lincoln, indie-Americana duo the Brother Brothers summon the sounds of ’60s folk outfits such as Simon & Garfunkel. Praised by NPR Music for their “fabulous old-time playing and sibling harmony,” identical twins Adam and David Moss serve up vintage-sounding originals with virtuosic acoustic instrumentation on cello, guitar and five-string fiddle.
Polar Flair 
Opens Friday, Nov. 20
Forest of Lights Credit: Courtesy
Vermont Institute of Natural Science’s Forest of Lights is back in Quechee — with a twist. A theme of “Arctic Animals: Survivors of the Cold” transports visitors to the North Pole to learn about the remarkable creatures that thrive in glacial temps. Expect a sparkly snowflake dome, a scintillating spiderweb, a twinkling tower, and illuminated narwhals, snowy owls and polar bears.
Laugh Factory 
Saturday, Nov. 21
Upright Citizens Brigade All-Stars Credit: Courtesy
Performing arts series KCP Presents welcomes intrepid improv troupe Upright Citizens Brigade All-Stars to St. Johnsbury Academy’s Fuller Hall. The acclaimed sketch-comedy act — assembled from the illustrious company that launched Amy Poehler and Kate McKinnon into stardom — shines with on-the-spot scenes and characters inspired by suggestions from the audience.
High Point 
Saturday, Nov. 21
The “Roof of the World” takes center stage at the 22nd annual Tibet Festival at Burlington’s O.N.E. Community Center. Celebrate the spiritually rich region — home to the Himalayas, Mount Everest’s northern face and the lineage of the Dalai Lama — with a vibrant display of its distinct heritage, including live traditional music, cultural dances, authentic cuisine, and arts and crafts.
Many Hands 
Saturday, Nov. 21 & Sunday, Nov. 22
Teapot by Clinton Pottery Credit: Courtesy
You know what they say: The early bird gets the handmade ceramic Christmas tree! Shoppers can try to check off every name on their list — before Thanksgiving — during the Celebrate Craft Holiday Fair at South Burlington’s DoubleTree by Hilton. The festive showcase from 90-plus vendors features wines and spirits, housewares, jewelry, artwork, and “you don’t see that every day” foods.
Walk This Way 
Ongoing
“Apple Adorned” by Sarah Wesson Credit: Courtesy
Ripton artist Sarah Wesson proves the best way to get artistic inspiration is to stretch your legs. The painter’s solo exhibit “Within Walking Distance: Act 3” at Town Hall Theater’s Jackson Gallery in Middlebury shows off the fruits of a three-year project gathering wild plants on daily walks. Delicate watercolors highlight the beauty of brittle dried flora that might otherwise be overlooked.






For more events across Vermont this week, consult the Seven Days calendar, sign up for the Notes on the Weekend newsletter and follow @sevendaysoutandabout on Instagram.
