name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Facing Down MassHealth’s Largest Cutbacks “in 61 Years”
description: The 2025 "One Big Beautiful Bill Act"  will drain $3.5 billion annually from MassHealth’s $13 billion in federal revenue—a staggering gap within the program’s $23 billion gross budget.
text:
EPISODE INFO

HOST: Paul Hattis & John McDonough
GUESTS: Ryan Schwarz, physician, Medicaid Director and Assistant Secretary for MassHealth, Massachusetts’s Medicaid and CHIP program







ON THE COMMONWEALTH BEACON podcast Health or Consequences, hosts Paul Hattis and John McDonough interviewed MassHealth Director Dr. Ryan Schwarz about sweeping challenges facing Massachusetts Medicaid. Drawing on seven years at MassHealth and 15 years strengthening health systems globally and at the World Bank, Schwarz characterized President Donald Trump’s 2025 “One Big Beautiful Bill Act” (OB3) as the largest set of cuts and eligibility changes in Medicaid’s 61-year history.
Once fully implemented over five years and if unamended, OB3 will strip coverage from 250,000 to 300,000 Massachusetts residents, including 175,000 to 200,000 MassHealth members, with 7,500 already losing coverage last October. Financially, the law will drain $3.5 billion annually from MassHealth’s $13 billion in federal revenue—a staggering gap within the program’s $23 billion gross budget.
To prevent enrollees from losing coverage due to bureaucratic hurdles when work requirements and twice-yearly renewals begin in January, Schwarz emphasized that MassHealth’s top priority is “coverage, coverage, coverage,” built on a three-part strategy. First, MassHealth is using internal state data to automatically exempt qualifying populations, such as pregnant individuals and parents of children under 14. Second, through a new data-sharing contract with Equifax, the agency will verify employment and salary compliance before members ever receive a renewal notice. Third, for remaining members, MassHealth has expanded eligibility staffing, launched a statewide awareness campaign with Health Care For All and 50 community organizations, and revived its signature bright blue envelopes alongside texts and robocalls.
These federal cuts arrive amid severe pre-existing financial pressures. Schwarz noted that healthcare costs across Medicaid, Medicare, and commercial markets have grown over 10 percent annually mostly because of pharmaceuticals, outpatient behavioral health, and long-term services, while state revenues grow just 2 to 3 percent. Though blockbuster weight loss GLP-1 drugs accounted for half of MassHealth’s drug spending growth, the broader portfolio is also expanding. Because about one in every four Massachusetts health care dollars flow through Medicaid, Schwarz warns that federal cuts will destabilize safety-net hospitals and ripple across the entire system, also driving up commercial healthcare costs.
Turning to delivery reform, Schwarz defended MassHealth’s nearly decade-old Accountable Care Organization (ACO) program. Citing an independent University of Massachusetts evaluation covering 2017 to 2022, he notes the ACO model improved care quality and member experience while saving $500 million. He highlighted MassHealth’s 2023 shift to capitated primary care payments across 1,000 practices, providing predictable monthly budgets that support team-based care and behavioral health integration. That initiative raised primary care’s share of MassHealth spending from 5 to 6 percent to 9 to 10 percent, aiming toward Gov. Healey’s 12 percent target by 2028, serving as a blueprint for pending primary care legislation.
Finally, Schwarz addressed two recent operational and political developments. Regarding recent disruptions in MassHealth’s dental program, reported in the November 7 edition of The Boston Globe, he called the provider and patient experience under former Dental administrator BeneCare “entirely unacceptable,” adding that MassHealth terminated BeneCare, returned responsibility to DentaQuest, cleared thousands of backlogged claims, and is launching a new provider portal by year-end.
Looking toward Washington, DC following November 3 Democratic victories in the US House and Senate, Schwarz declined to predict whether Congress might roll back OB3 cuts, stressing that MassHealth will stay laser-focused on protecting Massachusetts residents when federal changes take full effect in January.
Health or Consequences has launched as its own podcast feed, featuring the same in-depth health policy conversations you’ve come to expect from The Codcast. Follow hosts Health or Consequences on Spotify, Apple Podcasts, and YouTube to get notified of new episodes.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: CT Dems align behind Hakeem Jeffries’ bid to be House speaker
description: Democrats' internal election comes amid some pushback in Connecticut to Jeffries’ leadership. A full House vote will happen in January.
text:
Connecticut’s congressional delegation on Wednesday rallied behind Hakeem Jeffries’ bid to serve as speaker of the U.S. House of Representatives when Democrats assume control next year with one of the largest majorities in decades.
House Democrats’ internal leadership election is the first step in the process for the New York Democrat, but it puts him on track to become the first Black speaker when the entire House votes on Jan. 3 in the incoming session of Congress.
Jeffries has sought to shore up support across an ideologically diverse caucus that includes moderates representing the reddest parts of the country to progressives in liberal enclaves. With a 251-11 vote on Wednesday, Democrats hope any tension over his nomination is resolved.
The leadership elections happened behind closed doors, and the Democratic caucus — which included newly elected members of Congress — voted in secret. Aside from nominations for speaker, the party is also voting on nominations for other leadership roles, like caucus chair.
While Democrats saw massive wins in the midterm elections earlier this month, some voters argue that it’s an indication that they want to see new leadership in both the House and Senate. Local grassroots groups in Connecticut and elsewhere wanted lawmakers to support alternatives to Jeffries and Chuck Schumer, who is running to become Senate majority leader next year, a post he once held.
No formal challenger materialized against Jeffries for Speaker of the House. The Senate, meanwhile, has a contested race for majority leader that also features U.S. Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland. Schumer claimed Wednesday he has the votes to overcome that challenge in leadership elections that are slated for early December. (U.S. Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., said he supports Schumer for the role.)
In the lead-up to these leadership elections, groups like Connecticut 50501 encouraged people to make daily calls to the offices of their elected officials to support candidacies other than Jeffries and Schumer.
Even with opposition percolating, U.S. Rep. Jim Himes, D-4th District, had predicted for weeks that Jeffries would have no issue getting the speaker nomination. Jeffries has been serving as House minority leader since 2023 and is a close ally of former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi of California.
“I’ve had any number of conversations with people. I get the concern,” Himes said last week on Connecticut Public’s “The Wheelhouse.” “Hakeem is an unknown quantity. He’s stepping into Nancy Pelosi’s shoes, and she was the ultimate in known quantities.”
“My own view is that Hakeem deserves a chance,” he continued. “I also don’t want to necessarily run over or see run over the absolutely historic moment of an African American man serving as speaker of the House for the first time in 250 years.”
Himes is expected to take the helm of the House Intelligence Committee next year. As speaker, Jeffries would appoint Democrats to the committee.
U.S. Rep.-elect Luke Bronin confirmed during new member orientation that he’d support Jeffries for speaker. Bronin defeated U.S. Rep. John Larson in the Democratic primary for Connecticut’s 1st Congressional District.
Jeffries supported Larson’s reelection bid and came to Hartford to campaign with the longtime congressman before Connecticut’s summer primary. At the time, Bronin said leadership should spend “less time protecting people who’ve been in Congress for decades and more time working to lift up a new generation of Democrats to help us build a stronger, more energetic, more effective Democratic Party.”
In an interview a day before the speaker vote, Bronin said Jeffries has never gotten the chance to wield the gavel and lead from the majority party.
“He’s kept a Democratic caucus together in very difficult times, and he has stayed laser-focused on the twin missions of affordability for working families and accountability for a president who’s out of control,” Bronin said Tuesday. “And after two terms in the minority, without the votes to make make change, I think he’s earned the chance to lead a majority to make the change we need.”
That’s something U.S. Rep. Joe Courtney, D-2nd District, echoed as someone who’s been in the minority party for the past four years.
Courtney, who was first elected in 2006, said he’s served in the minority party in previous sessions and has seen more progress and even some victories this time around. He pointed to the number of discharge petitions, a procedural tool that allows the minority to force votes on the House floor if they collect a majority of signatures. The eastern Connecticut congressman also credited Jeffries with navigating government funding fights on top of not funding federal immigration agencies like ICE through regular appropriations.
“I think he really helped fashion the winning message, and I think the fact that there was no declared opponent kind of speaks volumes about the fact that people who know him up close really think he’s going to do good job,” Courtney said in an interview on his way into the House chamber to vote. “There definitely were some successful moments for a minority.”
For the remaining weeks of the session and in the new Congress, Jeffries will continue to work closely with U.S. Rep. Rosa DeLauro, D-3rd District, who is poised to take the gavel of the influential House Appropriations Committee.
Jeffries has pointed to DeLauro as one of the main negotiators working on government funding, which runs out after Dec. 11, and funding for the war in Iran. But by next year, DeLauro will be at the helm of the committee and will have a different negotiating posture.
Opposition efforts
A number of progressive and grassroots organizations in Connecticut have been rallying for alternatives to both Jeffries and Schumer.
Local groups such as Connecticut 50501 and Black Lives Matter 860 held a rally over the weekend in Hartford in the hopes of pressuring Connecticut’s lawmakers to vote differently. They want Blumenthal and U.S. Sen. Chris Murphy, who is currently recovering from a stroke at a rehabilitation center, to support Van Hollen over Schumer. And they wanted House members to support U.S. Rep. Ayanna Pressley, D-Mass., who was floated as a potential challenger but didn’t mount a formal bid.
“Both Chuck Schumer and Hakeem Jeffries have proven time and time again through their votes that they stand for the establishment, for the billionaire class, for corporations, and not for us,” Alison Greenlaw, CT 50501’s Hartford County lead organizer, said in a statement. “Both accept significant contributions from AIPAC, which lobbies on behalf of foreign Israeli interests, not those of the American people. Neither supports Medicare for all. Neither supports abolishing ICE. Neither will vote to end the war in Iran. These are the clearly articulated priorities of the American people. If they do not support our priorities, they cannot set the agenda for the next two years.”
Greenlaw said groups like hers haven’t heard from Connecticut’s federal lawmakers in response to their push. She said they’ll be drafting a letter to political leaders and “exploring additional methods of applying pressure, based on their responsiveness, including future protests.”
Courtney said some of the calls to his office were “couched with caveats” acknowledging no one’s challenging Jeffries or from people saying they ultimately trust Courtney’s judgment during the final speaker vote in January. But the congressman said others were “definitely very fired up.”
U.S. Rep. Jahana Hayes, D-5th District, said she also heard a lot of feedback from constituents and people around Connecticut.
“No one else is running. But also he’s done a good job, and he’s never led in the majority,” Hayes said in an interview outside of the Capitol on Tuesday afternoon. “I’ve got a lot of pushback, and I’ve tried to ask people, ‘Well, who would you suggest?’ And people either have no suggestions, or the names that they’re floating are people who are not even interested.”
“We have to be ready to lead on Jan. 3, so I don’t want us to be in a situation like the Republicans were with McCarthy,” Hayes said, referring to Republican Kevin McCarthy who struggled in multiple speaker votes in 2023 and was removed later that year.
Democrats are trying to look beyond leadership elections and give a sense of the agenda they’ll pursue next year with both majorities, though they’ll still need to contend with President Donald Trump’s veto authority over the next two years.
Jeffries has already outlined the early days of House Democrats’ majority. In a press conference a day before the internal elections, the congressman appeared to align with progressive U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders’ healthcare agenda with support for lowering the age for Medicare eligibility, including vision, hearing and dental care, and more. He said that’ll help “on our march toward universal health coverage.”
The New York Democrat said he also wants to end the war in Iran as well as Trump’s tariffs, restore the enhanced Affordable Care Act subsidies that expired at the end of 2025, reverse Medicaid cuts enacted through the GOP’s major tax bill and implement campaign finance reform.
When the 120th Congress convenes on Jan. 3, the full House will vote on speaker. Jeffries will need a simple majority.

name: Source New Mexico
title: Aging experts call for expanded early detection of mental health conditions in older New Mexicans
description: A panel of state health and aging experts this week emphasized the need for earlier detection of mental health conditions and cognitive decline in older New Mexicans to better connect them and their caregivers with available services.
text:
Attendees during lunch at the Annual Conference on Aging, hosted by the New Mexico Aging & Long-Term Services Department, Oct. 19–21, 2026, in Glorieta. (Photo by Leah Romero for Source NM)A panel of state health and aging experts this week emphasized the need for earlier detection of mental health conditions and cognitive decline in older New Mexicans to better connect them and their caregivers with available services.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The panel was part of a two-day Western Governors’ Association mental health workshop held in Santa Fe this week and hosted by Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham, Hawaii Gov. Josh Green. The healthy aging panel included New Mexico Aging and Long Term Services Department Secretary Emily Kaltenbach, Department of Health Secretary Gina DeBlassie, AARP New Mexico Director Joseph Roybal-Sánchez and CHRISTUS St. Vincent Center for Healthy Aging Medical Director Ann Garcia. 
Kaltenbach set the tone of the discussion by noting that one in four New Mexicans will be over the age of 65 by 2030, moving the state up to fourth in the country with the highest population of seniors. And currently, about 9% of seniors earn an annual income of only $10,000. The largely rural nature of the state means access to health services can be difficult for many to reach.
“We’re a very rural state, so social isolation is a significant issue here in New Mexico,” Kaltenbach said. “Twenty-seven percent of our older adults live alone, and many of them live in far reaches of the state. In fact, we have a county on the western part of the state that’s still designated frontier federally, and so people have to travel hours to get to their nearest service center.”
She said distance and financial barriers make senior centers and community health centers important places for older residents to connect with services, but also “entry points” where early detection of cognitive decline or mental health conditions can occur, if staff have the correct training. She added that mental health and cognitive challenges can go unrecognized because they are thought of as “normal parts of aging.”
Garcia said as a medical practitioner, she often finds that family members recognize subtle changes in older loved ones before they recognize it themselves, or before being seen by medical professionals. Other patients are brought in for mental health and cognition screenings by people they interact with at church, community programs or other non-clinical settings.
“But that process is challenging in itself. For them, it might take months, even years, to convince their family member to seek care,” Garcia said. 
DeBlassie added that her department sees an influx of people coming in for screenings around the holidays when family members are in town and spending extended time with older adults and start recognizing possible issues. She said DOH mobile health units can act in the same way for early detection, particularly in rural areas of the state.
“There’s no wrong door as it relates to recognizing when somebody is in need of help or support, and then with that, ensuring that the workforce that is out there or the community also knows where to refer individuals to get those services,” DeBlassie said. 
Roybal-Sánchez said the state and providers should be working to be more proactive than reactive in identifying issues and helping older adults connect with the services to support them in their communities, before these conditions worsen.
“We need to stop waiting for a crisis to happen to act,” he said. “Early identification should be a routine part of health aging, not something that happens only after being hospitalized, a fall at home or a family emergency.”
The panel agreed that growing the caregiving and health care workforce would improve outcomes for older adults, along with training them and informal caregivers in early detection of mental health conditions and expanding New MexiCare, or similar programs in other states, to pay and train caregivers. Roybal-Sánchez added that the federal Older Americans Act, passed in 1965 and most recently reauthorized in 2020, should be updated and reauthorized to better set up states with funding and care parameters.

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: Former Oklahoma legislator, teacher to serve as Education Department chief of staff
description: OKLAHOMA CITY — State Superintendent-elect Robert Franklin has chosen a former House education leader for a top role in his administration. Former Rep. Rhonda Baker, R-Yukon, will serve as Franklin’s chief of staff at the Oklahoma State Department of Education, the agency announced Wednesday. Franklin and his staff will take office in January. Baker was […]
text:
Rep. Rhonda Baker, R-Yukon, attends the governor's State of the State Address on Feb. 5, 2024, at the state Capitol in Oklahoma City. (Photo by Kyle Phillips/For Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY — State Superintendent-elect Robert Franklin has chosen a former House education leader for a top role in his administration.
Former Rep. Rhonda Baker, R-Yukon, will serve as Franklin’s chief of staff at the Oklahoma State Department of Education, the agency announced Wednesday. Franklin and his staff will take office in January.
Baker was a longtime English teacher before she served in the state House from 2016 to 2024, when she chose not to seek reelection. She led the House Common Education Committee and served on a subcommittee focused on school funding. Since leaving office, she’s worked as the education director for the Greater Oklahoma City Chamber.
“I have seen firsthand the dedication of our teachers and school leaders, and I believe strongly in what we can accomplish when we work together around common goals,” Baker said. “This is an opportunity to listen, build strong partnerships and help create a brighter future for every Oklahoma student.”
Chief of staff often serves as the right hand of the state superintendent in directing operations and staffing at the Education Department.
State Superintendent-elect Robert Franklin attends an Oklahoma Watch education forum Nov. 12 at Oklahoma City Community College in Oklahoma City. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)
Franklin said he’s building a leadership team at the agency “that understands education from the classroom to the state level.”
“Rhonda brings that experience, along with a deep commitment to public service and a proven ability to bring people together,” he said.
Franklin will succeed state Superintendent Lindel Fields, who was announced earlier this week as Gov.-elect Mike Mazzei’s incoming chief of staff.
Fields said he will support a smooth transition from his administration to Franklin’s.
“As we prepare for this transition, it is encouraging to see experienced education leaders stepping forward to serve,” Fields said. “Rhonda brings valuable knowledge and a commitment to Oklahoma’s students and educators.”

name: West Virginia Watch
title: West Virginia evaluating optional Medicaid work requirement grace period
description: The state of West Virginia is still deciding whether or not to take advantage of an optional six month grace period for Medicaid recipients who will be subject to work requirements under federal legislation.
text:
The West Virginia Department of Human Services' website, wvmedicaidhelp.org, explains the changes coming to the program in January on Nov. 11, 2026. (Photo by Leann Ray/West Virginia Watch)The state of West Virginia is still deciding whether or not to take advantage of an optional six month grace period for Medicaid recipients who will be subject to work requirements under federal legislation.
“No decision has been made, as our priority remains ensuring that any actions taken are in the best interest of the West Virginians who depend on these programs,” Angel Hightower, a communications specialist for the state Department of Human Services, wrote to West Virginia Watch in an email Tuesday.
Under Republicans’ One Big Beautiful Bill Act, low income adults who are on expanded Medicaid under the Affordable Care Act will be required to work, volunteer or train for 80 hours each month in order to keep their health coverage, unless otherwise exempt. 
The work requirements have been planned to take effect Jan. 1. The federal Centers for Medicare and Medicaid last week announced an optional “hold harmless” period through June 2027, during which time states will assess whether individuals meet the work requirement but not deny applications or disenroll people who are otherwise eligible for the program based on the work requirements. 
The grace period will give states time to “ improve and refine their systems,” and give them the “opportunity to learn from the early months of implementation to identify and address workforce training needs and improve the beneficiary experience,” CMS said in a news release. 
“States have made real progress, and they’ve been clear with us about what it takes to get this right for beneficiaries — at scale and for the long term,” Dan Brillman, deputy administrator and director of the Center for Medicaid and CHIP Services, said in the news release.
“If the state can use data to show that someone is working or qualifies for an exclusion, that person should not have to track down paperwork to prove it,” he said. “And when someone needs support, they should know exactly what to do, when to do it, and where to go. That’s how we build a Medicaid program that works better for people, connects them to work, education, and training opportunities, and supports paths to prosperity.”
About 40,000 West Virginia Medicaid recipients have been identified as not currently meeting the work requirements or qualifying for an exemption, meaning they could lose their healthcare under the work requirements, according to the latest estimate from the state Department of Human Services.

name: Honolulu Civil Beat
title: The AG’s Work Is Confidential. Except In This OHA Case
description: Stacy Ferreira reached out to the Attorney General’s Office asking for help. The Office of Hawaiian Affairs CEO hoped the state’s top law enforcement agency would investigate what she saw as misconduct by OHA’s board.  She claimed the board’s chair, Kai Kahele, had leaked private budget information to outside entities and coerced executive team members […]
text:
Stacy Ferreira reached out to the Attorney General’s Office asking for help. The Office of Hawaiian Affairs CEO hoped the state’s top law enforcement agency would investigate what she saw as misconduct by OHA’s board. 
She claimed the board’s chair, Kai Kahele, had leaked private budget information to outside entities and coerced executive team members to “fraudulently” certify a budget — allegations she claimed might violate laws or policies. 
Attorney General Anne Lopez has often emphasized that her office does not share information on pending matters so as not to jeopardize a potential case. Case information, her office has said, is confidential.
But apparently this one was not, according to records released by OHA this month as part of two internal investigations into the agency’s unfolding drama. After getting Ferreira’s tip, Lopez allegedly contacted Gov. Josh Green’s office. And then Green’s communications director Makana McClellan allegedly alerted the subject of the complaint: Kahele. 
“The Attorney General found it problematic that the CEO would solicit an investigation of OHA,” Kahele told an investigator, explaining how he learned about Ferreira’s complaint. “So much so that she contacted the Governor’s staff, and the senior-most staff member contacted me as the Chair to inform me.” 

Attorney General Anne Lopez addresses the ongoing bribery case involving an influential legislator.

Lopez’s office did not respond to questions about why her office notified Green’s staff about the complaint. An investigator hired by OHA ultimately found Ferreira’s claims without merit. 
Nevertheless, the suggestion that the state’s top cop would leak information to the governor and trigger a notice to the target of a complaint has sparked concerns among legal experts. The allegation seems to directly contradict the AG’s insistence that the office’s work is confidential and that the office is independent from political influence. And legal experts said it raises doubt about the office’s credibility with future whistleblowers, who often fear retaliation from those they’re complaining about. 
“We have problems if the system is rigged or leaked to the point where a whistleblower feels that they’re going to have their confidential information disseminated,” said Alexander Silvert, a retired federal public defender. “That’s going to be an issue with coming forward.”   
AG’s Office spokeswoman Toni Schwartz said in a statement that the AG conducts investigations independently and is committed to “protecting the integrity of those investigations.”
McClellan declined to discuss the situation and did not respond to requests to interview Green. 
“We cannot comment on pending legal matters,” she said. 
OHA chair Kai Kahele, middle, said Gov. Green’s communications director, Makana McClellan, told him last year that a complaint had been filed against him with the AG’s Office. Jamm Aquino/Civil Beat/2026
The report doesn’t say why the AG may have found Ferreira’s report “problematic,” as Kahele stated, but it notes Ferreira as CEO was supposed to get approval from the Board of Trustees before seeking a legal opinion from the AG’s Office, which she didn’t do. 
Ferreira directed a reporter to her attorney who did not reply to a request for comment. Bill Brennan, OHA spokesman, said Kahele was traveling and unavailable for comment. 
After Kahele was informed about the complaint against him, the Office of Hawaiian Affairs put Ferreira on leave. Ferreira then sued Kahele and the Board of Trustees, claiming he put her on leave in retaliation for making the report with the AG’s Office. That lawsuit is pending.
Latest From Civil Beat
OHA had hired two independent firms to investigate Ferreira’s claims against Kahele as well as allegations against Ferreira, including that she failed to disclose a romantic relationship with a nonprofit founder who was in the running for a grant and that she obstructed passage of the office’s 2025 budget.
The Hawaiʻi Whistleblower Protection Act is supposed to shield the type of retaliation Ferreira claims she faced. Though the statute doesn’t address when and how the AG’s Office is allowed to share information about complaints, whistleblowers who come forward have an expectation of confidentiality when they file complaints, said Scot Brower, a Honolulu attorney who specializes in whistleblower cases.  
Having the target of a complaint find out about it too soon could compromise any investigation, he said.  
“The person who’s allegedly committing the crime, they could destroy their records, they could hide stuff, they could take a plane out of town,” he said, speaking generally. “That’s why they have secret grand jury proceedings, because you don’t want the target to know what’s going on.” 
‘Prosecutorial Independence’ 
Hawaiʻi’s attorney general has a unique position providing legal counsel across state government to the governor, the Legislature and executive agencies. This means that lawyers within the same department may serve clients with distinct, and sometimes competing, interests. 
Simultaneously, as the state’s top law enforcement office, the attorney general may also be called upon to investigate those clients. 
That split role has, at times, attracted scrutiny. 
Lopez held a press conference in February to assure the public that she could operate completely independently of the governor who appointed her as she investigated some of his colleagues in the state’s most recent bribery scandal. The case centers on a local businessman who allegedly bribed state officials to secure lucrative Covid-19 testing contracts during the pandemic. 
Former Lt. Gov. Sylvia Luke was indicted on bribery charges in July after a nearly six-month investigation by the Attorney General’s office.  Craig Fujii/Civil Beat/2026
During the press conference, Lopez assured reporters that she hadn’t shared any information with the governor about the investigation that hadn’t already been made public. At the time, a coalition of government accountability advocates had called on Lopez to get a special prosecutor to investigate the corruption case, saying Lopez couldn’t conduct a fair investigation into Lt. Gov. Sylvia Luke, Green’s No. 2. 
But Lopez also assured the public that she wouldn’t be influenced by politics. 
“This prosecutorial independence is really important,” she said at the time. “And it’s one that (Green) and I have talked about since the very beginning and that we have both been committed to — that I promised I wouldn’t be a politician, and he promised that that prosecutorial independence is crucial to this department.” 
Five months later, an Oʻahu grand jury indicted Luke, three other state officials and a lobbyist in a sweeping conspiracy case. A trial is scheduled for Aug. 2. 
Green was vocal throughout the investigation that he was frustrated by its slow pace. On April 14, he told Hawaiʻi News Now’s “Spotlight Now” program that he expected to have an answer about Luke’s role in the case by the following Monday. That Wednesday, Luke’s attorney at the time, David Louie, confirmed she had received a target letter in the investigation. The following day, Luke announced she would take a leave of absence from her role as lieutenant governor. 
Green’s press secretary, Erika Engle, said in an email the AG often briefs Green on “matters that will be made public. Such briefings are distinct from providing substantive updates on an active investigation.” 
But the revelations about the OHA complaint have brought concerns about information sharing to a new level. 

Alexander Silvert, a former federal public defender, filed a petition with the Legislature in January asking them to investigate bribery allegations. Craig Fujii/Civil Beat/2026

In Silvert’s opinion, the information about the OHA complaint had no reason to reach the governor’s office. Leaks like this further blur the lines of independence and undermine public trust in the justice system, he said. 
“If a complaint’s filed, at some point you have to tell the person who the complaint’s against that there’s been a complaint filed against them so that they can respond,” he said. “That’s just due process.” 
But, he added, “You’re not supposed to hear it from the executive branch.” 
Robert Harris, executive director and general counsel of the state Ethics Commission, said the state law prohibits state employees from disclosing confidential information they learned through their work. 
For example, in 2023, a former legal clerk for the AG’s Office was cited $1,000 for violating the state code of ethics by emailing confidential information about a lawsuit to the opposing counsel. Back in 2019, an OHA board member was found to have violated the ethics code by disclosing information from executive session meetings. She was fined $1,500. 
In the case of the AG’s office sharing information about the OHA complaint with the governor’s staff, it isn’t clear whether the existence of the complaint would be considered confidential, Harris said. Some information, such as people’s medical information, is deemed confidential by statute, while other types of information are agency specific and internal policies dictate what is considered confidential and what’s not. 
Schwartz, the AG’s office spokesperson, did not respond to requests to provide any internal office policies regarding sharing information about pending investigations and the handling of whistleblower complaints. 
She did say, however, that “as a general matter, the Department of the Attorney General does not disclose the existence or status of investigations” in order to “protect and maintain the integrity of the investigative process.” 
She did not respond to a follow-up question about why, according to Kahele’s account, the office disclosed information about the OHA matter. 
Elected vs. Appointed 
Even though AGs are appointed by the governor, the governor can’t unilaterally fire them, unlike other department heads that serve at the pleasure of the governor. Removal of an attorney general requires a two-thirds vote of the Senate.  
This, some experts say, gives the AG a level of autonomy and independence. But critics of the model say it doesn’t make the AG independent enough. 
The governor can choose a new AG every time he or she reorganizes his cabinet, as Green has done. Green announced last week that Lopez’s first deputy, Matthew Dvonch, would succeed her. His appointment requires Senate confirmation. 
Gov. Josh Green nominated Lopez’s first deputy, Matthew Dvonch, to serve as his next attorney general. (Screenshot: Hawaiʻi Legislature hearing/2026)
Dvonch declined a request to discuss what level of confidentiality the AG’s office, under his leadership, will apply when it receives a request for an investigation. 
Camron Hurt, executive director of the government accountability group Common Cause Hawaiʻi, thinks the state should explore a constitutional amendment to require that attorney generals be elected, as they are in most other states. 
Hawaiʻi is one of only five states where the governor appoints the attorney general. 
“I believe that everybody truly does want to be independent, but how are you independent from your boss?” Hurt said. “If your boss is the people, then that’s who you’re working for, and those are the people who are going to hire and fire you, and I think that makes much more sense.” 
The Legislature did consider a bill in 2016 to make the attorney general and judges elected.  Then-state Sen. Gil Keith-Agaran, who introduced the bill, said he did so just to start a conversation about the idea. 
“I thought it was worth a listen, since we are an outlier,” he said.
The bill passed the Senate and was referred to the House Judiciary Committee, where it did not get a hearing. Then-state Rep. Karl Rhoads, who was chair of the committee at the time, said he didn’t like the idea of politicizing the role of attorney general. The provision of state law shielding AGs from being fired by governors in the middle of a term, in his view, is sufficient to ensure their independence. 
“I think that’s a good safeguard,” he said. 
Former Hawaiʻi Attorney General Doug Chin testified against a bill introduced in 2016 that would have changed attorney general to an elected position.  Kevin Fujii/Civil Beat/2023
While two individuals who testified in favor of the bill said they supported the idea and felt it would give more power back to the people, three former attorneys general testified against it, as did as Doug Chin, who was attorney general at the time.
Requiring attorneys general to campaign for re-election would distract them from their duties, Chin said. And asking them to fundraise could also subject them to accusations of being influenced by campaign contributors. 
“If an attorney general is not acting with the independence the State Constitution contemplates, then that attorney general should be reminded of the unique prerogative the State Constitution accords to the office,” he wrote. “It should not be necessary to abandon what has been the practice under the law in Hawaii for more than 150 years.”

name: Honolulu Civil Beat
title: Kamehameha Makes Its Case To Block Admissions Lawsuit
description: The lawsuit marks the fourth time the school's admissions policy has been challenged. School officials remain confident they will prevail again.
text:
Kamehameha Schools has asked a federal judge to dismiss a lawsuit challenging its more than 140-year-old admissions policy that gives a preference to students of Native Hawaiian ancestry.
The school was created from the estate of Princess Bernice Pauahi Bishop at a time of steep population decline among Native Hawaiians and shrinking opportunities for education. That estate now controls land and financial assets valued at well over $15 billion.
Last October, the group Students for Fair Admissions sued the school alleging that its admissions policy discriminates against non-Hawaiians and violates parts of the Civil Rights Act. 
In court and in legal filings, the group’s attorneys have turned prior civil rights cases on their heads: lawsuits originally intended to fight the segregation of Black and other minority students are being used in an attempt to pry open Kamehameha’s doors to other races too.
Lawyers and Kamehameha’s supporters have painted the lawsuit as not just an attack on the admissions policy but an assault on Native Hawaiians that seeks to take resources meant for them.
“This lawsuit,” Kamehameha lawyer John Bash said during a hearing Tuesday, “is trying to siphon off this wealth for the benefit of other people.”
The admissions policy is one of several landmark Hawaiian programs facing legal attacks including the Hawaiian Homes Commission Act — which guarantees a homestead lot to those who can prove they have 50% or more Hawaiian blood — and a Native Hawaiian health scholarship.
Kamehameha Schools CEO Jack Wong, middle, and attorney Joachim P. Cox, back, mingle with students, staff ahead of a key hearing on Tuesday. (Jamm Aquino/Civil Beat/2026)
“We enter this courtroom with the law on our side and an unwavering understanding of who we serve.” Crystal Rose, chair of Kamehameha School’s board of trustees
The admissions policy has been challenged at least three times before, with Kamehameha prevailing in each case. School officials remain confident they’ll be able to beat back this lawsuit as well.
“We enter this courtroom with the law on our side and an unwavering understanding of who we serve,” Crystal Rose, chair of the school’s board of trustees, said during a rally at Kamehameha’s downtown headquarters Tuesday morning. 
Rose was an attorney for Kamehameha 20 years ago, during the first admissions lawsuit.
Mason Fong, a senior at Kamehameha Kapālama, said students now have a duty to speak up and protect the school for future generations.
“Pauahi saw a future for us before we were born,” he said. “Today, we stand for the keiki we have yet to meet, so they have a place at Kamehameha.”
Hearing Focused On Admissions
Kamehameha students, all dressed in the school’s signature Navy blue polos, trustees and other school officials packed the federal courthouse for Tuesday’s hearing so much so that the court opened an overflow room for attendees who wanted to watch the hearing live.
As Kamehameha lawyers adorned with green maile lei took their seats and the legal team for the SFFA appeared on Zoom, court security took the unusual step of addressing the packed courtroom, warning that outbursts could result in immediate removal from the courthouse.
The princess did not create Kamehameha “as an ordinary school teaching reading, writing and arithmetic,” KS attorney Bash told the court, “but to preserve Native Hawaiian culture and Native Hawaiian sovereignty for her people.”
Bash asked the court to dismiss the lawsuit because the initial complaint filed in October 2025 included just the Students for Fair Admissions as plaintiffs representing two unidentified families, neither of whom actually applied to Kamehameha.
His other argument centered around the ability of two other plaintiffs added later, I.P. and E.S., to continue in the case. School lawyers have previously said that neither teen had the scores to advance to a stage of the admissions process where ancestry would be considered.
Lines of students, media and Kamehameha School officials snaked around the steps of the federal courthouse prior to the hearing. (Blaze Lovell/Civil Beat/2026)
The school has a two-step admissions process. In step one, applicants face a battery of tests and either participate in interviews or a classroom visit. Composite scores are compiled based on that stage as well as their recommendation letters and report cards from their previous schools.
Once applicants are ranked, the top scorers are offered seats and only then does ancestry come into play, according to a court declaration from a school admissions official.
Are Contracts Race-Based?
Based on his line of questioning, District Judge Micah Smith did not appear inclined to grant Kamehameha an outright dismissal of the case. Rather, he implied that he would allow Students for Fair Admissions and the other plaintiffs to amend their complaint and investigate Kamehameha’s claims that ancestry is not considered in the initial stages of the application process.
But attorneys for the plaintiffs said doing so could be unfair to them as it may result in the plaintiffs having to argue the core of their case — the admissions process — in front of the judge at a relatively early stage instead of in front of a jury.
“It’s the whole case: How does the admissions process work?” plaintiffs attorney Cam Norris said.
Latest From Civil Beat
In opposing the school’s motion to dismiss the case, Norris argued that because Hawaiians are not federally recognized, they are considered a race, like white, Black, Asian and Hispanic. He pointed to the U.S. Supreme Court’s decision in Rice v. Cayetano that eliminated Native Hawaiian-only voting in elections for the Office of Hawaiians Affairs as well as decades of court rulings that have struck down segregation of schools based on race.
Part of the SFFA’s case revolves around a section of the Civil Rights Act having to do with protection from discrimination in contracts. Since then, Kamehameha has attempted to recast its relationship with students as providing a gift in the form of free tuition instead of entering into a contract.
After Kamehameha made tuition free for all students last year, the Legislature, attempting to aid Kamehameha, subsequently passed a law that said such arrangements are considered gifts and not contractural obligations.
Norris said contracts between Kamehameha and its students still exist if there’s an implicit agreement that students receive a diploma at the end of their schooling. And he said contracts exist at Kamehameha in the form of such things as housing agreements, medical waivers, sports participation agreements, and even use of campus vending machines. And if those contracts are race-based, he argued, then the lawsuit should still stand.
On rebuttal, Bash said Native Hawaiians are not a race, but have a special political status and trust relationship with the federal government first demonstrated under the Hawaiian Homes Commission Act and dozens of other federal laws since then, including after the Rice v. Cayetano ruling in 2000.
As for the contracts and agreements Kamehameha still has on campus, Bash called them “gift conditions” and said none implicate race. For example, Bash — a white, Republican, former U.S. attorney from Texas and special assistant to President Donald Trump, who at one point was in the running to replace Ken Paxton as state attorney general — said he had no trouble using an on-campus vending machine recently.
In the end, the judge did not immediately rule on Kamehameha’s motion to dismiss the case. Smith also left the courtroom without indicating when he might issue a ruling, but previous decisions in the case have come in a couple weeks of a hearing.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: County employers oppose proposed 24% rate increase for West Virginia public insurance plan
description: Representatives of local governments whose employees use West Virginia state health insurance coverage raised concerns Tuesday with a proposal to raise the rates for one plan by 24% in the coming fiscal year.
text:
Kanawha County Sheriff Joey Crawford speaks to the West Virginia Public Employees Insurance Agency finance board Tuesday during a hearing about the agency’s proposals for fiscal 2028. (Photo by Lori Kersey/West Virginia Watch)Representatives of local governments whose employees use West Virginia state health insurance coverage raised concerns Tuesday with a proposal to raise the rates for one plan by 24% in the coming fiscal year. 
About 50 people attended a public hearing of the West Virginia Public Employees Insurance Agency finance board at the state Capitol Complex in Charleston, West Virginia, Tuesday evening. The meeting was one of six the board has held around the state this month to hear feedback about its proposals for the 2028 fiscal year, which starts in July 2027. 
The finance board has proposed a modest aggregate premium increase of 2% for state workers and employers and a 4% aggregate increase for non-state workers in the gold, silver and bronze high deductible plans. 
Medicare and non-Medicare retirees will not have premium increases in fiscal year 2028, according to PEIA’s proposal. 
For but for non-state employees who participate in the gold high deductible health plan, the board proposes a 24% increase. 
According to the board’s presentation, PEIA actuaries predict the non-state fund expenses will exceed premium revenues by around $10 million, mainly because of the gold high deductible plan’s poor performance. 
If the trends continue, PEIA projects the non-state fund will finish 2027 with a reserve of around $20 million, which would be below its 10% minimum statutory reserve and its actuarial reserve requirement of $26.3 million. 
PEIA director Brent Wolfingbarger said the plan is projected to finish the year with an “unsustainable” medical loss ratio of 119.4%, meaning the cost of medical claims exceeded premium revenue.
About 5,000 policy holders, amounting to 32% of nonstate employees enrolled in PEIA, are on the gold high deductible plan, he said. 
“The poor financial performance of the non-state fund gold high deductible health plan is longstanding and has not improved despite past premium increases and benefit changes,” Wolfingbarger said. “Moreover, the number of both non-state policyholders and non-state members enrolled in the old high deductible plan have almost quadrupled since fiscal year 2021, which has substantially increased the non-state fund’s overall financial exposure.”
He said the 24% increase is necessary to “properly price the plan’s risk” according to its historical performance and to reduce the medical loss ratio. 
With high deductible plans, policy holders pay less out of their paychecks in monthly premiums, and pay more out of pocket for medical costs like doctors visits. 
Local government employers sometimes contribute to employees’ health savings accounts to offset those out-of-pocket costs, a practice that Wolfingbarger discouraged. Officials said funding the health savings accounts lead to employees going to the doctor more often, which contributes to rising costs and the plan’s poor performance.
Kanawha County Commissioner Natalie Tennant said increasing the rate for the gold high deductible by a “staggering” 24% this year is unfair. 
“It’s our county employees who participate in PEIA in that very plan,” she told the finance board. “Yes, some folks were saying, ‘Who has that plan?’ It’s Kanawha County. We’re looking at 24% across county government and our participating independent agencies.”
Including Kanawha County, Kanawha County Metro 911 and the Kanawha County Ambulance Authority, about 600 workers use the gold high deductible plan, county finance director Kim Fleck said.
The plan saves money for the county and for employees, Fleck said. The county has funded the employee health savings accounts for the plans in lieu of offering pay increases, she said. 
Tennant said the gold high deductible plan saved the county nearly $1 million. Kanawha County officials disagreed with Wolfingbarger that funding employees’ health savings accounts leads to them going to the doctor more often. 
“We’re not encouraging them. We’re trying to just offer something a little extra to the employees because we can’t do things like the raises,” Fleck said.
Tennant asked the board to consider other solutions before implementing the rate increase, or consider implementing it in phases.
Kanawha Sheriff Joey Crawford echoed Tennant’s suggestion to spread out the proposed increase. He said PEIA rate increases make it difficult to recruit and retain deputies. 
“They apply, we tell them what their benefit packages are. We tell them what their salaries are, and we sit down and explain to them we want the best and the brightest. We want you to come to work for us. But then I have to go in and say, ‘last year our premium increase was 24%.’ That hurts,” Crawford said.
The PEIA finance board is expected to take up its proposals for 2028 at its December meeting, planned for 1 p.m., Dec. 3

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Lawsuit seeks federal action to protect North Pacific gray whales
description: Three conservation groups sued the Trump administration on Tuesday over its failure to grant Endangered Species Act protections to the gray whales that swim along North America’s West Coast. The lawsuit, filed in U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California, comes after gray whale numbers declined precipitously and a toll of dead whales […]
text:
A gray whale and her healthy calf swim in the Pacific waters off Washington. Calf production in the Eastern North Pacific gray whale population has dropped precipitiously. A newly filed lawsuit is seeking Endangered Species Act protections for the population. (Image courtesy of NOAA Fisheries/ Alaska Fisheries Science Center)Three conservation groups sued the Trump administration on Tuesday over its failure to grant Endangered Species Act protections to the gray whales that swim along North America’s West Coast.
The lawsuit, filed in U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California, comes after gray whale numbers declined precipitously and a toll of dead whales found from Mexico to Alaska has mounted.
The plaintiffs are Oasis Earth, which is based in Alaska; the Center for Biological Diversity, a national organization; and the California-based Earth Island Institute’s International Marine Mammal Project. The defendants are the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s National Marine Fisheries Service, its administrator and U.S. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, whose department oversees NOAA.
The lawsuit faults the Trump administration for missed legal deadlines to respond to an Endangered Species Act listing that Oasis Earth submitted in August of 2025.    
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX. 

That petition cited a sharp decline in gray whale abundance and calf births over the past decade. The number of Eastern North Pacific gray whales was about 26,960, according to a 2015-2016 estimate. But the 2025-2026 estimate puts the total number at about half that, around 14,500, according to NOAA’s California-based Southwest Fisheries Science Center
The latest tally puts this year’s gray whale die-off at 192 animals, including 31 deaths along the coast of Washington state and 27 in Alaska, according to the plaintiffs. That follows a designated “unusual mortality event” of 2019 to 2023, in which 690 gray whales were found dead between Mexico and Alaska. NOAA scientists said the deaths and a corresponding drop in the birth rate were likely the result of changes in sea ice cover in the Alaska summer feeding grounds and reductions in gray whale prey.
A spokesperson for NOAA, reached by email, declined to comment on the lawsuit filed Tuesday, citing the agency’s policy on pending litigation.
The listing petition “remains under consideration,” said the spokesperson, Michael Milstein of NOAA Fisheries’ Southwest Fisheries Science Center.
Eastern and Western populations
The lawsuit, which seeks to compel action on the listing petition, is specific to the Eastern North Pacific population segment of gray whales. Those whales migrate between Mexico and Alaska along the North American coast.
The Western North Pacific population segment, which is found off the coast of Asia, remains listed as endangered. That population segment is believed to have fewer than 300 animals, and they are found between Russia’s Sakhalin Island and Kamchatka Peninsula, according to NOAA.
The Eastern North Pacific population segment has been listed as endangered in the past. The endangered listing was removed in 1994 after the National Marine Fisheries Service, also known as NOAA Fisheries, determined that the population had rebounded to historic levels. A 1999 review affirmed that the population was healthy enough to not need Endangered Species Act protections.
But recent information about the population and effects of the die-offs has been hard to obtain, said Rick Steiner, Oasis Earth’s founder.
NMFS has not publicly released recent information on this year’s whale deaths, Steiner said by email. “The only conduit for this info to the public has been us asking NMFS for the updates and then us collectively releasing that data to the public,” he said. The agency had not released this year’s calf count, either, he said. The plaintiffs estimate this year’s calf count was as low as the record low recorded in 2025, he said. 
“The agency is obviously trying to hide the severity of the gray whale decline from the public,” Steiner said.
The 85 calves born in 2025 was the lowest count since agency counts began in 1994, according to NOAA.
According to the listing petition and the lawsuit that followed it, the main threat to Eastern North Pacific gray whales comes from climate change.
Because of climate change, which has induced sea ice loss and altered deepwater marine productivity and food ability, the feeding habitat in the Northern Bering Sea, Chukchi Sea and Beaufort Sea is “severely compromised,” the listing petition said.
Another threat is posed by ship strikes, which appear to have killed at least 14 gray whales this year, according to the lawsuit.
Threats also come from entanglements in fishing gear, oil spills and other pollution, according to the lawsuit and the listing petition.
A National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration-authorized team of marine mammal biologists perform a partial necropsy of a dead gray whale beached in the Copper River Delta, near Cordova, Alaska, May 17, 2019. The Coast Guard assisted in locating the whale and helping to collect tissue samples and photos of a 42-foot young adult female whale. Hundreds of dead gray whales have been found in recent years along the population’s West Coast migration route between Mexico and Alaska. (Photo by Petty Officer 3rd Class Tyler Demers/U.S. Coast Guard)

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Investigation finds Bemidji schools mishandled sexual harassment, assault allegations for years
description: At least a dozen Bemidji Area Public Schools employees, including an assistant principal, sexually harassed and assaulted students over the past two decades in a pattern of sex-based discrimination that violates state law, according to an investigation released Wednesday by the Minnesota Department of Human Rights.  The district routinely failed to report in[...]
text:
(Photo by Getty Images) At least a dozen Bemidji Area Public Schools employees, including an assistant principal, sexually harassed and assaulted students over the past two decades in a pattern of sex-based discrimination that violates state law, according to an investigation released Wednesday by the Minnesota Department of Human Rights. 
The district routinely failed to report incidents of sexual harassment and sexual assault to law enforcement and the Minnesota Department of Education, as mandated by law, according to a memorandum from the human rights department. 
On multiple occasions, either a school principal or the director of human resources referred an employee to an “employee assistance program,” rather than disciplining the employee or reporting the conduct to law enforcement or the state Department of Education. In multiple instances, district administrators deemed the reports of sexual abuse or sexual harassment made by girls not credible and did not investigate further.
“For years, Bemidji Area Schools received warnings that educators were sexually harassing students, including children as young as kindergarten. Yet the district repeatedly failed to take effective action. In some cases, educators continued to work with students after multiple complaints,” Department of Human Rights Commissioner Rebecca Lucero said in a statement. 
The district, which serves about 4,700 students, did not make changes to its training or policies after multiple law enforcement investigations revealed criminal sexual behavior involving district staff. All but one of the alleged incidents involved male staff members and female students.
The state will now seek an agreement requiring the school district to make changes, including new policies and practices, staff training and ongoing reporting to the state. If the state and the district cannot reach an agreement, the Department of Human Rights may file a lawsuit under the Minnesota Human Rights Act.
Jeremy Olson, the superintendent of Bemidji Area Schools since 2022, did not respond to messages Tuesday. In a statement to MPR news, district leadership said it “strongly disagrees with the Minnesota Department of Human Right findings” and that it continues to dispute charges.
“…the District takes all reports of sexual harassment seriously and promptly investigates the same. The District has policies in place prohibiting sexual harassment and conducts trainings for its staff regarding sexual harassment,” leaders told MPR.
The districtwide investigation was spurred by a June 2025 report from the parent of a female student who was subjected to “inappropriate behavior” by a male physical education teacher that culminated in “sexual abuse” in October 2024. The student now suffers from a range of impacts from the abuse, including panic attacks and suicidal ideation, according to the parent’s report.
The incident was also reported to local law enforcement. During the police investigation, investigators learned that the district knew about multiple previous incidents of sexual misconduct by the teacher. In a separate memorandum, the human rights department found probable cause that the district engaged in sex-based discrimination against the student assaulted in October 2024. 
The names of staff and students are redacted in the human rights department memoranda, as are the names of the schools where the alleged incidents took place.
Teacher 1
Teacher 1 was first alleged to have touched a kindergarten student under her underwear in 2008. The incident was reported to the state Department of Education and local law enforcement, but charges were not pursued. Similar incidents were reported in 2011, at which time the teacher was placed on leave. Teacher 1 was charged in January 2013 with “non-consensual sexual conduct” and died a week later.
Teacher 1 appears to be John Wangberg, who was charged in 2013 with two felony counts of sexual conduct in the second degree and a gross misdemeanor charge of non-consensual sexual conduct in the fifth degree. Wangberg died a week after his arraignment. Wangberg worked as a teacher in the school district from the mid-1980s through 2011.
Assistant Principal
State documents refer to an “Assistant Principal,” who was placed on leave from the district when law enforcement reported he was being investigated for criminal sexual misconduct in March 2017. At least 24 of his 50 alleged victims were district middle school students. He pleaded guilty to federal charges of “production of child pornography and coercion of a minor” and was sentenced to 300 months in prison.
The person appears to be Brandon Mark Bjerknes, who served as the assistant principal at Bemidji Middle School and was sentenced to 25 years in federal prison in 2018 for one count of coercion and enticement of a minor and one count of production of child pornography. 
Although the state does not find that the district could have prevented the crimes, investigators noted that the district “did not make significant changes to staff training or create policies or training on electronic communications with students” after learning from law enforcement about his criminal conduct. The district formally adopted a policy about employee-student relationships in 2026, according to the report.
Teacher 6
Teacher 6 was first reported to the school principal, Principal 3, for patting a student on the back and moving his hand down to touch her bottom in March 2017. Teacher 6 and Principal 3 transferred to a different elementary school in 2018, where additional allegations were made in 2019 and 2023 involving inappropriate comments to students and unwanted touching.
After an April 2023 incident, Teacher 6 was referred to the district’s employee assistance program and put on paid leave. Twelve days later, a therapist cleared him to return to work. Additional incidents were reported in November 2023, but Principal 3 did not file the mandatory reports with the state Department of Education or police.
The district’s then-human resources director sent a letter in 2024 to the state’s teacher licensing board, wrongly claiming the November incidents happened before the April incidents, and required no action. “The Minnesota Department of Human Rights’ investigation records did not support the timeline,” the human rights department memo states.
Another teacher reported Teacher 6 to the education department in March 2024, and the district received another report from an unnamed government agency about Teacher 6. The assistant principal interviewed the students involved in the alleged incidents and “concluded the reported incident was unfounded and took no further action.”
In October 2024, two students reported to their homeroom teacher that they felt uncomfortable around Teacher 6. Principal 3, the then-director of human resources and the student counselor were all notified. The district reported the incidents to the state and the parent of Student 4 reported the incident to local law enforcement. Teacher 6 was placed on paid leave.
In July 2025, Student 4’s parent filed a Title IX complaint with the school district, but the district found Teacher 6’s conduct did not meet the threshold of sexual harassment. 
The teacher’s last day of employment with the district was June 30, 2026.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Concern rises among Mississippians as US loses measles elimination status
description: Syringes are prepared for the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine at a clinic in Lubbock, Texas, on Feb. 26, 2025. (AP Photo/Mary Conlon)
text:
The United States lost its measles elimination status for the first time in more than 25 years, heightening concerns about a potential resurgence of the highly contagious, preventable illness in Mississippi.
State Health Officer Dr. Dan Edney warned Tuesday that, though the state has not reported an endemic case of measles since 1992, cases are “inevitable” as vaccination rates decline in certain parts of the state. 
“The way to protect our babies and our children from these vaccine-preventable illnesses is through vaccination,” Edney said Tuesday. “That is our best defense.” 
The Pan American Health Organization announced Tuesday that the U.S., Mexico and Bolivia lost measles elimination status, a designation for places that have halted sustained transmission of the virus for at least a year. 
There have been no endemic cases of measles in Mississippi since 1992, according to the Mississippi State Department of Health. 
“We haven’t seen measles in decades in Mississippi, but we know that it’s only a matter of time,” Dr. Anita Henderson, a Hattiesburg pediatrician and former president of the Mississippi chapter of the American Academy of Pediatrics, said Tuesday.


For years, Mississippi permitted only medical vaccine exemptions authorized by a doctor for school entry and boasted the highest kindergarten vaccination rates in the nation. That began to change in 2023 when a federal judge ruled that parents can opt out of vaccinating their children due to religious beliefs. 
During the 2025-2026 school year, vaccination rates for required kindergarten immunizations fell to 97.2% coverage. Eight counties fell below a 95% kindergarten vaccine coverage rate, the threshold experts consider necessary to prevent outbreaks of measles. These counties include Franklin, George, Jackson, Lincoln, Pontotoc, Tate, Tishomingo and Webster.
The number of religious vaccine exemptions increased by more than 60% during the 2025-2026 school year. That year, over 3,000 Mississippi students were approved for religious exemptions, compared to roughly 1,880 during the previous school year. 
Nationwide, more than 5,400 cases of the respiratory illness have been confirmed this year, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. The virus has largely spread among people who are unvaccinated.
State health departments have reported at least 10 deaths in 2026 alone. At least half of the deaths were children, including some who were too young to be vaccinated. 
International public health officials expect the U.S., Bolivia and Mexico to each submit a plan to stop transmission and regain elimination status, according to the Associated Press. 
Regaining measles elimination status will require coordinated action across public health agencies, health care providers, laboratories and communities, the CDC wrote in a Tuesday statement. 
“The measles elimination designation is not what protects Americans,” said CDC Director Dr. Erica Schwartz. “Vaccination does.”
In August and September, the CDC awarded $100 million in funding to support prevention and response to measles and other vaccine-preventable diseases.
Henderson said she urges parents to ensure their children are up to date on their measles vaccinations. She also advises parents of infants traveling internationally or to areas that have had measles outbreaks to speak with their pediatrician about early vaccinations. Adults, too, should ensure they are up to date on their vaccinations to protect children who are too young to be vaccinated.
“We’ve got to make sure that the adults and children around them are vaccinated,” Henderson said. 
Adults and children can receive vaccines at county health departments, Edney said. Measles, mumps and rubella vaccines are free for people without health insurance. 
Edney on Tuesday said the potential of a measles outbreak in Mississippi has broad ramifications for public health efforts, which are already underfunded. Preparation for a measles outbreak takes away funding from other work, like the state’s high infant mortality rates. 
“I’m having to divert resources to an area where we had achieved victory,” Edney said.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Two of Alaska’s legislative races are within five votes after ranked choice tabulations
description: One Republican member of the Alaska House of Representatives is losing his re-election bid by three votes, and another is winning by four after the Alaska Division of Elections conducted ranked choice runoff calculations Wednesday. According to Wednesday’s preliminary results, independents have won 7 of the 40 seats in the state House, Democrats have won […]
text:
Rep. Kevin McCabe, R-Big Lake, talks with Sen. Bill Wielechowski, D-Anchorage (right) during a joint session of the state House and Senate on Tuesday, May 7, 2024. At left is Rep. Zack Fields, D-Anchorage. (Photo by James Brooks/Alaska Beacon)One Republican member of the Alaska House of Representatives is losing his re-election bid by three votes, and another is winning by four after the Alaska Division of Elections conducted ranked choice runoff calculations Wednesday.
According to Wednesday’s preliminary results, independents have won 7 of the 40 seats in the state House, Democrats have won 17 and Republicans won 16. 
The state-level results appear to reflect the “blue tsunami” of Democratic-leaning outcomes in elections nationwide this month. 
Two years ago, Republicans won 21 seats in the state House, and the swing means the House will remain controlled by an emboldened coalition majority of Republicans, Democrats and independents.
The races will be certified Nov. 25, and recounts are possible afterward.


The two tight elections — both in the Matanuska-Susitna Borough — were among a handful of close races decided by Wednesday’s ranked choice tabulation.
In Alaska, all candidates for a particular office run together. The top four vote-getters in the August primary advance to the November general election, and voters are asked to rank the candidates in order of preference.
If one candidate gets at least 50% of the first-choice votes, they win. If none reach that threshold, the lowest finisher is eliminated, and votes for them go to their voters’ second choices. The eliminations continue until only two candidates are left, and the person with the most votes wins.
In the state Senate, where 10 of 20 seats were on the November ballot, Republicans still hold 11 seats, Democrats hold nine, and there is one independent — Sen.-elect Bryce Edgmon, I-Dillingham, whose election was confirmed by Wednesday’s tabulation. Edgmon replaces longtime Democratic Sen. Lyman Hoffman of Dillingham.
The Senate will be governed by an 11-person coalition majority, a smaller version of the coalition that has controlled it since 2023. 


All of the state’s closest legislative elections were in the Matanuska-Susitna Borough, where Democratic voters played an influential role in races with multiple Republicans.
In House District 30, which covers the western Mat-Su and the Denali Borough, Republican candidate Doug Massie is leading Republican Rep. Kevin McCabe by three votes.
McCabe led Massie in first-choice votes, but voters who backed Democratic candidate Sandra Loomis strongly favored Massie once Loomis was eliminated: Almost a fifth of her votes transferred to Massie, giving him a narrow lead. 
Next door, in the eastern Mat-Su’s House District 29, Republican Rep. Garret Nelson leads Republican challenger Steve Menard by four votes.
Nelson led Menard by fewer than 50 first-choice votes, but unlike in House District 30, the few Democratic-leaning voters who ranked at least one of the Republicans split evenly between them, allowing Nelson to preserve his advantage.
A similar pattern happened in House District 28, covering Wasilla. Republican Rep. Elexie Moore trailed Republican challenger Stephen Wright in first-choice votes but finished ahead of Democratic candidate Kit Kennedy. When Kennedy was eliminated, most of her supporters chose to rank neither Republican. A small plurality preferred Moore, but not enough to erase Wright’s advantage. He recorded a 46-vote win as of Wednesday night.
In Alaska, the state will pay for a recount if the margin is 20 or fewer votes, or less than 0.5% of the total of the votes for the two closest candidates. The recount must be requested by a candidate or 10 qualified voters in the area covered by the election.
McCabe said by text message that he intends to request a recount. It was not immediately clear whether Menard would do so.
Among the Mat-Su’s closely contested state Senate seats, Republican Sen. George Rauscher — appointed by Gov. Mike Dunleavy to replace Sen. Shelley Hughes, R-Palmer, after her resignation to run for governor — won election on his own merits in a ranked choice runoff.
Dunleavy also appointed Sen. Cathy Tilton, R-Wasilla, to replace Republican Sen. Mike Shower after he resigned to run for lieutenant governor. Tilton lost a ranked choice runoff to fellow Republican Ryan Berry by 467 votes.
Unlike in the close state House races, the elimination of Republican candidate Zane Vrvilo was enough to give Berry the edge; the subsequent elimination of Democratic candidate Pat Chesbro increased Berry’s lead via transfer votes.
Elsewhere in the state:

Sen.-elect Louise Stutes, R-Kodiak, was elected to replace Sen. Gary Stevens, R-Kodiak, in a three-way ranked choice runoff. Stutes had 49.9% of the first-choice votes, just barely short of the margin needed to avoid the runoff against two other Republicans.
Independent Brent Johnson defeated Republican Rep. Sarah Vance, R-Homer in a head-to-head race that was unresolved until Wednesday because of late-counted absentee ballots. Of 10,128 votes, Johnson defeated Vance by 59 according to the preliminary total.
In Anchorage, Republican Rep. Julie Coulombe defeated Democratic challenger Danni Hall by 131 votes out of 8,499 cast in House District 11. Democrats had spent heavily to boost Hall’s campaign.
Also in Anchorage, Democratic candidate Denny Wells confirmed his victory over Republican Rep. Mia Costello, winning in House District 15 by 669 votes in uncertified results Wednesday.
In Eagle River, Republican Rep. Jamie Allard won re-election in a four-way ranked choice runoff election that saw her leading in first-choice votes.
For the other Eagle River state House district, former Republican Rep. Ken McCarty won the election to replace retiring Republican Rep. Dan Saddler by defeating moderate Republican challenger Gina Wall. Though there were only two candidates, ranked choice tabulation was still used because neither had more than 50% of the vote, there were more than 100 write-in votes, and McCarty was leading Wall by just 19 first-choice ballots. The tabulation confirmed McCarty’s victory.
Rep. DeLena Johnson, R-Palmer, won re-election after a three-way ranked choice tabulation. She had led in first-choice votes.
North Pole Republican Rep. Mike Prax was re-elected after a three-way ranked choice runoff in House District 33. Republican challenger Barbara Haney was eliminated first, and Prax defeated independent Pepper McFarland in the final matchup. 
Democratic candidate Evelynn Trefon won the race to replace Edgmon in House District 37. She had 58.8% in the final tabulation, ahead of Republican candidate Brenda Wilson.
In House District 38, incumbent Democratic Rep. Nellie Unangiq Jimmie was re-elected after a ranked choice runoff. She had 58.2% in the final tabulation, ahead of second-place finisher and former Democratic Rep. CJ McCormick. 
Democratic incumbent Rep. Neal Foster, who had 49% of the first choice votes in House District 39, won in ranked choice tabulation. Independent candidate Tyler Ivanoff was second.
