name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Commentary: A river runs under it
description: One day in November 2024, Stephanie Pula returned home to the smell of sewage. She had left three days before to visit her grandmother. Upon her return, she saw the skirting around her manufactured home had been removed without notice. Underneath, she found towels soaked in cold sewage wrapped around the broken drain pipe that […]
text:
Stephanie Pula poses for a portrait outside of her house in The Meadows manufactured home community in Monticello, Minnesota the Thursday, Nov. 12, 2026. (Photo by Nicole Neri/Minnesota Reformer)One day in November 2024, Stephanie Pula returned home to the smell of sewage.
She had left three days before to visit her grandmother. Upon her return, she saw the skirting around her manufactured home had been removed without notice. Underneath, she found towels soaked in cold sewage wrapped around the broken drain pipe that connected her trailer to the park’s sewer system. No one — not park management, not her neighbors nor the plumbers who had visited her lot twice — could provide any information about the towels or who was responsible.
Raw sewage had been leaking into the ground beneath her home in Monticello for two weeks and would continue to leak for another four days. Pula was not alone. At least five additional sewage releases were recorded at her park from March to August 2025 along with a park-wide main line failure near the connection to the city of Monticello, according to Minnesota Pollution Control Agency incident reports obtained by the Reformer. In December 2025, the MPCA fined the park $13,957 following an investigation into the recurring pattern.
Roughly 180,000 Minnesotans live in manufactured home parks, renting the land and utilities beneath while owning the home above. All the while, these parks are rapidly changing hands from small family businesses to national corporations, while the laws that protect the residents are still being debated in the Legislature. 
Pula’s account, which is consistent with a series of Reformer stories on mobile home parks this year, is becoming all too common and underscores the problems that residents confront when they go up against powerful, multi-state landlords. Stories like this have prompted legislators to action, with Gov.-elect Amy Klobuchar supporting measures to cap lot rent alongside other protections. 
Eighteen days, or it’s coming from inside the house
Pula has lived in her manufactured home since 2016, and her family has called the park home since her parents moved in several years before that. Kjellberg’s, now known as the Meadows, was built in 1959 by the late Kent Kjellberg. The park operated on Highway 25 in Monticello for just over 60 years under the Kjellberg name until its sale in January 2021 to Lakeshore Management, an Illinois-based operator of manufactured home communities in 11 states, for roughly $23 million.
The troubles began when Pula’s toilet stopped flushing on Oct. 21, 2024. Roto-Rooter sent two technicians that day. The first technician couldn’t fix it, so the park chose to try again; the second billed The Meadows $2,745 for a three-hour hydro-jet job. Sewer lines beyond the trailer are the park’s responsibility, not the resident’s, according to the community’s lot rules and Minnesota state statute. 
Soon after, Pula said that the assistant manager, Rachael Sullivan, left her a voicemail stating that the line was clear and no damage was found. Pula believed her and let it go.
On Nov. 1, with her plumbing issues seemingly resolved, she left for an early Thanksgiving with her grandmother four hours north. Unbeknownst to her, since that initial visit and throughout her absence, sewage had been draining into the ground beneath her home, with another plumbing company, D&D Service and Repair, having written up a job while she was gone for her lot on request of the park “so it doesn’t overflow there.” 
When she returned on Nov. 4, she was surprised to find the smell had worsened, with odors permeating her children’s clothes and linens.
The Meadows manufactured home community in Monticello, Minnesota the Thursday, Nov. 12, 2026. (Photo by Nicole Neri/Minnesota Reformer)
Not enough sewage to clean up

	
Pula reported the backup and smell when she got home. Community manager Rebecca Miller, however, didn’t make the legally required call to the MPCA until Nov. 6. Miller told the duty officer that a “small amount” of sewage had backed up under the home, and that a vacuum truck was brought out but “not needed as there was not enough material,” according to the agency’s incident logs obtained by the Reformer. Miller listed the leak as starting Nov. 4, the day Pula had came home — meanwhile the park’s own plumbing invoices stretched back to the first call placed by Pula on Oct. 21.
The MPCA said, in an April 2025 violation notice that the park let wastewater sit on the soil for 18 days before it was cleaned up — only reporting the discharge after agency staff told them to do so.
On Nov. 7, D&D Service and Repair installed a new joint on the broken pipe. As explained in a recording shared with the Reformer, technician Daryl Cardinal told Pula the fix wouldn’t hold for long. “This has been an ongoing problem for a long time,” he said. When asked if it was a temporary fix, no one argued. D&D declined to comment for this story. 
The following day a truck from Roto-Rooter arrived, pumping roughly 100 gallons of sewage from the same location. Their technician told Pula the company had quoted Lakeshore roughly $1.6 million to replace sewer lines park-wide, work that the park never pursued, according to the technician. He continued, noting that the blockage would have to have been in the main line the whole time — the park’s responsibility. A few days before, park staff spread white powder, which the Minnesota Department of Health later said was “likely lime,” underneath and around Pula’s unit. 
The powder that was spread over the spill wasn’t the hydrated lime he would have expected, according to the Roto-Rooter technician in conversation with Pula at the time. She asked him what it was, and he said it was “plant food,” based on the fertilizer bags Pula found following another application by park maintenance workers. Roto-Rooter declined to comment for this story. 
On Nov. 15, Lakeshore attorney Clarice Scarnecchia told Pula there were no invoices because there weren’t records from vendors working on her lot back on Nov. 6. After Pula sent a video she had personally taken that afternoon, Scarnecchia wrote back stating she had found some records after all.
Nearly three weeks after the leak was resolved, on Nov. 26, Teresa Compton, the regional manager at Lakeshore, sent an email to Pula detailing that the “lime” covering the contaminated soil beneath and around her trailer would remain in place. She noted it would “absorb into the ground.” The wooden block used by D&D’s technician to prop up the cut pipe beneath Pula’s home, however? Pula should replace it herself. The pipe repair, cap replacement and replaced skirting were all described as acts of courtesy from park management. 
Pula argued in a Dec. 4 email that the plumbing under her home had never required repair until after the spill, and that she should not be responsible for fixing it now. She requested partial rent relief, reimbursement for proper decontamination, and a land survey to assess if her trailer shifted while standing over sewage. Lakeshore did not concede to any of her requests — they declined to survey, remediate, or do more than spray water on whatever they had laid down under her home, according to Pula.
These issues would bubble to the surface later as Pula and her family sought legal recourse. 
The Meadows manufactured home community in Monticello, Minnesota the Thursday, Nov. 12, 2026. (Photo by Nicole Neri/Minnesota Reformer)
Not just her lot
The pipes under Pula’s lot were failing long before the Lakeshore purchase. The park’s plumbing was never constructed to a uniform standard, according to interviews with former staff and residents. When asked for comment, the company declined to respond to any specific questions about the park or Pula’s lot.
Sean Sullivan, who served in maintenance at The Meadows for three years following Lakeshore’s 2021 acquisition, said sewer lines there often sit above the frost line and vary in diameter, with sections of 2-, 3- and 4-in.-wide pipe fitted together. “It’s over 70 years [old],” he said about the system. “Nothing’s been really properly maintained. It’s just been stitch it, repair it, and patch it.”
Since the sale in 2021, the biggest change has been staffing. Previously, the park had five maintenance staff, Sullivan said. During his three years with Lakeshore, this number dwindled to just one, often Sullivan himself. Throughout this period, rent has nearly doubled in the 5 years since Lakeshore took over, Sullivan noted, reaching $760 per month by October of last year, all while he remained the sole maintenance worker for the entire park and its over-300 sites. 
“You [went] from personal ownership to corporate ownership,” Sullivan stated. “This is a corporation… the corporation is money, money, money.”
Jean Weisbrich, a resident of the park for over three decades, recalled staff hauling away branches and bagged leaves and generally handling issues like plumbing problems before they escalated. All this ended under Lakeshore, she said. Last year, when branches overhanging her roof required trimming, she had to hire someone. 
“They just need to pay their techs more,” Sullivan said. “If they can keep the good techs, that place would look cleaner.”
Four days of odors, plus two years of hearings
In the four days following her return from her grandmother’s home, the Pula family stopped using their bathroom, instead driving to a nearby gas station or Walmart. They took showers at her father’s house, and did laundry at a laundromat across town. Mornings started earlier to allow her children to make bathroom trips before school.
Pula filed for emergency relief on Nov. 8, 2024 once disputes with the park began in earnest.
A judge in Wright County determined that raw sewage had indeed flooded the ground beneath Pula’s home and ordered Lakeshore to provide comparable lodging, which ended up being a rental home in another section of the park. By Nov. 20, the court considered the emergency over: Repairs to the sewer pipe had been completed, and the Minnesota Department of Health had inspected the ground, although they did not test inside Pula’s home, according to Pula. She was told that despite her reservations regarding the safety of her home, to return to Lot 6 within 48 hours.
On Dec. 6, a review hearing concluded the case. Patrick Flynn, an attorney for the Landlord Resource Network who was hired by Lakeshore for the case, informed Judge Richard Ilkka that the emergency had passed. While Pula noted that the leak had affected the condition of her home, Flynn carefully corrected the record on one point: the leak, he stated, “was not in the home at all. It was underneath the home.” Asked whether Lakeshore had turned over all of its records, Flynn remained noncommittal, stating he couldn’t say he’d provided everything “without knowing what it is that the court actually defines as that,” with Miller stating under oath that there was nothing else in her file.
Ilkka said of the hearing, “I’m making this record for this reason… at some future date, Ms. Pula has a lawsuit and says [Lakeshore] didn’t provide me with documentation, there’s going to be this record here today.” Ilkka closed the case, specifically noting no findings on habitability, or whether repairs or soil clean up were adequate. “All of these things could be true,” he said.
Pula filed again in the spring of 2025, asking to hold her lot rent in escrow for rent refunds, a fine and attorney’s fees. This time, her case was dismissed only a month later on grounds she had given inadequate notice, a claim Pula disputes.
New foundations built on soggy ground
Despite its outdated infrastructure, ongoing resident concerns, and history of regulatory investigation, Lakeshore is looking to grow the park’s footprint. Earlier this year, an associated developer pitched 226 new manufactured home units on 44 acres situated south of the park, plus two commercial lots facing the highway. City planning staff suggested a significantly smaller expansion of the park, about eight to ten acres, with single-family homes and townhouses on the remainder. The Lakeshore proposal is still under review.
In June 2026, a state health inspector revisited Pula’s lot and discovered a grayish-white substance still present beneath the home, likely a residue from the substance applied 19 months prior. No active sewage was found. The inspector instructed park management to remove the substance.
Pula filed for emergency relief once again, on Aug. 20, 2026, but was denied in days. She says she can still smell the odors coming from below and inside her home, the smell penetrating both her clothes and her children’s belongings.
“The only document since all of this that states whether my home is habitable is the first emergency order,” Pula said. “Nothing has been tested to show any treatments have been effective.” Looking back, Pula sighed. “[The Meadows] could have prevented this whole thing.” She continues to pay rent for her lot while figuring out what comes next.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Connecticut launches Mobile ID program with limited uses
description: Connecticut officials on Tuesday unveiled a Mobile ID program that allows residents to verify their identity with an app on their phone.
text:
Connecticut officials on Tuesday unveiled a Mobile ID program that allows residents to verify their identity with an app on their phone in a few limited settings.
“It’s an important step in modernizing government, and it gives residents another secure way to show their ID,” said Bryan Cafferelli, commissioner of the Connecticut Department of Consumer Protection.
The Mobile ID will be accepted by airport security at participating checkpoints, including Bradley International Airport and Tweed New Haven Airport.
Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles Commissioner Tony Guerrera said it’s easier to go through airport security without having to remove a physical ID from a wallet or pocketbook.
“Let’s be honest, we’ve all gone through airports, right?” Guerrera said. “Next thing you know, you’ve got to pull out your license. What do you do? You put your travel bag down, right? You’re pulling out your license, you’ve got to grab it.”
“Now, all you do,” Guerrera said, miming showing someone his phone. “Boom, and you walk right through.”
In a press release, officials said Mobile ID “is designed to complement, not replace a physical driver’s license or identification card. Individuals should continue to carry their physical credentials.”
“Law enforcement will not accept Mobile ID as a substitute for a physical driver’s license, and it cannot be used for voting,” the release continued.
Guerrera said law enforcement may ultimately end up accepting Mobile ID in the future, though he believed that would likely require an act of the legislature.
Connecticut businesses can choose whether or not they accept Mobile ID for age verification purposes for the purchase of items like alcohol and cannabis. Businesses must use a specialized mobile device app to verify Mobile IDs.
Cafferelli said he expects many businesses will adopt the technology over time.
“This will happen organically,” he said. “The more people who download it and present it at businesses, if they don’t have the app, they’re going to get on board and say, ‘Let me get that app because it’s the trend and it’s how people want to show their ID.’”
The Connecticut DMV said the Mobile ID program, which they call “a comprehensive secure technology infrastructure designed to support long-term operational needs,” cost the state $2.1 million to develop and implement.
The federal Transportation Security Administration reports 22 states plus Puerto Rico offer digital ID programs.
This story was first published Nov. 17, 2026 by Connecticut Public.

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: Judge dismisses lawsuit to block Hyundai steel mill dock
description: A St. John the Baptist Parish judge has dismissed a lawsuit seeking to block the construction of a sprawling riverfront dock for Hyundai’s new Ascension Parish steel mill. The suit alleged the financing plan for the dock was approved without the public input required by law.
text:
The logo for Hyundai. The company, in a joint venture with Pohang Iron and Steel Co. of South Korea, is spending $5.8 billion on an Ascension Parish steel mill. (Photo: Hyundai Media Center)A St. John the Baptist Parish judge has dismissed a lawsuit seeking to block the construction of a sprawling riverfront dock for Hyundai’s new Ascension Parish steel mill. The suit alleged the financing plan for the dock was approved without the public input required by law. 
Judge Kirk Vaughn ruled in favor of the Port of South Louisiana in a case brought by three plaintiffs: Rural Roots Louisiana, a community empowerment group; the Louisiana Bucket Brigade, an environmental group; and Harry Joseph Sr., a resident of the Modeste community where the Hyundai plant is being built. 
Their lawsuit alleged the port did not properly notify the public of its intention to approve $400 million in bond financing for the dock project. Vaughn ruled that the complaint was filed too soon because the port’s board has yet to OK the bond deal.  
“The court’s ruling to dismiss the case is a clear win for Louisiana and allows us to move forward,” the Port of South Louisiana said in a statement. “Our focus remains on delivering transformational projects that create opportunities for families and strengthen our region.”
The port board planned to vote on the bond issuance during a meeting at 9 a.m. Tuesday, the same time Vaughn had scheduled a hearing in his courtroom on the port’s request to dismiss the case. The judge issued a temporary restraining order Monday at the plaintiffs request to force the board to postpone its meeting.
The judge explained that he dismissed the lawsuit because “the time to sue … would be after the final bond authorization,” Bucket Brigade director Anne Rolfes said in an interview Tuesday.
According to Rolfes, the judge said the lawsuit did raise “significant constitutional questions” about the port’s process to approve financing for the dock. 
“We feel really pleased that the judge can see there are serious issues raised,” she said.
Rolfes said the plaintiffs will continue to challenge what she described as the “shadowy, hidden” processes surrounding the steel mill project, but she did not offer a specific plan.
“We will pursue a next step, but what that next step is remains to be seen,” she said.
Hyundai, in a joint venture with Pohang Iron and Steel Co. of South Korea, is spending $5.8 billion on the Ascension Parish mill. It will eventually employ 1,300 workers with an average annual salary of $95,000, CEO Hyung Jin Kim said. 
The lawsuit was filed in St. John, where the Port of South Louisiana is headquartered.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Churches ask for release of additional Homeland Security surveillance records
description: Three Twin Cities churches are asking a federal judge to order the federal government to release more records related to the surveillance of unions, activist organizations and houses of worship during Operation Metro Surge.  The churches — First Universalist Church of Minneapolis, Hennepin Avenue United Methodist Church, and St. John the Evangelist Episcopal[...]
text:
Interfaith leaders gather for prayer and a press conference Thursday, Jan. 8, 2026 at the spot near 34th Street and Portland Avenue where an ICE agent shot and killed Renee Good, 37, the previous day. (Photo by Nicole Neri/Minnesota Reformer)Three Twin Cities churches are asking a federal judge to order the federal government to release more records related to the surveillance of unions, activist organizations and houses of worship during Operation Metro Surge. 
The churches — First Universalist Church of Minneapolis, Hennepin Avenue United Methodist Church, and St. John the Evangelist Episcopal Church — filed a brief in the so-called “Minnesota 15” case, in which 15 Minnesotans are facing charges of conspiracy to impede or assault federal agents. 
The churches, represented by Groundwork Legal, support the defendants’ request for additional discovery — that is, that a judge order the Department of Homeland Security to turn over downloads of undercover agents’ phones and laptops; all reports related to surveillance of Minnesota unions, nonprofit organizations and activists; and communications between local prosecutors and their bosses in Washington, D.C.
Batches of records already released in the case revealed that undercover agents attended anti-Immigration and Customs Enforcement organizing meetings at several churches, including those named in the brief. In at least one case, as an undercover agent surveilled an anti-ICE organizing meeting at a Roseville church, other agents scanned license plates in the parking lot to build a database including attendees’ addresses, family and employment information and vehicle registration information, according to a filing by defense attorney Kevin Riach in the case.
“Sending undercover agents into houses of worship and tracking community members engaged in lawful activities strikes at the very heart of our democracy and religious freedom,” said Groundwork Legal CEO Irina Vaynerman in a press release. “Americans do not want to live in a surveillance state, and the federal government cannot hide behind a veil of secrecy.”
Minnesota clergy took an active role in opposing the swarm of federal agents that descended on Minnesota last winter. Progressive faith leaders were outspoken following the killings of Renee Good and Alex Pretti by immigration agents, and have opposed the opening of a detention center in Appleton. As thousands of people marched in downtown Minneapolis during the Jan. 23 general strike, about 100 clergy members were arrested while protesting at the Minneapolis-St. Paul International Airport, calling on the airport and airlines to stop facilitating deportations.
Groundwork Legal previously represented Minnesota faith leaders in a successful effort to help win access to detainees held in the Whipple Federal Building.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Inside the Newsroom: John Moritz talks offshore wind
description: Reporter John Moritz shares a peek into his reporting process, what made this story unique and challenges the story presented.
text:
Last Friday, The Connecticut Mirror, along with three other nonprofit newsrooms — ProPublica, the New Bedford Light and Ocean State Media — published a major reporting project on the Trump administration’s war on offshore wind construction in New England.
Trump’s effort to end future offshore wind development has led to massive uncertainty in the New London area, where residents were promised steady jobs and an economic boost from the industry.
John Moritz, our energy and environment reporter, has followed the progress of wind energy development in the region for years. For this project, he spent time with workers and leaders in New London to understand what the promise of this new industry meant to them — and how it feels to see it fade away.
Here’s the story behind that story.
This interview has been edited for length and clarity.
The CT Mirror: How did you first get wind of this story?
John Moritz: I’d been covering the renovation and overhaul of the State Pier dating back several years. During the Biden administration, the state, along with Ørsted and Eversource, invested about $300 million to basically turn what had been an old, underutilized public pier in New London into this massive heavy lift platform for the offshore wind industry.
And when the Trump administration started attacking that industry and trying to shut down some of these projects last year, I wanted to answer the question of what happens to that investment. What’s the long term impact going to be on the pier? And as it turns out, there were reporters at some of our partner publications in Massachusetts and Rhode Island where similar investments were being made, who had the same questions.
CTM: As you said, you’ve reported on offshore wind developments in Connecticut for years now. How did this story feel different?
JM: This story isn’t just a Connecticut story, it’s a global story. The companies that were coming to invest here are some of the biggest energy companies in the world. And these companies invested hundreds of millions of dollars. 
As part of our reporting on this project, we went through earnings calls that were being announced very early in the morning, our time, because these are European companies. And if you go into the meeting minutes of these calls, they’re saying they are now shifting their investments to Asia and the Pacific and South America. They’re not investing in the United States any longer because they see the political climate here as being too turbulent.
CTM: What would you say was the hardest part of reporting the story?
JM: The hardest part of the story was getting people to talk openly about the impact of the administration’s actions on their lives. There are so many people who recognize that this is an administration that can change policies kind of on a whim, seemingly. And no one wanted to be seen as the instigator of another fight that could potentially put people out of work or threaten hundreds of millions of dollars of investments.
CTM: How long have you been working on this project?
JM: I remember it was cold and dreary, our first meeting, so it makes me think it was sometime last winter [December 2025].
CTM: You’ve been working on this for a really long time. Can you walk me through how the story came together? 
JM: We really wanted to focus on the stories of real people that this was impacting. One of the things I focused on was the mayor of New London and his son. The mayor’s name is Michael and his son is Thomas. 
The mayor went to England for a trip to view that country’s offshore wind industry. He talked to me about his vision of having old shuttered factories in Connecticut be repurposed similarly to what he saw in England, which was one of the world’s leading producers of wind. And his son actually went to work as a union laborer on the pier. So it’s a multi-generational story of people who saw a resurgence happening in their community and now are left wondering what’s going to happen next.

title: The biggest upsets that changed who CA sent to Congress
description: Come January California’s GOP congressional delegation will be so small they can caucus in a Subaru. text:
Newsletter Header Placeholder (do not move)




Rep.-elect Randy Villegas speaks during an election night watch party at La Movida Nightclub in Bakersfield on Nov. 3, 2026. Photo by Larry Valenzuela, CalMatters




Come January California’s GOP congressional delegation will be so small they can caucus in a Subaru. We have more on that below, and another piece coming Thursday about what Republican losses mean for the Legislature. 
It’s also bonus season for California pension funds, and they had a good year. Check out the paydays in today’s newsletter. 
And, we have firefighting goats. Gotta love goats. 
California’s congressional delegation will return to Washington next year with what is likely to be the state’s smallest Republican delegation in nearly 90 years, reports CalMatters’ Maya C. Miller.
In 1937, California only had 20 U.S. House seats, and GOP members occupied four of those seats. After the Democratic blue wave earlier this month, California will also have just four Republicans in the House, along with 48 Democrats.
Of the five incumbent seats the GOP lost, perhaps the most stunning was Republican Rep. David Valadao’s defeat by Democrat Randy Villegas in California’s heavily Latino 22nd Congressional District, which stretches from Fresno to Bakersfield.
Out of seven elections during Valadao’s congressional career, he only lost once in 2018, and he later reclaimed his seat in 2020. But Villegas, a progressive newcomer endorsed by Sen. Bernie Sanders of Vermont and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio Cortez of New York, defeated Valadao by more than 35 percentage points.
As for the Democrats, intraparty battles between progressives and moderates defined several key races, and the results were mixed: Some progressive challengers handedly toppled establishment incumbents, while moderates prevailed in other districts.
The most disappointing loss for progressives took place in the “battle of the ages” race for the state’s 7th Congressional District, which encompasses parts of Sacramento, El Dorado and San Joaquin counties. 
Rep. Doris Matsui, who has held office since 2005 and is 82, kept her seat by nearly 5 percentage points from Sacramento City Councilmember Mai Vang, a 41-year-old progressive. Matsui won reelection with the help from Republican-leaning regions in the district.
In another case of moderate Democrats prevailing, political novice Eric Jones unseated incumbent Rep. Mike Thompson, a Democrat, by 5 percentage points to represent Northern California’s 4th Congressional District. Jones ran to the center and deployed ads that included anti-immigrant rhetoric and described Thompson as “soft on illegal criminals.”
Read more.



Focus on Inland Empire: Each Wednesday, CalMatters Inland Empire reporter Aidan McGloin surveys the big stories from that part of California. Read his newsletter and sign up to receive the next one.

Other Stories You Should Know


Bonus season for CalPERS and CalSTRS


The California State Teachers’ Retirement System offices in West Sacramento on Nov. 12, 2024. Photo by Miguel Gutierrez Jr., CalMatters




California’s two largest public pension funds paid their investment staff big bucks this year in bonuses, writes CalMatters’ Adam Ashton.
The California Public Employees’ Retirement System, which is valued at more than $646 billion as of Monday, paid $37.9 million in bonuses to its staff, compared to $37.7 million in incentives last year.
Meanwhile, the California State Teachers’ Retirement System paid $21.8 million in incentives to, up from $20.3 million last year. As of October, the fund is valued at $415 billion.Three executives — the chief investment officers at both funds and CalPERS’ chief executive — took home seven-figure bonuses.
Both funds describe the bonuses as important for recruiting and retaining investment staff, and asserted that the bonuses represent a small portion of the funds’ earnings in their reports to their boards.
Read more.



These adorable goats have a job to do 🐐


San Diego Gas & Electric uses goats to graze brush that grows along corridors of power transmission towers to reduce fire risk in San Diego on April 9, 2026. Photo by Kevin Carter, Getty Images




San Diego County’s latest weapon against fighting wildfires are furry, have four legs and tout horns. That’s right, they’re goats.
As CalMatters’ Deborah Brennan explains, county fire officials are piloting a program in Valley Center that uses herds of goats to curb wildfire risk by gobbling up vegetation around homes, vital roadways and potential evacuation sites.
While they look cute, their work is serious: In the last few decades, deadly wildfires have torn through San Diego’s backcountry, prompting the county to revamp its fire-fighting strategy. 
Officials are launching the pilot at Star Valley Park, a former ranch site, and recently received a $300,000 state grant to expand the grazing program to other high-risk fire areas.

Jake Enriquez, region manager for the county’s parks and recreation department: “Having a vegetation break here is very advantageous to the fire agencies. It gives them a defensible space to work off of. … And these goats do a fantastic job.”

title: Black tie meets rockabilly at Wilmington’s 50th Grand Gala

text:
The Stray Cats play Copeland Hall on Dec. 5, then the party moves up Market Street to the Hotel du Pont, where the Gold Ballroom has helped make the late-night celebration a Wilmington tradition.
WILMINGTON, Del. — The dress code calls for festive black tie. The band calls for an upright bass. At Wilmington’s 50th Grand Gala on Saturday, Dec. 5, guests will hear the Stray Cats at the Grand Opera House, then walk up Market Street to spend the rest of the evening among the chandeliers and gilded interiors of the Hotel du Pont.
The two addresses are part of the draw. The Grand opened in 1871 behind the ornate cast-iron facade that still fronts Market Street. The hotel opened in 1913, bringing Italian Renaissance architecture and European chandeliers to the corner of 11th and Market streets. The gala ties those landmarks together for one night, with a single ticket covering both the concert and the after-party.
A rockabilly night at The Grand
The 8 p.m. program in Copeland Hall opens with the Grand Medal for Excellence in the Performing Arts, which this year goes to Francis “Skip” Pennella. He spent 11 years as board chair, recently retired as executive director and now serves as a senior adviser.
Then come the Stray Cats. Guitarist and singer Brian Setzer, upright bassist Lee Rocker and drummer Slim Jim Phantom helped put rockabilly back on the charts in the early 1980s. The original trio brings the twang and slap bass behind “Rock This Town” and “Stray Cat Strut” to the same stage where Bruce Hornsby performed with the Delaware Symphony Orchestra at last year’s gala.
The Gold Ballroom and a party that moves room to room
The Hotel du Pont’s Gold Ballroom has given the Grand Gala some of its most memorable late-night moments. The French neoclassical ballroom dates to 1918, with a gilded ceiling and carved medallions honoring women from history and mythology. During the 2010 gala, Procol Harum singer Gary Brooker joined Wilmington-area band Club Phred there for a surprise encore of “A Whiter Shade of Pale.” Elsewhere in the hotel that night, a jazz trio played in the Du Barry Room and guests found desserts in the Green Room.
For the 50th gala, The Grand is bringing back that room-to-room format. Its Ultimate After Party will feature gourmet food, signature cocktails at themed open bars and live performances by local musicians. There are no assigned tables. Guests can sample the food in one room, catch up with friends over a cocktail in another and stay out dancing until 1 a.m. The concert and the hotel party are included with every gala ticket.
Past galas have drawn hundreds of arts supporters, and this year’s mix makes for one of Wilmington’s most distinctive nights out. Where else on the holiday calendar can you dress in black tie for the Stray Cats, walk up Market Street to a century-old hotel and spend the rest of the night with people who help keep live performance within reach for Wilmington families?
Gold and Platinum guests can begin at 6:30 p.m. with a VIP reception at the baby grand. The Platinum package for two extends the evening into Sunday, with premium concert seats, an overnight stay at the Hotel du Pont, hotel parking and a Sunday brunch gift certificate.
What the evening supports
Gala proceeds support The Grand’s community programs, including Stages of Discovery school matinees, sensory-friendly performances and Summer in the Parks. The Grand says its community engagement and outreach programs reach more than 20,000 students and Wilmington residents. An anonymous donor is matching donations through Dec. 1, according to the gala site.
TO GO

The 50th Grand Gala takes place Saturday, Dec. 5, in Wilmington. The VIP reception begins at 6:30 p.m. for Gold and Platinum guests. Doors open at 7:30 p.m. for Silver and Bronze guests. The medal presentation and concert begin at 8 p.m. in Copeland Hall at the Grand Opera House, 818 N. Market St.
The after-party follows at the Hotel du Pont, 42 W. 11th St., and ends at 1 a.m. Guests walk between venues. The dress code is festive black tie. Bring your ticket and wristband for entry.
Individual tickets are $250 for Bronze, $350 for Silver and $550 for Gold. The Platinum package for two is $1,650. All tiers include the concert and after-party.
The Grand’s box office is at 302-652-5577. Tickets, donations and sponsorships.

description: TOPEKA — Kansas lawmakers gathered Monday to consider their options ahead of the 2027 legislative session after failing earlier this year to pass online protections for children. text:
The parent company of Instagram and Facebook agreed to settle a nationwide lawsuit by paying up to $17.1 billion and implementing safety features on its platforms to protect children. (Photo by Anna Kaminski/Kansas Reflector) TOPEKA — Kansas lawmakers gathered Monday to consider their options ahead of the 2027 legislative session after failing earlier this year to pass online protections for children.
A group of lawmakers said Monday they are interested in trying again to pass legislation that restricts Kansas children’s access to addictive social media platforms, age-inappropriate apps and potentially dangerous situations online.
Kansas was among the first wave of states in 2026 that attempted to legislate against unfiltered content consumption among minors, but Senate Bill 372 failed when the House declined to pick up the legislation. 
It would have enacted the App Store Accountability Act, which would have created age verification and parental consent requirements in app stores. A succession of tech sector lobbyists spoke with several members of the House when the bill had a hearing in March. The full Senate and a House committee recommended it be passed.
A bipartisan group of lawmakers appeared interested Monday in revisiting the app store accountability proposal in 2027 and crafting additional legislation.
Sen. Brad Starnes, a Riley Republican, suggested disallowing phones with full capabilities for children, favoring simpler devices with different modes and restrictions for nighttime and school.
“If we can’t control the particulars of the software and programs and et cetera, then the possibility of controlling the device itself, so that a person of whatever age we determine cannot have a phone or a device that allows them to even enter into programs until a certain age,” Starnes said.
Rep. Cyndi Howerton, a Wichita Republican, proposed adding age restrictions to the purchasing of burner phones.
Rep. Jo Ella Hoye, a Lenexa Democrat, said Kansas should explore a bill like Nebraska’s Legislative Bill 525, a two-pronged law that passed the state’s unicameral legislature unanimously in April. In addition to data protections for the agricultural industry, the bill contained the Conversational Artificial Intelligence Act, which requires AI disclosures and safeguards against inappropriate and misleading content.
Hoye said the bill was “on the right track” in regulating children’s access to potentially harmful content and platforms.
Under the law, if a minor is interacting with AI, a platform would have to disclose immediately AI in use and periodically remind the user.
“There are some things that would intervene here should violence or sexual content come up,” Hoye said.
The lawmakers heard from roughly two dozen lobbyists, experts and officials about the policy landscape and the reality of children’s online experience. Some, such as the Computer and Communications Industry Association, advocated against blanket changes to the way children access smartphones and the internet.
“Existing tools already let families set the right protections in just a few clicks,” said Megan Stokes, state policy director for the association. “Kansas lawmakers should focus on empowering families through these tools and digital literacy education rather than adopting measures that undermine free expression and user privacy.”
Throughout the hearing, committee members and guest speakers repeatedly emphasized the importance of taking into consideration First Amendment concerns and privacy protections.
It is likely the issue will be in court no matter what, said Kansas Attorney General Kris Kobach.
He said legislation and litigation could work in tandem. He has been part of five lawsuits against tech companies in recent years, including against social media platforms, he told the committee. Three of those lawsuits are ongoing, he said. One against Meta, the parent company of Facebook and Instagram, resulted in a $17 billion settlement for most states, including $134 million for Kansas, which must be used to remediate the harm done to children.
How exactly to make up for harms suffered isn’t obvious, Kobach said.
“It’s things to encourage kids to get outside again and to not be on their phone and to be able to do other things rather than getting sucked into this digital world,” he said.

name: Mississippi Today
title: ‘I’m no superhero’: Jackson schools superintendent to depart district next summer
description: Jackson Public Schools Superintendent Errick L. Greene in attendance at a Tuesday evening JPS Board of Trustees meeting, Nov. 18, 2025.
text:
Jackson Public Schools Superintendent Errick Greene will leave the district at the end of the school year. 
Greene announced his decision Tuesday at the end of a school board meeting. He expressed confidence in the district’s “ability to continue the great work we’ve done.” He also described his time at JPS as the “absolute highlight and honor” of his career. 
Greene’s departure concludes eight years with the school system, marking a chapter of gradual improvements under his leadership.
“I’ve endeavored to lead with a sense of purpose and promise and to center our scholars in every decision that we make,” he said. “I’m no superhero who swooped in to carry out this massive vision and effort on my own, and there is clear evidence to show this district is far better today than when we arrived.”
Greene joined Mississippi’s third-largest district in 2018 as it was facing the possibility of a state takeover. Under his leadership, JPS weathered the COVID-19 pandemic, improved its state-assigned accountability grade and closed and consolidated a number of schools. The district also raised staff pay and spent millions in school renovations, he said. 
Superintendent of Jackson Public Schools Errick Greene listens as a student expresses her concerns about school closures during a JPS community meeting at Forest Hill High School in Jackson, Miss., Monday, Oct. 9, 2023. JPS announced its plan to close or consolidate 16 schools. Credit: Eric J. Shelton/Mississippi Today
During his tenure at JPS, the district also achieved the highest graduation rate in its history, established the state’s largest early childhood collaborative and created a grants management office that has secured $30 million in federal dollars, a district press release stated.  
School board president Barbara Hilliard said while trustees were sad to hear of Greene’s departure, they are grateful for his “tireless leadership and service.” 
Mayor John Horhn announced Greene’s departure at Jackson city council meeting on Tuesday. 
“Leading a school district is demanding work,” Horhn said in a press release sent after the meeting. “Our schools are central to Jackson’s future. As mayor, I am grateful for those who choose to serve our young people and help them prepare for life beyond the classroom.”
Greene’s contract will end on June 30. Until then, he said he would spend the school year “completely focused on leading this district to even greater achievement levels.” It’s unclear what he will be doing next.
Greene ended his remarks on Tuesday with a series of quotes that he ruminated on while weighing his decision to leave the district. Some were hopeful, while others were somber, conveying a range of complicated feelings about a difficult job. 
“Be careful what you ask for because you just might get it,” he started.
Then, “My soul looks back and wonders how it got over,” Greene added, and the audience applauded.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Steward’s collapse left patients and health care workers exposed. Massachusetts must ensure accountability for those who were in charge.
description: The collapse of Steward Health Care exposed systemic failures that extend far beyond one corporation. Massachusetts now has an opportunity to address them.
text:
IMAGINE A FIREFIGHTER entering a burning building. The structure is failing, the exits are compromised, and people are trapped inside. She knows the risks. She enters anyway. 
Now imagine that, after the fire is extinguished, she discovers the building’s owner neglected its safety obligations and failed to maintain adequate insurance. Yet somehow, she is left responsible for the damages. 
She did not start the fire. She should not be left with the bill. 
This is the predicament facing health care workers who remained at Steward Health Care hospitals as the company’s financial empire collapsed around them. 
Physicians, nurses, physician assistants, and other professionals continued caring for patients amid staffing shortages, dwindling resources, and mounting uncertainty. They were encouraged to stay, reassured that their malpractice insurance remained intact, and praised for their commitment. 
Then Steward filed for bankruptcy in May 2024. 
What followed exposed the difference between having insurance and having insurance that can actually pay a claim. 
Steward relied on TRACO, a captive malpractice insurer domiciled in Panama. Its financial arrangements reportedly relied heavily on obligations between affiliated companies rather than independently available reserves. 
The Boston Globe reported that there were 517 pending or settled but unpaid malpractice claims, with estimated resolution costs approaching $200 million. TRACO reportedly had only about $3.5 million in available cash. 
As Steward’s hospitals deteriorated, clinicians faced greater exposure to liability and diminishing financial protection against it. 
Today, patients face uncertainty over compensation while health care workers confront lawsuits, legal expenses, and the possibility of personal financial ruin. Massachusetts intervened to preserve hospital services. Yet many patients and health care workers remain exposed to the financial consequences of Steward’s collapse. 
Neither group created this crisis. Both deserve protection. 
That principle inspired the formation of PROTECT: Patients and Providers for Reform, Oversight, Transparency, Equity, and Clinical Trust, a coalition advocating greater health care accountability. 
Steward exposed systemic failures that extend far beyond one corporation. Massachusetts now has an opportunity to address them. 
First, establish a Steward Recovery Fund. Massachusetts responded to a malpractice insurance crisis in 1975 by creating a mechanism to preserve coverage. A temporary fund could now compensate valid claims while protecting health care workers from financial ruin. 
The Commonwealth should retain the right to recover those expenditures from Steward, TRACO, affiliated corporations, and, where legally justified, the personal assets of responsible executives. Public intervention must not become private absolution. 
Second, strengthen malpractice insurance oversight. Hospitals should not promise insurance backed by inaccessible offshore assets or unsecured obligations between related companies. Massachusetts should require appropriately regulated coverage, independently verified reserves, and enforceable financial protections. 
Insurance that disappears precisely when it is needed is not much use to anyone. 
Third, pursue executive accountability. The attorney general should investigate potential civil and criminal violations and bring proceedings wherever the evidence warrants. If charges are not justified, the public deserves a comprehensive explanation. 
Fourth, investigate predatory malpractice insurance practices. Clinicians who were assured they had adequate coverage should not face exorbitant replacement or tail insurance costs because their employer failed to honor its obligations. Improper charges should be recoverable, with appropriate penalties helping finance the recovery fund. 
Fifth, modernize malpractice accountability. Our malpractice system must evaluate the totality of circumstances leading to patient harm, not simply the actions of the last clinician involved. 
Hospitals are powerful institutions that control staffing, scheduling, resources, and the conditions under which care is delivered. Liability should follow control. 
Malpractice tribunals should be able to examine institutional failures alongside individual negligence. Massachusetts should also reconsider its $100,000 charitable liability cap, which can limit compensation from qualifying health care institutions. 
Equally important, reforms promoting independence in clinical decision-making should ensure health care teams can exercise professional judgment without unnecessary administrative restrictions or corporate interference. 
Finally, strengthen whistleblower and worker protections. Health care workers are often the first to recognize unsafe conditions, yet speaking out can jeopardize their livelihoods. Massachusetts should strengthen retaliation protections through meaningful penalties, a private right of action, and recovery of attorneys’ fees.  
The Legislature must also eliminate special Wage Act exemptions that shield charitable health care institutions from accountability. A withheld paycheck can become a powerful instrument of control, silencing the employees best positioned to expose wrongdoing. Charitable status should never excuse financial coercion or diminish workers’ rights. 
These reforms do not excuse individual medical negligence. Patients deserve justice when they are harmed. But responsibility must follow the evidence, including into executive offices and corporate boardrooms. 
Steward’s collapse was not merely a failure of hospital management. It exposed weaknesses in how Massachusetts regulates health care institutions, financial risk, and corporate accountability. Those weaknesses matter as hospitals confront continued consolidation, financial pressures, and uncertainty over looming Medicaid cuts. 
Without reform, Steward may prove less an exception than a preview. Massachusetts demonstrated that it could act decisively when hospitals faced collapse. The question now is whether that commitment extends to the patients and health care workers left behind. 
We cannot celebrate the professionals who stayed, praise their sacrifice, and then leave them financially responsible for arrangements they neither designed nor controlled. 
A firefighter who accepts the danger of entering a burning building should not have to assume the financial consequences of its owner’s negligence. Neither should the health care workers who stayed at Steward. 
They didn’t start the fire. They shouldn’t be left with the bill. 
Duncan Daviau, a physician assistant and emergency medicine clinician, is a health care advocate writing on behalf of PROTECT (Patients and Providers for Reform, Oversight, Transparency, Equity, and Clinical Trust).

title: Salesianum and Appoquinimink will Meet in 2026 DIAA Division One Boys Soccer State Championship Game after Semifinal Victories
description: Salesianum defeated Charter School of Wilmington, 6-0, and Appoquinimink defeated Cape Henlopen, 1-0, on November 17 punching their ticket to the 2026 DIAA Division One Boys Soccer State Championship game.   FREDERICA, Del. — Salesianum and Appoquinimink will meet in the state championship game for the first time since 2018 when the two teams play in the 202[...]
text:
The Salesianum boys soccer team celebrates their semifinal win with a group picture. The team will play Appoquinimink in the 2026 DIAA Division One Boys Soccer State Championship game on November 20. Photo Credit: Ryan Colasanti
Salesianum defeated Charter School of Wilmington, 6-0, and Appoquinimink defeated Cape Henlopen, 1-0, on November 17 punching their ticket to the 2026 DIAA Division One Boys Soccer State Championship game.
 
FREDERICA, Del. — Salesianum and Appoquinimink will meet in the state championship game for the first time since 2018 when the two teams play in the 2026 DIAA Division One Boys Soccer State Championship Game, Friday, November 20.
Salesianum defeats Charter School of Wilmington, 6-0
Salesianum junior Bryan Perez-Herrera dribbled the ball down the left side of the field and settled about 15 yards away from the goal. Two Force defenders stood a couple feet away ready to defend the juniors’ attack. 
Perez-Herrera dribbled a little farther down the line then stopped his momentum and made a move to his right to evade the first Force defender. A second evasion got Perez-Herrera past a second defender and created enough space for a right footed shot. The shot curved left as it neared the goal and drifted past the dive of senior Scott Honisch in goal. It drifted so far the shot hit the left post. The ball bounced in on the right side of the net for the first score of the second half.
Perez-Herrera finished the half with a hat-trick that helped Salesianum defeat the Charter School of Wilmington Forces, 6-0, Tuesday night.
Sallies scored five goals in the second half starting with Perez-Herrera’s first in the 45th minute. Perez-Herrera struck again in the 49th minute with a shot to the middle of the net which was set up by an Esser assist, and his third came just two minutes later on a shot that snuck right between the goalkeeper and the right post. Perez-Herrera celebrated each goal by landing a flip, spinning in the air three times. Perez-Herrera said it was the first hat-trick of his high school career.
“It feels great,” Perez-Herrera said postgame. “Just proud of myself honestly.”
Esser scored for the Sals right after his fellow junior’s third goal and a goal by senior Sawyer Valle in the 64th minute completed Sallies’ total. Salesianum senior Nico Rossi scored the first and only goal of the first half on a shot to the back left of the net off an assist by Esser. The Sals’ finished the game with its sixth game scoring six or more points and the team’s tenth shutout of the season. 
“We switched our formation, but they have one guy who’s a game changer. We stayed tight on him in the second half,” Rossi said about the team’s defense. “Once we got on him, didn’t really do anything and kept it [a] clean sheet.”
The Sals are returning to the state championship game for the 17th consecutive season and will try to win their second straight state title in as many seasons. Salesianum has won 14 of the last 16 state championship games. 
Appoquinimink defeats Cape Henlopen, 1-0 (OT)
Appoquinimink sets up for a throw in during its semifinal game against Cape Henlopen. Photo Credit: Ryan Colasanti
Appoquinimink senior Luke Talley placed the ball on the turf in the corner on the right side of the net. Talley took a few steps back, waited for the official’s whistle and served a pass into the box with three minutes elapsed from the first overtime period. 
Talley’s pass soared through the dark night sky and over the heads of Cape Henlopen defenders. The Vikings goalkeeper, Kasen Adams, leaped to try and deflect the pass but the ball flew over his outstretched arm. Jaguar sophomore Aiden Messinger made contact with the pass on an attempted header that hit his chest instead. The ball ricocheted into the air, off the crossbar and back toward Messinger in front of the goal. Messinger’s second attempt hit nothing but net. 
Messinger’s header in the third minute of overtime was the game winning score in Appoquinimink’s, 1-0, overtime victory over Cape Henlopen, Tuesday night.
“I saw the ball go up and first Gabe [Arbuet] on the back post hit it, hit crossbar, it went straight to me [and] I knew I had to put it in the back of the net to finish the game,” Messinger said. 
The game was evenly matched throughout the night. Neither team could gain much momentum and most of the game was played along the edges of the field. 
The Vikings had the best scoring opportunity in the first half on a shot by junior Kihara Ngido that went just high over the top of the goal. The Jaguars generated a corner opportunity late in the half, but the play was defended well and the two teams went into the half without a score.
The Jaguars attempted their first of two free kicks near the goal in the first four minutes of the second half, but the set piece was knocked away by a Cape Henlopen defender. The Jaguars kept the pressure on the Viking defense during the final 20 minutes of the half, but each time Appoquinimink looked like it might break through the Viking defense came up with a stop. Adams was integral to the staunch Viking defense, finishing the game with nine saves.
The Jaguars’ defense played just as well with strong communication along their back line, led in part by senior Reed Holliday. Appoquinimink only allowed a couple shots near the goal and each one was saved by Jaguar goalkeeper, Lincoln Neubauer. The Jaguars continued to create scoring opportunities in the final minutes of the second half, but were turned away by the Viking defense until Messinger’s game winning goal in the first overtime period. 
Appoquinimink is returning to the state championship game for the first time since 2022 and will try to earn the program’s first state championship title since 2020. The Jaguars beat the Sals for the championship title in 2020 and will have to do so again for the 2026 honor. 
The 2026 DIAA Division One Boys Soccer State Championship Game will be played at 7:30 p.m. on Friday, November 20, at DE Turf Sports Complex.

title: State marker to honor Laurel church’s ties to town’s first school for Black children
description: New Zion United Methodist Church traces its roots to the 1830s and now supports youth programs in West Laurel. The public is invited to Friday’s unveiling. text:
New Zion United Methodist Church traces its roots to the 1830s and now supports youth programs in West Laurel. The public is invited to Friday’s unveiling.
LAUREL, Del. — The building that housed Laurel’s first Black Methodist congregation went on to become the town’s first school for Black children. On Friday, Nov. 20, the state will honor that history with a marker at New Zion United Methodist Church on West Sixth Street.
The Delaware Public Archives announced that the unveiling will begin at 11 a.m. at 1042 W. Sixth St. The ceremony is free and open to the public, with remarks planned from community members, local and state officials and Archives representatives.
From church to schoolhouse
Black and white Methodists in Laurel worshipped together in the early 1830s, according to a church history published by Operation West Laurel. As the Methodist congregation outgrew Zion Meeting House, its trustees gave the building to Black residents. In 1833, it was moved to Townsend Street, where it became their first church.
In the 1860s, the Black congregation bought a second church building, known as New Zion, and moved it to a site across from the present sanctuary. The Townsend Street building then became Laurel’s first school for Black children. A history preserved by the Delaware Public Archives says the school remained there until the county built a replacement and that the old building was torn down in 1924.
That same year, the congregation built the sanctuary it uses today under the Rev. D.G. Waters, according to the church history. The concrete-block building was known as Waters New Zion Methodist Episcopal Church. The adjoining cemetery connects the site to generations of congregants.
New Zion later became part of the Peninsula-Delaware Conference after the region’s separate Black and white Methodist conferences merged in 1965. The United Methodist Church was formed through a national denominational merger three years later.
Worship and youth outreach today
The Peninsula-Delaware Conference lists the Rev. Vanessa Stephens Lee as New Zion’s pastor and gives 10 a.m. as the church’s main worship time.
Outside of worship, New Zion supports Operation West Laurel, an interfaith group that formed after a series of fatal shootings involving young people in Laurel. The church provides space for some of the group’s programs and has helped fund its work, Operation West Laurel organizer Crystal Stevens told Spotlight Delaware in 2025.
The group’s SOAR program offers homework help and reading and math support for children in grades two through six who have been exposed to gun violence. Project RISE offers tutoring, mentoring and job preparation for high school boys. Operation West Laurel also organizes neighborhood prayer walks that give volunteers a chance to hear directly from residents.
