title: Weapons remain leading cause of non-medical deaths for Alabama children in 2025
description: Weapons were the leading cause of “non-medical, unexpected or unexplained” deaths in 2025 for children under 18 in Alabama, and most of those were caused by firearms, according to a report released Thursday. “These are all tragic. Many of them, most of them, are preventable,” said State Health Officer Dr. Scott Harris during a meeting […]
text:
An unloaded Glock 19X handgun sits next to a magazine and 9 mm ammunition at a gun range. Weapons remained the leading cause of "non-medical, unexpected or unexplained deaths" among Alabama children in 2025. (Amanda Watford/Stateline)Weapons were the leading cause of “non-medical, unexpected or unexplained” deaths in 2025 for children under 18 in Alabama, and most of those were caused by firearms, according to a report released Thursday.
“These are all tragic. Many of them, most of them, are preventable,” said State Health Officer Dr. Scott Harris during a meeting of the State Committee on Public Health on Thursday. “It really sheds a light on what’s happening with Alabama’s kids.” 
Of the 711 deaths of children in the state reported in 2025, 223 were classified as non-medical, unexpected or unexplained deaths. The State Child Death Review Team reviewed almost 90% of the deaths that met the criteria. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The team reviewed 199 child deaths in 2025. Most of the non-vehicle deaths occurred in the child’s home, and most of all deaths occurred in suburbia. 
There were 57 bodily force or weapon-related deaths, and about 95% of them were caused by firearms, according to the report. Guns are the leading cause of death for children in the United States.
Report: Weapons were leading cause of death for Alabama children in 2024

In 28 of the firearm-related deaths (51.8%), the firearm was not locked away, an increase from 31.1% in 2024. In less than five of the reviewed deaths (under 9.3%) the firearm was locked away, but the child still gained access to it. 
Alabama law does not require firearms to be stored in homes with children. Rep. Barbara Drummond, D-Mobile, has filed bills that would effectively require parents and legal guardians to store firearms requiring a key or other unique mechanism to access the weapon. Should a minor access the firearm, the parent or guardian would be guilty of a Class A misdemeanor, punishable by one year in jail and a fine up to $6,000.
Drummond, a gun owner, has filed the bill multiple times, but it has never made it to the House floor. She said in a phone interview Tuesday afternoon that she plans to file the bill in 2027, but will try to change the messaging of the bill to gain support.
“It doesn’t take away anybody’s rights or anything like that. It simply says that people have got to be responsible. We’re going to continue that fight,” Drummond said. “We’re going to try to make sure that we start pushing it more as a school safety and parenting bill rather than a safe storage bill because that’s exactly what it is.”
According to Everytown, an advocacy group to lessen gun violence, 26 states have a safe storage law. The Child Death Review Team encouraged the safe storage of firearms, separating ammunition from firearms, storing guns unloaded and ensuring they are not accessible to children. The team also recommended the Legislature “improve gun safety laws.” 
Drummond said the statistic of children who died by an unsecured firearm was “horrific.” 
“What the Department of Public Health is saying about firearms, that’s data. Data doesn’t lie. This is not a right or a left issue for me. It is a responsibility issue. It’s a safety issue,” Drummond said. “That’s what’s so tragic. These are young lives that are being lost. I just think that we as policymakers can do something to help that situation.”
In 21 of the firearm-related deaths (38.8%), the owner of the firearm was a caregiver, parent or direct family member of the child who died, according to the report. In nine of the reviewed deaths (16.7%) the owner of the firearm was a stranger to the child, and in less than five of the reviewed deaths (less than 9.3%) the owner of the firearm was a friend of the child, according to the report. 
 
 If you or someone you know is in a crisis, call, text or chat the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline at 988. For a list of Crisis Centers in Alabama, visit the Alabama Department of Mental Health’s website. For help with grief and loss, the American Foundation for Suicide Prevention offers advice and resources.


In 24 of the firearm-related deaths (44.4%) the child intentionally or accidentally caused injury to themselves, according to the report. In 15 of the deaths (27.8%), the firearm was used in the commission of a crime, and in seven (13%), the child was injured in a drive-by shooting. In five of the deaths (9.3%) the child was playing with the firearm, according to the report. 
The team also recommended increasing funding for mental health and children’s services, as well as increased collaboration with the Alabama Suicide Prevention and Resources Coalition.
A message seeking comment was left Tuesday with House Majority Leader Rep. Paul Lee, R-Dothan, the only active lawmaker on the 2025 review team and a former chair of the House Health Committee.
In sleep-related deaths, the children are typically less than one year old. There were 38 sleep-related deaths and 18 sudden unexpected infant deaths (SUID), which are not mutually exclusive and have significant overlap, according to the report. Sleep-related deaths were mostly unchanged from 2024, when 35 were reported, but there was a significant drop from the 51 SUIDs, according to that year’s report. 
According to the 2025 report, the team has worked to educate county coroners, medical examiners and law enforcement on what classifies as a SUID. The department has also invested in safe sleep education. 
In most sleep-related and SUID cases, the child slept in an unrecommended surface, like an adult bed or a couch. According to the American Academy of Pediatrics, safe sleeping is a baby sleeping alone, on their back, in a crib with no additional pillows, blankets or stuffed animals. SUID is the leading cause of death for infants.

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Pro-voucher group spent big on Blackburn, but not in the state House, throwing expansion into doubt
description: Gov.-elect Marsha Blackburn received millions in support from a pro-private-school-voucher group during the 2026 election cycle, but won’t say whether she’ll push for expanding the program next year. Todd Rapp, press secretary for Blackburn’s gubernatorial transition, did not answer a question about whether her administration plans to push for a voucher expa[...]
text:
Gov.-elect Marsha Blackburn is in favor of private school vouchers but hasn't said whether she'll push to expand the program this year. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout).Gov.-elect Marsha Blackburn received millions in support from a pro-private-school-voucher group during the 2026 election cycle, but won’t say whether she’ll push for expanding the program next year.
Todd Rapp, press secretary for Blackburn’s gubernatorial transition, did not answer a question about whether her administration plans to push for a voucher expansion during the coming year’s legislative session. 
But he said by email that Blackburn supports the concept of vouchers. 
“With more than 17,000 students still on the waitlist, it is clear that Tennessee families support the Education Freedom Scholarship Program,” said Rapp. “Governor-elect Blackburn will not stop working to expand education freedom until every Tennessee parent has the opportunity to send their child to the school that best fits their needs.”
The leading group pushing for private-school voucher expansion nationally ran a political action committee supporting Blackburn that spent nearly $13 million during the 2026 election, campaign finance reports compiled by the Lookout show. The group, called Tennessee Freedom Fund, was the largest single independent spender during the gubernatorial race. 
But the group spent no money on Tennessee state legislative races and potentially lost eight pro-voucher votes in the state House, casting doubt on the possibility of expanding the program. 
Staffers at the conservative group Club for Growth run the Tennessee Freedom Fund PAC. Club for Growth operates several federal and state PACs. These include Club for Growth Action PAC, the School Freedom Fund, and the Tennessee Freedom Fund. The group’s PACs are primarily funded by billionaire Jeff Yass. 



Quotation







When a program like that requires such a significant amount of funding, then there’s an opportunity for budget debate.


– Rep. John Ray Clemmons, Chair, House Democratic Caucus


Tennessee enacted its universal private school voucher program in 2025 after Gov. Bill Lee and the School Freedom Fund led a concerted effort to win a handful of state House and Senate seats. 
During the 2024 election cycle, the School Freedom Fund spent nearly $3.3 million in Republican primaries to successfully boost their slate of pro-voucher candidates. 
The victories gave Lee enough votes in the state House to pass a program creating 20,000 vouchers worth $7,300 apiece for parents to send their kids to private schools. Then, in 2026, Lee pushed lawmakers to expand the program, which narrowly passed in the state House 52-43. 
But during the 2026 cycle, eight House members who voted for vouchers lost. Two Republicans who voted for the expansion lost in the primaries, and six more GOP members who voted for vouchers lost to Democrats in the general election. 
Nashville state Rep. John Ray Clemmons, the House Democratic Caucus chair, said Democrats will put forward a bill to repeal the voucher program entirely, but expects the debate to turn into a budget fight. 
“When a program like that requires such a significant amount of funding, then there’s an opportunity for budget debate,” said Clemmons. “I don’t know if it will get repealed, but it could be defunded.”
School Freedom Fund helped Blackburn put Senate money into the race
During the 2026 cycle, Club for Growth and School Freedom Fund played a crucial role in backing Blackburn’s gubernatorial run. 
The Tennessee Freedom Fund’s largest contribution was $4.81 million from the School Freedom Fund and $1 million from Yass. The group purchased ads praising Blackburn and attacking her opponents in the primary and general election.
Club for Growth also served as a conduit for Blackburn to put her U.S. Senate campaign account money into the governor’s election. 
Blackburn gave $4.8 million to Club for Growth Action PAC in May, and then three months later the School Freedom Fund gave a total of $4.81 million to the Tennessee Freedom Fund. The same staff is registered to all three PACs. 
Blackburn moves $4.8M from US Senate campaign account in apparent legal ‘workaround’

Brendan Glavin, the director of insights with OpenSecrets, a nonpartisan organization that tracks political spending, said in August the transactions looked like a “workaround to get her remaining federal campaign war funds into the state race.”
Glavin said the layering of money makes it seem like the cash supporting Blackburn is “technically coming from another source.”
“But it is hard to ignore the obvious connection between the transactions,” Glavin said.
Under Tennessee law, Blackburn is not allowed to directly spend her U.S. Senate campaign money in the governor’s race. Federal law does not prohibit such transactions.
The Lookout has made multiple attempts to reach Club for Growth, including sending detailed questions about transactions and whether the donations were connected. As of publication, no one from Club for Growth has answered questions.
The School Freedom Funds money came at a crucial time in the Republican gubernatorial primary, when polling showed Blackburn’s lead narrowing. U.S. Rep. John Rose, Blackburn’s main rival in the primary, had nearly matched her campaign spending by putting nearly $13 million of his own money into the race. 
Rapp did not respond to Lookout’s questions about Blackburn’s campaign finances, but said that Blackburn “fundamentally believes” in vouchers because “no parent should have to win the lottery to ensure their child has access to a quality education that fits their unique needs.”

name: West Virginia Watch
title: Commentary: The West Virginia small business owner who cannot afford to look struggling
description: Think about the people who run the small businesses in your county. The woman who owns the hardware store on Main Street. The couple behind the diner that opens at 5 a.m. The man with three HVAC vans and a phone that never stops ringing. If one of them were quietly falling apart, how would anyone know?
text:
West Virginia has 118,045 small businesses, and about four in five of those have no employees at all. For most owners, there is no human resources office, no employee assistance program and no one to cover the counter on a bad day. (Getty Images)Think about the people who run the small businesses in your county. The woman who owns the hardware store on Main Street. The couple behind the diner that opens at 5 a.m. The man with three HVAC vans and a phone that never stops ringing. If one of them were quietly falling apart, how would anyone know?
Most likely, no one would. The owner would make sure of it. That is how entrepreneur loneliness works: plenty of people around, and no one to tell.
West Virginia runs on these people. According to the U.S. Small Business Administration’s Office of Advocacy, the state has 118,045 small businesses, and they employ 47.4% of West Virginia’s employees. Of those businesses, 93,669, about four in five, have no employees at all. For most owners, there is no human resources office, no employee assistance program and no one to cover the counter on a bad day. The owner is the business.
I am a licensed clinical social worker, and I want to explain why so many owners keep their struggles hidden, and why that silence is a risk West Virginia should take seriously.
Why owners stay quiet
A 2026 CEREVITY report, 64% of Founders Conceal Mental Health Strain from Investors, reviewed 318 founders and venture-backed operators who sought therapy through the CEREVITY network. About 64% said they had actively hidden mental health strain from their investors or board, and the most common reason was fear of professional or funding consequences.
Most West Virginia owners do not answer to a venture capital board. But they answer to someone: a banker who holds the line of credit, a landlord, a supplier extending terms, a spouse who co-signed the loan and customers who are also their neighbors. The calculation is the same. If people sense that the owner is not holding up, the owner fears they will start to doubt the business.
In a small town, that fear has extra weight. The local counselor may be a regular customer. A car parked outside a therapist’s office is easy to recognize. So the owner keeps going, opens on time and tells everyone things are fine.
What silence costs
Strain that is hidden does not go away. It shows up as sleepless nights, short tempers at home, a drink that becomes two and decisions made from exhaustion. Clinicians see the pattern often: people who wait tend to arrive only when a crisis forces the issue, after a health scare, a marriage in trouble or a business decision they regret.
When a one-person business goes down, there is no one to take it over. The job goes, the service goes, and a storefront on Main Street goes dark. In a state where so many people work for small businesses, an owner’s mental health is not only a private matter. It is part of the local economy.
A private first step
The good news is that the first step can be small and private.
Owners can talk with a licensed clinician by telehealth, outside their own town and professional circle, so no one sees a car in a parking lot. West Virginians can also call or text 1-844-HELP4WV at any hour for help finding mental health and substance use support, a line West Virginia Watch has described as the state’s only 24/7 call line of its kind.
Lenders, chambers of commerce and small-business advisers can help, too. They already hand owners checklists for taxes, permits and cash flow. Adding one line about confidential mental health resources would cost almost nothing and would tell owners that taking care of themselves is part of running a sound business.
And owners can tell one person. Not the whole town. One trusted person who can hear the truth without it becoming news.
West Virginia depends on people who open the doors every morning no matter what. They deserve a way to get help before the doors close for good.
If you or someone you know is in crisis, call or text 988 at any hour.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: West Virginia earns F for preterm births in annual March of Dimes report card
description: Slightly fewer West Virginia babies were born prematurely in 2025 compared with 2024, though the rate has increased overall in recent years, according to data compiled by the March of Dimes.
text:
West Virginia earned an F on the 2026 March of Dimes Report Card for having a preterm birth rate of 12.7% in 2025. (Getty Images)Slightly fewer West Virginia babies were born prematurely in 2025 compared with 2024, though the rate has increased overall in recent years, according to data compiled by the March of Dimes. 
West Virginia’s preterm birth rate was 12.7% in 2025, down — but not significantly — from 13.4% the year before. The state earned an F on its 2026 report card, released Tuesday from the organization. The state earned the same grade in 2025. 
“Even though the overall grade is an F because the preterm birth rate is high, the preterm birth rate is actually improving, and so that’s encouraging for us to see, and lets us know that progress is possible,” Dr. Michael Warren, chief medical and health director for the March of Dimes, told West Virginia Watch.
West Virginia’s preterm birth rate has increased from 11.3% in 2015. It’s higher for Black women, who had a rate of 17% in 2025. 
Warren said the number of preterm births offers a good snapshot of how mothers and babies are doing overall. Preterm birth is the leading cause of infant mortality in the United States, he said. It’s also more broadly reflective of the overall health of a population.
“For example, we know in the United States and in states like West Virginia, there are high rates of chronic disease, like high blood pressure and diabetes and unhealthy weight before pregnancy,” Warren said. “Those not only pose risks to mom but also to baby, including a higher risk of being born pre-term.
“So the rate of preterm birth is really a nice measure that allows us to to really put a finger on the pulse of mom and baby health,” he said. 
The state’s rate of smoking, hypertension and unhealthy weight prior to pregnancy all contribute to the number of preterm births, according to the organization. 
Overall the United States earned an D+ for preterm births in 2025. Half of all states earned a D or an F. 
Warren said to improve preterm birth rates, there has to be a focus on the health of both mothers and babies.  
“We know that the health of those is linked very closely,” he said. “So addressing those chronic diseases before pregnancy, making sure that women continue to get into care early, making sure that women get all the care that they need, is really vital.”
Medicaid covers four out of every 10 births in the United States, including 6,939 West Virginia births in 2025, and it’s “vital” that the program is strong, Warren said. 
The organization recommends that West Virginia’s Medicaid program start reimbursing for doulas, or nonclinical professionals who tend to women in pregnancy and delivery. 
“Some states are reimbursing for that through their Medicaid program. West Virginia is not currently, so that really represents an opportunity for good policy movement,” Warren said. 
Republican’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act, or H.R. 1, made historic cuts to Medicaid, including imposing work requirements for those who are part of the expansion program. In West Virginia, state officials estimate that about 40,000 residents don’t meet the new requirements and don’t automatically qualify for an exemption, which means they could lose their coverage when the requirements take effect. 
The Rural Health Transformation program is another aspect of the law that Congress added as concerns were raised that Medicaid funding cuts in the bill could lead to the closures of rural hospitals. The five-year federal program aims to “transform the existing rural healthcare infrastructure and build sustainable health care systems that expand access, enhance quality of care, and improve outcomes for patients.” The program gave West Virginia about $202 million for 2027, and $199 million in 2026. 
“While the infusion of funds for rural health is great, we do worry that the cuts that are coming to Medicaid are going to outweigh the benefits to the Rural Transformation funds,” Warren said. “Four in 10 births in this country are covered by Medicaid, and when the United States is among the most dangerous developed countries in the world for giving birth, slashing the funding that supports four out of every 10 births is not a way for us to change those overall birth statistics.”

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Photo essay: The Equity Alliance, building Tennessee’s Black community for a decade
description: Just over a week after the 2016 presidential election, six Black women gathered in a Nashville casual restaurant.  One, Christiane Buggs, was elected to the Metro Nashville Schools Board in August. Another, Tequila Johnson, managed Bugg’s campaign. Charlane Oliver, a marketing director for a suburban chamber of commerce, had volunteered her communications sk[...]
text:
More than 100 members and volunteers with The Equity Alliance, a Black-led civic and political network, marched on Oct. 17, 2026 as part of the Tennessee State University Homecoming Parade. (Photo by John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)Just over a week after the 2016 presidential election, six Black women gathered in a Nashville casual restaurant. 
One, Christiane Buggs, was elected to the Metro Nashville Schools Board in August. Another, Tequila Johnson, managed Bugg’s campaign. Charlane Oliver, a marketing director for a suburban chamber of commerce, had volunteered her communications skills. The other three, Aerin Washington, Verlinda Darden and Mariah Cole, worked on the campaign.
In the wake of Buggs’s win and more recently, the election of Donald Trump as president, the group members asked themselves the question often asked in portentous times: What’s next? 
“I was angry about Black Lives Matter,” said Oliver, referring to the movement that grew as a response to the 2013 killing of Black teenager Trayvon Martin in Florida and 2014 police killings of Michael Brown in Missouri and Eric Garner in New York. “When Donald Trump got elected, that was the straw that broke the camel’s back.”
They discussed the needs of Nashville’s Black communities, based on their recent work in electoral politics. With each pledging to kick in $250 to launch an organization aimed at educating and mobilizing Black voters, they founded The Equity Alliance on Nov. 18, 2016.
Ten years later, the organization has spun off five other entities, including state and federal political action committees, registered hundreds of thousands of Black Tennesseans to vote — in 2018 alone, The Equity Alliance registered more than 91,000 through the Tennessee Black Voter Project — aided young, Black entrepreneurs in setting up shop and fed thousands through monthly community meals in three cities. 
Oliver, who served as the Alliance’s first executive director before leaving the group in 2022 for a successful state Senate run, said politics was the organization’s first focus.
“We wanted to make sure candidates we were supporting and endorsing at least had a ground group of people who were going to vote for them,” she said. “We wanted people to understand how powerful their vote was and to reach people averse to politics and expand the electorate.” 
Tequila Johnson and state Sen. Charlane Oliver, founders of The Equity Alliance, photographed at the Tennessee Women Suffrage Monument in Nashville’s Centennial Park in 2022. (Photo by John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)
Red berets of response
Lipstick-red berets have become the uniform of the Equity Alliance: they are hard to miss and evoke an era when groups like the Black Panthers organized in streets, challenged the political establishment and demanded that a nation live up to its promises.
But the Alliance’s story isn’t about a return to the past. It is about what happens when a new generation of Black women takes the lessons of earlier movements and joins them to politics in the present, in a state where Republican lawmakers have diminished Black voting power by gerrymandering and harsh redistricting, a state in which political power can determine who gets heard, who gets represented and whose neighborhood receives the resources it needs.



Quotation







It’s not enough to show up and get people physically engaged when their basic needs aren’t being met.


– Tequila Johnson, CEO, The Equity Alliance


Johnson, now CEO, said Alliance leaders realized soon after launching that to achieve success through civic and political means, they needed to help meet the everyday needs of the Black Tennesseans they were trying to reach. 
“It’s not enough to show up and get people physically engaged when their basic needs aren’t being met,” said Johnson.
The women developed a community engagement pyramid the women developed based on Maslow’s Hierarchy of Needs, a five-tier psychological theory developed by American psychologist Abraham Maslow. Like Maslow’s structure, the Equity Alliance model seeks to ensure community members have tools for survival and stability before they can be free to grow into higher levels, including leadership and advocacy. 
Rapid response following environmental disasters, including a catastrophic Nashville tornado in March 2020 and a January 2026 ice storm that led to power outages in Memphis and Nashville, meet the first level on the pyramid.
“Feed the Block” is another, offering monthly gatherings in Memphis, Nashville and Clarksville neighborhoods,in which local food trucks sponsor and cater community suppers. 
Island Marshall, age 6, preparing for an event in Memphis. Her mother, Kat Marshall, is communications director for The Equity Alliance. (Photo by John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)
The next generation
After 10 years, Alliance leaders are again asking, “what’s next?”
“We are in a place where we need to grow and diversify our leadership,” said Johnson. “We are looking at 20 or 30 years from now. I want to see 20 more ‘mes.” I want to see 20 more young Black leaders.” 
She wants a rapid response hub, a community center through which people can get food, generators, and find temporary housing following emergency situations. Johnson sees herself as growing into a national voice for the South, calling attention to the latent political power here and the benefits of investing in civic infrastructure.
Oliver said she once dreamed of raising enough money to hire an executive director; now, the organization has 20 full time staff members and employed 250 in Memphis during the recent election cycle. 
“It’s hard to put into words, sitting back, not being attached to the organization,” said Oliver. “I beam when I hear they are adding staff.”
“We planted seeds, we didn’t know how it was going to sprout,” she said. “It had ripple effects. That’s how change happens. You don’t get to control the end result.” 
“You do your part and be hopeful the next person catches the baton and carries it forward.”

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: Commentary: Idaho lawmakers should build on the momentum, support we are giving to kinship caregivers
description: Forty years ago, I was a child growing up in my grandparents’ house in Mountain Home. To me, it was simply home. I didn’t think of my grandparents as caregivers or understand what they had taken on to raise me. I understand it now. As program manager for the Idaho Caregiver Alliance, I see their […]
text:
More than 11,000 Idahoans are raising children whose parents cannot, and roughly 9,000 Idaho children are being raised by relatives with no parent in the home. These kinship caregivers are grandparents, aunts and uncles, older siblings, Tribal members and close family friends, writes guest columnist Sheila Weaver. (Photo by Lourdes Balduque/Getty Images)Forty years ago, I was a child growing up in my grandparents’ house in Mountain Home. 
To me, it was simply home. I didn’t think of my grandparents as caregivers or understand what they had taken on to raise me.
I understand it now. As program manager for the Idaho Caregiver Alliance, I see their story repeated in families across the state. This National Family Caregivers Month, those families deserve recognition – and support that reflects on their selflessness and needs.
More than 11,000 Idahoans are raising children whose parents cannot, and roughly 9,000 Idaho children are being raised by relatives with no parent in the home. These kinship caregivers are grandparents, aunts and uncles, older siblings, Tribal members and close family friends. 
For every Idaho child in foster care living with a relative, about 18 more are being raised by kin outside foster care entirely. Most of these families never receive support from the state system. 
That is what makes this work so easy to overlook. Kinship caregivers often step in overnight providing stability in a situation that can be highly emotional for a child. They keep a child in a familiar place while taking on homework, doctor’s appointments and everyday responsibilities.
That commitment carries a cost. More than 40% of caregivers surveyed reported spending at least $1,000 more each month than before they stepped into the role. In a statewide survey the Idaho Caregiver Alliance conducted, 88% of caregivers had been providing care for at least a year. More than 60% were raising two or more children. 
Community partnerships can help families find stability. Support from partners like Molina Healthcare of Idaho has helped us offer education and skill-building programs that help caregivers address trauma, strengthen family well-being, and connect with others who understand their challenges. For one grandmother, these gatherings helped her feel less alone raising her grandchild. 
Beyond meeting immediate needs, Idaho is working to make support easier to find. For two years, the Idaho Department of Health and Welfare, the Idaho Department of Correction and the Idaho Caregiver Alliance have worked together through the Bridging Systems for Kinship Families initiative. 
The goal has been to improve coordination among state agencies and community organizations that serve these families. 
This year, through Senate Resolution 118, the Idaho Senate endorsed developing a state blueprint for kinship caregivers, the first in the nation. That plan draws on surveys and focus groups with caregivers across the state and is expected in early 2027.
When the Idaho Legislature returns to the state Capitol this January, lawmakers have an opportunity to build on this momentum by listening to kinship caregivers and making their needs a priority. 
As the state plan’s recommendations take shape, policymakers will need to work together with partners like Molina to support the families who are standing behind these children and their kinship caregivers.  
My grandparents never thought of themselves as caregivers. They just made a home for me, and it took me years to understand what it took to make it that way. Every child raised by kin deserves that same sense of home, and the people providing it deserve to be seen and supported.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: Thousands of WV tax deeds could be set aside due to alleged process server forgeries
description: Potentially thousands of deeds for tax delinquent properties sold by the state Auditor’s Office were found to be fraudulently notarized, an investigation by the Secretary of State’s Office found.
text:
An investigation found that potentially thousands of deeds for tax delinquent properties sold by the state Auditor’s Office were fraudulently notarized. (Photo by Amelia Ferrell Knisely/West Virginia Watch)Potentially thousands of deeds for tax delinquent properties sold by the state Auditor’s Office were found to be fraudulently notarized, an investigation by the Secretary of State’s Office found. 
And some people were found to not have been served at all, the investigation showed. This could open the door to deeds being contested and set aside in court. 
“There are a lot of ramifications for a process server, whether it be in litigation, serving a copy of someone’s complaint, or serving a copy of the notice of the tax sale at a property,” said state Sen. Ryan Weld, an attorney who deals in property law. 
The issues with the process server don’t relate to the federal indictments against Auditor Mark Hunt announced Monday by prosecutors. But it is another in a series of issues brought to light about the Auditor’s Office, which have included hiring a state senator for contract work, irregularities in tax sales and a potential conflict of interest with a used car lot. 
Over the summer, Falcon Express — a process server that has worked for the Auditor’s Office to serve interested parties in properties up for tax sale — alerted the Secretary of State’s Office that one of its subcontractors was using a notary who did not appear to exist. 
The number of documents, issued between 2022 to 2026, could be in the thousands, according to a report filed in the investigation. That means those with an interest in a property gone to tax sale could potentially have been robbed of the chance to pay the back taxes if they hadn’t been served at all, or those buying a tax sale property could have their ownership contested even if they did all the right things. 
Property owners who may have been improperly served could have the tax delinquent deed set aside, according to West Virginia state code.
During a tax delinquent property sale, a buyer of the property must conduct a title search to find any property owners or any entity with a lien on it. For instance, a piece of property could be split between the five children of a deceased person and all would need to be served. 
The results of the title search are then given to the state Auditor’s Office, who in turns uses their contracted process server to contact everyone with legal claims to the property to let them know about the sale. 
Any tenant renting a property up for tax sale would also have to be served. Weld said this could potentially give them the opportunity to buy it themselves — and improperly serving them could jeopardize that. 
“If you have a kind of a slumlord as your landlord, someone who isn’t really taking care of the property, doesn’t really care what happens, and they’re not paying the property taxes, you could be robbed of the place that you live at because you never even knew,” he said. “You can’t do anything about something you don’t know about.”
Madyln Alqutub, a spokesperson for the Auditor’s Office, confirmed that Falcon Express is still being used by the office, stating issues with a subcontractor were “identified and addressed.”
“Our office is presently in litigation and is unable to make further comments regarding this matter,” she wrote in a statement. 
The notary stamps in question appeared on sworn affidavits that stated the server had made contact with the interested party and given them the legal documents. 
An investigator with the Secretary of State’s Office — which is in charge of keeping a list of authorized notaries — traveled to the Eastern Panhandle to find the notary listed in affidavits verifying papers were served. 
During the course of the investigation, the Secretary of State’s Office obtained a forged notary stamp. The investigator also confirmed that an additional 30 documents that appeared to have been notarized by a registered notary were not signed by the person whose signature appeared on them. 
The investigation also found multiple instances where a person who was supposed to have been served was not, according to the report. 
The subcontractor died shortly after the investigation culminated in a search warrant at their house. 
The Secretary of State’s Office closed the case as non-prosecutable due to the subcontractor’s death. The office forwarded the findings to the state’s Auditor Office, according to David Cook, the Secretary of State’s general counsel. 
Alqutub, a spokesperson for the Auditor’s Office, said the office never heard from the Secretary of State about the findings. 
Falcon Express was initially hired during the latter half of then-auditor, now Attorney General JB McCuskey’s administration. 
Kallie Moore, a spokesperson for McCuskey, said the Auditor’s Office had no issue with the processor at that time. Falcon Express declined to comment. 
The Auditor’s Office has paid a little more than $1 million since 2020 to Falcon Express for serving papers, according to West Virginia Checkbook, an online database of state account transactions. 
About $35,000 has been paid since the investigation concluded.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: Health Care Authority green lights CAMC, Ronald McDonald House mobile care unit
description: A West Virginia regulatory agency this month signed off on a plan by a Charleston hospital and a nonprofit organization to operate a mobile health unit serving women and children in underserved areas of West Virginia, despite an objection from a competing healthcare system. Charleston Area Medical Center told the West Virginia Health Care Authority […]
text:
The Care Mobile, a project of Charleston Area Medical Center and Ronald McDonald House of Southern West Virginia, aims to bring care to women and children in underserved parts of the state beginning next year. (Rendering courtesy of Ronald McDonald House) A West Virginia regulatory agency this month signed off on a plan by a Charleston hospital and a nonprofit organization to operate a mobile health unit serving women and children in underserved areas of West Virginia, despite an objection from a competing healthcare system.
Charleston Area Medical Center told the West Virginia Health Care Authority earlier this month of plans to work with Ronald McDonald House of Southern West Virginia on a “fully equipped medical clinic on wheels” to provide free or reimbursed care underserved areas of the state, according to a Nov. 2 letter on file with the Health Care Authority.
CAMC’s letter asked the Health Care Authority for a determination that the hospital does not need to obtain a certificate of need for the project. 
Certificate of need is a regulatory process overseen by the state Health Care Authority. West Virginia state law requires that when adding or expanding services, healthcare providers get a document stating that those new services fit an unmet need in the area. 
CAMC argued that the project is essentially the same as one to provide mobile specialty physician services that was deemed to be exempt from certificate of need review in 2023.
“The only difference is that it will have pediatric and obstetric physician services and target areas where the residents lack access to those physician specialties,” an official for the hospital wrote. “Thus, we are adding a second physician specialty bus which should not require review.”
A healthcare financial analyst with the Health Care Authority asked CAMC in a followup letter whether the mobile unit would be a shared healthcare service between two or more hospitals.
“Yes, the Ronald McDonald Care Mobile unit will share pediatric and OB physician services from Vandalia Health’s CAMC Women and Children’s Hospital across the Vandalia Health footprint and will be on Vandalia Health hospital campuses and Vandalia Health ambulatory care sites providing Pediatric and Obstetric specialty physician services,” David Jarrett, a healthcare planning consultant for Vandalia Health, wrote in a letter responding to the health care authority.
In a letter dated Nov. 6, Alaina Crislip, a Charleston attorney representing WVU Medicine’s Thomas Memorial Hospital, wrote to the Health Care Authority, requesting that the hospital be listed as being affected by CAMC’s mobile care unit proposal. 
“We represent (Thomas Memorial Hospital), which provides services similar to those under review in the above-captioned matter and which will be significantly affected by the project proposed therein,” Crislip wrote.” “…As further discussed below, TMH respectfully submits that CAMC has failed to establish that its proposal is not subject to CON review.”
She wrote further that CAMC’s request had a ‘fundamental problem’ in that it doesn’t have a CON for mobile services it wants to establish. 
“The mobile mammography determination on which CAMC relies permitted the addition of a second unit under an existing CON,” Crislip wrote. “Here, CAMC has no underlying CON to expand upon. Simply put, CAMC must first obtain the CON that its request assumes it already has.”
At its meeting last week, the Health Care Authority sided with CAMC, determining that the project is not reviewable, and that it’s exempt from needing a certificate of need because of a shared services exemption for a mobile unit that’s used by more than one hospital.  
The “Care Mobile,” a 40-foot vehicle with two exam rooms, will provide obstetric and pediatric care to the southern and central regions of West Virginia, home to many of the families served by the Ronald McDonald House, executive director Brooke Hylbert told West Virginia Watch Monday. 
“We really just want to ensure that we are beginning to bring those healthcare services into communities that may be experiencing a gap or an access to care issue,” Hylbert said.
CAMC Women and Children’s hospital will staff the mobile unit. The project will cost about $1 million, to be paid for by Ronald McDonald House.
Terry Cox, system director of mobile health and telemedicine services with CAMC’s Mobile Medical Administration, described the healthcare system’s work with Ronald McDonald House as the perfect collaboration. 
“Their vision is to take what they do here locally in Charleston, and try to support families where they live in rural areas, especially,” Cox said. “You pair that with what we can do from a pediatric and prenatal standpoint at Women and Children’s Hospital and the specialty care that we provide, and it just seems like a great opportunity for us to partner.”
CAMC and Ronald McDonald House officials hope to take possession of the mobile unit by the end of the first quarter of 2027, and have it on the road by the end of the second quarter, Cox said. 
Hylbert said the mobile unit will help the Ronald McDonald House take its mission of providing a home away from home to families while their children are getting medical care in Charleston a step further. 
“This Care Mobile kind of allows us to take that mission a step further and reach those families potentially before they ever even have to make that journey,” she said. “It’s really just a natural extension of our mission to provide those essential services, remove barriers, strengthen families, and promote access to healthcare when children need it.”
In an email to West Virginia Watch, Kristin Anderson, a spokeswoman for WVU Medicine Health Thomas Memorial Hospital, said the hospital supports ensuring healthcare services are available throughout the state, and it also respects the processes in the state’s CON law and the health care authority’s obligation to enforce those processes. 
“The Nov. 2, 2026, letter from CAMC to the West Virginia Health Care Authority did not provide sufficient information to support the request to circumvent the required Certificate of Need Application process, as evidenced by the Health Care Authority’s request for additional information from CAMC,” Anderson wrote.  “Thomas Hospitals does not object to additional health care services being made available in West Virginia and supports following the processes associated with approval for those services.”
A spokesman for CAMC declined to comment on the letter from WVU Medicine.
Hylbert, with Ronald McDonald House of Southern West Virginia, said from their perspective, healthcare is not a competition. 
“I think our responsibility here at the Ronald McDonald House is to bring resources together and address needs of the community,” she said. “And this program is something that we feel will do that.”

title: Hearing set for Thursday on Barnes County hog farm
description: North Dakota’s environmental regulatory agency will hold a public meeting in Valley City on Thursday about plans for more than 8,000 hogs at a Barnes County farm.  The Department of Environmental Quality will host the public hearing on the animal feeding operation permit for Blackhawk Farms from 5 p.m. to 8 p.m. at the Barnes […]
text:
Hogs are shown in a barn. A large hog farm near Valley City, North Dakota, is the subject of a public hearing Thursday. (Photo by Scott Olson/Getty Images)North Dakota’s environmental regulatory agency will hold a public meeting in Valley City on Thursday about plans for more than 8,000 hogs at a Barnes County farm. 
The Department of Environmental Quality will host the public hearing on the animal feeding operation permit for Blackhawk Farms from 5 p.m. to 8 p.m. at the Barnes County Courthouse.
The application was submitted by Justin Roelofs, the vice president of relationship management with Pipestone, a Minnesota-based company that provides management for hog farms. 
The Blackhawk Farms plan is for a maximum of 8,461 head of swine inside barns at a site 14 miles north and 7 miles east of Valley City. 
The pigs will be on slatted floors with manure falling into pits, according to the application. 
The site is not within a mile of any aquifers, sensitive groundwater areas, source water protection areas, or wells, according to a fact sheet with the application. Given that, under state law, the farm will be required to install monitoring wells. 
There are five private wells within 2 miles of the farm.
The department says in the fact sheet that it proposes to issue this permit for five years. The permit application includes limits and conditions to protect human health, aquatic life and water. 
The public can speak at the hearing or provide written comments. A public comment period ends Nov. 30.
People can find details about the permit application and submit comments through the agency’s  website. Emails, calls, and letters can be directed to sfeld@nd.gov, 701-328-5237, or ND Dept. of Environmental Quality, Division of Water Quality, 4201 Normandy St., Bismarck, ND 58503.

name: WyoFile
title: Wyoming voters soundly rejected a major property tax cut. Here’s why.
description:
While voters don’t love taxes, many preferred a more targeted approach to property tax relief than Proposition 1 offered.
The post Wyoming voters soundly rejected a major property tax cut. Here’s why. appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
No county more soundly rejected Prop 1 — the sweeping statewide property tax cut — on Wyoming’s ballot this year than Niobrara, the least populated county in the nation’s least populated state.
Rep. JD Williams lives in Lusk, Niobrara’s county seat, and represents his home county along with neighboring Weston and Goshen counties. The Republican lawmaker, who frequently communicates with constituents via social media, describes his community bordering Nebraska and South Dakota as deeply conservative. 
That means residents are OK with paying their own way, he said. One way they do that is through special districts, which collect property taxes in exchange for providing services such as the senior center, fire department and weed and pest control.
Proposition 1 would have hit their special districts hard, which Williams called a “deal breaker.” 

Rep. JD Williams, R-Lusk, during the 2026 Wyoming Legislature budget session in Cheyenne. (Mike Vanata for WyoFile)

“I would say that’s why Niobrara County rejected it at a higher percentage than any other county in the state,” he said. “Just because we are not interested in giving any more control, decision-making authority or taxing authority to the state of Wyoming, and that’s what it would have done.”
As Williams sees it, the ability to fund special taxing districts keeps power closer to home. 
“It would have moved local decision-making authority to the Legislature, away from local boards, specifically our county commission,” Williams said. 
On Nov. 3, Wyoming voters soundly rejected Prop 1, which received less than 42% support. Even in a deeply conservative state, only one county backed the measure: Lincoln County, with support from 57% of the voters. On the other end was Niobrara County, where less than 30% of voters wanted to enact this type of tax relief. 
WyoFile teamed with partner publications to examine why Wyoming’s disparate counties voted the way they did on Proposition 1. Also known as The People’s Initiative to Limit Property Tax in Wyoming through a Homeowner’s Property Exemption, the initiative landed on the Nov. 3 general election ballot with the backing of more than 30,000 valid signatures collected around the state. If passed, it would have exempted 50% of a primary residence’s assessed value from property taxation, causing Wyoming’s annual property tax revenues to drop.


The state’s first citizen initiative to land on the ballot in 30 years, Prop 1 needed approval from more than 50% of those voting in the general election to pass. 
Although many expected a close vote, the measure’s failure caught some by surprise. Along with a potential loss of local control and services, voters remained leery of Prop 1 for many reasons, including worries that it would raise other types of taxes, benefit Teton County billionaires and unleash unintended consequences. 
Lincoln County lone yes
While Niobrara County anchors Wyoming’s eastern flank, Lincoln County sits on the opposite side of the state, bordering Idaho. Former Rep. Marti Halverson, a Republican who represented northern Lincoln County and southern Teton County for six years, rallied for Prop 1 in the only county that ultimately supported it.
Halverson described her own community as split before Election Day. But in Star Valley, in the northern part of the county, she said, people “voted for it overwhelmingly enough to override the undervotes, overvotes and the no votes in Opal, Kemmerer, Diamondville, Frontier and Cokeville.”
In places like Star Valley, the real estate market caught fire amid the COVID-19 pandemic, as people from around the country escaped to rural communities. As buyers snapped up properties, home prices — and property tax bills — soared. 
“I have two close neighbors who saw their property taxes double,” Halverson said. “Now, these are working families with mortgages, and their mortgages went up $400 to $500 a month.” 
Looking north across Star Valley in northern Lincoln County on Sept. 6, 2026, from Salt River Pass. Average residential fair market value in Lincoln County jumped 186% from 2015 to 2025. (Ryan Dorgan/WyoFile)
The rise in property values varies widely across the state. Historical average residential fair market value jumped 257% (183% after exemptions) and 186% (116%) in Teton and Lincoln counties respectively, the two highest increases, followed by Sheridan at 109% (48%). In contrast, Niobrara saw a 44% increase, which dropped to just 6% once tax exemptions were applied, during the same period from 2015 to 2025, according to a Legislative Service Office analysis. Campbell and Big Horn counties saw similar increases of 65% (12%) and 67% (19%), respectively during the same period.
State lawmakers heard homeowners’ concerns and responded with a slew of new and expanded tax breaks. But Prop 1 supporters saw more room to cut. While disappointed Prop 1 didn’t pass, Halverson said she “wasn’t surprised with over $2 million being spent against it.” 
Property tax vs. sales, income tax
The initiative’s failure has given Halverson “hope” that talk of increasing sales tax or imposing a state income tax is now “off the legislative table.” 
“I don’t think with the failure of Prop 1 that the Legislature can, in good conscience, raise any taxes,” she said. 
The risk that sales tax or a state income tax could eventually backfill revenue lost from the property tax cut drove some of the opposition to Prop 1. 
Tom Harrington spearheaded “Concerned Citizens of Big Horn County,” a group that rallied against Prop 1, waving signs at motorists traveling through Shell Canyon in north central Wyoming every Sunday for about six weeks ahead of the election. He shares Halverson’s desire to avoid sales and income taxes.
“I’m against both of them, especially the sales tax, which is regressive and will unfairly impact the lower income people in our community,” Harrington said. “And income tax, I think, is just anathema to Wyoming, and I don’t think that’ll ever fly.” 
Harrington served as a judge in Big Horn, Hot Springs and Washakie counties before retiring. These days he helps out with the Greybull and Basin wrestling program. He still sees room for targeted property tax reform, especially for longtime Wyoming residents and specifically, single people, be they widowers or widows on fixed incomes and over age 65. 
But he saw Prop 1 as a chainsaw approach that would damage local services.
Likewise, Steve Helburn voted against Prop 1, in part, because of potential cuts to libraries, Meals on Wheels and law enforcement. He also didn’t like that the “benefit was primarily for the billionaires in Teton County, and little benefit to much less benefit to other parts of the state.” 


The Greybull resident already qualifies for property tax relief as a veteran and senior who has paid property taxes for more than 25 years in Wyoming. “I can get both of those,” Helburn said. “I don’t always, but they’re available to me.” 
Harrington also qualifies for existing tax relief programs, and has used them in the past. But he’s considering not applying in the future to support local services. 
The Wyoming Taxpayers Association, which opposed Prop 1, estimated that Big Horn County alone had lost more than $2 million in revenue from 2025 tax exemption programs, excluding the veteran’s exemption and refund and deferral programs. Had Prop 1 passed, the association estimated the county could have lost nearly $1.9 million more.
Big Horn County Commissioner Bruce Jolley, a Lovell Republican, also qualifies for the relatively new exemptions. But Jolley typically opts instead for the veterans discount because it doesn’t pinch the county budget since the state reimburses the county for that relief program, he said. Gov. Mark Gordon included $16.6 million to extend property tax relief programs in his supplemental budget announced Monday.
Jolley fielded many calls from constituents asking his position on Prop 1, which he opposed. Most were concerned about the county, towns, schools and special districts losing funding, Jolley said. “I see firsthand how it affects the budget of the county.” 
He’s also leery of one tax cut opening the door to raising other types of taxes.  
“I am especially against any kind of tax backfill because that means our sales tax will rise, which in northern Wyoming, especially in Washakie, Hot Springs and Big Horn counties, that is going to directly affect our small business,” he said. “More people will utilize the option of going to Montana to buy their goods and services.”
Tax-rich county declines cut
In the county with the highest property tax values in Wyoming, voters not only opposed giving themselves a property tax break this general election but also decided to increase taxes for the local hospital and maintain a tax for environmental conservation.
Roughly 63% of Teton County voters opposed Prop 1. Some voters coming out of the polls Nov. 3 were conflicted.
“I ultimately voted against it,” Austin O’Bryhim, 33, said. “Not because I don’t agree with property tax relief — because I think in this county, specifically, it’s well needed — but they did not demonstrate the ability to make up for that budget deficit elsewhere.”
The estimated financial impact was significant. The Wyoming Department of Revenue and Legislative Service Office estimated there could be roughly $109 million to $125 million exempted from residential property tax bills statewide in the first year. In Teton County alone, nearly $37 million could have been exempted, according to the Wyoming Taxpayers Association.
Residential property tax dollars don’t go to the state’s general fund, but rather to public education and local governments. Roughly two-thirds of residential property taxes pay for Wyoming schools. The remaining one-third funds county government such as administration, roads and general operations; special districts, including fire protection, hospital districts, weed and pest control and water/sewer; and city and town budgets, according to the revenue department.
Voters arrive to cast ballots in the general election Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026, at the Old Wilson Schoolhouse in Teton County. (Bradly J. Boner/Jackson Hole News&Guide)
Margo Krisjansons, who has lived in Teton County since 1973, also voted against property tax relief.
“I’m a little guy. I’m not a billionaire,” Krisjansons said, “so I got to think about the long-term for what’s good for me as a homeowner in Kelly.”
The death of Prop 1 took some Teton County voters like Republican Werner E. Minshall by surprise. He’s frustrated by the lack of overarching tax relief, and although he said he could afford his high tax bill at around $36,000, others couldn’t.
“It’s extremely unfortunate,” Minshall said about Prop 1 failing. “So, now we’re going to have a bloated government in Teton County.”
Big Horn County conservatives, who also supported Prop 1, blamed scare tactics for its failure. 
“I believe that it’s humanitarian in the way that it helps families that are buying property, families that are trying to hold on to property and older folks and even regular folks trying to pay their bills,” said Gordon Preis, a Republican committeeman who lives in Emblem. Preis joined other conservative voters in Big Horn County to buy an advertisement in the Greybull Standard urging fellow citizens to support Prop 1.
“The real issue is they don’t want to lose their tax money, the state, the county,” Preis said. 
Preis compared it to how he pens his cows, getting them a little hungry and then leading them into the pen. “People fall into the trap every time.”
‘Prop 1’ splits two ways in Campbell County
Campbell County voters were close to evenly split on the ballot initiative. After Lincoln and Park counties, Campbell County came the closest to passing Prop 1. That it failed, winning about 48% of the vote, shocked many in a county where mineral taxes bankroll many services. Minerals generate about 78% of Campbell County’s property tax revenue.
Even though he opposed Prop 1, Campbell County Commissioner and former Republican legislator Scott Clem said it’s hard to say why the initiative didn’t pass.
“Being able to pay less (in property tax) is certainly appealing,” Clem said. “I still wonder how much the public is aware about the tax remedies that have been implemented in the past couple of years.”
Campbell County Commissioner Scott Clem poses for a portrait in downtown Gillette on Nov. 11, 2025. (Jonathan Gallardo/Gillette News Record)
Only 40% of eligible Campbell County taxpayers have applied for the relatively new exemptions for the 2026 tax year, Assessor Erin Slattery wrote in an email. The other 60% may choose to pay property taxes to fund local services or not know their options. 
Governments can do a better job informing taxpayers about existing tax exemptions and relief options, Clem said.
Gillette real estate agent Josh McGrath gave multiple presentations about initiatives called Prop 1. There was Prop 1, the statewide initiative.
But Campbell County also had its own local Prop 1, asking voters to renew a penny sales tax to fund local services for another four years. The penny tax was promoted in Gillette with signs of Abraham Lincoln, reminding voters the local tax funds more than $18 million in infrastructure, maintenance, public safety and other programs around town. 
While the statewide initiative failed, voters renewed the penny tax by nearly 68%. 
Messaging from Campbell County groups combined with campaigning from outside organizations, such as the Wyoming Taxpayers Association, could have impacted the results, McGrath said.
“I think it’s because they saw the benefit of the (penny tax), and I think that maybe had a bit of a residual effect. Like, ‘Hey, I’ve seen what this has done as a benefit,’” McGrath said. “They’re both named Prop 1, but I don’t have a great reason for why it’s split. It was one of those hot topics where you’re either for it or against it, and there’s not any middle ground.”
Wanda Lieneman was a regional campaign manager for Cody Republican Brent Bien’s gubernatorial run and helped gather some of the more than 30,000 signatures for the initiative he helped get on the ballot. She pointed to negative ads from groups like the Wyoming Education Association and Wyoming Taxpayers Association as the biggest reason it didn’t pass. 
She called the results of her petition work “devastating.” Lieneman started working on the initiative after seeing friends get taxed out of their homes, she said. Her own property tax bill on her home has more than doubled in the past five years, but she takes advantage of the 50% exemption for seniors.
She disagreed that local services would suffer, suggesting local governments could be supported by interest income generated from the state’s and other rainy day funds. Revenue for school districts, law enforcement and other public services doesn’t have to come from property taxes, she said. 
Lieneman said Prop 1 could be the last time Wyoming residents see a ballot initiative like it.
“What can I do? We did everything we could to get it through, and the lies went out that we were not telling people the truth,” Lieneman said. “I’m going to continue to fight for it, I’ll go down to the Legislature and do my part there, but as far as the initiative goes, it’s dead.”
For Commissioner Clem, a lack of relief for renters and the potential for unintended consequences added to the list of reasons he voted against Prop 1. 
“All taxes suck. No one likes them, not even me, but they are a necessary evil for a functioning 21st Century society,” he said. “In this case, the devil you know is better than the devil you don’t know.”
