name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: Federal permitting bill splits South Dakota Republicans, causing some to align with Democrats
description: Federal legislation that could accelerate permitting for large energy and infrastructure projects has scrambled political allegiances in South Dakota, leading two Republican U.S. senators to vote differently while splitting Republican state lawmakers and causing some of them to align with Democrats. Fifty state lawmakers and lawmakers-elect from South Dakota[...]
text:
The South Dakota House of Representatives meets at the Capitol in Pierre on Feb. 10, 2026. (Photo by Makenzie Huber/South Dakota Searchlight)Federal legislation that could accelerate permitting for large energy and infrastructure projects has scrambled political allegiances in South Dakota, leading two Republican U.S. senators to vote differently while splitting Republican state lawmakers and causing some of them to align with Democrats.
Fifty state lawmakers and lawmakers-elect from South Dakota — including 37 Republicans, 12 Democrats and one independent — sent a letter on Monday to Republican U.S. Senators John Thune and Mike Rounds urging opposition to the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act. It would streamline federal review and approval for projects including power plants, transmission lines and pipelines. It would also require data centers to cover their electrical infrastructure costs. 
Supporters say the changes would reduce project delays and costs, while critics say they would weaken environmental oversight, local control and public input.
The letter says economic development, affordable energy and infrastructure investment “must not come at the expense of environmental protections, agricultural interests, private property rights, tribal sovereignty, local control, or the health and well-being of our communities.”
State senators Joy Hohn, R-Hartford, and Red Dawn Foster, D-Pine Ridge, were the first two signers of the letter. Foster is a member of the Oglala Sioux Tribe. Hohn, who won reelection earlier this month, is a vocal opponent of a carbon-capture pipeline that was proposed to run through eastern South Dakota. 
“This bill is an incremental erosion of our fundamental rights,” Hohn told South Dakota Searchlight.
Other letter signers include a county commissioner and various Republican Party officials.
Sen. Joy Hohn, R-Hartford, speaks on Feb. 11, 2026, in the South Dakota Senate at the Capitol in Pierre. (Photo by Makenzie Huber/South Dakota Searchlight)
Lawmaker disagreement
State lawmakers sometimes approve resolutions urging support or opposition of federal actions. A news release from Hohn and Foster about the letter said that because lawmakers don’t begin their annual legislative session until January, they “do not have the opportunity to formally address this issue through a legislative resolution.”
“Recognizing the concerns being raised by constituents throughout South Dakota, participating legislators have come together through a joint letter to ensure those voices are heard at the federal level,” the news release said.
Judging solely by the signatures, the letter does not have enough support to pass as a resolution, partly because some of the signers lost their bids for reelection or did not run for another term. The letter has 20 signatures from state House members who will be in office in January, short of the 36 needed for a majority, and 12 signatures from state Senate members who will be in office in January, short of the necessary 18.
Sen. Casey Crabtree, R-Madison, the state Senate’s majority leader-elect, did not sign the letter. Nor did any other member of the incoming Republican legislative leadership teams in the state House or Senate. 

Sen. Casey Crabtree, R-Madison, speaks in the South Dakota Senate on Feb. 11, 2026, at the Capitol in Pierre. (Photo by Makenzie Huber/South Dakota Searchlight)

Crabtree said he supports the federal permitting legislation and said lawmakers should commend U.S. Senate Majority Leader Thune for working in a bipartisan manner to “deliver affordable electricity, fix our roads and bridges, upgrade our telecommunications systems and maintain strong protections for South Dakotans.”
“The American people are united behind the issue of affordability,” Crabtree said. 
All of the members of the incoming Democratic legislative leadership teams in the state House and Senate signed the letter. That includes both of the party’s Senate members who will be in office in January, and 10 of the 12 Democrats who will be House members in January. 
Senate Minority Leader-elect Erik Muckey, D-Sioux Falls, said trying to cut red tape for infrastructure development may sound great on its face. 
“But the thing is, you can accomplish that without having to have very drastic, negative impacts on environmental law, the Endangered Species Act, the Clean Water Act, all the way to the utter disregard of tribal sovereignty, local control and even, frankly, the state Public Utilities Commission,” Muckey said. 
House Minority Leader-elect Eric Emery, D-Rosebud, acknowledged that federal permitting needs work. He said the bill goes too far. 
“As a Native legislator from Rosebud, I can’t get past what this bill does to tribes,” he said. 
Emery said the bill narrows what states and tribes can review under the Clean Water Act, and it allows 150 days to challenge a federal permit in court, which he said is too short. He also opposes what he described as a watering-down of tribal consultation requirements. The Great Plains Tribal Chairmen’s Association and some other tribal organizations oppose the legislation.
“Consultation on sacred sites and cultural resources is part of what the United States owes tribal nations under the treaties. It shouldn’t be optional,” Emery said. “This is one issue where I agree with a lot of my Republican colleagues here at home. Local control and tribal sovereignty don’t belong to one party in South Dakota.”
Rep. Eric Emery, D-Rosebud, sits at his desk in the South Dakota House of Representatives during the 2024 legislative session. (Photo by Makenzie Huber/South Dakota Searchlight)
Not just lawmakers opposed
South Dakota Public Utilities Commission Chair Chris Nelson, a Republican, said the commission is “adamantly opposed” to provisions that would allow transmission line developers to seek federal approval if state regulators deny a permit or impose conditions developers consider too burdensome.
“What it really does is it takes away the South Dakota PUC’s ability to evaluate projects fairly under our statute and to work with landowners here, to work out their concerns, and make a final decision here,” Nelson said.
Nelson also raised concerns about federal eminent domain authority and whether federal regulators would be required to consider landowner objections. Eminent domain is a legal power granted to some developers for gaining access to land without landowner consent, while paying just compensation to the owner. It’s been a divisive issue in South Dakota the last several years because of a proposed multi-state carbon capture-pipeline that would have passed through the eastern part of the state. The Legislature and Republican Gov. Larry Rhoden banned eminent domain for carbon pipelines last year.
Bill moves forward in D.C.
Sen. Rounds was the only Republican to cast a procedural vote against the legislation earlier this month. Afterward, he posted comments on social media expressing some of the same concerns expressed by Nelson. Rounds said at the time that he hoped to work with his colleagues to address the concerns.
The bill passed that procedural vote 73-25 and awaits a final vote in the Senate.  
Permitting overhaul splits SD’s US senators but advances with tepid bipartisan support

Thune voted to advance the bill and has said permitting reform is necessary to lower energy costs, create jobs and prevent infrastructure projects from being delayed for years by federal bureaucracy.
“Too often, projects are bogged down in bureaucratic delays for months, and often years, at a time,” Thune said during a Tuesday speech in the Senate. “Delays cause project budgets to balloon, which then leads to higher costs for American consumers.”
Thune said the bill would also reduce permitting burdens on farmers and ranchers, provide technical assistance to communities considering a data center, and require data centers to cover their own energy-related costs.
“Whether that’s their operating and construction costs or the cost of grid improvements needed to accommodate them,” he said. “This legislation ensures those costs don’t show up on household utility bills.”
Thune’s office told South Dakota Searchlight the legislation would not override South Dakota’s ban on eminent domain for carbon pipelines.
U.S. Rep. Dusty Johnson, R-South Dakota, shared his support for the bill last week on social media, calling it “the most important affordability bill in decades.”
“If we want lower taxes, lower energy bills, better roads and bridges, we have to right-size our regulatory approach,” Johnson said, adding that the bill “does that while protecting property rights and forcing data centers to pay their fair share.”

title: ‘SEIZED’ documentary about Marion newspaper raids to premiere on HBO
description: TOPEKA — The lead headline on the front page of the Marion County Record’s Aug. 16, 2023, edition read in big, bold font: “SEIZED…but not silenced.” The paper’s weekly issue came five days after local law enforcement seized computers, cellphones and materials from the Record, its reporters and editor Eric Meyer’s home. An HBO Original […]
text:
Copies of the Aug. 16, 2023, edition of the Marion County Record rest on a countertop in the newspaper office. Staffers pulled an all-nighter to get the newspaper out after their equipment was seized by law enforcement. (Sherman Smith/Kansas Reflector)TOPEKA — The lead headline on the front page of the Marion County Record’s Aug. 16, 2023, edition read in big, bold font: “SEIZED…but not silenced.”
The paper’s weekly issue came five days after local law enforcement seized computers, cellphones and materials from the Record, its reporters and editor Eric Meyer’s home.
An HBO Original documentary, “Seized,” traces the raid, the lawsuits that ensued, and the staff that remained to continue covering the community.
It will debut at 8 p.m. CT on hDec. 1 on HBO and will be available to stream on HBO Max.
The documentary, directed by Sharon Liese, premiered at the Sundance Film Festival in January.
“Told with humor and candor, the saga of The Record raises salient questions about the role of local newspapers, often underfunded, under attack, and disappearing fast,” a press release said. “The film is an affectionate portrait of small-town America and how one small town became a flashpoint in the global discourse about the urgency of independent journalism.”

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: As Dems take control, advocates see opportunity to upend the energy status quo
description: With Wisconsin sitting on the precipice of total Democratic control of state government and voters in the state more focused than ever on both their rising utility bills and the system behind them, the state’s Citizens Utility Board held a forum on energy affordability Tuesday to discuss policy solutions for bringing those costs down.  Residents, […]
text:
Solar panels in Boone, Iowa. Participants at a Citizens Utililty Board meeting in Madison on Tuesday said an integrated resource plan is crucial to bringing down utility costs in Wisconsin. (USDA photo)With Wisconsin sitting on the precipice of total Democratic control of state government and voters in the state more focused than ever on both their rising utility bills and the system behind them, the state’s Citizens Utility Board held a forum on energy affordability Tuesday to discuss policy solutions for bringing those costs down. 
Residents, advocates, policymakers and experts gathered at the Park Hotel in Madison where the results of the election earlier this month were cast as an opportunity to upend an energy status quo. In recent years, participants said, Wisconsin has prioritized the development of fossil fuel burning plants, investment returns to utility shareholders and the needs of tech companies building massive data centers over the finances of regular citizens.
Kristy Nieto, a member of the Wisconsin Public Service Commission — the regulatory body that oversees the state’s utility companies — said at the event that Wisconsin was previously a national leader in regulating utilities in ways that benefited regular people and the environment. She argued that the commission should be given the staffing, budget and authority to restore that leadership. 
“We have to fundamentally rethink how we approach affordability and the tools that we have to mitigate rate increases,” she said. “Business as usual won’t cut it, but despite the challenges that we face, I think there’s something important that Wisconsin has going for it right now. We have an opportunity to lead again. Sometimes we’ll hear the argument that the commission shouldn’t do something because the commission hasn’t done it before, or because other states don’t do it …  Wisconsin would be an outlier. I say that when done thoughtfully, competently and rationally, being an outlier can be a good thing. We were an outlier when we established modern utility regulation in the progressive movement, in environmental stewardship, and we shouldn’t be afraid to be an outlier again.”
Nieto said that to successfully make energy in Wisconsin more affordable, the state should pull three levers — establish a more holistic planning process for the state’s energy portfolio, give the PSC more tools to prioritize lowering costs when setting electric rates and increase the capacity of PSC’s staff to regulate an increasingly complex industry. 
Policy advocates speak at the Citizens Utility Board’s Nov. 17 energy affordability forum in Madison. (Photo by Henry Redman/Wisconsin Examiner)
In the weeks since the November election, during which Democrats were swept into power on promises to  increase the affordability of basic needs such as energy, lawmakers, environmental groups and affordable energy advocates have settled on “integrated resource planning” as a top priority for Democrats once the legislative session begins in January. 
Integrated resource planning means the state’s utility companies would have to submit their future plans to the PSC for approval, forecasting how much power a company will need to generate, where that power will come from and how it will pay for that generation. That process will include public input and, advocates say, will help lawmakers push the utility companies toward building more renewable energy sources. 
Wisconsin is one of just a few states that doesn’t already have an integrated resource planning requirement. 
Emma Heins, who works on Wisconsin policy for the clean energy trade group Advanced Energy United, said that as data centers put stress on Wisconsin’s energy system, the state needs a way to address the broader energy landscape rather than tackling energy demand issues on a case-by-case basis. 
“Wisconsin is really, really overdue for an integrated resource plan,” Heins said, adding that the system has benefits for the regulators, who would be able to see the whole picture at once, for the utilities, who would have more regulatory certainty, for labor, which would be able to plan for 20 years of job opportunities, and for lawmakers, who would have a clearer picture of the decisions being made. 
A number of speakers at the forum argued that once the planning process is in place, the Legislature needs to keep the  pressure on the utilities and that regulators need the tools necessary to do their job. 
“The Legislature, you all have the bully pulpit. You have the microphone, the voice, to get out to the media, to leverage your constituents and to apply pressure in a holistic sense to utilities and what they are requesting of commissions,” Tremaine Phillips of the energy affordability group Powerlines said. “The other way is on personnel. Our commissions as well as consumer advocates are outgunned, outmanned in these proceedings.” 
The Legislature, he said, needs to give regulators adequate staff and resources to do their job. 
Beyond structural change to the planning process and the potential benefits of giving the PSC more manpower and teeth to regulate the state’s utility companies, a number of advocates at the forum said the state can save a lot of money by supporting energy efficiency programs and giving residents incentives to use less power and lower demand on peak energy days. Wisconsin has a number of existing programs that help people make their homes more energy efficient. Forum speakers said these could simply be given bigger budgets to achieve larger results. 
“I think there’s still a misconception that it’s not enough, or it’s so marginal that it doesn’t actually help the situation,” Heins said of the state’s existing energy efficiency programs. “So I think people think about, well, in my own home, I didn’t see 30% savings because I replaced LED light bulbs or something like that. And so then they extrapolate that to the grid and say, ‘Well, how much could energy efficiency actually do?’ When we know it’s a lot.”
If Wisconsin fully takes advantage of its available programs to reduce energy demand, the state could save up to $1.5 billion on energy costs, according to Citizens Utility Board analyst Jeff Adams.
“I mean, you factor in commercial and industrial and kind of multiply things to the scale of an entire grid — it can fix a lot of problems,” Heins said.

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: North Dakota students try on legislative roles, tackle AI
description: North Dakota students brainstormed answers to AI and technology use this week, hoping state lawmakers will take up the baton in January. Nearly 50 student senators from across North Dakota debated and advanced bills on artificial intelligence and student technology use during the first Student Legislative Summit at the Capitol. The students met on Monday […]
text:
Adam Said, a junior at Sheyenne High School, speaks on the Senate floor during the first Student Legislative Summit at the Capitol on Nov. 17, 2026. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)North Dakota students brainstormed answers to AI and technology use this week, hoping state lawmakers will take up the baton in January.
Nearly 50 student senators from across North Dakota debated and advanced bills on artificial intelligence and student technology use during the first Student Legislative Summit at the Capitol.
The students met on Monday and Tuesday to form committees, subcommittees, debate and vote on both topics as bill drafts were created from their work. The bills will be made available to state lawmakers as they begin the 2027 legislative session Jan. 5
“It was a lot of debates. A lot of, not heated discussion, but respectful discussion around topics that truly matter,” Adam Said, a junior at Sheyenne High School in West Fargo.
Said said it was a unique experience and he believes the students did a good job putting their viewpoints into the summit’s bill drafts. He also hopes state lawmakers take their opinions to heart.
“Parents and students do actually have a voice and our voices should matter, especially with AI that changes how education is viewed and how education is operated,” he said.
Thomas Unser, a student at West Fargo High School, speaks on the Senate floor during the first Student Legislative Summit at the Capitol on Nov. 17, 2026. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)
Superintendent of Public Instruction Levi Bachmeier said one of his favorite units as a state government teacher was the mock Congress and thought he could recreate that type of environment at the Capitol with high school students.
“I genuinely have appreciated and learned so much from these students,” Bachmeier said. “Just having the opportunity to hear from such thoughtful and passionate young people has helped develop my thinking and I hope that lawmakers view it the same way.”
He said the goals of the summit were to expose student leaders to the legislative process, but also give the student perspective on issues that state lawmakers may need to grapple with.
“They are smart and they are engaged,” said Sen. Kathy Hogan, D-Fargo, of the students attending the summit. 
Hogan said she hopes the students will stay involved and come back to Bismarck to sit with their representatives during the regular legislative session.
Kierstin Hurtt, superintendent of Valley-Edinburgh School District, and parent of one of the students participating, said she was watching the next generation of engaged leaders in North Dakota, in real time.
Brody Kramer, a senior at Bismarck Legacy High School, speaks on the Senate floor during the first Student Legislative Summit at the Capitol on Nov. 17, 2026. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)
“It’s inspiring. It’s hopeful. It’s massive,” Hurtt said. “You are really learning what it’s like to be a stakeholder and how everything is about building a relationship with other stakeholders to achieve a common goal.”
She said she was impressed that students were asking each other for clarity on their different points of view and opinions.
Hurtt added she hopes student senators will be able to use the voting board and the proceedings will be live-streamed in the future.
Brody Kramer, a senior at Bismarck Legacy High School, said it’s good for students to interact with others from across the state and expressing viewpoints constructively on complicated topics is an important skill to learn.
“I think the bills we’re talking about should be pushed into the legislative session and talked about there,” Kramer said. 
He said the committee work and debating with other students inspired him to consider running for public office.
The bill outlining rules for artificial intelligence use in schools passed on a 40-8 vote.
The bill would allow students to use artificial intelligence tools beginning in ninth grade, unless under the direction of a teacher during classroom instruction. However, it would not allow students to use the tools to complete assignments.
Hazel Albert, a student from Hope-Page High School, speaks on the Senate floor during the first Student Legislative Summit at the Capitol on Nov. 17, 2026. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)
The bill would also require teachers to list when AI use is permitted and not permitted as part of course instruction. Teachers would not be able to use AI to input grades into a gradebook or assign final grades, but they can use AI tools to assist with grading assignments and to create lesson plans.
A bill regulating the use of technology during the school day was approved on a 47-0 vote.
The school technology bill outlines that school districts must use technology as a support to learning and not a replacement for essential instruction. It also requires the technology must be used in a “manner reasonably suited to a student’s academic level, age, accessibility needs, and educational circumstances.”
“The seeds are being planted to have good public servants and there’s a whole Senate full of them right now,” Hogan said.
North Dakota Monitor reporter Michael Achterling can be reached at machterling@northdakotamonitor.com.

title: New ‘Opportunity Zones’ designated in Idaho, allowing tax breaks for new development
description: The U.S. Department of the Treasury approved all of Idaho’s 25 requested areas to be eligible to receive federal tax incentives to spur development.  The agency on Tuesday announced that the areas, which are located in 14 Idaho counties, are designated as Opportunity Zones. The federal program allows certain housing or economic development projects to […]
text:
A construction crew works outside a new development in Boise. Five of Idaho's new "Opportunity Zones" will be located in Boise. The designation allows for certain developments there to receive tax breaks. (Photo by Abigail Gerstein/Idaho Capital Sun)The U.S. Department of the Treasury approved all of Idaho’s 25 requested areas to be eligible to receive federal tax incentives to spur development. 
The agency on Tuesday announced that the areas, which are located in 14 Idaho counties, are designated as Opportunity Zones. The federal program allows certain housing or economic development projects to qualify for tax breaks. 
The Opportunity Zone program was created under the first Trump administration through the 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act. Congress last year made the program permanent through the One Big Beautiful Bill Act.
Idaho’s Republican Gov. Brad Little gives an interview to a reporter during a GOP election night watch party on Nov. 3, 2026, in Downtown Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun)
“Idaho is committed to encouraging private investment, creating good-paying jobs and strengthening communities across our state,” Idaho Gov. Brad Little said in a press release.  “Our first round of Opportunity Zones brought millions of dollars in investment to Idaho. With these new designations, we have another opportunity to build on that success, support rural and urban communities alike and ensure Idaho continues to be a place where businesses can grow and families can thrive.”
Nine of the 25 designated zones in Idaho are considered rural and will qualify for enhanced tax breaks, according to a press release. The most new zones are located in Ada County followed by Canyon County. 
Five of the designated zones will be in Boise, two in Nampa, two in Pocatello and two in Moscow. There will be a zone designated in Caldwell, Emmett, Twin Falls, Post Falls, Rexburg, Jerome and Lewiston, and other cities and unincorporated areas. 
U.S. Sen. Mike Crapo, R-Idaho, talks with attendees of the Idaho GOP election night watch party at the Grove Hotel in Boise, Idaho, on Nov. 8, 2022. (Photo by Otto Kitsinger for Idaho Capital Sun)
“By making Opportunity Zones permanent and strengthening incentives for rural communities, we’ve laid the groundwork to attract long-term private investments to Idaho in areas that need it most,” U.S. Sen. Mike Crapo, R-Idaho, said in the release.  “This is about generating economic growth in our communities and creating opportunities for Idaho families to prosper.”
The new designations take effect Jan. 1, 2027. 
Here are some of the new zones: 

Boise: Areas off West Main Street downtown, south of downtown and Shoreline Drive, in West Boise near the Boise Towne Square Mall, off South Broadway Avenue, and near Boise State University and West University Drive. 


Nampa: Downtown around 12th Avenue South and First Street South, as well as the 11th Avenue North corridor. 


Pocatello: The downtown Main Street corridor and Portneuf River area and areas around Yellowstone Avenue, Pole Line Road and West Quinn Road. 


Moscow: North of Main Street, along Highway 8 and Highway 95, and south of Moscow near the University of Idaho campus and Schweitzer Engineering Laboratories. 
Twin Falls: Downtown, near Main Avenue and Shoshone Street. 

The area in Twin Falls was home to Idaho’s first Opportunity Zone project, a food hall. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
 Results of previous Opportunity Zones are hard to measure 

In 2025, U.S. Housing and Urban Development Secretary Scott Turner traveled to Idaho with Crapo to discuss housing issues in the state. Turner, who led the first iteration of the program, said it would be a continued focus for developing more housing to meet the needs. 
Idaho to submit ‘Opportunity Zone’ proposals seeking tax breaks for economic development 

Turner said at the time 700 new housing units had been built inside Idaho Opportunity Zones and 4,000 new jobs had been created.
The first version of the program didn’t have reporting requirements, according to the Idaho Department of Commerce. 
A 2021 Brookings Institution analysis of the program nationally found some increased economic activity in urban areas, but not in rural areas, Stateline reported. However, that study’s data was limited by the effects of the COVID-19 pandemic.
The updated program, called Opportunity Zones 2.0, provides larger incentives for rural investments compared to urban ones and has a reporting requirement.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Commentary: Alaska Board of Game should not close hunting, trapping for a road that doesn’t exit yet
description: The state is considering restricting public hunting and trapping opportunities in Northwest and Interior Alaska to accommodate planning for a proposed private road. While I call Juneau home, I’ve spent a bit of time in the Brooks Range and have long-time friends who live in and have deep ties to the region. I engage with […]
text:
The John River is seen from the sky , along the proposed Ambler Road route in the Southern Brooks Range. (Photo by Mary Glaves)The state is considering restricting public hunting and trapping opportunities in Northwest and Interior Alaska to accommodate planning for a proposed private road.
While I call Juneau home, I’ve spent a bit of time in the Brooks Range and have long-time friends who live in and have deep ties to the region. I engage with the Alaska Board of Game both personally and through my professional work. I’ve made a point of believing in their public process, even when I disagree with an outcome. That is why the way that this proposal is moving forward concerns me.
On Nov. 20, the Board of Game will meet by web conference to consider closing roughly 420 square miles of hunting and trapping country in Units 23 and 24. The proposed closure would extend one mile on each side of the proposed Ambler Road, a 211-mile private industrial road planned to connect the Dalton Highway to the mining district. Amendments to 5 AAC 92.510 and 92.550 would prohibit hunting and trapping there from July 1, 2029, through Jan. 1, 2036, unless extended. People could still travel through the area, but they could not hunt or trap.
The road hasn’t been built. Geotechnical and permafrost studies took place along the corridor this past season, and exploration continues in the mining district. But survey crews and drill rigs are not a road. There is no roadbed, final alignment or drivable surface. Fish and Game’s own materials acknowledge: “The Ambler Road has not been constructed, and submission of this proposal will assist in the planning process for future construction and use of the road.”
That distinction matters. I understand that a road could raise legitimate questions about safety and access. Those questions may need to be addressed if it is built. But why impose a broad closure before there is a road—or a demonstrated wildlife-management need?
I continue to participate in the Board of Game process because it gives Alaskans a public forum to weigh competing interests and bring local knowledge and experience to the table. The process is not perfect, and people will not always agree with the board’s decisions. But it should be open, consistent and worthy of the public’s confidence.
The board first considered this proposal in July at a special Fairbanks meeting. The Fairbanks Advisory Committee voted 13-0 against it, and many people testified in opposition. The board tabled it for its January meeting in Kotzebue, in the affected region, offering local residents an opportunity to weigh in. Instead, the proposal is back on Nov. 20, at a web conference with no oral testimony. Written comments were due by 8 a.m. on Monday, Nov. 16—just four days before the meeting.
For rural Alaskans who live in or near the corridor, that is a significant limitation. Oral testimony is an important way to participate, particularly in communities where internet access, time and travel can be barriers. A decision affecting this much country deserves a genuine effort to hear from the people most directly connected to it.
The proposal originated from a confidential memorandum among state agencies, Native corporations, a mining company and the federal government. The report describes a “Hunting Buffer” section in which the parties agreed that the Fish and Game commissioner would propose this closure. The Anchorage Press reported on this earlier this year, in February. This raises a fair question: how does that agreement relate to the department’s responsibility to manage fish and wildlife in the public interest? Decisions about hunting and trapping opportunity should be made through the state’s public process, with the rationale and supporting information available for scrutiny.
The proposed road would be private, gated, staffed around the clock and off-limits to the public. Yet the proposal would restrict hunting and trapping on surrounding public land before the road is built, regardless of whether construction moves forward.
A closure of this scale should be grounded in a clear wildlife-management rationale or demonstrated need. As presented, the proposal identifies no biological necessity, such as a declining population or unsustainable harvest, and documents no current safety problem created by an existing road. Instead, it sets a future date: July 1, 2029. If a date tied to a road that has not been built can close roughly 420 square miles to hunting and trapping, what precedent does that set for the next road, pipeline or mine? It also raises another question: Does preemptively closing approximately 420 square miles of public land to hunting and trapping meaningfully advance the Department of Fish & Game’s first guiding principle: “provide for the greatest long-term opportunities for people to use and enjoy Alaska’s fish, wildlife, and habitat resources”?
The Board of Game should not ignore legitimate concerns that may arise if the Ambler Road is built. I am asking that the state honor its own process, its purpose, and the public’s role in it. I want to continue believing that decisions about hunting and trapping are considered openly, on their merits, and with respect for the people who live, work and recreate in the affected areas.
The board can reject the proposal or take no action. At a minimum, it should allow the public process to work as intended and ensure any restrictions are supported by a clear need and considered through a fair, accessible process. I still believe in that process. I want the state and the board to give Alaskans good reason to keep believing in it.

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico Information Technology Department seeks $30M funding boost amid cyberattack ‘crisis’
description: The New Mexico Department of Information Technology is seeking a funding boost in the upcoming fiscal year to harden state and local networks against increasingly common cyberattacks, Secretary Manny Barreras told a legislative committee this week.
text:
The New Mexico Department of Information Technology is seeking a one-time, $30 million appropriation in the upcoming legislative session for cybersecurity boosts, Secretary Manny Barreras told lawmakers Nov. 16, 2026. (Photo via Getty images)The New Mexico Department of Information Technology is seeking a funding boost in the upcoming fiscal year to harden state and local networks against increasingly common cyberattacks, Secretary Manny Barreras told a legislative committee this week.
In addition to a roughly 5% base budget increase, the department is seeking a one-time, $30 million allocation to the department’s Office of Cybersecurity, which the New Mexico Legislature created in 2023. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The funding, if the Legislature approves it at the upcoming legislative session beginning Jan. 19, would go toward vulnerability analyses and patching of IT systems for an array of state and local governments, including state agencies, universities, public school districts, tribes, wastewater systems and small towns and villages.
“Many of them, especially the small and rural ones, don’t have the resources to do this on their own,” Barreras told lawmakers on the Legislative Finance Committee on Monday.
The department’s request comes amid a spate of high-profile IT failures that have grounded airplanes nationwide or interrupted major email service. Lawmakers on the committee also referenced a recent cyberattack at the University of New Mexico Hospital, which resulted in ambulances being diverted to other hospitals and patient appointments being canceled. 
“We’re in a crisis right now. We have several things that are going on worldwide that’s impacting how we do business,” Barreras told lawmakers.”We don’t know the whole story behind a lot of these at this point. It’s still under speculation, but we got to get serious about this.”
The one-time funding the department is seeking will evaluate current vulnerabilities and help governments prepare for “newer risks” to their online infrastructure and data, Barreras said, including from artificial intelligence and quantum computing. 
The Office of Cybersecurity assists 442 public entities statewide with cybersecurity. Over the last year, the office received 56,000 cybersecurity-related alerts and helped entities through 37 “incidents,” Barreras said. 
Separate from the one-time appropriation, the department is seeking a base budget of $118.5 million in the upcoming fiscal year, which represents a 4.6% increase, or $5.2 million, over the current year. 
That recurring budget increase includes $3.8 million for the department’s Office of Broadband Access and Expansion, which leads the state’s efforts to connect New Mexico households to high-speed, affordable internet, including in rural and tribal areas.
US Senate Dems call for pause on router installation that caused air travel ground stop

Much of that new funding would enable the office to increase staffing from 15 to 20, including hiring three new mapping and data employees, as well as a deputy director and public information officer. 
“Good broadband decisions start with good data,” Barreras told lawmakers about why the staff increase is needed. Connectivity requires “knowing exactly which homes and businesses lack service and where infrastructure is planned or needed,” he added. 
The rest of the department’s recurring budget increase request would go to the Office of Cybersecurity for statewide risk assessments and safety audits, according to the department.
Lawmakers on the committee said they shared the department’s concern about cyberattacks and would consider legislation ensuring local entities adopt best practices and adhere to statewide standards. 
LFC Chair Rep. Nathan Small (D-Las Cruces), however, noted that the Legislature is receiving funding requests for cybersecurity upgrades from a host of different state and local entities, including state-funded hospitals and district attorneys’ offices. 
He said he is “at a loss” about why the Legislature would fund both the state IT department’s cybersecurity requests and those for individual entities to “go their own way with very different standards.”
According to an LFC analysis, several dozen state agencies collectively are requesting $153 million in the upcoming fiscal year for various IT upgrades, many of which relate to cybersecurity or modernizing obsolete systems. 
Barreras said he agrees the Legislature should consider legislation that creates “more centralization, standardization statewide” on the cybersecurity front. 
“You know, one mission, one system, one network,” he said. “And we’re all working together.”

name: National
title: It’s official: Measles is endemic again in the US
description: A panel of global health authorities announced formally Tuesday that the United States is no longer a country that has eliminated measles, urging public health leaders to step up vaccinations and stop the spread of outbreaks. The determination by the Pan American Health Organization had been expected after 12 continuous months of measles outbreaks in […]
text:
Children can receive their first dose of the MMR vaccine, above, after 12 months of age. The United States lost its measles elimination status in mid-November 2026 after more than 25 years. (Photo by Joshua Haiar/South Dakota Searchlight) A panel of global health authorities announced formally Tuesday that the United States is no longer a country that has eliminated measles, urging public health leaders to step up vaccinations and stop the spread of outbreaks.
The determination by the Pan American Health Organization had been expected after 12 continuous months of measles outbreaks in the country, the first beginning in West Texas in fall 2025, and the most recent surging through Pennsylvania. This year, at least 10 people have died of measles, including two deaths announced last week. 
Also this week, nearly a dozen scientists with the federal Centers for Disease Control and Prevention independently published a public health alert noting that  at least 112 pregnant women and 13 newborns have been infected with the virus, some with dire outcomes.  
“Once the measles gets a foothold in a community, it’s very contagious, and can include people who are pregnant,” said Dr. John Gaudet, a retired pediatrician and associate professor at the William Carey University College of Osteopathic Medicine in Mississippi, who was unaffiliated with the public health alert. 
Measles is a highly contagious respiratory virus with symptoms that include fever, cough and rash. The disease can cause complications including pneumonia, encephalitis and blindness and can lead to death. But it also can be prevented through a two-dose vaccine known as MMR, or measles, mumps and rubella. 
The Pan American Health Organization (PAHO), a regional office of the World Health Organization, concluded in2000 that the U.S. had essentially eliminated measles because spread had been squashed for 12 months or more. 
After convening last week, a panel of experts at PAHO determined the United States’ “measles elimination status” has been reversed. The organization made the same determination for Bolivia and Mexico. Canada, which lost its status a year ago, was determined to have disrupted transmissions and to be making progress toward regaining elimination status.
PAHO noted in its announcement that measles outbreaks can be concentrated in particular communities or geographic regions within a country.
“National vaccination figures can mask these disparities, while barriers to health services, missed vaccinations, misinformation and vaccine hesitancy leave children, adolescents and adults vulnerable to infection,” the statement said. 
In the United States, many public health experts are worried because children, who generally don’t get their first MMR dose until at least  one year of age, are highly susceptible, including those who contract the virus before birth. 
There were 112 confirmed cases of measles in pregnant women and 13 cases of congenital measles between Jan. 1, 2025, and Sept. 28, 2026, according to the public health alert published Monday in the journal NEJM Evidence. (The authors defined congenital measles as cases transmitted to newborns in utero or with a positive test or febrile rash within 10 days of birth to a woman with confirmed measles.) . All but two of the women had not received the MMR vaccine or had an unknown vaccine status. 
Among the pregnancy cases with reported outcomes, 19 women experienced live births and two lost their pregnancies, the alert said. Of the live births, eight were preterm and eight had to be admitted into the neonatal intensive care unit. Thirteen of those newborns tested positive for congenital measles, and six developed measles-related symptoms, including one infant who showed symptoms related to a life-threatening brain-swelling condition, according to the health alert. The other pregnancy cases either had unknown outcomes or were in women who were still pregnant as of Sept. 28.
Gaudet said one of the often-fatal neurological complications of measles known as subacute sclerosing panencephalitis, or SSPE, usually shows up between two and 10 years after a measles infection in older children and young adults. But if the infection is contracted in utero, he said, it can happen much earlier. 
“The whole timeline is compressed if it’s congenital,” Gaudet told Stateline.
Infant mortality rates in the United States are high compared with other high-income countries worldwide, with a rate of about 5.5 deaths per 1,000 live births in 2024-2025, according to provisional CDC data. That rate is more than double among Black infants. 
“Health care systems and clinicians should be prepared to provide care to pregnant women and their infants with measles, particularly in communities with a high proportion of unvaccinated people,” the health alert said. 
The United States had 5,412 reported measles cases as of Nov. 12, according to the CDC, more than double the 2,289 cases through all of 2025. Among this year’s cases, nearly 18%, or 951, were among children below the age of 5. 
Throughout his leadership, U.S. Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has been an outspoken critic of vaccinations and is opposed to many vaccine mandates, including recommending fewer vaccines for children at the same time that many Republican-led states have ended vaccine mandates for their populations. At least 39 states now have MMR vaccination rates below 95% — the threshold considered necessary for herd immunity. 
In a statement posted to the social media site X on Tuesday, Kennedy blamed the decline in vaccinations on the COVID-19 pandemic and said that the agency has been responding to measles outbreaks. 
“I continue to recommend MMR vaccination as the most effective way to prevent measles,” Kennedy wrote.
“Worldwide COVID-era disruptions interrupted routine childhood vaccination, leaving gaps in protection here and abroad,” Kennedy wrote. “CDC has worked alongside state teams in Texas, South Carolina, Virginia, Kansas, New Mexico, and Wisconsin to help bring their outbreaks rapidly and successfully under control. CDC is also supporting Pennsylvania and New York with epidemiologists and other experts.” 
“The measles elimination designation is not what protects Americans. Vaccination does. We know where transmission is occurring and we’ve invested $100 million in state and local health departments to reach those communities,” CDC Director Dr. Erica Schwartz, said in a written email statement to Stateline. “Losing a designation doesn’t mean we abandon an evidence-based approach. It means we remain focused on stopping outbreaks.” 
Dr. Susan Kansagra, chief medical officer of the Association of State and Territorial Health Officials, a group representing local health officials, told Stateline that it’s critical that state health departments are well funded enough to carry out a public health campaign to vaccinate their populations. 
But without vaccination mandates, she said, pediatricians play a pivotal role in informing parents about the safety and efficacy of the MMR vaccine. 
“They are the most important because we know in lots of surveys, lots of what we hear on the ground, that providers are the most trusted members of the community, and that one-on-one physician-patient or provider-patient relationship is so important,” Kansagra said. 
“They’re also the first folks that will see somebody that might walk in that could have measles. And making sure that they have the tools they need to be able to respond appropriately is also really important.” 
Gaudet said in his three decades as a practicing pediatrician, he never saw a case of measles. But as he teaches medical students, he said he shows them textbook pictures and gives them as much information as he can. 
“I tell them, ‘I’ve never seen the measles, but you will. Be ready.’”
Stateline reporter Shalina Chatlani can be reached at schatlani@stateline.org, and reporter Kelcie Moseley-Morris can be reached at kmoseley@stateline.org.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: No veto overrides in the NC House for now, but GOP leader expects at least one before 2027
description: The state House Tuesday didn’t touch the four vetoed bills lingering on its calendar, teed up for override votes.   House Speaker Destin Hall, R-Caldwell, told reporters Tuesday he still wants to override the vetoes, and the House will have another chance. No more votes will come this week, but Hall said he expects legislators will […]
text:
North Carolina House Speaker Destin Hall, R-Caldwell, speaks to reporters after the legislative session's opening day on Jan. 8, 2025. (Photo: Galen Bacharier/NC Newsline)The state House Tuesday didn’t touch the four vetoed bills lingering on its calendar, teed up for override votes.  
House Speaker Destin Hall, R-Caldwell, told reporters Tuesday he still wants to override the vetoes, and the House will have another chance.
No more votes will come this week, but Hall said he expects legislators will have one more day of work before the end of the year. Republican leaders have set aside a three-week window, from Nov. 30 through Dec. 18, to come back for an additional voting session before their terms end Jan. 1.
Hall said he didn’t know which vetoes the House would try to override. “I expect we’ll take up at least one or more of them,” he said.

Three House Republicans were absent Tuesday. All Democrats and unaffiliated members were present. 
With three absences, House Republicans did not have enough votes on their own to override vetoes. Overrides require the votes of three-fifths of the members present and voting. With 117 House members present, 70 votes are needed for an override. Republicans had only 68.
North Carolinians brace for House override vote on permitless carry veto

The potential veto overrides remaining are for Senate Bill 50, which would allow most people 18 and older to carry a concealed handgun without a permit or gun safety training. It did not pass the House with a veto-proof majority. Gov. Josh Stein vetoed the bill in June 2025. 
The state Senate has already overridden the veto of Senate Bill 50. A House override would make it law.
House Bill 437 bans “unauthorized camping” by homeless people, NC Newsline reported. It opens local governments to liability if they allow homeless people to sleep anywhere other than shelters or approved campsites. Stein vetoed the bill in July. It passed the House 73-40, with enough votes to override Stein’s veto. With all House members present, 72 votes are needed to override a veto. 
House Bill 377 would allow the state Supreme Court chief justice to suspend trial court judges without pay on the recommendation of the N.C. Judicial Standards Commission when judges are being investigated. Opponents warned it would politicize the courts. The House passed the bill 62-45. Stein vetoed it in August. 
Veto coming on the GOP’s big elections bill, NC Gov. Stein says

House Bill 958 would make wide-ranging changes to election laws that clear a path for more ballot challenges, election audits and registration removals, NC Newsline reported. It would also cut the early voting period in primary elections from 17 days to 10 days. The bill passed the House 62-47 with only Republican votes. Stein vetoed the bill in August. 
Asked about the potential veto overrides Tuesday morning, Stein advised against taking them up. 
“I think if anything was clear from two weeks ago it’s that the people of North Carolina are sick and tired of games,” Stein said. “They want legislators who are working on issues that will make their lives better.”

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Hartford seeks criminal charges against “problem landlord”
description: Hartford officials said the out-of-state landlord is violating CT building code and hasn't fixed major issues, including vermin infestations.
text:
Hartford officials have asked the State Attorney’s Office to pursue criminal charges against a “problem landlord,” Shlomo “Sam” Sarot, accusing him of violating state building code.
“This landlord has been subject to many orders of the housing division, the building code division, and has failed to comply with those orders,” said Judith Rothschild, the city’s deputy director of development services, at a press conference on Tuesday.
Sarot lives in Woodmere, N.Y., but owns five properties in Hartford, according to city officials. Sarot was on Mayor Arunan Arulampalam’s December 2025 “problem landlord” list for issues of mice and cockroach infestations, non-working sinks and excessive heat.
Residents at one of Sarot’s buildings, at 57-59 Sumner St., told The Connecticut Mirror that they’ve been dealing with cockroach and mice infestations, among other problems, ever since Sarot took over the building in July 2025. Rothschild said open violations exist at other Sarot-owned buildings, but 57-59 Sumner St. is “the worst of them at this point.”
Several residents at 57-59 Sumner Street don’t keep any food in their cabinets because mice keep raiding their supplies, pictured here on Tuesday, Nov. 17, 2026. Credit: Sandy Battulga / CT Mirror
Several residents told the CT Mirror that they can’t keep any food in their cabinets because mice consistently get into the products. As such, they have resorted to ordering food every day.
“Everyone’s still having issues with mice. I don’t have anything in my cabinet. I don’t cook in my pots and pans,” resident Natori Mitchell told CT Mirror on Tuesday. “I’m a whole diabetic. I’m supposed to eat salad and fruit and everything, supposed to cut it up on the counter. You can’t do anything like that if there’s mice droppings everywhere. I have to put aside $30, $40 dollars just so me and my daughter can go eat. Unhealthy. It’s just not fair.”
Her daughter, Ariya Howington, said she sometimes feels “stuff tap on me.
“I think there’s like bugs crawling on me,” the 8-year-old said.
In an emailed response to the CT Mirror, Sarot said the city’s decision to refer him to the State Attorney’s Office “came as a surprise.”
“We have been working with City inspectors to address the building’s conditions and have repeatedly requested clarification and another meeting,” he wrote. “Despite follow-up attempts, that meeting has not been arranged.”
Mitchell has lived in the building since 2021, but said the previous owners maintained the building well. It was only when Sarot took over that she began experiencing major problems.
In addition to vermin infestations, city officials also said the building hasn’t had a working elevator since June. Also, over the July 4th weekend this past summer, the roof collapsed due to water damage. Arulampalam said Sarot hired an “unlicensed contractor” to fix the issue and the contractor ended up doing more damage, which led to the fifth, sixth, and seventh floors of the building becoming unlivable. As such, the city helped pay for tenants on those floors to relocate to other housing.
A dead cockroach and mice droppings decorate the floor of one resident’s apartment on Tuesday, Nov. 17, 2026. Credit: Sandy Battulga / CT Mirror
The mayor said the city “made a number of demands” to Sarot to fix the problems in the building over the past four months, including suspending his rental license in October, but Sarot has not fixed the building violations or paid any associated fees or liens.
Violating state building code is a misdemeanor, according to Rothschild. That means if the state attorney decides to pursue legal action for violating that code and the landlord is found guilty, the maximum penalty he could face is between $200 and $1,000 in fines, six months in jail or both.
Rothschild said the state attorney now has to review the city’s filing and decide whether to pursue legal action. Rothschild was formerly a state housing prosecutor and said that this kind of legal action is “common” in her experience, but she did not say how often Hartford has pursued this kind of action against landlords.
Several remaining tenants told the CT Mirror that they want to move out and have tried communicating with Sarot about the infestations they’re facing and other problems in the building but the problems persist.
“The absolute need to relocate depends on the severity of the conditions. If there is severe infestation, then relocation is possible,” Rothschild said. “At this point, we have not yet ordered any vacates for the floors based on just that.”
Regarding the mice and cockroach infestations, Sarot told the CT Mirror that he “promptly arranged professional extermination” after learning of the tenants’ complaints, “followed by treatments every two weeks.”
Sarot also wrote that efforts to replace the broken elevator “have begun” but he doesn’t have a “firm completion date” yet.
But several tenants of the building say exterminators have not visited their units. Mice droppings, dead mice, and numerous dead cockroaches were evident in multiple apartment units and in the apartment building’s stairwell.

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: Commentary: Valar’s nuclear/data center paradise will be hell for everyone else
description: Americans across the political spectrum (including Utahns) have been remarkably united in opposing data centers. Someone should tell the Carbon County commissioners. They just voted to hang that albatross around the county’s neck.  They also voted to expose their 20,000 residents to more radioactivity. Repercussions will ripple throughout the state. Reasonab[...]
text:
(Illustration by Alex Cochran for Utah News Dispatch)Americans across the political spectrum (including Utahns) have been remarkably united in opposing data centers. Someone should tell the Carbon County commissioners. They just voted to hang that albatross around the county’s neck.  They also voted to expose their 20,000 residents to more radioactivity. Repercussions will ripple throughout the state.
Reasonable people wouldn’t get on an airplane whose pilot had never flown anything more than a kite. You wouldn’t let someone crack your chest and bypass your coronary arteries who had never finished high school, never went to medical school, never operated on a patient before, but just felt supremely qualified because, “How hard could it be?” But the commissioners were undaunted in turning their county’s future over to someone grossly unqualified, blinded by his own ambitions of becoming a nuclear prima donna, manifesting a complete lack of understanding or concern for the consequences to others. 
Valar Atomics is a 3-year-old company whose founder and CEO, Isaiah Taylor, is a 27-year-old high school drop-out. His previous work experience included teaching himself computer coding and working in an auto-repair shop. He has little formal education in anything, and none in nuclear physics, radiation, or public health. That should not be an indictment of anyone, unless that person insists on imposing his dangerous lack of expertise on everyone else.
Taylor’s company has developed “SMRs,” or “fun size” nuclear reactors. The idea of SMRs (small modular reactors) has been around for decades, its theoretical advantage is they could be mass produced in a factory reducing nuclear’s exorbitant costs. But that’s only true if hundreds, perhaps thousands were built. Other SMR projects failed because they didn’t reduce costs. Currently only two SMRs are operating commercially in the entire world, one in Russia, one in China. There is nowhere near enough real-world experience with SMRs to confirm their safety and viability.
Taylor’s nuclear career should have ended when he claimed that a person could hold one of his spent nuclear fuel rods in his hand for five minutes and not be exposed to any more radiation than from a single CAT scan. Actual experts say that person would be dead within seconds. 
Taylor could be a smart kid despite his lack of education. But raw intelligence itself is no reason to trust someone with policy that could harm the entire state. Elon Musk has plenty of raw intelligence. Big Tech oligarchs — Peter Thiel, Mark Zuckerberg, Larry Ellison, Sam Altman, Jeff Bezos, Jensen Huang — are all smart people. But they lack what’s more important: wisdom, judgement, common sense, self-restraint, and a commitment to the common good. What Taylor lacks in these qualities he makes up for in hubris.  
Actual experts calculate Valar’s nuclear powered hyperscale data center megalopolis would wreak environmental and public health havoc on Carbon County in multiple ways. For example, in a study commissioned by Carbon County residents, two experts in atmospheric modeling calculate that the project would raise regional temperatures 5-12 degrees Fahrenheit as far out as 15 miles downwind. That would desiccate local agriculture and ecosystems. Taylor is unperturbed by information like this that throws cold water on his ambitions and his investors’ expectations.
Last week, Valar’s men came to the Carbon County Commission for approval of the first stage of Taylor’s nuclear fantasy — the largest nuclear power complex the world has ever seen, a farm of 456 SMRs using unproven technology, nuclear fuel manufacturing and factory assembly lines, slap dash storage of high-level nuclear waste, natural gas power plants and large hyperscale data centers, even larger than Stratos.
Taylor’s ambitions have been boosted by a state taxpayer paid propaganda campaign dispensing utter nonsense: “nuclear plants emit less radiation than bananas,” “a nuclear plant is safer than a chair,” “nuclear waste storage is safer than your leftovers,” and “nuclear energy is cleaner than a candle.” The deceitful campaign paved over the painful reality that tens of thousands of Utahns have died from “downwinder” cancers, and more will in the future, because of radiation they were promised was safe. If any state should refuse more radiation exposure it should be Utah. The commissioners were warned by experts that the project would launch a steady stream of radioactivity into the county in perpetuity on top of all the other data center environmental disasters. They were warned cancer rates are higher in communities with nuclear plants. They approved it anyway.
Real experts predict Valar’s nuclear/data center paradise will be hell for everyone else. Nuclear gimmicks should not be just the latest stepping stone for Big Tech to take even more control over our lives. And the world’s most dangerous and complex technology should not be toyed with by profiteering amateurs, using Utah as their guinea pig.

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Bipartisanship touted as slew of new Democrats join Indiana Legislature still run by Republicans
description: Republican legislative leaders expressed a willingness for more bipartisanship on the day that more Democrats sat as members of the Indiana General Assembly than any time since 2010.
text:
Indiana House members take their oaths of office during the Legislature's Organization Day on Tuesday, Nov. 17, 2026. (Photo by Tom Davies/Indiana Capital Chronicle)Republican legislative leaders expressed a willingness for more bipartisanship on the day that more Democrats sat as members of the Indiana General Assembly than any time since 2010.
The Statehouse hallways and galleries were filled Tuesday with family members and friends of 37 freshman members joining the ranks of 150 total senators and representatives taking their oaths of office during the Legislature’s Organization Day.
Republican Ben Smaltz of Auburn was elected without opposition as the new House speaker — a promotion to the top leadership post following the unexpected election defeat of former Speaker Todd Huston.
Democrats gained 16 House seats in this fall’s election, narrowing the Republican House majority to 54-46.
Smaltz acknowledged that shift in a speech to the House after being sworn in as speaker, telling Democrats that they have “a greater opportunity to help shape the direction of this chamber and I encourage you to bring your ideas forward.”
“To my Republican colleagues, we still hold the majority, but the dynamics have changed,” Smaltz said. “I encourage you to listen, engage, and look for opportunities to work with our Democrat colleagues without abandoning our principles. The makeup of this chamber may be different, but our responsibility remains the same — to represent Hoosiers, to find common ground, and to deliver results.”
Top Senate Democrat urges “common ground”
Republican and Democratic leaders in the Senate also emphasized the importance of bipartisan cooperation in a chamber that will include 13 new senators among the 50 members. That includes five more Democratic senators that cut the Republican majority 35-15.
New Republican Senate President Pro Tem Chris Garten said he would seek to preserve civil debate.
“We can be firm in our convictions without being disrespectful,” Garten said in a speech to the Senate. “We can debate with passion without sacrificing professionalism, and we can disagree on policy without questioning one another’s character.”
Senate Democratic leader Shelli Yoder of Bloomington speaks to the Senate on Nov. 16, 2026. (Photo by Casey Smith/Indiana Capital Chronicle)
Senate Democratic leader Shelli Yoder of Bloomington urged lawmakers to consider whether the state’s economic policies are actually improving residents’ lives as they prepare to write a new two-year budget during the 2027 session that starts in January.
Yoder said she welcomed Garten’s emphasis on cooperation and believed that was possible on affordability, public schools and government transparency.
“That’s what we’re going to be finding common ground on and working very hard to the very end to make sure Hoosiers know that we are a chamber and a body that works for them,” she said.
House Republicans turn down rules changes 
That spirit of bipartisanship, however, only went so far Tuesday as Republicans voted along party lines to reject proposed House rules changes that Democrats argued would make legislative action more transparent and allow more public input.
One proposal would have prohibited the House from considering bills that include provisions adopted by joint House-Senate conference committees that were not approved by at least one chamber. Such conference committees often negotiate in private the final agreements on bills in the final days of a legislative session.
Rep. Matt Pierce, D-Bloomington, cited language that was added to the state budget bill in the final hours of the 2025 session that eliminated the election of some Indiana University Board of Trustees members by IU alumni.
“I’ve seen over and over again this process favor the insiders, favor the people who have influence, and we have an opportunity today to say we can do better,” Pierce said during debate before the proposed rule change was voted down.
Rep. Ryan Kominakis, D-Valparaiso, poses for a picture with his sons on the House floor on Nov. 16, 2026. (Photo by Niki Kelly/Indiana Capital Chronicle)
Another proposal from Democrats would have allowed so-called “blast motions” under which a bill that hasn’t been acted upon by a committee could be advanced to the full House with the support of at least 51 members.
Republican Rep. Alex Zimmerman, the new chair of the House Rules Committee, argued such a change would undermine the process of properly considering legislation.
“This blast motion takes away the voice of the people that we are elected to serve,” said Zimmerman, R-North Vernon. “When they show up to a committee meeting, we let them testify on every bill that is heard in committee.”
Apparent deal on House committee splits
A point of contention between Republican and Democratic leaders since the election has been the partisan makeup of House committees, through which all bills that come up for consideration must clear.
Under the previous Republican supermajorities of the past 14 years, most House committees have been made up of nine Republicans and four Democrats.
The much tighter House membership had Democrats arguing for 7-6 committee splits. 
A pending agreement would expand most committees to 14 members, with eight Republicans and six Democrats.
Smaltz told reporters that such a split was “a reasonable assumption” and that he anticipated a list of committee assignments would be completed within about 10 days.
House Democratic leader Phil GiaQuinta of Fort Wayne said his caucus was never going to accept a suggested 8-5 Republican control of committees.
“The majority is going to want you know to have their two-person spread,” GiaQuinta said of the 8-6 committees. “It is a reflection of where we’ve been in the past. Good number to land on.”
