title: Scholten, Michigan Head Start Association criticize Trump rollback of teacher pay increases
description: A new federal rule rolled back an expected $10,000 pay raise for most Head Start program teachers, as well as basic benefits for full-time staff — a move that has met pushback in Michigan from an association of teachers and U.S. Rep. Hillary Scholten (D-Grand Rapids). The rule, promulgated by the U.S. The Department of […]
text:
Preschool children line up to go outside at the Ralph Hawley Head Start Center in Emeryville, Calif., in December. The Trump administration has proposed major changes to the Head Start program. (Photo by Florence Middleton for CalMatters)A new federal rule rolled back an expected $10,000 pay raise for most Head Start program teachers, as well as basic benefits for full-time staff — a move that has met pushback in Michigan from an association of teachers and U.S. Rep. Hillary Scholten (D-Grand Rapids).
The rule, promulgated by the U.S. The Department of Health and Human Services under President Donald Trump, was finalized over the weekend. Issued in May, the “Restoring Flexibility to Support Head Start Program Access” rule cancels the mandatory pay increase for Head Start teachers and expanded benefits set forward in 2024 by the administration of former President Joe Biden.
Head Start leaders had requested an overall 4.97% cost-of-living adjustment, often referred to as COLA, which would have allowed programs to pay staff at a more competitive rate. That increase also had the potential to retain experienced educators while allowing families to continue receiving consistent Head Start services.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The Health and Human Services rule rescinded requirements put forward by the Biden administration to provide full-time staff with health care coverage, paid leave and behavioral health access. Part-time staff were also eligible for healthcare access and other benefits. 
Although it is separate from an August Health and Human Services proposed rewrite of Head Start performance standards, concern remains for Head Start teachers now cut out from receiving higher pay and benefits. The Biden rule would have affected more than 250,000 teachers and staff, and the Trump course change may put nearly 716,000 children and their families’ education access at risk.
“Programs will no longer be required to move toward pay comparable to public preschool teachers by 2031, leaving currently low wages stagnant for Head Start educators and encouraging qualified and valued individuals to seek other employment opportunities outside of our programs,” the Michigan Head Start Association said in a social media post. “Our educators are the heart of our classrooms and the foundation of Head Start’s success. Without the professional and supportive education they provide, fewer children and families can be served in Head Start programs. Families will lose access to critical early learning and interventions because of insufficient operational and financial federal investment.”


Scholten also criticized the new rule, noting that she joined a June letter opposing the decision.
“The Trump Administration’s decision to cancel cost-of-living adjustments for Head Start teachers sends a clear message about its priorities: penny-pinching educators’ salaries while covering the White House in gold. This is unacceptable,” Scholten said in a statement. “For more than 60 years, Head Start has supported early education, health and dental care, and healthy meals while connecting families to job training and housing support. Now, the program is asking for the bare minimum: funding to maintain its operations and to help absorb higher costs amid the affordability crisis.”
Scholten added that the decision would force Head Start programs to “choose between a livable wage for educators, spaces for more children, and healthy meals on the table.”
“I have heard directly from my constituents who run these programs about how this will negatively impact our community,” Scholten said. “This is unacceptable, and I will keep fighting to protect Head Start, because the educators and families who depend on it deserve better than this.”

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: NJ warns feds might be forging ahead on Roxbury migrant jail
description: NJ officials told federal judges Monday that the feds have ignored their requests for details on its plan to put a migrant jail in Roxbury.
text:
A U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement vehicle is parked outside a Roxbury warehouse slated to become a migrant detention center. (Photo by Benjamin Leynse / New Jersey Monitor)New Jersey and the Trump administration remain at a standoff over the feds’ plan to detain migrants in a warehouse in Roxbury, with state officials suggesting in a new court filing that U.S. Department of Homeland Security officials are flouting judicial orders that they pause the plan to allow an environmental review.
Attorney General Jennifer Davenport said state officials have repeatedly sought details on a $31.8 million contract Homeland Security officials signed earlier this month to convert the 470,000-square-foot warehouse it bought in February into a processing center for detained migrants.
But the feds have not forked over the contract or otherwise answered questions, despite the state’s and township’s “urgent need for information,” Davenport told U.S. District Court Judges Jamel K. Semper and James B. Clark III in a joint status report filed Monday.
“If Defendants have already committed resources to converting the facility, then any forthcoming EA (environmental assessment) will be mere window dressing for a decision that has already been made — subjecting Plaintiffs to a wide range of infrastructure, environmental, and public health harms without the required review,” Davenport wrote.
Converting the warehouse into a mass detention center would overwhelm local sewer and water infrastructure, and environmental assessments, “if properly done, would confirm that the warehouse is unsuitable as a site for a detention center,” Davenport added.
The status report is the latest filing in a lawsuit Gov. Mikie Sherrill’s administration and Roxbury’s GOP-leadership filed in March to stop the plan. The state and township succeeded in May in putting a temporary hold on it. The Trump administration has gone back and forth in subsequent court filings about whether the plan is moving forward.
In a terse response filed with Monday’s status report, Department of Justice officials insisted they’re cooperating with the state’s request for information.
Immigration and Customs Enforcement officials signed a contract Nov. 5 for the maintenance, design, and environmental analysis of facility, said Adam R.F. Gustafson, principal deputy assistant attorney general in the Justice Department.
They informed state officials the next day that “ICE intends to retain the Roxbury facility and renovate it to some level of detention capacity, among other uses, and will do so in accordance with” federal judges’ May order requiring an environmental review before further construction.
Since then, Gustafson said, Homeland Security officials “have been working to respond to Plaintiffs’ informal request” for the contract and details. He did not explain any reasons for their delay in providing the requested information.
Immigration agents have been using the warehouse parking lot to process people they detain, which also has prompted objections from the state. In Monday’s status report, Davenport raised concerns about agents also holding detainees inside the facility, something Homeland Security officials have denied.

name: WyoFile
title: Detention conditions at Wyoming Boys’ School were ‘well below the standard of care,’ expert witness testifies
description:
During trial for civil rights lawsuit brought by former resident, boys’ school employees testify they frequently interacted with the plaintiff while he was confined in detention rooms. 
The post Detention conditions at Wyoming Boys’ School were ‘well below the standard of care,’ expert witness testifies appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Detention rooms at the Wyoming Boys’ School “were well below the standard of care and, when compared to other juvenile facilities, way more dangerous,” an expert witness testified Tuesday at a trial concerning alleged abuse, including unconstitutional isolation, at the state facility.
Forensic psychologist Dr. Max Wachtel said that based on his evaluation, Blaise Chivers-King, the former boys’ school resident suing school staff, had PTSD that was “directly caused by his isolation time at the Wyoming Boys’ School.” Because of his previous trauma history, which includes witnessing domestic violence and being removed from his home when he was 12, Chivers-King faces greater challenges to healing, Wachtel said. “The boys’ school damaged him further in a way that’s going to be a lot worse than a kid who didn’t have that prior trauma.” 
Wachtel’s 239-page report on conditions at the boys’ school and their impact on Chivers-King was based on his review of medical documents, school records, video and images. He testified that he asked Chivers-King’s attorneys if he could visit the school but wasn’t given a tour.
Chivers-King is one of six former boys’ school residents who sued school staff in 2024. The school, which detains delinquent boys ages 12 to 21, is a 38-acre residential facility near Worland that’s overseen by the Wyoming Department of Family Services. Chivers-King, who spent time at the boys’ school between 2020 and 2022, alleged school staff violated his 14th Amendment rights by placing him in isolation, using excessive force and infringing on due process. Chivers-King is suing school staff in part for days he spent locked in 7-by-10-foot cinderblock rooms under conditions that his attorneys consider solitary confinement. One of those stints lasted two weeks. 
Surveillance cameras watch over dormitories at the Wyoming Boys’ School on Dec. 10, 2021 in Worland. (Lauren Miller/Casper Star-Tribune)
Boys’ school employees argue that they interacted with Chivers-King frequently while he was confined, though the school’s logbook doesn’t reflect some of those visits. 
Wyoming Boys’ School employee Chisun Bennett testified that staff would talk with Chivers-King “quite often” while he was confined. “I don’t believe in leaving kids alone,” Bennett said. Staff also offered the former resident exercise, school work and reading material while he was in the detention room, though he often declined, Bennett testified.  
“It’s much more work to keep a student like Blaise on detention status,” boys’ school employee Mike Nelson, a defendant in the case, testified. “It’s just resource intensive. And it’s stressful.”
Wachtel testified that getting even four hours of interaction with staff in a day doesn’t change that the child is in isolation. “It’s also an indication that the kid doesn’t need to be in isolation anymore,” he said. 
In his experience working with juveniles, Wachtel said on average kids might be held in a detention room for an hour to an hour and a half. If it took them longer to calm down, he would call an ambulance to get the child to a higher level of care at a hospital where the juvenile could be put on a mental health hold — when a person is held against their will in a medical setting for a period of time if they show a substantial likelihood of hurting themselves or others. 
Isolation for juveniles can cause PTSD, “significant depression and anxiety” and “acute anger and aggression,” Wachtel said. Prolonged isolation can also lead to psychosis and breaks from reality, as well as “acute and chronic” cognitive problems, according to Wachtel. For kids with prior mental health challenges, those risks are magnified. “It greatly increases the risk of suicide or some sort of self-harm. That’s extremely common.”
Videos and images show Chivers-King attempting to strangle himself in the detention room and the injuries he sustained after banging his head against a detention room wall. He testified that he began hearing voices when he was confined.
A defense attorney suggested that calling an ambulance would simply pass off the responsibility to someone else. Wachtel testified that it would be appropriate to get a child to a hospital where staff could use emergency medicine and “more ethical restraints,” including chemical restraints. Using chemical restraints long term is “absolutely barbaric,” but though it’s “not ideal,” it’s the standard of care to use them short term, Wachtel testified.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Report: Mayo Clinic was the nation’s least charitable hospital in 2023
description: Mayo Clinic’s flagship Rochester hospital ranked last in the nation in how much it gave in financial assistance relative to how much it received in tax breaks in 2023, according to a new analysis from Massachusetts-based think tank The Lown Institute. Nonprofit hospitals are required to provide charity care — financial assistance for people who […]
text:
Mayo Clinic in Rochester, Minn. (Photo by Max Nesterak/Minnesota Reformer.)Mayo Clinic’s flagship Rochester hospital ranked last in the nation in how much it gave in financial assistance relative to how much it received in tax breaks in 2023, according to a new analysis from Massachusetts-based think tank The Lown Institute.
Nonprofit hospitals are required to provide charity care — financial assistance for people who can’t pay for their care — and other community health programs in exchange for tax-exempt status, a trade that health policy experts have said is hard to monitor.
The think tank analyzed 2023 tax data for around 3,000 hospitals across the country, along with Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services hospital cost reports and local property assessments, to calculate the difference between how much hospitals received in tax breaks and how much they spent on charity care and other community investments.
The report found that Mayo Clinic’s Rochester hospital received $366 million more in tax breaks than it gave in charity care and other community investments. The second worst offender in the state, HealthPartners’ Methodist Hospital in St. Louis Park, had a far smaller difference: $21 million. Minnesota hospitals altogether received $591 more in tax breaks than they gave in charity care.
Half of the country’s nonprofit hospitals received more in tax breaks than they give in charity care, according to the report.


A Mayo Clinic spokesperson disputed the findings, calling The Lown Institute’s methodology “deeply flawed.” The analysis does not count the significant investments Mayo Clinic makes as a world-renowned research institution into developing new treatments and training the next generation of physicians.
“The methodology excludes important categories of Community Benefit identified by the IRS, including Medicaid shortfall, medical research and health professions education,” the statement reads.
The Minnesota Attorney General’s Office began investigating Mayo Clinic in 2022 after reports in the Rochester Post Bulletin that the health system sued patients who were eligible for charity care over medical debt. The investigation found that Mayo instructed staff to avoid discussing charity care and had an overly complicated charity care application.
Mayo doubled the amount of charity care it provided from 2022 to 2024, after the investigation began.
The Lown Institute’s analysis time frame predates a settlement agreement between the attorney general and Mayo in 2025 that required the health system to use better charity care applications and provide charity care to some patients who are eligible without needing to apply.
A KFF Health News and Star Tribune joint investigation earlier this year found that Minnesota’s hospitals and health systems give less financial aid as a percentage of their operating budgets on average than hospitals in almost every other state, making them among the least charitable in the country.

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: Leaked bill could allow Ohio data centers to seize land
description: A leaked Ohio bill could allow data centers to qualify as “public utilities,” giving them the ability to seize private property. Ohioans rejected data centers on every ballot measure this election, but after that massive loss, Republican lawmakers may be moving to allow tech hubs one way or another. For decades, Gretchan Francis has been […]
text:
A farm in Hudson, Ohio (John Greim/LightRocket via Getty Images)A leaked Ohio bill could allow data centers to qualify as “public utilities,” giving them the ability to seize private property.
Ohioans rejected data centers on every ballot measure this election, but after that massive loss, Republican lawmakers may be moving to allow tech hubs one way or another.
For decades, Gretchan Francis has been fighting to keep her multigenerational family farm.
“It’s not the farm that it once was,” Francis said in an interview. “It’s only 60 acres; it’s not 160 acres.”
Using eminent domain law, which allows the government to take property for public use, the state has seized her land numerous times for highway development.
“I understand that it is necessary, but I think it has to be done in the right way,” she said.
While the Ohio Department Of Transportation has always been able to do this, farmers like her are fearing that new legislation would take their livelihoods for a controversial cause.
A draft bill leaked to WEWS exclusively would expand the list of who qualifies to take land. The draft changes the definition of “public utility,” which is currently just an entity being owned or operated by municipal corporations, an electric cooperative, and an agency holding a certificate of public convenience and necessity granted by the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission.
The legislation adds “and an agency holding a certificate of environmental compatibility and public need from the power siting board for constructing an electric transmission line and associated facilities or gas pipeline and its associated facilities.”
This could mean a transmission developer may be able to seize land to power or place a data center, according to legal experts.
“That would be devastating,” Francis said. “I think anybody would feel the same way if their personal land was taken for a data center. That sounds like it’s a corporate, private, for-profit type of need, not for a public need.”
In June, the Ohio Business Roundtable, a powerful trade group that lobbies at the Statehouse, recommended that lawmakers change eminent domain law, and “should extend possession authority to energy infrastructure projects once public use and necessity have been established.”
The Ohio Farm Bureau, which is adamantly against changing eminent domain, had been preparing for this fight since.
“We are aware of efforts to further erode the limited protections that landowners have, allowing for quick take of property without first paying for the property and determining a landowner’s rights and compensation through a court of law,” the Bureau’s Evan Callicoat said.
The Farm Bureau isn’t opposed to data centers, but they are opposed to a violation of property rights, Callicoat said. He feared that the proposed idea is broad enough that farmers could lose their land to data centers, not getting paid for months or years.
The Roundtable calls the program “deposit and build,” and it’s modeled after a system that 45 other states use.
“This recommendation is about making sure that Ohio’s grid is reliable and affordable for Ohioans and that economic development can continue in the state,” the Roundtable’s Alexandra Denney said in an interview Monday.
The Ohio Power Siting Board controls the installation of utility facilities, including power lines, some gas pipelines, and wind farms. The Public Utilities Commission of Ohio can also help utility companies acquire land.
A utility will approach a homeowner for land and must provide them with a “fair” market price. If the owner refuses to sell, the utility company will take them to court and will need to determine “necessity” for the land. If a court sides with the utility company, deeming it necessary to take, the appraised value of the land is given to a court account.
However, the owner can appeal this decision to fight for more money. While this court battle is going on, construction is not allowed to begin.
The draft bill changes the appraisal process, making it easier to seize land immediately.
“Ratepayers and Ohioans are paying the price because it’s driving up costs and it’s also delaying the critical infrastructure that we need to have a reliable grid,” Denney said about construction delays.
While Denney was aware of the appraisal portion of the legislation, she categorically denied any changes to eminent domain. After the bill was read to her, she said she would need to “look at” the changes in the definition of public utilities.
She said that Ohioans choosing to restrict or ban data centers in 21 different cities has nothing to do with the timing of this proposal.
“That is not the intent of the Ohio Business Roundtable to expand the ability to use eminent domain to anybody that doesn’t already have that ability,” Denney said.
The soon-to-be Senate president, Republican Bill Reineke (R-Tiffin), is working on the bill, and echoed her sentiment.
“We keep talking about lowering costs, and one way we can do that is expanding infrastructure for public utilities to keep rates down. That’s what this is about,” Reineke said in a statement. “It’s important to me that landowners keep their rights, and this would not extend eminent domain to anyone who doesn’t already have that privilege — rather, it is a framework to simplify our existing process that would put us in line with 45 other states.”
He added that one of his top focuses was to make sure there was enough energy and lower costs.
But the legislation does specifically change who is considered a public utility, both for electrical transmission and for gas. Even without being a private electric transmitter who applies for a certificate, Francis believes it is feasible that a utility company can help take land in order to power a data center.
For farmers, they want Ohioans to know that this won’t just impact their land, but anyone else’s. Plus, Francis said, no economic development proposal is worth losing memories.
“It’s very important,” the farmer said, choking up. “I want my kids to know where they came from. It’s hard to describe when you have roots not just to a family, but to a place.”
The farming community plans to start calling their lawmakers to demand that they stop the bill.

name: California
title: Fiscales piden a la Corte Suprema de California que detenga las conmutaciones de la pena de muerte de Newsom
description: Los fiscales de California y un grupo de defensa de las víctimas de delitos están pidiendo a la Corte Suprema estatal que bloquee la conmutación generalizada de las sentencias de muerte por parte del gobernador Newsom.
text:
This article is also available in English. Read it here.
Los fiscales de distrito de 30 condados argumentaron en una demanda presentada el lunes que el tribunal supremo del estado debería detener las conmutaciones de penas de muerte ordenadas por el gobernador Gavin Newsom.
La demanda , presentada ante la Corte Suprema de California, alega que Newsom actuó ilegalmente cuando propuso conmutar las sentencias de 548 presos sin darle a las víctimas de sus crímenes la “oportunidad de ser escuchadas”.
 “Solo este tribunal puede detener el desprecio del gobernador por la ley, su abuso de poder”, escribieron los demandantes a la Corte Suprema de California.
 La petición distingue las facultades de conmutación de Newsom de las facultades de indulto de un presidente: el indulto presidencial no tiene límites, salvo el juicio político. En cambio, cuando los presos condenados a muerte en California solicitan una conmutación, los gobernadores deben notificar al fiscal de distrito donde se cometió el delito, así como a las víctimas o sus familias.
 Quizás anticipándose a este argumento, Newsom emitió una declaración explicativa en la que detallaba por qué no era necesario notificar a las víctimas ni a sus familias. Un factor clave fue que ninguna de las conmutaciones propuestas provenía de una solicitud de un preso condenado a muerte. Al proponer una conmutación generalizada, Newsom afirmó que no se aplicaba ninguno de los requisitos legales.
 La sección del código penal de California que destacaron los fiscales de distrito “no se aplica cuando el gobernador actúa por iniciativa propia para conceder el indulto sin que haya una solicitud”, escribió Newsom en la explicación.
 Añadió que, tras presentar las propuestas de conmutación de penas ante el Tribunal Supremo, su oficina notificaría a los fiscales de distrito de los condados en los que se cometieron los delitos y solicitaría su ayuda para realizar las notificaciones.
 El Tribunal Supremo de California intervendrá en casi 400 de las conmutaciones de penas de Newsom. La ley estatal exige que el tribunal revise estos casos porque los presos fueron condenados por múltiples delitos graves. Los representantes del tribunal no han especificado cómo ni cuándo se llevarán a cabo dichas revisiones.
 En 2019, Newsom decretó una moratoria sobre las ejecuciones y posteriormente ordenó el desmantelamiento de la cámara de ejecución en la prisión estatal de San Quentin. Su sucesor, el gobernador electo Xavier Becerra , se ha comprometido a extender la moratoria cuando asuma el cargo.

name: Virginia Mercury
title: After Lucas pleads not guilty, Locke warns against Senate inquiry
description: Hours after Virginia Sen. Louise Lucas of Portsmouth pleaded not guilty to federal corruption charges relating to her cannabis business, a Democratic colleague warned Monday that a proposed state Senate investigation that could lead to her expulsion would set an “awful precedent” before her criminal case is resolved.  Sen. Mamie Locke, D-Hampton, made the re[...]
text:
Virginia Sens. Mamie Locke, D-Hampton, left, and Louise Lucas, D-Portsmouth. Locke spoke against a proposed Senate investigation that could lead to Lucas’ expulsion hours after Lucas pleaded not guilty to federal charges tied to her cannabis business. (Photo by Markus Schmidt/Virginia Mercury)Hours after Virginia Sen. Louise Lucas of Portsmouth pleaded not guilty to federal corruption charges relating to her cannabis business, a Democratic colleague warned Monday that a proposed state Senate investigation that could lead to her expulsion would set an “awful precedent” before her criminal case is resolved. 
Sen. Mamie Locke, D-Hampton, made the remarks during an hourlong virtual rally organized by the L. Louise Lucas Legal Defense Fund. She said she doubted the proposal would advance and accused President Donald Trump’s administration of targeting prominent Black women in public office. 
Lucas, the Senate’s president pro tempore, appeared to join the call with her camera and microphone off; she did not speak. Earlier Monday, she was arraigned in the U.S. District Court in Newport News, where she entered a not guilty plea. Her trial is scheduled for Sept. 13, 2027. 
Lucas faces five federal charges: racketeering conspiracy, conspiracy to distribute and possess with intent to distribute marijuana, money laundering conspiracy, conspiracy to commit honest-services fraud and maintaining drug-involved premises.
Prosecutors allege she helped run an operation that distributed large quantities of marijuana, laundered the proceeds and used her legislative position for personal financial gain. 
The Virginia Senate Republican Caucus on Tuesday called on Senate Democrats to require Lucas to step aside as chair of the Senate Finance and Appropriations Committee while she faces federal charges. 
“She still chairs the committee that directs billions of taxpayer dollars. The decision rests with the Senate Democratic Caucus, and it is time for them to exercise their responsibility and act,” the caucus said in a statement. 
Lucas has said she intends to remain in the Senate and continue chairing the committee while her case, which began under President Joe Biden’s administration, proceeds. 
 Locke challenges Senate inquiry 

Republican Sen. Bryce Reeves of Spotsylvania filed Senate Resolution 173 for the 2027 legislative session. It would direct the Senate Privileges and Elections Committee to review evidence underlying the federal charges, including recordings and financial disclosures, to determine whether Lucas violated state law. 
The committee could recommend disciplinary action, including expulsion, which would require a separate resolution and at least 27 votes in the 40-member Senate. 
“It would be an awful precedent for us to take up a resolution against an individual who is presumed innocent,” Locke said in response to a question from Laura Maretich, an attorney with the defense fund who moderated the event.
Locke called the proposal “out of order” and said she doubted it would reach the Senate floor. 
Reeves told The Mercury earlier this month that the Senate has an obligation to examine possible misconduct regardless of the outcome of the federal prosecution. 
He pointed to allegations that Lucas failed to disclose business interests on required financial forms. His resolution acknowledges that she is presumed innocent and calls for any disciplinary actions to be based on the committee’s findings. 
 Supporters question federal prosecution 

Locke compared Lucas’ case to recent federal probes of several other prominent Black women, including New York Attorney General Letitia James, Federal Reserve Gov. Lisa Cook and U.S. Rep. LaMonica McIver of New Jersey. 
She also cited Trump’s attacks on Fulton County District Attorney Fani Willis, who prosecuted the Georgia election interference case against him. 
“Why do so many powerful Black women who challenge political power find themselves having to defend not only their ideas, but their offices, their reputations, their careers and sometimes their very freedom?” Locke said. 
Other speakers questioned the timing of the federal charges. 
FBI agents searched Lucas’ Portsmouth legislative office and a cannabis shop she owns in May, following Virginia’s redistricting referendum. The indictment was unsealed Oct. 22, less than two weeks before the midterm elections. 
During a news conference in Norfolk, U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche denied political motivations, saying the investigation began before Trump returned to the White House. 
Civil rights attorney Phillip Thompson questioned Monday why federal prosecutors were pursuing Lucas when licensed businesses in other states openly sell recreational marijuana despite the federal prohibition. 
Virginia legalized adult possession of marijuana in 2021, but recreational sales are not scheduled to begin until July 2027.
 Prosecutors allege Lucas’ business sold marijuana while operating under the guise of a hemp retailer and that she sought to influence marijuana legislation for her own financial benefit. 
Salaam Bhatti, a public interest attorney and former Democratic congressional office hopeful, criticized remarks Blanche and FBI Director Kash Patel made during the news conference announcing the charges. 
Bhatti accused Blanche of applying a double standard by criticizing Lucas for allegedly putting her financial interests ahead of her constituents. He questioned whether the same scrutiny would be applied to Trump and his family’s business dealings. 
Bhatti also challenged Patel’s suggestion that Lucas had a responsibility to enforce law. 
“Legislators don’t enforce the law, they make it. The executive branch enforces it,” he said. 
Bhatti argued that the officials’ comments could prejudice potential jurors. 
“They came to Norfolk, where the jury is going to be chosen,” he said. “In front of that community, they said this stuff out loud.”
Lucas’ attorneys raised similar concerns in court, asking a judge to sanction Blanche, Patel and First Assistant U.S. Attorney Theophani Stamos.
The defense argued that their statements at the news conference violated a court rule restricting public comments that could interfere with a fair trial. 
A spokesperson for the U.S. Attorney’s Office declined to comment on the motion. The Justice Department told The Associated Press that it stood by its case and declined to comment further on the pending litigation. 
Brian Woolfolk, chief counsel for the defense fund, said donations would help Lucas defend herself in federal court and respond to any efforts in Richmond to strip her of Senate leadership positions or remove her from the chamber. 
Given the complexity of the case, Woolfolk said he expects extensive pretrial motions.

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: Commonwealth Court Judge Lori Dumas announces candidacy for state Supreme Court
description: The election will be another chance for Republicans to change the makeup of the court, which has had a majority of justices elected as Democrats since 2015.
text:
The Pennsylvania Supreme Court. (Jen Barker Worley/ Administrative Office of Pennsylvania Courts)Commonwealth Court Judge Lori Dumas will run as a Democrat for state Supreme Court, for one of two seats expected to be up for election next year, she announced Monday.
Dumas has served on Commonwealth Court, one of Pennsylvania’s appellate courts, since she was elected in 2021. The winners of next year’s election will take the seats currently held by Justice Christine Donohue and Chief Justice Debra Todd.
“I’m running to be a justice on Pennsylvania’s Supreme Court because I believe Pennsylvanians deserve a justice who brings experience, independence, compassion, and an unwavering commitment to the rule of law to the bench,” Dumas said, adding that as a mother of three, her commitment to those ideals is deeply personal.
Commonwealth Court Judge Lori Dumas. (Photo courtesy of the Administrative Office of Pennsylvania Courts)
The election will be another chance for Republicans to change the makeup of the court, which has had a majority of justices elected as Democrats since 2015. The retention election for three Democratic justices in 2025 prompted intense voter influence campaigns from outside groups that spent millions of dollars in addition to $14 million the justices’ campaigns raised.
The court now has four Democrats, two Republicans and one Independent. Justice David Wecht announced in May that he was leaving the Democratic Party over what he described as anti-Jewish actions and rhetoric becoming mainstream within the party.
Once elected, Pennsylvania judges must face voters in a retention election every 10 years to remain in office.
Todd, who was first elected in 2007 and retained in 2017, faces mandatory retirement in 2032.
“At the present time, the Chief Justice is not planning to seek retention in 2027,” court spokesperson Stacey Witalic said, noting Jan. 4 is the deadline for judges to file notices if they are seeking retention. 
Donohue, first elected in 2015 and retained in 2025, will reach the mandatory retirement age of 75 next year and must retire.
Before her election to Commonwealth Court, Dumas served for 19 years as a Philadelphia Court of Common Pleas judge, where she presided over family, civil and criminal cases.
“The law must work the same for everyone who walks into a Pennsylvania courtroom — no matter their ZIP code, their income, or their circumstances,” Dumas said, noting that as a trial court judge she protected children, families and victims of violence.
“I have been tasked with balancing the power of government with the voice of the people. I am running for the Supreme Court to bring that same fidelity to the law — and to every Pennsylvanian it serves,” she said.
The Supreme Court is the court of last resort in Pennsylvania, handling appeals ranging from death penalty cases to family court disputes. In recent years, the court’s role in redistricting has had an impact on the commonwealth’s representation in Congress and the General Assembly. 
The court also hears disputes over challenged laws and policy decisions, such as the court’s consequential ruling in June that skill games are illegal under the state Gaming Act and Crimes Code.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: NC House Dems elect Reives, Butler to 2027 leadership roles
description: The full state House of Representatives will vote on key leadership positions on Jan. 13 when lawmakers come to Raleigh for the 2027 session.
text:
House Democratic Leader Robert Reives (D-Chatham) speaks to reporters after the North Carolina House voted to pass three constitutional amendments on May 20, 2026. (Photo: Christine Zhu/NC Newsline)The North Carolina House Democratic Caucus elected Rep. Robert Reives as their choice for Speaker of the House Monday, according to an announcement by the caucus. 
Reives, 54, has represented Chatham County since 2014. His caucus elected him House Democratic leader in December 2020, a position he has served in for six years. He will be the second Black House speaker in state history, following Dan Blue. 
“Our House Democratic Caucus is ready to hit the ground running to make life more affordable for North Carolinians,” Reives said in a statement. “We have a great leadership team and I look forward to working with them in the weeks ahead to prepare for the upcoming biennium.”
The House Democratic Caucus met in a private meeting for current and new elected members on Monday at the Albemarle Building, across the street from the Legislative Office Building. 
The full state House of Representatives will vote on key leadership positions on Jan. 13 when lawmakers come to Raleigh for the 2027 session, according to Reives’ office. Republicans can also nominate their own ticket, but with Democrats holding a 71-49 majority, their choice will win.
Rep. Deb Butler, 65, will serve as Speaker Pro Tem. She has represented New Hanover County in the House since 2017. 
Who will be the NC Senate’s next leader and money man?

The caucus selected Reps. Terry Brown and Beth Helfrich, both from Mecklenburg County, as majority leader and deputy majority leader, respectively. 
Rep. Phil Rubin of Wake County will be the House’s joint caucus chair.
The group elected six party whips: Reps. Mary Belk of Mecklenburg, Gloristine Brown of Pitt, Allison Dahle of Wake, Jordan Lopez of Mecklenburg, Marcia Morey of Durham, and Amos Quick of Guilford counties. 
Reps. Eric Ager from Buncombe County and Allen Buansi from Orange County will serve as conference chairs. 
Lawmakers from Mecklenburg County have the most representation in House Democratic leadership, holding four positions.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: DeSantis sued (again) for delaying special election for Senate seat in Miami-Dade
description: The ACLU of Florida has filed a lawsuit on behalf of a voter, calling on Gov. Ron DeSantis to fulfill his constitutional obligation to call a special election to fill the vacancy in Florida Senate District 39 in Miami-Dade County. The district has gone without representation for 84 days, since Republican then-Sen. Bryan Ávila resigned […]
text:
Gov. Ron DeSantis hosted a news conference on Wednesday, Nov. 4, 2026, at the Florida Capitol following the midterm elections. (Photo by Jay Waagmeester/Florida Phoenix)The ACLU of Florida has filed a lawsuit on behalf of a voter, calling on Gov. Ron DeSantis to fulfill his constitutional obligation to call a special election to fill the vacancy in Florida Senate District 39 in Miami-Dade County.
The district has gone without representation for 84 days, since Republican then-Sen. Bryan Ávila resigned to run for lieutenant governor.
“The Governor’s failure — inaction longer than any of his predecessors in known history — leaves the district’s half a million constituents without representation and deprives them of a voice in the Capitol during the 2027 legislative session and interim committee weeks that begin in thirteen days,” reads the lawsuit, filed Tuesday in the Florida Supreme Court on behalf of Alejandro Peñuelas, a resident of Doral, one of the cities the district.
ACLU attorneys claim in the lawsuit that this is the 10th vacancy over which voters have had to go court to force the governor to call an election. They call that “a disturbing pattern that both undermines our republican form of government and wastes judicial resources.”
In nearly every case, DeSantis has set the election date only after those lawsuits were filed.
“There is no good reason for this governor to keep resisting timely special elections,” said Nicholas Warren, ACLU of Florida senior staff attorney, in a written statement. “From Jeb Bush to Rick Scott, prior governors consistently acted quickly to ensure Floridians retained their voice in government. Governor DeSantis’s refusal to do the same is as perplexing as it is illegal.”
The ACLU says that had the governor acted quickly after Ávila resigned his seat on Aug. 25, a special primary or general election could have been held concurrently with already-scheduled municipal elections in late November or December. They contend the delay is likely to cost taxpayers more to hold a separate election.
In 2024, Ávila won the seat by nearly 40 percentage points. It was previously held by Republican Sen. Anitere Flores.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Declining enrollment and unpaid costs for special education affect Kansas education budget
description: TOPEKA — Decreased public school enrollment and requests to fully fund special education generated confusion and questions in an interim legislative committee. Although the education department decreased projected fiscal year 2027 funds because of enrollment losses, other needs pushed the budget request up, including $110 million in additional funding for sp[...]
text:
Rep. Kristey Williams, an Augusta Republican, shown here speaking to a reporter on June 5, 2026, in Overland Park, says a new graphic on the Kansas State Department of Education website shows the monies that go into special education funding. (Photo by Anna Kaminski/Kansas Reflector)TOPEKA — Decreased public school enrollment and requests to fully fund special education generated confusion and questions in an interim legislative committee.
Although the education department decreased projected fiscal year 2027 funds because of enrollment losses, other needs pushed the budget request up, including $110 million in additional funding for special education, said Dylan Dear, Kansas Legislative Research Department assistant director for fiscal affairs.
Dear summarized agency requests for the 2026 Kansas Special Committee on the State Budget, which met Nov. 12.
Once again, the Kansas Department of Education asked for dollars to fund special education.  Kansas budget director and administration secretary Adam Proffitt said in January that the state hasn’t fully funded special education to the 92% required in statute for 15 years. 
Committee chairman Rep. Troy Waymaster, R-Bunker Hill, questioned requested education budget increases, saying he was “perplexed” by the fact that education enrollment decreased but the department was “asking for more money for special education.”
“We’ve already had the discussion in past legislative sessions that we do allocate funds for special education and somehow it’s not counted towards special education,” he said.
Waymaster highlighted a contentious argument ongoing between legislators and state school officials regarding the complexity of special education funding and how to fix the issue. 
In 2024, a task force created to address the issue couldn’t even agree on who would hold leadership positions and limited the input from school officials because, according to Sen. Renee Erickson, a Wichita Republican, “We have their input, which is just more money. We don’t need a task force to convene to discuss that part.”
Even with an annual increase built into the school finance formula, “we’re still having increases,” Waymaster said at last week’s budget meeting. The general fund appropriation for fiscal year 2027 for special education is $617 million, he said.
Rep. Barbara Ballard, a Lawrence Democrat, questioned Waymaster about his reference to funds that weren’t being counted, saying she would like that statement clarified to communicate it to school officials in her district.
“I wish we would get to that point that we find out where that is because I’ll just use my own school district — they claim we’re not getting as much as the state says we’re actually getting,” she said. “We had a real good discussion about this last year. So if there’s additional funds, then maybe we need to identify them as such.”
Waymaster said it had been an ongoing issue in recent years that special education funding is received from different agencies or departments that isn’t counted toward the funding total.
“I think when we look forward in fiscal year 2028, we need to actually have an understanding of how much money is actually being spent out of these state coffers,” Waymaster said.
Rep. Kristey Williams, an Augusta Republican, said the money is included in accountability reports on the education department’s website, in a new section about special education financial accountability.  
“On that, you will find the missing money that you are referencing that is outside of the formula,” she said. “It is $219.6 million for 25-26, and if you’re asking yourself what is that money, that is taxpayer money that is both state equalized for (local option budget) or supplemental, and also locally raised for special education students. It’s $220 million that is not counted in the formula required by law to be placed into their special education fund and used for that purpose.”
Frank Harwood, deputy commissioner, division of fiscal and administrative services with the education department, said federal funds and Medicaid reimbursements schools receive are accounted for in the school formula, as well as what the state appropriates and money received from the local option budget.
“State law allows a local school board to levy a local tax for up to 33% of their general fund budget,” he said. “It’s called the local option budget. It is equalized based on the average valuation per pupil, but the local school board determines what percentage of the general fund they will make for the local option budget.”
The state minimum is 15% but the average statewide is about 32.6%, he said.
“When the LOB was put in, there was no indication that it would be used for anything other than whatever the local district decided,” Harwood said. “Over time, the Legislature has put more restrictions on the local option budget, requiring a transfer to special education — that happened in 2024. Before that it was on bilingual and at-risk funds.”
Harwood said special education was underfunded by about $225 million in fiscal year 2026, based on the statute that says the state must fund 92% of excess costs. Based on consensus revenue estimates released recently, the excess costs for fiscal year 2027 would be about $250 million.
School districts cover the special education costs that aren’t funded by transferring money from either the general fund or the LOB into the special education fund, he said.
Final accounting for the 2025-26 school year will be completed after Thanksgiving, Harwood said, but in 2024-25, school districts transferred about $40 million to support special education.
“All 284 districts are approaching that differently,” he said.
Harwood pointed to Johnson County as an example, which last year eliminated orchestra in middle school. Four school districts there are considering suing the state for failing to fully fund special education.
In May, they announced in a news release that they are talking with legal representation. 
“Despite longstanding legal requirements, the Legislature and state elected officials have consistently and deliberately chosen to shift those costs onto school districts and local taxpayers rather than fulfill their legal obligation,” the districts said in the news release.
Decreasing enrollment will bring more pressure on district budgets, Harwood said. When a district loses students, they don’t lose them in a way that allows them to eliminate a fifth or 12th grade teacher, for instance, he said.
Students are lost throughout the grade levels, which means faculty are needed in the same numbers, Harwood said. Some districts are disorganizing, which means they will merge with surrounding districts. Some are closing buildings.
Multiple factors are at work on district budgets. 
“If you look just at this past year, the base state aid went up by 2.9% and enrollment came down by 1.8%, so the inflationary increase that’s built in is greater than the enrollment decline,” he said. “Just the math shows you there would be an increase in costs.”

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: ‘We Live Here’ charts a course through New London’s housing history
authors: Alexis Zanghi | Special to The Connecticut Mirror
description: The collaborative exhibition, at New London's Garde Arts Center, examines the history and present of housing in southeastern CT.
text:
“WE LIVE HERE.”  
That’s the text on the transom above 305 State St. in downtown New London. The all-caps signage, bold and striking on the Garde Arts Center’s marquee, is visible to pedestrians from a block away. 
Wide-ranging and collaborative, the exhibition examines the history and present of housing in southeastern Connecticut, and imagines new potential for the places residents call home.
“We” was the animating idea behind the exhibition. At every stage, decisions large and small were informed by a citizens’ advisory board of 30 community members, bringing together tenants, tenant organizers, activists, advocates, care workers, city officials, and other stakeholders. Curator Anna Vallye, who is an assistant professor of art history and architecture studies at Connecticut College, co-directed the project with Beth Sabilia, director of the Center for Housing Opportunity of Eastern Connecticut.
“Their work is evident throughout the exhibit,” Sabilia said during an interview last week. 
The design of the exhibition — shaped with feedback from the citizen’s advisory board — is intended to make visitors feel as if they’re “behind the scenes of a construction site,” Vallye said. 
The interior space is divided by plywood sheeting, styled as construction hoarding. The walls are covered in a forest green that evokes vinyl mesh windscreen wrapped around construction fencing. (The color is also a nod to the New London High School Whalers.) 
The storefront location was purposeful, too: State Street is one of the city’s main thoroughfares for pedestrians and vehicles, Vallye said, and the team wanted to locate the exhibition where “any passerby” might “encounter” the project. Inside, visitors will find interviews with neighbors, portraits of residents and advocates, infographics and a chronology of housing history. They’ll also see speculative designs for a future New London: parks, markets, buildings and homes that have yet to be built. 
Visitors are encouraged to follow a historical timeline, which Vallye described as the exhibition’s “spine.” As it charts twin histories of urban development and housing policy, the timeline allows visitors to “glimpse into how national trends and patterns are reflected in local issues.”
“We Live Here/New London” is an exhibition that looks at housing as the framework of community life. Credit: Sean D. Elliot / Connecticut College
Early in the timeline are photographs of a settlement house in Chicago and images from “How the Other Half Lives” by Jacob Riis, whose muckraking photographs inspired progressive reformers to advocate for better housing in cities around the country, including in New London. As a reporter, Riis accompanied police and health inspectors on tenement raids, where residents — startled, frightened, half-asleep — may not have agreed to be photographed.
There are political cartoons and opinion-editorials from archives of the local newspaper, The Day; maps of redlined neighborhoods; clippings from campaign ads and shelter magazines. There are photographs of the construction and later, the demolition, of the Pruitt-Igoe complex in St. Louis, Missouri. 
Comments from visitors, handwritten on postcards, contribute additional insights. One advocates for “modest homes,” a return to the smaller, more efficient housing of previous decades. Another, nestled beneath images of twentieth-century tract housing, reminds visitors that Black veterans were excluded from the GI Bill, which provided housing and college for so many white Americans. 
Data visualizations appear throughout the space, documenting the impact of exclusionary zoning, charting the pace of gentrification, and contrasting the mismatch of available housing with household sizes. An interactive map of the New London metropolitan area prompts visitors to pin where they live, using a yellow pin for single-family homes and orange for multi-family housing.
“We Live Here/New London” is an exhibition that looks at housing as the framework of community life.  Credit: Sean D. Elliot / Connecticut College
The “overwhelming dominance of the single-family home in Connecticut,” and the impact of restrictive land-use policies, are some of the observations Vallye hopes visitors take from the exhibition. Equally important is a feeling of “place-based solidarity.” For her, it’s no coincidence that crises of affordability and housing have escalated just as participation in civic life has declined. 
“We all live somewhere,” Vallye said. “We belong to a specific place, whether we’ve lived there for months or for generations, and organizing for collective action, especially at the local level, can make a real difference in people’s lives.”
“We Live Here” celebrates that collective action. Members of the advisory committee contributed interviews and testimony, and it was their recommendation to feature portraits of “people who are doing the work.” At the exhibition’s entry, a display of large portraits features a pastor and his partner, a couple and their garden, and other members of the New London community. 
In one photograph, a man in a U.S. Navy baseball cap faces the camera, daylight glinting from the saltwater and his sunglasses, his back to the ocean. After two tours aboard the SS America, he stepped onto land in New London and knew he was home. 
The portraits are Sabilia’s favorite part of the exhibition. Representing the experiences of tenants has a fraught history, one that “We Live Here/New London” carefully navigates. A collection of interviews with residents plays on a loop inside a storefront window. Conducted and edited by Connecticut College students, film major Johanne Wartelle said the videos were shot as dialogues, with each participant level to the camera and with each other.

“We Live Here/New London” is an exhibition that looks at housing as the framework of community life.  Credit: Sean D. Elliot / Connecticut College

The exhibition’s timeline ends today, in 2026, but around the corner in the next room visitors will find ideas for what New London can be. Architectural models appear atop plywood pedestals, anchored by concrete deck blocks. 
In the future New London, buildings in disrepair, underutilized lots, and fixtures of the local economy are rehabilitated with tabby bricks made from salvaged oyster shells. Highways and structures from the urban renewal era are repurposed as multifunctional sites for living and working. 
Yesterday’s bridge trusses support tomorrow’s kelp farming. A decommissioned highway deck hosts temporary workers and houses market stalls. Flood-resistant modular housing, constructed as a continuous deck, weaves together neighborhood third spaces with overhead catwalks. A participatory design-a-thon challenges top-down decision-making and encourages residents to determine their own zoning and building regulations. 
Exhibitions about housing have long featured designs for newer, better homes. These “speculations” by students at Yale School of Architecture envision better shared lives, co-created alternatives to the present. 
The community behind “We Live Here/New London” isn’t waiting to create those alternatives. Guided by the citizens’ advisory committee, the exhibition’s programs have included a block party, organizer trainings by the Connecticut Tenants Union, a panel about housing policies proposed during the most recent legislative session in Hartford, and another on what “moved the needle” for community advocates. 
This month, the Southeastern Connecticut Community Land Trust led a two-part film screening and discussion about alternative economies and community control. On December 1, The Day will stage a forum on housing equity, hosted at Connecticut College. 
The show suggests that property is power. The relationships at work in “We Live Here/New London” — between photographer and subject, landlord and tenant (or tenant union), mortgage lender and homeowner, town and gown — might be power dynamics that shape our present. Aware of these tensions, the exhibition doesn’t try to design today’s problems away. Instead, it begins construction on a shared future.
“We Live Here/New London” is on view at the Garde Gallery, 305 State St. in New London, through December 18. More information is available here.

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Republican Senate leader Chris Garten asks Indiana Supreme Court to let him take office
description: Attorneys for Republican state Sen. Chris Garten have asked the Indiana Supreme Court to throw out a judge’s order blocking him from taking the oath of office Tuesday with other newly elected legislators.
text:
Sen. Chris Garten, R-Charlestown, speaks during a February 2026 Senate session. (Photo by Leslie Bonilla Muñiz/Indiana Capital Chronicle)Attorneys for Republican state Sen. Chris Garten have asked the Indiana Supreme Court to throw out a judge’s order blocking him from taking the oath of office Tuesday with other newly elected legislators.
The court filings come just hours before the Senate’s Organization Day session scheduled for 1:30 p.m. Tuesday, when the majority Republicans planned to install him in the chamber’s top position of president pro tem.
Garten’s attorneys argue that Scott County Circuit Court Judge Jason Mount exceeded his authority by issuing a temporary restraining order Monday preventing Garten from “presenting himself to take the oath of office as, or to be seated as, the Senator from District 45.”
The Supreme Court did not make any immediate rulings Tuesday morning.
The restraining order sought by the Clark County Democratic chairman argued that voting equipment problems on Election Day in Jeffersonville leave questions about the accuracy of the reported election results.
Judge issues order blocking Indiana Senate GOP leader Chris Garten from starting new term

The tallies for Senate District 45 — which includes all of Clark County and a portion of Floyd County — show Garten ahead of Democratic challenger Nick Marshall by 297 votes, or about two-thirds of a percentage point.
Garten’s attorneys argue that the state constitution gives each house of the Legislature the exclusive authority to determine “the elections, qualifications, and returns of its own members.”
“The order stops the certification the recount statutes assume, and it purports to forbid a Senator-elect from presenting himself to the Senate,” they say in a court filing. “That is a court impermissibly deciding who may be heard by the Senate on its organizing day.”
Garten is represented by prominent conservative attorney James Bopp, along with Ted Nolting and Philip Lashutka of the Indianapolis firm Kroger, Gardis and Regas.
Democrats argued that Garten should not be allowed to be sworn in for a new four-year term before the Indiana Recount Commission can review the race.
Democrats maintain the Clark County Election Board — controlled 2-1 by Republicans — failed to adequately review problems involving four precincts that voted at Jeffersonville High School, where a ballot scanner malfunction was reported on Election Day.
Mount, a Democrat, was assigned as the special judge after a Clark County judge’s recusal from the case, according to court records. Mount is the brother of Republican U.S. Rep. Erin Houchin, who served in the state Senate with Garten.
Democrats have said they intend to seek a recount of the Senate race results. Candidates have until Tuesday to file recount petitions, with county party chairs having a Friday deadline.
Garten’s attorneys argue that state law lays out a recount as the proper process that should be followed.
“A recount and contest before the Recount Commission is the remedy the General Assembly created for the claims Petitioner raises,” they said in court filings.
State law says the Recount Commission must complete a legislative recount by December 20, unless it extends the deadline for good cause.
