name: Honolulu Civil Beat
title: This Unlicensed Contractor Will Take Your Cash But May Not Finish The Job
description: Cheryl Ryan isn’t optimistic that she will get back any of the $30,000 Rocky Aviguetero owes her for work on her backyard pool, which she says he never finished. But the teacher sued the unlicensed contractor in September anyway after a pool resurfacing job this spring turned into a horror show by June.   “I’m sitting […]
text:
Cheryl Ryan isn’t optimistic that she will get back any of the $30,000 Rocky Aviguetero owes her for work on her backyard pool, which she says he never finished.
But the teacher sued the unlicensed contractor in September anyway after a pool resurfacing job this spring turned into a horror show by June.  
“I’m sitting here beating myself up for having trusted him. There’s a lot of shame associated with falling for this,” the Kāneʻohe resident said. “I now have a hard time hiring and trusting other people.”
Ryan’s pool, it turns out, was just a sample of the trail of damage that Aviguetero’s been accused of leaving behind. Once she started looking, Ryan quickly found there were others who said they had paid Aviguetero for projects never completed and materials never delivered. 
In court records, Ryan discovered three civil claims against Aviguetero worth more than $55,000 from the last four years and another 16 claims or civil suits against him dating back as far as 1988. Courts have entered a dozen default judgments against him since 2008. And those were only the cases, like Ryan’s, that ended up making it to court.
Aviguetero, who hasn’t hired a lawyer in the last seven years, turned up for only one online hearing in all that time, according to a review of court records by Civil Beat.
The Department of Commerce & Consumer Affairs also sued Aviguetero in 2008 and got a court to impose a $15,000 fine against him and his then wife for contracting without a license on Kauaʻi. Details of the complaint that led to the fine are not readily available online, and the court docket doesn’t specify if the fine was ever paid. 
In Hawaiʻi, engaging in contracting activity without a license is a misdemeanor crime that can become a felony if done habitually. But the court judgments against Aviguetero have been in civil court and were not related to licensing issues. 
Ryan’s situation is illustrative of the the difficulty consumers have when trying to hold an unlicensed contractor accountable in Hawaiʻi. Their options — seeking recourse either through the courts or the state’s licensing agency — are apparently not enough to stop some accused bad actors from operating.
Cheryl Ryan hired Rocky Aviguetero to do landscaping as well as work on her swimming pool.  (Jamm Aquino/Civil Beat/2026) Jamm Aquino/Civil Beat/2026
That discovery only fired up Ryan more. 
“I went through the shame process, and now I’m just in the angry process,” she said. “The only thing I can do is make sure this doesn’t happen to other people.”
There are two other pending consumer complaints against Aviguetero from this year and 2024, according to the Hawaiʻi Regulated Industries Complaints Office website. Separately, DCCA issued a cease and desist letter to Aviguetero in 2024 for allegedly selling unregistered securities. 
Attempts to contact Aviguetero by phone, text and email were unsuccessful. 
Despite this lengthy pattern of allegations about unethical behavior and the financial harm to consumers, Aviguetero remains active. 
After he talked Ryan into an “off-the-books” deal, took cash deposits and partially completed the project, he stopped working and failed to return nearly $24,000 and unused materials as agreed, Ryan’s lawsuit alleges.  
Landscape Worker Offered To Help
Ryan first met Aviguetero in March when she called Koʻolau Landscaping, a licensed landscaping business based on Oʻahu’s Windward side. 
She wanted four coconut trees on her property removed, and Aviguetero turned up in a Koʻolau Landscaping truck and uniform to provide a quote for the work. The work was done well, and she paid him $3,500 and $200 tip, according to her lawsuit complaint. 
Ryan said that Aviguetero’s role as a Koʻolau Landscaping employee was one of the reasons that she hired him for the pool work. 
That’s when he said he could also do other backyard projects through a separate arrangement, she said.
“You really need to have your pool resurfaced. I got a guy who can help you with that. I’ll do the prep work, and he’ll come in and he’ll do the plaster and we got you,” Ryan recalls Aviguetero saying. 
Aviguetero represented that he was licensed and qualified, according to her lawsuit complaint. She said she later discovered that neither were true.
He then told her that if she could pay cash, he would get a better price for materials.
“It’s better for you. It’s better for me,” she recalls him saying. Ryan said it was not the first time somebody’s asked her for cash to do a job and thought, “OK, it’s worked out before.”
Ryan kept a detailed record of the timeline of the work and provided Civil Beat with documentation of payments, statements, receipts and text messages related to the project. 
On April 6, Aviguetero said he paid $475 for the pool renovation permit, the complaint states. Ryan said she later discovered that wasn’t the case, the lawsuit says.
A week later he texted that he had secured the materials for the pool renovation and asked for $10,000 in a cashier’s check and $8,000 in cash, the complaint states. That was followed by a $1,098 payment for permit processing and tiles, the lawsuit states, and $7,760 for electrical work and additional materials. 
Cheryl Ryan said that she and Rocky Aviguetero agreed that he would return nearly $24,000 after he failed to complete the work. That never happened. (Jamm Aquino/Civil Beat/2026) Jamm Aquino/Civil Beat/2026
Then on June 22, Ryan got a text from Aviguetero’s son saying that his father was in hospital for emergency surgery, the lawsuit states. Throughout July, he offered “various excuses and promises to send others to perform the work,” but no one came, according to the lawsuit.
On Aug. 18, the court filing said Ryan spoke with Aviguetero and they made a verbal agreement that he would return $23,460 and materials to her, the lawsuit alleges.
Aviguetero didn’t respond to a text message from Ryan documenting the agreement, according to the filing. 
Aviguetero has been employed by Koʻolau Landscaping, company owner Asher Eisenpress said in a text last week. 
“However he did not have authority to represent the company or sign contracts on its behalf. Koʻolau Landscaping did not provide a quote, enter into an agreement, perform any work or receive any payment,” for the work on Ryan’s property, Eisenpress said.
Eisenpress did not respond to a follow-up question about whether Aviguetero is still employed by the company. 
Ryan says she’s resigned to the fact she likely won’t get her money back from Aviguetero. 
“That’s hard for me to swallow. I’m a school teacher and I’ve been working really hard to save up the money to make these improvements on my house,” she said. “And ultimately he screwed me over.”
Ryan has a court date scheduled for next month. 
Latest From Civil Beat
Licensing Rules Not Always Enforced
In Hawaiʻi, anyone doing construction or contracting work that is more than the bare basics — painting and minor drywall, non-structural woodwork and yard maintenance — needs to have a license. The only exception is for handymen doing projects that cost less than $1,500.
Depending on the scope of the work, contractors in Hawaiʻi working on a pool need one of three license types, including for full construction, renovation and repairs, and to install prefabricated hot tubs and above ground pools. 
Aviguetero doesn’t have any of those, state licensing records show. 
Rogue operators like Aviguetero are just the tip of the iceberg, said Steve Maratta, the owner of Aquatic Solutions. His company ended up fixing Ryan’s pool at a discount rate, Ryan said.
Maratta said the practice is far more widespread than the enforcement records show. Unlicensed or improperly licensed companies do pool construction and renovations all the time, Maratta said. His company has been registered in Hawaiʻi since 2012, has 15 employees and an annual revenue of $8 million, he said.
Maratta said that in his opinion, the state Department of Commerce and Consumer Affairs is not doing enough enforcement against contractors like Aviguetero or larger companies that aren’t licensed for pool construction. 
Steve Maratta, of Aquatic Solutions, stands near the swimming pool he’s currently constructing at his home in Hawaiʻi Kai. Maratta said he’s fixed many swimming pools that had been inadequately constructed. Maretta said that enforcement of unlicensed pool contractors was more proactive in the state of Nevada where he used to operate. (Jamm Aquino/Civil Beat/2026) Jamm Aquino/Civil Beat/2026
“When I was living in Las Vegas, the municipality would really go after these guys,” he said. 
In Nevada, even submitting a bid for work valued at over $1,000 without a license is a criminal offense, even if no work is done. And after three strikes, it becomes a felony.
California, Arizona and Florida regulations allow agencies to go as far as conducting sting operations and jobsite sweeps on pool construction site. They even use undercover investigators to catch unlicensed operators. 
Esther Brown, who heads the state industry complaints office, did not return a message left with her office Monday. 
A Civil Beat review of the last six years of DCCA’s unlicensed enforcement actions shows only two times that a pool company or a contractor was fined for doing work without the required license. 
Neptune Pools and Spa Service based in Honolulu was fined $5,000 in June for carrying out work as a specialty pool contractor without a valid contractor’s license.  
The company’s co-owner, Alish Fernandez, said their license lapsed through an oversight and they were working to get certified again, but the process is expensive and cumbersome for small family businesses like hers. 
Maratta filed a formal written complaint with the DCCA in June about a different company he said was doing a backyard pool project without proper licensing. The agency informed him that they had closed the case after sending a warning letter. 
Meanwhile, Maratta holds a pool construction license in addition to general building and engineering licenses, and even so, his company has not been immune from enforcement action. His company was fined $8,500 after consumer complaints about the quality of work related to his pool projects were filed in 2021 and 2023.  
Few Options For Consumers Wronged
If a contractor abandons a project or fails to deliver materials, homeowners can be reimbursed up to $12,500 per contract through a state recovery fund, with maximum total compensation capped at $25,000 per individual contractor. 
But the fund only applies to cases involving contractors who are licensed. The consumer also has to win a civil judgment in court first, and the contractor needs to show they are unable to pay. 
The options for consumers narrow quickly when it comes to unclicensed contractors. 
“Then you’re just dealing with another person,” Ryan’s attorney Addison Bonner said. “Your remedies are essentially trying to negotiate a resolution or filing a breach of contract.”   
Consumers who are wronged can take their contractor to court, but it’s no guarantee they’ll get their money back. (Cory Lum/Civil Beat) (Cory Lum/Civil Beat/2014)
It becomes even harder if the customer did a cash deal for promised discounts.
“Then it becomes a question of what that cash was paid for,” he said, “and whether that cash was paid at all.” 
Ryan’s lawsuit against Aviguetero alleges breach of contract, deceptive business practices and unjust enrichment. She is seeking damages and attorney fees, the filing shows. 
Under certain circumstances, consumers could file a police report, if for example, a contractor asks for a deposit to buy materials that never appear.
“That could be theft, in my mind,” Bonner said, but added as a former prosecutor, charges would be an unlikely outcome.
Ryan did talk to police, she said, and they told her to take civil action. 
“I can’t guarantee that there’s going to be any recovery.”Attorney addison bonner
Ryanʻs experience with Aviguetero is similar to Kapolei resident Shannondore Cuesta, who paid him $11,100 for soil, bricks, concrete and irrigation equipment for a yard project that he never finished, according to her detailed court filing this year. 
She and her husband just got a default judgment for the full amount plus costs against Aviguetero. She declined to speak on the record. 
Chelita Muratsuka paid $10,500 starting in November 2022 to install artificial turf at her Mililani residence that she alleged in her court filing was never completed. She managed to get a default judgment against Aviguetero in 2024, but the court records show the court order sent to Aviguetero was returned in the mail. 
Garrett Yamamoto of Wahiawā hired Aviguestero to have his yard leveled and artificial turf installed. Now he is out of pocket nearly $4,000, court records state. 
Even if the courts rule in favor of consumers like Ryan, court records suggests they are unlikely to recoup money from Aviguetero, who has multiple tax liens and other judgments, according to background checks. 
Bonner said that his law office fields calls from consumers like Ryan on a weekly basis, but in most of the cases, it may not be financially worth pursuing, “unless we’re well into the six figures.” The attorney’s fees may exceed any potential award. 
“I can’t guarantee that there’s going to be any recovery,” he said. 


Is Your Contractor Licensed?
Working with licensed contractors offers more protection for Hawaiʻi consumers. Here are some available resources. 
Is the contractor licensed?
Ask the company or contractor for their license numbers. Some contractors list them on their website while others do not. You can verify a professional license at the state’s Department of Commerce and Consumer Affairs websites here. Search business registrations here. 
DCCA also publishes a list of licensed contractors, electricians and plumbers and engineers, architects, land surveyors and landscape architects. 
What licenses are required?
A license is required for any work that is valued at more than $1,500. So anything more than light handyman work like painting or non-structural woodwork likely requires a licensed contractor. Check if the job requires a specific license.
Have they ever been sanctioned for working without a license?
You can search through judgments and disciplinary actions here and here. 
Does the contractor company have a history of complaints from consumers?
Check the Regulated Industries Complaints Office website for records of any complaints.

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Indiana reviewing possible Medicaid work requirement grace period
description: The Indiana Family and Social Services Administration is reviewing new federal guidance allowing states to delay enforcement of Medicaid expansion work requirements set to begin in January. The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services updated its guidance to states last week to create an optional six-month transition period, during which states can roll out [...]
text:
Indiana’s Home and Community-Based Services Medicaid waiver helps children and adults with intellectual, physical, or developmental disabilities and older adults live at home instead of in a nursing home or facility. (Getty Images)The Indiana Family and Social Services Administration is reviewing new federal guidance allowing states to delay enforcement of Medicaid expansion work requirements set to begin in January.
The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services updated its guidance to states last week to create an optional six-month transition period, during which states can roll out the new 80-hour work rule without disrupting coverage for otherwise eligible people who aren’t yet in compliance.
Able-bodied adults between the ages of 19 and 64 insured through the Healthy Indiana Plan, or Medicaid expansion, must show they are working, volunteering or in school for at least 80 hours a month starting in January, unless they meet an exception or meet a monthly income threshold.
The work reporting rules are required by state and federal law.
Indiana will use a three-month look-back window to determine compliance, meaning Hoosiers must show they met the requirements three months before applying for coverage or undergoing the eligibility redetermination process.
While work reporting rules will still take effect Jan. 1, it is unclear whether the Family and Social Services Administration will delay enforcement.
Marcus Barlow, a spokesperson for the agency, told the Indiana Capital Chronicle that FSSA is reviewing the CMS guidance on the optional enforcement delay, as well as the agency’s statutory authority and state requirements.
“We are carefully evaluating the guidance and its implications and will provide additional information as it becomes available,” he said.
The optional six-month grace period follows a district court ruling in October which found CMS exceeded its authority in narrowing the definition of medical frailty to qualify for an exception from work requirements.
CMS wrote in a statement last week that it’s established an “optional hold harmless period” to give state governments more time to update their systems and improve the processes they have in place.
“States have made real progress, and they’ve been clear with us about what it takes to get this right for beneficiaries—at scale and for the long term,” Director of the Center for Medicaid and CHIP Services Dan Brillman wrote in the statement.
“If the state can use data to show that someone is working or qualifies for an exclusion, that person should not have to track down paperwork to prove it. And when someone needs support, they should know exactly what to do, when to do it, and where to go. That’s how we build a Medicaid program that works better for people, connects them to work, education, and training opportunities, and supports paths to prosperity.”
Democrats in Congress raised concerns as recently as this week that states hadn’t had enough time to prepare for the new 80-hours-a-month requirement.
House Energy and Commerce Committee ranking member Frank Pallone Jr., of New Jersey, and Senate Finance Committee ranking member Ron Wyden, of Oregon, wrote in a letter dated Wednesday that administration officials use their “discretion to give states additional time to implement work reporting requirements and protect eligible beneficiaries from losing coverage.”
The provision in the law requires Medicaid enrollees between the ages of 19 and 65 to work, participate in community service, or attend an education program for at least 80 hours a month.
The law detailed several exceptions, including for pregnant people, parents of dependent children, people who have complex medical conditions, tribal community members, those in the foster care system, people who were in foster care who are below the age of 26 and individuals released from incarceration in the last 90 days, among others.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Kim Davis violated rule on disclosing her assets in decade-long case
description: Kim Davis, the former county clerk who owes more than $500,000 after refusing to issue a marriage license to a gay couple a decade ago, violated a rule on disclosing her assets, a federal judge said. Now the question is what punishment Davis will face as a result, if any. Davis said in a document […]
text:
Kim Davis, then the Rowan county clerk,  waved to supporters at a rally outside the Carter County Detention Center on Sept. 8, 2015 in Grayson. Davis was ordered to jail for contempt of court after refusing a federal court order to issue marriage licenses to same-sex couples. (Photo by Ty Wright/Getty Images)Kim Davis, the former county clerk who owes more than $500,000 after refusing to issue a marriage license to a gay couple a decade ago, violated a rule on disclosing her assets, a federal judge said.
Now the question is what punishment Davis will face as a result, if any.
Davis said in a document filed Nov. 16 that she shouldn’t face any sanctions.
Davis said that’s because she believed she was giving a truthful answer when she said in a court document that she doesn’t own any real property– property that could go toward paying the judgment against her.
“I had no intent then, and have no intent now, to conceal anything or to otherwise answer in any way other than the truth,” Davis said in the document.
An attorney for the couple trying to collect from Davis said he doesn’t buy it.
“This is all made up to try to get out of trouble now,” Michael J. Gartland said of Davis’ latest responses.
Court sanctions against Davis could include an order for her to pay attorney fees for the gay couple trying to collect money from her.
A decade-long fight
The controversy is the latest development in a court fight that started more than a decade ago and has drawn international attention at times.
Davis was county clerk in Rowan County in June 2015 when the U.S. Supreme Court ruled that same-sex couples have a constitutional right to marry.
County clerks in Kentucky issue marriage licenses, and Davis soon received requests from gay couples for licenses.
Davis refused the requests, arguing that as an evangelical Christian, she believed marriage was only proper between a man and a woman.
Davis said that issuing a marriage license with her name on it to a gay couple would violate her religious beliefs and rights.
Her office turned away several gay couples who requested licenses, leading to demonstrations and widespread news coverage.
U.S. District Judge David L. Bunning had Davis jailed for several days for contempt of court for refusing to issue marriage licenses in accordance with federal law.
A clerk in Davis’ office ultimately issued marriage licenses to same-sex couples, but several who had been turned away earlier sued Davis, arguing she had subjected them to public embarrassment and emotional distress.
“For me it was a heaven or hell issue,” Davis, who lost reelection in 2018, testified at one point.
However, federal judges rejected the idea that Davis’ personal conviction justified not issuing marriage licenses to gay couples.
The First Amendment shielded Davis as a private citizen, but when she acted as a public official, it didn’t allow her to violate the rights of others, a federal appeals panel said in one ruling.
The judges said “when an official’s discharge of her duties according to her conscience violates the constitutional rights of citizens, the Constitution must win out.”
In one case, the state of Kentucky had to pay $225,000 to attorneys who represented eight people who had sued Davis, and in another, a jury awarded $50,000 each to David Ermold and David Moore, one of the couples Davis turned away several times when they sought a marriage license.
That’s the judgment at issue in the continuing legal fight.
Couple denied wedding license by Kim Davis allege she has covered up assets owed them

With attorney fees, costs and interest added to the initial $100,000 judgment, Davis owed $565,285 to Ermold, Moore and their attorneys as of last July, according to a court document.
In trying to collect, attorneys for Ermold and Moore sought information about Davis’ assets.
Davis said in responses in late 2025 that she did not own any real property and had not transferred property worth more than $2,000, according to the court record.
A mistake or on purpose?
However, Joseph D. Buckles, a Lexington attorney who, along with Gartland, represents the couple trying to collect from Davis, later found records in Morehead showing Davis had transferred houses and a 50-acre farm to family members or a trust in April and May 2025, according to the court record.
Davis didn’t receive any money for the transactions, which came not long after a federal appeals court affirmed the financial judgment against her.
Davis had received a 50 percent interest in the property and bank accounts – an estate worth hundreds of thousands – after her mother died without a will in January 2025, Buckles and Gartland argued in court documents.
Davis concealed the property transfers in her answers in federal court, Ermold and Moore and their attorneys have alleged.
“No fact-finder could hear this record and find that a debtor who lost her appeal, deeded her entire inheritance to her family for nothing within weeks . . . and then denied it all under oath, acted with any purpose other than to hinder, delay, or defraud the creditors she has been promising to outlast for a decade,” Buckles and Gartland argued in a state court motion.
Ermold and Moore filed a lawsuit in Rowan County seeking to void the property transfers.
Davis has not filed a formal answer to the allegations in that lawsuit.
But in the federal lawsuit, Davis filed a declaration denying she was trying to hide anything and that she intentionally failed to disclose property transfers to Ermold and Moore as required.
Davis said the property transfers at issue were done to honor her late mother’s wishes, and that she received nothing from the estate
“I made no personal transfers of property that I owned because I was merely the conduit and administrator transferring property in the manner that my late mother explicitly stated was her desire,” Davis said. “My mother specifically requested that the property be distributed in the manner in which it was distributed so that the caretaking of long familial property would continue to the subsequent generations of the family.”
Davis said she believed at the time – and still does – that the answers she gave in federal court about not owning or transferring property were true based on her understanding.
If that was wrong, she said, “then it was completely and honestly the result of misunderstanding or mistake, but not intent.”
U.S. Magistrate Judge Edward B. Atkins ruled in early November that Davis violated discovery rules by not disclosing her assets and providing records about the property transfers.
That ruling was on a motion by Buckles and Gartland seeking to have Davis held in contempt of court and for sanctions against her.
Atkins declined to hold Davis in contempt, but did order her to file updated answers about the property transfers and show why she shouldn’t face sanctions.
Davis’ answers this week were in response to that order.
Her attorneys said Atkins should deny the request for sanctions because Davis had shown she did not knowingly provide false answers and had no intent to deceive the people trying to collect from her.
“Davis’s answers were at best an honest mistake and should not be sanctionable,” her lawyers wrote.
Davis is represented by Liberty Counsel, a conservative Christian legal organization.
Gartland called the answers Davis filed this week “nonsense” and said he would continue pressing for sanctions against her.

name: Honolulu Civil Beat
title: Does Waikīkī Need An Economic Rescue?
description: The state is looking to boost development in parts of the tourist zone by tapping into a federal tax break program aimed at drawing investors to impoverished and under-resourced communities.
text:
Waikīkī, the bustling heartbeat of Hawaiʻi’s tourism industry, doesn’t usually spring to the top of lists of economically depressed neighborhoods and low-income communities.
Yet, much of the neighborhood north of Kalākaua Avenue is now being described that way by the state, which has selected it for a federal program intended to spur investment in downtrodden areas through tax breaks that can include big capital gains tax savings. 
The governorʻs office says the move is aimed at benefiting both residents and visitors by improving the area’s older residential buildings and hotels on the side streets makai of Ala Wai Canal stretching to Kalākaua Avenue.
“From a tourism point of view, the hotels are needing to go through a refresh to keep up with competition. But there’s also aging housing stock there,” said Scott Glenn, Gov. Josh Green’s senior advisor for federal affairs, climate and housing. “This can be a financing tool to help with housing as well as the tourism and economic development side.”
Elsewhere on Oʻahu, tracts were selected in Iwilei, Chinatown, the North Shore, Wahiawā, ʻAiea and Mōʻiliʻili. In West Oʻahu, the Kalaeloa tract — 3,700 acres of a former U.S. Navy air station — was chosen. Economically struggling Westside communities such as Waiʻanae and Nānākuli were not, though both were eligible under the guidelines.
Data on the federal program’s outcomes is limited because it previously lacked robust reporting requirements, experts said. But it has been criticized for benefiting relatively wealthier neighborhoods, which based on some data have attracted the most investment, and because states can’t control what projects get the tax breaks the program provides.
However, economists say Hawaiʻi is taking advantage of the program in the best way it can, and the state is exploring how to direct investment to projects it wants to support.
Glenn was on a team of state officials Green chose to select the so-called opportunity zones. The Treasury Department gave the state a list of 88 census tracts it determined were eligible to be zones under poverty and household income guidelines. Hawaiʻi was allowed to choose 25. 
Five of Hawaiʻi’s 25 new economic opportunity zones are located in Waikīkī.  (Screenshot/Hawaiʻi State Office Of Planning/2026)
Nineteen zones were chosen on Oʻahu, five in Waikīkī. The world famous district — home to glitzy businesses ranging from Chanel to La Mer to the Ritz-Carlton —  accounted for nearly $9 billion in tourist spending in 2024. But it also has a large population of retirees and service industry workers with limited and lower incomes among its roughly 20,000 residents. 
In those zones, “typically, there are much smaller, older buildings with cheaper rent there and the people that are living there aren’t necessarily the wealthiest,” said Steven Bond-Smith, an economist with the University of Hawaiʻi Economic Research Organization. 
Eligible census tracts had to have a poverty rate of at least 20% or a median family income 70% or below that of the metropolitan area or state.
It is the second round of the program, with designations lasting a decade. While the Waikīkī tracts were eligible before, this was their first time being selected. 
Some in the neighborhood questioned the decision, saying the program wouldn’t ultimately benefit residents.
“If you wanted to give somebody local a tax break to build something, then I could understand. But what you’re really doing is you’re just bringing in people who already have a ton of money. They could afford to pay the taxes,” said Todd Ferguson, a Liliʻuokalani Avenue resident who works for the nearby Ala Wai Golf Course.

Cleghorn Street sits in one of the new economic opportunity zones in Waikīkī.  (Kevin Fujii/Civil Beat/2026)

“As a local resident, I don’t get any tax breaks, and neither does anybody else around here,” Ferguson said.
But others said the approach held promise.
“It’s a good idea if they are smart about their resource spending and if it’s more toward helping the community,” said Jason Song, who lives in Kakaʻako but owns Discount Vapes on Kūhiō Avenue.
The state should ensure investments go toward a mix of business and housing projects, Song said, and housing that is developed should be affordable.
“It should be for bringing in tourists or new housing,” he said, “but not charging astronomical prices for rent if they’re gonna use tax breaks.”
Some Struggling Communities Excluded
While the absence of communities such as Waiʻanae, where 27% of residents live below the poverty level, from the list of zones stands out, economists and elected officials said that was likely due to obstacles they face including a lack of ongoing investment, challenges including limited access and traffic congestion, and a lot of property that is Hawaiian homelands, making it harder to develop projects.
“We don’t have large swaths of land there where a developer is going to come in and bring houses or businesses,” said Honolulu City Council member Andria Tupola, who represents West Oʻahu. “We definitely need it in Kalaeloa. It’s basically no man’s land out there.”
Though West Oʻahu is often seen as an area with a greater need for economic investment, no communities on the Waiʻanae Coast were selected for the program.  (Kuʻu Kauanoe/Civil Beat/2021)
The program is best suited to benefit zones already experiencing some economic investment and growth, experts said.
“What we’re seeing it less likely and able to do is take an extremely disinvested neighborhood and make a market there,” said Brady Meixell, a senior research associate at the Urban Institute, a nonpartisan research organization. “The market fundamentals still have to be in shape to bring investment into an area.”
That, Bond-Smith said, means the state had to focus on areas where pre-existing opportunities make greater returns on investment more likely.
“Waikīkī, particularly the more rundown parts of Waikīkī, there’s probably some big investment opportunities there that will generate a bigger return for investment in Hawaiʻi than investments in Nānākuli,” he said.
In selecting the zones — their designation lasts 10 years — the state team focused on issues ranging from housing to energy and healthcare projects, Glenn said. The need for housing was the chief criterion guiding decisions, and the speed at which projects could get up and running was another.
Glenn said the first question the team usually asked was, “Is there an opportunity for housing here?”
Two zones on Maui were named. One — Lahaina’s Front Street — was ruled eligible only after state and county officials and University of Hawaiʻi Mānoa economists convinced the government that the neighborhood, destroyed in the 2023 wildfire, desperately needed investment.
Four zones on Hawaiʻi island were also named in last week’s announcement, three in Hilo and one in North Kona.
In a statement, Green, a physician, said that with early investment in places where resources are scarce, “you prevent a lot of pain down the road.”
“That’s as true for our communities as it is for our patients,” he said. “These designations will catalyze investments to build a healthier and more affordable Hawaiʻi for our local people.”
Few Guardrails
Experts who researched the first round of opportunity zones have varied perspectives on how they have worked so far.
Based on data from Ohio, which required investors who made use of the tax breaks to include that on their state tax returns, new housing was the main outcome, Meixell said.
“People thought it would be more of a small business program in some cases,” Meixell said. “But for a lot of structural reasons based on how the incentive is given, it really has become more of a housing program.”
Hawaiʻi is pursuing the best use of the program by focusing it on tracts with better odds of attracting investment in new housing, Meixell said.
Other experts said the program also has too few guardrails when it comes to what investors choose to do; for example, the state cannot select which projects get the tax breaks.
“There’s nothing to force investors or even encourage them to do things that benefit the low income people who live in an opportunity zone,” said David Wessel, senior fellow in economic studies at Brookings Institution, a nonpartisan policy research group.
At least a dozen projects on Kaua‘i’s South Shore, a hub of hotels and tourism activity on island, appear to have taken advantage of the last round of economic opportunity zone designations.  (Nathan Eagle/Civil Beat)
Wessel, who has written about how the program has favored the wealthiest zones, said that nationally, real estate projects other than housing have attracted more investment through the zones.
“The challenge is we’re talking about private investors, rational, profit seeking private investors who are going to go for the highest return possible with the lowest risks. And in many cases, that has been hotels rather than housing,” he said. 
Likewise, Wessel said, “a lot of the housing has been more like the high end condos because they’re more profitable.”
On Kauaʻi, the two zones selected in the 2018 round included the resort community of Kukuiʻula and Hanalei. Projects there have included the purchase of a $1.87 million vacation rental in Poʻipū, a $721,000 vacant parcel in Kukuiʻula and a proposed $227 million resort and wellness center in Poʻipū that never got off the ground. 
No Kauaʻi tracts were eligible in the latest round.
In Waikīkī the five zones cover an area that stretches roughly from Ala Wai Boulevard to Kalākaua Avenue and Nāhua Street, from Ala Wai Boulevard to Kūhiō Avenue and ʻŌhua Avenue to Kaʻiulani Avenue, and from Kūhiō Avenue to Kalākaua Avenue and Kaʻiulani Avenue to Kapahulu Avenue.  
Those areas of ​​Waikīkī, with some older hotels and apartment buildings whose age and conditions have kept rents lower, “might be just the place where a little bit of a tax break could provide some incentive to get some investment there,” Wessel said. “I just hope they get the housing and not just the renovated hotels.”
Steering Investment
On its second go round, “Hawaiʻi is being innovative” in its approach to the program, trying to fashion ways to best leverage the tax breaks and direct investment to the types of projects it wants, Meixell said.
Some strategies the state is considering: Making it cheaper for opportunity zone investors to borrow money, aligning state and federal tax laws to investors’ advantages and creating portfolios of projects to bring multiple investors together to lower their individual risk, said Gwen Yamamoto Lau, executive director of the Hawaiʻi Green Infrastructure Authority. 
There are three tax benefits for investors in opportunity zones: They can temporarily put off paying taxes on capital gains they invest in a zone; if they leave their money invested for at least five years, they pay less tax on those profits; and if they hold onto an investment in a zone for at least 10 years before selling it, they pay no capital gains tax at all on the new profit, potentially a major jackpot. 
A vacant lot on Liliʻuokalani Avenue, which sits in a newly designated economic opportunity zone.   (Kevin Fujii/Civil Beat/2026)
Money invested in opportunity zone projects must be placed in what are termed opportunity zone funds; the state hopes those may also be a way to steer capital toward the types of housing and other projects it wants to see.
For example, Yamamoto Lau said, it might be that investors in a luxury housing project would start their own fund to do that and qualify for the tax breaks, however they might not be eligible for state support.
“We cannot stop investors from doing what they want. But we can encourage investors in things that are important to us,” she said.
The opportunity zone program, the nation’s largest ongoing federal community economic development initiative, produced $100 billion in investment overall in its first round, with Hawaiʻi getting an estimated $310 million of that. It’s projected to cost the federal government more than $40 billion between 2025 and 2034.
“Compared to other states, we’re lagging a little bit on opportunity zone investments,” Yamamoto Lau said. “We really want to ramp that up.”
That’s desperately needed in Kalaeloa, an area of more than 3,300 residents that was selected as a zone in the first iteration, too, Tupola said.
“Honestly, it had zero impact,” she said, attributing that to zoning rules put in place by the Hawaiʻi Community Development Authority, which is responsible for regulating housing in the area, and a lack of infrastructure.
“We need to make a better plan and pitch it to someone willing to invest,” Tupola said. “It could help in any of the private sector things that the district needs.”
The opportunity zone will be just one tool in driving investment there, she said, along with business improvement districts and state enterprise zones, which also offer tax incentives.
“We have 10 years to figure this out. And in government terms, 10 years is kind of fast,” she said. “So we have to get on this right away.”

name: Source New Mexico
title: Federal food aid paperwork taking toll on New Mexico Health Care Authority staff, secretary says
description: Major changes to the federal Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program contained in the “One Big Beautiful Bill Act” enacted last year are taking a financial toll on the New Mexico Health Care Authority, Secretary Kari Armijo told lawmakers on the Legislative Finance Committee on Monday.
text:
New Mexico Health Care Authority Secretary Kari Armijo told a legislative committee Nov. 16, 2026, that the authority needs an 11% budget increase due to new costs it has incurred administering the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program. (Photo by Daniel Montaño/KUNM)Major changes to the federal Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program contained in the “One Big Beautiful Bill Act” enacted last year are taking a financial toll on the New Mexico Health Care Authority, Secretary Kari Armijo told lawmakers on the Legislative Finance Committee on Monday.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The bill, known as the “One Big Beautiful Bill Act” or H.R.1, imposed new paperwork requirements on roughly 460,000 New Mexicans who receive SNAP assistance and placed new costs on state agencies that oversee the program, Armijo said. The new paperwork requirements went into effect in May and require SNAP recipients to provide additional documentation regarding their income and expenses. 
That requirement has resulted in a 16-fold increase in records SNAP recipients send to HCA caseworkers, along with an 81% increase in eligibility verifications that state workers are now required to conduct, according to new data Armijo released Monday. 
“The impacts of H.R.1 are not just policy impacts or financial impacts,” Armijo told lawmakers. “They are workload impacts for our agency. We have to equate all of this work into tasks and a frontline workforce that can manage those tasks.”
In addition to the increased workload, the spending bill, which President Donald Trump signed in July 2025, increased the share the state is required to pay for SNAP administration from 50% of costs to 75%, which imposed an additional $6.7 million on the authority.  
The authority is anticipating additional costs as more provisions of the bill go into effect next year. As a result, Armijo’s budget request seeks a $14.1 million increase in recurring funding for the authority’s Income Support Division, which administers SNAP and other programs including Temporary Assistance for Needy Families and Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program.
Thousands of New Mexicans could lose food assistance under federal proposal, state says

The requested funding for the upcoming state fiscal year — $1.56 billion — amounts to a roughly 11% increase over the division’s previous budget. 
Armijo requested an additional $5 million in recurring funding dedicated to New Mexico food banks, which are seeing increased demand due amid rising grocery prices and at least 18,000 New Mexicans losing SNAP since H.R. 1 went into effect. 
The Legislature, in a special session shortly after the bill went into effect last year, approved $8 million for food banks in a one-time appropriation, but Armijo noted that the food banks are still receiving “a lot of demand” and that funding for them is needed on a recurring basis. 
Armijo’s presentation Monday related only to the authority’s budget requests for the Income Support Division and two other divisions. Armijo will provide a separate budget presentation in the coming weeks regarding H.R.1 impacts on Medicaid, the low-income health insurance program, which the authority also oversees.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Rural healthcare in Kansas receives $226 million boost
description: TOPEKA — Kansas received $226 million in federal money to fund 24 rural healthcare programs across the state, state and federal officials announced Monday. The additional funding brings the state’s two-year total to nearly $450 million. In the program’s first year, rural communities received money for new healthcare facilities, improvements to existing healt[...]
text:
U.S. Sen. Jerry Moran speaks before President Donald Trump takes the stage at a Nov. 1, 2026, rally in Salina. (Photo by Sherman Smith/Kansas Reflector)TOPEKA — Kansas received $226 million in federal money to fund 24 rural healthcare programs across the state, state and federal officials announced Monday.
The additional funding brings the state’s two-year total to nearly $450 million. In the program’s first year, rural communities received money for new healthcare facilities, improvements to existing healthcare infrastructure, new equipment and technological advancement.
The Rural Health Transformation Program is a $50 billion nationwide effort born out of the One, Big Beautiful Bill Act that passed by Congress in 2025.
Democratic Gov. Laura Kelly said Monday the state took great strides in the first year of the program “to build a health care system that works for all Kansans — regardless of ZIP code — at a time when rural communities are particularly vulnerable and need support the most.” 
In the program’s first year, the Kansas Department of Health and Environment, which oversees the state’s money, dispersed almost $99 million directly to rural healthcare providers and community groups. The program funds have been used to boost prevention efforts, increase local access to primary care, build a rural healthcare workforce, provide care to specific populations, and improve data and technology. 
U.S. Sen. Jerry Moran, R-Kansas, said the program’s resources “address the unique needs of rural communities in our state.
“This is an important investment in rural healthcare across Kansas, and these resources will provide long-term upgrades for technology, staffing and equipment to better meet the needs of Kansans in small towns across our state,” he said
Kansas was among the top recipients in the country, receiving the sixth-largest amount each year. U.S. Rep. Ron Estes, a Wichita Republican who represents south-central Kansas in Congress, said the state “made a strong case for what rural providers here actually need.” 
“This funding pays for the staffing, equipment and technology that hospitals and clinics in our small towns rely on every day,” he said.
Moran and Estes helped craft and voted in favor of the federal legislation that created the program. The legislation also instituted sweeping cuts to Medicaid, which are expected to eliminate $930 million from the public health insurance program over the next 10 years.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Trump administration gives states a delay on new Medicaid rules but KY can’t take it
description: The Trump administration on Friday offered states extra time to implement work requirements for Medicaid, but the Beshear administration says Kentucky cannot take advantage of the optional delay.  Beth Fisher, a spokesperson for the Cabinet for Health and Family Services, said that the state has to align with timeline requirements in Kentucky’s House Bill 2,[...]
text:
Hundreds of Kentuckians with disabilities and their loved ones and advocates came to Frankfort and pleaded with elected officials to find a way to protect the services they receive through Medicaid waivers, on July 17, 2026. (Photo by Sarah Ladd/Kentucky Lantern)The Trump administration on Friday offered states extra time to implement work requirements for Medicaid, but the Beshear administration says Kentucky cannot take advantage of the optional delay. 
Beth Fisher, a spokesperson for the Cabinet for Health and Family Services, said that the state has to align with timeline requirements in Kentucky’s House Bill 2, which says the state has to implement the new work requirements in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act on Jan. 1. 
The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services wrote in a statement that an “optional hold harmless period” will give state governments more time to update their systems and improve the processes they have in place. 
“States have made real progress, and they’ve been clear with us about what it takes to get this right for beneficiaries—at scale and for the long term,” Director of the Center for Medicaid and CHIP Services Dan Brillman wrote in the statement.
States have 6 more months to implement Medicaid work requirement, administration says

Under the rules, people covered by Medicaid between the ages of 19-64 will have to spend 80 hours a month either working, participating in community services or attending an educational program. Some people have exemptions, including those with physical, intellectual or developmental disabilities. 
“Gov. Beshear has repeatedly pushed back against these harmful Medicaid cuts, which will put 35 Kentucky rural hospitals at risk of closing and strip 250,000 Kentuckians of their health insurance,” Fisher said in a statement.
Medicaid is the federal-state program that pays for 1 in 3 Kentuckians’ health care. 
“Team Kentucky believes healthcare is a basic human right and values the critical role of Medicaid in providing coverage for 1.4 million Kentuckians,” Fisher said.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Hattiesburg songwriter explains why local music matters
description: The Saenger Theater in downtown Hattiesburg on Nov. 13, 2026.
text:
Mississippi Today Ideas is a platform for thoughtful ideas to be shared about our state’s past, present and future. Opinions expressed in guest essays are the author’s own and do not necessarily represent those of Mississippi Today. You can read more about the section here.  

You can live in a town for years and still feel like you’re visiting. You know the streets, where to buy groceries, which restaurant you like. Belonging takes something more.
For me, local music has often been how that happens.
You start going to a room. You recognize a few faces. You hear someone play a song they wrote, and something in it stays with you. You come back. Eventually, you have people to say hello to, a favorite song to ask for and a friend you want to bring along.
You have a place in what’s happening.
When I talk about local music, I’m thinking particularly about original music: people writing songs and making records in the communities where they live. Hearing a song from its writer offers a connection you can follow. You might hear an early version, then watch it become a record. The song becomes part of your history with a place.
I grew up in Doraville, Georgia, outside Atlanta. We had a local band, the Atlanta Rhythm Section, that became nationally known. They even wrote a song called “Doraville.” People elsewhere were hearing a band from our backyard sing about our home. It gave us something to claim.
Later, at the University of Georgia in Athens, I found that feeling again, this time playing in a band myself. The work being made around us mattered. You didn’t have to leave town before people took you seriously.
There’s an attitude I still run into: “If you’re so good, why are you still here?” That’s a strange thing to ask someone whose work might be one of the reasons a place is worth living in.
Drew Yiung performs at the Keg & Barrel in Hattiesburg in 2025. Credit: Courtesy photo by Rob Walker
I recently spoke with producer and engineer John Keane, who recorded my band’s first album in Athens. We talked about musicians and visual artists moving through the same circles. Bands grew out of an art community where trying something unfamiliar was part of the point. The audience expected to be surprised, too.
John remembered people arriving for school and staying because of the friends they made in music and art. Others moved away and came back. Athens offered a life they wanted, with people they wanted to be around.
That matters when communities talk about attracting and retaining people. A job may bring someone to town. What happens after work can help them decide whether to stay.
Mississippi has spent years making sure the world remembers the musicians who came from here. We’ve built museums, marked highways and put considerable effort into telling those stories. That’s work worth doing.
But I wonder whether we’re giving the same attention to the people writing songs and making records here today. We ought to be able to celebrate our musical history while making it possible for the next generation to earn a living creating it.
I came to Hattiesburg for an artist-in-residence position and apparently forgot to leave. Getting to know the musicians here had something to do with that.
My master’s in economic development at the University of Southern Mississippi and my work with Greater New Orleans Inc. and Visit Mississippi gave me another way to think about what surrounds a song.
Shows involve sound engineers, venue staff and promoters. Recording brings work to studios, producers, designers and photographers. A musician’s ability to keep working affects people beyond the band.
Touring musicians also carry their hometowns with them. We tell audiences where we’re from, talk about the people we play with and recommend places to hear music. Someone who has never visited Hattiesburg can leave our show knowing a little more about it.
Music tourism can begin with a drive from the next town. Staff at the historic Saenger Theater in downtown Hattiesburg say the theater’s audiences regularly include visitors from Mobile, the Mississippi Gulf Coast, Jackson and New Orleans, with some traveling from Texas, Florida and Tennessee.
The staff says multiple downtown restaurants have reported additional customers when the theater has a show. Some visiting patrons ask for hotel recommendations, and touring artists and production crews also need overnight accommodations.
The theater does not have figures measuring the restaurant spending or hotel stays its events generate. Those accounts give us a place to start asking how music supports downtown businesses, and what more we could learn by tracking it.
Residents benefit, too. Young people should be able to imagine an interesting life in their hometown. Retirees still need places to meet people or hear a good band on a Tuesday.
Hattiesburg already offers several ways in. I recently played a Thursday lunchtime concert in the Brown Bag series. Live at Five and programming at Midtown Green give people other places to gather. FestivalSouth brings performances into the city’s calendar across several art forms.
Museum shows can put songwriters in front of listeners who might never hear them in a club.
Hattiesburg is hardly alone in this. Across Mississippi, communities are finding different ways to bring people together through music. The challenge is making sure musicians have places to play, audiences willing to listen and opportunities to keep doing the work.
When and where we present music matters. Bringing music into parks, museums, libraries and other public spaces introduces it to people who might never walk into a nightclub. Some people work early. Some have children or someone at home who needs them. Others simply prefer an afternoon concert to a late night out. These performances widen the audience and make music a more natural part of everyday community life.
That’s particularly important in a place like Hattiesburg, which has been positioning itself as an attractive place to retire. Access to music, art and culture is part of what makes a community appealing at any age. People aren’t just looking for somewhere affordable to live. They’re looking for somewhere interesting to live, with opportunities to get out, meet people and feel connected.
The musicians need a workable life, too. Can they afford somewhere to live and rehearse? Are there rooms where they can develop an audience? Are publicly supported events paying them fairly? Can younger players find a place to start?
On Nov. 20, I’ll be part of the Hattiesburg Music Showcase at the Saenger, alongside Blue Mountain, Jacob Arnold & The Bird Dogs and Grits & Greens. Four acts offer only a glimpse of the music being made here, but they give listeners a chance to hear different approaches to writing and playing original songs.
The Saenger opened in 1929 and underwent a major interior renovation in 2000. Preserving a theater gives us a stage. What we put on it, and whether we show up, helps determine what that investment makes possible.
Come for someone you know. Take a chance on someone you don’t. Then find another show, bring a friend and come back when something catches your ear.
Eventually, a song reminds you of a room, the people and a particular time in your life.
You remember being there. You remember belonging.

Drew Young is a Hattiesburg-based songwriter, educator and cultural producer. He has worked with Visit Mississippi and Greater New Orleans Inc. and writes about music, culture and community for “TIDAL” and on his Substack. He is the creator of “Back Roads & Back Stories” and holds a master’s degree in economic development from the University of Southern Mississippi.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Weddle makes unusual legal move to try again to move his contributions case to Franklin County
description: Former London Mayor Randall Weddle is asking a second time to move his trial for allegedly making excess campaign contributions to Gov. Andy Beshear from Laurel County to Franklin County. On Monday, Weddle’s attorney Guthrie True filed an unusual petition with the Kentucky Court of Appeals asking it to reverse a ruling by Laurel Circuit […]
text:
Randall Weddle, mayor of London, Kentucky, speaking at Gov. Andy Beshear's press conference on May 18, 2023.(Screen grab from Gov. Andy Beshear's YouTube Channel)Former London Mayor Randall Weddle is asking a second time to move his trial for allegedly making excess campaign contributions to Gov. Andy Beshear from Laurel County to Franklin County.
On Monday, Weddle’s attorney Guthrie True filed an unusual petition with the Kentucky Court of Appeals asking it to reverse a ruling by Laurel Circuit Judge Michael Caperton which would keep the case in Laurel County.
In a case being prosecuted by Attorney General Russell Coleman, the Laurel grand jury indicted Weddle last spring on four counts of intentionally exceeding the legal limits on campaign contributions. The indictment alleges that Weddle did so by giving $18,000 too much to Beshear’s 2023 campaign for governor and as much as $205,000 too much to the Kentucky Democratic Party in late 2022 by donating the money in the names of his family members, friends and employees. 
Those amounts are far above the limits set by law at the time of the donations – $2,000 to a candidate’s campaign per election, and $15,000 per year to a state political party.
Weddle pleaded not guilty, and True immediately asked for a change of venue to Franklin County – the motion Caperton denied last month.
True is now taking an extraordinary step in filing what in effect is a pre-trial appeal – petitioning for a “writ of mandamus” from the appeals court that would say Caperton was wrong and order that he transfer the case to Franklin. 
The 28-page petition says that by bringing the indictment in Laurel County Coleman “engaged in forum shopping – plain and simple – in the hopes of some strategic advantage.”
True argues that Kentucky law clearly allows any case alleging illegal campaign contributions can be brought to Franklin because that is the county where all state political campaigns and committees file their reports. Otherwise, he argues the law requires that such cases be brought in the county in which the contributions were “solicited, made or accepted.”
In this case, True says all parties in the case agree the contributions were solicited from Franklin County, accepted in Franklin County, and made by Weddle on his credit card while he was on a family vacation in the Bahamas.
The petition states that Weddle “will suffer great injustice and irreparable harm if he is compelled to go through trial in the wrong venue and risk conviction followed by a retrial in the correct venue.”
Last month Caperton rejected True’s arguments and agreed with attorneys on Coleman’s staff that Laurel is a proper venue – primarily because Weddle has a Laurel County address on his credit card and Laurel County is where Weddle lives. “A donation is ultimately ‘made’ from the place where the card is registered, not where the Defendant physically happens to be at the particular time he is using his phone and pushes the ‘donation’ button,” Caperton said in his order.
A spokesman for Coleman’s office told the Lantern they could not comment on “an open investigation.”
In a footnote of Monday’s petition, True repeated his basic case for Weddle – a case True previously gave to the Kentucky Registry of Election Finance while that body was initially investigating the matter. “When Mr. Weddle learned of a problem with the contributions … he reported the problem – ultimately to the candidate himself, Governor Beshear – and the contributions were refunded. In the end, there were no contributions at all,” True stated in the footnote.
The election registry later deferred its investigation when Coleman’s office began looking into the matter.

text:
U.S. currency is seen in a close-up photo. (Getty Images)The Alaska Division of Banking and Securities is planning to approve Northrim Bank’s takeover of Oregon’s People’s Bank of Commerce, it said in a public notice Thursday.
The purchase, announced in July by Northrim, marks the first time that Northrim has expanded outside the state of Alaska. People’s Bank of Commerce has 11 branches in southern Oregon and the Willamette Valley. Northrim, based in Alaska, has 21 branches spread across the state.
Under the terms of the purchase, Northrim will give stock in Northrim to the owners of People’s Bank, who will own more than 22% of the enlarged company.
People’s Bank shareholders approved the deal in October, and the companies expect the arrangement to become final on Jan. 1.
The Knoll Bond Rating Agency, which analyzed the deal this summer, concluded that it would strengthen Northrim and is aligned with the bank’s efforts to expand outside Alaska.

name: California
title: California sues OpenAI over hacking that stoked AI fears
description: The first woman to lie in state in the California Capitol wasn’t a lawmaker. That recognition belongs to Dolores Huerta, the labor leader who inspired legions of Californians with her decades of activism. Our visual editor Miguel Gutierrez Jr. spent Monday at her memorial, and you’ll want to make time for the images he captured.  […]
text:
Attendees gather at the OpenAI DevDay 2026 conference in San Francisco on Sept. 29, 2026. Photo by Jeff Chiu, AP Photo




The first woman to lie in state in the California Capitol wasn’t a lawmaker. That recognition belongs to Dolores Huerta, the labor leader who inspired legions of Californians with her decades of activism. Our visual editor Miguel Gutierrez Jr. spent Monday at her memorial, and you’ll want to make time for the images he captured. 
It was a big day in legal news: California sued OpenAI; the Trump administration lost once again in its attempt to cancel already-awarded university grants; and a group of district attorneys filed an appeal asking the state Supreme Court to block Gov. Gavin Newsom’s death penalty commutations. We have more on all of those stories in today’s newsletter. 
California is suing artificial intelligence giant OpenAI over an AI-driven cybersecurity incident that the state claims was the result of the company prioritizing “growth and rapid model development over safety and accountability.”
As CalMatters’ Colin Lecher explains, OpenAI, the maker of ChatGPT, was evaluating internal research models when it discovered that its AI agents had hacked their way into Hugging Face, an online platform where users can submit tools and data related to AI.
The high-profile breach underscored the dangers of AI, and intensified concerns that so-called “rogue” AI agents could damage critical infrastructure or compromise military weapon systems.
In September California Attorney General Rob Bonta said his office would investigate the incident, but according to the lawsuit — filed Monday in San Francisco Superior Court — OpenAI has failed to comply with the probe.

The lawsuit: “The company has responded to … subpoenas with just a smattering of publicly available information, self-serving blog posts, and redacted copies of a few dozen external communications containing highlevel descriptions of select security incidents.”

OpenAI also knowingly tested a risky AI model without sufficient oversight, while misleading and endangering the public, Bonta said at a press conference announcing the lawsuit. 
An OpenAI spokesperson told NPR that the company has “engaged — and will continue to engage — constructively with the Attorney General’s office to share information and advance, strong, practical safety standards for the entire industry.”
In its latest funding round earlier this month, OpenAI raised about $11 billion, and is estimated to reach a valuation of $1.25 trillion. 
Read more.



CalMatters Ideas Festival: 2027 Ideas Festival will expand to Los Angeles, Sacramento and San Francisco. One full day of candid conversations in each, with the leaders, innovators and changemakers shaping California’s future. Learn more.

Other Stories You Should Know


‘The power of ordinary people’


Dolores Huerta’s casket lies in honor at the state Capitol in Sacramento on Nov. 16, 2026. Photo by Miguel Gutierrez Jr., CalMatters




Hundreds of people gathered in Sacramento Monday to honor the late Dolores Huerta. The civil and labor rights leader is the first civilian and woman to lie in honor at the state Capitol. She passed away on Oct. 28 at the age of 96 after a battle with cancer.
A late morning procession of lowrider cars and marchers walked behind a white hearse carrying Huerta. Some were holding the red United Farm Workers flag while the crowd chanted, “Sí se puede” — the famous “Yes we can” rallying cry that Huerta coined as an advocate for farmworkers. 
In a private ceremony, Gov.-elect Xavier Becerra, U.S. House Speaker Emerita Nancy Pelosi and leaders for the state Senate and Assembly gave joint remarks, describing Huerta as “the heart and soul” of America’s Latino community.

Becerra: “Huerta taught a nation that there is a power greater than wealth and stronger than fear: The power of ordinary people who stand together to tear down the walls of injustice. Because she lived, California is more just and America is more free.”

Services honoring Huerta are expected to move to Bakersfield, where a vigil will be held Thursday, followed by a memorial the day after.
See more photos from the service from CalMatters visuals editor Miguel Gutierrez Jr.:
Hundreds of mourners, with some chanting “Sí se puede!,” march down Third Street towards Capitol Mall to commemorate Huerta. Photo by Miguel Gutierrez Jr., CalMatters

Huerta’s hearse, with “Sí Se Puede” flags at the front, sits at Crocker Park in Sacramento. Mourners cried and waved as the procession made its way to the state Capitol. Photo by Miguel Gutierrez Jr., CalMatters

Members of Kalpulli Itzkuauhtli and Xiuhcoatl Danza Azteca perform a ceremony in honor of Huerta at the state Capitol. The scent from the burning copal was heavy in the air as the dancers readied to perform their ceremony. Photo by Miguel Gutierrez Jr., CalMatters



UC wins again against Trump


Tré Willingham works inside a lab in Rowland Hall at UC Irvine on June 15, 2026. Photos by Ariana Drehsler for CalMatters




The Trump administration lost its last attempt to cancel research grants from the University of California after the Supreme Court rejected its request to review rulings that ordered it to continue funding those projects, reports CalMatters’ Mikhail Zinshteyn.
Trump last year issued a series of executive orders to defund so-called diversity, equity and inclusion efforts, including research grants. Between January and July 2025, federal agencies terminated more than $900 million in grants to UC researchers. 
Lawyers for the U.S. Department of Justice argued that agencies had the right to cut the grants because they did not comply with Trump’s executive orders, even though the UC researchers broke no rules in how they used the money. But attorneys for the UC researchers, in a legal brief to the high court, said the move is “a quintessential First Amendment violation.” 
Read more.



And lastly: DAs sue to block Newsom’s death row clemency


An officer opens the gate for an incarcerated person leaving the exercise yard at San Quentin State Prison’s death row in San Quentin on Aug. 15, 2016. Photo by Justin Sullivan, Getty Images




Dozens of California district attorneys filed a lawsuit Monday to stop Newsom’s commutations of over 500 people on death row. The lawsuit claims that the governor abused his power and acted unlawfully by granting prisoners clemency without allowing victims of their crimes the “opportunity to be heard.” Read more from CalMattes’ Nigel Duara.






California Voices
CalMatters contributor Liz Carlisle: UC Santa Cruz researcher Joji Muramoto redefined how farmers treated one of California’s most chemically intensive crops — a legacy that highlights the innovation at risk under hostile immigration policies.
