name: New Jersey Monitor
title: Critics condemn police purchases of cars, K9s, gym gear from NJ opioid funds
description: New Jersey police spent millions in opioid settlement funds on cars, canines, surveillance, and more. New legislation would bar such uses.
text:
New Jersey police spent millions in opioid settlement funds on cars, canines, surveillance, and more. New legislation would bar such uses. (Photo by Dana DiFilippo/New Jersey Monitor)In Ocean County, a day’s work might mean Elizabeth Burke Beaty, a harm reductionist, helps someone struggling with drug addiction by getting them a ride to treatment, connecting them with a food pantry or housing assistance, or even traipsing into the woods to bring them a new tent.
Law enforcement agencies in Ocean County, though, have decided that helping people beat addiction means splurging on new police cars, canines, surveillance cameras, street signs, body armor, and more.
Police across New Jersey have commandeered millions of dollars that pharmaceutical companies have paid New Jersey, its 21 counties, and 241 of its largest municipalities since 2022 to settle lawsuits over the deadly opioid epidemic.
With the state set to receive over $1.1 billion in settlement funds through 2038, advocates now are demanding that lawmakers tighten oversight of spending to ensure it meets approved uses — addiction prevention, treatment, and support services for people in recovery.
“The police have been well-funded for very, very long, and they’re not recovery specialists,” said Burke Beaty, founder and CEO of Sea Change Recovery Community and Harm Reduction Center. “The money that they’re taking is not in the spirit of repairing all the harms caused by Big Pharma.”
A New Jersey Monitor analysis of municipalities’ spending reports and records on the watchdog site Opioid Audit shows that police spent opioid funds in all sorts of ways that don’t directly help people harmed by addiction.
Seventeen agencies spent more than $1.5 million on cars, lights, lettering, vehicle wraps, and related expenses. Eleven departments spent more than a half-million dollars on police canines, kennels, canine training, and veterinary care. Seven bought surveillance cameras and automated license plate reader systems.
At least 20 spent money on technology including drones, digital roadside billboards and radar systems, e-bikes, vape detectors for schools, police radios, mapping software and investigative databases, drug analyzers and breathalyzers, and defibrillators.
Scores more used settlement funds to pay for officer training, salaries and overtime, staff wellness programs, bicycles, gym equipment, subscription renewals, body armor, clothing, National Night Out costs, junior police academies, school assemblies, and associated promotional materials.
The departments typically characterized the spending as prevention, harm reduction, community engagement and education, and recovery support.
But officials often stretched the definition of those terms.
Wall Township explained spending more than $30,000 of opioid funds on treadmills, weights, and other gym equipment as an investment in the “mental health of first responders.” Garfield police cited public awareness as the chief goal of $5,450 they paid for a vehicle wrap and thousands more spent on a “Let’s Knock Out Opioid Use Together” festival that featured a live DJ, several inflatable bounce houses, food vendors, a pop-up party area, and a helicopter landing display.
While the settlement requires officials to invest in evidence-based strategies to reduce addiction and repair harms, some police spending seems to flout that rule. In Highland Park, police bought 10 anti-choking devices for $605 last year even though state health officials issued a cautionary statement about the devices and the federal Food and Drug Administration has warned that using them carries risks.
In many cases, police invested opioid funds in things that have historically been paid for out of their budgets, such as police salaries, vehicles, and safety gear. Watchdogs have long warned against using opioid money as “slush funds” or to plug budget gaps.
Much of such spending would be barred under new legislation Assemblywoman Maureen Rowan (D-Atlantic) introduced Monday.
Rowan’s bill would prohibit police and public officials from using opioid funds on any activities, equipment, or technology that normally would be paid out of municipal, county, or state budgets. It also would forbid spending the funds on police training and salaries not specifically tied to addiction remediation, drug takeback programs, and anything related to surveillance, crime detection, search and seizure, evidence gathering, and criminal processing.
It lists specific policing items as disallowed, including drones, traffic enforcement signage, drug simulation goggles, high-dose naloxone, and agency marketing and promotional items. And it would set a 5% cap on how much opioid funds an agency could spend on administrative expenses.
John Donnadio is executive director of the New Jersey Association of Counties. (Photo by Dana DiFilippo/New Jersey Monitor)
John Donnadio, who heads the New Jersey Association of Counties, welcomes the clarity.
His group and the New Jersey State League of Municipalities have pushed state officials to provide more guidance on acceptable spending, even though quite a bit already exists, including approved uses listed in the national settlement itself, a memorandum of agreement former Attorney General Andrew Bruck issued in 2022, a law New Jersey lawmakers passed in 2023, a lengthy strategic plan a state advisory panel put out last year, and guidance from harm reduction groups.
“Maybe if they were more specific, we would avoid this,” Donnadio said. “Like the state, or the Department of Human Services, the Attorney General’s Office, or whatever office said, ‘Alright, this is an inventory of what’s good: naloxone kits, transportation for individuals to treatment if they can’t afford it, reaching out to the homeless population.’ And ‘bouncy houses are bad things. Car wraps are bad things,’” he said. “I don’t know if that’s the answer, but I think that would be helpful. Then there’s no wiggle room. There’s no gray area.”
League officials didn’t respond to requests for comment. But Raymond Heck, a past president of the group and Millstone’s mayor, told lawmakers last month at a public hearing on opioid spending that many local governments want more detailed guidance.
Heck, a state correctional officer and member of the New Jersey Police Training Commission, denied any ill intent in past spending decisions.
“I don’t believe the municipalities, the counties, are doing wrong. The ones that are questionable? We just want to make it better. Give them direction,” Heck said.
Restrictions on police use of opioid funds are reasonable — and overdue, considering law enforcement historically has treated addiction as a crime instead of a public health crisis, harm reductionists say.
“Why would we be giving more money into that same system of criminalization?” said Eva Mancini of the New Jersey Organizing Project.
Katie Carter lost her mother to an overdose five years ago and struggled with addiction herself. She credited her recovery largely to help from harm reduction groups including Atlantic City’s Oasis. She now works with Mancini to help others still fighting for sobriety.
“In my own experience, the way people who use drugs are treated by police is not kind,” Carter said. “That’s personally why I think that they don’t deserve the money.”

name: Washington State Standard
title: AG pushes harsher arson penalties after devastating WA wildfires
description: The Old Trails wildfire, one of the three that burned hundreds of homes in the Spokane area over the summer, was allegedly started by Aaron Farinacci, who planned the arson and had set many other fires. Standing near where the fire burned, Attorney General Nick Brown on Monday unveiled legislation he’s pushing to increase the […]
text:
A Cal Fire firefighter works amid the remains of homes destroyed in the Old Trails Fire on Aug. 6, 2026 in Spokane, Washington. (Photo by Mario Tama/Getty Images)The Old Trails wildfire, one of the three that burned hundreds of homes in the Spokane area over the summer, was allegedly started by Aaron Farinacci, who planned the arson and had set many other fires.
Standing near where the fire burned, Attorney General Nick Brown on Monday unveiled legislation he’s pushing to increase the punishment for blazes set intentionally. 
Currently, the harshest charge prosecutors can file is first-degree arson, with a standard prison sentence of 21 to 27 months if convicted. In a press conference, Brown argued that means “opportunities for justice for the victims and for communities like Spokane are woefully low.”
“Washington state’s arson laws do not fit the punishment for the level of destruction borne out by these types of events,” he said. “This new piece of legislation that we’re announcing today is an attempt to close that gap.”
The bill, set to be sponsored by Spokane state Sen. Marcus Riccelli, would create the charge of aggravated arson. It would heighten the penalties for intentionally setting fires that cause “great bodily injury,” damage at least five homes or cause more than $10 million in property damage.
The standard sentencing range for aggravated arson would be roughly seven years to 26 years in prison, with severity depending on other factors. The criminal charge wouldn’t apply to those who accidentally set devastating fires; prosecutors would have to prove the fires were knowingly and maliciously set. The potential sanction would only apply to future fires, not Farinacci and Old Trails, for example.
Supporters of the proposal hope the punishment will serve as a deterrent. Brown said the bill would bring Washington in line with Oregon and California, which have similar statutes on the books. 
Riccelli said his family had to evacuate during the complex of fires. His wife’s childhood home burned down. 
“This is about ensuring those who commit these heinous crimes are held accountable to the fullest extent of the law,” the Democratic state senator said.
The Chelan Hills Fire, which burned nearly 10,000 acres, destroyed at least 100 structures and killed one person, was also intentionally set, according to criminal charges.
Washington experienced its second-worst fire season ever this year, with thousands forced to evacuate and more than 900,000 acres burned, fueled by a warming and drying environment. While many fires are caused by humans or lightning, climate change creates conditions for them to spread rapidly. 

SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX. 
The damage to homes burned across the state was worth at least $188 million, according to Gov. Bob Ferguson’s office. Ferguson is pushing for federal financial aid to help residents rebuild. The toll for public infrastructure was tens of millions of dollars in damage.
The governor is also urging lawmakers to pass legislation offering rebates on state and local sales and use taxes for costs stemming from efforts to rebuild after a disaster.
The 105-day legislative session starts Jan. 11. Lawmakers can start filing bills Dec. 7. The Legislature will also consider a renewed request from the state’s public lands commissioner for $60 million annually for wildfire prevention efforts.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Commentary: Q & A: ‘Funding levels are down, scientific grants have been pulled’ for mental health research
description: The Nobel Prize for Physiology or Medicine was recently awarded to Drs. Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel for their work on optogenetics, a method that has led to better understanding of how brain cells work, which could lead to more effective targeted treatments for people with mental illnesses.  This was remarkable: You can […]
text:
Dr. Sophia Vinogradov poses for a portrait in this courtesy image. (Photo courtesy of Dr. Sophia Vinogradov)The Nobel Prize for Physiology or Medicine was recently awarded to Drs. Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel for their work on optogenetics, a method that has led to better understanding of how brain cells work, which could lead to more effective targeted treatments for people with mental illnesses. 
This was remarkable: You can count the Nobel Prizes for research related to mental illnesses on one hand. 
The lack of research on mental illnesses is troubling, so I interviewed Dr. Sophia Vinogradov, the department chair of psychiatry and behavioral sciences at the University of Minnesota Medical School, to learn more about the research being conducted in the field.
This interview has been edited for length and clarity. 
What research on mental illnesses — including a better understanding of the brain or new treatments — is emerging that will give people hope?
There are two main areas emerging. One is around medications. The “third generation of antipsychotics” focuses on decreasing the side effects and increasing the impact on cognition. There is also more emphasis on precision medicine. For example, some medications “fail” during their controlled clinical trials and never go to market because it only helped a modest percentage of people. Now we are doing research to learn why a medication did or did not help specific individuals and using technology to see how the brain is reacting. Each mental illness plays out differently in different individuals, and researchers now understand that we need to focus on tailoring treatment.
The second exciting area is understanding brain circuitry. The brain is made up of circuits or networks of cells that operate together to enable all of the things that make us human — there are brain circuits for concentrating and remembering, for different emotions, for motivated behavior, for impulse control, for problem solving — and all of them can be impacted by mental illnesses. When we understand how they work, we can study what happens when they malfunction and explore ways to make them work better. It opens a window into addressing the things that are really challenging for people with mental illnesses.
Schizophrenia can be so difficult for both the person and their family and is considered to be one of the most disabling conditions in the world. Are we finding more effective treatments?
The past 15 years of research has demonstrated unequivocally that intervening as early and vigorously as possible is very effective. Programs like Navigate that focus on early intervention for psychosis have been extremely helpful in changing the trajectory of young people’s lives. 
We’re now entering a second phase of research, where we are studying how to tailor those programs to help the 20 to 25% of individuals who have a more severe form of the illness and are not responding to the current treatments.
We also need to work on making these programs more accessible in Greater Minnesota. These programs rely heavily on grants, since neither Medicaid nor private insurance pays for all the needed treatment components, which include individual therapy, family therapy and supported education and employment, in addition to medication treatments. So, we need to expand grant funding, require insurance to pay for it and continue to look at collaboration and technology to increase access.
One successful example is a new collaborative program between our team at the U and clinicians at CentraCare in Saint Cloud, which has allowed us to share our expertise with practitioners in central Minnesota.
The mental health community was very concerned that legalizing cannabis would result in more young people experiencing psychosis. What have you seen in Minnesota?
The research clearly shows that cannabis can trigger psychosis symptoms in vulnerable individuals, including those with certain genetic backgrounds. In these people, symptoms don’t go away when they stop using cannabis, and the treatment approach has to be tailored so they can learn to understand the unique effect that cannabis has on their brain. I have also seen individuals with cannabis-induced psychosis where the symptoms disappeared once they stopped using and engaged fully in treatment. In general, such people have insight into their experience, a lot of family support, are willing to take medication for a while and fully commit to leading a healthy lifestyle.
It’s a spectrum, of course, like everything. But I would add that the science shows us that using cannabis before age 26 has important brain effects and is not recommended, especially for people in their early teen years.  
The younger the exposure to cannabis, the worse the mental health outcome across the board.
We have seen rising rates of mental illnesses in our children and youth. Do we know why?
It’s a complicated and interesting question. One of our faculty members is looking at how social media use can be toxic to youth mental health. Also, the School of Family and Social Sciences is analyzing data to see how youth and parents are using social media and comparing it to their self-assessments of mental health symptoms, wellbeing and parent interactions. We are trying to pinpoint where it is having a negative impact.
We find that if you are prone to depression, for example, you may be attracted to things that will make your depression worse, versus visiting sites that could help you. We find that youth struggling with social and peer relationships will turn even more to social media, which doesn’t address the problem — and even makes it less likely that they will learn healthy ways to relate to others.
I will note that children and youth in general are leading less healthy lives. They are exercising less, have less unstructured play and physical activity, are bombarded with violent and sexualized imagery in the media, have parents that are more distracted and overwhelmed and are inundated by very unhealthy fast-food choices. Children’s brains and bodies are not meant to be looking at screens, sitting in isolation, remaining physically inactive and eating empty calories.
Increasing access to mental health treatment requires addressing workforce shortages, especially in psychiatry. Who is interested in this field now?
Psychiatry is now one of the most popular residency programs. This didn’t used to be the case. Now, almost 1 in 10 graduating medical students want to be psychiatrists — and yet there are not enough residency slots to meet this demand. We also need to improve our training opportunities for psychiatrists and other mental health workers to serve rural communities. The good news is that the residents I work with are very committed and dedicated and deeply interested in people as individuals.
The number of research grants awarded during fiscal year 2026 by the National Institutes of Health was 12% less than in fiscal year 2024. Has this impacted research in your department?
Major changes at the federal level have had a serious impact on our research. Funding levels are down, scientific grants have been pulled or stopped in the pipeline. Personnel have left the National Institute of Health, and some of our long-standing relationships with dedicated program officers at the National Institute of Mental Health are gone. I am deeply concerned that the U.S. is going to  lose its position as the pre-eminent country for cutting edge research.
What changes have you seen recently in support of research into mental illnesses and the brain, and what would you like to see going forward?
Researchers from many different areas of expertise are coming together to focus on mental illnesses. We are seeing teams comprising doctors, engineers, computer scientists and others working together, and consortia of teams across the country —  and world — are coming together to share information and findings on specific topics such as schizophrenia and autism.
Lastly, we know we need to involve more people with lived experience in guiding our research. These are complex and nuanced illnesses, and researchers need to understand how they impact people differently and how they impact people’s lives. Research is about finding ways to improve people’s lives, and doing so in the ways that matter most to each individual.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: No evidence marshals impeded ICE arrest in Meriden court, report finds
description: An investigation found no evidence judicial marshals interfered with ICE agents at the Meriden courthouse, contradicting allegations federal authorities made.
text:
An investigation by the Connecticut Judicial Branch found no evidence judicial marshals interfered with ICE agents during an operation inside the Meriden courthouse, contradicting allegations made by federal authorities.
The U.S. Department of Homeland Security previously accused court officers of impeding and threatening ICE agents during the Sept. 23 incident, during which masked federal agents entered the building and arrested one person.
After reviewing surveillance video and interviewing marshals who were present, an investigator from the Judicial Branch found no evidence to support the allegations.
In a report released this month, the investigator determined claims that marshals blocked the elevator and exits and told the man to hide upstairs were “unfounded.”
In a public statement released to the media after the incident, DHS also accused an unnamed marshal of threatening an ICE agent and saying, “I’ll catch you outside and rip your face off.” The investigator determined evidence was lacking to support the allegation.
Marshals told the investigator none of them said or heard the remark, though one acknowledged he “exchanged words” with an ICE agent and couldn’t recall what was said.
Asked for comment on the findings, DHS responded by providing a copy of the same statement it released previously.
Immigrant advocates and others sharply criticized the ICE operation, which they said may have violated Connecticut law and procedures put in place by court authorities.
Connecticut has expanded and enacted new protections for immigrants in recent years. A state law that went into effect in May prohibits most civil immigration arrests on courthouse grounds without a signed judicial warrant. It also bars law enforcement officers from wearing face coverings in court without a medical need.
Records obtained previously by the American Civil Liberties Union of Connecticut show ICE officers had an administrative warrant issued by DHS, and not the kind of signed judicial warrant required under Connecticut’s new law.
According to DHS, immigration officers were seeking an Ecuadorian man who illegally entered the United States near Hidalgo, Texas, in 2022 and was ordered removed from the country the following year. His criminal history includes two counts of driving under the influence of alcohol and two other motor vehicle offenses, the agency said.
On the day of the arrest, an ICE “spotter” entered the courthouse shortly after noon and spoke with a judicial marshal, according to the report.
In an interview, the marshal told the investigator he asked the ICE spotter to wait until the man the agents were seeking left the building to arrest him.
Surveillance video shows the spotter left the building, then returned and spoke with several marshals, according to the report. Asked about the conversation, one marshal said the spotter showed him a text message on his phone “that read something to the effect of, ‘We don’t give a [expletive], we are going to do what we want,’ and ‘they can’t tell us what to do,'” according to the report.
Video shows a larger group of ICE agents then entered without stopping, showing identification or signing a sheet for law enforcement officers.
According to the report, they first removed the wrong person — an unidentified man who had been seated next to their intended target earlier in the day — then came back, walked unimpeded to the elevator, rode it to the second floor and apprehended the other man in a bathroom.
The last ICE agent to leave the building used pepper spray on at least one woman and a building maintenance worker, one marshal told the investigator.
“He added that the woman was older and not provoking the agent,” the report reads.
The Judicial Branch previously denied a request from Connecticut Public to release video of the incident, citing an exemption to the state public records law for material that poses a safety risk. Releasing the video footage “would provide a roadmap to individuals who may be inclined to counteract or circumvent Judicial Branch security measures,” a court official wrote.
Protesters, local officials and others denounced the incident last month. Some called on the state to enforce a recently passed law that allows for prosecution of federal law enforcement officers for violating civil rights.
Meriden City Councilor Yvette Cortez said during a demonstration in October that it’s important for residents to show solidarity, including by continuing to accompany immigrants to court appearances.
“We can be there for our neighbors and support them and stand beside them through this horrible time,” Cortez said.
Dan Barrett, ACLU’s legal director in the state, said the incident exposed potential weaknesses in Connecticut’s protections for immigrants.
“We have an interest in justice being administered here,” Barrett said, “and so we ought to really think critically about whether our laws adequately protect against what we saw in Meriden.”
This story was first published Nov. 16, 2026 by Connecticut Public.

name: Missouri Independent
title: Commentary: The abortion ban is dead. Missouri Republicans should support actual pro-child policy.
description: After President Donald Trump won reelection in 2024, his supporters spread the slogan “Your body, my choice” across social media.  That same election, Missourians voted to protect the right to abortion in the state constitution. Our Republican elected officials essentially responded, “No. Your body, my choice” by putting the abortion ban back on the ballot. [...]
text:
Dr. Margaret Baum, chief medical officer of Planned Parenthood Great Rivers, embraces Margot Riphagen, president and CEO of Planned Parenthood Great Rivers, during an Amendment 3 watch party in St. Louis. The crowd celebrated after the ballot measure aimed at banning abortion was voted down by Missourians on Nov. 3 (Anna Spoerre/Missouri Independent).After President Donald Trump won reelection in 2024, his supporters spread the slogan “Your body, my choice” across social media. 
That same election, Missourians voted to protect the right to abortion in the state constitution. Our Republican elected officials essentially responded, “No. Your body, my choice” by putting the abortion ban back on the ballot.
The ban failed. But abortion opponents’ fundamental failure long predates the losses at the ballot box.
A criminal law is a rule enforced by the threat of state force. Thus, an abortion ban is an attempt to use physical force to make someone do something with her body against her will. The reason anti-abortion leaders must resort to this physical coercion is that they have failed so completely to persuade women that abortion is immoral. A 2024 study projected that roughly one in four U.S. women will have an abortion by age 45.
And the reality is that bans do not necessarily reduce the abortion rate, and have not since the fall of Roe. Women who do not want to be pregnant will go to extraordinary lengths to end their pregnancies. Bans primarily serve to punish, humiliate and endanger women by forcing them to have later abortions after having to travel out of state, figure out how to obtain medication online or wait dangerously long for miscarriage care. 
We know the proponents of criminalization are well aware that their ban punished women without reducing abortions (except for the poorest and youngest in need) from their efforts to enact laws even more extreme than the ban. State Sen. Mary Elizabeth Coleman sought to block women from obtaining abortions out of state. State Sen. Mike Moon pursued legislation that could subject women who obtain abortions to the death penalty. 
With the ban defeated once again, State Rep. Brian Seitz plans to introduce legislation to stop women from accessing abortion via the mail. Medication abortion has transformed access to early abortion care, and made self-managed abortions far safer than the dangerous methods women sometimes resorted to before Roe v. Wade.
Anti-abortion leader Sam Lee wants more tax dollars for the state’s Alternatives to Abortion program and more millions in tax credits for unregulated antiabortion pregnancy resource centers known to pose as medical clinics. He’s also suggested abortion opponents may collect signatures to put another measure on the ballot now that the passage of Amendment 6 restricts the legislature’s ability to reverse voters. 
But a few Republican leaders have suggested they should listen to voters and back off the attempts at coercion, at least for now. Some have even suggested focusing on support for children and mothers. Indeed, given that poor economic circumstances are the most common reason women cite for needing abortions, getting Missouri’s social safety net funded and functioning is the best way to support people carrying unplanned pregnancies to term willingly.
That is where all our focus should be, not on repeatedly raising millions of dollars to fight over something we’ve voted on twice. 
This is not a pro-life state in the sense of prioritizing the health, safety and potential of children and families. We are failing on access to prenatal care, maternal mortality, preventable stillbirths from syphilis, infant mortality, child and teen deaths, funding our schools as set out in law and dropping kids from food assistance and medicaid because we can’t administer our programs properly. 
And it is about to get much worse. We have a looming budget hole and massive cuts to Medicaid and SNAP set to hit Missouri on Jan. 1. This is all thanks to the One Big Beautiful Bill that all of our purportedly pro-life Republican senators and congressmembers voted for, and which our state legislators have done little to prepare for.
Instead, our anti-abortion Republican officials have engineered one scheme after another to further reduce taxes for the wealthy.
It’s not polite to say it, but the available evidence indicates that the proponents of abortion criminalization are motivated by the desire to dominate and punish rather than concern for the welfare of children. 
I am begging them to prove me wrong. Urgently. This legislative session.  
Voters told them twice that my body is not their choice. They should move on to policies that support families rather than coerce women. Whether Missouri kids get treatment for preventable conditions and have enough food to eat is their choice — and their responsibility.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Nebraska widow’s big win against life insurer is in legal limbo; she seeks action from state agency
description: OMAHA — Twice she won a jury trial against an insurance provider who denied a claim after her husband died of COVID-19. But Vaneza Ramos, a widowed mother of 10, has yet to see any of the roughly $12 million awarded.  Farmers New World Life Insurance has not answered Ramos’ request to pay even a […]
text:
Vaneza Ramos, husband Jose Gaytan and one of their children at a ribbon cutting ceremony for their second La Michoacana store along the South Omaha 24th Street corridor. (Photo courtesy of Pesek Law)OMAHA — Twice she won a jury trial against an insurance provider who denied a claim after her husband died of COVID-19. But Vaneza Ramos, a widowed mother of 10, has yet to see any of the roughly $12 million awarded. 
Farmers New World Life Insurance has not answered Ramos’ request to pay even a portion for now, namely the $350,000 value of the original policy, said her attorney. Instead Farmers has asked for another trial, or that a judge reduce the award amount.
On Monday, Ramos’ legal team turned to the Nebraska Department of Insurance for action. 
In a regulatory complaint to Insurance Director Eric Dunning, attorney Ross Pesek of Pesek Law asked that the agency investigate what he alleged could be a systematic “bad faith” practice by Farmers. He wants the state to find out whether other Nebraska families have been denied benefits through similar Farmers procedures and if laws were violated.
Pesek Law attorneys Ross Pesek and Alejandra Ayotitla represented the Omaha widow and mother of 10 in a life insurance trial case against Farmers Insurance. (Photo courtesy of Pesek Law)
Pesek described the alleged practice as selling life insurance policies without obtaining available medical records, collecting premiums and, after a death, obtaining  medical records to retroactively justify denying a claim. 
Ramos’ husband, Jose Gaytan, died within a two-year timeframe when a claim can be contested. Farmers denied the $350,000 life insurance claim that named Ramos as beneficiary, saying Gaytan had a history of a heart attack and that a post-death investigation showed he failed to disclose the medical condition on his application. 
The company instead tried to send Ramos a $17,360 check, the amount Gaytan had paid into the policy. Two different Douglas County juries later sided with Ramos, one awarding the policy amount plus attorney and court costs, and the second calling upon Farmers to pay $11.3 million for bad-faith damages, bringing the total judgment to roughly $12 million.
Pesek said in his Monday complaint that the Nebraska Supreme Court has interpreted state law to require an insurer seeking cancellation of a policy based on misrepresentation to prove the policyholder made the incorrect statement knowingly and with intent to deceive.
He cited testimony from the Ramos trial and a separate Nebraska appellate case involving Farmers to support his request for a deeper look. 
“Only an examination of Farmers’ actual claim files can establish the scope of this problem,” he wrote. 
Martin Swanson, deputy director of the Nebraska Department of Insurance, said Monday the department does not comment on investigatory matters.  
Farmers’ lawyers did not respond to requests for comment. 
Farmers, however, did file a motion in Douglas County District Court late last month seeking a new trial or for a reduction in the Ramos award amount. The company argues that financial damages presented during trial totaled less than $200,000.
In challenging the bad-faith amount, Farmers attorneys argued that it was excessive and appeared to be punitive damages — which they said are not allowed under Nebraska law.
“If an award of damages shocks the conscience, it necessarily follows that the award was the result of passion, prejudice, mistake, or some other means not apparent in the record,” the insurer said in a court filing.
The jury verdicts came from two separate Douglas County panels: In March, one jury found that Farmers breached its contract when it declined to pay the life insurance policy on Gaytan. Last month, the second jury found that Farmers acted in “bad faith” and awarded the $11.3 million.
Pesek said the family’s recent request that Farmers at least pay the original policy amount has gone unanswered.
The two verdicts came six years after Gaytan’s death in 2020 of COVID-19 — just 20 days after Ramos gave birth to the couple’s last baby. In rejecting the claim, Farmers said Gaytan had a history of a heart attack and that a post-death investigation showed he had failed to disclose the medical condition on his application. 
The jury factored in emotional distress and financial hardship when determining an amount, Pesek said. The family owns two La Michoacana diners that feature frozen treats. Ramos’ mother had to move in to help; an 18-year-old son set his plans aside to work at the business. The family’s truck was repossessed. She fell behind on vendor bills, impacting their business reputation. They borrowed money.
Pesek acknowledged the state Insurance Department probably cannot get Ramos paid, saying that fight is likely headed to the Nebraska Supreme Court. But he said the department can offer lawmakers a sense of whether Nebraskans in other Farmers cases might have been improperly denied benefits. 
He asked the department to use its authority to examine Farmers’ personnel training, policy forms and other records to shed light on denied claims and practices. If violations are revealed, the complaint asks that the department determine corrective action.
“People go to jail for stealing $100 from a cash register,” Pesek said. “Farmers has been allowed to steal $350,000 from a Nebraska family without any consequence for six years.”
Pesek said he has spoken to at least one state lawmaker and will push to have the Legislature take up changes in the coming session, including allowing punitive damages in bad-faith cases, with the money going to the state’s public school fund; making pre-judgment interest automatic in bad-faith claims; and allowing attorneys’ fees on the full bad-faith award, not just the contract amount.

title: ‘This kiddo is struggling’: Community clinics address Oklahoma’s youth mental health crisis

text:
Ashley Showalter wears pins on her lanyard during an interview at on Tuesday, March 31, 2026, in Oklahoma City. (Photo by Nate Billings/For Oklahoma Voice)Editor’s note: This story discusses suicide and mental health crises. If you or someone you know needs help, call or text 988, the U.S. suicide and crisis lifeline, or access online chat at 988lifeline.org.
OKLAHOMA CITY — In south Oklahoma City, a team of behavioral health providers spend their days in schools, working with teachers and administrators to speak with students who need help and finding time for them to participate in therapy, counseling or other interventions. 
The goal: boosting students’ well-being and attendance, which makes it much easier for them to learn. 
Oklahoma youth have long struggled with higher rates of mental illness than the national average, but face hurdles accessing care. Amid growing mental and behavioral health challenges, the state’s certified community behavioral health clinics are working to reach youth where they are to provide or connect them with other specialized care – whether that’s in their school, at home or through peer-to-peer support. 
Oklahoma’s network of private certified community behavioral health clinics operate a plethora of youth-focused programs, providing care both in and out of schools. This federally designed healthcare model provides access to a series of core, required mental, behavioral and substance use services, regardless of someone’s ability to pay. 

This is the second of a three-part series on Oklahoma’s certified community behavioral health clinics.

The hope is that by addressing youth’s challenges early on, it will help cut down on Oklahoma’s high rates of incarceration, hospitalization and emergency room visits by preventing an issue from reaching the point of an arrest or a call to 911.
People struggling with mental or behavioral health often languish in Oklahoma’s jails and prisons because of a lack of available beds at mental health facilities. 
The federal government originally paid for a higher share of the cost for these nine private clinics to get them started, but that extra funding ended last year. These clinics, which serve more than 150,000 people a year, are at risk if the cash-strapped state Legislature can’t find a way to help foot the bill for the increasing cost of care. 
Barriers to care
Between 2018 and 2024, the percentage of these community behavioral health clinics providing school-based services grew from 51% to 88% nationally, according to a report from the federal Office of Behavioral Health, Disability, and Aging Policy.
In south Oklahoma City, Family & Children’s Services, formerly known as Hope Community Services, is one of those clinics. They have 28 clinicians who work in teams across 28 different public and charter schools in what is traditionally a lower income area. Officials said they could not provide a list of the specific schools they operate in for privacy reasons. 
Heather Helberg, the provider’s central region president, said embedding clinicians in schools isn’t a requirement, but these health clinics are required to respond to community’s needs, which often include providing services for schools. 
Heather Helberg, the central region president for an Oklahoma City provider with Family & Children’s Services, is pictured Jan. 16, 2026 in Oklahoma City. (Photo by Emma Murphy/Oklahoma Voice)
Clinics in other areas of the state provide similar services, such as Grand Mental Health, which serves most of northern Oklahoma. 
“We can also go out and we go into their homes and meet them where they’re at when it’s convenient for them,” Helberg said. “We also have telehealth options, so I think the school is kind of the entry point for us to find the folks, because the teachers and the counselors have said, ‘Hey, this kiddo is struggling.’”
She said that as of Aug. 31, the clinicians in Oklahoma City schools had received nearly 270 referrals since the beginning of the school year between all the sites they serve.
“We have had an overwhelming response from schools saying we need these services,” she said. 
The longer people go without treating mental illness, Helberg said, the worse it becomes. So the earlier kids can get services, the better. 
“Twenty years from now, we’re looking down the road and we have a healthier Oklahoma,” she said. “And so I think that’s kind of the big picture of all this — we want to do something that’s actually going to help our community in the future, not just now, but just is going to make our kiddos healthier in the long run.”
Access to youth services
More than 1 in 10 Oklahoma children, ages 12 to 17, had serious thoughts of suicide in 2024, according to an annual report from Mental Health America. 
Nationally, there’s been a sharp rise in preteen suicides over the past decade, often attributed to stressors such as COVID-19, social media use, bullying, overexposure to media and restrictions on accessing healthcare like gender-affirming care. 
‘Somebody stepped in and helped’: Advocates press to keep Oklahoma’s mental healthcare ‘safety net’

For nearly a decade, the federally designed certified community behavioral health clinic model has provided healthcare services hundreds of thousands of Oklahomans. Oklahoma was one of the first states to pilot this program. 
During the pilot years, which lasted from 2017 through most of 2025, the federal government paid for a larger portion of the program. But, as expected, it shrunk by about 23%, leaving the state responsible for tens of millions of extra dollars. 
Brittany Hayes, senior vice president of policy at Healthy Minds Policy Initiative, an Oklahoma nonprofit, nonpartisan policy group that researches mental health and substance use, said common barriers for youth include transportation, scheduling or not knowing where to start. These community providers have been helpful in breaking down these obstacles, she said. 
“They are designed to be a no-wrong-door access point, so families in need can show up or call and get what they need, regardless of what that is,” she said. 
Community clinics have also developed partnerships with schools, which helps staff know how to help students get help in moments of crisis, Hayes said. 
The number of children and adolescents served by certified community behavioral health clinics increased by 24% in the first five years of the program, according to a report issued by the federal Office of Behavioral Health, Disability, and Aging Policy.
Tiffany Scott speaks during an interview on Tuesday, March 31, 2026, in Oklahoma City. (Photo by Nate Billings/For Oklahoma Voice)
Youth services can extend beyond a child’s 18th birthday and be offered through their early 20s. 
Tiffany Scott, the youth program director at the Oklahoma City provider, said that by embedding clinicians, young people and parents have a starting point to reach out for help. Otherwise, many just don’t know whom or where to turn to. 
While the number of students seeing clinicians varies by site, she said, the ultimate goal is to have a team of clinicians assigned to each school. 
At one of the schools where clinicians have worked since January, Scott said they’re seeing about 24 kids. The frequency depends on the level of need — whether that’s weekly, biweekly or monthly. At newer sites where relationships with school staff, teachers and students are still growing, clinicians are seeing around six to 10 students, but those numbers are climbing along with the number of referrals. 
The clinicians work with teachers and administrators to meet the culture and needs of the school to find time to meet with students in a way that does not disrupt academics, Scott said.
While the reasons students work with clinicians vary by situation and school, Scott said that in elementary schools, they’ve seen a lot of disruptive behavior or kids not understanding classroom structure. In middle or high school, clinicians are more often working with children struggling with depression, anxiety, suicidal ideation or self-harm.
Oklahoma City Public Schools said in a statement that they are “grateful” for the partnership and have worked to build a network of partners to provide mental health resources to students and families. 
“These partnerships complement the work of our OKCPS Mental Health Specialists and school teams, helping us provide a more comprehensive, wraparound approach to supporting students,” the spokesperson said in a statement. “We value this collaboration and welcome opportunities to expand access to mental health support across the district.”
Ashley Showalter speaks during an interview on Tuesday, March 31, 2026, in Oklahoma City. (Photo by Nate Billings/For Oklahoma Voice)
‘Envisioning a future’ 
The work goes beyond the walls of schools.
Ashley Showalter has been a youth case manager with Family & Children’s Service for two years and is also a certified peer. 
As a “certified peer,” she is able to share her own experiences with clients, which often helps build trust and relationships. Showalter said she is bipolar and has post-traumatic stress disorder, anxiety and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, so she is able to talk about recovery and treatment with clients who have similar diagnoses. 
Showalter works with teens and young adults, typically aged 16 to 24, in things like learning healthy coping skills, rehabilitation, finding housing and creating goals. She helps them learn life skills, such as creating a resume, filling out job applications, budgeting and building a support system. 
“I can encourage and offer suggestions,” she said. “But at the end of the day — I like to use this metaphor when I explain the program to kids — I might be driving the car, but you’re telling me where to turn. I’m not going to turn anywhere without your permission, but I’ll help guide you.”
Ashley Showalter, right, checks in with Layla Broeker after they gave an interview, Tuesday, March 31, 2026, in Oklahoma City. (Photo by Nate Billings/For Oklahoma Voice)Ashley Showalter listens during an interview, Tuesday, March 31, 2026, in Oklahoma City. (Photo by Nate Billings/For Oklahoma Voice)Layla Broeker speaks during an interview, Tuesday, March 31, 2026, in Oklahoma City. (Photo by Nate Billings/For Oklahoma Voice)Layla Broeker, left, and Ashley Showalter pose for a photo, Tuesday, March 31, 2026, in Oklahoma City. (Photo by Nate Billings/For Oklahoma Voice)Layla Broeker, left, speaks next to Tiffany Scott during an interview, Tuesday, March 31, 2026, in Oklahoma City. (Photo by Nate Billings/For Oklahoma Voice)Wall of Hope at Family & Children's Services, previously Hope Community Services, is pictured Tuesday, March 31, 2026, in Oklahoma City. (Photo by Nate Billings/For Oklahoma Voice)
Showalter has been working with Layla Broeker, 18, to prepare the teen for her future. That assistance has included finding work study programs to pay for housing in college, looking for scholarships and exploring major programs. 
Broeker said she wasn’t able envision a future or create substantial goals for herself when she was suicidal and struggling with major depressive disorder. 
After spending time at an inpatient facility, the 18-year-old was referred to an Oklahoma City certified community behavioral health clinic for outpatient care. The support and independence she learned there sparked a change, Broeker said. 
“I think if I look back at my goals initially, there wasn’t really a foreseeable future in my perspective,” she said. “And I really came here because I had to. But then over time, I did realize that having agency and having support, I was able to do things independently and I was able to actually have my own goals and have goals to begin with.”
Broeker said she was assigned a therapist, case manager and peer services. This year, she was accepted to the University of Oklahoma and offered a scholarship. 
“Eventually, it shifted from just not having any goals to just even minor things,” Broeker said. “Like, my grades last year were terrible; I didn’t do anything in school. But now I even look forward to things like school, which are generally mundane tasks, and I feel like my goals now are more practical rather than emotional.”

title: Wyoming analysis debunks common argument for feeding elk regardless of deadly CWD
description:
Study compared the winter home range size of free-ranging elk in the Laramie Mountains to those that dwell on feedgrounds — and one has 327 times more room to roam.
The post Wyoming analysis debunks common argument for feeding elk regardless of deadly CWD appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Time and again while planning to modify Wyoming’s elk feedgrounds, biologist Ben Wise heard an argument for why the elk that bunch up around the state-supplied hay will be just fine as potentially devastating chronic wasting disease spreads through the gathered herds. 
The argument has been an almost reflexive retort by parties, such as hunting outfitters, who’ve long resisted making changes to Wyoming’s historic system of feeding elk. In essence, their contention is that Laramie Peak Herd elk have had CWD for four decades, also form super-sized winter herds and they’re doing just fine — they’re even so overpopulated it’s a problem. So why would feedground elk fare differently?
“I was sitting in all those [feedground] meetings and hearing that [argument] just over and over and over,” said Wise, a disease biologist for the Wyoming Game and Fish Department’s Jackson Region. 
Wise knew that the six feedground-dependent elk herds were intrinsically different. In southeast Wyoming, he said, “we’re not replenishing that winter range every day with a tractor or a sleigh.”
Elk chow down on hay at a state feedground in Northwest Wyoming. (Mark Gocke/Wyoming Game and Fish Department)
Wyoming wildlife managers happened to have the hard data on hand to prove Wise’s point. Because of an unrelated research project looking at elk-mule deer overlap in the Laramie Mountains, there were existing data from 129 GPS-marked elk there. And there was movement data from another 675 collared elk in the feedground region. With help from Game and Fish’s Science, Research and Analytical Support Unit, he set out to analyze how the two cohorts used the landscape differently in the winter. 
Wise explained his methodology and relayed the results at the Wyoming Game and Fish Commission‘s Nov. 6 meeting. He defined core home range sizes based on where individual elk spend the top 20% of their time during the heart of winter, from Jan. 15 to March 1. 
In southeast Wyoming’s Laramie Peak and Iron Mountain elk herds, the median size of an elk’s core home range was 1,959 acres. Animals that gathered on Wyoming’s 21 feedgrounds and the National Elk Refuge had a dramatically smaller core winter home range: just 6 acres. 
Free-roaming southeast Wyoming elk, in other words, had a winter home range that was about 327 times larger than their feedground-gathering counterparts. 
“They’re totally different,” Wise told WyoFile. 

Wyoming Game and Fish Department biologist Ben Wise on the National Elk Refuge in December 2018, shortly after the refuge instated mandatory testing for chronic wasting disease in all hunter-killed elk after an infected mule deer was found in Grand Teton National Park. (Ryan Dorgan/Jackson Hole News&Guide)

In human terms, the size gap is the same as the difference between a two-person college dorm room and a typical Safeway grocery store. From a disease perspective, it makes a world of difference. In a shared space, it’d be a lot easier for a human to catch a cold in the dorm room — or for an elk to pick up always-lethal CWD on a feedground. 
“We can’t compare these two populations and say, ‘What’s happening in Laramie Peak is going to happen in the feedground herds,’” Wise said. “They’re just not the same critters doing the same thing.” 
Elk in the Laramie Mountains have indeed held up well with CWD, which occurred at just 4% prevalence in the most recent assessment. Cow elk hunting there on private land is unlimited, and other extraordinary measures have been taken, yet the herd has remained about double its desired population. 
But wildlife disease experts predict a dramatically different outcome for the feedground herds in the southern Greater Yellowstone Ecosystem. Chronic wasting disease is still in the early stages of spreading there — it was first detected in 2024, and has since been found at five-state run feedgrounds plus the National Elk Refuge. Long term, the outlook for the six elk herds that use the feedgrounds is much poorer. Populations and hunting opportunities are expected to plummet regardless of management because of CWD, but continued feeding is expected to result in the worst-case scenario. 
There was more purpose to Wise’s analysis than debunking the common look-at-Laramie Peak argument that elk herds will be fine in the face of CWD. It’ll be useful data as the state adjusts its feedgrounds operations, he said. (The authority to close a feedground was stripped away by the Wyoming Legislature, and the governor now makes that decision.) 
A herd of about 300 elk grazes private land in the Iron Mountain area in February 2024. (Mike Koshmrl/WyoFile)
“Are there ways that we could spread elk out more?” Wise asked commissioners. “Are there other techniques we could use to increase their distribution on the landscape to reduce their overall density during that time period where we’re actively feeding them?” 
There were some nuances in the home range size data that were encouraging from a disease perspective. Collared elk on the National Elk Refuge, for example, tended to roam a significantly larger territory. The median core home range was 202 acres, roughly 40 times that of elk that dwelled on state-run feedgrounds. 
The state agency has tried with some success to emulate that more diffuse, disease-friendly elk distribution. After the winter of 2022-23 caused a historically lethal flare of foot rot, the Horse Creek Feedground south of Jackson was expanded out of the river valley onto an adjoining bench.
“It’s working really, really well,” Wise said. “The elk showed that they’ll go up there. If they get hungry, they’re going to go where the food’s at.” 
Game and Fish will have the chance to find similar opportunities to spread elk out. The state agency just wrapped up “feedground management action plans” for the Jackson and Pinedale herds, which identify specific steps managers will take to reduce the impact of CWD. Action plans for the four remaining feedground elk herds — Fall Creek, Afton, Piney and Upper Green — are being completed this winter. 
“We had committed to being done in early 2027,” Wise said, “so we’re feverishly working toward that.”

title: New trails, disc golf, showerhouse mulled for Wyoming mountain bike hotspot Curt Gowdy
description:
Wyoming State Parks seeks public comments by Friday on master plan proposals. 
The post New trails, disc golf, showerhouse mulled for Wyoming mountain bike hotspot Curt Gowdy appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Curt Gowdy State Park, a mountain biking hotspot in southeastern Wyoming that draws hundreds of thousands of annual visitors, is set to get a facelift. 
Wyoming State Parks is developing a new master plan for the 3,552-acre park between Laramie and Cheyenne, and is considering upgrades like a disc golf course, strider park, showerhouse and additional trails. Park staff are soliciting feedback on the process, and the public can fill out an online questionnaire through Friday. 
The agency aims to create a document that reflects Curt Gowdy’s existing and future needs, according to Superintendent Adam McKay. Outdoor recreation has undergone an evolution since the current master plan was drafted in the late 1980s. 
The plan that emerges will shape management for the next 10 to 15 years, and come at a time when outdoor recreation is growing as an economic industry in the state. 
New trails and growing users
Established in 1971, Curt Gowdy encircles three small reservoirs: Granite Springs, Crystal and North Crow. For much of its early existence, the park functioned as a water-activity and camping park. 
Curt Gowdy began to transform in the early 2000s, when crews and volunteers started constructing what amounted to more than 40 miles of trails. State Parks partnered with experts from the International Mountain Bike Association on design, resulting in a multi-level network designed for maximum mountain biking fun. 





Click to enlarge: This map shows proposed site improvements at the Hidden Falls Trailhead in Curt Gowdy State Park, which would entail a new restroom and formalized parking. (Wyoming State Parks)

The additions also raised Gowdy’s profile as a mountain bike destination. With shoutouts in publications like Bike and Outside magazines and three “epic” trail designations from the International Mountain Bicycling Association, cyclists from all over have trekked to the park. 
The park felt the impacts acutely in the summer of 2020 as people flocked to open spaces amid pandemic restrictions. Mountain bikers, campers and hikers poured into the 3,552-acre park, which experienced a 130% spike in visitation in June of that year, according to Wyoming State Parks. 
The trend has slowed but not reversed. Annual visitation now hovers around 600,000 — up roughly 27% from 2019. In 2025, the park was the third most-visited state park in Wyoming’s system, with 594,000 visitations. More than half of the park’s out-of-state visitors are from nearby Colorado. 
That trend helped spur the master planning process. Along with mountain bikers, people visit to camp, hike and ride horses on equestrian trails. 
Future concepts
Today, Curt Gowdy is home to 50 miles of trail along with more than 180 reservable lodging sites — from campgrounds to cabins and a lodge. The park’s visitor center was built in 2014.
Since launching the planning process this summer, Wyoming State Parks staff has conducted open house meetings in Cheyenne, Laramie and the park. Going forward, it is considering improvements including upgrades to the park amphitheater, day-use areas and parking facilities along with new amenities like trails and the showerhouse. 
Administrators hope for public comment to help identify gaps, understand what visitors value and build a shared vision for the park. 
Master planning has caused contention for Wyoming State Parks in recent years. In Fremont County, opposition mobilized after Sinks Canyon State Park released a 2020 master plan that called for, among other amenities, a via ferrata to be built on a cliff face where peregrine falcons historically nested. The state later abandoned that project.

title: Wyoming’s congressional delegation won’t have Barlow’s back on public lands
description:
The governor-elect clearly opposes sale of public lands, but he won’t find Wyoming allies at the U.S. Capitol, columnist Kerry Drake writes.
The post Wyoming’s congressional delegation won’t have Barlow’s back on public lands appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
I’m confident that President Donald Trump’s proposal to sell federal public lands to state, local and tribal governments will be opposed by the state under Gov.-elect Eric Barlow.

Opinion

But what about Wyoming’s congressional delegation? Based on their past statements and actions, plus strong negative public reaction to what they’ve done, I have little confidence that the three GOP members have the  level of support for protecting public lands as the vast majority of Wyomingites want from their federal lawmakers.
Barlow has well established that he opposes the selling of public lands in Wyoming.
Last Friday, Barlow told Cowboy State Daily that the U.S. Department of Interior’s new strategic plan “is not what Wyoming wants regarding its federal lands.”
On the campaign trail to a resounding win in the governor’s race, Barlow repeatedly said, “Wyoming’s public lands are not for sale.”
This year, Barlow successfully sponsored a joint resolution to send a message to the president, Congress and Wyoming’s delegation that the Legislature opposes any policy promoting broad or indiscriminate disposal of public lands.
So, how does Wyoming’s incoming congressional delegation — Rep.-elect Chuck Gray and Sen.-elect Harriet Hageman, who will be joining Sen. John Barrasso — compare with Barlow’s public land stands?
Gray, as secretary of state, hasn’t dealt with federal public lands. But in April he went on “The Jenny Beth Show,” hosted by Jenny Beth Martin, who co-founded the Tea Party in 2009, and explained his public land positions.
“We are all for keeping our public lands in public hands. We want to protect our multiple use, our recreation uses, but we also need to be able to reach our full potential on public lands,” Gray said. “So, speeding up leasing of coal, oil and gas. 
“In the One Big Beautiful Bill, Congressman Hageman and the great work of the Trump administration, that work has been getting going in the Trump administration,” he said.
Gray added that Wyoming needs responsible management of public lands. But how does he define that?
“The Trump administration has been doing great work in reversing the problematic policies of Obama and Biden,” he said. “And we need a Congress that will back him up in codifying these executive orders, codifying these executive actions.” 
What would happen if Trump’s current public land policy is rebuffed by the current Congress or is, most likely, dead on arrival when the new Democratic-controlled House and Senate take over in January? If the president signs an executive order to accomplish it, would Gray really risk opposing Trump after spending the past decade trying to stay in his good graces?
And what about that public land sale provision that was once in the One Big Beautiful Bill, sponsored by Sen. Mike Lee of Utah? Hageman’s support of it is the basis of much of the criticism she’s received on public lands.
Hageman was an early backer of Lee’s plan in 2025 to add a provision to Trump’s budget bill that would allow public lands to be sold if they were used for affordable housing.
Environmental organizations quickly united to tie Lee and Hageman to an unpopular public lands position. Hageman’s opponents took control of the narrative, and she spent much of the next week writing op-eds and telling reporters she wasn’t in favor of selling huge parcels of America’s federal lands.
Hageman said the provision was about affordable housing and “disposing useless land,” which didn’t track with the fact it had no affordability mandate, no environmental reviews and no requirement to consult local communities or tribes.
Selling any public land that is owned by all Americans and considered sacred, and calling it “useless,” was an egregious political error which many will never forgive her for.
It didn’t matter when Hageman said Lee’s provision in the One Big Beautiful Bill would only potentially impact between 2-3 million acres of public land in 11 Western states. That’s way too much if one of your core principles is that it should be no acres.
“We never, ever, ever talk about ever disposing of any federal lands under any circumstance whatsoever,” a frustrated Hageman said at a June 2025 town meeting in Powell. “That absolutely makes no sense whatsoever in a growing country.”
She followed her observation by noting the need for affordable housing and the potential income public land sales could bring into the federal treasury.
“When you talk about wanting your grandchildren to be able to access these public lands, I want my grandchildren to not have to face a $70 trillion debt of their federal government,” Hageman told the crowd.
I don’t think most supporters ever believed the real reason for the sale of public lands was to build more affordable homes. But when Hageman tossed in the hand grenade that the money generated would pay off a tiny fraction of the enormous debt an out-of-control Congress keeps building up, people stopped listening. And if Hageman was truly worried about the debt, then the best solution would have been to vote against the Big Beautiful Bill, which will add $3.4 trillion to the national debt over the next 10 years.
The Wilderness Society released a map that contended if one just considered the possible sales that might be made from Lee’s measure as written, it could impact up to 15 million acres in the West.
Lee argued but realized it was “turn out the lights, the party’s over” time, and pulled his provision.
U.S. Sen. Cynthia Lummis — who didn’t run for reelection this year — and Barrasso were in favor of Lee’s proposal to sell public lands for affordable housing. 
But Hageman’s support for a Utah lawsuit the previous year that would have forced the U.S. to dispose of 18 million acres of public land in that state — plus hundreds of millions of acres more across the country — was what really made Hageman the villain on the issue.
Of course, it isn’t all about selling public federal lands. Hageman’s determination to overturn key protections for public lands, like getting rid of the Roadless Rule enacted under President Bill Clinton, added to her anti-environmental reputation. 
Trump already asked the U.S. Forest Service and Agriculture Department to begin the process of rescinding the Roadless Rule in August 2025, before Hageman introduced a House bill to nullify the rule. Barrasso and Lummis also supported both actions.
Out of more than 370,000 public comments on the USFS proposal to rescind the roadless rule, a new analysis last month by the Center for Western Priorities found that 99.1% opposed the idea.
Faced with such overwhelming evidence that the public hates something, most politicians would stop backing it and move on.
Why is that likely the last thing Hageman, Barrasso and Gray will do? It’s because Trump wants it. Hageman has the benefit of knowing she just got elected with 65% of the vote, and is in office for the next six years.
Barrasso, who just got elected Senate minority whip, has no choice but to do Trump’s bidding on this and just about any issue. He’s danced with the devil he’s known for more than a decade, and it’s too late for him to look for another political partner. I doubt Gray would ever consider jumping ship, even if it’s sinking.
Barlow might be wondering if he can count on the congressional delegation for support in opposing Trump’s plans to sell public lands to state, local and tribal governments, or anyone else.
I wouldn’t waste time turning around to see if they have your back, governor. I think they’ve probably made their political calculations and already moved on. So that leaves it up to Wyoming’s public land lovers to let their congressional delegation know they stand with their soon-to-be governor.

title: Lansing City Council hears calls for emergency homelessness response, delays action
description: LANSING – In the wake of a sweep of a homeless encampment in Lansing’s Old Town neighborhood, city council members heard hours of public testimony calling for a broader response to homelessness as winter weather approaches.  Councilmember Deyanira Nevarez Martinez, who represents the city’s second ward, has proposed an ordinance to enact a 60-day moratorium [...]
text:
Khadja Erickson, the executive director of the Mid-Michigan Tenant Resource Center speaks about the need for greater support for the unhoused community in Lansing, including a proposed moratorium on encampment sweeps, at a council meeting on Nov. 16, 2026. (Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance)LANSING – In the wake of a sweep of a homeless encampment in Lansing’s Old Town neighborhood, city council members heard hours of public testimony calling for a broader response to homelessness as winter weather approaches. 
Councilmember Deyanira Nevarez Martinez, who represents the city’s second ward, has proposed an ordinance to enact a 60-day moratorium on sweeps of homeless encampments in certain city parks. It would not apply to sweeps on private property, such as the most recent sweep, which took place on Thursday.
Nevarez Martinez was clear that she does not believe such a moratorium is a permanent or long-term solution to homelessness, but that time is needed to develop a strategy and identify shelter options for those facing homelessness.
“We do not have sufficient options for people, and then we criminalize them for having nowhere else to go. That is unacceptable. I believe we need to address this crisis on multiple fronts: sufficient low-barrier emergency shelter, transitional housing, and permanently affordable housing,” she said. “My goal is not to pit our unhoused neighbors against our housed residents, our schools, or our business community, we all have a stake in making Lansing a safer, healthier, and more compassionate city.”
Lansing City Council member Deyanira Nevarez Martinez speaks about her proposed ordinance to enact a temporary moratorium on homeless encampment sweeps in Lansing at a council meeting on Nov. 16, 2026. (Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance)
Meanwhile, Council President Peter Spadafore has introduced a resolution to establish an ad hoc committee on homelessness strategy. The resolution was expected to come before the council Monday, but Spadafore said email issues had delayed its consideration until the next meeting.
Both the moratorium and the establishment of the committee are expected to be considered on Dec. 7, the next meeting of the council.
Nick Cook, the director of public policy at the Michigan Coalition Against Homelessness, was among the many speaking during the public comment period who emphasized the harms that can be done to residents in an encampment when it is swept. 
“Let’s be honest about what is happening. People are not sleeping in tents because they want to; they are sleeping in tents because there’s nowhere else to go. Shelters are full. Affordable housing is scarce. Supportive housing is insufficient,” Cook said. “Yet, instead of addressing those realities, our response has too often been to push people from one piece of public property to another and call it progress. It is not progress. An encampment sweep does not house a single person. Does not treat mental illness. Does not help someone find employment. It does not connect people to stability. What it does is scatter vulnerable people, destroy what little property they have left, sever ties with outreach workers, and make survival even harder.”
Many also focused on the long-term solutions necessary to address homelessness in a sustainable fashion — and the fact that the city council has had repeated hearings about the same issues in recent months. 
“If you want encampments to go away, the solution is very simple. It’s housing. That’s how you prevent them from returning,” Khadja Erickson, the executive director of the Mid-Michigan Tenant Resource Center, said. “That’s how you prevent from experiencing this: a bunch of people coming to talk to you about homelessness. I promise you, I am just as tired of talking about it as you are of hearing about it.”
Erickson, along with others, also repeatedly noted that a more long-term response was necessary, especially one that allows better access to wraparound services, as well as access to water and safe heating sources.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“You keep lauding these 70 shelter beds. As many people have come up here and said, in 2026 we found over 800 people in our point-in-time count,” Erickson said. “70 beds is not even 10% of that number.”
Multiple members of Lansing’s unhoused community also spoke at the meeting. 
One speaker, who identified himself as a disabled combat veteran, argued that people experiencing homelessness are already living throughout the city and should be allowed to remain where they are. He said existing shelters are inadequate and described the Capital City Rescue Mission’s requirements and crowded conditions and said he would rather remain outdoors than stay in those conditions.
Alyssa Clark, who identified herself as a small business owner near the recently-swept encampment, said that she has had clients cancel appointments and “question whether they feel safe coming here.”
“Over the past nine months, we’ve dealt with people sleeping in fire escapes, unattended fires, encampments in the parking lot, discarded needles, trash, human waste, and recurring sewage problems. These aren’t just inconveniences; they’re serious safety and sanitation concerns that are affecting my business,” she said. 
However, most speakers emphasized the humanity of those who are facing homelessness and the need for people to have a safe location to go if there are encampment sweeps.
Reverend Elijah Burton, pastor of First Christian Church in Lansing, said that he was present at Thursday’s sweep and was angry about the treatment of unhoused individuals in Lansing.
“What kind of refuge requires someone to pack up their life every morning? What kind of safety exists when people must constantly fear being displaced?” Burton asked. “We have become so concerned with the visibility of homelessness that we are losing sight of the actual crisis. People do not have homes. Moving someone does not house them. Removing a tent does not create a shelter bed somewhere, and making people disappear from our parks does not make homelessness disappear from our city.”

title: SpaceX cleaning up 5,000 gallon chemical spill at Southaven facility
description: SpaceXSI said it is working to clean up an estimated 5,000-gallon chemical spill after a “misconfigured hose” released chemicals into a drainage ditch near its facility in Southaven, Mississippi Saturday. Much of the spilled propylene glycol — a low-toxicity chemical used by chemical, food and cosmetic industries as antifreeze, among other things — was conta[...]
text:
xAI powers its Memphis Colossus data centers using gas turbines at its power plant across the state line in Southaven, Mississippi. About 5,000 gallons of chemicals spilled at one of xAI's Southaven sites on Saturday, Nov. 14, 2026. (Mississippi Free Press / Illan Ireland)SpaceXSI said it is working to clean up an estimated 5,000-gallon chemical spill after a “misconfigured hose” released chemicals into a drainage ditch near its facility in Southaven, Mississippi Saturday.
Much of the spilled propylene glycol — a low-toxicity chemical used by chemical, food and cosmetic industries as antifreeze, among other things — was contained onsite. Some of the liquid flowed into a nearby drainage ditch and onto adjoining properties.
“The SpaceXSI team immediately stopped the flow to prevent further travel down the ditch and initiated cleanup,” a company spokesperson stated Monday. “Cleanup began within hours and is expected to be completed by the end of the day today.”
The Mississippi Department of Environmental Quality, MDEQ, visited the site and approved the company’s response plan. The propylene glycol remained in the drainage ditch and did not reach nearby Horn Lake Creek, the state regulator said Monday.
“Water samples are being collected for laboratory analysis as MDEQ continues to monitor cleanup activities and assess potential environmental impacts,” MDEQ stated.
The chemical spill appears to have started on a staging yard leased from Bearden Integrated SCVS LLC, according to MDEQ. Bearden Integrated owns three parcels along Tulane Road across from SpaceXSI’s property on Stanton Road, according to DeSoto County property records.
SpaceXSI said the spill was caused by a “misconfigured hose attached by a contractor to a mobile tank.”
The chemical entered the drainage ditch, crossing onto property owned by Beruk Construction Inc. and a private citizen, according to MDEQ. SpaceXSI is working with the property owner to conduct cleanup on affected land, the company stated.
A battle over data centers heats up along the Mississippi-Tennessee state line

MDEQ stated Monday that soil excavation is complete near the tank and silt fence, and no further excavation is planned. The regulator will continue to assess the situation and determine whether further action is needed.
SpaceXSI stated it is in “constant communication” with MDEQ on cleanup progress, potential post-cleanup testing and its investigation into the spill’s cause. The company did not respond to questions about the frequency and footprint of its promised post-spill inspections.
The Southaven Police and Fire departments also responded to the scene Saturday.
Propylene glycol is a colorless, odorless synthetic liquid that absorbs water and is used to maintain moisture in some food products, medicines and cosmetics, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. It is also used in polyester compounds, as a runway and aircraft deicing solution, as a solvent for food colors, and to create artificial fog.
The chemical can mix with water and soak into soil, typically breaking down within a week, according to the CDC. But it consumes oxygen as it degrades in water, posing potential harm to any aquatic organisms that depend on oxygen, according to the Cumberland River Compact.
Protect Our Aquifer, a nonprofit dedicated to protecting the Memphis Sand Aquifer, stated Sunday that the organization is “in contact with neighbors in (Mississippi) to take water samples.” It encouraged followers to avoid fishing in Horn Lake Creek.
MDEQ is separately seeking an estimated $6.1 million in fines from SpaceXSI, which it says proceeded with “land-disturbing construction activities” at three sites before receiving a construction stormwater permit, according to the company’s quarterly report filed in October to the Securities and Exchange Commission.
“The Company is cooperating with MDEQ and is in discussions to resolve the matters through a single agreed order,” the report states.
MDEQ recently rejected an appeal of SpaceXSI’s air permit, which allows the company to use 41 methane gas turbines at its power plant in Southaven to power its Colossus 2 data center in nearby Memphis.
The company also faces an NAACP lawsuit alleging that it installed and operated the “mobile” gas turbines prior to obtaining a permit and without “regard for the health and safety of people living nearby.” A federal judge rejected SpaceXSI’s attempt to dismiss the lawsuit in late October.
