title: Black Belt food insecurity higher than state average, says analysis
description: The Black Belt suffers from higher rates of food insecurity than Alabama averages, according to an analysis from the University of Alabama. The issue brief from the Education Policy Center reported that an average of 18.5% of residents in the Black Belt face food insecurity compared with 17.2% of residents outside the region. Researchers calculated […]
text:
Bananas and cereals at a grocery store in Fairfax, Virginia, on March 3, 2011. A new analysis from the University of Alabama found that food insecurity is higher in the Black Belt than the state as a whole. (USDA Photo by Lance Cheung)The Black Belt suffers from higher rates of food insecurity than Alabama averages, according to an analysis from the University of Alabama.
The issue brief from the Education Policy Center reported that an average of 18.5% of residents in the Black Belt face food insecurity compared with 17.2% of residents outside the region. Researchers calculated the number based on figures obtained from the 2026 Map the Meal Gap report that Feeding America, a hunger-relief organization, published at the end of July.
“It is not even about skipping meals, but even worrying about, ‘Am I even going to be able to eat?’” said Garrett Till, a senior fellow with the Education Policy Center and one of the authors. “Whenever you are not eating, you are probably not going to be able to perform greatly at work. It plays into health; it plays into lifespan.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The U.S. Department of Agriculture defines food insecurity as having limited or uncertain access to adequate food based on the economic and social conditions faced by a household.
The issue is particularly acute for children. According to the analysis, 29% of children in the Black Belt experience food insecurity, compared to about 23% in the parts of the state that are not considered part of that region.
The prevalence of food insecurity is higher in Alabama than in other parts of the country, according to the analysis. Nationally, about 48 million people living in the United States, roughly 14.4% of the total population, are food insecure. About 21% of American children experience food insecurity, while 24% of Alabama children are food insecure.
Poverty is but one factor that contributes to food insecurity, but a host of other issues, such as living in a food desert, also play a role. Some people living in rural areas lack access to adequate and nutritious food.
“It is based on geographic factors like the distance to an actual grocery store, actual locations that provide healthy food choices,” said Tessa Pickens, a graduate research associate at the University of Alabama and a coauthor of the analysis. “And again, it is that inability to overcome that cost barrier to get healthy food. That is what is going to go into that metric.”
The issue brief includes a map of Alabama that indicates roughly two-thirds of the Black Belt have both low income and little access to food sources. People in those areas must drive longer distances to purchase nutritious food.
“Even if you have the transportation, which is going to be a more stark number in the Black Belt, you have to have the transportation to get to a proper supermarket,” Till said. “Then you also have to weigh out, ‘Gas prices are going up, do I really want to burn the gas to go the 10, 15, 20-minute plus journey to buy healthy food.’”
The issue brief cited an example of using public funds to financially assist grocery stores. Illinois’ Grocery Initiative, for example, provides grants to reopen local grocery stores in food deserts. The issue brief also proposed food pantries partnering with local retailers to provide people with additional resources.

title: North Dakota’s rural health money allocated but details not yet public
description: The $199 million North Dakota received for the first year of a massive federal rural health care grant has been allocated, though the state says it will likely be weeks before all of the award recipients are public. The money comes from the Rural Health Transformation Program, a $50 billion, five-year funding package approved by […]
text:
An ambulance departs the Sanford Medical Center in Fargo, North Dakota, on Sept. 13, 2025. (Photo by Jeff Beach/North Dakota Monitor) The $199 million North Dakota received for the first year of a massive federal rural health care grant has been allocated, though the state says it will likely be weeks before all of the award recipients are public.
The money comes from the Rural Health Transformation Program, a $50 billion, five-year funding package approved by Congress last year as part of its budget reconciliation law. The program guarantees every state at least $500 million in grant money.
States had until the end of October to obligate all of the money given to them for year one of the program. North Dakota last week announced it met this goal in part by contracting with third party organizations to help with the application and award process.
North Dakota to use ‘anchor partners’ to manage Rural Health grants

The award recipients have been chosen but contracts are still being finalized, Alysia Huck, the program’s communications manager, said in an email. Specific award amounts are still being decided, she said.
“Once those agreements are finalized and signed, we’ll be able to provide a more detailed breakdown of award recipients and funding amounts,” Huck said.
Program Director Krissie Meyer said she expects this process to be complete by the end of the year or early January.
Some states have already made most of their year one Rural Health Transformation Program grants public. Nebraska, for example, has a dashboard featuring the funds that were awarded and spent through September 30, 2026.
North Dakota is set to receive roughly $206.4 million from the federal government for year two of the grant, the state announced last week. The award is about $7.4 million more than it received for the first year — the largest percentage increase of any state.
The state received a total of 800 applications for its first year grant opportunities according to the Department of Health and Human Services’ website. The department hasn’t disclosed the total number of award recipients.
The grants are split across four initiatives: expanding rural health care access, addressing workforce issues, promoting healthy lifestyles, investing in technology and data.
The Department of Health and Human Services recently began working with third party organizations to help process applications and administer the grants.
In August, the department made details of about roughly $11.2 million in grants public in a report to the federal government.
That included money for hospital staff recruitment and retention, nutrition programs and a mobile dental unit, according to the report.
Meyer said the state is considering adding more third-party partners for the second year of the program.
While states have already submitted their draft budgets for year two to the Centers for Medicaid Services, the final budgets have yet to be approved. Budget revisions are due by the end of November, Meyer said.

title: Younger Colorado voters more in favor of recent tax ballot measures, poll shows
description: Younger voters in Colorado propelled two major tax reforms to victory in November’s elections, according to bipartisan exit polling. Seven in 10 voters between 18 and 44 years old supported Proposition NN and 68% of that age group supported Amendment 87, compared to 45% and 38% of older voters, respectively. Together, those two measures will […]
text:
Chris Kennedy, center, president of the Bell Policy Center, spoke as Amendment 87 supporters declared victory at a press conference in Denver's La Raza Park on Thursday, Nov. 5, 2026. (Photo by Chase Woodruff/Colorado Newsline)Younger voters in Colorado propelled two major tax reforms to victory in November’s elections, according to bipartisan exit polling.
Seven in 10 voters between 18 and 44 years old supported Proposition NN and 68% of that age group supported Amendment 87, compared to 45% and 38% of older voters, respectively. Together, those two measures will restructure longstanding tax rules in the state and add a significant amount of additional tax revenue to the state’s coffers for healthcare and public education.
“It was really those younger voters that pushed some of these major changes to our taxes and fiscal system here,” Lori Weigel with the Republican-aligned group New Bridge Strategy said during a Monday media briefing on the poll results. “This major change was very much grounded in those young voters wanting to make a real shift.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
New Bridge Strategy and the Democratic-aligned Aspect Strategic conducted the exit poll for the Colorado Polling Institute with Rose Community Foundation between Oct. 30 and Nov. 5, sandwiching Election Day on Nov. 3. They reached 606 voters through an online survey and oversampled in Denver and El Paso counties. The statewide margin of error was plus and minus 3.98%.
Proposition NN will increase public school funding over the next decade by permanently increasing the state’s revenue cap set by the Taxpayer’s Bill of Rights. Instead of returning money to taxpayers in some years, the state can keep more and direct it to education. Amendment 87, which passed by a smaller margin, creates a graduated income tax system in the state in which people and companies who earn more than $500,000 annually will pay a higher tax rate.
The two measures are among the biggest transformations to Colorado tax policy in over 30 years.
Supporters of Colorado’s graduated income tax measure celebrate victory

Older voters were more likely to support Proposition 136, an unsuccessful ballot measure that would have capped the state income tax at 4.4%. About 49% of people older than 45 said they voted for that proposition, compared to just 39% of younger voters.
Voters also like the direct democracy that ballot measures offer: 82% said they like voting on specific policy questions.
The poll showed a 48% favorability rating towards the incoming Democratic Gov. Phil Weiser, who won the governor’s race by a 27-point margin over Republican Victor Marx. And for the first time, CPI found that a majority of voters hold an unfavorable opinion on Gov. Jared Polis, the Democrat leaving office. Last November, 46% of voters didn’t approve of him. That number is now 58%.
Polis has made a series of controversial and unpopular decisions in the last year. He commuted the sentence of election denier Tina Peters and vetoed a round of progressive bills after the legislative session.
“Usually parties are not abandoning their leader even at the very end,” Weigel said. “In fact, sometimes as governors are going out, they’ll get a halo effect where people are more positive towards them as they leave office. I think it is a real shift, especially among Democrats.”
The Democratic Party as a whole also has a net-negative rating, according to CPI. About 52% of voters view it poorly, a 7-point increase from last November. Voters view the Republican Party worse, with 64% seeing it unfavorably. Around 21% of voters said they had unfavorable views of both political parties, but they were likely to vote for Democratic candidates, and they had a nearly 90% negative view of President Donald Trump.
A plurality of voters, 46%, said the recent midterm elections for Congress was a vote to signal opposition to Trump. Three of Colorado’s Republican congressional seats flipped to a Democrat, leaving the state with a 7-1 Democratic U.S. House delegation. Voters in El Paso County, who elected a Democrat in the 5th Congressional District for the first time, were more than twice as likely to say their vote was a signal against Trump.
While Democrats were almost uniformly supportive of Weiser, only 85% of Republican respondents said they were in favor of Marx, signaling how the controversial Republican nominee divided the party this year. Marx’s favorability was 9 points higher among Republican men than Republican women.
Pollsters also asked voters what they want the incoming state Legislature to tackle next year. Their priorities are addressing healthcare costs at 88%, how to balance the state budget at 87% and improving public schools at 86%. About 70% also said they want state lawmakers to address data centers in some way, which comes after two regulatory bills on the issue died last year and local governments continue to pass their own policies about development.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: NJ has low preterm birth, infant mortality, but maternal deaths and racial disparities persist
description: New Jersey has low preterm birth and infant death rates, a new report shows, but racial disparities and high maternal mortality persist
text:
A new annual report from the March of Dimes shows New Jersey compares well nationwide when it comes to preterm birth and infant morality, but the news is less positive for maternal deaths and racial disparities. (Stock photo by Coral222/Getty Images)New Jersey has one of the nation’s lowest infant mortality rates and preterm births are relatively rare, but maternal mortality rates — and the racial disparities in those death rates — remain higher here than they are nationwide.
The latest annual March of Dimes report card, released Tuesday and based on data from multiple years, ranked New Jersey second nationwide for its infant mortality rate of 3.4 deaths per 1,000 live births, and eighth for number of babies born before their due date, 9.2% pregnancies that are carried full term.
“New Jersey’s strong rankings in preterm birth and infant mortality are encouraging and reflect important progress in maternal and infant health. But the state’s maternal mortality ranking and persistent racial disparities remind us that there is still significant work to do, and we cannot afford to lose momentum in ensuring that every mother and baby benefits from that progress,” said Adelisa Perez-Hudgins, a vice president at the nonprofit Health Care Quality Institute, which has prioritized maternal child health.
Nationwide, 10.4% of the babies born in 2025 were preterm, or delivered before 37 weeks, increasing their risk of health issues, according to the maternal and infant health advocates annual report. The infant death rate averaged 5.5 out of 1,000 live births in 2024, when about 20,000 babies died before their first birthday, it said.
New Jersey’s maternal death rate — once among the highest nationwide — continued to hover above the national average, with 24.8 women dying while pregnant, while giving birth, or up to 42 days later, out of every 100,000 healthy births, based on data from 2020 through 2024, according to the report. Nationwide, the maternal mortality rate averaged 23.1 over those five years.
The report did not provide single-year state-level maternal mortality data for 2024 or 2025.
That report found the maternal mortality rate averaged 14.4 per 100,000 live births over those three years. It also showed Black women were nearly seven times — and Hispanic women some 3.5 times — more likely to die than white New Jerseyans.
Perez-Hudgins said the state has taken important steps to improve outcomes, but the data available doesn’t yet show how it’s working.
“What we do know is that far too many women, particularly Black women, face unacceptable risks during pregnancy and after childbirth,” she said.
Racial gaps also persist nationwide, the March of Dimes found, especially in infant mortality.
Black babies in America died at more than twice the rate of white and Hispanic infants, and nearly three times the rate of Asian babies, according to data from 2022 through 2024. In New Jersey, the death rates were lower over those years, but the disparity was more severe, with a death rate of eight per 1,000 for Black infants and 2.3 per 1,000 for white babies, according to the report.
To improve outcomes in New Jersey, birthing hospitals have adopted best-practice protocols and the state invested in the perinatal workforce and made other policy changes to protect moms and babies. The March of Dimes report credits the state for extending Medicaid coverage for pregnant women for the first year after they give birth, ensuring nonclinical birth coaches called doulas can get paid by insurance, and having a commission to review these deaths.
New Jersey also created an authority to oversee maternal and infant health, which is building a headquarters in Trenton and working to expand birthing options and other services there. And it launched a nurse home visit program for new moms that has proven to reduce emergency room visits and connect families with services, which is slated to operate statewide starting next year.

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Appeals court dismisses challenge to retroactive TN sex offender registry placements
description: A federal appeals court has dismissed a challenge to Tennessee law that requires sex offenders convicted in decades-old crimes to be newly classified as “violent offenders” or “offenders against children” and placed on a public registry that didn’t exist at the time of their offenses.  The decision by the 6th Circuit Court of Appeals on […]
text:
The 6th Circuit Court of Appeals has dismissed a challenge to Tennessee law requiring individuals convicted in decades-old sex crimes to be added to a public-facing offender registry. (Photo from United States Courts of Appeal)A federal appeals court has dismissed a challenge to Tennessee law that requires sex offenders convicted in decades-old crimes to be newly classified as “violent offenders” or “offenders against children” and placed on a public registry that didn’t exist at the time of their offenses. 
The decision by the 6th Circuit Court of Appeals on Friday overturned a lower court ruling that found the new rules imposed on individuals whose crimes predated 1995, and the creation of a public registry, were an unconstitutional retroactive punishment.
The federal appeals court concluded instead that placement on the registry was not a form of punishment; instead, it found placing individuals names, addresses and photographs on a public registry furthered a public interest in accessing information. “Public disclosure bears a rational relationship to Tennessee’s stated purpose of providing information to the public,” the three-judge panel wrote.
Tennessee has long had a sex-offender registry available to law enforcement, but in 2004 state lawmakers acted to make it public. Three years later, they extended registration requirements for the public-facing registry to offenders convicted before 1995.  
The challenge was brought by eight individuals convicted of pre-1995 sex offenses whose individual lawsuits were consolidated in one 2021 case.  In legal filings, their attorneys estimated thousands of Tennessee residents are impacted by the registration and classification requirements. 
The lawyers also challenged the new sex offense classification system as imposing new legal consequences on crimes committed prior to 1995, including the ability to live, work or visit locations near children. Among the plaintiffs, whose identities are shielded in the lawsuit, is a grandfather prevented from overnight visits with his grandchildren and an individual who could not buy a house because it was near a child care center.
The judges dismissed those claims without prejudice, leaving the plaintiffs open to challenging them in the future. The panel concluded that those geographic restrictions were not the responsibility of David Rausch, director  of Tennessee Bureau of Investigation, who is the named defendant in the lawsuit.

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: Commentary: The exhausting 2026 election is behind us. Now, the work of improving Idaho elections begins.
description: With the anticipated certification of Idaho’s general election on Nov. 24, this exhausting 2026 cycle will come to a blessed end. Before the wrap, the League of Women Voters of Idaho believes a review of lessons learned and suggestions for next steps are in order.  We have learned: Idaho voter registration laws, policies and procedures […]
text:
Informative voting pamphlets are on display in South Hills Middle School gymnasium on Election Day in Twin Falls, Idaho, Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Andrew Eakin for the Idaho Capital Sun)With the anticipated certification of Idaho’s general election on Nov. 24, this exhausting 2026 cycle will come to a blessed end. Before the wrap, the League of Women Voters of Idaho believes a review of lessons learned and suggestions for next steps are in order. 
We have learned:

Idaho voter registration laws, policies and procedures privilege men.
Time is up on incumbents who refuse to meet their challengers in public forums.
Fallout from voter fraud lies has weighed most heavily on county election officials. 
Life must be breathed back into the notion of nonpartisan support for voters.
Idaho’s obsolete campaign finance laws are harmful to voters and increasingly ignored.

League leaders across the state sound a clarion call to executive and legislative branch office holders: Laws, policies, and administrative procedures must change. Addressing each of the five lessons above will help reset Idaho’s electoral course.
 Revise state edicts that unequally protect the voting rights of men over women

Her name is Alice. At 80-something, she moved into assisted living and relinquished her driver’s license. As a life-long voter, Alice was ready in early September with a U.S. birth certificate and proof of residency to request a voter ID, register and vote in November.
Voting rights groups say Idaho laws from 2023 create hurdles to register and vote

Under Idaho’s 2023 voter identification law and the 2024 Only Citizens Will Vote Act signed by the governor, her right to vote now rested in the hands of the Idaho Division of Motor Vehicles, the voter ID issuing agency. She did not get her ID in time because she was not born male and because she accepted the norm of changing her last name upon marriage. 
If, as a male, Alice had been married three times (the fact in her case), the birth certificate and proof of residency would have been enough for the ID to be issued. Unlike a man, Alice must prove she is a U.S. citizen and, because she followed marital customs, she must also provide all documents required for her “proof of identity trail.” This means securing three certified marriage licenses obtained from different counties over 60 years. 
These additional documents all come with a price, both in terms of monetary cost and time. Women lacking resources to shoulder these extra burdens sometimes resign themselves to becoming non-voters as an accident of birth and marital conventions. Alice, and women of her age, rarely bucked the societal expectation that their husband’s last name would become theirs. 
Now, to vote in Idaho, they must pay the price.
The fix

Stop referring to Idaho’s voter ID as “free.” Even for men, the documents required typically come with a cost.


Revise Idaho laws, policies and administrative procedures that fly in the face of the Equal Protection Clause of the 14th Amendment to the U.S. Constitution.


Relatedly, revise Idaho laws, policies and administrative procedures that apply an unequal poll tax to women who must obtain documentation that men do not.


If decisions are made to maintain the status quo, establish a state-funded structure to support all Idahoans required to collect identity trail documentation necessary to be issued a state-issued voter ID.

 Turn the lights back on in the court of public opinion

For more than 30 years, Idaho Public Television and the Idaho Press Club partnered with the League to sponsor Idaho Debates, a forum for incumbents and challengers to air and compare their views before a statewide audience.
Where are the debates? Idaho incumbents largely forgo debates and forums this year. 

In 2023, the refusal of incumbents to appear with their opponents doomed Idaho Debates and nearly all events like them. The fits and starts involved in inviting, scheduling, rescheduling, reinviting and, finally, going without recalcitrant candidates have exhausted nonpartisan voter education organizations and frustrated the voting public. 
While voter guides are useful, the League knows that voters headed to the polls this November with less quality information than they had when all political candidates were willing to meet each other and the public face-to-face. Excuses incumbents give for refusal to appear with their challengers run thin and can be reduced to a single fear: “If I meet with my challenger, I run the risk of voters choosing someone else.”
While not as prevalent as among Republican office holders, some Democratic incumbents have chosen not to participate in some nonpartisan voter education efforts. 
Candidates who fail to provide information to nonpartisan voter guides, for example, may believe this outreach to their constituents is unnecessary or burdensome. Proliferation of voter guides has not helped.
The fix

Political parties must partner with voter education organizations to structure public forums that meet fair, nonpartisan and high-quality standards.


Candidates should expect to be encouraged and trained by their political parties to engage in civil discourse with their political opponents.


A state-funded, printed voter guide of candidates and issues should replace the current voter pamphlet sent to every Idaho household by the Office of the Secretary of State. Candidates should expect to provide campaign information to a state voter guide that draws high quality, open-ended questions from existing nonpartisan guides.

 Acknowledge the heavy burden carried by county election staff members resulting from voter fraud lies

Every cause of long voting lines in Canyon County and uncounted ballots in Latah and Bannock counties may never be identified, but there is no doubt county elections staff were overly burdened with reassuring voters that this election was secure. One head of elections who was asked how voters were feeling in her county said voters were more fearful and confused this year. 
Voters wanted their ballots to count; they worried about being stricken from voter rolls, about mailing in their absentee ballots, and about something going wrong in the counting process that would exclude their votes. Voter fraud lies, perpetuated through social media, talk radio and cable news, drained county election staff members. 
Also, new this cycle, were more questions about which state and federal laws prohibit on-duty law enforcement officers and federal agents from congregating near polling places. 
Poll workers were trained on Idaho Code § 18-2318 which protects the “freedom of voters to exercise their franchise without interference or intimidation and to ensure the administration of an election at any polling place is undisturbed.” Training also included discussions of 18 U.S. Code § 593 which forbids armed forces from intimidating qualified electors or interfering “in any manner” with an election officers discharge of his or her duties. 
Yes, unprecedented turnout and lengthy ballots seem to have complicated this election. Lies upon lies about widespread voter fraud added unnecessary weight to the work.
The fix

Begin now to ask which, if any, laws, policies, and administrative procedures have been implemented that may have been an over response to now-widely acknowledged falsehoods about rampant voter fraud. Do the advantages of using the less-than-perfect Department of Homeland Security’s Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements, or SAVE, data system, for example, outweigh the taxpayer-funded administrative costs?
Reinforce messages that voter privacy is paramount in Idaho and that the federal government has no role in setting the times, places and manner of state-run elections except when Congress may choose to adjust the rules.
Ask county officials to review support levels for county election offices to ensure they are adequate to meet demands.

 Revive Idaho’s long-held belief in nonpartisanship

As lies about voter fraud have seeped into our political discourse, fewer people believe that supporting voters could be a nonpartisan service. 
This June, the U.S. League of Women Voters warned its volunteer members that the federal government was targeting nonprofits it suspected of engaging in voter fraud. That month, without warning, federal agents stormed the offices of one Ohio nonprofit looking for such fraud. None was found. 
In late September, LWVUS was forced to address allegations by the Kansas attorney general that League members in Leavenworth were “buying” the votes of college students. The offense? Members of that League were distributing $5 Starbucks gift cards to students walking by their voter education table. 
Closer to home, a public complaint was lodged against one of Idaho’s local Leagues alleging that two members were engaged in electioneering. The two were involved in a private conversation at a weekly public event. After years of participation, the League’s standing invitation to that event was rescinded. Suspicions dogging nonprofit voter service organizations have not produced evidence of wrongdoing, but they have succeeded in throttling our mission-driven work.
The fix

Nonprofit voter service organizations should welcome scrutiny by political parties into the support they offer voters. Sunlight is the best disinfectant.  


Nonprofit voter service organizations should conduct internal audits to ensure that their 501(c)3 activities follow the spirit and letter of the law. Such an audit is continuous at the Idaho League. 


Candidates, office holders, political parties and nonprofit organizations must consider themselves partners in creating an informed electorate and act accordingly.

 Pull campaign finance law reform to the top of the legislative agenda

Time was, an Idaho legislative candidate could spend $2,500 to run a successful campaign. The state’s campaign finance laws were written for that time. 
Today, tens of millions of dollars are poured into Idaho’s elections and, by law, candidates and organizations are allowed to anonymize many of their funding sources. 
In this environment, helping voters identify sources of information and verify claims has become increasingly difficult. Producers of materials distributed in opposition to Idaho’s Reproductive Freedom and Privacy Initiative (Proposition 1) were primary in flouting the requirement that a funding source be identified. 
Idaho’s Secretary of State Phil McGrane attributed the violations to naivete and relatively poor organization. McGrane acknowledges that many candidates in Idaho are also engaged in a campaign funding “arms race” that Idaho law is inadequate to patrol. Rank and file Idaho voters tell League members they are exhausted and confused by the rhetorical onslaught this money buys. 
The noise increasingly serves to induce fear and to obfuscate, not to educate. 
The fix

Idaho legislative leaders: Finally make good on perennial promises to update campaign finance laws. The central players in American elections are informed voters, not candidates, political parties or campaign financiers. Idaho law governing campaigns should reflect this hierarchy. 


Conduct a serious study of the “Montana Plan” approved this month by more than 60% of voters in Idaho’s neighboring conservative state. The plan changes state code to prohibit entities incorporated in Montana from spending money to influence elections at local, state and federal levels. It reaffirms that corporations are “creatures of state law” and, as such, are subject to the state’s authority to grant or rescind their powers, including the power to spend money to influence politics. While the initiative is already facing court challenges, several other states have cued up to learn more.


Evidence of campaign finance violations committed during this election cycle still exists in yard signs, flyers, brochures, door knocking scripts and other materials. Where possible, violators must be identified and fined albeit at the current inadequate levels ($250 each for candidates and $2,500 each for political action committees). Additional state resources will undoubtedly be necessary to conduct this investigation.

 The wrap

The 2026 cycle will be remembered by many as an unending slog. Idaho voters deserve a respite but myriad issues that contributed to the slog should not await redress. This immediate task belongs to everyone who believes in equal access to the ballot and in securing the integrity of elections.

title: Tower Hill Completes the 3-Peat with 2026 DIAA Girls Volleyball State Championship Win
description: The Tower Hill Hillers defeated the St. Mark’s Spartans, 3-0, to win the 2026 DIAA Girls Volleyball State Championship on November 16.   NEWARK, Del. — Tower Hill junior, Jillian Truesdell, spent most of the game’s final rally patiently waiting around the middle of the net.  The initial action took place to her left. Tower Hill set up a couple ... Read More
text:
The 2026 Tower Hill Volleyball team poses for a team picture after winning the 2026 DIAA Girls Volleyball State Championship, the program’s third straight state title. Photo Credit: Ryan Colasanti
The Tower Hill Hillers defeated the St. Mark’s Spartans, 3-0, to win the 2026 DIAA Girls Volleyball State Championship on November 16.
 
NEWARK, Del. — Tower Hill junior, Jillian Truesdell, spent most of the game’s final rally patiently waiting around the middle of the net. 
The initial action took place to her left. Tower Hill set up a couple chances for junior Cadence Davis that were dug by the Spartans on the opposite side of the net. The Spartans retaliated with a hit that was fielded by eighth-grader Lizzie DiSabatino and passed to senior Parker Lewicki at the center of the net. Lewicki set the ball straight up for Truesdell who was positioned right next to her.
Truesdell placed the ball on the front left edge of the court just beyond the Spartan defense and just within the out of bounds line. As the ball hit the court, Truesdell turned around, raised her arms in the air and was swarmed by her teammates in celebration.
Tower Hill defeated St. Mark’s, 3-0, for the third straight season and won the program’s third state championship title in as many years.
“Throughout the game they’d been blocking the middles and it’s kind of been hard to find open spots, but I just went up there and I knew it had to get done,” Truesdell said postgame. “I found an open spot on the court and it felt amazing.”
The Hillers controlled the action throughout most of the match and never trailed by more than three points in any set. The only time Tower Hill trailed by that margin was early in the second set when the Spartans jumped out to a 4-1 lead. The Hillers followed by scoring three straight points to tie the game and then put together three more stretches where they strung together three straight points to win the set, 25-17. The Hillers won the first set, 25-16, and finished the game with a 25-20 set victory. 
“We had a pretty good gameplan I thought and it played out pretty close to where, to what we thought it was, but, you know, you have to be able to perform,” Tower Hill head coach Michael Sachs said. “Our passing really held up well tonight and that was one of the keys so we were able to kind of play the game we expected it to be.”
While the game might’ve gone to plan, the team’s arrival to the Bob Carpenter Center did not. Tower Hill’s bus experienced issues after hitting a pothole and was halted about a mile away from the stadium along South College Avenue near the intersection of South College Avenue and East Chestnut Hill Road. The team had to walk the rest of the way into the facility, but the trek didn’t hinder the Hillers’ demeanor.
“Well we did have to walk a mile, but I think it really pumped us up more than put us down,” Cadence Davis said. “We were really hype walking on the sidewalk, but it’s ok because, I don’t know, we’re a hype team, it was a lot of energy and we had fun no matter what.”
Davis finished the game with 15 kills and battled through an injury to her left arm she sustained in the team’s semifinal game against Archmere on November 12. Senior Sydney Fischer tied Davis for the team lead with 15 kills herself, finishing the postseason with 90 kills across four games. 
The Hillers finished the season undefeated for the first time in program history and lost only three sets throughout the year. The championship is the program’s fourth volleyball state title all won under Sachs in the past five seasons. The first came in 2022 and set a blueprint for the five seniors (Fischer, Lewicki, Madison Squire, Gianna Laird and Wren Steiner) to sustain.
“The first year we won the state championship in 2022 we never imagined it was even possible for us and that team had some great leaders,” Sachs said. “And they just, they passed down the leadership year after year after year and that’s really been the key.”
The group has done an admirable job of contributing to that sustained success losing only two games over the past three seasons. 
“They have a lot of fun playing, but they are very even keeled,” Sachs said about this team’s seniors. “They never really get high up. They never get too far down. We used to talk about how it was like a business trip to them. They never get out of their heads and the other thing is they just support each other so much.”
“It feels incredible,” Truesdell said about winning her third straight state championship. “We’ve been working towards this all season and it’s just amazing to be able to win with all my best friends.”
The Spartans end the season with a 15-4 overall record and their third straight state championship game appearance.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: Commentary: There is no place for Islamophobia in West Virginia
description: We all live in America, where we say we value the First Amendment and the freedom of religion. But religious freedom can’t be something we defend only for a select few. I want religious freedom for me, and also for you.
text:
Author Cindy Briggs-Biondi's children hold a "Love thy neighbor" sign at a No Kings Protest in March 2026. (Photo courtesy of Cindy Briggs-Biondi) To my Muslim neighbors in West Virginia: I know that right now, in the aftermath of the midterm elections, you are experiencing a climate of renewed hostility, suspicion and Islamophobia. I see the kind of broad, sweeping statements that are being made to denigrate and dehumanize you. I notice the ways that people, many times Christian, mischaracterize Islam as a categorically extremist religion, intent on imposing “Sharia law” on the rest of the country. But I know that the overwhelming majority of Muslims simply practice loving God and loving your neighbor.
I see the rhetoric aimed at Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed and Mayor Zohran Mamdani, and the ways that their Muslim identity has been made a target. I recognize that when a Muslim public figure is portrayed as inherently dangerous because of his faith that you may feel those same sentiments directed toward you. So I want to say clearly: I see what is happening, I know it is wrong, and I want you to know that you do not face it alone.
Islamophobia is a moral and spiritual failure and a form of religious bigotry that diminishes all of our humanity. I reject the conflation of Islam with terrorism, extremism and violence, just as I reject the conflation of the way of Jesus with dominance, control and conquest. I see the way you are continually being told to prove your loyalty or your patriotism over and over again. We all live in America, where we say we value the First Amendment and the freedom of religion. But religious freedom can’t be something we defend only for a select few. I want religious freedom for me, and also for you.
I write to you as a Christian pastor and follower of Jesus, and also on behalf of the leadership of the West Virginia Faith Collective. For me, Jesus is the example by which I seek to live. Jesus commanded me to love God and love my neighbors as myself. You are my neighbor, and I love you. I want a life of wholeness and flourishing for you, just as I wish it for myself. Jesus demonstrates in stories like the parable of the Good Samaritan that religious and cultural “outsiders” are the ones who can teach me what it means to be a good neighbor. The Bible also communicates from the very beginning that every human being possesses inherent dignity because every single one of us is created in the image of God. In the congregation I serve, we regularly say to one another, “You are a beloved child of God, precious and beautiful to behold.” You, my Muslim siblings, are also beloved children of God, precious and beautiful to behold.
I am thankful for the relationships I have been able to begin to cultivate with some of you. I have experienced your hospitality when I’ve been invited to sit down at an interfaith iftar meal. I’ve witnessed your work for justice when we have stood together at the Capitol demanding an end to war, violence and genocide. I’ve seen how you help your neighbors with regular food deliveries. I have heard your cries for peace, lighting candles for those who have no peace.
Our great state of West Virginia is made better by your presence. You are a part of the fabric of our communities, contributing to our shared life, health, economy and well-being of our state. Your children play with my children. I refuse any attempt to define what it means to be a “real” West Virginian or a “real” American in ways that exclude you because of your faith.
So here is what I, as a pastor and a follower of Jesus promise to you: I promise that I will speak out when you are stereotyped, scapegoated or dehumanized. I will disrupt Islamophobic rhetoric wherever I encounter it, and I will defend your right to worship freely and safely, just as I will defend my own. I will continue to seek opportunities to develop genuine relationships, conversation and cooperation with you to make West Virginia a better place for all of us.
As a follower of Jesus, I won’t remain silent when anyone is made to feel unwelcome, or unsafe, or less than human. Jesus calls me to love my neighbor, to welcome the stranger and to stand with those who are mistreated. There are no exceptions, not even for people whose faith is different from mine. On behalf of the West Virginia Faith Collective, I say to you, our Muslim neighbors: You are not strangers to us. You are not a threat to us. You belong here, and we are grateful that you are a part of the life of this state.
In faith and solidarity,
Rev. Cindy Briggs-Biondi and the West Virginia Faith Collective Leadership Team

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: WKY gas pipeline agency is spending state dollars on engineering, litigation, lobbying
description: Critics of a public agency in Western Kentucky that’s trying to build a 53-mile natural gas pipeline have scrutinized the project as the agency has sued landowners, wielding eminent domain, in an effort to secure remaining easements needed to build the pipeline.  Among the questions that these critics, including landowners being sued, have: how the […]
text:
An image showing the proposed natural gas pipeline route through Greg Davenport's family farm in Christian County. Much of the proposed route follows along Interstate 24 in Western Kentucky. (Screenshot/Court exhibit)Critics of a public agency in Western Kentucky that’s trying to build a 53-mile natural gas pipeline have scrutinized the project as the agency has sued landowners, wielding eminent domain, in an effort to secure remaining easements needed to build the pipeline. 
Among the questions that these critics, including landowners being sued, have: how the agency is spending a $30 million appropriation from the Kentucky legislature in 2022 to jumpstart the agency’s efforts, the sole funding source that the Todd County-based Pennyrile Regional Energy Agency has relied on.
Elected officials in the two small Todd County cities of Guthrie and Trenton, with a combined population of fewer than 2,000, formed the public agency in 2019 as the Todd County Natural Gas District. In 2021, the agency rebranded and proposed to build the regional pipeline as part of efforts to expand the region’s natural gas supply as an economic development boon to supply customers including the Fort Campbell military installation and to an existing Novelis aluminum recycling facility for a potential expansion.
But Milton Furman Cook, a Lyon County farmer among the landowners currently being sued, told the Lantern he doesn’t believe the other Western Kentucky counties along the pipeline route — Lyon, Trigg, Caldwell, Christian — will benefit in the same way Todd County will. 
“My tax dollars are being used to condemn my property on a project that will have no benefit for the people in my community,” Cook said. “This would be one thing if this was an interstate that was going to help a lot of people. This is a small group of people that it’s going to benefit.”
A Kentucky Lantern analysis of a recent 12-month window of spending by the agency shows that among the biggest expenditures by the agency are staying local in and around Todd County: payments for engineering fees going toward a local engineering firm in Todd County, and payments to a natural gas consulting firm located in Tennessee right across the Todd County line. The expenditures were obtained through the state’s Open Records Act.
The agency is also spending considerable funding for a Lexington law firm it’s hired to litigate a number of the eminent domain lawsuits it is entangled in with landowners, along with spending to hire a prominent lobbying firm based in Frankfort. 
In a phone interview, Eston Glover, the chair of Pennyrile Regional Energy Agency’s board, refuted the notion that the pipeline was primarily to the benefit of Todd County, saying the entity started in Todd County because local representatives “saw the need” for it. 
“The opportunities to grow from it and to develop a place for our kids to come back and work are going to be occurring in every county,” Glover said. “We want anybody that touches this line to be able to get gas through our pipe to their property.” 
Engineering, litigation and lobbying
Among the top expenditures that PREA reported from October 2025 through September 2026 included: 

D2 Energy, a consulting firm for natural gas transportation based just miles away from Guthrie, one of two Todd County cities that created the agency through an interlocal agreement. PREA spent $373,750 for engineering fees toward D2 Energy. 
Payments for easements ranging in the tens of thousands of dollars for each payment to landowners. PREA made $253,116.00 in payments for easements over the 12-month time frame. 
McGhee Engineering, a Todd County-based engineering firm that has worked on wastewater and drinking water infrastructure projects in Western Kentucky. McGhee Engineering has received $548,900 for engineering fees from PREA. 
Sturgill, Turner, Barker & Moloney, PLLC, a Lexington-based law firm that PREA has hired as counsel for litigation against landowners over pipeline easements and litigation against Kentucky’s utility regulator. The law firm has received $287,599.39 from PREA. 
Commonwealth Alliances LLC, a prominent Frankfort-based lobbying firm whose leader was among the highest paid out of all lobbyists in Frankfort. Commonwealth Alliances LLC received $55,256.00 from PREA. 
Tim Thomas, a consultant with Paducah-based Cleaview Consulting LLC, who served previously as the former co-chairman of the Appalachian Regional Commission and was a field representative for U.S. Sen. Mitch McConnell. Thomas’ firm received $56,592.37 from PREA.


Glover said that the agency picked D2 Energy and McGhee Engineering because the firms were “familiar with the area” and the agency. Glover said D2 Energy manages Guthrie’s existing municipal natural gas system, which supplies the existing Novelis plant; McGhee Engineering had also built a gas line extension to the plant. 
“We hired them to do some preliminary engineering. But when we got into the process of going forward, our board decided that they had proven themselves, and we chose them to be our guides for developing this project,” Glover said.
When asked if other firms besides D2 Energy and McGhee Engineering were considered, Brock, the agency’s executive administrator for the agency, said only McGhee Engineering had responded to a request for qualifications sent out by the agency in 2022. 
In a deposition for one of the eminent domain lawsuits in Christian County, McGhee Engineering President Michael McGhee told an attorney representing sued landowners that his firm had not designed a gas pipeline before as large as the 16-inch pipeline that PREA was planning to build. McGhee was also briefly a board member for the local economic development nonprofit Todd County Industrial Foundation, according to the deposition. 
Glover also said the agency hired Tim Thomas for his political connections, along with hiring the prominent lobbying firm Commonwealth Alliances LLC to have a presence in Frankfort. 
“We felt it behooved us to know what was going on legislatively or what was going on around the state that could impact or affect what we’re trying to do with this project,” Glover said. “There’s not many organizations that are trying to do something as broad as we are that do not have some type of lobbyist or information gatherer.” 
The Pennyrile Regional Energy Agency did lobby state lawmakers during the legislative session this year, with Rep. Jason Petrie, R-Elkton, the powerful chair of the Kentucky House Appropriations and Revenue Committee, successfully passing a state law that provided PREA an exception from being regulated by the Kentucky Public Service Commission, the state’s utility regulator. 
When asked about what issues the agency had lobbied in Frankfort, Glover declined to comment because of the agency’s ongoing litigation. 
With that spending, PREA has about $21.8 million in its bank account as of September 2026, according to a bank account balance sheet. The agency has received income in the form of interest payments from its account with the local bank Elkton Bank & Trust Co.; Glover, the agency’s vice chair Gary Traughber and the agency’s attorney Jeff Traughber, who serves as the elected Todd County attorney, also serve on the bank’s board of directors. 
In a deposition earlier in the Christian County court case, Glover told an attorney representing sued landowners that there were no specific state reporting requirements for the $30 million appropriation but that PREA conducted its own audits. He said he updated Petrie, the local state representative, and Gov. Andy Beshear “orally, personally” about the agency. 
A spokesperson for House GOP leadership referred questions about reporting requirements for the funding to the state executive branch. 
In an emailed statement, Scottie Ellis, a spokesperson for Gov. Andy Beshear’s office, said the 2022 law that appropriated the $30 million for the Pennyrile Regional Energy Agency did not include any reporting requirements for the funding. Ellis said the Department for Local Government within the governor’s office does require a completion report for the earmark. 
Glover said his agency has tried to be open to the public, saying their goal is to “put the facts out there” and “not to discredit or to tear down anybody else’s thoughts.” The agency has recently spent funding on advertising. The agency’s website, which previously had no information when the board meets, now features a tentative webpage under construction titled “Board Meetings”. 
“We feel like our records are just exactly the way that they’re supposed to be handled. We have not avoided sharing that information with anybody that wanted to see it, and it’s open to be seen every day,” Glover said. “We’ve learned that there’s so many things that need gas in our general area, and that just reinforces our belief that we’re doing the right thing.”

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Commentary: Kentucky missed the tax trigger. Here’s how to hit it.
description: For the second consecutive year, and the third time in four years, Kentucky has failed to meet the revenue benchmarks required to further cut the state income tax. The shortfall this time wasn’t even close, as General Fund receipts fell short of the threshold needed. Kentucky’s new tax regime has cut the personal income tax […]
text:
In January, at a pro-housing rally, Sen. Robby Mills, R-Henderson, said bills to tackle the housing shortage should be moving soon in the Kentucky legislature. (Kentucky Lantern photo by Liam Niemeyer)For the second consecutive year, and the third time in four years, Kentucky has failed to meet the revenue benchmarks required to further cut the state income tax. The shortfall this time wasn’t even close, as General Fund receipts fell short of the threshold needed.
Kentucky’s new tax regime has cut the personal income tax rate from 5 percent to 3.5 percent. In an analysis for the Bluegrass Institute, Rea Hederman Jr. and Sai Martha found that reaching 3 percent would add $810 million in GDP and $370 million in private investment in its first year, and by 2034 would generate $850 million in annual investment and 7,000 new jobs. Our large rainy day fund and the healthy General Fund surplus confirm that Kentucky is not spending recklessly; this means the problem is on the growth side of the ledger.
The commonwealth’s competitors aren’t slowing down. Iowa, Louisiana and Idaho cut individual income tax rates in 2025, and this year Montana did. Both Mississippi and South Carolina have enacted revenue-triggered phase-outs aimed at eliminating the income tax, and Oklahoma has cut its rate with triggers for future cuts.
Senator Chris McDaniel, R-Ryland Heights, chairman of the budget committee, said Kentucky’s miss this year demonstrates the “responsibility” and “reactiveness” of the model. He’s clearly right on the first count, but reactiveness is the wrong posture for a state that has set elimination of its income tax as a long-term goal. Kentucky needs a proactive growth agenda that expands the tax base by making the commonwealth a better place to start a business, build a home, and earn a living.
Three simple reforms, none of which require new spending, would accomplish exactly that.
 Cut the red tape
Kentucky’s regulatory code contains more than 127,000 restrictive requirements spread across 6.4 million words. Between 2020 and 2024, the commonwealth’s regulatory burden grew 8.8 percent – double the national median of 4.4 percent. Every one of those restrictions is a barrier between a would-be entrepreneur and satisfied customers.
Patrick McLaughlin of the Hoover Institution, writing for the Bluegrass Institute, documented what happens when states take this problem seriously. When British Columbia cut its regulatory burden by 40 percent, GDP growth surged. Virginia’s 25 percent reduction saves residents an estimated $1.2 billion a year. McLaughlin’s model projects that a 20% cut in Kentucky would leave Kentucky’s economy roughly $14 billion larger by 2037.
Frankfort should begin with a systematic review of the commonwealth’s administrative code by adopting regulatory transparency, identifying rules that are no longer useful and sunsetting them. The Bluegrass Institute’s own research finds that even a 10% reduction in restrictions would raise growth. The General Assembly should give regulatory reform the same priority as income tax reduction – the two are indelibly connected.
 Let Kentuckians build
People follow opportunity, and homes are where jobs go to sleep at night. In the Lexington and Bowling Green housing markets, median home prices are near historic highs relative to household income, pricing out workers and families Kentucky needs to attract.
The cause is not a lack of demand, it is a thicket of mostly local regulations – minimum lot sizes, parking mandates, and permitting timelines that stretch months past any reasonable review period. This artificially constrains supply. The Bluegrass Institute’s “Menu of Options for Kentucky Housing Reform” lays out a detailed deregulatory agenda: permitting shot clocks, by-right approval of accessory dwelling units and small multifamily buildings, elimination of arbitrary lot-size minimums and adoption of the “Golden Girls Rule” that lets unrelated adults share a home without local government meddling.
Virginia’s regulatory streamlining, which included simplifying housing rules, is projected to cut roughly $24,000 from the cost of a new home. More homes mean more property tax revenue, more construction jobs, more appliance and furniture sales, and more families putting down roots in Kentucky communities, which all show up in General Fund receipts.
Here in Kentucky, lawmakers failed to deliver on housing affordability when the omnibus housing bill died in the final hours of the 2026 session. This is in spite of the fact that the Kentucky Housing Task Force, co-chaired by Sen. Robby Mills and Rep. Susan Tyler Witten, embraced many Bluegrass Institute recommendations that would expand housing supply at no cost to taxpayers. Too often, the legislature has substituted new government programs like trust funds, loan subsidies, and tax credits for the genuine deregulation that would let the market build. The next session should finish what the task force started.
 Open the door
Kentucky requires a government license to work in 132 of 246 occupations tracked by the Archbridge Institute, making us the ninth-most-burdensome licensing regime in the US. The Institute for Justice’s License to Work report finds that Kentucky licenses 38 of 102 lower-income occupations it studied, ranking the commonwealth 13th in licensing burden for the workers who can least afford it.
Research suggests occupational licensing reduces employment by up to 27 % in licensed fields. It is a barrier that keeps people out of the labor force, and is exactly the opposite of what a state trying to grow its tax base should do. Kentucky’s July unemployment rate was 4.7%, above the national average of 4.1%. Neighboring Indiana, which licenses fewer occupations, had an unemployment rate of 3.3%. Correlation is not causation, but the pattern is worth examining.
Every barber, auctioneer, florist and massage therapist who is deterred from working in Kentucky by months of mandatory training, hundreds of dollars in fees and exams that test academic knowledge rather than practical competence is a taxpayer the commonwealth never gains.
The Bluegrass Institute has identified occupational licensing reform as a key move to improve Kentucky’s economic freedom. Kentucky ranks in the bottom half of states on the Fraser Institute’s economic freedom index and is the second-most federally dependent state in the nation. Reducing licensing barriers is one of the fastest ways to change both numbers.
 The path forward
Kentucky’s income tax trigger mechanism was designed to ensure that tax cuts are undertaken by a stable government with dependable revenues, not revenues borrowed from future taxpayers. But missing the trigger year after year should not be treated as an acceptable outcome; it should be treated as a policy signal that Kentucky’s private sector is not growing fast enough.
The General Assembly reconvenes in January. Lawmakers who are serious about finishing what HB 8 started should arrive in Frankfort with an agenda that matches their ambition. The path to zero runs through a bigger, freer Kentucky economy.

name: Virginia Mercury
title: Virginia lawmakers weigh using marijuana taxes to fund school substance use programs
description: Virginia lawmakers on Monday discussed using future marijuana tax revenue to expand substance use prevention and counseling in public schools, after a new survey found that few secondary schools screen students for substance use risks or have specialized counselors.  The Joint Commission to Oversee the Transition of the Commonwealth into a Cannabis Retail Ma[...]
text:
Virginia lawmakers are weighing whether to use tax revenue from future retail marijuana sales to expand substance use prevention and counseling in public schools. (Photo by Getty Images)Virginia lawmakers on Monday discussed using future marijuana tax revenue to expand substance use prevention and counseling in public schools, after a new survey found that few secondary schools screen students for substance use risks or have specialized counselors. 
The Joint Commission to Oversee the Transition of the Commonwealth into a Cannabis Retail Market learned that just 13% of secondary schools surveyed in September use formal screening to identify students at risk, while about one in five have a substance use counselor.
Del. Cia Price, D-Newport News, urged the state to help schools pay for screening, evidence-based prevention programs and alternatives to suspension while the Virginia Department of Education studies staffing needs and costs. 
“I don’t want to wait until 2028 to find out that we should have done something this year,” Price said. 
Virginia is preparing to launch legal retail market sales July 1, 2027. A briefing by the Behavioral Health Commission projected that the forthcoming state retail cannabis tax of 6% to 8% could generate $11.3 million in fiscal 2028, rising to $74 million by fiscal 2032. 
The money would be divided among several designated purposes, including K-12 education and substance use prevention and treatment through community service boards. The joint commission is responsible for recommending how the revenue should be spent. 
 Schools struggle to intervene early

John Barfield, a policy analyst for the Behavioral Health Commission, told lawmakers that youth substance use has declined over the long term and that Virginia generally fares better than the national average. 
But vaping on school grounds remains a concern, he said, particularly as nicotine concentrations in vaping products and THC potency in marijuana have increased. 
Virginia schools already cover substance use in health classes. Yet only 11% of elementary schools and 29% of secondary schools represented in the survey of school counselors reported combining classroom instruction with evidence-based prevention programs and community partnerships. 
Barfield said research shows that approach has the strongest lasting effect on student behavior.
Formal screening could also help identify students who need intervention before their problems worsen. According to Barfield, research shows universal screening identifies more than twice as many at-risk students as informal methods such as staff observation.
Some schools, however, expressed concern that screening could reveal more students needing help than their staff could accommodate. 
“I think the concern, in many instances, is, if we discover that a significant portion of our students have a problem and we don’t have the resources to address that problem, where does that leave us?” Barfield said. “Counselors or nurses could screen students and refer those at highest risk for services.”
Del. Katrina Callsen, D-Albemarle, said screening could also give parents information to help address problems at home. Barfield said parental consent would be required. 
The survey found that about a quarter of responding secondary schools offered diversion programs as alternatives to suspension. 
Price tied that finding to testimony the commission heard in September from RISE for Youth, which warned that increasing penalties for public marijuana use could place additional financial burdens on families. 
State data cited by the group showed that marijuana-related juvenile intake complaints declined 30% from fiscal 2019 to fiscal 2024, even as the share originating in schools rose from 17% to 54%. 
“About 60% of responding secondary schools partnered with an outpatient provider, usually a community services board,” Barfield said. “About a third brought clinicians into schools, easing transportation and scheduling barriers.” 
 Getting money to school divisions

The Behavioral Health Commission has adopted recommendations to fund a new position at the Virginia Department of Education in the 2027 budget, assess school divisions’ substance use prevention and treatment needs by Dec. 1, 2027, and conduct follow-up surveys every two years beginning in 2028. 
Barfield estimated the new position would cost about $120,000. The employee would help school divisions select evidence-based programs, train staff and put prevention efforts into practice. 
Asked what could help schools sooner, Barfield pointed to certified substance use counselors.
“They seem to be, based on our site visits, kind of the glue that holds all of it together, and they have the capacity to go out and make those community partnerships,” he said. “They have the capacity to kind of identify those evidence-based programs, and they have the necessary training to do early intervention really well.”
Virginia has no dedicated funding stream for substance use services in schools, Barfield said. 
Much of the existing support comes from grants, while general state education funding helps pay for school counselors who often handle substance use concerns alongside their other responsibilities. 
Nathalie Molliet-Ribet, executive director of the Behavioral Health Commission, suggested providing every school division with a baseline allocation to support at least one employee focused on substance use. 
She said competitive grants can put less-resourced divisions at a disadvantage because they may lack the staff needed to prepare applications. 
Sen. Lashrecse Aird, D-Henrico, who chairs the commission, asked how lawmakers could make sure divisions spend the money on the intended services. 
Molliet-Ribet suggested defining eligible expenses and requiring divisions to report how they used the funding. 
Del. Will Morefield, R-Tazewell, cautioned against requiring local governments to hire additional employees without providing enough state money to cover the costs. 
“The majority of rural counties, especially in the area that I represent, just simply can’t afford to take on another position,” Morefield said. 
Other states already direct marijuana tax revenue toward education and substance use services, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures. 
Colorado has used marijuana revenue to fund grants that help schools to hire behavioral health professionals. 
Molliet-Ribet said members of the Behavioral Health Commission would introduce the budget amendments needed to carry out their recommendations. 
Aird said the joint commission could also put forward its own recommendations as lawmakers prepare for the 2027 legislative session, which begins Jan. 13.

name: Virginia Mercury
title: Commentary: Getting back to Virginia amid the FAA chaos wasn’t ‘The Odyssey,’ but it certainly was a pain
description: It was around the fifth delay message Saturday from American Airlines, while stuck at a shoulder-to-shoulder gate of would-be passengers at the New Orleans airport, that I wanted to emit a blood-curdling scream. Probably would’ve been apropos, given that The Boss and I repeatedly failed to leave the city often synonymous with voodoo. Yes, we […]
text:
A plane flies over Norfolk Tower at Norfolk International Airport. (Photo courtesy of Norfolk International Airport)It was around the fifth delay message Saturday from American Airlines, while stuck at a shoulder-to-shoulder gate of would-be passengers at the New Orleans airport, that I wanted to emit a blood-curdling scream.
Probably would’ve been apropos, given that The Boss and I repeatedly failed to leave the city often synonymous with voodoo.
Yes, we were among the tens of thousands of fliers across the country affected by the nationwide ground stop on Friday evening. We originally had been set to leave New Orleans around 4:15 p.m. CST (bound for Charlotte before eventually arriving in Norfolk) when things came to a halt. It was only the second such stoppage since 9/11.
We knew little about what caused the crisis in those first few hours. Given the various explanations since then, I’m not sure the oft-incompetent Trump administration knows what’s going on even now.
The incident affected 532 flights from four major Virginia airports, my colleague Nathaniel Cline reported.
FAA ground stop disrupts 532 flights at 4 Virginia airports

Now, don’t get me wrong: The Boss and I were in a much better position than most folks. We’re retired. We didn’t have infants stuck to us. We’re ambulatory. We didn’t have to sleep on chairs or the floor, as other passengers were forced to do. 
And we could easily afford any unplanned expenses. For example:
As The Boss waited for a gate agent to reschedule our initial flight Friday night for Saturday, I searched hotels for fast-dwindling rooms nearby. Cost: $163.
We scoured Uber – which jacked up prices to more than $60 for the two-mile ride. We instead queued up with dozens of others waiting for cabs outside the airport. Cost: $22, with tip. We caught Uber the next morning to return to the airport. (The fee had miraculously dropped to $11 since the surge in demand had plummeted.)
We both got overpriced, middling lunches at an airport restaurant. They were $56 with tip.
Now, multiply those fees thousands of times, and you get an idea of the extra dough that passengers forked over this past weekend – if they could spare it. You can’t measure the inconvenience and exasperation.
In the meantime, we endured more than a dozen flight delays Saturday. My wife had to repeatedly tell me to chill out and watch college football on nearby TV screens, since we were figurative prisoners at the airport.
After fleeing the New Orleans airport during the nationwide ground stop on Friday evening, my wife (aka, “The Boss,”) and I spent several long hours — and many dashed hopes — trying to catch flights that would return us to Norfolk. It was exasperating, and a little costly for us. (Photo by Roger Chesley/Virginia Mercury)
When we finally boarded Saturday evening and then arrived in Charlotte, we sprinted through the terminal to barely make our connection to Norfolk.
I mean, it wasn’t Matt Damon in “The Odyssey.” We didn’t have to navigate Scylla and Charybdis, after all. 
But it wasn’t any fun, either.
