name: Florida Phoenix
title: Will Florida Republicans make a change in leadership or stay the course?
description: While Florida Republicans fared better than most of their compatriots around the nation in this month’s midterm elections, they still took major losses in the Florida Legislature, with Democrats netting 16 seats in the state House. One of the questions party members are considering ahead of an election for party chair in January is whether […]
text:
Republican Party of Florida Chairman Evan Power at the RPOF's Sunshine State Showdown on June 27, 2026 (Photo by Mitch Perry/Florida Phoenix)While Florida Republicans fared better than most of their compatriots around the nation in this month’s midterm elections, they still took major losses in the Florida Legislature, with Democrats netting 16 seats in the state House.
One of the questions party members are considering ahead of an election for party chair in January is whether the results were a one-off due to Donald Trump’s unpopularity, or because Florida voters are showing real discontent with the GOP after three decades of one-party rule in Tallahassee.
That’s the backdrop for the campaign for leadership of the Republican Party of Florida (RPOF), as Chairman Evan Power faces a reelection challenge from Martin County State Committeeman James Campo. The vote will take place in Orlando on Jan. 9.
James Campo is the assistant treasurer of the Republican Party of Florida and a State Committeeman from Martin County (Photo from James Campo’s website)
Campo, 62, announced his candidacy in June, when he surmised that the seat would be vacant as Power ran for election in Florida’s Second Congressional District. However, the best-laid plans for both men changed in August after Power finished third in the GOP primary, resulting in his pivot to seeking reelection for chair.
“I think it’s basically a race of the grassroots versus the inside-Tallahassee beltway,” Campo told the Phoenix in an interview last week. “I’ve been to 60 counties listening intently on the issues and not just repeating talking points set by the RNC.”
Campo is part of the RPOF now, serving since 2023 as assistant treasurer. A certified financial planner, he previously worked in local government for a decade as both mayor and town commissioner of Sewall’s Point.
Power, 45, is a registered lobbyist with Tallahassee’s Ramba Consulting Group who has served as party chair since 2024. (He previously served as Leon County Republican Executive Committee chair). He’s proud that, under his watch, Florida Republicans have continued to build a voter registration lead that’s now more than 1.5 million over the Democrats, and boasts that while much of the country went blue on Election Day, “We held the line and stayed red and elected all of our statewide officers.”
He dismisses any concerns that Florida — which survived the blue tsunami but still saw its top-of-ticket candidates win only narrowly — might be shifting back to its former status as a swing state. He notes that the political party in power historically loses congressional seats in midterm elections.
“I think that when you look at the voters, we have voters turn out. They did not turn out in this election,” Power said. “We, obviously, in Florida will give them a reason to turn out again moving forward by delivering on the promises that we made on the campaign trail. So, I think that we’re a red state. We’re going to remain a red state, and this is probably the closest that the Democrats will get to success for a long period of time.”
Internal problems
One issue that has arisen place during Power’s tenure as the head of the RPOF has been the removal of numerous party members for various alleged transgressions. In some cases, it was because those members were accused of violating membership rules. Power says the idea was to stop individuals from joining Republican Executive Committees with the intent “to do damage.”
“Look no further than Bobby Williams and Frank Collige, who ran Republican campaigns and then immediately supported Democrats,” he said, referring to candidates for governor and chief financial officer this year, respectively, who after losing in their primaries endorsed the Democratic candidates in the general election.
In fall 2024, Power and the RPOF executive board suspended the entire Manatee County Republican Executive Committee, alleging “numerous grievances,” such as lawsuits against leaders and police reports, as reported by the Bradenton Herald.
“What we have done under my chairmanship is actually enforce the rules for the first time in a long time,” Power said. “And it’s been an unbiased enforcement of the rules across the state. And what’s happened is that we’ve cleaned up some situations where people are being alienated and not allowed to join their RECs so people can get control, and yes, sometimes people get upset because they can’t be in charge. But if you’re that upset for not being in charge, maybe you’re not in this for the right reasons.”
Campo disagrees.
“I think there’s some selective enforcement of rules, which has created some alienation amongst party leaders,” he said.
Campo pledges that, if elected chair, he won’t seek nor hold public office during his term. He says Power was distracted from his party duties when he ran for Congress.
“I think there’s a conflict,” Campo said. “The Bible says you can’t serve two masters. And I think that he was distracted running for Congress and receiving full salary and being the chair for seven months.”
Power counters that he’s been “the most active and engaged chairman on the county level,” noting that he’s traveled more than 350,000 miles crisscrossing the state for years, attending Lincoln Day Dinners and other local party events.
Two former RPOF chairs — Blaise Ingoglia and Joe Gruters — simultaneously served in the Legislature while leading the party over the past decade.
Endorsements
The universe of voters who will make this decision is around 240 or 250 individuals — county party chairs, state committee members, some appointees of the governor, members of the Florida Senate and House, and members of Congress.
Campo claims nearly 90 commitments to vote for him.
“People in private are telling me that we need some new energy and we need to be outside of the beltway in Tallahassee and they like my background,” he said.
Power initially rolled out 60 endorsements for his campaign, and now says he’s up to 70 endorsements. He has the support of some of the biggest members of the party, including Rick Scott, Ashley Moody, and, as of Friday, the incoming titular head of the party, Gov.-elect Byron Donalds.
“Evan Power has delivered results for Florida Republicans,” Donalds announced on X. “His focus on voter registration, turnout, and a strong grassroots organization helped our team win in 2024 and 2026.”
Some observers noted that Power did Donalds a solid in June when he announced, to the disappointment of many, including Gov. Ron DeSantis, that there would be no debate between the Republican candidates in the gubernatorial primary during the party’s “Sunshine Showdown” in Broward County. Power announced that only Donalds had reached the criteria to qualify.
Meanwhile, at least one group is campaigning against Power’s reelection bid.
The America First Party of Florida became a ballot-qualified political party in Florida last year, formed by disaffected MAGA conservatives. Their vice chairman is Trent Wayman, a former Manatee County state committeeman whom Powers removed in 2024. The group released a written statement over the weekend saying that another term for Power “would be a setback for principled conservatives and legitimate conservative leadership in the State of Florida.”
“Out objection is straightforward: we believe Power’s leadership puts insiders first and treats grassroots activists as a problem when they challenge the establishment,” said Wayman, in an email to the Phoenix. “Those activists do the work, knock the doors, and turn out the voters. They deserve a voice, not pressure to fall in line or get out of the way.”

name: Maryland Matters
title: Supreme Court won’t take up Maryland gun rights case
description: The U.S. Supreme Court on Monday let stand a lower court's ruling that upheld the Maryland law placing restrictions on carrying guns in "sensitive places" frequented by the public, including state parks, amusement parks and mass transit.
text:
The U.S. Supreme Court on Monday let stand a lower court's ruling that upheld the Maryland law placing restrictions on carrying guns in "sensitive places" frequented by the public, including state parks, amusement parks and mass transit. (Photo by Aristide Economopoulos/New Jersey Monitor)The U.S. Supreme Court on Monday let stand a lower court’s ruling that upheld the Maryland law placing restrictions on carrying guns in “sensitive places” frequented by the public, including state parks, amusement parks and mass transit.
The court refused to hear an appeal by gun-rights groups of a January ruling by the 4th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals in Novotny v. Moore, which upheld most of the 2023 law. That means Maryland’s restrictions will stand.
In a separate statement on the case, Justice Clarence Thomas said he was “skeptical” that each portion of the Maryland law restricting gun-carrying is consistent with Second Amendment principles. But Thomas also said he agreed with the court’s decision to reject the Maryland case for a hearing, because “the breadth of petitioners’ challenge would complicate our review.”
The Maryland Attorney General’s Office, which was defending the law, did not immediately respond to a request for comment Monday, but gun-rights groups said they were disappointed with the decision.
Feds consider next steps after losing challenge to Montgomery County gun law

Some of Maryland’s location-specific constraints on carrying weapons are long-standing. But some were added or amended by the General Assembly in the 2023 law, including restrictions on properties hosting children and vulnerable people (such as daycare facilities, schools and hospitals), government buildings and special event and entertainment areas.
Bill Sack, senior director of legal operations at the Second Amendment Foundation, said his organization — which was among the petitioners — was “disappointed” to see the high court reject the case, arguing that Maryand “has extinguished the Second Amendment rights of its residents” by creating “multiple categories of so-called sensitive places.”
“We are encouraged, however, with Justice Thomas’ statement in which he casts serious doubt as to the constitutionality of laws like Maryland’s,” Sack wrote.
The foundation has a narrower case pending before the Supreme Court, focused squarely on New York’s sensitive places carry ban in public parks, Sack noted.
“We are hopeful the Court takes a very hard look at that case and elects to restore the right to carry for the Americans all over the country that are subject to these unconstitutional laws,” Sack wrote.
Another petitioner, Maryland Shall Issue, also bemoaned the Supreme Court’s rejection of the Maryland case.
“The Court’s order is, of course, a disappointment, but we will continue to press appropriate challenges to misguided legislation that is designed for no other reason than to eviscerate the general right to publicly carry arms for self-defense,” read the group’s statement.
The high court’s decision came one week after a U.S. District Court judge in Maryland upheld a similar law from Montgomery County, dismissing a challenge that had been filed by the U.S. Justice Department.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: How America’s first hospice took root in CT
description: The work Kübler-Ross set out to do remains unfinished. Let us recommit ourselves to three remedies for problems she identified during her life's work.
text:
Elisabeth Kübler-Ross was born 100 years ago this past July. She is remembered, almost entirely, for five words: denial, anger, bargaining, depression, acceptance. They make up a model of grief so thoroughly absorbed into the culture that it now turns up in sports commentary and breakup advice. 
The five stages made her famous, but another lasting legacy of hers took root in Connecticut. A never-published letter from her archives shows how the ambitions she shared with a Yale nursing dean helped give the country its first hospice, and how far American end-of-life care still has to go.
Earlier this year, her family shared with me a letter she typed on Jan. 1, 1971, to Dame Cicely Saunders, the British physician who had opened St. Christopher’s Hospice in London four years earlier. Buried in casual conversation about her 10-year-old son and an upcoming trip, she asks whether Saunders knows that she and Florence Wald, former dean of the Yale School of Nursing in New Haven, have “secret ambitions to have a St. Christopher in USA.”

That phrase deserves translation. In 1971, the United States did not have a single hospice program. The ambitions did not stay secret long. Nineteen months later, on Aug. 7, 1972, Kübler-Ross told the U.S. Senate Special Committee on Aging that Yale had applied for grants to start a hospice like St. Christopher’s.
By 1974, Wald’s team of nurses, physicians and clergy was caring for seriously ill patients in their homes from a small office in New Haven. Their organization, now known as Connecticut Hospice, was the nation’s first hospice. That year, state regulators approved construction of the country’s first hospice facility in Branford, which opened to inpatients in 1980. Connecticut Hospice still cares for patients on the Branford waterfront today.
Idaho Sen. Frank Church opened the 1972 hearings by noting that at least 80% of Americans were then dying in institutions. During her testimony, Kübler-Ross recounted a story that crystallized the problem: a 28-year-old mother of three with liver disease had been moved to the last room at the end of a long hallway, far from the nursing station, with no visitors. One day Kübler-Ross found her sitting on the edge of the bed, holding the telephone receiver off the hook. When asked what she was doing, the woman replied that she simply wanted to hear a sound.
By the time she testified, Kübler-Ross had interviewed more than 500 dying patients. Her research found that people at the end of life were not, for the most part, terrified of death. They were terrified of being left alone with it. She told the Senate that patients needed, besides hope, reassurance that they would not be deserted, even though most felt deserted anyway.
A decade later, in 1982, Congress passed the bipartisan Medicare hospice benefit, widely regarded as one of the great achievements in American health policy, with roots traceable directly to Kübler-Ross’s “secret ambitions.” Today, the benefit provides care to more than 1.8 million American seniors each year at a cost of $28 billion and growing. In 2024, for the first time, a majority of Medicare decedents, 52.9%, were in hospice when they died. Roughly a third now die at home, the most common single place of death.
The results are extraordinary. Yet the work Kübler-Ross set out to do remains unfinished. In her centennial year, let us recommit ourselves to three remedies for problems she identified during her life’s work. Those problems persist today, and they are as much psychological as they are matters of policy.
First, pay for palliative care from the moment of diagnosis, not after the last treatment fails. The median hospice stay in America is 19 days. Kübler-Ross envisioned relationships measured in months — enough time for denial, anger, and bargaining to do their work, enough time to finish what she called unfinished business. Nineteen days is barely enough to learn a family’s names. 
In her Senate testimony, she drew a distinction clinicians should find uncomfortable: most of the nursing-home patients she met had not reached acceptance but resignation, which she described as a feeling of defeat. Acceptance takes time and company. Resignation only takes waiting. The clinical case for early palliative care is settled; Medicare’s payment structure should follow it. And we should reimburse providers commensurate with the level of care delivered, rather than the one-size-fits-all per diem in place since the benefit’s creation.
Second, protect the integrity of the Medicare hospice benefit. In 1972, Kübler-Ross told the Senate that Medicare and Medicaid, as designed, “tend to enhance institutionalization” — the very first response, she said, was “Let’s hospitalize the patient.” Today’s distortion is different but no less harmful. 
When Medicare first certified hospices in 1983, one in ten was for-profit; by 2024, four in five were. Nonprofit hospices have declined nearly 15 percent in just five years while for-profits grew by 60 percent, and research published in Health Affairs last fall found that private-equity-owned hospices reported the highest margins and the lowest spending on direct patient care. The market has grown at a pace no oversight system was built to police — fraud severe enough that in May, Medicare froze enrollment of new hospices nationwide. Yet enrollment records still do not require hospices to disclose private equity ownership, and regulators cannot police what they cannot see. Ownership transparency, real oversight to root out fraud, and quality measures that assess whether a person’s life was better — not simply how many days were billed — are overdue. 
Legislation introduced this spring would attempt the first real modernization of the benefit since 1982. Congress should take it up on a bipartisan basis. Scale, which was always the goal, has become the problem; quality must become the standard.
Third, treat connection as clinical care. The abandonment Kübler-Ross documented is now a public health epidemic we call social isolation. In 2023, the U.S. Surgeon General issued an advisory on loneliness calling it “far more than just a bad feeling – it harms both individual and societal health.”  Roughly one in four adults over 65 reports being socially isolated, and the consequences are staggering: chronic loneliness is linked to a 50 percent increased risk of dementia, a 29 percent increased risk of heart disease, and a 32 percent increased risk of stroke — as harmful to health, research has found, as smoking 15 cigarettes a day. 
In March of last year, I testified before the same Senate committee she did, 53 years on. The terminology has changed; the need has not. We should screen for isolation the way we screen for pain, and we should support the roughly 59 million family caregivers providing more than $1 trillion in unpaid care annually — increasingly the frontlines of care for our aging population — with real financial, emotional, and workplace support.
Kübler-Ross understood that hospice was never merely a service delivery model. It was a philosophy of care grounded in dignity, honest communication, and accompaniment. The dying are not problems to be managed. They are people to be met, heard, and supported.
One hundred years after her birth, the question before us is whether our health care system will continue to honor that legacy.  I can think of no better way to mark her centennial than to advance her “secret ambitions” together.
Andrew MacPherson is senior adviser to the National Partnership for Healthcare and Hospice Innovation (NPHI), serves on the board of the Elisabeth Kübler-Ross Foundation, is founder and executive chair of the Foundation for Social Connection Action Network (F4SC-AN), and co-founded the Global Initiative on Loneliness and Connection. He is the founding principal and managing partner of Healthsperien, a Washington health care advisory firm.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: A baby’s mental health begins before birth
description: Black women accounted for just 13 percent of live births in Connecticut but 27 percent of pregnancy-associated deaths.
text:
A baby’s mental health story begins earlier than most people realize. It starts before birth, shaped in part by the health, stress, safety and support experienced by the mom carrying that child.
Pregnancy can bring extraordinary joy. It can also bring uncertainty, fear and stress. Those emotions are a normal part of life, and experiencing them does not mean a mother is harming her baby. We know that persistent stress and the conditions surrounding a pregnancy can affect maternal well-being and the environment in which a baby develops.
That is why supporting maternal mental health is also an investment in infant mental health.
I was reminded of this recently when I attended the launch of “Big Work Happens Here,” a new Connecticut initiative focused on infant mental health and the role each of us can play in shaping the well-being of the next generation. The campaign calls that collective effort “Team Baby.” Importantly, the work starts before a baby is born.
Research has linked prenatal stress with changes in birth weight and heightened stress reactivity later in life. That makes the environment surrounding pregnancy important, from the quality and accessibility of healthcare to whether a mother feels safe, supported, heard and able to get help when she needs it.
In my work in maternal health, I have seen how seemingly simple things can change a pregnancy experience: A provider who takes time to listen; a family member who recognizes that a mother is struggling; a doula who helps her understand her choices; a care team that connects her with resources before stress becomes a crisis.
But that support does not reach everyone equally.
For Black women, pregnancy occurs against the backdrop of disparities in maternal health. And Connecticut is not immune. Despite our state’s reputation for wealth and health, significant differences in maternal outcomes remain. According to the 2026 Connecticut Maternal Mortality Review Committee report, Black people accounted for just 13 percent of live births in Connecticut but 27 percent of pregnancy-associated deaths.
Those numbers are not abstractions. Black women know them. Their families know them. They see these experiences in their communities. The knowledge itself can add another layer of worry to a time that should be filled with joy and anticipation.
Nor can these disparities simply be explained away by education or economic opportunity. National research found that Black women with a college degree or higher were 1.6 times as likely to die from pregnancy-related causes as white women who had not completed high school. Among women with college degrees, Black women were 5.2 times as likely as white women to die from pregnancy-related causes.
Perhaps most troubling is that research has found that more than 80 percent of pregnancy-related deaths are preventable.
We can and must do better.
These statistics can be frightening, and women should know them. But knowledge should empower, not paralyze. Every woman deserves the opportunity to reclaim the joy of pregnancy and to be an active participant in her care.
That means knowing maternal warning signs. It means choosing providers who listen and take concerns seriously. It means asking questions and participating in decisions about the birth experience. When something does not feel right, it means speaking up and being heard.
Healthcare providers have an enormous responsibility, but we cannot do this work alone. That is what I find so compelling about the idea of “Team Baby.” The team extends far beyond the obstetrician’s office or hospital walls. It includes nurses, doulas, behavioral health professionals and other caregivers. But it also includes partners, grandparents, childcare providers, friends, neighbors and others who surround a growing family. You do not need a medical degree to make a difference.
Sometimes support begins with asking a mother how she is really doing, and then taking the time to actively listen to the answer. It can mean offering help, recognizing when someone is struggling or simply making sure that a mother knows she is not alone.
Those moments may seem small however, their impact can be anything but.
The work of building a healthier generation begins long before a child takes a first step. It begins before birth, with healthier, safer and better-supported mothers and families. Every one of us has a place on that team.
Daileann Hemmings is System Director of Maternal Health Equity at Hartford HealthCare.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Maryland Democrats celebrate election victories at state, county levels
description: Gov. Wes Moore (D) said the overwhelming Democratic victories in this month's elections "speak for themselves" -- but that didn't stop state Democrats from speaking about them anyway Monday, when they boasted about flipping 27 state and county from red to blue.
text:
Gov. Wes Moore (D) touts the party's Election Day successes at an event Monday at the Maryland Democratic Party headquarters in Annapolis. with Party Chair Steuart Pittman, right, and six Democratic candidates who won in state and county races. (Photo by William J. Ford/Maryland Matters)Gov. Wes Moore (D) said the overwhelming Democratic victories in this month’s elections “speak for themselves” — but that didn’t stop state Democrats from speaking about them anyway Monday.
Moore, flanked by party officials and six successful candidates at the Maryland Democratic Party headquarters in Annapolis, touted the party’s success on Nov. 3.  Party leaders said about 27 state and county seats flipped from “red to blue” in state and county races.
This was the first year since 1974 that Democrats fielded a candidate in every single legislative district in the state, party officials had said.
“This does not happen by accident. This happens because we have leaders who understand their community,” the governor said Monday. “This is an important time for us to enlarge the Democratic base, and I think that’s exactly what we are seeing since our inauguration. We’re proud to say that the results and the numbers speak for themselves.”
Party leaders said that about 1.6 million texts were sent to voters over the course of the campaigns, 966,000 phone calls made and volunteers knocked on more than 340,000 doors statewide. Anne Arundel County Executive Steuart Pittman, who is serving as the Democratic party chair, said the party’s success was due to “neighbor-to-neighbor organizing.”
Maryland Democratic Party Chair Steuart Pittman speaks Monday at the party’s headquarters in Annapolis. (Photo by William J. Ford/Maryland Matters)
“People sometimes think campaigning is all done on the internet now, and that it’s not personal anymore,” he said. “But Democrats understand that people trust their neighbors much more than … what they see that was generated by AI [artificial intelligence] or some political party’s digital operation.”
According to governor’s campaign, the Moore-Miller campaign invested about $1.3 million toward the party’s Coordinated Campaign. About $23,000 went directly to help three Democratic candidates unseat Republican incumbents in the legislature.
Approximately $8,500 went to the campaign of Democrat Josh Hastings in his successful campaign to unseat Del. Barry Beauchamp (R) in District 38B in Wicomico County. Hastings received 8,189 votes in unofficial returns, or 61% of the vote, to Beauchamp’s 5,309 votes, or 39% of the vote.
Another $8,500 was sent to Democratic candidate Chuck Cook, who unseated Republican Del. Stuart Schmidt Jr. in District 33B in Anne Arundel County. State Board of Elections’ unofficial results Monday gave Cook 11,598 votes, or nearly 55%, to Schmidt’s 9,514 votes, or 45%.
The county’s Board of Elections was conducting a post-election mail-in ballot canvass Monday.
If results stay the same after the state Board of Canvassers certifies results Dec. 3, the Democratic supermajority in the legislature will remain and grow slightly. Democrats added one state senator, and will now hold 35 of 47 seats in that chamber, while Republicans in the House saw their numbers slip from 39 to 35 delegates, leaving Democrats in control of 106 House seats.
Blue wave meets blue line in Frederick, as sheriff’s race just one of Democrats’ wins

History made
One of the most surprising results in the state came in Frederick County, where Democrats flipped a Senate seat, two House seats and won most county races, including the ouster of longtime Sheriff Chuck Jenkins.
About $6,000 went to Democratic nominee Laura Westdorp, who managed to defeat Republican Sen. William G. Folden to represent legislative District 4. According to results posted Sunday by Frederick County’s Board of Elections, Laura Westdorp defeated Folden by 2,305 votes.
Early returns on Election Day give Folden a 52-48 advantage, but as mail-in and provisional ballots came in, Westdorp took the lead and held it, flipping the 52% to 48% advantage in her favor.
The race for three House seats in that same legislative district was even closer. The top two vote-getters were Democrats Jerry Donald and Andrew Duck with 29,901 votes and 29,160 votes, respectively, followed by House Minority Whip Jesse Pippy, whose 28,015 votes was just 127 votes more than Democratic candidate Alleria Stanley.
Republican Del. April Miller came in fifth, trailing Stanley by 804 votes. By ousting Miller and taking the seat left vacant by the retirement of GOP Del. Barrie Ciliberti, Democrats took what was a solidly red district and made it one with three Democrats and just one Republican, Pippy.
Cat Carter, who won a seat on Howard County Council, speaks Monday at the Maryland Democratic Party headquarters in Annapolis. (Photo by William J. Ford/Maryland Matters)
The state’s Democratic leadership also touted the election of Natalie Ogilvie, who unseated incumbent Republican Amanda Fiedler to represent District 5 on the Anne Arundel County Council. Ogilvie, a small business owner, became the first Latina ever elected to the council, and the first Democrat elected from that district since 1986.
In unofficial results, Ogilvie received 20,129 votes, or 51% of the vote, to Fiedler’s 19,083 votes, or 49%.
Cat Carter said it’s been 42 years since a Democrat represented District 5 on the Howard County Council until her victory this month. Carter received 17,667 votes, or about 56% of the vote, to beat Republican Ryan P. O’Connor, who got 13,924 votes, or 44% of the vote.
Carter will replace current Councilman David Yungmann, who chose not to seek reelection. She said Monday that council district had not elected a woman before.
“But this November, voters chose different and I believe the reason is simple: We listened, we showed up and we earned their trust,” said Carter, who runs a cybersecurity business with her husband.
“That victory is more than turning this district from red to blue,” she said. “It’s about earning the confidence of people who may not agree on every issue, but who want their government to work for them.”

name: Washington State Standard
title: WA governor looks to sharply pare spending in face of $4B budget shortfall
description: Washington Gov. Bob Ferguson on Monday directed state agencies to make deeper spending cuts after the latest economic forecast showed tax receipts will not make a dent in a projected $4 billion shortfall next fiscal year. Ferguson wants agency leaders to find ways to reduce costs and pare expenditures by up to 15% through mid-2028, […]
text:
Gov. Bob Ferguson wants state agency leaders to find ways to cut up to 15% of their spending to deal with a projected $4 billion budget shortfall. Here he speaks to reporters in 2025. (Photo by Jacquelyn Jimenez Romero/Washington State Standard)Washington Gov. Bob Ferguson on Monday directed state agencies to make deeper spending cuts after the latest economic forecast showed tax receipts will not make a dent in a projected $4 billion shortfall next fiscal year.
Ferguson wants agency leaders to find ways to reduce costs and pare expenditures by up to 15% through mid-2028, underscoring the state’s lingering financial difficulties amidst slow and steady growth in the economy. 
“Between rising costs and billions of dollars in federal cuts, including massive cuts to health care, we are facing a significant challenge in the first year of the next budget. Today’s revenue forecast does not change that,” Ferguson said in a statement.
“We now project an approximately $4 billion shortfall in the first year of the next budget. Bridging that one-year shortfall will not be easy,” he said.
It’s a better situation in the second year when the new income tax on high earners that Ferguson championed is expected to generate roughly $3.5 billion. 
“The good news is our budget situation will be stable beginning July 1, 2028,” he said.
Ferguson issued his statement shortly after the bipartisan Economic and Revenue Forecast Council learned tax receipts will be $195 million higher for the budget that ends June 30, 2027, and $75 million lower in the next biennial spending cycle than what chief economist David Reich predicted in September.
Overall, the forecast shows $76.5 billion will be available for the current budget and $82.5 billion for the 2027-29 biennium.
Ferguson will rely on those data points for two documents he will release by Dec. 20: a supplemental spending plan for the current fiscal cycle and a full operating budget for the 2027-29 biennium. Those blueprints will serve as templates for legislative budget writers in the 2027 session.
Late Monday, K.D. Chapman-See, director of the Office of Financial Management, sent a memo to agency leaders highlighting areas of the operating and transportation budgets to consider for savings. The memo also went to presidents of colleges and universities, and other state elected officials.
The directives call for eliminating, reducing and delaying programs or services that do not meet the agency’s core mission or directly support essential services for residents.  Chapman-See also instructs leaders not to submit proposals that create savings for their agency but increase costs for another program or agency.
Options for additional reductions are due to the budget office by Nov. 23. The short timeline  indicates Ferguson is looking for more items to include in his budget proposal.
Ferguson also plans to update the freezes on hiring, travel, contracts and discretionary purchases, according to the memo.
The governor, who relied on new and higher taxes to balance the current budget, has said he would not propose doing so in his budget.
“I think the governor has been very consistent in his comments, both publicly and privately, that we’re not considering new revenue as part of our solution for the budget problem,” Chapman-See said in Monday’s meeting of the forecast council.
More taxes are not on the drawing board of Rep. April Berg, D-Mill Creek, chair of the House Finance Committee.
“We’re not looking at revenue sources at this time,” Berg said during the council meeting. “There’s not a revenue package per se that’s coming up. We’re looking at implementation of current bills and current legislation, and looking forward to just figuring out a sustainable path forward given our budget challenges.”

Asked the same question, Rep. Ed Orcutt, R-Kalama, a council member and the ranking Republican on the finance committee, joked, “when have I ever had tax increases on the table?”
Asked if he thought the Democrats could overcome the shortfall without new or higher taxes, he said, “They absolutely can. The question is, will they?”SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Budget challenges and taxes have defined Ferguson’s tenure thus far.
When he settled into office in January 2025, he claimed the chasm between incoming revenues and ongoing expenses was $16 billion. One of his first actions was to call on agencies he oversees to pare spending by 6%.
In his first session, he signed a two-year $78 billion budget crafted by majority Democrats that was balanced with spending cuts and billions of dollars in new and higher taxes. The tax package Democrats assembled totals around $9.4 billion over four years to fully cover the gap. 
In the 2026 session, Ferguson championed a statewide income tax, insisting it be imposed on households with an annual income in excess of $1 million. Democrats used their majorities in the House and Senate to pass it and voters upheld the tax in the Nov. 3 election. 
The tax, if it survives a legal challenge, is set to take effect in January 2028, with the first payments due in 2029. Reich estimates it will generate $3.5 billion in its first year, with collections rising in future years.

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: Utah advocates ask Cox to pause Flock cameras on state roads until new law is finalized
description: A Utah group advocating for more regulation of automated license plate readers is asking the governor’s office to turn off the Flock cameras installed on state highways by the end of this month and until a new regulatory framework is established. The Utah Civic Compact, a nonprofit that has investigated how the Flock Safety cameras […]
text:
Flock Safety cameras are mounted on a pole in the parking lot of the Home Depot in Salt Lake City on Tuesday, Aug. 25, 2026. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)A Utah group advocating for more regulation of automated license plate readers is asking the governor’s office to turn off the Flock cameras installed on state highways by the end of this month and until a new regulatory framework is established.
The Utah Civic Compact, a nonprofit that has investigated how the Flock Safety cameras are used in the state amid intense scrutiny over misuse and surveillance concerns, says the Utah Department of Transportation has exceeded its authority by establishing a rule that requires the department to sign a license agreement with the company to operate on state right-of-ways. 
“No statute gives UDOT the power to license the vendor,” Jarom Gillins, director of policy at the Utah Civic Compact said at a Monday news conference.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
A Utah 2023 law allowed UDOT to issue permits for the use of the cameras on state highways if law enforcement agencies request them. However, the Utah Civic Compact criticized that the department of transportation’s license agreement with Flock established conditions for camera operations “regardless of which (law enforcement agency) has contracted for the company’s services,” according to the document.
Utah group says there’s a faster way to block Flock cameras  — without legislation

The Utah Civic Compact has been analyzing UDOT’s agreement with Flock for over a month, hoping to find a way to turn off the cameras installed on state property. 
In October, the group asked UDOT to cut its contract with the company, arguing that UDOT is able to terminate the agreement if it “determines that the public does not support the Company’s activities.” On Monday, the group switched that request for a direct call to Gov. Spencer Cox to pause the cameras’ operations until new legislation is enacted.
“If vendors are going to be part of plate reader systems on state highways, the Legislature should set the terms in statute, with the agency responsible for every camera and no vendor license the law does not provide for,” Gillins wrote on the organization’s website. “The Utah Privacy Commission’s task force has recommended that agencies own and control the data their systems collect and that vendors process it only on the agency’s behalf.”
However, John Gleason, a spokesperson for UDOT, said the department’s role is only focused on ensuring the equipment is properly permitted and secured so it doesn’t cause any issues with traffic. 
“We don’t install the equipment and we don’t use Flock cameras. We really have no involvement in the use of the equipment,” Gleason said. “We’re just required by state law to issue the permits if they’re for law enforcement use, and to ensure that the equipment is safely installed and not posing a concern for traffic.” 



Let us know what you think...


 


Utah lawmakers have been studying legislative proposals during their off-session meetings after the Utah Civic Compact revealed that the vast majority of searches for Flock Safety data from cameras installed in Weber County were made by out-of-state law enforcement agencies, a fact that the governor said had him “deeply troubled.”
The question, lawmakers said, isn’t whether the state should allow the cameras, but how to regulate them. 
Utah law limits searches of license plate camera databases to active criminal investigations, outstanding warrants, or to search for a missing or endangered person or a stolen vehicle. But, concerns about misuse have recently emerged as police officers in other states have been accused of using Flock camera data to track people they know, and not for their jobs.
Earlier this month, a KSL investigation revealed a former Tooele County Sheriff’s Office detective had searched the department’s license plate reader system for a vehicle belonging to the estranged husband of a woman he was dating, using a case number from a closed investigation to do so.
“Ideally, we want all network surveillance paused across the state of Utah until the legislature can act and regulate these systems properly, and we know exactly where our data is going and what is happening with our data,” Gillins said.

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: Commentary: Candidate is right that no party is above scrutiny — including his own
description: The Sunday night before Election Day, I read a point/counterpoint column from Dan Ahlers, the Democratic candidate for governor, in The Dakota Scout. With an impending blue wave expected to wash over the nation, it was with a certain degree of anticipation that I read Ahlers’ missive. In this new age for Democrats, perhaps Ahlers […]
text:
South Dakota Democratic nominee for governor Dan Ahlers talks to attendees at the Democratic Party election night gathering in downtown Sioux Falls on Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Makenzie Huber/South Dakota Searchlight)The Sunday night before Election Day, I read a point/counterpoint column from Dan Ahlers, the Democratic candidate for governor, in The Dakota Scout. With an impending blue wave expected to wash over the nation, it was with a certain degree of anticipation that I read Ahlers’ missive. In this new age for Democrats, perhaps Ahlers had something unique to say, a fresh vision for the state and the challenges it faces.
Sadly, no. Ahlers started off with a Democratic oldie but goodie — bemoaning the dangers of one-party rule. “When one party holds power for generation after generation, there is a danger that accountability becomes less of a priority,” Ahlers said, adding later, “No political party should be above scrutiny.”
In this last-ditch attempt to sway voters, Ahlers uses “one-party rule” like it’s a curse word or the name of a crime or the result of a conspiracy. It’s not. One-party rule in South Dakota is the fault of one party — the Democratic Party. You certainly can’t blame Republicans for being the only candidates to show up on the ballot.
Democrats gain seats in South Dakota Legislature for the first time since 2008

For decades, the Democratic Party in South Dakota has been, at best, an afterthought. At worst, it’s a punchline. That played out in the recent election as Democrats lost, again, every statewide office. Democrats hamstrung themselves in statewide races, failing to field candidates for U.S. Senate and state attorney general.
In the Legislature, Democrats will have two members in the 35-member state Senate and 10 in the 70-member state House. There has been some crowing on the part of Democrats, since their showing included the addition of four new representatives in the Sioux Falls area, the best they’ve done in an election since they sent 16 members to Pierre in 2018.
In their post-election afterglow, Democrats are busy strategizing how they can replicate their Sioux Falls gains in the rural areas of the state. That will be a big task. The Democratic Party allowed Republicans to have majorities in both chambers before a single vote was cast. When all the pre-election paperwork had been filed, Republicans were guaranteed 52 seats in the Legislature — 21 in the Senate and 31 in the House.
That’s how this state earned a tradition of one-party rule. It’s tough to have a two-party system when one of the parties doesn’t show up. Ahlers had been the executive director of the Democratic Party in South Dakota. It was his job to oversee the recruitment of candidates for the Legislature. Unfortunately, he fell short by 52 candidates before he decided to recruit himself to run for governor.
Don’t mistake this as an endorsement of the state’s Democrats or their ideas. It is an endorsement of the idea that South Dakota voters and taxpayers deserve a real debate on the issues. Lately the only election debates have been in the Republican Party primaries between candidates who largely agree with each other. Once the general election rolls around, some Republican legislative candidates don’t have anyone to debate, anyone to challenge their ideas, anyone to offer voters a choice in November.
A blue wave drenched the rest of the nation on Election Day. In South Dakota, the outcome resembled something that drips from a leaky faucet. Ahlers was right when he said that no party should be above scrutiny. Take a close look at the Democratic Party in this state and you’ll find it’s the reason why South Dakota has a long tradition of one-party rule.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Moore announces new set of appointments as staff shakeup continues
description: Gov. Wes Moore (D), in a statement, called the four appointees "seasoned and talented public servants, and we are excited and grateful that they will be assuming these critical leadership roles."
text:
The shuffling continues on the second floor of the State House, as Gov. Wes Moore on Monday announced four new appointees to administrative positions in his office, including the nearly created position of chief administrative officer. (File photo by Danielle E. Gaines/Maryland Matters)The shuffling continues on the second floor of the State House, as the governor’s office announced a new batch of appointments Monday.
The four appointees named to administrative positions in Gov. Wes Moore’s office, including a new position of chief administrative officer, were hailed by the governor as “seasoned and talented public servants, and we are excited and grateful that they will be assuming these critical leadership roles.”
Moore named Joseph “Joh” Sedtal as the new principal deputy chief of staff, filling the job vacated by Manny Welsh when Moore named him chief of staff earlier this month.
Sedtal was deputy secretary at the Department of General Services, and before that he served as deputy secretary of administration at the Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services. Sedtal earned a bachelor’s degree from Tulane University and a law degree from the University of Maryland Francis King Carey School of Law.
Asma Mirza will serve as Moore’s chief administrative officer — a new position whose duties had previously been tied to one of the governor’s deputy chiefs of staff.
“After evaluating the current structure and to align with the needs for the second term, the principal deputy chief of staff and chief administrative officer positions are being intentionally decoupled. While these positions will interact closely, they have distinct roles and responsibilities going forward,” said Rhyan Lake, a spokesperson for Moore.
Maryland environment secretary to step down, in latest shakeup to Moore’s Cabinet

“The principal deputy chief of staff, alongside other deputy chiefs of staff, will manage the day-to-day operations of government, whereas the CAO will focus on successful implementation of major executive branch priorities that will have the highest impact on Marylanders over the next four years and beyond,” Lake said.
Mirza joined the administration in 2023 as chief performance officer. Prior to that she served as the deputy for implementation management for the White House Infrastructure Implementation Team and special assistant to the President.
Mirza also spent nearly seven years as a performance manager in the federal Office of Management and Budget during President Barack Obama’s two terms. In between her two stints in the White House, she worked for three years for the international consulting firm McKinsey & Co.
She earned a bachelor’s degree in leadership and change management and operations information management from Georgetown University. She earned an MBA from the University of Maryland.
Moore also named Kristina Broadie-Jeter as executive secretary. She currently serves as chief of staff for executive operations and protocol. In her new role, she will manage “core operational units of the Governor’s Office, including budgetary, personnel, constituent services, and protocol matters.”
Broadie-Jeter previously served as assistant chief of protocol in for ceremonials in the U.S. State Department and held similar positions under U.S. House Speaker Nancy Pelosi, in addition to working in the Obama-Biden White House. She earned a bachelor’s degree from Duke University.
Finally, Moore named Walter Donoughe assistant chief of staff. He most recently served as assistant administrative officer for the governor.vDonoughe graduated from Towson University with a bachelor’s degree in Political Science.
Since winning a second term on Nov. 3, Moore has announced a new chief of staff as well as other changes to his Cabinet: Last week, the secretaries of State, Veterans and Military Affairs, and Public Safety and Correctional Services all cleaned out their desks and were replaced immediately by interim directors. He also recently announced the changes in leadership within the state Department of the Environment and the Department of Emergency Management.

title: Democrats re-elect Jinkins as House speaker in WA Legislature
description: Democratic state lawmakers in Washington on Monday re-elected Rep. Laurie Jinkins as House speaker in the wake of a midterm election in which Democrats flipped 10 Republican-held seats to attain a supermajority. Jinkins overcame the challenge of Rep. April Berg, D-Mill Creek, who focused on their differences in style and looked to ride the recent […]
text:
Speaker of the House Laurie Jinkins, D-Tacoma, gives her opening remarks for the 2026 legislative session which began on Jan. 12. (Photo by Jacquelyn Jimenez Romero/Washington State Standard)Democratic state lawmakers in Washington on Monday re-elected Rep. Laurie Jinkins as House speaker in the wake of a midterm election in which Democrats flipped 10 Republican-held seats to attain a supermajority.
Jinkins overcame the challenge of Rep. April Berg, D-Mill Creek, who focused on their differences in style and looked to ride the recent election’s wave of political change.
“I’m glad we could have a contested but not contentious conversation around leadership,” said Berg, chair of the House Finance Committee. “I’m super excited to continue my role with the caucus.”
House Democrats, who are on course to hold 69 of the chamber’s 98 seats, made the decision in a meeting Monday afternoon at the state Capitol.
They also re-elected Rep. Joe Fitzgibbon, D-West Seattle, as House majority leader and chose Rep. Liz Berry, D-Seattle, as floor leader, and Rep. Brianna Thomas, D-West Seattle, as caucus chair.
Rep. Chris Stearns, D-Auburn, was elected Speaker pro tem. Jinkins and Stearns must be formally voted on by the full House of Representatives on the first day of the 2027 session.
The battle for speakership is the most important of Monday’s decisions. Jinkins will lead a caucus with immense political power in the upcoming session, including the ability to advance constitutional amendments and override vetoes from a governor without any Republican votes.
Jinkins, Senate Majority Leader Jamie Pedersen, D-Seattle, and Gov. Bob Ferguson, who will meet this Friday, will be in regular contact during the 105-day session as they discuss policy and budget matters. With a caucus of 69 members, House Democrats will, at times, hold greater sway in three-way negotiations on a particular controversial piece of legislation or budget provision.
Democrats did not reveal exact vote counts of the leadership election. 
In interviews ahead of the meetings, some returning lawmakers wondered how the 20 caucus newcomers — who’ve dubbed themselves The Tidal 20 — would cast their votes, since some had campaigned as disrupters of the political status quo.
Jinkins, first elected to the House in 2010, has been speaker since January 2020 and is the first woman and the first lesbian to ever hold the position. She succeeded Frank Chopp, Washington’s longest serving and arguably most powerful speaker in the history of the House of Representatives.
During her tenure, the caucus has grown from 57 members to 69. This year’s incoming class of Democrats has 20 people: the 10 who won Republican-held seats and 10 others who won Democrat-controlled seats, some held by incumbents.
Berg won her House seat in 2020 and she shepherded this year’s controversial income tax law through the chamber. She began her bid to unseat Jinkins in the spring.
The Senate Democratic Caucus re-elected Pedersen as majority leader on Nov. 5. Democrats outnumber Republicans in the chamber by a margin of 30-19.
Senate Republicans are scheduled to hold their reorganization votes on Dec. 6 with the House Republican Caucus choosing their leaders on Dec. 11. 
The 2027 legislative session is scheduled to begin Jan. 11.SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Environmental groups petition EPA to lower nitrate standard from 10mg/L to 1 mg/L
description: A group of environmental groups has submitted a petition to the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency urging it to revise and significantly lower the current safe drinking water standard for nitrate.  EPA established a maximum contaminant level of 10 milligrams per liter for nitrate contamination in drinking water in 1975, then officially implemented the leve[...]
text:
Environmental groups are petitioning EPA to lower its safe drinking water standard for nitrate. (Photo by Cami Koons/Iowa Capital Dispatch)A group of environmental groups has submitted a petition to the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency urging it to revise and significantly lower the current safe drinking water standard for nitrate. 
EPA established a maximum contaminant level of 10 milligrams per liter for nitrate contamination in drinking water in 1975, then officially implemented the level in 1991. Petitioners argue that in the more than 30 years since the limit was set, dozens of epidemiological studies have demonstrated a link between lower levels of nitrate exposure and certain types of cancer, thyroid disease and adverse birth outcomes, yet the EPA has not changed the standard. 
Petitioners, which include Food & Water Watch, Environmental Law & Policy Center, Union of Concerned Scientists, Environmental Working Group, Natural Resources Defense Council and other groups, are asking the EPA to revise the limit to 1 mg/L. 
In the petition, which is more than 50 pages in length, environmental groups are presenting findings from more than 30 peer-reviewed human health studies, along with a benefit-cost analysis they commissioned to show that “there are serious risks to human health from nitrate levels well below the current standard” and that the public health benefits of lowering the standard to 1 mg/L “substantially exceed” the costs. 
“Nitrates in drinking water are causing a public health crisis across the country,” the petition says. “The current crisis is not a surprise. Elected officials and regulators at the federal, state, and local levels have systematically ignored or failed to respond to the causes of this pollution for decades, leading to widespread drinking water contamination.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The petition directs the EPA to address nitrate pollution “at the source” with stricter regulations to stop the “overapplication” of manure and commercial fertilizers and the “irresponsible management” of waste from confined animal feeding operations, or CAFOs. It also notes areas where the EPA could direct existing funding to support drinking water treatment facilities and protection projects. 
Tyler Lobdell, a senior staff attorney with Food & Water Watch, spoke about the petition at a Monday news conference and said it laid out a “roadmap” for the EPA to “protect public health and begin holding industrial agriculture accountable for this problem.”
“On behalf of our millions of members, and on behalf of communities from coast to coast, we’re here to demand that EPA protect our water at the tap and at the source,” Lobdell said. 
A spokesperson for the EPA said in a statement Monday it would review the petition and that the agency is “committed to ensuring all Americans have access to clean drinking water.” 
The agency also noted that it is required by the Safe Drinking Water Act to review drinking water regulations every six years. As part of its most recent review in 2024, the statement from the EPA said, the agency had “determined that the nitrate rule was not a candidate for revision at the time.” This determination was based on a “robust evaluation” of available studies and data on nitrate contamination. 
“As EPA begins its evaluation for the next Six-Year Review, the agency will deploy gold-standard science and consider newly available recent studies to inform its decision making,” the EPA statement said. 
In a separate but related matter, Food & Water Watch is suing the EPA for failing to comply with their Freedom of Information Act request for reports and communications surrounding a “scuttled” assessment from the agency on the human-health impact of the oral consumption of nitrate and nitrite.
What is nitrate contamination?
The petition says nitrate is a “prevalent contaminant” in both ground and surface water sources and that contamination is “most likely where vulnerable surface or groundwaters meet intensive agricultural practices on the landscape.” 
An analysis from petitioners of data from the National Water Quality Monitoring Council found that from January 2015 through August 2026, the states with the highest mean levels of nitrate in surface waters, listed in descending order, were: Iowa, Minnesota, Delaware, Illinois, Indiana, Kansas, California, Maryland, Pennsylvania and Utah. 
Iowa had 274 monitoring sites with an average nitrate level of 4.22 mg/L per site, while Minnesota, the next highest on the list, had 806 monitoring sites and an average nitrate level of 3.60 mg/L. 
Anne Schechinger, senior director of agriculture and climate research at the Environmental Working Group, said Monday that while nitrate “mainly” gets into water from commercial fertilizer and manure application in agricultural settings, even large cities like Los Angeles, Philadelphia, Phoenix and Las Vegas have elevated levels of nitrate in their drinking water. 
According to Schechinger and data in the petition, there are around 120 million people in the U.S. with drinking water sources at or above the 1 mg/L standard proposed by the petitioners. 
Permitting overhaul advances in US Senate with tepid bipartisan support

“Science has advanced since the EPA set the 10 mg/L (limit) more than three decades ago, so we now know that even low levels of nitrate exposure in drinking water can increase the risk of health harms in people,” Schechinger said in the news conference Monday. 
That figure doesn’t include people sourcing their water from private wells, which are not subject to EPA standards or regular testing.
The petitioners’ analysis of groundwater nitrate levels from federal water quality data found Colorado, Montana, Washington, Arizona, Delaware, Nevada, Wisconsin, New Mexico, Iowa and California had the highest mean values of nitrate in groundwater. Colorado, at the top of the list, had a mean groundwater nitrate concentration of 7.89 mg/L according to the petition. 
Utilities already struggle to meet current standard
Utilities with source waters that are high in nitrate concentrations either need nitrate removal systems or to blend water from multiple sources to meet safe drinking water standards.  
In Iowa, nitrate contamination is a prominent issue and even became a key policy point among candidates in the recent election. Despite a massive nitrate removal system in Des Moines, the city’s regional water authority, Central Iowa Water Works, has had to issue lawn watering bans the past two summers to lower demand on the system and keep nitrate levels below the EPA’s limit of 10 mg/L. 
The city’s treatment facility sources water from the Des Moines and Raccoon rivers, but nitrate concentrations well above 10 mg/L in the rivers made it difficult for the system to meet high water demand in the summer and safe drinking water standards. 
Nitrate levels haven’t exceeded the EPA limits in Des Moines, but the “finished” water leaving the treatment facilities regularly has nitrate levels above 5 mg/L, according to data from Des Moines Water Works. 
Tami Madsen, the executive director of Central Iowa Water Works, said the regional water authority was reviewing the petition from environmental groups and needed “time to evaluate” the motion before it could comment.
“Our focus remains on providing safe drinking water to the one in five Iowans we serve and protecting the sources our communities rely on,” Madsen said in an email.
At the EPA’s current limit of 10 mg/L, nitrate contamination violations are the most common health-based standard violated by public water supply systems in Iowa and many smaller communities can’t afford to implement a nitrate removal system. 
Petitioners said that addressing the issue “at the source,” by adding regulations and limitations on fertilizer application and livestock systems, would “lower the compliance cost” for public water systems.
Nancy Stoner, a senior attorney with the Environmental Law & Policy Center, said that public health benefits would be 3.9 times as great as projected costs, over the next 50 years, of lowering the nitrate standard to 1 mg/L. 
Swimmers weren’t warned about nearly 30 high E. coli tests at beaches this summer

According to the benefit-cost analysis included in the petition, the annualized cost of meeting the recommended threshold breaks down to about $53 per household per year for people in large water systems.
“Everyone should be able to drink the tap water anywhere in the U.S. safely, and that’s what the Safe Drinking Water Act requires,” Stoner said. 
The petition said the benefit-cost ratio is an underestimation because the analysis only looked at the effect lowering the standard would have on three health outcomes: colorectal cancer, ovarian cancer and very low birth weight. 
EPA’s 10 mg/L standard was based largely on studies of nitrate contamination and blue baby syndrome or methemoglobinemia, a potentially fatal condition where an infant is unable to properly carry oxygen in their blood. 
Stacy Woods, the research director for the Union of Concerned Scientists, said the research in the petition provides “substantial evidence that the current standard does not adequately protect against serious health effects” including ovarian cancer, colorectal cancer, thyroid disease, low birth weight and birth defects. 
“We joined this petition because we know that the current standard for drinking water is insufficient to protect public health,” Woods said. “… The EPA must update the nitrate drinking water standard to reflect today’s science and protect public health.”

name: Honolulu Civil Beat
title: Makana Eyre: Hawaiʻi’s Literary Boom Gains Momentum On Kauaʻi
description: Kauaʻi Writers Garden has created an event rooted in place and making a statement about homegrown culture.
text:
Hawaiʻi is in the midst of a literary breakout.
There have always been landmark books from Hawaiʻi authors – the sort of work that could attract major New York publishers and national reviews.
But for decades, they appeared piecemeal. A single work would carry the mantle until another one, often years later, came along to take it forward.
That began to change five or six years ago, with 2023 being the first of several banner years.
Since then we’ve seen a string of important titles, including Mariah Rigg’s “Extinction Capital of the World,” Sara Kehaulani Goo’s “Kuleana,” and, this year, new novels by acclaimed writers T Kira Madden and Kawai Strong Washburn.
Any good literary scene needs an ecosystem around it. That is starting to thrive too. MIA, Hawaii’s longest-running reading series, is back. Bamboo Ridge Press, which has nurtured generations of local writers, seems as vital as ever. We also have the Hawaiʻi Review of Books, an ambitious and finely-edited forum for culture, ideas and criticism.



Ideas showcases stories, opinion and analysis about Hawaiʻi, from the state’s sharpest thinkers, to stretch our collective thinking about a problem or an issue. Email news@civilbeat.org to submit an idea or an essay.


Read More

The newest addition to the literary scene is the Kauaʻi Writers Garden, a speaker series and writing community in Līhuʻe celebrating its first anniversary this month.
Over the last year, the Garden has brought in an impressive list of writers, poets and publishers to the island including Brandy Nālani McDougall, Lee Tonouchi, Megan Kamalei Kakimoto, Ingrid Rojas Contreras and Scott Kikkawa. 

 Hawaiʻi Poet Laureate Lee Tonouchi (Courtesy: Olivia Franco)

The Garden grew out of a friendship between the writer and musician thomas iannucci (who stylizes his name in lower case) and Kauaʻi County Council member Addison Bulosan. 
At the time, iannucci, a three-time Nā Hōkū Hanohano Award-winning rapper, was shifting his focus from music to fiction. Bulosan, known for his patronage of the arts, asked him how they could nurture a Kauaʻi literary community. iannucci had an answer.
Since getting his first short story published in 2023, iannucci had been flying back and forth from Kauaʻi to Oʻahu to do readings and mix with other writers. Yet it didn’t take long for the commute to grow expensive and taxing.
“You gotta ask plenty favors, sleep on somebody’s couch,” he told me.

Ingrid Rojas Contreras at a Garden event co-sponsored by the National Book Foundation. (Courtesy: Olivia Franco)

Flying over also made him uneasy. He could manage the trip to Honolulu and take part in opportunities there. But many of his fellow Kauaʻi writers could not. That sparked an idea. Why not bring the opportunity to Kauaʻi?
There was something else he wanted to change. Hawaiʻi was producing top first-rate writers. But they often earned more recognition nationally than in the islands. He reckoned that if there were a venue to introduce them to folks outside Oʻahu’s usual – and sometimes insular – writing circles, people would come.
iannucci’s theory proved right. Since its first event in November of last year, the Garden has grown into a centerpiece of Kauaʻi’s burgeoning literary community.
With Bulosan as its patron and co-founder, and with the help of two other Kauaʻi writers, co-founders Jonathon Medeiros and Mason Bundschuh, this event has become a bright spot for local culture.
Today, it operates under the Rice Street Business Association, a nonprofit aimed at revitalizing downtown Līhuʻe, with support from donors including Hawaiian Telcom and HMSA. It has an ongoing partnership with the Hawai’i Council for the Humanities and has collaborated with the National Book Foundation.
It’s tempting to see the Garden in a narrow sense: as a story about cultivating local culture. But it goes much further than giving writers a platform and residents a place to engage with their work.
For decades, the implicit message we’ve all soaked up is that to experience culture at its highest levels, you have to leave the neighbor islands – if not the state altogether. Literature? Film? Photography? Painting? That was the domain of New York or Washington or San Francisco. The Garden shows us that Hawaiʻi – even a little town such as Līhuʻe – can be a cultural destination.

Kauai County Council member Addison Bulosan is the patron and co-founder of the Kauaʻi Writers Garden. (Kevin Fujii/Civil Beat/2024)

Don Wallace, an author and editor of the Hawaii Review of Books, put it to me this way, “What Kauaʻi has accomplished for its local writing community in a tumultuous, awful, very bad year for weather and humans is proof that it isn’t the distance from New York (or Honolulu) that matters. It’s the ferocity of your commitment to your fellow writers and readers.” 
There’s also a larger story about who participates in and shapes culture in the islands and beyond. The Garden stands in welcome contrast to the Kauai Writers Conference, an annual literary gathering that brings together authors, editors and agents for workshops and networking.
Held at an upscale resort in Līhuʻe each November, the three-day event this year will cost attendees $895. Master classes cost another $895. Food, lodging and travel all costs extra.
“What Kauaʻi has accomplished for its local writing community in a tumultuous, awful, very bad year… is proof that it isn’t the distance from New York that matters.”Don Wallace, an author and editor of the Hawaiʻi Review of Books
The conference clearly has a stellar lineup of authors. But some local writers have bristled at an event long seen to cater to visiting writers rather than local talent – or anyone without the deep pockets to afford such an expense. The conference has offered scholarships and modest kamaʻāina discounts, and it has collaborated with some local authors.
iannucci is determined to do it differently: the Garden is free, rooted in place, and features many of the best contemporary writers with links to Hawaiʻi.
What does the Garden have in store for 2027? A lot. Its speaker list is already nearly fully booked. Alicia Upano, author of the recently published “Everything to the Sea,” will get the year started in January.
iannucci, who himself is known for writing in pidgin and has a forthcoming book, is full of ideas. The Garden plans to launch new collaborations with Bamboo Ridge and Bess Press, and it will soon announce appearances by several prominent authors slated for 2027. 
Even as they look to the future, iannucci and his colleagues are proud of what the Garden has already achieved. Kauaʻi councilmember Addison Bulosan put it this way, “What’s magical about it is how open and welcoming everyone is and how many of these guests find a home. It’s like being amongst a long-lost family member.”
