name: Maryland Matters
title: Officials give final OK to limit state health plan spending on Ozempic, Jardiance
description: State officials gave final approval Monday to regulations that cap how much state and local governments are willing to pay for two high-cost drugs by setting “upper payment limits” on treatments for Type 2 diabetes and other conditions.
text:
During a virtual meeting Monday, PDAB member Dr. Georges Benjamin oversaw the vote that finalized new regulations capping how much state and local governments will pay for two prescription drugs on state health plans. (Photo by Danielle J. Brown/Maryland Matters)State officials gave final approval Monday to regulations that cap how much state and local governments are willing to pay for two high-cost drugs by setting “upper payment limits” on treatments for Type 2 diabetes and other conditions.
The Prescription Drug Affordability Board action set payment limits on two prescription drugs covered by state healthcare plans: Jardiance, a brand name for the drug empagliflozin, and Ozempic, a name brand for semaglutide.
The vote finalizes language that now goes to the state register for final evaluation. If no problems arise there, the new regulations would go into effect on Jan. 1, 2027, marking the first time the board has limited spending on high cost drugs since it was created in 2019.
“This landmark move will save state and local government millions of dollars,” Vincent DeMarco, president of the Medicare Healthcare for All coalition, said during public comments ahead of the board votes Monday.
Jardiance and Ozempic are both used to treat Type 2 diabetes among other conditions.  Ozempic has also gained new attention for its use as a weight-loss drug. Healthcare advocates estimate that state and local governments could save around $6.1 million with upper payment limits set for those two drugs.
That may be a fraction of the $3 billion budget shortfall state lawmakers will likely need to address in the 2027 legislative session, but DeMarco called Monday’s vote is a “critically important step,” more possible savings on the horizon.
Board votes to cap how much state, local governments spend on Ozempic

It the upper payment limits take effect on Jan. 1, it would also start the clock on a possible expansion of the board’s authority from just state health plans to the private insurance market in 2028. A 2025 law authorized the expansion, but delayed it until one year after upper payment limits were set on two prescription drugs under its current authority.
Savings would increase significantly if the board’s authority expanded to reach private insurance, according to an analysis from Steve Ports Consulting, commissioned by Maryland Health Care for All.
That analysis said the expected $320,000 in Jardiance savings for state health plans could balloon to between $9 million and $16 million a year if expanded out to all Maryland health plans. Projected Ozempic savings would go from $5.8 million a year to somewhere between $113 million and $165 million a year.
Certain patient advocacy groups for people with chronic or rare diseases worry that upper payment limits will risk their ability to access their medications. And drug manufacturers warn that actions taken by the board may not result in out-of-pocket savings for patients at the pharmacy counter.
“These policies can introduce new incentives for insurers and pharmacy benefit managers (PBMs) that may ultimately restrict access to needed treatments through greater utilization management, formulary reshuffling, or adverse tiering,” according to a written comment to the board by the EACH/PIC coalition, a group of almost two dozen patient-advocacy groups for specific conditions.
“These shifts risk delaying or disrupting care, and … insurance barriers, not price alone, are often the real drivers of patient hardship and perceived ‘unaffordability,’” the statement said.
Advocates ‘thrilled’ by state decision to cap spending on diabetes drug Jardiance

State officials respond by saying that upper payment limits are not expected to limit access, but if they do, the board can alter the policy to address the issue.
Meanwhile, other healthcare advocates say expanding the board’s authority to the private market will result in even more savings that could free up state and local funds to go toward other healthcare programs.
“Beyond reducing costs, these measures could expand access to lifesaving medications,” said Sara Westrick, AARP Maryland’s advocacy director, said in a written comment to the board. “Greater affordability may also allow more patients to start treatment and continue taking their prescribed medications, thereby improving adherence and potentially increasing appropriate utilization.”
DeMarco is also leading the charge on proposed 2027 legislation that would let the board more easily set upper payment limits for prescription drugs based on the Maximum Fair Price, which is negotiated between federal officials and pharmaceutical companies to offer lower prescription drug costs for those on Medicare.
Advocates claim that could yield over $665 million in savings on the 25 drugs already negotiated under the Maximum Fair Price policy, with additional savings added as federal officials continue to negotiate lower prices for other medications covered by Medicare.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Comer announces candidacy for Kentucky governor in 2027
description: Republican U.S. Rep. James Comer has made his long-rumored campaign for Kentucky governor official.  The congressman, who was just elected to serve a sixth term in the U.S. House last month, made the announcement in a livestream Monday evening.  In the months leading up to launching his gubernatorial bid, Kentucky Republicans have largely cleared the […]
text:
U.S. Rep. James Comer and his wife TJ wave to the crowd during the Fancy Farm Picnic on Saturday, Aug 2, 2025. (Austin Anthony for the Kentucky Lantern)Republican U.S. Rep. James Comer has made his long-rumored campaign for Kentucky governor official. 
The congressman, who was just elected to serve a sixth term in the U.S. House last month, made the announcement in a livestream Monday evening. 
In the months leading up to launching his gubernatorial bid, Kentucky Republicans have largely cleared the field in preparation for the 2027 primary. Secretary of State Michael Adams, who is term-limited in his current role, was considering running for governor. However at the Fancy Farm Picnic in August, Adams said “the best thing I can do for my team is to call on all Republicans to join me in supporting James Comer to be our next governor.” 
“The Democrats are going to pull out all the stops to claw onto the one office they can still win,” Adams said at the time. “We absolutely have to nominate our strongest ticket. The first thing we must do to strengthen our chances is to avoid some messy primary where we all attack each other.” 
Comer later said at the Kentucky Farm Bureau Ham Breakfast he’d likely make an announcement after the November election. Current Gov. Andy Beshear, a Democrat, is term-limited. 
Democrats already have a choice to make on their side in May between Lt. Gov. Jacqueline Coleman and Rocky Adkins, a former Beshear senior adviser and member of the Kentucky House. In early October, Adkins’ campaign reported raising more than $1.75 million and Coleman’s reported $540,000.
Comer, who now represents the state’s 1st Congressional District, has become a prominent figure in national politics as the chair of the House Oversight Committee. Under Comer’s two terms as chair, the House Oversight Committee has made national headlines for its fiery debates. In 2024, U.S. Rep. Jasmine Crockett, D-Texas, asked if a committee member could discuss someone’s “bleach blond bad built butch body” after former U.S. Rep. Majorie Taylor Greene, R-Georgia, accused Crockett of wearing “fake eyelashes.” The committee has also led queries into Democrats, like Hunter Biden, the son of former President Joe Biden, and his laptop usage. Earlier this year, the committee held former President Bill Clinton and former U.S. Secretary of State Hillary Clinton in contempt for refusing to testify as part of the committee’s investigation into convicted sex offender and financer Jeffery Epstein. 
Comer previously ran for governor in 2015, losing the GOP primary to future Gov. Matt Bevin by 83 votes. The election was tense and got personal as Comer was accused of abuse by an ex-girlfriend from college, which he denied at the time. He later told the New York Times in a 2023 profile that he leaked emails suggesting coordination between a local blogger who wrote about the alleged abuse and the husband of the running mate of another opponent in the race, Louisville developer Hal Heiner, which the Lexington Herald-Leader described in May 2015.
Before that, Comer was Kentucky’s agriculture commissioner and served in the Kentucky House of Representatives.

title: DHHS Disability and Aging Division Director Tony Green to retire Feb. 2
description: LINCOLN — Tony Green, director of Nebraska DHHS’ Division of Disability and Aging, will retire Feb. 2.  Gov. Jim Pillen announced Green’s retirement in a press release Friday afternoon.  “Tony’s leadership led to the elimination of the state’s developmental disability waiting list, which was one of the first and highest priorities of my administration,” Pill[...]
text:
Tony Green, director of the Division of Developmental Disabilities in the Nebraska Department of Health and Human Services, greets Anna Keyzer of Lincoln and her son, Simon, during a meeting of the Nebraska Olmstead Advisory Committee. Dec. 19, 2025. In July 2026, the division was renamed the Division of Disability and Aging. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)LINCOLN — Tony Green, director of Nebraska DHHS’ Division of Disability and Aging, will retire Feb. 2. 
Gov. Jim Pillen announced Green’s retirement in a press release Friday afternoon. 
“Tony’s leadership led to the elimination of the state’s developmental disability waiting list, which was one of the first and highest priorities of my administration,” Pillen wrote. “He has worked hard to strengthen program eligibility and enrollment operations, so they provide the greatest level of service for as many people as possible. I wish Tony all the best as he takes on new pursuits.”
Green was first hired by the Department of Health and Human Services in 1990, according to the press release. He later was executive director for a community-based disability provider. After returning to DHHS, he served in multiple leadership roles within the Division of Disability and Aging. 
Twice he was appointed interim director of the Division of Children and Family Services. He also served as interim director of the Division of Behavioral Health.
According to his bio on the DHHS website, in 2024, he was elected to the Board of Directors for the National Association of State Directors of Developmental Disability Services.​
Green’s department has come under fire by some advocates of disabled Nebraskans who criticized the agency’s implementation of a tool that essentially determines the level of publicly assisted care, services and funding for those with developmental disabilities.
“It’s been an honor to spend my entire career to date supporting Nebraska’s most vulnerable citizens,” Green said in the release. “We’ve accomplished historic milestones during my time as director of the Division of Disability and Aging. It has been an honor working with some of the most hard-working and dedicated staff I’ve ever known. Thank you, Governor Pillen, for your trust in appointing me to lead this important division on behalf of Nebraska.”
An announcement about interim leadership for the division will be made later, according to the release.

text:
Assemblymember Selena Torres-Fosset during the 2025 legislative session in Carson City. (Photo: Richard Bednarski/Nevada Current)Nevada Democratic Assemblymember Selena Torres-Fossett announced Monday she is resigning from the state Legislature. 
“My commitment to the people of Nevada remains unwavering, but I recognize that this chapter of my life calls for a different kind of leadership: being present for the family I’ve fought hard to build,” she said in a statement.
Torres-Fossett was first elected to serve Assembly District 3 in Las Vegas in 2018, a year Democrats in Nevada as well as nationwide saw sizable legislative wins.  
She most recently won reelection by a substantial margin, garnering 11,540 votes, or 64% of the vote. 
During her time in the Legislature, she has served as chairs of the Education and Government Affairs committee as well as the vice chair of the Nevada Latino Legislative Caucus. 
“Throughout her time in the Legislature, Selena has brought a unique perspective, an unwavering commitment to her constituents, and a genuine desire to make Nevada a better place for everyone,” Assembly Speaker-designate Elaine Marzola said in a statement. 
Clark County Commissioners will be tasked with selecting someone to fill the vacancy.

name: WyoFile
title: Gordon would extend property tax relief with new supplemental budget
description:
Outgoing governor seeks $527 million for “absolutely unforeseen or emergent” issues.
The post Gordon would extend property tax relief with new supplemental budget appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Gov. Mark Gordon unveiled his supplemental budget online and at a news conference Monday, seeking $527 million for social services, property tax relief, natural resource conservation and education, among other things.
The supplement, which the Legislature will consider early next year, addresses “emergent, unanticipated, or obligatory expenses” and completes “commitments already underway,” he said.
The request includes $16.6 million to extend property tax relief programs. The two-year budget the Legislature passed this year paid for the programs for only one year, ending in June 2027. Gordon’s request would avoid curtailments through June 2028.
He called the failed Proposition 1 that voters rejected in the Nov. 3 election an axe where a scalpel is a more appropriate tool. Prop. 1 would have cut in half property taxes a primary residence — not land — but was rejected in the face of draconian impacts to local government services.
Nevertheless, the governor called on the Legislature to take a long look at the several property tax relief, refund and exemption programs “and clarify what has become a pretty complicated system.”
A real estate company listed this Jackson house and lot in 2024 for $2.7 million. The property, which could be redeveloped with several units, had property taxes amounting to $9,951. (Angus M. Thuermer Jr./WyoFile)
Gordon also asked for money to bolster social service programs, including for special needs and long-term care patients through Medicaid programs that enable residents to receive help at home.
The waiting list for help for certain Wyoming residents needing long-term care and other assistance “is too long,” he said. The supplemental request would “accommodate those on the waitlist longer than 24 months.” Some of the supplemental funds would boost reimbursements “to help retain caregivers who provide essential long-term care, best assuring our neighbors can stay at home.”
He wants money for the Wyoming Business Council to continue its work while the Legislature figures out that agency’s future.
The governor also wants to continue the SUNBucks summer nutrition program, seeking one-time funding of $436,000 to prepare for next summer and 575,000 for the state’s 50% share of administrative costs for the federal program.
“Last summer, around 37,000 Wyoming school children qualified for the needs-based program,” he said.
We have seen when kids suffer from hunger that decreases their ability to learn.”Gov. Mark Gordon
“I have heard repeatedly over the course of this year how important that program was to making sure kids were not dealing with hunger and were ready to learn, ready to do well,” he said. “We have seen when kids suffer from hunger that … decreases their ability to learn.”
Fully $40.4 million would go to the University of Wyoming for science initiatives, the School of Energy and to complete two new dorms.
He touted achievements at Laramie. “We were able to get the university into a research-one level status that only a very few institutions in the country have,” Gordon said.
He is asking for $30 million for the Wyoming Wildlife and Natural Resource Trust to continue invasive species control, wildfire mitigation and fire recovery work.
The governor wants $100 million added to permanent savings, noting that the state’s investment portfolio was also its leading revenue generator.
Rachael Price and Sarah Wilzbacher of Anam Cara Caregiving chat during a work meeting. The Lander nonprofit offers in-home caregiving services that Gov. Mark Gordon’s supplemental budget would boost. (Katie Klingsporn/WyoFile)
Gordon supports $31.6 million for schools as recommended by a legislative committee, money that would help insure the equitable distribution of money to large and small schools and districts.
“It is important,” Gordon said, “that people remember that our constitution requires that every child get a good education and they be equally funded. That is a state responsibility.”
The supplemental request includes $500,000 for the attorney general to defend Wyoming’s share of Colorado River Basin water, water running through the Green and Little Snake rivers. The legal account also would support Wyoming’s efforts to ship coal and other products to foreign customers, efforts sometimes challenged by West Coast states.
State attorneys also could use some of the supplemental funds to defend Wyoming’s right to prohibit abortion, he said. Lawmakers have repeatedly attempted to ban or restrict abortion here, but the courts have consistently rebuffed those efforts.

title: Idaho Fish and Game commissioner pleads guilty to misdemeanor hunting charges
description: Idaho Fish and Game Commissioner Brody Harshbarger has pleaded guilty to two misdemeanor criminal hunting charges in exchange for prosecutors dropping poaching and trespassing charges, court records show.  Harshbarger, of Ashton, was originally charged with seven total hunting, poaching and trespassing charges after an Idaho Department of Fish and Game law e[...]
text:
Idaho Department of Fish and Game Commissioner Brody Harshbarger recently agreed to plead guilty to two hunting related charges. (File photo by Getty Images)Idaho Fish and Game Commissioner Brody Harshbarger has pleaded guilty to two misdemeanor criminal hunting charges in exchange for prosecutors dropping poaching and trespassing charges, court records show. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Harshbarger, of Ashton, was originally charged with seven total hunting, poaching and trespassing charges after an Idaho Department of Fish and Game law enforcement officer responded to a Citizens Against Poaching hotline call Dec. 20, 2025, court records show. 
Earlier this month, Harshbarger agreed to plead guilty to two of the misdemeanor charges – hunting without a valid tag and shooting from or across a public highway.
In exchange, the state dropped:

Two charges of unlawfully taking or killing a big game animal.
One charge of hunting with the aid of a motorized vehicle.
One charge of failure to make a reasonable effort to retrieve a six-point bull elk that was killed.
One charge of trespassing to hunt or fish.

Harshbarger is due back in court on Dec. 9 for sentencing, court records show. 
According to the plea agreement, Harshbarger faces a $500 fine for each of the two charges he pleaded guilty to, as well as the revocation of his hunting license for a period of one year.
Idaho Fish and Game commissioner Brody Harshbarger (Photo courtesy of the Idaho Fish and Game website)
Harshbarger’s appointment to the Idaho Fish and Game Commission is not scheduled to expire until June 30. 
Efforts to reach Harshbarger and his attorney, Mark Fuller, were not immediately successful Monday.
Idaho Fish and Game Commission members are appointed by the governor and responsible for establishing hunting regulations and overseeing the Idaho Department of Fish and Game.
As of Monday afternoon, Harshbarger continued to serve as an Idaho Fish and Game commissioner, said Emily Callihan, a spokeswoman for Gov. Brad Little.
Little has not asked for Harshbarger’s resignation, Callihan said Monday afternoon.
“The Governor’s Office is aware of Commissioner Harshbarger’s plea agreement,” Callihan said in an email to the Idaho Capital Sun on Monday. “Gov. Little will be working with the Idaho Department of Fish and Game and stakeholders in the coming days to ensure the responsibilities of the position are fulfilled.”
However, Harshbarger’s picture, name and bio did not appear on the Idaho Fish and Game Commission’s website on Monday. The names, bios and photos of the other six commissioners did appear on the website Monday.  
The Idaho Fish and Game Commission’s next meetings are scheduled for Tuesday and Wednesday in Lewiston. 
 Why was an Idaho Fish and Game Commission member facing criminal hunting charges?

According to sworn probable cause documents filed with Harshbarger’s case, Harshbarger and another man, Eric Murphy, were hunting elk near Spring Hollow boat ramp in eastern Idaho’s Fremont County. 
Harshbarger did not have a valid elk tag at the time because he had just filled his elk tag the weekend prior, according to court records. 
According to the probable cause documents, Harshbarger and Murphy both fired shots across Spring Hollow Road, and Harshbarger shot from the driver’s seat of his vehicle. Court documents indicate that a six-point bull elk was killed unlawfully on private property and an antlerless bull elk was killed unlawfully on Bureau of Reclamation property. 
“Neither Brody Harshbarger nor Eric Murphy called the landowners to request permission to retrieve the six-point bull and did not make a reasonable effort to retrieve the six-point bull elk …,” the probable cause statement reads. 
“Neither individual had permission to be shooting onto the private property, in violation of Idaho Code,” the report continued. 
In March, after the charges against him became public, Harshbarger agreed to “postpone the performance” of his duties as an Idaho Fish and Game commissioner until the criminal charges were resolved, according to a March 10 letter from Little’s then-chief of staff Zach Hague.
Now that Harshbarger has agreed to plead guilty to two of the hunting charges, some members of the public are asking for answers and asking who will represent them on the commission. 
“This is an extremely important matter to the thousands of hunters and anglers who have been unrepresented on the IDFG Commission since Mr. Harshbarger was charged,” Sheryl Hill of Ashton said Monday.

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: Judge stops meeting to approve $400M for Hyundai steel mill dock
description: A Louisiana judge granted a temporary retraining order Monday afternoon preventing the Port of South Louisiana from holding a public hearing on how it will finance riverfront infrastructure for the Hyundai steel mill project in Ascension Parish with state bonds.
text:
A freight ship heads south on the Mississippi River in southern Louisiana in June, 2024. Aerial support provided by SouthWings.
(Tegan Wendland/Mississippi River Basin Ag & Water Desk)
A Louisiana judge granted a temporary retraining order Monday afternoon preventing the Port of South Louisiana from holding a public hearing on how it will finance riverfront infrastructure for the Hyundai steel mill project in Ascension Parish with state bonds. 
Judge Kirk Vaughn of the 40th Judicial District Court said in his order that the public hearing on the proposed issuance of up to $400 million in bonds would cause “immediate and irreparable injury” to plaintiffs who are suing the port if the meeting took place as scheduled.


The meeting was planned for 9 a.m. Tuesday, and the port board’s agenda included a vote on the final decision whether to approve the bonds. The vote could have taken place at the exact same time as a court hearing on the lawsuit.
Lawyers for two of the plaintiffs, Rural Roots Louisiana and the Louisiana Bucket Brigade, successfully argued the scheduling conflict prevented them from testifying in the court hearing and at the public meeting. 
“We’ve asked the court to order the court to postpone that public hearing while the court determines these questions as to the legality of this bond issuance,” Pam Spees, a lawyer with the Center for Constitutional Rights who represents the plaintiffs, said in a news media briefing Monday morning. 
The Port of South Louisiana wants to approve the bond financing to support its construction of a deepwater dock facility and marine terminal on the Mississippi River to be exclusively used by Hyundai for its steel mill.
“It’s a cheaper way for these corporations to get financing, and then it’s another way that taxpayers lose out,” Spees said.
The port’s decision has been the subject of lawsuits from local community and environmental groups that allege the port did not properly disclose its decision to finance the project to the public. 
A court hearing on whether to dismiss the lawsuit will continue as scheduled at 9 a.m. Tuesday.
There was no information immediately available on when the Port of South Louisiana might reschedule its board meeting. The Port of South Louisiana declined to comment.
There was also no immediate response from the Hyundai-Posco joint venture that has teamed to build the $5.8 billion steel mill. 
This is a developing story.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Alaska State Troopers chip away at high vacancy rate with new academy grads
description: The Alaska Department of Public Safety announced 24 new law enforcement officers graduated from its basic training academy earlier this month. Among the cohort, 15 new state trooper trainees are helping continue the trend of reduced vacancy rates statewide. State law enforcement officials have reported progress on filling state trooper roles and reducing the[...]
text:
Alaska State Troopers sat in a classroom in the Alaska Law Enforcement Training Academy in Sitka Alaska in Spring 2022. (Photo courtesy of the Department of Public Safety.)The Alaska Department of Public Safety announced 24 new law enforcement officers graduated from its basic training academy earlier this month. Among the cohort, 15 new state trooper trainees are helping continue the trend of reduced vacancy rates statewide.
State law enforcement officials have reported progress on filling state trooper roles and reducing the vacancy rate in recent years, which they have said has impeded the agency’s ability to conduct criminal investigations. 
There are now 52 officer vacancies out of 411 funded positions within the agency, about a 13% vacancy rate, according to Austin McDaniel, a spokesperson for the Department of Public Safety. He said the agency saw a number of retirements this year, but also more applicants. 
That number has dropped from 62 vacant positions in 2024, or a roughly 15% vacancy rate.    
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX. 

“We’re certainly seeing improved recruitment numbers here over the last few academies, which is helping us lower the number of vacancies statewide we have in the state trooper and wildlife trooper job class,” McDaniel said. 
Nine of the recent graduates are headed to police departments in Bethel, Kenai, Soldotna, Seward, Palmer and Sitka. Two trainees are assigned to the Fairbanks Airport Police and Fire department. 
During 17 weeks and 1,000 hours of basic training at the residential academy in Sitka, law enforcement trainees receive classroom and hands-on instruction, including in use of force and de-esclation tactics, physical fitness, driving and firearms training. Trainees also learn about criminal law and police procedure. McDaniel said the course focuses on scenario-based training for new officers, and training is “constantly evolving based on things like case law, based on best practices we’re learning from the field.”
This year, five applicants did not complete the basic training academy — nearly one-fifth of the cohort. “It’s a highly stressful environment,” McDaniel said. “If you are struggling to handle stress appropriately in a controlled environment like a training academy, you know, the law enforcement profession, where there is a lot of stress every day in the job, may not be the best fit for folks.” 
After the 17 weeks of basic training, trooper recruits head to a 19-week field training and evaluation program based in Fairbanks, Soldotna or Palmer. If trainees successfully complete the program, they are promoted to the role of trooper within roughly one year of beginning the academy.
McDaniel credits the interest in Alaska law enforcement and improvements in trooper hiring and retention to a variety of factors: ongoing recruitment efforts by the department — including a reality TV show spotlighting the Alaska State Troopers — and competitive salary and benefits. 
“(They’re) all helping us move the needle towards recruiting more Alaska state troopers,” he said. 
Average pay for a new trooper in their first year is estimated at $145,000, including salary and overtime pay, McDaniel said. That’s a boost of roughly 12% from an average of $127,000 last year. The state offers the same base pay of $97,000 for new recruits plus incentives such as bonuses for rural posts, retirement benefits, moving expenses, retention pay and subsidized housing.
 

The Alaska Department of Public Safety Training Academy in Sitka is seen on Oct. 6, 2025. The academy offers specialized programs and hands-on training for a variety of law enforcement roles, including police and Alaska State Troopers (Photo by Corinne Smith/Alaska Beacon)
 

Rent and utilities are now free for troopers living in state-owned housing, which is covered by the state following a new contract negotiated this year by the Public Safety Employees Association. Legislators and the governor approved nearly $2 million in the budget for the subsidy this year. The state manages 86 housing units — for troopers, court service officers and fire and safety personnel —  in 21 communities, including Bethel, Nome, Kotzebue and Dillingham. 
The Public Safety Employees Association union did respond to a request for comment on the new contract on Monday. 
Following the first year-long probationary period, troopers may be reassigned to rural posts across the state through a department bid process. McDaniel said troopers are required to make at least one transfer within two to five years of working for the department. 
Staffing rural law enforcement positions has been a challenge for years, especially in Western Alaska. But the department doesn’t recruit directly to rural posts, McDaniel said. Instead the department opens positions and bids based on a variety of factors. “It’s going to be based on call volume. It’s going to be based on how many other employees we have in that area — kind of what is the need, the department’s need at that time,” he said.
Some rural posts are staffed by troopers in a two weeks on and two weeks off rotation, and those officers are still required to live in the state, McDaniel said. 
McDaniel said the revived reality TV show featuring the troopers has been renewed for another season. State officials have said they agreed to the show to help with recruitment, but McDaniel said it’s too early to determine a direct link to an increase in law enforcement applicants. 
“We see that as a positive thing,” he said. “But I’d say that instead of crediting the contract or the TV show or our recruitment efforts, I think it’s the fact that we are pulling all of the levers at the same time in an effort to make us a competitive agency for people looking at law enforcement in Alaska.”

title: Arkansas lawmaker proposes prohibiting Franklin County site from being used for prison
description: Republican Sen. Brad Simon filed a bill Monday that would prohibit Arkansas from using a Franklin County property purchased by the state for a future prison site.  Senate Bill 3 would prohibit the state from using the 815 acres it bought for nearly $3 million in 2024 for a correctional facility, detention facility or any […]
text:
The entrance to the Franklin County prison site on Nov. 13, 2025. (Photo by Ainsley Platt/Arkansas Advocate)Republican Sen. Brad Simon filed a bill Monday that would prohibit Arkansas from using a Franklin County property purchased by the state for a future prison site. 
Senate Bill 3 would prohibit the state from using the 815 acres it bought for nearly $3 million in 2024 for a correctional facility, detention facility or any temporary or permanent facility in which people are held in custody. 
The proposed bill would require the entity that holds the title for the Franklin County property and any other entity that has a property interest in the site to “execute and record a restrictive covenant” that would prohibit the land from being used for a correctional or detention facility. 
Franklin County prison project not canceled, Arkansas corrections secretary says

The prison project has faced criticism from elected officials and the local community since the state first announced plans to construct the facility in an effort to address overcrowding in correctional facilities. The project has been placed on hold after facing resistance in the Legislature.
Simon won a special election this year to fill a vacancy in the Arkansas Senate left by the death of Republican Sen. Gary Stubblefield, an outspoken critic of the prison project. 
Monday was the first day state lawmakers could start filing bills ahead of the legislative session that begins Jan. 11. 
Another bill filed Monday seeks to repeal the Generating Arkansas Jobs Act of 2025. The legislation, which allows utilities to begin recouping the costs of building new power generation facilities from ratepayers before those facilities are completed, has been blamed for Arkansans’ increasing electricity bills. Senate Bill 2, which aims to repeal the 2025 law, is co-sponsored by eight Republican lawmakers and two Democrats.

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Braun ‘fired up’ to seek second term in 2028
description: Gov. Mike Braun kicked off his 2028 reelection campaign Monday with a fundraiser and a promise to Hoosiers that he will “listen to the customer” on kitchen table issues should voters choose him again. “I love the competition. I love the battle and I’ve never been more fired up about doing something again,” he told […]
text:
Gov. Mike Braun, flanked by First Lady Maureen Braun, speaks to supporters during his reelection announcement on Monday, Nov. 16, 2026, in Speedway. (Photo by Niki Kelly/Indiana Capital Chronicle)Gov. Mike Braun kicked off his 2028 reelection campaign Monday with a fundraiser and a promise to Hoosiers that he will “listen to the customer” on kitchen table issues should voters choose him again.
“I love the competition. I love the battle and I’ve never been more fired up about doing something again,” he told a crowded room of supporters at the Indianapolis Motor Speedway Museum. Among those attending were donors, lobbyists and staffers from his administration.
Braun spent more than 20 minutes going over accomplishments from his first two years — including targeting utility rate increases and cutting property taxes.
He won the 2024 race with 54% of the vote, compared to 41% for Democrat Jennifer McCormick. He previously served one term in the U.S. Senate. Prior to that he was in the Indiana House and a local school board member in his hometown of Jasper.
Braun’s approval rating has dipped, recently. An October Free Press Indiana poll found that 48% disapproved of his job performance, with 38% approving. An Indiana Chamber of Commerce poll from the same time showed Braun’s disapproval was 47% and approval 35%.
At 70, he was the oldest person ever to be elected governor in Indiana. He will be 74 by the time the 2028 general election hits.
Braun has closely aligned himself with President Donald Trump, including calling a special session last year to redistrict Indiana’s congressional boundaries early. That effort ultimately failed.
Republicans were routed in the Nov. 3 midterm election, losing two statewide offices, one congressional seat and 21 legislative seats. Democrats also picked up many local offices. The chair of the Indiana Republican Party — handpicked by Braun — resigned and a successor is being sought.
A crowd of supporters for Gov. Mike Braun at the Indianapolis Motor Speedway Museum on Monday, Nov. 16, 2026, in Speedway. (Photo by Niki Kelly/Indiana Capital Chronicle)
Braun mentioned those results several times during his speech.
“So, what do you take from what we learned a couple weeks ago? Just like in business, you got to listen to the customer. If you’re not listening to the customer, they’re probably not going to be buying from you,” he said, standing beside first lady Maureen Braun.
As of June 30, Braun had $3.1 million in his campaign coffers. But he has continued bringing in large contributions — at least $1.6 million more since July 1, according to state Election Division filings.
During the first two years of his term, Braun has focused on affordability in multiple ways. He remade the Indiana Utility Regulatory Commission and has urged the commission’s members to turn down rate increases sought by Indiana utilities. Those moves haven’t resulted in change, though, as the board is bound by statute and precedent.
He suspended state gasoline taxes since last spring, saving Hoosiers more than $1 billion.
Braun also put $200 million into vouchers to help low-income parents with childcare costs.
In the 2025 legislative session, he championed property tax savings of $300 for homeowners. But that legislation — Senate Enrolled Act 1 — has caught criticism from both sides. Some believe the savings are coming at the expense of local schools and governments losing funding and others don’t believe the bill went far enough to reign in growing property tax bills.
Braun also touted a trimmer state government and alluded to larger increases for K12 schools in the next state budget.
A multimedia display welcomed supporters for Gov. Mike Braun to the Indianapolis Motor Speedway Museum on Monday, Nov. 16, 2026, in Speedway. (Photo by Niki Kelly/Indiana Capital Chronicle)
“We’ve cut taxes, created new opportunities for jobs and high wages, and led the nation in affordability,” he said. “Now it’s time to build on those to deliver even more opportunities in savings for Hoosiers, and I will be working with both sides of the aisle, just like I did in D.C.”
A big question about Braun’s renewed candidacy is whether he will welcome Lt. Gov. Micah Beckwith onto the ticket or choose another person to be his running mate. Beckwith was not part of the program Monday night.
Republican delegates will choose the lieutenant governor candidate in the GOP state convention in the summer of 2028. The party faithful picked Beckwith over Braun’s choice of then-state Rep. Julie McGuire in 2024.
Beckwith and Braun have operated largely separately during the first term, with Braun regularly being asked to comment on controversial things Beckwith does or says.
Braun didn’t take questions from reporters afterward and Beckwith didn’t respond to a text message sent earlier in the day about his plans.
At least one local GOP leader isn’t behind Braun’s reelection bid.
Wells County Republican Chairman Preston Wright commented on the current state of the Indiana Republican Party, including Braun.
“I’ve been telling my fellow county and district chairmen for months that I’m unhappy with the direction of the state party. Those concerns have never been personal,” he said in a statement last week. “Indiana was not immune to the wave of support for Democrats across the country … There are bigger issues with the direction of the party and how Hoosiers view us that won’t be fixed by changing the chairwoman.
“Until we have a new Governor, I expect more of the same.”

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: CT lawmakers mull priorities, practices for 2027 legislative session
description: Lawmakers will get raises, but the 2027 legislative session's committee assignments and other key details are still under discussion.
text:
The names, salaries and top leaders of the new General Assembly are settled, but most committee assignments and other details key to how business will move at the Capitol are a work in progress as the legislature prepares for the arrival of 39 new members and even more lopsided Democratic majorities.
Legislative salaries will increase in the two-year term that begins on Jan. 6 by 3.6% in 2027 and 3.2% in 2028, a consequence of a bipartisan bill passed in 2022 that pegs pay to a federal measure of wage growth, the Employment Cost Index. The first raise pegged to the index came in the 2025-2026 term.
The second calculation under the indexing provision will raise the base legislative pay in the part-time legislature to $46,608. Pay for the top two leaders, the House speaker and Senate president pro tem, will go to $60,591.
No lawmaker gets only the base pay. An additional $4,500 for unvouchered expenses is paid to House members, $5,550 to senators. Also, many lawmakers have a leadership title that come with higher pay, such as the $54,182 paid to committee co-chairs and assistant leaders.
The election two weeks ago produced Democratic majorities of 33-3 in the Senate and 116-35 in the House, the biggest ever in the Senate and the largest in the House since the post-Watergate election of 1974. Democrats currently hold advantages of 25-11 and 102-49.
House Speaker Matt Ritter, D-Hartford, and Senate Majority Leader Bob Duff, D-Norwalk, who has been endorsed by his caucus to become the Senate’s top leader, president pro tem, said in separate interviews they are working on committee assignments and legislative priorities. 
“To me, my moonshot is true property tax reform,’’ Ritter said, declining to provide details. “There’s a lot of conversations I have to have. It covers special education, it covers PILOT. Let’s go big.” 
PILOT is payments in lieu of taxes, the method for the state to at least partially reimburse municipalities for revenue lost due to hospitals, universities, state offices and other institutions exempt from local property taxes.
Duff cast his priorities more broadly, all falling under the umbrella of affordability:
“Anything we can do to help make our state more affordable for the working class, for the middle class, for seniors,” Duff said. “It’s the No. 1 issue we heard at the doors on the campaign trail. What all that looks at like the end of the session is up for debate.”
The legislature is not expected to expand the number of standing committees to accommodate the larger Democratic majorities, but the leaders are likely to increase the number of subcommittees.
“The approach for me is really to think about the legislature as an institution and the role we have right now. The states are where the action is at,” said Duff, the president-elect of the National Conference of State Legislatures. “We now have very big issues that states are working on, because Congress in Washington is not functioning. We have to think differently about how we approach policy. Adding more committees doesn’t address that issue.”
Democrats regained control of the U.S. House and Senate, but the new Senate majority will not be filibuster proof. And the blue wave, of course, leaves President Donald Trump and his veto pen in the White House.
Sen. Rob Sampson, R-Wolcott, who will be the leader of the three-person state Senate minority, said Monday that the diminished minority will require adjustments in how three senators will be able to staff the two dozen joint committees of the General Assembly.
“It’s going to be a combination of leaning on our House Republican counterparts and our Senate Republican staff,” Sampson said. “They’ve got to become an early warning system for three senators, so we can pick our shots. We have no choice.”
The current Senate minority leader, Sen. Stephen Harding of Brookfield, lost his reelection bid, but he is expected to return as a senior adviser to Sampson.
“There is nothing public yet,” Sampson said. “We have not finalized our staffing budget with the majority.”
But Sampson left no doubt he wants Harding to return on his staff.
“Sen. Harding is fabulous asset to the caucus,” Sampson said. “I am hoping he will remain in the picture.”
Sampson said he will be seeking a rule change necessary to maintain a modicum of GOP influence — the ability of a single senator to request a roll call on amendments offered on the Senate floor, as opposed to a voice vote. 
Under current rules, 20% of the body must favor a roll call on an amendment. With only three Republican senators, the GOP will control only 8% of the seats. With 35 of the 151 seats, House Republicans will continue have more than 20% of the membership.
“Whether you have 35 or 50, procedurally the rules fall the same way,” said House Minority Leader Vincent J. Candelora, R-North Branford. “The approach has to be that Republicans have to get in the game early and be an active participant in the process.”
Candelora said that means being involved at the committee level in the development and screening of legislation, which he says has been the approach of his caucus.
Committee assignments generally are not made public until December, and Ritter will begin to interview his 26 new members Wednesday to assess their desires for committees.
Three major committees will see no change in their House chairs.
Ritter said Monday that Rep. Toni Walker of New Haven will return to Appropriations, Rep. Maria Horn of Salisbury to Finance, Revenue and Bonding, and Rep. Steven Stafstrom of Bridgeport to Judiciary.
One potentially awkward seating assignment has yet to be made: The House chamber has four seating sections, and the one where Candelora and most other Republicans now sit has 36 desks. 
On Jan. 6, there only will be 35 Republicans — meaning one Democrat will have to sit across the aisle.

name: Daily Montanan
title: Merger of NorthWestern Energy, Black Hills lands in court
description: The same day NorthWestern Energy announced its merger with Black Hills Corp was complete, a state agency decision to approve it landed in court. In a joint press release Monday, the utilities announced they’d formed a new company, Bright Horizon Energy. “Today marks the beginning of an exciting new chapter as Bright Horizon Energy,” said […]
text:
Electricity pylons (Photo by Getty Images). The same day NorthWestern Energy announced its merger with Black Hills Corp was complete, a state agency decision to approve it landed in court.
In a joint press release Monday, the utilities announced they’d formed a new company, Bright Horizon Energy.
“Today marks the beginning of an exciting new chapter as Bright Horizon Energy,” said Brian Bird, president and CEO of Bright Horizon, former CEO of NorthWestern, in a statement.
“By bringing together our talented employees, complementary operations, and shared commitment to safety, reliability and affordability, we are creating a stronger, more resilient company positioned to meet the growing energy needs of our 2.2 million customers across eight states.”
The $15.4 billion merger proposal was announced in August 2025, and last week the Montana Public Service Commission approved it on a 3-2 vote.
Montana was the final state that needed to grant approval for the merger to close.
But Monday, two parties that participated in the Public Service Commission case filed a petition in Lewis and Clark County District Court to declare the PSC’s final order on the proposal void.
The PSC closed part of the meeting last Tuesday.
In their petition, 350 Montana and Montana Farmers Union alleged the closure violated the Montana Constitution’s requirement that government meetings be open to the public.
The groups argue the PSC’s move to shut out the public “without notice, explanation, or any legal reason to do so” was an infringement on people’s right to know and participate in the decisions of their government.
In a related public records request also filed Monday, the groups asked for information about who participated in the closed session, what took place, and “what materials were considered or changed.”
Represented by lawyer Monica Tranel, the groups also allege the PSC did not account for the risks of the merger on Montana ratepayers, and as such, is compelling them to “pay for the capital Bright Horizon has promised to AI data centers.”
The order said Bright Horizon capital is obligated in eight states to 40 entities including Microsoft and Meta, and Montana will lose oversight of investment decisions in the merger.
Additionally, the parties argue the PSC didn’t adequately evaluate the 370 megawatts that NorthWestern Energy acquired from Puget Sound Energy at the Colstrip Power Plant.
Court filings ask the judge to void the PSC order on the merger “to the extent it authorizes merger consummation” and to stop the deal because “loss of control of Montana’s largest utility is at stake.”
The court filing said once the merger closes, the Montana PSC’s regulatory leverage disappears because corporate control of the enterprise will be in South Dakota.
Monday, Tranel said the merger isn’t yet final; it remains subject to reconsideration for 30 days, and the court filing said the closure is extended to Feb. 18 to account for potential judicial review.
The petition also asks the judge to stop the utilities and unregulated affiliates from selling or transferring the Puget shares of the Colstrip Power Plant.
A spokesperson for the PSC said the commission had not been served and had no comment. A spokesperson for NorthWestern said the utility does not comment on pending litigation.
In 2026, NorthWestern Energy and Black Hills Energy reported $19.9 million in merger related costs, according to NorthWestern. A utility spokesperson said those costs are paid for by shareholders and will not be recovered through customer rates.
The combined merger costs for 2025 were not available Monday from NorthWestern.
The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, Nebraska Public Service Commission, and South Dakota Public Utilities Commission earlier approved the merger.
Although the merged company has a new name, the news release Monday said local customers should not expect immediate changes to branding, payment processes, outage reporting or customer support.
The new company is expected to serve electric and natural gas customers in Montana, Arkansas, Colorado, Iowa, Kansas, South Dakota, Nebraska and Wyoming.
At PSC meetings including the one last week, many members of the public expressed opposition to the merger, citing concerns Montanans would have to subsidize the costs of data centers.
But a couple of representatives of the business community urged the PSC to support the deal as a tool for economic growth.
PSC President Jeff Welborn and Commissioner Randy Pinocci voted against the merger. Commissioners Jennifer Fielder, Annie Bukacek and Kirk Bushman supported it.

name: Nevada Current
title: Ford’s transition team co-chaired by attorney whose firm represents Kalshi against Nevada
description: Parties in Nevada’s court battle against the prediction market Kalshi are declining to comment on Governor-elect Aaron Ford’s inclusion on his transition team of John Bailey, a founding partner in the law firm that is representing Kalshi against the state.  “We have no comment,” a spokesperson said Monday on behalf of the Nevada Gaming Control […]
text:
(Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)Parties in Nevada’s court battle against the prediction market Kalshi are declining to comment on Governor-elect Aaron Ford’s inclusion on his transition team of John Bailey, a founding partner in the law firm that is representing Kalshi against the state. 
“We have no comment,” a spokesperson said Monday on behalf of the Nevada Gaming Control Board, which is warding off Kalshi’s bid to compete with the state’s sports books, absent the required license.  
The Nevada Resort Association, which represents major resorts and is a party to the lawsuit, also declined to comment. 
Ford, who as AG, has represented Nevada gambling regulators in their effort to rein in Kalshi, raised eyebrows last month when his campaign sent out a news release touting Kalshi’s odds of Ford unseating Gov. Joe Lombardo. 
Lombardo’s spokesperson deemed the campaign pitch a conflict of interest and called Ford’s news release “absolutely absurd.” 
Now, Ford is seeking guidance from Bailey, an expert in gaming law, whose firm enjoys Kalshi’s legal largesse.
Bailey will serve as a co-chair of Ford’s transition advisory committee, along with Lieutenant Governor-elect Sandra Juaregui and Ford’s wife, Berna Rhodes-Ford, the campaign announced Thursday. 
Bailey also served on Gov. Steve Sisolak’s transition team. 
In a separate move Monday, Ford named Asha Jones as chief of staff, a position she previously served in for Nevada’s Democratic U.S. Rep. Steven Horsford. Prior to that she was district director for former Nevada U.S. Democratic Rep. Ruben Kiehuen. Jones has also worked for Sen. Harry Reid and Shelley Berkley, the former Democratic congresswoman who is now mayor of Las Vegas. More recently, Jones served as a vice president of corporate affairs for Brightline West, and as director of development for Boyd Gaming.
Politics is replete with instances of strange bedfellows – relationships that confound common sensibilities.
“That’s not a way to endear yourself to the gaming industry. It’s curious,” former gaming executive Richard Schuetz, who also served as a member of the California Gaming Control Commission, said of Ford’s selection of Bailey. 
“It’s always good to have a diversity of opinions. You don’t want to just listen to people reading off the same song sheet,” Schuetz said. “But I think it’s important to understand that Bailey’s influence could have a dramatic impact on the gaming industry.”
Ford’s campaign did not immediately respond to a request for comment. 
Earlier this year, a three-judge panel of the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals ruled against Kalshi, which is fighting an order from Nevada gaming regulators to stop taking sports bets in the state. 
The prediction market is represented by Bailey’s partner, Dennis Kennedy. 
Nevada is among a number of states fighting Kalshi and other prediction markets in court. 
In November, the Ninth Circuit denied Kalshi’s request for a rehearing before the entire court. Kalshi is expected to appeal the ruling to the U.S. Supreme Court. 
Disclosure: Bailey, who previously represented hard money lender Jeff Guinn, the son of former Gov. Kenny Guinn, alleged this reporter accepted gifts and money in exchange for writing stories about Guinn, who was being sued by investors. The Nevada Supreme Court ruled in 2013 that Guinn was attempting to circumvent the Nevada Shield Law that protects reporters.

title: Trial scheduled in Van Buren County animal-neglect case
description: A Van Buren County dog breeder facing 34 counts of animal neglect is scheduled to go to trial early next year. In late July, Van Buren County officials criminally charged Wuanita Swedlund, 35, of Farmington, with 27 counts of simple misdemeanor animal neglect without death or serious injury, plus seven serious misdemeanor counts of animal […]
text:
This dog was photographed by USDA inspectors in January 2023 at a kennel operated by Wuanita Swedlund of Iowa. (USDA photo courtesy of Bailing Out Benji)A Van Buren County dog breeder facing 34 counts of animal neglect is scheduled to go to trial early next year.
In late July, Van Buren County officials criminally charged Wuanita Swedlund, 35, of Farmington, with 27 counts of simple misdemeanor animal neglect without death or serious injury, plus seven serious misdemeanor counts of animal neglect with injury.
Swedlund has pleaded not guilty to all of the charges and a trial is now scheduled for Jan. 27, 2027.
In an affidavit attached to the criminal complaints, Deputy Sheriff Spencer Rider alleged Swedlund had failed to provide adequate food and water to the confined animals on her property, causing the animals unjustified distress and suffering.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
During a June visit to Swedlund’s kennels, Rider alleges, officials observed water bowls containing no potable water for animals to drink; food bowls contaminated with feces; kennels with an excessive buildup of feces and organic matter, indicating the kennels had not been cleaned for a prolonged period of time; a flea infestation, and a Yorkshire terrier that was in need of dental care.
On June 30, 2026, deputies seized 32 dogs, plus one cat and one rabbit, from Swedlund’s property.
In June 2026, the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service sued Swedlund for allegedly barring federal officials from conducting “unannounced” inspections of her dog-breeding operations. The USDA asked the court to issue an injunction granting the agency access to the property.
On July 10, 2026, U.S. District Judge Stephen Locher issued the injunction, stating that Swedlund’s noncompliance with the federal Animal Welfare Act “goes well beyond bureaucratic handwringing. The evidence shows that Swedlund has housed hundreds of dogs since acquiring her USDA license in 2023. She has consistently failed to provide her animals with adequate facilities, access to water, or access to medical care. It is evident that the animals in Swedlund’s care suffered needlessly — precisely the type of harm that the Animal Welfare Act sought to prevent.”
Van Buren County District Court Judge Joel D. Yates has transferred ownership of the animals to the PAW Animal Shelter in Fort Madison for eventual adoption. In his ruling, Yates said the evidence showed the “animals were neglected by not having access to appropriate food, potable water, sanitary conditions, proper ventilated shelter and necessary veterinary care.”
Swedlund spoke to the Iowa Capital Dispatch in July, saying she doesn’t believe any of the animals suffered from any type of neglect. “All my animals were healthy,” she said at the time.
Court records indicate USDA first issued Swedlund a license in July 2023. Since then, the records show, she has been cited for numerous violations of the Animal Welfare Act, some of which were tied to the death of eight puppies from three different litters.
In that case, USDA alleged Swedlund told inspectors she had found three dead bulldog puppies after feeling a strong, cold draft at the front of their enclosure. Inspectors reported Swedlund had placed duct tape over the hole that caused the draft, but the tape was peeling away at the time of the inspection and the cold draft could still be felt.
Three more puppies from a litter of rottweilers were found dead, the USDA says, and one puppy was severely injured and later euthanized after a husky broke into an enclosure housing a sheepdog and her newborn litter. A week later, another of the puppies from that litter was apparently eaten by its mother.

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Arkansas still set to enforce Medicaid work requirements Jan. 1 despite option of 6 extra months
description: The Arkansas Department of Human Services still plans to enforce work requirements for Medicaid enrollees starting Jan. 1, despite the federal government allowing states six more months to put the mandate in place. The Arkansas Department of Human Services is “reviewing the details” of the additional six months allowed before implementation but has not chang[...]
text:
The Arkansas Department of Human Services building on Main Street in downtown Little Rock. (Photo by John Sykes/Arkansas Advocate)The Arkansas Department of Human Services still plans to enforce work requirements for Medicaid enrollees starting Jan. 1, despite the federal government allowing states six more months to put the mandate in place.
The Arkansas Department of Human Services is “reviewing the details” of the additional six months allowed before implementation but has not changed its plan to put the mandate in place Jan. 1, acting communications chief Keith Metz said in an email.
The U.S. Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services announced the six-month grace period Friday, a day after two top Congressional Democrats raised concerns that states needed more time to put systems in place to keep eligible Americans from losing Medicaid coverage.
Many states unsure how to implement new Medicaid work requirements, KFF survey finds

Most Medicaid enrollees between the ages of 19 and 65 will be required to work, participate in community service, or attend an education program at least 80 hours a month in order to keep their health insurance, according to the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, a sweeping 2025 tax and spending cut bill.
Officials in multiple states said earlier this year that they were unsure how exactly to determine if someone meets the new work requirements or is exempt.
Those exempt from the work requirements include pregnant people, parents of dependent children, people who have complex medical conditions, tribal community members, those in the foster care system, people who were in foster care who are below the age of 26 and individuals released from incarceration in the last 90 days, among others.
The Department of Human Services has been preemptively working to determine Medicaid enrollees’ continued eligibility before the work requirements go into effect.
Arkansas Advocates for Children and Families said Monday that the extra time allowed was encouraging and the state’s decision not to take that time was frustrating.
“Arkansas’s Medicaid participants are already going through many changes that are confusing,” the organization said in a statement. “Arkansas should take the maximum amount of time allowed to make sure the reporting system is as accurate as possible, as other states have chosen to do, rather than rushing implementation of the work reporting requirements.”
More than 800,000 low-income and disabled Arkansans receive some form of Medicaid coverage. As of Nov. 1, nearly 209,000 are on the state’s hybrid Medicaid expansion program, known as Arkansas Health and Opportunity for Me, or ARHOME.
Official: Moving Arkansas Medicaid expansion enrollees to new program would take more than 6 months

In July, the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services verbally denied a five-year extension of the expansion. Human Services Secretary Janet Mann asked for a two-year reprieve to develop a new program. The Trump administration informed Mann earlier this month that it will keep ARHOME active for six months starting Jan. 1.
Six months is not long enough to transfer all Medicaid expansion enrollees to either managed care or fee-for-service Medicaid, state Division of Medical Services Director Elizabeth Pitman told lawmakers last week.
Formulating a new expansion model will be a high priority in the legislative session that begins in January. Pitman and Mann both told lawmakers that ending the program completely is not an option.
Arkansas’ program uses Medicaid money to purchase private insurance for low-income residents. The first-in-the-nation model was approved in 2013 as an alternative to expanding Medicaid under the Affordable Care Act.
Arkansas was the first state to impose work requirements on Medicaid expansion recipients, a mandate that was approved during President Donald Trump’s first term. More than 18,000 Arkansans lost coverage before a federal judge blocked the policy in 2019.

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: Burleigh County ballot mistake did not affect results, election official says
description: A ballot mixup at Burleigh County polling location on Election Day would not have changed any election results, according to a county election official. County canvassing boards met Monday to certify local election results ahead of North Dakota’s State Canvassing Board meeting Wednesday.  Dozens of voters in Burleigh County were given the wrong ballot by […]
text:
Thomas Larson, election coordinator for Burleigh County, speaks to the Burleigh County Canvassing Board while holding a stack of set-aside ballots on Nov. 16, 2026. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)A ballot mixup at Burleigh County polling location on Election Day would not have changed any election results, according to a county election official.
County canvassing boards met Monday to certify local election results ahead of North Dakota’s State Canvassing Board meeting Wednesday. 
Dozens of voters in Burleigh County were given the wrong ballot by election judges at one Bismarck  polling location.
The ballots involved legislative candidates from District 7 on the northside of Bismarck. There were 134 District 7 voters who were given a ballot for District 8, which did not have any legislative candidates competing this year.
Election error caused some Bismarck voters to receive wrong ballot

Sen. Michelle Axtman, R-Bismarck, would go on to defeat her District 7 Democratic-NPL challenger Kevin Horneman 4,402 to 1,914. Republican House candidates Greg Vetter and Steve Sauter received 4,147 and 4,029, respectively, and defeated the Dem-NPL District 7 House candidates Tiffany Williams-Rice and Jason Thoms, who received 1,866 and 1,786 votes.
The margins of victory were large enough that the 134 votes would not have affected the outcomes. 
“Essentially, the judges were giving out the wrong ballots,” said Thomas Larson, election coordinator for Burleigh County. 
The polling location had four different ballots that could have gone to voters depending on where they lived, he added.
“None of our other polling locations had this issue. It was an isolated situation,” Larson said.
Thomas Larson, election coordinator for Burleigh County, speaks to the Burleigh County Canvassing Board on Nov. 16, 2026. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)
The mistake was discovered Election Day morning but voters were unable to change their ballots once they were inserted into the tabulation machines.
“Once a ballot is cast, there’s nothing you can do about it,” Larson said. He added the county plans to conduct more immersive training for election judges ahead of the 2028 election to ensure they are set up and prepared for the issue “not to happen again.”
He said the error at a single polling location does not reflect the accurate work of election workers across the county in the lead up to Election Day during the early voting period.
“At the Event Center, for 10 days during early voting and on Election Day, we have 33 different ballot styles there and this wasn’t an issue,” Larson said.
North Dakota Monitor reporter Michael Achterling can be reached at machterling@northdakotamonitor.com.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: CT delays Medicaid losses from work requirements until July 2027
description: The “hold harmless” period means that while work requirements go into effect Jan. 1, no one will lose coverage for noncompliance before July.
text:
New federal work requirements for the Medicaid HUSKY D program are slated to go into effect in January, but Connecticut residents who fail to comply won’t lose coverage before July, according to a Monday announcement by Gov. Ned Lamont and the state Department of Social Services commissioner Andrea Barton Reeves.
Beginning Jan. 1, HUSKY D enrollees must meet work requirements, also being referred to as “community engagement requirements.” 
To keep coverage, HUSKY D enrollees will have to prove they work at least 80 hours or earn a minimum of $580 per month. The requirement can also be fulfilled by demonstrating at least 80 hours of monthly participation in school, community service or a qualified training program. Several exemptions exist.
On Friday, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services announced it would provide states the option of implementing a “hold harmless” period through and including June 30, 2027. During these six months, HUSKY D members who are otherwise eligible won’t lose coverage just because of failure to meet the work requirements.
The decision is meant to give states more time to implement the changes. Lamont and Barton Reeves announced on Monday that Connecticut will elect to implement the “hold harmless” period.
“This additional time will help our residents meet the changing federal requirements and ensure our systems are working the way they should,” Lamont said in a statement. Barton Reeves called the “hold harmless” period “a true benefit to our members.”
The work requirements were originally passed in 2025 as part of House Resolution 1, commonly referred to by President Donald Trump as the “One Big Beautiful Bill.”
Sen. Matt Lesser, D-Middletown, co-chair of the state legislature’s Human Services Committee, said the federal government’s decision to extend a hold harmless period could be the result of the Democrats’ sweep in the midterm elections.
“Elections have consequences,” Lesser said. “My hope is that this is the sign that the writing is on the wall for the president’s disastrous domestic policy agenda.”
The hold harmless period is only a six months reprieve from coverage losses, and as of now, the Medicaid work requirements are still going into effect. But several Democrats who won their races in the midterm elections campaigned on permanently reversing some of Trump’s healthcare policies, including the Medicaid changes.
Even with Democratic majorities in both chambers, Trump still has the power to veto any proposal to reverse the Medicaid changes. Overriding his veto would require getting Republicans on board. Or Democrats could opt to negotiate a deal with Trump, if he’s open to it.
Last week, before the announcement of the hold harmless period, State Comptroller Sean Scanlon said state officials hoped Democrats would be able to repeal the Medicaid changes, but their success likely depends on Trump’s willingness to negotiate.
“We’re really hoping that that is something that they get done in the first couple weeks of a new Congress,” Scanlon said. “Of course, the president is still the president. What his appetite is to do deals with the Democrats and resolve some of these things is really unclear and I don’t think anybody knows at this point.”

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: Newly elected Oklahoma senators take oath of office ahead of start of Senate term
description: OKLAHOMA CITY – They came to the Senate chamber humbled, with a sense of gratitude, awe and excitement for the future. Oklahoma Chief Justice Dustin P. Rowe on Monday administered the oath of office to the newly elected and reelected senators in the Senate chamber. Some fought back tears. Others thanked voters and introduced friends […]
text:
Sen.-elect Jessica Winegeart, R-Calumet, introduces her family after taking the oath of office Monday in the Senate chamber. (Photo by Barbara Hoberock/Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY – They came to the Senate chamber humbled, with a sense of gratitude, awe and excitement for the future.
Oklahoma Chief Justice Dustin P. Rowe on Monday administered the oath of office to the newly elected and reelected senators in the Senate chamber.
Some fought back tears. Others thanked voters and introduced friends and family members.
They will officially become senators on Wednesday. 
House members will be sworn in on Tuesday.
“I’m not one to be a big crier, but I was welling up, you know, just to see all the hard work that I and several other people that helped me through the process come to fruition, come to the beginning and end at the same time,” said Sen.elect Aaron Forst, R-Owasso.
Forst defeated incumbent Sen. Dana Prieto, R-Tulsa, in the Republican primary.
“It’s been a year and a half of campaigning,” Forst said. “It’s been a long trail. We had a lot happening. This was not your standard race in our case by far. It’s taken a toll on my family.”
His main focus will be on childcare.
“It’s overregulated, underfunded and we’ve got to do something to fix that,” he said.
Sen.-elect Curtis Erwin, R-Elgin, is replacing Sen. Dusty Deevers, R-Elgin, who didn’t make it out of the primary.
“The race was long, but all of my opponents were very respectful,” he said. “They ran really clean races.”
Sen.-elect Jessica Winegeart, R-Calumet, decided to run for senate after serving on her local school board. She replaces Sen. Darcy Yech, R-Kingfisher, who was term limited.
“I was able to affect change in my community, to see the positive outcomes, to see the things that I could be involved in,” she said. “And I want to do that on the next level.”
She said being sworn in was “completely surreal, overwhelming.”
“You know, I really had to hold it together because it’s such a huge moment in your life,” she said. “It’s such a huge honor, but also a huge responsibility. You feel the weight of that.”
Senate President Pro Tem Lonnie Paxton, R-Tuttle, said his advice to the newcomers is to build relationships and stay in contact with constituents.
“Don’t get isolated,” he said. “Don’t get tunnel vision. Don’t think we are better than anybody else. We’re here serving the public, and they’re not serving us.”

title: New Mexico workforce department awards $250K for youth internship programs
description: The state Department of Workforce Solutions announced Monday it awarded $250,000 in contracts to expand youth internship programs.
text:
The New Mexico Department of Workforce Solutions announced on Nov. 16, 2026, that it has awarded two contracts to boost youth internship programs. (Photo of Mayfield High School students in Las Cruces by Leah Romero for Source New Mexico)The state Department of Workforce Solutions announced Monday that it awarded $250,000 in contracts to expand youth internship programs. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The funding, via a $270,000 appropriation earlier this year from the Legislature, follows a request for proposals by DWS for youth-based internship programs to serve youth ages 16-24. 
Lawmakers this year have consistently focused on the statewide issue of youth engagement, particularly in the aftermath of an April Legislative Finance Committee report that found approximately 32,000 New Mexicans between the ages of 16 and 24 neither work nor go to school.
Future Focused Education, an Albuquerque-based secondary education nonprofit, will receive $187,500 for its ‘X3’ paid internship program for high school and early college-age students. The awarded funds will help students in the X3 program get hands-on experience and mentorship in the healthcare, behavioral health and agriculture career fields, DWS said in a news release. 
According to Future Focused Education, the X3 internship program has 2,140 active internships with 229 employer partners.
“Paid internships do more than prepare young people for careers,” Kim Lanoy-Sandoval, executive director of Future Focused Education, said in a statement. “They give them the chance to discover their potential, build meaningful connections, and contribute to the communities they call home. “
Santa Fe Public Schools received $62,500 from DWS to provide additional internships through the district’s Work-Based Learning Program, available for junior and senior high school students. Students in the program will earn $15.40 per hour, increasing to $17.50 per hour starting Jan. 1, 2027, according to the news release. 
“This investment creates meaningful opportunities for our students to connect what they learn in the classroom with real-world career experiences,” Christine Griffin, SFPS superintendent, said in a statement. 
DWS added that student interns in the program will also receive additional support, including transportation and child care assistance, as well as financial literacy resources.
“By bringing educators, employers and workforce partners together, we are investing in young people while helping businesses build the skilled workforce they need to grow and succeed,” DWS Secretary Sarita Nair said in a statement

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Federal government fights Arkansas’ efforts to sue Kalshi
description: The federal government has asked a judge to block Arkansas’ lawsuit against the online prediction market Kalshi, saying the state doesn’t have the authority to regulate the company. The Commodity Futures Trading Commission filed a lawsuit last week in federal court in Arkansas against the state over its investigation into Kalshi. Attorney General Tim Griffin[...]
text:
(Getty Images)The federal government has asked a judge to block Arkansas’ lawsuit against the online prediction market Kalshi, saying the state doesn’t have the authority to regulate the company.
The Commodity Futures Trading Commission filed a lawsuit last week in federal court in Arkansas against the state over its investigation into Kalshi. Attorney General Tim Griffin earlier this month sued Kalshi and accused the company of running an illegal gambling operation.
The CFTC complaint, however, said that federal law gives the commission exclusive jurisdiction to regulate prediction markets like Kalshi.
“To restore the commission’s exclusive jurisdiction, the state’s pending enforcement action against Kalshi, as well as any future enforcement actions or investigations against federally regulated (designated contract markets) and related entities, must be enjoined immediately,” the commission’s lawsuit said.
Arkansas is the 11th state the CFTC has sued over regulation of prediction markets, the agency said. 
“As prediction markets continue to prove their value in being useful for risk management and providing the public with valuable information about the future, Arkansas seeks to shut down event contracts ranging from sports and politics to other important world events,” Chairman Michael S. Selig said in a news release.
Griffin’s office on Monday said it disagreed with the commission’s argument and said that Arkansas regulates gambling to protect consumers. 
“Instead of obtaining the licenses, submitting to the oversight, complying with the restrictions, and paying the taxes required of lawful gambling operators in Arkansas, Kalshi opened its platforms to Arkansas consumers, including individuals as young as 18 years old, encouraged them to wager real money on sporting and entertainment events, and profited from those wagers,” spokesperson Jeff LeMaster said in a statement.

title: DeSantis administration agency chiefs, other top staff told to submit resignations
description: Gov. Ron DeSantis’s administration is asking that its department heads and other high-ranking officials submit resignations by close of business Monday to smooth the transition to Gov.-elect Bryon Donalds.
“With Inauguration Day approaching on Jan. 5, 2027, the Governor would like to ensure an orderly and seamless transfer of leadership to the incoming Donalds administration,” the email, obtained by the Florida Phoenix, says. 
“As is consistent with previous gubernatorial transitions, I ask that all agency heads who are receiving this email submit their letter of resignation effective at the close of business on January 4, 2027.”
