name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Parent leaders hold our communities together. It’s time the state built a pathway to support them.
description: Parent leaders need a pathway that connects their leadership to college and careers, and a direct line from their lived experience to the agencies and organizations that need it.
text:
HUONG VU WAS a television journalist in Vietnam. Peace Junaid was a nutritional biochemist in Nigeria. When they immigrated to Massachusetts years ago, both put their careers on hold for their families, and neither expected to find a way back to their careers. 
Today, Massachusetts families turn to parent leaders when the rules change overnight. Housing, health care, and child care now cost more than many families can bear, and federal changes have already unraveled much of the safety net beneath them. When families are left guessing where to turn, the answer is often a parent who has already figured it out, at school pickup, in a frantic WhatsApp thread, or at an after-school meeting. 
Systems across Massachusetts already understand that parent engagement matters, and many have worked hard to make room for it. Yet despite those efforts, too many parent voices are still underrepresented. Real leadership, where parents help shape the decisions that affect their families and then help carry them out, is not yet happening. That is not for a lack of caring. It is a lack of infrastructure. 
Parent leaders already carry valuable skills: outreach to families others miss to help them navigate and connect to the right resources and systems; communication that bridges languages, cultures, and the gap between families and institutions; and advocacy that pushes their needs to the forefront. What they need is a pathway that connects their leadership to college and careers, and a direct line from their lived experience to the agencies and organizations that need it. Goodwill does not scale. Infrastructure does. 
The two of us came to this from opposite directions. One of us arrived from Colombia 30 years ago with a law degree, became a mother, and eventually did family engagement work to elevate parent leaders, something she has done for the past 20 years. The other spent 30 years in corporate strategy, then 15 more in pro bono consulting and funding early childhood programs across Massachusetts. 
We reached the same conclusion: The stability of our communities rests on parent leaders, and they need a foundation to grow. 
So we co-founded Mass ParentCorps to build a statewide infrastructure for parent leadership, together with parent leaders and the organizations that support them. We raise awareness of what parent leaders contribute, expand their pathways to college and careers, bring their voices into policy, and attract investment to the field.  
We started with the Mass ParentCorps credential, which honors the expertise of parents already leading in their communities. They take a course at one of our partner community colleges and present an applied learning project, earning six to nine college credits along with the credential. Then we connect them to opportunities to continue their education or pursue new work. 
We started by listening to the Departments of Early Education and Care and Elementary and Secondary Education, to the parent leaders, and to community agencies, including Families First, Union Capital Boston, East Boston Social Centers, Family Nurturing Center of Massachusetts, and Vital Village Networks, which helped shape the model. And then we went to Urban College of Boston, where President Yves Salomon-Fernandez opened the door without hesitation. 
Together, with support from Eastern Bank and the Commonwealth Children’s Fund, we recruited 19 parent leaders, representing 10 community agencies, into our first credentialing cohort. This fall, we partnered with Middlesex Community College to launch a second cohort of 21 parents. Joanna Geller, director of policy, research, and evaluation at the NYU Metropolitan Center for Research on Equity and the Transformation of Schools, is researching and evaluating the model. 
From one parent leader a whole ecosystem rises. As a parent gains a path forward, their children see a leader at home, communities are engaged, and responsive systems add up to a healthier economy.  
Huong’s path shows what infrastructure can do. After she arrived here, her career stopped, until a home visitor brought her a basket of resources and led her to a parent-child playgroup run by the Dorchester Family Engagement Network at the Boys & Girls Clubs of Dorchester.  
That playgroup became her workplace. She began as a volunteer with a Vietnamese book club, was promoted to parent leader, and was among the first parents there trained to use a developmental screening tool to help families understand how their children are growing. Today she is a full-time family engagement specialist on the club’s staff, working with hundreds of families every year. What she wants next is for policymakers to see her work for what it is: a profession. 
At that same Boys & Girls Club, Huong saw a leader in Peace Junaid before Peace saw it in herself, and offered her a role as a parent partner. “It takes others to see something in us to help lift us up,” Peace says. Both women were part of our first cohort. Today, Peace plans to combine her training as a biochemist with her leadership to help women care for their own health, and to become, in her words, “the CEO of my own dreams.” 
Their stories echo those of hundreds of parents across Massachusetts who run family nights at community centers, sit on school councils, and connect a newly arrived family to a pediatrician, a food pantry, and an English class in the same afternoon. They work as parent partners, parent leaders, and family engagement specialists at family engagement networks, community centers, family resource centers, early education programs, and youth organizations. 
Some organizations already understand what parent leaders are worth. These have long trained and paid them, often stretching limited budgets to do it. That deserves real credit. Elsewhere, many parent leaders are still treated as volunteers, doing essential work on the side until they burn out. 
Massachusetts already knows how to invest in families. It is the only state to make pandemic-era child care grants permanent, with $475 million for Commonwealth Cares for Children this year, and free community college has reversed a decade of enrollment decline. But these policies work only when families know about them, trust them, and can navigate the paperwork.  
Parent leaders make that happen. The bridges are being built. Now we must invest in the people who walk families across them. 
It is time to make parent leadership a Commonwealth priority: 

Recognize parent leadership as a skill set. State agencies should recognize a parent leadership credential in hiring and contracting, so Huong’s work counts as the profession it is. 


Build on what’s working. Fund at scale the paid roles many agencies already offer parent leaders. 


Connect leadership to college and careers. Parent leadership training should carry credit toward certificates and degrees, so a biochemist like Peace builds on her science background instead of starting over. 


Put parents at the table. Parent leaders should help write the policies that shape families’ lives. 

On Tuesday, November 17, our first cohort will share their experiences at a forum at Urban College of Boston. Joined by college leaders, researchers, and community partners, they will discuss how parent leadership can open doors to higher education, strengthen communities, and inform statewide policy. We invite policymakers, funders, and employers to listen and help turn these lessons into action. 
Huong and Peace each carry the skills of a leader. Massachusetts has depended on parent leaders like them to hold our communities together. Now it is time to do more than celebrate their contributions. It is time to recognize their value, invest in their potential, and build the pathways that allow their leadership to flourish. 
Magda Rodriguez-Villafane is president and co-founder of Mass ParentCorps. Don Hawley is CEO and co-founder of Mass ParentCorps.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Demographic cliff poses concern for neighbor-state enrollment, Iowa Board of Regents reports
description: Jason Pontius’s first comment to the Iowa Board of Regents about enrollment trends was his prediction for headlines — enrollment at Iowa’s three public universities remained more-or-less flat from last year to this year. However, the underlying story stretches into the future of high school graduates, both their number and who decides to pursue higher […]
text:
The Iowa Board of Regents met on Nov. 12, 2026. States bordering Iowa are set to see worse declines in high school graduates than Iowa itself, potentially harming university enrollment. (Photo by Brooklyn Draisey/Iowa Capital Dispatch)Jason Pontius’s first comment to the Iowa Board of Regents about enrollment trends was his prediction for headlines — enrollment at Iowa’s three public universities remained more-or-less flat from last year to this year.
However, the underlying story stretches into the future of high school graduates, both their number and who decides to pursue higher education.
Colleges and universities across the U.S. have been preparing for the demographic cliff of fewer students graduating high school for years, including those in Iowa despite the state projecting to see less of a dip than other states.
Pontius, associate chief academic officer for the board of regents, said in past meetings he hesitated to call the decline a “cliff,” but told board members at its November meeting that the number of Iowa high school graduates right now is likely the highest the state will see for the next 20 years. States surrounding Iowa will also see their graduating classes sink, impacting out-of-state student enrollment.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“These are the traditional students we’re talking about,” Pontias said. “That pool has gotten smaller, and so it provides additional challenges for us going forward. Our undergraduate population is about 95% traditional students right now.”
Total student enrollment at the University of Iowa, Iowa State University and University of Northern Iowa decreased by one half of a percentage point — 352 students — between fall 2025 and fall 2026, according to the enrollment report discussed by the board at its November meeting last week. Undergraduate student enrollment across the universities grew by .2%, or by 98 students.
Overall, total student enrollment at the three universities in fall 2026 was 71,520, the highest seen since 2022 but nearly 10,000 students below the higher education system’s peak in 2016.
While Iowa lags one year behind the rest of the U.S. in the enrollment cliff, Pontius said new data projects further declines in high school graduates from 2036-2041, which will represent itself in Iowa as a second decline after a brief level period.
“This is the highest number of high school graduates in the state of Iowa we are likely to have in the next two decades,” Pontius said.
Declines in high school graduates are expected across the U.S., Pontius said, varied between states but averaging out to a 12% drop over the next 15 years.
From 2026 to 2041, Pontius said Iowa is expecting a 9% decline in high school graduates. In the top five states Iowa universities bring students from, Nebraska will also drop by 9%, followed by Minnesota with 13%, Missouri at 14%, Wisconsin at 16% and Illinois at 29%.
Despite other states already dealing with the enrollment cliff, Pontius said out-of-state enrollment increased for this year by 1.3%, to a total of 26,142 students. UNI, which offers in-state tuition to students from neighboring states, saw a 28% increase in Illinois students and a 55% jump among Minnesota students, alongside growing numbers from other states.
“We get about 11,400 students right now from the state of Illinois,” Pontius said. “So a major decline there is problematic and adds an additional challenge to our attempt to kind of maintain enrollment in our three public universities.”
Shifts in student’s choices for their education are also impacting enrollment, Pontius said, with midwestern public flagship institutions seeing growth between 2009-2024 and regional public institutions seeing declines. Many things could contribute to this trend, he said, and while the University of Northern Iowa hasn’t been entirely exempt, it has been “bucking this for the last few years.”
UNI was the only state university to see enrollment growth from fall 2025 to fall 2026, increasing by 1.8% while the UI saw a .6% decrease and ISU saw a 1.1% decrease.
Data from surveying Iowa high school students for their post-graduation plans and enrollment numbers show that for community colleges, both intent to enroll and actual enrollment have been dropping, while going straight into employment has been rising and intent and actually going to a state university has been “holding roughly flat.”
One question Pontius said he often gets when enrollment declines at Iowa public universities is whether students are leaving the state to attend college, which has not been happening. In the 15 years that metric has been tracked for, Pontius said it “has been very flat the entire time.”
“We retain a very large number of our students who go to college in the state of Iowa, and that has always been the case,” Pontius said.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Judge orders filings unsealed in Greenville missing DNA evidence case
description: Circuit Court Judge Richard A. Smith addresses prosecutors and defense attorneys at King Brown Jr.'s sentencing hearing at the Washington County Circuit Court in Greenville, Nov. 2, 2026.
text:
Circuit Judge Richard A. Smith has ordered all court filings unsealed in a Greenville homicide case in which over 100 pieces of DNA evidence went missing. They will be made available to the public on the Mississippi Electronic Court system on Dec. 7.
Smith sealed the court filings after he canceled a hearing in May, when public officials were set to testify on the chain of custody of the missing evidence. The evidence ranged from a rape kit to fingernail scrapings to a strip of tape, and was tied to a rape and manslaughter appeal by King Brown Jr. Brown was convicted in 2005 after a third trial of the rape and killing of a 6-year-old Greenville girl. 
King Brown Jr. listens to the judge during his sentencing hearing at the Washington County Circuit Court on Nov. 2, 2026. Credit: Leonardo Bevilacqua/Mississippi Today
Smith said he did not want to subject the public officials set to testify to undue embarrasment. 
Several circuit clerk employee affidavits suggested district attorney’s office employees visited the evidence room prior to the specimens’ disappearance. An unsigned district attorney’s office statement denied the allegations.
Additional testimony by Washington County Circuit Clerk Barbara Esters-Parker, Deputy Clerk Cynthia Lakes and Deputy Clerk Willinna Hawkins were provided under seal in May.
In June, Andrew Coffman, an attorney for the Reporters Committee for the Freedom of the Press, made a motion on behalf of Mississippi Today to restore public access to information on whether district attorney’s office employees or circuit clerk’s office employees bear blame for the evidence’s disappearance.
Coffman also argued that Smith’s previous order violated the right to review court records, which are public records by default. 
His motion was granted over five months later on Monday.
That ruling came two weeks after Smith suspended the remainder of Brown’s sentences, which had totaled 50 years. Now, Brown will serve five years of supervised release. Without the evidence that might have exonerated him, he remains a rapist and killer under Mississippi state law.

name: VTDigger
title: Dismissed Bennington County murder case heads back to court
description:
The suspect is currently in custody serving a 12½-year prison sentence on federal drug and firearm charges.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Dismissed Bennington County murder case heads back to court.
text:
The Vermont Supreme Court in Montpelier on Tuesday, June 30, 2026. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger

The prosecution and defense are taking different views of a recent Vermont Supreme Court decision in a Bennington County murder case.
The state’s highest court, in a decision issued Friday, called on Judge Kerry McDonald-Cady to consider specific factors laid out in case law before deciding whether to dismiss a murder charge against Deven Moffitt, 36, formerly of Bennington, with prejudice, meaning it could not be refiled by the prosecution.
The judge had sided with Moffitt’s attorney more than a year ago in dismissing the charge with prejudice, prompting the appeal. 
Moffitt was charged in 2022 with second-degree murder in the 2019 death of his former girlfriend, Jessica Hildenbrandt, 43, of Ballston Spa, New York. Her remains, according to police, were found near an abandoned gravel pit in Searsburg. 
“We conclude that the court had authority to impose a sanction up to and including dismissal with prejudice, but that it should have considered the Sauve factors before permanently ending the prosecution,” Justice Nancy Waples wrote in the Vermont Supreme Court’s unanimous ruling.
Those factors, from the 1995 case State v. Sauve, include the seriousness of the charged offense, the evidence of guilt and the existence of any misconduct in the investigation and prosecution.
“We appreciate the opportunity to continue the pursuit of justice for Jessica and her family,” Bennington County State’s Attorney Erica Marthage said in a statement Friday. 
Vermont Defender General Matthew Valerio, whose office represented Moffitt in the appeal, said in an interview Monday that he didn’t expect the outcome of the case to change.
“It seems like a good one for the defense,” Valerio said of the high court’s ruling. “The court could write a more detailed opinion that includes the Sauve factors and come to the exact same result. So, it wasn’t the result that was wrong.”   
The Vermont Supreme Court decision is the latest legal twist in the case that had been working its way through the court system for several years and included prosecutorial missteps along the way.
In the case, there was an initial DNA match using a database linking the remains found in Searsburg to Hildenbrandt, according to court records. 
However, when additional testing to confirm the identity of the remains was not completed by the start of a scheduled trial in early 2025, the prosecution asked for delay to allow for expedited testing.
McDonald-Cady, the judge, ruled that the delay was not reasonable as the state already had enough time leading up to the trial to do that testing, with the original case filed against Moffitt in 2022.
The prosecution then moved to dismiss the case without prejudice, allowing it to be refiled at a later time. Moffitt’s lawyer in turn filed a motion to dismiss the case with prejudice, meaning it could not be filed again.
The judge agreed to dismiss the case with prejudice, concluding that the prosecution was improperly attempting to grant itself the continuance that the court had denied. 
The prosecution appealed that ruling to the Vermont Supreme Court leading to Friday’s decision.
Moffitt is currently in federal custody. He had been sentenced in June 2025 to 12½ years in prison following his convictions on federal drug and firearms charges.

text:
House Speaker Kyle Hilbert, R-Bristow, speaks to news reporters at the state Capitol in Oklahoma City on May 8, 2025. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY — The leader of the Oklahoma House on Monday was nominated by the chamber’s Republicans to continue in his role next session. 
Rep. Kyle Hilbert, R-Bristow, was selected by his Republican peers during a closed-door caucus meeting and is likely to serve as the next Speaker of the House, according to a news release.
“I am honored to continue serving the people of Oklahoma in this role,” Hilbert said in a statement. “I recognize the weight of this responsibility and the work that lies ahead. There are significant challenges in our state and our responsibility is to take on those issues with a long-term vision, making meaningful progress today while laying the groundwork for a stronger Oklahoma for generations to come.”
He still needs to be elected during a public vote by the full chamber during its organizational day Jan. 5 when all 101 members are present. 
House members are set to be sworn in Tuesday for the upcoming session. 
As speaker, Hilbert oversees the House’s operations, appoints lawmakers to committees and leadership positions, and directs the flow of legislation. 
He is also third in line to replace the governor, behind the lieutenant governor and leader of the Oklahoma Senate. 
Hilbert’s party will maintain control over the House in the upcoming session, but it will shrink slightly as Democrats were able to flip six seats previously held by the GOP. 
He was first elected by his caucus in 2024 as the youngest House speaker in the state’s history. 
Hilbert was reelected by his constituents this year for another two years, marking his fifth of six potential terms. 
House Democrats also selected Rep. Melissa Provenzano, D-Tulsa, to lead their caucus for the upcoming session. She said she was “honored to serve with such a diverse, smart, and compassionate team.” 
“We will not waste time taking advantage of this incredible opportunity,” Provenzano said in a statement. “The work has already begun, and we look forward to doing the job Oklahomans entrusted us to do.”

name: WyoFile
title: Gordon stalls $13M grant to trona company that’s cutting 350 jobs in southwest Wyoming
description:
The grant is on hold until the state examines “the economic impacts to Sweetwater County … from the shifting global dynamics affecting Wyoming trona production,” Gov. Mark Gordon said.
The post Gordon stalls $13M grant to trona company that’s cutting 350 jobs in southwest Wyoming appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Gov. Mark Gordon will take “no action” for now on a $13 million state taxpayer-funded grant request by WE Soda, the London-based trona miner and soda ash producer that plans to cut 274 workers in southwest Wyoming beginning in January and a total 350 over the next two years.
“The conversation has changed, as a whole, from when this [Wyoming Energy Dominance Fund] application was first submitted,” Gordon said in a prepared statement Monday. “Before committing state severance tax resources, we need to have a better understanding of what the overall conditions this critical industry is facing, and what the future may look like.”
WE Soda announced Nov. 4 it would reduce its Wyoming workforce from about 850 to 500 over the next two years, primarily due to its new plan to shift its Westvaco trona mine from underground mining to drill-and-pump solution mining. 
WE Soda workers wait at a bus stop in Rock Springs for a ride to work their shifts at the company’s trona mine and soda ash operations. (Dustin Bleizeffer/WyoFile)
Prior to the announced layoffs, the company applied for — and the Wyoming Energy Authority recommended — a $13 million grant from the state’s new Energy Dominance Fund. WE Soda said it would use the money to build a “high-pressure natural gas supply connection from the Williams’ MountainWest Overthrust Pipeline system” to its Westvaco operations, an investment that’s not immediately tied to its plan shift to solution mining.
The union representing workers at WE Soda’s trona and soda ash operations — United Steelworkers Local 13214 — rallied workers and the community to implore Wyoming officials for help and for Gordon to pump the brakes on the grant and to instead “find a way to support the workers who made that corporation successful.”
Many southwest Wyoming leaders and residents echoed the sentiment.

The Brewery in Green River. (Dustin Bleizeffer/WyoFile)

“The whole thing sucks,” a Green River bar manager told WyoFile on Thursday. She didn’t want to share her name for fear of retribution toward workers and local businesses. “I don’t think the state should subsidize an industry that is depleting our job market. We struggle with that anyway. This is going to make it worse.
“WE Soda,” she added, “can take a flying fuck into a rolling donut.”
The Energy Authority, which administers the state’s Energy Dominance Fund, told WyoFile last week that it had recommended the $13 million grant be approved before it learned of the company’s plans for major job cuts.
Gordon on Monday directed the agency “to conduct an expedited thorough examination of the economic impacts to Sweetwater County and the state from the shifting global dynamics affecting Wyoming trona production.”
The Energy Authority “stands ready to deliver on Gov. Gordon’s request to examine how this global market is changing and what those changes could mean for Wyoming,” Energy Authority Executive Director Rob Creager said in a prepared statement. “This work will give the state a stronger foundation for evaluating investments and identifying where support can make a lasting difference.”
A handful of companies mine trona in southwest Wyoming and process it — on site — into soda ash, the primary material used to make glass, myriad household products and industrial products such as large batteries. Wyoming once held about 14% of the global soda ash market worth some $1.3 billion in exports, and its operations directly employed some 2,500 workers in 2025.
Shifting Westvaco operations from underground mining to drill-and-pump “solution” recovery is necessary, WE Soda has said, due to market pressures from China and Mongolia flooding the global market with cheaper-to-produce soda ash.
WE Soda workers, joined by their families, attend a union meeting Nov. 12 in Rock Springs. (Dustin Bleizeffer/WyoFile)
The proposition of a state grant to help Wyoming operators compete in the tightening global market, local elected officials have said, is enticing but confounding due to the fact WE Soda’s job cuts are going to devastate the economy in southwest Wyoming.
“People won’t be able to pay their taxes, houses will go up for sale because people are going to lose their jobs,” Mayor-elect Stan Blake told WyoFile. “We have to help the miners who live in Green River.”
Gordon commended WE Soda for “working to get out in front of these major shifts.” But, he said, “the state needs to better understand how to efficiently and effectively support the industry, workers, families, and ancillary businesses that Sweetwater County depends on. State support through the WEA’s ongoing work in this area is vital.”

title: 4 companies to split $12M in federal funds to connect final eligible Nebraska locations to broadband
description: LINCOLN — Nebraska’s Broadband Office announced roughly $12 million in new federal funding would be distributed across four companies looking to connect the final 12% of locations across the state eligible for broadband internet connections under the Broadband Equity, Access and Deployment program. The NBO reopened its BEAD applications for a second round ea[...]
text:
An ultra fast broadband tower is seen on a rural farm. (Sandra Mu/Getty Images)LINCOLN — Nebraska’s Broadband Office announced roughly $12 million in new federal funding would be distributed across four companies looking to connect the final 12% of locations across the state eligible for broadband internet connections under the Broadband Equity, Access and Deployment program.
The NBO reopened its BEAD applications for a second round earlier this year after at least three companies backed out of signing their subgrants following changes to the program under a new presidential administration.
A BEAD on Nebraska broadband: State reopens provider applications with over $300M still in limbo

In late 2025, state lawmakers learned of changes coming to BEAD through President Donald Trump’s “Benefit of the Bargain” initiative. The update came a day after Gov. Jim Pillen announced that Nebraska had planned to use just $44.5 million of the $405 million the state was initially awarded through BEAD to connect unserved Nebraska locations to broadband.
In May, NBO announced the seven companies that did sign subgrants, following three weeks of repeated questions from the Examiner about the contracts. The companies were tasked with connecting 88% of the roughly 14,000 BEAD-eligible locations in the state.
The remaining 12% represented about 1,705 eligible locations, according to Monday’s press release, that will now be served by four companies that provide both fiber and licensed fixed wireless. An additional $11.9 million of BEAD funding has been approved with these awards along with about $4.1 million in matching funds.
Among the awardees are:

AMG Technology Investment Group LLC/Nextlink – serving 1,461 licensed fixed wireless locations
Midstates Data Transport LLC/Stealth – serving 155 fiber locations
Northeast Nebraska Telephone Co. – serving 224 fiber locations
Quick Current – serving four licensed fixed wireless locations

SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
While federal officials and Pillen had argued the original BEAD program was ineffective due to burdensome regulations imposed under the Biden administration, not all of Nebraska’s broadband advocates were convinced.
Gage County farmer Emily Haxby expressed concerns about the restructured program’s de-emphasis on fiber internet, which she said was unmatched in its scalability and reliability compared to other methods. However, it’s also one of the most expensive methods.
Nearly 80% of the second round BEAD awards went to providers looking to provide licensed fixed wireless broadband over fiber. Nebraska’s BEAD technology composition now stands at 10% fiber, 67% fixed wireless and 23% satellite, according to the press release.
U.S. Sen. Deb Fischer and others were concerned about what would happen to the more than $300 million in leftover BEAD funds for Nebraska. The NBO said the office is preparing for a new round of BEAD funding and has received a list of supplemental BEAD locations in Nebraska from the National Telecommunications and Information Administration.
Jay Omar, spokesman for Nebraska’s Department of Transportation, clarified that the upcoming round of BEAD funding, along with the additional $11.9 million in federal funds, all will come out of Nebraska’s initial $405 million allocation.
“These are more positive steps forward in connecting Nebraskans and communities around the state to reliable, high-speed broadband,” Pillen said in the press release. “But there is still work to be done. We have just received guidance on the next step of the program to capture additional unserved locations. My office is already working hard to bring the next phase of this federal investment home to Nebraska.”

name: Mississippi Today
title: Retrial in New Albany stabbing will proceed
description: This still from a video captures the moment when Lane Mitchell stabs Russell Rogers in the neck at the Tallahatchie Gourmet in New Albany , Miss., on Feb. 9, 2019. The photo is time stamped 21:18:27.
text:
The U.S. Supreme Court declined Monday to consider double jeopardy issues raised in the case of a north Mississippi man whom a judge acquitted of attempted murder and is set to be retried.
Attorneys for Lane Mitchell asked the nation’s high court last month to hear his case, arguing that a 5-4 Mississippi Appeals Court decision violated their client’s protection from being tried twice for the same charge. 
Mitchell’s case was one of over a 100 petitions for review denied without explanation by the court. Typically, the U.S. Supreme Court accepts very few requests for review. 
Before the high court considered the petition, parents of the victim, Russell Rogers, shared their concerns about how the case was presented to the justices, including how it contained what they called misstatements. 
In 2019, Mitchell, then 18, stabbed Rogers of Collierville, Tennessee, at the Tallahatchie Gourmet restaurant in New Albany, believing the man posed a threat to his father, who was working as a bartender, and to a female waitress. 
After a 2023 trial, Union County Circuit Judge Kent Smith entered an order of acquittal based on the victim’s absence at court, which he said violated Mitchell’s right to confront the accuser of the crime. The defense and prosecutors didn’t present closing arguments, and the  jury hadn’t begun deliberations.
Two years later, the state Court of Appeals said the judge ruled incorrectly and reversed the ruling and sent it back to be tried again. Retrial is scheduled for March 2027.
When reached Monday after the U.S. Supreme Court’s decision, Maridonna Rogers wondered how a new trial will be any different if it is tried with the same judge in the same county.

text:
Gov. Kay Ivey speaking at the unveiling of her gubernatorial portrait in the Old Senate Chambers in the Alabama State Capitol in Montgomery, Alabama, on Nov. 16, 2026. A bust of the governor was also unveiled in front of the Gov. Kay Ivey Office Building on Washington Avenue immediately following the portrait. (Anna Barrett/Alabama Reflector)Gov. Kay Ivey reflected on her historic tenure as a portrait and bronze bust were unveiled on the Capitol Complex Monday morning. 
In the Old Senate Chambers – where Ivey took the oath of office in 2017 – the governor thanked Alabamians for trusting her during her nearly 10 years as governor, which will end in January.  
“When I was sworn in as governor on April 10th, 2017, in this very room, I said to the people of Alabama that serving as your governor is no small task, but that I would do my very best. Even 10 years later, I am proud,” she said. “Alabama has made significant and truly historic gains. And y’all, that would not have been possible without all of you and many others.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Ivey took office following former Gov. Robert Bentley’s resignation following a misdemeanor plea to campaign finance law violations and the threat of impeachment in April 2017. Ivey later won two terms in her own right, but is constitutionally barred from seeking a third consecutive term.
Ivey grew up in Camden in Wilcox County before becoming a high school teacher. She then worked as a banker before becoming the assistant director of the Alabama Development Office – now the Alabama Department of Commerce. 
For 13 years, she worked at the Alabama Commission on Higher Education as the director of government affairs and communications before running for state treasurer in 2002, an office she held until 2011. In 2010, she ran for lieutenant governor, which she held until she became governor in 2017. 
Ivey’s agendas have consistently revolved around education and economic development. Chief of Staff Liz Filmore said Monday morning that Ivey “hit the ground running” with policies like the Literacy and Numeracy Acts, and attracting billion-dollar companies to the state. 
“Governor Ivey truly believes in our students, and that education and jobs go hand in hand,” Filmore said. “These and many other achievements were accomplished in part because Governor Ivey established and maintained an excellent rapport with the Alabama Legislature. Governor Ivey’s greatest asset is her determination to get things done, no matter what the peanut gallery has to say. And I’m here to tell you, we’ve got a lot of peanuts in Alabama.”
Jo Bonner, former chief of staff and current president of the University of South Alabama, recognized the significance of Ivey’s impact on women and girls in Alabama. When she leaves office in January, she will make history as Alabama’s longest consecutive serving governor, and the nation’s longest-serving female governor. She is also an alumna of Alabama Girls State, a leadership program that many of Ivey’s staff are also alumni of, including Filmore. 
“The governor has spent a lifetime demonstrating that where you begin does not determine where you can go or how far you can go,” he said. “For those of us who are privileged to be with you today, thank you. Thank you for letting us be a small part of a story of a young girl from Camden, Alabama, who went on to become an incredible leader for our state.”
Her tenure has not always been smooth. During the COVID-19 pandemic, Ivey and Lt. Gov. Will Ainsworth sharply disagreed on how to handle the public health crisis. In October, House Speaker Nathaniel Ledbetter, R-Rainsville, a close ally of Gov.-elect Tommy Tuberville, called for a pause in Ivey’s namesake prison project in Escambia County amid rising costs of a second modern prison.
Gov. Kay Ivey standing next to a bronze bust of herself in front of the Gov. Kay Ivey Office Building on Washington Avenue in Montgomery, Alabama, on Nov. 16, 2026. (Anna Barrett/Alabama Reflector)
Alabama’s prisons are notoriously overcrowded and the state’s Department of Corrections is set to go to federal trial at the end of the month for reported conditions. To address overcrowding, the Legislature in 2021 approved $1.3 billion for two 4,000-bed facilities, but one prison alone has reached nearly $1.25 billion and the other has yet to break ground. 
The portrait was painted by Huntington College graduate Ann Kenyon. She has also painted portraits of President Donald Trump and his family for their personal collection. The bronze bust, which is displayed in front of the Gov. Kay Ivey Office Building on Washington Avenue, was sculpted by Alabama native and Montgomery resident Claudetta Fulmer. She also sculpted the statue of Rosa Parks by the Montgomery Fountain and Revolutionary War General Richard Montgomery. 
“It’s an honor to share this day with you, ladies and gentlemen, it remains the highest honor of my life to serve and be your governor,” Ivey said. “To the people of Alabama, thank you for giving me the incredible opportunity to serve you.”

name: California
title: Prosecutors ask California Supreme Court to halt Newsom’s death penalty commutations
description: California prosecutors and an advocacy group for crime victims are asking the state Supreme Court to block Gov. Newsom's blanket commutation of death sentences.
text:
In summary
California prosecutors and an advocacy group for crime victims are asking the state Supreme Court to block Gov. Newsom’s blanket commutation of death sentences.


The district attorneys of 30 counties argued in a lawsuit filed Monday morning that the state’s high court should halt Gov. Gavin Newsom’s commutations of people on death row. 
The lawsuit, filed at the California Supreme Court, asserts that Newsom acted unlawfully when he proposed commuting the sentences of 548 prisoners by failing to afford the victims of their crimes the “opportunity to be heard.” 
“Only this court can stop the governor’s disregard of the law — his abuse of power,” the petitioners wrote to the California Supreme Court. 
The petition distinguishes Newsom’s commutation powers from the pardon powers of a president — the presidential pardon doesn’t have any limits, other than impeachment. By contrast, when condemned California prisoners apply for a commutation, governors must notify the district attorney where the crime took place, and the victims or their families. 
Perhaps anticipating this argument, Newsom issued an explanatory statement laying out why he didn’t need to issue notifications to victims or their families. A central factor was that none of these proposed commutations stemmed from an application from a prisoner on death row. By proposing a blanket commutation, Newsom asserted that none of the statutory requirements applied. 
The section of the California penal code highlighted by the district attorneys “does not apply when the governor acts on his own initiative to grant clemency absent an application,” Newsom wrote in the explanation. 
He added that, after he submitted the proposed commutations to the Supreme Court, his office would notify the district attorneys in the counties in which the crimes were committed and seek their help with notifications.
The California Supreme Court will get a say on almost 400 of Newsom’s commutations. State law requires the court to review those cases because the prisoners were convicted of multiple felonies. Representatives of the court have not said how or when those reviews would take place.  
Newsom in 2019 issued a moratorium on executions and later ordered the dismantling of the death chamber at San Quentin State Prison. His successor, Gov.-elect Xavier Becerra, has committed to extending the moratorium when he takes office.

text:
Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen, center, smiles with local private school students after ceremoniously signing a proclamation for "National School Choice Week" in the state. Jan. 28, 2026. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)LINCOLN — Nebraska organizations that want to award funds through the new Federal Scholarship Tax Credit program to offset K-12 educational costs can now apply for certification.
Gov. Jim Pillen announced the opening of applications Monday and directed interested organizations to the Nebraska Department of Revenue at revenue.nebraska.gov/federal-scholarship-tax-credit. Pillen’s office said the agency will review applications to determine whether organizations meet federal requirements for participation. 
Nebraska will submit the list of approved scholarship-granting organizations to the U.S. Department of the Treasury. The Revenue Department later will publish the list.
“The FSTC creates a new opportunity for Nebraskans to support educational opportunities in their communities through federal tax credits,” a news release from Pillen’s office states. “The program does not reduce existing state appropriations to public schools.”
Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen talking in front of U.S. Reps. Adrian Smith and Mike Flood at St. Teresa Catholic School in Lincoln on Sep. 29, 2025. (Photo by Juan Salinas II/Nebraska Examiner)
Beginning Jan. 1, taxpayers can donate to approved scholarship-granting organizations nationwide and claim up to $1,700 for federal income tax credits, or $3,400 for married couples filing jointly. Unused tax credits can be carried forward for up to five years.
Approved organizations will receive student applications, determine scholarship eligibility and distribute funds for qualified K-12 costs, according to Pillen’s office. Covered expenses include tutoring, special-needs services, school- or class-related equipment and full or partial tuition.
Students in any education setting — public, private and home schools — are eligible, so long as their household income is below 300% of the area median gross income.
Taxpayers nationwide, including those in states not opting in to the federal program, can donate to approved Cornhusker State organizations for the tax credit.
Pillen made Nebraska the first state to opt into the program shortly after President Donald Trump signed it into law in the “one big beautiful bill” in July 2025. U.S. Rep. Adrian Smith, a Republican who represents Nebraska’s sprawling 3rd Congressional District, ushered the law through Congress.
Nebraska voters repealed a similar state program using taxpayer dollars to offset private costs of attendance in November 2024.
Pillen’s office encouraged interested organizations to apply by Jan. 15.
“Applications received after that date cannot be considered for inclusion on the 2027 certification list,” the Governor’s Office said.

title: Board suspends license of Iowa nurse after her third disciplinary case
description: An Iowa nurse previously accused of being incapacitated by drugs while working and of having a personal relationship with an inmate-patient is now being sanctioned for alleged drug use. The Iowa Board of Nursing’s disciplinary history with licensed practical nurse Rachel Blair of Ankeny dates back to 2020 when the board charged Blair with attempting […]
text:
(Photo courtesy of the Iowa Board of Nursing)An Iowa nurse previously accused of being incapacitated by drugs while working and of having a personal relationship with an inmate-patient is now being sanctioned for alleged drug use.
The Iowa Board of Nursing’s disciplinary history with licensed practical nurse Rachel Blair of Ankeny dates back to 2020 when the board charged Blair with attempting to initiate a personal relationship with a patient.
According to the board, Blair was working at a county jail in April 2019 when she participated in personal telephone calls with an inmate. “At times, the calls were sexually explicit in nature,” the board alleged. According to the board, Blair was then fired from the jail for providing “treatment” for an inmate despite the lack of a physician’s order, and for admitting to having “feelings for an inmate.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Court records show that a Polk County Jail inmate at the time told jail officials that a nurse, later identified as Blair, had been providing tobacco, drugs and sex to an inmate known as “Casper.” According to a search warrant application filed by the sheriff’s department, Blair admitted to providing “Casper” with unordered, undocumented “massaging treatments,” approximately 15 times over four to six weeks, in a private treatment room at the jail.
According to the warrant application, a subsequent review of the jail’s recorded telephone calls uncovered communications between Blair and the inmate that included “sexual content and comments referencing a personal relationship.”
A review of text messages then uncovered 199 written exchanges between Blair and the inmate, according to the warrant application. The messages also included 21 photos of Blair, the sheriff’s department alleged. In addition, the warrant application alleged that money had been deposited into the inmate’s account three separate times by depositor “Clare Loren,” Loren being Blair’s middle name and the name associated with the text messages attributed to Blair.
According to the application, Blair admitted to destroying potential evidence in the case during the initial stages of the sheriff’s investigation of the matter.
In that case, the Board of Nursing suspended Blair’s nursing license, pending the completion of a mental health evaluation, and also required her to complete an educational course on professional boundaries. At the end of the suspension, Blair’s license was reinstated and placed on probation for two years.
In 2024, the board alleged Blair was working at an unspecified Urbandale care facility when the medication count was reported as being off during her shift, indicating the staff was unable to account for missing drugs.
According to the board, the facility was missing one fentanyl patch, an opioid painkiller. During that same shift, the board alleges, Blair “fell to her hands and knees and struggled to stand.” Paramedics were called to the scene and administered Narcan — a drug commonly used for emergency treatment of an opioid overdose — to Blair.
As a result of that incident, the board charged Blair with misappropriating the medications of a patient or agency, then agreed to settle the case by providing Blair with a warning that any future violations could result in some form of disciplinary action. As part of that settlement, Blair agreed to participate in the Iowa Practitioner Health Program and to comply with any requirements of the program.
On July 20, 2026, the board charged Blair with failing to comply with a board order and violating an agreement with the Iowa Practitioner Health Program. The charges stemmed from allegations that in January 2026, Blair tested positive for amphetamine use and that she declined to participate in the Iowa Practitioner Health Program as ordered by the board.
Recently, the board suspended Blair’s license for six months, after which she can apply for reinstatement by showing proof of sobriety. If her license is reinstated, it will be subject to two years of probation that will involve additional chemical screening and board oversight.
The Iowa Capital Dispatch was not able to reach Blair for comment.
Other Iowa-licensed nurses recently sanctioned by the board include:
Haley J. Evans of Hamilton, Illinois — The board recently issued an emergency suspension of Evans’ license as a registered nurse after charging her with failing to respond to, or comply with, a board investigation or a subpoena.
According to the board, it investigated a complaint related to Evans work in Iowa and concluded that she had “engaged in conduct that could create an unreasonable risk to public safety” and that she “poses an immediate danger to the public.” The board has opted not to publicly disclose the date, location or nature of the alleged conduct. A hearing on the matter is scheduled for Dec. 16, 2026.
The Iowa Capital Dispatch was not able to reach Evans for comment.
Trisha M. Davis of Holstein — In July 2026, the board charged Davis, a registered nurse, with not possessing the required knowledge or skill to discharge her professional obligations; deviating from the standards of learning or skill ordinarily possessed by an Iowa nurse; willfully or repeatedly failing to practice nursing with reasonable skill and safety; committing an act that might adversely affect a patient’s welfare; and failing to assess or accurately document a patient’s status.
The board alleges that in February 2026, while working at the Cherokee Regional Medical Center, Davis was assigned to the CCU/telemetry unit, which is typically the unit that provides continuous heart monitoring for patients in a coronary care, or cardiac care, unit. According to the board, Davis was not actively monitoring patients in the unit and was “nonresponsive” when one patient experienced a change in their mental status and a second patient was in respiratory distress. The board alleges Davis was fired by the hospital a few weeks later.
Board records indicate Davis denied the allegations but recently agreed to a three-month suspension of her license to be followed by a two-year probationary period.
The Iowa Capital Dispatch was not able to reach Davis for comment.
Susan L. Peden, aka Susan L. Deo, of Bondurant — In June, the board charged Peden, an advanced registered nurse practitioner, with lacking the knowledge or skill needed to fulfill her professional obligations; deviating from the standards of learning or skill ordinarily possessed by a nurse; committing an act that might adversely affect a patient’s welfare; prescribing or administering drugs in an unsafe manner;  and prescribing or administering drugs without accurately documenting it or without the proper patient assessment or instruction.
According to the board, Peden was employed by RC Dermatology, also known as Radiant Complexions Dermatology, in West Des Moines when, at some undisclosed point in time, she failed to perform or document the required tests and labs on a number of patients prior to prescribing them medications. She was also accused of failing to perform or document risk/benefit assessments and of sending a patient refills of prescription medications without having seen the patient at least once per year.
To resolve the case without a hearing, the board recently agreed to dismiss three of the five charges against Peden — lacking knowledge or skill, committing an act that might adversely affect a patient’s welfare, and improperly sending a patient prescription refills — and Peden agreed to be cited for the two remaining charges. As a result, the board ordered that her license be suspended for two months and that it then be placed on probationary status for two years. Peden must also complete 20 hours of educational training on dermatology and medical documentation.
The Iowa Capital Dispatch was not able to reach Peden for comment.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Crews are cleaning SpaceXSI chemical spill in Southaven as data center company faces another environmental issue
description: A truck approaches a closed construction site on Tuesday, Oct. 6, 2026 in Southaven, where SpaceXAI has had a power plant since August 2025.
text:
The recently renamed SpaceXSI — the Elon Musk-owned data center company formerly called SpaceXAI and xAI before that — is at the center of yet another environmental controversy in Mississippi.  
After an incident where a “contractor removed a pump” at SpaceXSI’s facility at 8235 Tulane Road in Southaven, the company allowed 5,000 to 6,000 gallons of a propylene glycol mixture to spill into a neighboring drainage ditch, state officials told Mississippi Today on Monday.
The Mississippi Department of Environmental Quality said it was still figuring out when the chemical spill occurred, but officials learned of the incident Saturday night.
“Preliminary information indicates the release occurred when a contractor removed a pump, causing a connected hose to siphon fluid from the tank,” MDEQ spokesperson Jan Schaefer said Monday. “The fluid overflowed the containment area and entered a nearby drainage ditch.”
The chemical in question comes from a “heat transfer fluid” made by manufacturing giant Dow and commonly used in HVAC systems. Schaefer said the spill posed no “immediate threat to public health or safety.” 
Since Saturday, a Mid South Environmental Services crew hired by SpaceXSI has vacuumed and excavated around the incident area to clean up remnants from the spill. Schaefer said the soil excavation finished Monday, and vacuuming was expected to be done Monday, as well.
While MDEQ is conducting water tests to monitor any natural impacts, Schaefer said none of the fluids that overflowed into the ditch reached nearby Horn Lake Creek. 
“Berms were installed upstream and downstream of the affected drainage ditch to contain the material,” Schaefer said.
The news, first reported over the weekend, came less than a month after the company’s announcement that it could face over $6 million in fines for starting construction at multiple Southaven facilities without water runoff permits. Those issues coincide with a long, ongoing battle between residents and SpaceXSI over its use of temporary gas turbines and the noise they produce. 
Schaefer said MDEQ could not comment on whether the recent spill would result in any enforcement action from the agency. 
While the spill has since been contained, chemicals did reach neighboring property owned by a “private citizen” and Beruk Construction Inc., Schaefer said. She said SpaceXSI connected with the private citizen, who agreed to let the contractor clean up on their land.
In addition to water testing, Schaefer said the facility will “transition to precautionary maintenance and periodic inspections.”

name: Source New Mexico
title: New report offers guidelines for how New Mexico can upgrade power grid, hit clean energy goals
description: Expanding and modernizing New Mexico’s power grid while tapping into new resources, such as geothermal energy, and offering workforce training in these new areas will help state officials meet projected demand while complying with upcoming clean energy goals, according to a new report.
text:
A new report from the New Mexico Energy, Minerals and Natural Resources Department offers state officials and utility leaders recommendations for meeting projected energy demand while meeting the state’s clean energy goals. (Photo by Danielle Prokop for Source NM)Expanding and modernizing New Mexico’s power grid while tapping into new resources, such as geothermal energy, and offering workforce training in these new areas will help state officials meet projected demand while complying with upcoming clean energy goals, according to a new report.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The New Mexico Energy, Minerals and Natural Resources Department on Friday announced its “Comprehensive Energy Transition Strategy,” which outlines five categories of steps state and energy sector officials can take to facilitate New Mexico’s energy transition.
Specifically, it recommends modernizing the grid to deliver renewable power; ensuring an adequate energy supply; managing demand and improving efficiency; supporting the state’s workforce for the energy transition; and expanding the state’s energy data infrastructure.
“We have created a forward-thinking strategy that recognizes that reliability, economic development, affordability and emissions reductions are not competing priorities,” EMNRD Acting Secretary Erin Taylor said in a statement. “They are mutually reinforcing goals that position New Mexico to remain an energy leader while building a stronger, more resilient future for generations to come.”
State environmental officials recently told a panel of state lawmakers that at its current rate, New Mexico will not hit its goal to significantly reduce greenhouse gas emissions by 45% by 2030.
The new transition strategy from EMNRD, however, highlights specific recommendations such as cutting red tape for new geothermal energy projects and creating virtual power plants as options for meeting increased demand with renewable sources.
A virtual power plant is a network of small devices in a house or business, including smart thermostats and water heaters, that a utility company can manage during peak hours rather than putting stress on a traditional power plant.
Energy industry leaders earlier this year told state lawmakers that attracting power-hungry projects such as data centers could actually help to modernize the state’s outdated grid — if the developers behind them are willing to pay for the upgrades they need.

name: VTDigger
title: Montpelier appoints new police chief
description:
Burlington’s current deputy police chief is becoming Montpelier’s police chief in January.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Montpelier appoints new police chief.
text:
The Montpelier Police Department on Wednesday, July 8, 2026. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger
Montpelier has selected a new police chief to lead the force: Burlington Deputy Police Chief Jonathan Young.
“I look forward to this new role in the capital city,” Young said in a press release issued by the Montpelier city manager’s office Monday. “My goals are always to leave people feeling safer, calmer and more valued after every interaction with the police.”
This hire closes a months-long search for the state capital’s police chief after both the chief and the deputy chief left for Northfield in May.
Young is a veteran of the U.S. Marine Corps and has 26 years of law enforcement experience, according to the release. He is currently working as an adjunct professor of criminal justice studies at Champlain College alongside his police duties.
As police chief, Young will oversee 17 sworn officers and 10 dispatchers. He will assume the role on Jan. 4.
The position, most recently held by Eric Nordenson, was vacated in May after Nordenson decided to leave to become Northfield’s police chief. Nordenson, who first joined the Montpelier force nearly three decades ago, was promoted to deputy chief in 2020 and was sworn in as chief in December 2022. 
Former Deputy Chief Kevin Moulton also departed Montpelier in May and was named Northfield’s deputy chief. He joined Montpelier’s police department in 2007 and rose from sergeant to deputy chief in 2023.
Moulton had been serving as Northfield’s interim chief since January while still working for Montpelier under an agreement between the two municipalities.
Two other Montpelier officers, Diane Mathews and Alesha Donovan, also resigned to join Northfield’s police department. The four departures left Montpelier with 11 officers and six vacancies, prompting the city to assess whether it could maintain around-the-clock coverage.

READ MORE

Montpelier’s city manager, Kelly McNicholas Kury, appointed Detective Sgt. Jeffrey Pearson to serve as interim chief on July 6.
The City Council on July 8 approved spending about $40,000 on a nationwide search led by JW Leadership Consulting, an Arlington firm that recruits law enforcement executives. Kury told councilors on Nov. 12 that she had interviewed four candidates, narrowed them down to two, and was negotiating with the finalist, whom Kury did not name at the time.
Kury said she is confident Young’s experience in Vermont law enforcement, as well as his knowledge of Vermont-specific public safety concerns, will set him up for success in the onboarding process, according to the release.
“Young demonstrated through a rigorous hiring process that he possesses the knowledge and
sensitivity that our city demands for a police chief to lead with the community in mind,” Kury said.
“I believe he will demonstrate the values of our city and department honorably.”

name: West Virginia Watch
title: House Speaker Hanshaw says Auditor Hunt should resign; impeachment proceedings imminent if not
description: House Speaker Roger Hanshaw has called on State Auditor Mark Hunt to immediately resign after a multi-count indictment alleged the auditor’s involvement in a property stealing scheme within his office.
text:
House Speaker Roger Hanshaw, R-Clay, has called on State Auditor Mark Hunt to resign following a multi-count indictment by a federal jury on Monday. (Photo by Perry Bennett/West Virginia Legislative Photography)House Speaker Roger Hanshaw has called on State Auditor Mark Hunt to immediately resign after a multi-count indictment alleged the auditor’s involvement in a property stealing scheme within his office. 
“These serious allegations cast a long shadow over the Office of the State Auditor and its role of maintaining the integrity of other state and local officials,” said Hanshaw, R-Clay. 
West Virginia Auditor Mark Hunt
On Monday afternoon, a federal grand jury indicted Hunt on charges alleging he schemed to steal multiple properties from lawful owners to benefit Charleston-area lawyer Robert L. Johns, a longtime friend and business associate. Hunt signed nine tax delinquent deeds for Johns, and the auditor defended actions as legally justifiable in his role.
Federal prosecutors said Hunt, 66, of Charleston, overruled career employees at the Auditor’s Office and issued the deeds after they found Johns had not complied with the law. 
U.S. Attorney Moore Capito announced the indictments on Monday with stern words about Hunt’s activities, including, “The rules governing public office are not optional.”
Within an hour of the announcement, Hanshaw said in a statement that Hunt should resign.
“Every American is entitled to due process and the presumption of innocence in every criminal proceeding, but the public is entitled to leadership from the officers it elects; Mountaineers should always be free from the sort of taint these indictments create,” said Hanshaw in a statement.
“Auditor Hunt should immediately resign from his office. If he resolves to do otherwise, the House of Delegates will take swift action in January to restore integrity to the Office of the West Virginia State Auditor.”
The House of Delegates could initiate impeachment proceedings against Hunt if he remains in office.
Senate President Randy Smith, R-Preston, declined to comment at this time.
Hunt and Johns have been charged with nine counts of theft of more than $5,000 by a public official, for which Hunt faces up to 10 years in prison for each count.
Hunt has also been charged with one count of bank fraud, for which he could face up to 30 years in prison. 
The grand jury also issued indictments against employees in Hunt’s office, including Deputy Chief of Staff David Cole, 57, of Charleston, who a West Virginia Watch investigation revealed was running a car lot with Hunt. Federal authorities say Cole and another member of staff, Frederic Caudill, 59, of Charleston, West Virginia, helped create the property deeds.

Cole and Caudill have also been charged with a count of lying to FBI agents during the investigation.
Separate indictments allege that Marie Ann Hoffmann, 66, an employee of the state auditor’s office, committed bank fraud while aided and abetted by Hunt and Cole.
All five defendants are presumed innocent unless and until proven beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law.
Senate Minority Leader Mike Woelfel, D-Cabell, shown March 4, 2026, says that if the allegations against Auditor Mark Hunt are true, they are “beyond troubling.” (Photo by Will Price/West Virginia Legislative Photography)
Senate Minority Leader Mike Woelfel, D-Cabell, said that if the allegations against Hunt are true, they are “beyond troubling.”
“It’s odd that it appears that many of the allegations are really undisputed,” said Woefel, an attorney, when reached by phone Monday. “I don’t have an opinion on what Mr. Hunt should do. I will tell you that I believe if I was the auditor, I would choose to resign so that I could focus on my defense to these very serious federal charges that are contained in the indictment.”
Both the West Virginia Republican and Democratic Parties have called on Hunt to resign. 
“These charges say Mark Hunt used the power of that office to take property from West Virginia families. That is a betrayal of the public trust, and our party will not defend or tolerate it,” said West Virginia Republican Party Chairman Josh Holstein. 
West Virginia Democratic Party Chair Mike Pushkin said, “The West Virginia State Auditor’s job is to investigate waste, fraud and abuse across state agencies — not to be the creator of waste, fraud and abuse. For Mark Hunt to remain in office under these circumstances would be like leaving the fox in charge of the henhouse.”
Woelfel stressed that the role of auditor is “critical in state government.”
“If we can’t trust the gatekeepers, the auditor, then that’s just going to undermine the public’s view of state government in general. That’s another extremely troubling aspect of the indictment,” Woelfel said.
Gov. Patrick Morrisey said in a statement to reporters that the allegations in the federal indictments are “troubling and must be taken seriously.”
“West Virginians have every right to expect honesty, integrity and accountability from those entrusted with public office,” the governor said through a spokesperson. 
Hunt, a Republican, was elected in 2024 and previously served in the state Legislature. He is an attorney with Mark A. Hunt & Associates PLLC, where he has continued to practice law while working as a state official.

name: Missouri Independent
title: Missouri school funding task force delays recommendations as budget cuts loom
description: A Missouri task force that spent nearly 18 months studying how to overhaul the state’s public school funding formula will delay its recommendations until July 2027, after lawmakers have approved the next state budget. State Sen. Rusty Black, a Chillicothe Republican who chairs both the task force and the Senate Appropriations Committee, announced the delay [[...]
text:
Missouri Gov. Mike Kehoe, pictured speaking during a meeting of the Missouri School Funding Modernization Task Force in September of 2025, has agreed to delay the task force's report until after legislative session (Annelise Hanshaw/Missouri Independent).A Missouri task force that spent nearly 18 months studying how to overhaul the state’s public school funding formula will delay its recommendations until July 2027, after lawmakers have approved the next state budget.
State Sen. Rusty Black, a Chillicothe Republican who chairs both the task force and the Senate Appropriations Committee, announced the delay Monday, citing looming budget cuts and legislative proposals to reduce property taxes, a major source of funding for public schools.
“Beginning (the political process) in this chaotic year that we are in is ill-advised,” he told the group at the end of its meeting Monday morning. “So that is the choice I have made.”
The decision comes after the task force learned that its proposed changes could increase the cost of Missouri’s school funding formula by more than $600 million. Meanwhile, the existing formula is already projected to be underfunded by roughly $300 million next fiscal year.
 The group was scheduled to review a draft report of recommendations during its meeting in October. Six days beforehand, Black cancelled the meeting, citing scheduling conflicts.
Monday’s meeting did not include a review of the report but instead focused on the state’s deteriorating financial outlook. Adam Koenigsfeld, director of Missouri Senate appropriations staff, estimated that lawmakers will have to cut $1.5 to $3.5 billion from the funding requested by state agencies.
This will be a major focus of the legislative session beginning in January, Black said, alongside proposals to reduce property taxes, which drastically impact school funding.
“As we go through this next year with two major things on the plate in the legislature… I’ve asked the governor’s office and the governor, and he has agreed to wait until the end of July to accept this report,” he said.
The report has not been made public. When The Independent asked the Missouri Department of Elementary and Secondary Education for a copy, a spokesperson referred the question to Black’s office.
The department has not yet responded to a request under Missouri’s open records law for a copy of the report.
Democrats have been calling out what they see as a lack of transparency and asking for a public release of the group’s recommendations.
“It is incredibly disappointing that the governor’s handpicked task force has worked for almost 18 months to research and craft a responsible funding formula and after 18 months of work, they are not going to issue any findings,” state Sen. Maggie Nurrenbern, a Kansas City Democrat and former educator, told The Independent. “I think the public deserves to know: What did the task force discover and why are they failing to release the report?”
State Sen. Doug Beck, a Democrat from Affton who previously served on his local school board, told The Independent that he was frustrated that the report is still in the dark.
“All I can assume is (GOP leaders) didn’t like the results of the extra money being spent, and they decided to can it,” he said. “I don’t see why they would do this, go through all this work, people’s time, valuable time from different people across the board, and then at the end say you’re not going to even come forward with the report that you’ve already completed.”
Gov. Mike Kehoe created the task force through an executive order in January 2025, asking for a report by Dec. 1 with recommendations to update Missouri’s 21-year-old formula.
His office said in a statement Monday that Kehoe “remains committed to developing a school funding foundation formula that reflects the needs of today’s students, families and educators” but supports the delay.
Kehoe initially asked the group to create a formula that would cost roughly the same in its first year of implementation as the $3.875 billion provided in fiscal year 2025. Changes to the formula and a new public school accountability system has increased the cost to $4.53 billion for fiscal year 2028.
“A lot of times when you ask a school superintendent, ‘where are the problems?….’ They ask for more money,” Kehoe said during the task force’s first meeting in June 2025. “That is not a great answer to me… That can’t always be the answer to every problem.”
Despite the state’s financial pressures, some task force members said Monday that they remain confident in their recommendations, even if lawmakers cannot afford to fully fund them.
“I would rather underfund a new formula than continue to fund a formula that is already making the inequities greater,” state Rep. Ed Lewis, a Republican from Moberly who lost his bid for State Senate in the August primary.
Michael Podgursky, a semi-retired economics professor from the University of Missouri-Columbia and affiliated scholar at the Sinquefield Center for Applied Economic Research, said the group had identified needed fixes for the formula.
“We need to come up with a rational basis going forward, independent of revenue projections,” he said. “Maybe it won’t get fully funded for some years, but at least underlying the projections is a rational structure for identifying need and equity across the districts.”
Black offered conflicting reasons for the delay, saying the state’s financial situation is worse than when the group first began meeting.
“The assumptions were that the money is going to be there and we are going to be able to have an impact,” he said. “Those assumptions I believe have changed tremendously.”
But he also noted that the budget situation was predicted years prior as the state spent down its reserves.
“The idea that we were going to cut $2 to $2.5 billion,” he said. “People around the state budget put those numbers in front of me two or three years ago.”
Beck wondered if Kehoe and other Republican officials did not like the outcome of the task force’s work, which called for an increase to education funding rather than tamping it down to 2025’s level.
“I thought (the task force) was going to be used as a way to underfund our schools, and I think that’s what they thought was going to happen,” he said. “Then when it turned out that they had to put more money in just to basically keep the status quo, it caused a problem for them.”
House Minority Leader Ashley Aune, a Democrat from Kansas City,  said at a news conference Monday afternoon that the delay means public schools will remain tied to a dated funding system.
“What that means is that we are going to go through another budget process in the upcoming session,” she said, “where appropriators are going to be asked to work on a foundation formula that our own governor says is not working.”
The task force will not meet in coming months, but Black encouraged members to remain part of the group.
“We will see what it looks like at the end of session when we reset and what we can do,” he said.
Kehoe’s policy director, Halle Herbert, said the governor is expecting a report around the end of July.
“We are all very much appreciative of the hard work,” she said. “And we know that the efforts are not done yet.”

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: Black Hills Corp., NorthWestern Energy complete merger to create $15 billion company
description: South Dakota-based utility companies Black Hills Corp. and NorthWestern Energy have completed their merger, forming Bright Horizon Energy, a company serving a combined 2.2 million electric or natural gas customers across eight states. The company announced the merger’s completion on Monday. Filings with the South Dakota Public Utilities Commission list the n[...]
text:
Signs identify the locations of a Black Hills Energy office in Rapid City and a NorthWestern Energy office in Huron. (Photos and illustration by South Dakota Searchlight) South Dakota-based utility companies Black Hills Corp. and NorthWestern Energy have completed their merger, forming Bright Horizon Energy, a company serving a combined 2.2 million electric or natural gas customers across eight states.
The company announced the merger’s completion on Monday. Filings with the South Dakota Public Utilities Commission list the new company’s value at $15.4 billion. 
The company announced the merger’s completion on Monday. It said customers will see no immediate changes to their billing or online account access.
“Today marks the beginning of an exciting new chapter as Bright Horizon Energy,” said Brian Bird, the new CEO who formerly led NorthWestern. Black Hills CEO Linden Evans is to retire.
Bright Horizon Energy will serve 195,705 customers in South Dakota, and 2 million more in Montana, Wyoming, Colorado, Nebraska, Kansas, Iowa and Arkansas. The merged company is headquartered in Rapid City. NorthWestern was headquartered in Sioux Falls.
The merged company has about 4,500 employees, about 39,000 miles of electric lines and about 60,000 miles of natural gas lines.
The South Dakota Public Utilities Commission approved the merger on June 24. Montana was the final state to do so, with regulators there signing off on Nov. 10.

name: Mississippi Today
title: [Register now] How Scott Colom won a Senate race: A post-election Q&A with Mississippi Today’s politics team
description: Mississippi Today's politics team is having an online Q&A session about Scott Colom's victory in the U.S. Senate race. The free event is at 2 p.m. Wednesday.
text:
No incumbent U.S. senator from Mississippi had lost since 1942. Then came the 2026 election cycle.
Democrat Scott Colom defeated Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith in one of the most closely watched races in the country. The tight election drew extra scrutiny because the vote counting process took more than a week. Colom became the first Black person ever elected to the U.S. Senate from Mississippi by popular vote. Deep South politicos will study his win for years.
So how did it happen? Why did DeSoto County flip from red to blue, and how did Colom appeal to voters waiting in line at a Trump rally? Why did it take so long to call the race? And what does a Democratic win in deep-red Mississippi mean for the 2027 governor’s race, the rest of the South and the road to the 2028 presidential election?
Mississippi Today’s politics team covered this race from the first campaign stop to the last affidavit ballot. Now they’re taking your questions.
