Space is limited, so register soon. We’ll email you a link to join after you sign up, so keep an eye on your inbox, including your spam folder.
Have a question for our reporters? Send it ahead of time to events@mississippitoday.org, and we’ll try to answer it live.

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Judge issues order blocking Indiana Senate GOP leader Chris Garten from starting new term
description: Democrats asked a judge on Monday to block Republican state Sen. Chris Garten from taking the oath of office for a new term ahead of an expected recount of his tight race for reelection.
text:
Sen. Chris Garten, R-Charlestown, speaks during a 2025 legislative meeting. (Photo by Whitney Downard/Indiana Capital Chronicle)A judge on Monday issued an order blocking Republican state Sen. Chris Garten from taking the oath of office for a new term ahead of an expected recount of his tight race for reelection.
Democrats sought the temporary restraining order against Garten ahead of the Legislature’s Organization Day on Tuesday, when the Senate’s majority Republicans planned to install him in the chamber’s top position of president pro tem.
The order issued by Scott County Circuit Court Judge Jason Mount said “Chris Garten is restrained from presenting himself to take the oath of office as, or to be seated as, the Senator from District 45.”
A court hearing on the request from Democrats for a preliminary injunction is set for Wednesday afternoon in Jeffersonville.
Garten did not immediately respond to questions about the legal action sent to his Senate and campaign offices. Garten last week said he was confident that his reelection would stand and called the claims from Democrats “political theater.”
The restraining order sought by the Clark County Democratic chairman argued that voting equipment problems on Election Day in Jeffersonville leave questions about the accuracy of the reported election results.
The tallies for Senate District 45 — which includes all of Clark County and a portion of Floyd County — show Garten ahead of Democratic challenger Nick Marshall by 297 votes, or about two-thirds of a percentage point, with 21,817 votes to 21,520 for Marshall.
Democrats eye seeking recount in Republican Senate leader Chris Garten’s tight reelection race

The court filing argues that Garten should not be allowed to be sworn in for a new four-year term before the Indiana Recount Commission can review the race.
Democrats maintain the Clark County Election Board — controlled 2-1 by Republicans — failed to adequately review problems involving four precincts that voted at Jeffersonville High School, where a ballot scanner malfunction was reported on Election Day.
The court filing said time is needed to “resolve the discrepancies in the poll pad records or determine whether all of the votes cast at Jeffersonville High School were counted through the transition from one machine to another: the machine’s results tape reports 1,640 ballots; 474 ballots were cast before the machine was replaced, but only 333 voters had signed in by 11:08 a.m.; and the poll pad records show more than 100 voters signing in after 7:00 p.m., an hour after the polls closed.”
Republican Clark County Clerk Ryan Lynch, a county election board member, did not immediately reply Monday to an email seeking comment on the court filing.
Mount, a Democrat, was assigned as the special judge after a Clark County judge’s recusal from the case, according to court records. Mount is the brother of Republican U.S. Rep. Erin Houchin, who served in the state Senate with Garten.
The judge’s order also blocks the Clark County Election Board from certifying the election results until he decides whether to grant an injunction.
Democrats have said they intend to seek a recount of the Senate race results. Candidates have until Tuesday to file recount petitions, with county party chairs having until Friday to do so.
Clark County Democratic Chair Miguel Hampton, state Democratic Chair Karen Tallian and Ninth Congressional District party Chair Adam Dickey said in a joint statement that the “Clark County Election Board left us with no other option but to resolve this issue in the courts.”
“The voters deserve to have their ballots counted fairly and accurately, and we cannot just look the other way and not worry about what happened or whether the results are even legitimate,” they said. “The fact that this election affects one of the most powerful Republicans in state government makes this situation unique.”

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: NC’s Attorney General moves to block merger of two largest distributors of vet supplies
description: If you’ve ever had to take the family pet to the vet, you know how expensive it can be. If a proposed merger between the nation’s two largest veterinary supply distributors goes through, that next visit could be even more expensive. North Carolina Attorney General Jeff Jackson is suing to block Covetrus and MWI Animal […]
text:
North Carolina Attorney General Jeff Jackson is joining a lawsuit to block Covetrus and MWI Animal Health from merging because he believes it will lead to higher prices at veterinary clinics and larger bills for people seeking care for their pets. (Stock photo by Oscar Wong/Getty Images)If you’ve ever had to take the family pet to the vet, you know how expensive it can be. If a proposed merger between the nation’s two largest veterinary supply distributors goes through, that next visit could be even more expensive.
North Carolina Attorney General Jeff Jackson is suing to block Covetrus and MWI Animal Health from joining forces because he believes it will lead to higher prices at veterinary clinics and larger bills for people seeking care for their pets.
Jackson and a bipartisan coalition of 12 other states and the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) are seeking a court order to rule the merger illegal.
“Pet owners are already paying hundreds of dollars a year for veterinary care,” said Jackson in a statement. “The last thing they need is two giant companies merging so they can charge veterinarians more, knowing those costs will get passed along to pet owners.”
Jackson said veterinary clinics looking to purchase medication or equipment can currently negotiate between the two companies in hopes of getting the best price possible. If the $3.5 billion merger between Covetrus and MWI goes through, Jackson says an already-concentrated marketplace becomes more so, and North Carolina’s vets will have less bargaining power. When veterinary clinics pay more for those supplies, the cost gets passed on to consumers.

Today, AG @JeffJacksonNC announced a lawsuit against two of the nation’s largest veterinary supply distributors to stop a merger that could raise costs for pet owners. https://t.co/73odI3ml4M https://t.co/BAF3RttEFw
— NC Attorney General (@NCAGO) November 13, 2026

Ben Wolin, Chief Executive Officer of Covetrus, said in February that the combined companies would make animal healthcare more affordable and accessible.
“By bringing MWI’s strong distribution capabilities and expertise to our business, we can offer more solutions to more customers, improve logistics, create savings and develop innovative new ways to support the animal health ecosystem, including veterinarians, producers, manufacturers, distributors and pet parents,” said Wolin in announcing the merger.
Jackson said eliminating competition in the industry could impact 80% of North Carolina households who own pets.
Last year, dog owners reported spending an average of nearly $600 on veterinary care, while cat owners spent about $530, according to the American Veterinary Medical Association.
North Carolina joins ‘overcharging’ lawsuit against Dollar General

The merger and the prospect of higher prices is also drawing scrutiny from local animal shelters and rescues.
“Basic veterinary care shouldn’t be a luxury,” said Mondy Lamb of  SPCA of Wake County in a statement. “Vaccinations, spay/neuter surgery, and treatment for sick or injured pets are essential services that every pet owner should be able to afford.”
More than 1,000 pet owners reach out to the Wake SPCA annually for help in covering care for their pets. The nonprofit recently opened a new low-cost spay and neuter clinic.
North Carolina will be joined in the lawsuit by the attorneys general from Arizona, Arkansas, California, Colorado, Maine, Michigan, Minnesota, Nebraska, New York, Ohio, Oregon, and Texas.

name: Georgia Recorder
title: Georgia House GOP to shuffle leadership after election losses
description: House Republicans will be led by a new leader when Democrats take control of the chamber in January. The caucus elected Republican state Rep. Todd Jones from South Forsyth as minority leader Monday in a close race against Mulberry Republican state Rep. Chuck Efstration, who served as leader under the Republican majority. State Rep. Jon […]
text:
Rep. Todd Jones, a South Forsyth Republican, makes a speech during a session of the Georgia House of Representative at the state Capitol in Atlanta on March 3, 2026. Alander Rocha/Georgia RecorderHouse Republicans will be led by a new leader when Democrats take control of the chamber in January.
The caucus elected Republican state Rep. Todd Jones from South Forsyth as minority leader Monday in a close race against Mulberry Republican state Rep. Chuck Efstration, who served as leader under the Republican majority. State Rep. Jon Burns, a Republican from Newington who served as House speaker since 2023, did not run for the top position but was selected to serve as House speaker emeritus.
Jones, who was first elected to the state House in 2016, said after the vote that he was drawn to the position after leading a startup over the last 25 years and felt that he would be a right fit as the party navigates stepping into the minority for the first time in 20 years.
“I love the idea of finding a way to basically navigate different challenges, and this was an amazing challenge,” Jones said. “We want to make sure that 11 million Georgians understand that there’s an opportunity for us to basically shift the ship, and we’re going to be able to do that in two years.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Jones said that Republicans need to “pivot and make sure that (the caucus is) serving 11 million Georgians,” but he declined to say how they plan to win the House in the next election.
“The last time I saw Kirby Smart, he didn’t tell me how he’s going to beat South Carolina on Saturday, and I’m going to go ahead and keep that kind of tight to the chest right now,” he said, referring to the celebrated University of Georgia football coach.
Hugley is officially nominated as Georgia House speaker as Democrats choose their leaders

House Democrats are set to hold a razor thin majority in the chamber after winning at least 91 seats in the November elections, the exact number they needed to take control of the chamber, and their caucus last week elected Columbus state Rep. Carolyn Hugley as their nominee for House speaker. Three districts remain uncalled, with one headed to a December runoff. 
Jones seemed open to working with Democrats on bipartisan issues, but aside from saying that mental health and substance use is a “top policy matter” for him, he declined to specify what those issues might be.
“I think it’s important that we are able to move forward in this state, and we understand there are going to be times that we’re going to be able to put bipartisan measures onto the table. And I think that’s something that we need to consider very strongly,” Jones said.
House Republicans also elected Waycross state Rep. James Burchett to serve as minority whip, Fayetteville state Rep. Josh Bonner as minority caucus chair, Moultrie state Rep. Chas Cannon as minority caucus vice chair, Concord state Rep. Beth Camp as minority caucus secretary, Bonaire state Rep. Shaw Blackmon as minority caucus treasurer and Elberton state Rep. Rob Leverett as minority caucus chief deputy whip.
Senate Democrats, who will remain in the minority in that chamber, also elected their leaders Monday. Augusta state Sen. Harold Jones will remain minority leader, and Stone Mountain state Sen. Kim Jackson will keep her minority whip position. Savannah state Sen. Derek Mallow will serve as caucus chair, replacing Atlanta state Sen. Elena Parent, who did not run for reelection. Smyrna state Sen. Jaha Howard will serve as caucus vice chair, replacing Atlanta state Sen. Sonya Halpern, and Atlanta state Sen. Sally Harrell will serve as vice chair of finance, replacing Grayson state Sen. Nikki Merritt. Atlanta state Sen. Nan Orrock will keep her post as secretary.
Lt. Gov-elect Josh McLaurin is set to be the first Democrat to preside over the Senate since 2007, though his actual power could be limited with Republicans in the majority.
The 2027 legislative session is scheduled to begin on January 11.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Workers compensation rates ordered lowered by average 7.4% in 2027
description: Costs are increasing but not for everything. Florida Insurance Commissioner Mike Yaworsky issued a final order Monday approving a statewide overall rate decrease of 7.4% for workers’ compensation policies. The reduction applies to both new policies and renewals. The reduction matches the recommendation by the National Council on Compensation Insurance (NCCI)[...]
text:
Workers compensation costs are being reduced for Florida businesses again (Photo by Nicole Neri for Minnesota Reformer)Costs are increasing but not for everything.
Florida Insurance Commissioner Mike Yaworsky issued a final order Monday approving a statewide overall rate decrease of 7.4% for workers’ compensation policies. The reduction applies to both new policies and renewals.
The reduction matches the recommendation by the National Council on Compensation Insurance (NCCI), submitted earlier this year.
“Approving a 7.4% rate reduction for Florida’s workers’ compensation policies is another major win for our business community heading into the new year. Lowering these mandatory coverage costs frees up capital for Florida employers to reinvest in their workforce, expand operations and drive economic growth,” Yaworsky said in a prepared statement.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Workers’ compensation is a no-fault system that aims to protect employers from getting sued by injured employees and provide workers injured on the job with the care they need to return to work. Employers are required to compensate for lost wages if an employee misses more than eight days of work due to an injury.
Most employers in Florida are required to carry workers’ compensation insurance but there are exceptions for businesses with four or fewer employees and for construction companies with four or fewer officers. While those firms aren’t mandated to carry the coverage, they must file for exemptions with the state.
According to the OIR statement, it’s the 11th consecutive that years workers’ compensation rates were ordered reduced.



“Eleven consecutive years of workers’ comp rate decreases is a great thing for Florida job creators and their employees,” Florida Chamber Vice President for Government Affairs Carolyn Johnson told the Phoenix in a statement echoing many of Yaworsky’s sentiments. “Not only does this trend continue to point toward safer workplaces, but it means savings that businesses can use to reinvest back in their business, their employees and in their communities.”

name: Missouri Independent
title: Missouri AG agrees to let Torch Electronics keep slot machines in veterans, fraternal halls
description: SPRINGFIELD — Torch Electronics will pay the state $13.5 million over two years and keep its illegal slot machines out of for-profit businesses to avoid state prosecution for violating gambling laws, Attorney General Catherine Hanaway said Monday. But under the agreement, the company can continue operating its machines in veterans halls, fraternal clubs and [...]
text:
Missouri Attorney General Catherine Hanaway shows the markings on a Torch slot machine Monday, Nov. 16, 2026, during a news conference in Springfield. She was joined by, from left, Major Steven Wilhoit, Lt. Don Jones and Sgt. Jason Trammell of the Missouri State Highway Patrol. (Rudi Keller/MIssouri Independent)SPRINGFIELD — Torch Electronics will pay the state $13.5 million over two years and keep its illegal slot machines out of for-profit businesses to avoid state prosecution for violating gambling laws, Attorney General Catherine Hanaway said Monday.
But under the agreement, the company can continue operating its machines in veterans halls, fraternal clubs and other qualifying nonprofit locations.
Torch, the largest vendor of the cash-prize games once common in convenience stores and bars, did not admit its games violate state laws against unlicensed games of chance. The company also will be allowed to enroll new nonprofit locations until Jan. 1, 2027, Hanaway said.
“This marks a significant step forward in our efforts to eradicate illegal gaming in Missouri,” Hanaway said. “It’s a big deal. This is a big win for us. It’s a big win for the people of the state.”
Torch declined to comment on the agreement.
Lawsuits challenge Missouri attorney general crackdown on gambling machines

Hanaway announced the agreement in Springfield, where city officials have spent years trying to remove Torch machines and similar games. In October, an appeals court upheld the city’s authority to deny Torch a license to place its games.
The agreement protects Torch and its owner, Steven Miltenberger, as well as employees, vendors, retailers and others from state prosecution for their involvement with Torch as long as they comply with its terms.
Torch agreed to pay $4.5 million this week, plus $4.5 million in each of the following two years. The agreement calls for an additional $6.5 million payment if Torch violates its terms.
The payments are classified as fines for federal tax purposes, meaning Torch cannot deduct them as business expenses. But the company is not admitting to any wrongdoing.
“Based on current and future ongoing litigation risk, Torch is willing to resolve the claims with the state without making an admission of liability,” the non-prosecution agreement states.
Torch began installing its machines in the years before the COVID-19 pandemic. Hanaway has estimated that 25,000 similar machines — not all owned by Torch — were operating in the state before she began an enforcement crackdown late last year.
On Monday, Hanaway said she could not recall how much profit Torch had made during the years its machines operated statewide or how much money the machines handled in March, the last full month before Torch agreed to limited operations.
The $13.5 million settlement was negotiated down from the state’s initial demand of 21% of Torch’s gambling revenue, matching the tax Missouri imposes on casinos’ adjusted gross receipts, Hanaway said. She did not disclose how much the initial demand would have totaled.
“The estimates have been that across all the machines, revenue, gross revenue, might be as much as $1 billion, but the claimed payout and these are some things that we can’t 100% verify,” Hanaway said.
Hanaway pressured Torch to shut down its machines in retail locations in April amid the threat of possible state and federal prosecutions.
The April shutdown did not extend to nonprofit locations such as veterans organizations and fraternal clubs, Hanaway said. The new agreement preserves that exemption, which she described as a matter of prosecutorial discretion.
“We have to use prosecutorial discretion and resources, and we wanted to go after sort of the biggest and the baddest first,” she said. “So Torch was obviously the largest company, but also, it does make a difference that the businesses that had these machines were putting the money in their own pocket, as opposed to the VFW or the Elks Club who are doing something good to support the community.”
The exemption applies only to what Hanaway termed “bona fide” nonprofit organizations. For-profit businesses cannot qualify simply by reorganizing as nonprofits or creating nonprofit affiliates, she said.
The St. Louis Post-Dispatch reported last month that several businesses had restarted their Torch machines after setting up new entities.
Hanaway said Torch insisted on retaining the exemption.
“It’s tough to negotiate an agreement like this,” Hanaway said. “We’ve already had these machines shut down for about six months, and they’re shut down into the future. We want to work towards an agreement, and also the not-for-profits, like they will tell you that they have been relying on these machines.”
Federal judge rules Missouri’s gas station slot machines are illegal gambling devices

Torch machines will remain shut down in retail locations, the agreement states, until the company wins a court decision, upheld on appeal, that its machines do not violate state law or the General Assembly legalizes the games.
The agreement also leaves open another path for Torch’s machines to return to retail locations. If state lawmakers authorize the Missouri Lottery to offer video lottery games, Torch machines could operate during the transition period between passage of the bill and the start of the state-regulated games.
The debate over video lottery drew millions of dollars into this year’s legislative elections. State Rep. Bill Hardwick, one of the most prominent supporters of video lottery legislation, won a state Senate seat, as did one of its vocal opponents, Springfield Democrat Betsy Fogle.
Torch is the largest but not the only vendor of the gambling machines. Hanaway said her office is pressuring other vendors to shut down their games and has begun negotiating with some of them.
“We absolutely are going to be going after those other companies,” Hanaway said. “We’re already in negotiations with some of them.”

name: Honolulu Civil Beat
title: Hawaiʻi Special Education May Leave Thousands Behind, Report Says
description:
Compared to mainland schools, Hawaiʻi enrolls a smaller percentage of special education students and puts them in mainstream classrooms less often, a new UHERO report found. 
The post Hawaiʻi Special Education May Leave Thousands Behind, Report Says appeared first on Honolulu Civil Beat.
text:
Nearly 7,000 Hawaiʻi students with disabilities may be missing out on federally-mandated services in schools, according to a recent report from the University of Hawaiʻi Economic Research Organization. 
Hawaiʻi enrolls the smallest percentage of special education students in the nation, said report author and UHERO research economist Daniela Bond-Smith. In the 2024-25 school year, around 11% of Hawaiʻi public school students received special education services, compared to the national median of 15%. 
That disparity is raising concerns that kids aren’t receiving the support they need to learn. 
The education department’s low enrollment rates might be expected if more students with disabilities attended private schools or received services outside of schools’ special education programs, the report says. But that’s not the case.
“These facts indicate that fewer students are being identified for and receiving special education services in Hawai‘i’s public schools than would be expected,” Bond-Smith said in the report.  
A new UHERO report found that Hawaiʻi’s special education enrollment lags behind the rest of the nation, raising concerns that some students aren’t receiving the services mandated under federal law. (Craig Fujii/Civil Beat/2026)
Hawaiʻi is required under federal law to support students with disabilities in public schools and receives around $50 million from the federal government each year. Services can range from one-on-one aides to physical and speech therapy.
“It’s really about enabling the child to be educated,” Bond-Smith said.
The education department is working to strengthen special education services and recognizes that improvements are needed, said Hawaiʻi schools’ communications director Nanea Ching. The estimate of nearly 7,000 local students possibly qualifying for special education is based on national enrollment rates, she said, not the actual number of students who have been evaluated for these services.
“National benchmarks offer helpful context, but special education eligibility and placement decisions must be based on individual student needs, not predetermined identification or inclusion targets,” she said in an emailed statement. 
Students may qualify for special education under a range of disability categories, ranging from developmental delays and hearing loss to autism and traumatic brain injuries. 
Students Staying Under The Radar
The state’s low enrollment rates suggests that some special education students – particularly those who need lower levels of support for their disabilities – are going unidentified in schools, according to the UHERO report. Those who are identified likely receive services at a later age than their mainland peers. 
Research has found that students who don’t receive necessary special education services may be less likely to finish high school and enroll in college. 
Enrollment in special education also varies by island and student characteristics. Those with speech and language disabilities in Hawaiʻi may be less likely to receive services than their peers on the mainland. Local Native Hawaiian and Pacific Islander students tend to be overrepresented in special education, while Asian students are much less likely to receive these services. 
Special education enrollment tends to peak later in Hawaiʻi schools compared to the rest of the nation, raising concerns that some students are missing out on services in their early years.  (Screenshot/University of Hawaiʻi Economic Research Organization)
Kauaʻi had the lowest rate of special education enrollment in the state, with roughly 9% of students receiving services. The other islands all reported an enrollment rate of roughly 11%. 
There’s a number of reasons why Hawaiʻi’s special education numbers lag behind the rest of the country, Bond-Smith said. The process of identifying students likely varies among schools, while some parents may have concerns about their children receiving a special education designation, especially when academic outcomes for these students tend to be relatively poor.    
Long-time special education teacher Shannon Kaʻaʻa said schools may also try different strategies to support students before evaluating them for special education services. If students show some short-term improvement, she said, their evaluation may get pushed back until they’re facing additional challenges later on.    
Attorney Eric Seitz said it’s only become harder for families to compel schools to provide services for their children since the Trump administration began dismantling the federal Department of Education. The administration has shuttered seven civil rights enforcement offices and laid off staff, further reducing support for families. 


Many of the challenges families face aren’t new. In the 1990s, Hawaiʻi was put under 12 years of federal court oversight to ensure students with disabilities would receive special education services after Seitz filed a class action lawsuit against the state. 
More recently, the state settled an $8 million claim this spring alleging the education department failed to serve a student with severe disabilities. The family alleged that the student experienced post-traumatic stress disorder and a regression in skills after the education department failed to provide adequate services for several years.   
Now, Seitz said, he’s working on another lawsuit alleging that the education department is failing to identify students with disabilities and provide them appropriate services in a timely manner. The state may also face greater consequences from the federal level if the U.S. Department of Education reasserts itself, he said. 
“I would suspect that within a few years, the functions of the Department of Education are going to be restored, and there is going to be better federal oversight,” Seitz said. “Hawaiʻi’s going to find themselves in the aims of the department as being one of the worst offenders in the country, and there are going to be repercussions.” 
Latest From Civil Beat
More Inclusivity Needed
Hawaiʻi also lags behind the nation when it comes to inclusion rates, which represent the number of special education students who spend most of their day in class with the rest of their peers. The state reported a five-year inclusion rate of 53%, below the national median of 69%.  
The low inclusion rates are partially because the state isn’t serving some special education students with lower needs, who would likely be able to spend most of their day in a classroom with the rest of their peers, according to the UHERO report. Students already receiving special education services are also less likely to learn in a mainstream classroom compared to their mainland peers.
Advocates say it’s important to teach special education students in the same setting as their peers because it gives them the opportunity to learn the same material as their classmates and engage socially with other kids their age.  
In 2017, the education department launched an initiative to train schools on inclusive practices and support students with disabilities in traditional classroom settings. The two-year program improved schools’ inclusion rates as well as the math achievement of their special education students, according to the UHERO report. Math and reading scores for all students at participating schools were around the same as those who didn’t participate in the initiative. 
The education department, headed by then-Superintendent Christina Kishimoto, announced in 2019 that it would award $10,000 salary bonuses to special education teachers starting the following year. Some educators say schools still need more qualified staff to effectively include special education students in classes with the rest of their peers. (Cory Lum/Civil Beat/2019)
But the rollout was limited to schools that opted into the program, and those that participated had varied success with improving their inclusion rates in the long run. The department continued offering training at a majority of campuses, although these offerings are typically more limited in scope than the original 2017 program.
“These kids primarily sit in general education classrooms. They’re primarily served by general education teachers, so we really need to frame this as an issue for all teachers,” Bond-Smith said, adding that schools are capable of closing the inclusion gaps between Hawaiʻi and the mainland and should try to design their lessons to support all types of learners. 
The education department is continuing to improve its training by offering more professional development around inclusion and coaching to encourage collaboration among teachers, Ching said. The department also provides annual training on special education eligibility and evaluations and is improving its use of data to identify and support students’ individual needs, she said. 
To effectively implement inclusion, schools need more educators who also receive proper training, said Kaʻaʻa, who now serves as a teachers’ union representative for educators in Central Oʻahu. For example, she said, teachers may require additional professional development around how to support students with behavioral issues in traditional classroom settings. 
Justin Hughey, a special education teacher on Maui, said staffing can be a barrier to inclusion. The state has historically struggled to hire special education teachers and now offers a $10,000 bonus to attract more educators. 
“If we paid teachers a competitive salary when factored in the cost of living,” Hughey said in a written statement, “we would easily fill the teacher shortage with certified teachers.” 
The post Hawaiʻi Special Education May Leave Thousands Behind, Report Says appeared first on Honolulu Civil Beat.

text:
Officials with the Maine Secretary of State's Office prepare ballots for ranked-choice tabulations for three primary elections in Augusta on June 12, 2026. (Photo by Jim Neuger/ Maine Morning Star)Democrat Elizabeth Bosworth was declared the official winner of Maine Senate District 18, defeating Republican John Andrews by just over 50 votes following a Monday recount.
The final tally, according to the Maine Secretary of State’s Office, was 10,413 to 10,360. 
Bosworth’s victory confirms another seat for legislative Democrats, who emerged from the Nov. 3 election with even stronger majorities in both the Maine Senate and House of Representatives. In the Senate, the party now holds a 24-seat supermajority, the first since 1985, according to the Senate President’s Office.
Bosworth will replace outgoing Sen. Rick Benentt, who left the Republican Party last year to run as an independent for governor. Bennett has represented the district, which includes parts of Oxford, Androscoggin and Cumberland counties, since 2022.
There will be two more legislative recounts this week, along with a recount for a Kennebec County Commission seat. The recounts are  all open to the public at the Maine Public Safety Building in Augusta and live-streamed on the secretary’s office Youtube page.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Man said he asked questions about Nolan Wells case, then was jailed
description: Event attendees stand outside holding signs in support of Nolan Wells’ family during a vigil for Wells at Greater St. John AME Church in Biloxi on Wednesday, Aug. 19, 2026.
text:
A New York man accused of making terroristic threats relating to the Nolan Xavier Wells case is now in a Mississippi jail weeks after he said he was just asking questions about the case. People on social media are calling out a lack of transparency about his arrest. 
The Jackson County Sheriff’s Department took Christian Anthony Claudio, 25, into custody after his extradition from Otsego County New York on Saturday. By Monday morning, department officials listed him on its jail docket with a felony charge of making terroristic threats. 
In an affidavit in Jackson County Court uploaded Monday afternoon, Claudio is accused of threatening to travel to Mississippi to kill chancery court clerks “due to findings of a high profile death investigation.” 
He had a first appearance in Jackson County where his bond was set at $50,000, and one of his bond conditions was to stop posting about the case on social media. 
Before his extradition, Claudio, a resident of Oneonta, New York, denied threatening anyone or making “crazy, malicious” statements when he called the Jackson County clerk’s office. 
“I never had no intent, I simply had questions about Nolan Wells, and I had called down there because in my heart, it felt wrong where I was just trying to understand what was going on,” he said in a video call from the Otsego County jail posted Friday on TikTok.
Wells, 18, went missing from Horn Island on July 4. He arrived by boat with friends who departed without him. The friends told investigators that Wells said he would get a ride back on another boat. Two days later, his body was found in waters off the barrier island along Mississippi’s Gulf Coast. On Sept. 21, a Jackson County grand jury declined to indict anyone relating to Wells’ death. 
In a Sunday video, Claudio’s family said he made it to Mississippi and the Jackson County jail, but he doesn’t feel safe there. 
Claudio had been scheduled for a Monday afternoon hearing in New York related to an out-of-state arrest warrant from Mississippi, but Claudio has already been picked up, Cara Tangorra, deputy chief clerk of the Otsego County Court, told Mississippi Today Monday morning. 
If prosecutors gather enough evidence, Claudio could be the sixth person charged with making threats against Jackson County public officials and witnesses tied to Wells’ death investigation. 
Joseph Alfredo Vasquez Dumarce of California plans to plead guilty, according to court records. He is accused of threatening to kill and bomb the office of a Jackson County chancery judge who is the stepmother of one of the friends Wells was last seen with. A man from Illinois who also made threats is scheduled for trial in February.
Claudio was first booked into the Otsego County jail Oct. 31, and he was held there until picked up by Mississippi deputies. 
He began posting on social media shortly after his arrest. Public outcry followed in which people on social media asked to see proof of the phone calls Claudio made to the Jackson County clerk’s office. 
Claudio shared his own account of what happened in a video featuring his sister Nicole Kaura posted Saturday on his TikTok account. Kaura was not immediately available for comment Monday. 
Days after the grand jury’s decision, Claudio called the Jackson County Chancery Clerk’s Office twice to ask a clerk questions about the Wells case. 
Three hours later, her brother received a call from Jackson County Sheriff John Ledbetter, who asked about Claudio’s calls earlier and if he had any questions about the case. Claudio said he did not. Kaura said Claudio was not told at the time that officials issued a warrant for his arrest. 
On Oct. 30, Claudio went to help a friend who had car issues. Law enforcement who were already at the scene ran his license and found he had an outstanding warrant.
In a Sunday video of that arrest also posted to TikTok, Claudio can be heard asking multiple times about what the warrant is for. 
Kaura said in the video that Sheriff Ledbetter signed the arrest warrant. The warrant alleged Claudio threatened the clerk over the phone and said he would come to Missisisppi.
Ledbetter was not immediately available for comment Monday.
While he was still in New York, Claudio’s family started a GoFundMe to raise money for legal representation. 
“This has been an incredibly difficult and stressful time for us,” his sister Kaura wrote. “I am barely sleeping or eating because I am constantly worried about Christian and what he is going through. As his sister, it is heartbreaking to feel helpless while he needs support the most.”
Claudio doesn’t have a prior criminal record, has a job working with children with disabilities and owns his own house, Kaura said. 
“All he did was make a phone call to a clerk and now he is being charged with something he did not do,” Kaura said in the Saturday TikTok video. “… All I’m asking is why him? Why Nolan (Wells)?” 
Update 11/16/26: This story has been updated with developments in Claudio’s case.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: CT extends deadline to get gift cards to ex-SNAP beneficiaries
description: Thousands of former recipients of federal nutrition assistance benefits in CT now have until Dec. 31 to claim $300 grocery store gift cards.
text:
Gov. Ned Lamont’s administration is giving thousands of former federal nutrition assistance beneficiaries an extra month to claim the $300 grocery store gift cards first pledged to them in early June.
Department of Social Services spokeswoman Christine Stuart confirmed Monday the administration has extended its self-imposed deadline from Nov. 30 to Dec. 31 to get cards to an estimated 25,000 former recipients of Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program benefits.
The department, which is working with regional nonprofit community action agencies, will send another round of text messages to eligible residents in hopes of disbursing as much relief as possible.
“Residents are advised to visit their local community action agency, show ID, and get their card on the spot,” the department wrote in a memo to state legislators about the deadline extension.
A full list of action agencies and their contact information is available on the Connecticut Association for Community Action website.
“I hope residents are able to take advantage of it,” said Sen. Matt Lesser, D-Middletown, co-chairman of the Human Services Committee and one of the lawmakers who pressed Lamont to intensify Connecticut’s response to federal human services cutbacks. “I know that the demand is significant.”
Lamont has faced increasing pressure to intervene since July 2025, when Congress and President Donald Trump ordered major cutbacks to SNAP and other federal human services programs.
Veterans, people experiencing homelessness, former foster youths and parents with children older than 14 all face tougher work requirements. Many lawfully present immigrants, including refugees, lost eligibility. And critics say tougher error penalties from Washington have led states to unfairly disqualify many SNAP applicants.
The Center on Budget and Policy Priorities, a fiscal policy group based in Washington, D.C., reported in mid-October that SNAP enrollment is at its lowest point nationwide in 17 years. Connecticut Voices for Children, a local policy and research organization, noted in August that nearly 63,000 Connecticut residents, including almost 19,000 children, had lost federal nutrition benefits since July 2025.
Lamont has invested millions of state dollars in Connecticut Foodshare, a nonprofit that supports hundreds of food pantries, shelters, community kitchens and other community-based assistance programs.
But anti-hunger advocates say food pantries and related programs can mitigate only a fraction of the problem created when households lose access to SNAP benefits.
The governor, who recently was reelected to a third term, announced on June 3 he would use state surplus funds to send $7.5 million, in the form of $300 grocery store gift cards, to 25,000 former SNAP recipients.
Distribution was set to begin Aug. 4, but the administration has struggled to get relief to eligible residents.
As of Oct. 27, aid had been provided to about 2,000 of the 25,000 residents, only about 8%. The social services department announced at that time it would streamline efforts to process claims for cards. And while it had used text messages and postcards last summer and fall to notify those eligible, another round of texting is planned.

name: Delaware
title: Gov. Meyer’s office says it’s still reviewing the $1,700 scholarship tax credit, with 46 days left
description: Thirty-one states have opted in, and all three of Delaware’s members of Congress back bills to repeal the credit. DOVER, Del. — Starting Jan. 1, the credit lets taxpayers give up to $1,700 to approved K-12 scholarship groups and take the same amount off their federal taxes. Those gifts can help Delaware students only if Delaware opts in. Delaware LIVE asked [...]
text:
Thirty-one states have opted in, and all three of Delaware’s members of Congress back bills to repeal the credit.
DOVER, Del. — Starting Jan. 1, the credit lets taxpayers give up to $1,700 to approved K-12 scholarship groups and take the same amount off their federal taxes. Those gifts can help Delaware students only if Delaware opts in.
Delaware LIVE asked Gov. Matt Meyer’s office if they are reviewing the tax credit that 31 other states have approved. The Governor’s office stated that they are still reviewing federal rules for a new $1,700 scholarship tax credit and will decide whether Delaware joins when that review is done, the office said in an email to Delaware LIVE on Friday. The state has until Jan. 1 to sign up.
Three things to know
1. No decision until the office finishes its review
“We are currently in the process of reviewing the lengthy Treasury guidelines and will have a decision when our internal deliberation is completed,” the governor’s office said.
2. All three of Delaware’s members of Congress back repeal
Sen. Chris Coons, D-Del., and Sen. Lisa Blunt Rochester, D-Del., are original co-sponsors of S. 4297, a U.S. Senate bill that would repeal the credit. Rep. Sarah McBride, D-Del., is an original co-sponsor of a similar U.S. House bill, H.R. 9289.
Both bills remain in congressional committees, where they have been since their introduction in April and June, respectively, according to congressional records. The offices of Sen. Coons, Sen. Blunt Rochester and Rep. McBride did not respond to emails Friday seeking comment.
3. Thirty-one states have joined, and New Mexico is the latest
The Internal Revenue Service (IRS) named 27 states in its June 8 announcement. Republican governors signed up 26 of them.
Four more have joined since, according to the IRS list of participating states (as of Nov. 13). New Mexico, the most recent, opted in Nov. 4, according to a news release from Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham, a Democrat. Delaware’s neighbors, Maryland, New Jersey and Pennsylvania, are not on the list.
You can claim the credit either way, but only an opt-in helps Delaware students
As Table 1 below shows, two things change if Delaware opts in. They are highlighted in yellow.

Table 1: What changes if Delaware joins the federal scholarship tax credit




What a Delaware taxpayer can do
If Delaware stays out
If Delaware opts in




Claim the federal credit, up to $1,700 per person, or $3,400 for a married couple filing jointly
Yes
Yes


Give to a scholarship group in another state, if that state has opted in
Yes
Yes


Give to a scholarship group in Delaware
No
Yes


Choose to help Delaware students with the donation
No
Yes




(Note: The highlighted rows are the ones that change if Delaware opts in. Source: Section 25F of the federal tax code; Treasury Department proposed rules [Oct. 2, 2026])

The scholarships can pay for tuition, tutoring, books and other costs at “a public, private, or religious school,” under federal law. A student qualifies if the household earns up to three times the area’s median gross income. That limit applies to students, not donors. The Treasury Department estimates it covers about 95% of U.S. children.
Donors who owe little or no federal income tax can still give, but the credit only lowers tax they owe. Any unused amount carries over for up to five years.
A state lawmaker and two Delaware groups want Delaware in
Some Delawareans have already made their case to the governor. On Aug. 21, state Rep. Mike Smith, a Republican, urged Gov. Meyer to opt Delaware in, according to a Delaware House Republican Caucus news release. “We can empower parents and help students succeed without costing our state taxpayers a single penny,” Rep. Smith said in the release.
Two Delaware groups are also asking. The Catholic Diocese of Wilmington runs an online campaign titled “Make Sure Gov. Meyer Opts-In to the Federal Scholarship Tax Credit on Behalf of Students in Delaware” (undated, checked Nov. 13, 2026).
The Caesar Rodney Institute asks readers to sign a petition “urging Governor Meyer to make this new educational opportunity available to Delaware students,” according to a June 25 post on its website.
Two bills in Congress would repeal the credit, and two would take the choice away from governors
Others want Congress to end the credit before it starts. “If we want to keep improving education to build a better future for the next generation, we have to start with keeping public funds in public schools that serve all kids,” Sen. Mark Kelly, D-Ariz., the Senate bill’s sponsor, said in a news release April 15.
Delaware’s teachers union, the Delaware State Education Association, is on a list of state groups endorsing S. 4297, the U.S. Senate repeal bill, posted on Sen. Kelly’s website (undated, checked Nov. 13, 2026).
The U.S. Senate bill would end the credit for all of 2027, even if it passed partway through the year.
Republicans in the U.S. House have filed a bill that goes the other way, H.R. 10412, filed Sept. 16. It and a related U.S. Senate bill, S. 5421, would “eliminate the State opt-in requirement,” according to their official titles. That would take the decision away from governors. None of the four bills has moved past committee, according to congressional records.
Three Democratic governors said no, and lawmakers overrode them
Not every governor wanted in. In Kansas, Kentucky and North Carolina, Democratic governors vetoed state bills opting their states in, and lawmakers overrode the vetoes.
“My veto allows time for proper vetting and educated decision-making,” Kansas Gov. Laura Kelly wrote in her April 8 veto message.
The choice is Gov. Meyer’s, and the deadline is Jan. 1
Under the law, the choice “shall be made by the Governor of the State” unless state law names someone else.
For 2027, the state must sign up by Jan. 1 and then send its list of approved scholarship groups by Feb. 15, according to the Treasury Department’s temporary rules (Oct. 2, 2026).

name: VTDigger
title: Forced drug switches are burying clinics in paperwork
description:
Every insurer-driven switch to a cheaper biologic sets off new approvals and appeals, and stable patients end up paying for it.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Forced drug switches are burying clinics in paperwork.
text:
This commentary is by Teresa Fama, a practicing rheumatologist at University of Vermont Health. 
Vermont and the nation are struggling with how to reduce healthcare costs. Much of the increase is due to prescription drugs and labor, particularly as the latter makes up 65% of UVM Health’s total expenses. To highlight the compounding effect on costs from these two aspects of healthcare, let’s look at Vermont’s Act 193.
Vermont’s Act 193 requires pharmacists to dispense the lowest-priced interchangeable biologic medication to patients. These interchangeable biologic medications are biosimilars of the reference product, meaning they are highly similar with no clinically meaningful differences in safety, purity or potency — think similar to “generic.” Act 193 was enacted in 2018 when not many biosimilars were available. For example, Humira, the most prescribed biologic to treat rheumatoid arthritis, had three biosimilars approved in 2018. Today, there are 10. 
Act 193 was intended to reduce the cost of healthcare by reducing prescription drug prices. And indeed, a national analysis of Medicare data found that each new biosimilar on the market is associated with a 10% to 13% drop in the price of the brand-name drug. This analysis, however, does not consider consequences for patients and the administrative costs to the healthcare system.
Switching medication based on formulary and not on treatment failure can cause harm to patients. As the number of biologics and biosimilars has increased, insurance companies’ formularies change based on deals with pharmacy benefit managers, often resulting in patients’ having to change medication every year. As a rheumatologist who prescribes biologic medications for inflammatory autoimmune diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis, I find it’s not uncommon for patients to have tried a few biologics before finding the one that works for their condition. Once patients are on a biologic that works, having them switch again creates enormous undue stress and often patient suffering. 

READ MORE

Switching also creates high costs for healthcare clinics, and subsequently the healthcare system, due to a significant increase in prior authorizations, where the burden is on the clinic to process the paperwork. An increase in prior authorizations increases the time for clinicians to review and, in some cases, appeal a prior authorization decision; it also generates more phone calls from patients and office visits. Our clinical pharmacists and nurses, along with members of a prior authorization team, spend a significant amount of time on phone calls or processing paperwork pursuing prior authorizations and appeals. We would rather clinical pharmacists and nurses spend most of their time on patient education, clinician assistance and education, and medication protocols.
As many of these biosimilars are considered interchangeable and have been shown to work similarly to the reference product  — for example, Yuflyma is considered interchangeable with Humira, according to the Food and Drug Administration — the biosimilar should be exempt from the standard prior authorization protocols for the reference product. In other words, if Humira had been approved in the past, then a prior authorization for Yuflyma should not be required. However, we find that these drugs are treated as stand-alone and are subjected to the same cost tier, even though they are supposedly cheaper, and regularly prompt prior authorizations. 
And in some cases, we’re often told that a patient must fail on a certain number of biosimilars before they can return to the reference product. In essence, step therapy — an insurer requirement that patients try and fail on cheaper drugs before coverage of the prescribed one — has been created for biosimilars despite them being interchangeable, a process not originally intended for biosimilars.  
What can be done? The Vermont Legislature should reconsider mandating that patients switch to biosimilars in the absence of treatment failure. Treat interchangeable drugs as intended, thus barring practices such as standard prior authorization protocols and step therapy. Follow the money — investigate who is really benefiting from these practices, as it is not obvious that patients are — and quantify the administrative costs to our healthcare system.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Forced drug switches are burying clinics in paperwork.

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: Next Oklahoma governor selects Lindel Fields as chief of staff, chooses literacy director
description: OKLAHOMA CITY — While pointing to education as his top priority, Gov.-elect Mike Mazzei tapped Oklahoma’s head of public schools as his chief of staff and chose a literacy director to lead a turnaround in reading scores. Mazzei, a Republican, announced Monday he is “sending a clear message” by selecting state Superintendent Lindel Fields as […]
text:
State Superintendent Lindel Fields speaks at a press briefing Oct. 7, 2025, at the Oklahoma State Department of Education in Oklahoma City. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY — While pointing to education as his top priority, Gov.-elect Mike Mazzei tapped Oklahoma’s head of public schools as his chief of staff and chose a literacy director to lead a turnaround in reading scores.
Mazzei, a Republican, announced Monday he is “sending a clear message” by selecting state Superintendent Lindel Fields as his chief of staff. He said his incoming administration is “serious about building a world-class education system in Oklahoma” and delivering a Mississippi-style leap in elementary literacy.
The governor-elect also announced Rebecca Pellam as his statewide literacy director, having promised throughout his campaign that the role will be a day-one hire. Pellam, from the town of Goodwell in the Oklahoma Panhandle, is a literacy-focused academic consultant and tutor who has worked as a teacher, instructional coach and college professor.
“As Governor-Elect, my first announcement is about education because Oklahoma’s current education system has let down our students, parents, and teachers for far too long, and fixing our broken education system is my number one priority,” Mazzei said in a statement.
Republican Mike Mazzei gives a victory speech at the Arvest Convention Center in Tulsa on Nov. 3 after winning the general election for Oklahoma governor. (Photo by Ace Cuervo/For Oklahoma Voice)
Pellam has spent 15 years in education policy, teacher preparation and classroom teaching. Mazzei said she brings the right knowledge and experience as his administration aims to emulate Mississippi, which improved its fourth-grade reading scores by heavily investing in literacy instruction and holding back struggling readers in third grade.
Oklahoma passed a similar law this year that requires added academic support and will retain children in third grade if they score too poorly on state tests.
Pellam said she will work with “parents, teachers, and school leaders to strengthen reading instruction, give teachers the tools they need to succeed, and make sure every Oklahoma child learns to read.”
“As a teacher and literacy researcher, I have seen firsthand the challenges facing our students, parents, and teachers,” she said. “We know how to teach children to read, and we know that reading is the foundation for success in every other subject.”
As chief of staff, Fields will be central to the Mazzei administration’s goals for academic improvement in K-12 schools, the governor-elect said. 
Fields also will help lead the incoming governor’s push for growing the economy, making the state more affordable, eliminating the state income tax and abolishing property taxes for seniors and veterans.
“As State Superintendent, I’ve seen what’s possible when we support educators and keep students at the center of our decisions,” Fields said in a statement Monday. “I’m ready to help turn that commitment into results, ensuring every child has the gift of literacy, and every teacher has the support they need to succeed.”
Gov. Kevin Stitt appointed Fields, a longtime CareerTech center administrator, to lead the Oklahoma State Department of Education in October 2025 after state Superintendent Ryan Walters’ turbulent tenure ended with an early resignation from office. 
Gov. Kevin Stitt, left, introduces Lindel Fields as his appointee to the vacant state superintendent position during a news conference Oct. 2, 2025, at Eisenhower International School in Tulsa. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)
Mazzei said Fields “helped calm the waters, restore stability and put the focus back on education.”
He also chose two allies of Walters to take part in his gubernatorial transition team. 
Suzanne Reynolds voted in lockstep with Walters while serving on the state Board of Education in 2023 until Stitt appointed her to the board of regents for the University of Science and Arts of Oklahoma. Reynolds, a pharmacist from Nichols Hills, will lead the “Mazzei Higher Education Working Group,” the governor-elect announced Monday.
Mazzei also announced conservative commentator and former Oklahoma Wesleyan University President Everett Piper as part of his education transition team. It’s unclear what Piper’s specific role will be. 
Walters in 2024 chose Piper and other conservative advocates and media personalities to help rewrite Oklahoma’s academic standards for social studies. The Oklahoma Supreme Court later threw out Walters’ controversial social studies standards over violations of the state Open Meeting Act, and Fields’ administration produced a new, less-polarizing draft.
While Mazzei’s brother, Dan Mazzei, leads the transition team, former state Sen. Marty Quinn, R-Claremore, will serve as deputy chair, the team announced Monday. Quinn, an insurance agent, ran unsuccessfully for state insurance commissioner this year.
Quinn and Mazzei briefly overlapped as state senators from 2014 to 2016.
It’s not immediately clear whether the transition team is being compensated.
