text:
Advance Notice graphicNews in brief

Hertel endorsed by Michigan’s Democratic congressional delegation — After historic wins, Curtis Hertel is seeking reelection to his position as chair of the Michigan Democratic Party. On Monday, he was endorsed by the whole of the state’s incoming congressional delegation. In a news release, U.S. Reps. Debbie Dingell, Rashida Tlaib, Hillary Scholten, and Kristen McDonald Rivet; and U.S. Reps.-elect Christina Hines, Will Lawrence, Sean McCann, Donavan McKinney, and Jeremy Moss all endorsed Hertel. Gov.-elect Jocelyn Benson and U.S. Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed endorsed him last week.

 

Savit to step down as Washtenaw prosecutor in preparation for AG role —  Michigan Attorney General-elect Eli Savit will step down from his current role as Washtenaw County’s prosecutor on Dec. 4, and will focus his efforts on transition into the Michigan Department of Attorney General. Savit defeated Republican Doug Lloyd for the role in the November general election. A successor to Savit will be appointed by judges on the Washtenaw Circuit Court bench. Until a successor is appointed, Washtenaw’s Chief Assistant Prosecuting Attorney Victoria Burton-Harris will assume the role. Savit has endorsed Burton-Harris to take up the position permanently for the remainder of this vacant term.

 

Camilleri announces new additional staff as he prepares for Senate majority leader position — State Sen. Darrin Camilleri (D-Trenton), who was recently selected to become the chamber’s majority leader in January, on Monday announced several new staff roles for the upcoming term. Rachel Plawecki will serve as senior deputy chief for strategy; Alissa Small will serve as deputy chief for public affairs; and Jonathan Mason, current chief of staff to Camilleri, will serve as deputy chief of staff overseeing operations.

 

Michigan AG special litigation chief receives national consumer advocate nod — Michael Moody, the special litigation division chief with the Michigan Department of Attorney General was honored by the National Association of State Utility Consumer Advocates with its Manifold Award. The association consists of 63 consumer advocates in 45 states, representing the interests of utility consumers before the courts and state and federal regulators. NASUCA also has advocates in Puerto Rico, Jamaica, and the District of Columbia. Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel, in a statement, called Moody “a valued member of our office for decades, and his expansive work has been absolutely essential in recent years, during an especially challenging period in Michigan history.”

 
ICYMI

Slotkin ‘seriously’ considering presidential bid, says decision could come soon — U.S. Sen. Elissa Slotkin said she is giving serious thought to making a run for president in 2028, as Democrats debate the party’s future leadership following the midterm elections. “I’m looking at it seriously, but I haven’t made any decisions, whether it’s me or somebody else,” the Michigan Democrat said Friday at the “What’s Next” conference in Denver, hosted by the group Majority Democrats.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: Commentary: NC GOP leaders kneecap state and local government on their way out the door
description: While the magnitude of recent Democratic gains in North Carolina state legislative races ended up being much larger than what even many optimistic partisans had predicted and hoped for, the general trend was not, in the end, surprising. Ever since primary voters sent veteran Senate Leader Phil Berger packing last March, it’s felt increasingly as […]
text:
North Carolina voters passed three constitutional amendments on Nov. 3, 2026 to authorize lawmakers to impose limits on local governments’ power to raise property taxes, cap the state income tax, and require photo ID for all voters — not just those voting in person. (Photo: Clayton Henkel/NC Newsline) While the magnitude of recent Democratic gains in North Carolina state legislative races ended up being much larger than what even many optimistic partisans had predicted and hoped for, the general trend was not, in the end, surprising.
Ever since primary voters sent veteran Senate Leader Phil Berger packing last March, it’s felt increasingly as if state Republicans have been running on fumes and that change was in the air. Between the strange and inexplicable divisions that prevented large legislative majorities from producing timely state budgets, the whiffs of scandal that have plagued several prominent party members, and the massive and debilitating weight of the chaotic Trump presidency, it was clear that the GOP would be losing seats this fall.
Unfortunately for our state and its future, however, it’s clear that Republican leaders read their impending comeuppance in the tea leaves well. And that fact helps explain one of the most regrettable results of the election: the approval of two destructive amendments to the state constitution on the subject of tax policy.
For more than 15 years, Republican legislative leaders have taken repeated steps to transform what had been a moderately progressive state with decent-to-above-average public services and structures and a much-admired public school system into a threadbare laboratory for what one of their most visible and reactionary national activists once described as “drowning [government] in the bathtub.”
And make no mistake; they made significant headway in this ghoulish endeavor. Thanks to repeated and regressive tax cuts that disproportionately benefitted the super-rich, total state and local government funding as a share of the state’s economy has, quite remarkably, plummeted by more than a third during the GOP reign. 
Think about that for a moment. Is it any wonder that our once widely envied public schools, higher education systems, and other middle class support structures are now relegated to the backwaters of national rankings? Or that pressure to rely on regressive fees, sales and excise taxes continue to grow? In comparison, Elon Musk’s destructive DOGE assault from last year looks like child’s play.
Amazingly, however, such widespread carnage and expanded inequality were insufficient to satisfy the ideological bloodlust that infected much of the right-wing establishment. And so it is that this past summer, with the demise of their longtime majorities coming into focus, Republican legislative leaders rammed through the latest in a long run of simplistic tax proposals – in this case, a pair of constitutional amendments — that are designed to lock in actions of the last decade-and-a-half and greatly debilitate future state leaders when it comes to undoing the damage.
The first of the amendments caps the state’s fairest and most progressive tax – the state income tax — at a rate less half of where it stood for wealthy North Carolinians and corporations when the Republicans took control of the legislature in 2011. And while those higher rates have already been flattened and lowered below the new cap via legislation over a period of several years, a constitutional limit establishes a huge roadblock to raising new revenue in a way that would require the rich and big corporations to pay something closer to their fair share. 
The second amendment seeks to inflict similar impacts on local government – the place to which so many responsibilities have fallen as state government structures have crumbled – by empowering the General Assembly to meddle with and limit local property tax rates. 
And while numerous fiscal policy experts repeatedly explained and warned of the long-term folly of both proposals – especially in an era in which natural disasters like Hurricane Helene continue to multiply and federal aid of all kinds has been slashed – the notion that voters would reject either amendment absent any kind of well-funded opposition or real explanation on the ballot of the state’s actual fiscal plight was never a serious possibility.
Indeed, given this backdrop, the fact that both passed by only 3-2 margins is a rather surprising outcome.
So, what happens now? Can and will Democratic leaders find a path to a place where they can commence rebuilding North Carolina’s battered state government? 
The guess here is that for now, even if they somehow were to obtain control of the state Senate by eking out a win on the closely contested race in Robeson County, Democrats will, like their colleagues in Washington, have to focus in the near term on staunching the bleeding. 
This will mean, for the foreseeable future, working to shift some current funding priorities by, for instance, winding down the state’s costly, discriminatory, unaccountable and destructive school voucher program, and working to build the kind of public awareness that, in the long run, might allow future legislatures to revive and restore a progressive state income tax.
In other words, Republicans have succeeded in kneecapping state and local government on their way out of power. And, for now, the best Democrats can do is try and fashion a fiscal splint that will give both institutions the chance to gradually heal.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: State energy and environment secretary leaving Healey administration
authors: Colin A. Young I State House News Service
description: The transition comes as energy costs are a top concern for residents, the state is struggling to maintain momentum for its policy-backed clean energy transition, and amid debate over whether the state can meet its midcentury decarbonization targets or should backtrack from them.
text:
THERE’S MORE TURNOVER in Gov. Maura Healey’s Cabinet as the governor gears up for a second term.
Energy and Environmental Affairs Secretary Rebecca Tepper announced Monday that she will depart the administration after almost four years on the job, giving Healey an opportunity to pick a new point person for energy affordability, one of the governor’s second-term priority issues. It also means a transition at a time when energy costs are a top concern for residents, the state is struggling to maintain momentum for its policy-backed clean energy transition, and amid debate over whether the state can meet its midcentury decarbonization targets or should backtrack from them.
Tepper’s last day is December 4, the administration said, and Healey will appoint Undersecretary for Environment Stephanie Cooper to serve as interim secretary until a permanent successor is named.
Healey called Tepper a “national leader” in the field.
“Secretary Tepper has been a strong advocate for Massachusetts communities, working to protect our natural resources, build resilience to climate change, and advance environmental justice. She has also been a leader among leaders by guiding a northeast coalition of states and Canadian provinces on energy production and transmission. She helped move forward major clean energy projects, including Vineyard Wind and the NECEC transmission line, despite significant federal opposition, and cut red tape to bring more solar and storage onto our grid,” Healey said.
Tepper was chief of the energy and environment bureau in the attorney general’s office under Healey and she joined the administration from the get-go almost four years ago. Tepper’s departure follows last week’s exit by Climate Chief Melissa Hoffer, another day-one Cabinet member for Healey.
“I’ve been proud to serve Governor Healey for over a decade, working together to keep ratepayer costs down, standing up for Massachusetts’ energy independence, and protecting our beautiful state from climate change and environmental harm,” Tepper said. She added, “In my time in this role, I’ve been laser-focused on building clean energy infrastructure and safeguarding natural resources. I always say the best time to start a new energy project is today. I believe Massachusetts is well-positioned to continue to advance our energy independence in the years to come.”
Before joining the attorney general’s office in 2015, Tepper worked for four years as general counsel for the Department of Public Utilities and was director of the Massachusetts Energy Facilities Siting Board from 2009 through 2011, according to her LinkedIn profile. She worked in the private sector for 15 years as a partner at Rubin and Rudman before joining state government.
Cooper has held a slate of senior roles under the Executive Office of Energy and Environmental Affairs umbrella, having overseen regulatory and policy efforts for clean air and water, solid waste and climate change; guided about $55 million in annual conservation and park development investments; and as DCR acting commissioner led a strategic evaluation that invested in state parks and strengthened core services. She worked in New York City government before moving to Massachusetts.
Asked Thursday about retaining Cabinet members in the administration’s second term, and if any secretaries have been asked to make commitments to stay on, Lt. Gov. Kim Driscoll said, “We definitely have an agenda. We want to deliver for the next four years. We want to make sure we have the right people to do that.”
Healey has experienced significant Cabinet turnover since taking office in 2023, losing the majority of its leadership ahead of this month’s reelection. Administration and Finance Secretary Matthew Gorzkowicz, Technology Services and Security Secretary Jason Snyder, and Labor and Workforce Development Secretary Lauren Jones are the only original Healey Cabinet members who remain.

name: Source New Mexico
title: Thousands of New Mexicans could lose food assistance under federal proposal, state says
description: Thousands of New Mexicans could lose food assistance under a new federal proposal that would change a provision of the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, according to the state Health Care Authority.
text:
New Mexico lawmakers, officials and food banks voiced their opposition to a Nov. 11, 2026, federal proposal that would end food assistance eligibility for an additional 6 million Americans. (Photo of food distribution at The Food Depot in Santa Fe in 2025 by Julia Goldberg/Source NM)Thousands of New Mexicans could lose food assistance under a new federal proposal that would change a provision of the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, according to the state Health Care Authority. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The proposal, which the U.S. Department of Agriculture made public last week, would end provisions — known as categorical eligibility — that automatically make households eligible for SNAP if they also meet requirements for the Temporary Assistance for Needy Families program.
According to USDA’s analysis, the proposed changes would cut SNAP benefits by more than $45 billion over five years and remove about 17% of SNAP beneficiaries from the program — or 6.3 million people — beginning in 2029, the first year the rule would be in full effect. The department estimates that approximately 1.7 million children would no longer be categorically eligible for free school meals with the rule change. The agency is taking public comment on the proposal until Dec. 12. 
New Mexico Health Care Authority spokesperson Timothy Fowler told Source NM in a statement that the rule could “result in thousands of New Mexicans losing food assistance.”
“The proposed eligibility rule would fundamentally change how New Mexico administers SNAP, with significant consequences for both vulnerable households and state operations,” Fowler said. “The HCA is currently assessing the eligibility change impacts to New Mexico and preparing to submit our comments.”
On Monday, U.S. Sen. Ben Ray Luján (D-N.M.), along with 11 Democratic senators, sent a letter to USDA Secretary Brooke Rollins urging the agency to withdraw the proposal. 
“Children should not go hungry, seniors should not have to spend down their savings to afford groceries and working families should not lose assistance while they are still struggling to make ends meet,” the senators wrote, adding that the proposed program change would put more families at risk of food insecurity while making the program more challenging for states to administer.
Jill Dixon, executive director of The Food Depot, told Source NM that after previous SNAP cuts from the Trump administration’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act in 2025, along with rising costs, New Mexico food banks have seen food distributions increase by 70% across the state. The Food Depot helps distribute food for northern New Mexico. 
‘It’s shameful’: New Mexico veterans increasingly turn to food banks after SNAP rollbacks

“We have grave concerns about further changes to the program that would further affect eligibility and create more confusion,” Dixon said. 
Katy Anderson, the vice president of strategy, partnerships and advocacy of Roadrunner Food Bank, echoed those concerns, telling Source NM in an email that the proposal will increase food insecurity for New Mexicans and that the 30-day window to provide public comment “minimizes the time that communities can speak to how this rule change will impact millions of Americans and thousands of New Mexicans.”
State Rep. Elizabeth “Liz” Thomson (D-Albuquerque), chair of the Legislature’s Health and Human Services Committee, also criticized the USDA proposal, saying it amounts to “cruelty.” Referencing the midterm elections Nov. 3, widely seen as a rebuke to the Trump administration,  she said: “If the elections didn’t show them that people are hurting and not liking what you’re doing, it just baffles me.”
Last year, Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham called a special legislative session to extend food benefits during the government shutdown. Thomson said she anticipates the Legislature will step up again as needed.
“I think our leadership has shown that we, as the Legislature, will do whatever we can to make sure that New Mexicans are not kicked off their Medicaid, that they have enough food,” she said. “I am 100% certain that we will do everything that’s within our power and within our budget to take care of people.”

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: NJ challenges $11M verdict against cop who arrested stroke victim for drunk driving
description: A NJ state trooper whose roadside blunder left a motorist permanently disabled just made a mistake and should get immunity, the state says.
text:
A New Jersey state trooper whose roadside blunder left a motorist permanently disabled just made a mistake and should get immunity, the state says. (Photo by Dana DiFilippo / New Jersey Monitor)New Jersey went to court Monday to ask a state appellate panel to vacate an $11.3 million jury verdict against a rookie state trooper whose mishandling of a minor car accident left a Jersey City woman permanently disabled.
The state’s attorneys argued that a trial judge got it wrong when he refused to give Trooper Jennifer Albuja immunity for failing to recognize that Cheryl Rhines hit a guardrail on her way to work in 2017 because she had a stroke — not because she was driving drunk, as Albuja wrongly deduced.
Cops make mistakes, and Albuja reasonably and sincerely suspected Rhines’ disorientation, slurred speech, and inability to stand suggested inebriation and warranted arrest, attorney Michael T.G. Long argued.
Long asked the three-judge panel to vacate the January 2025 verdict and grant immunity to Albuja, who’d graduated from the police academy the year before she responded to the call for motorist aid on Route 78.
But Dennis M. Donnelly, Rhines’ attorney, urged the panel to uphold the verdict, saying Albuja’s deliberate indifference, negligence, and failure to follow police training defeat any immunity claim.
Albuja acknowledged she had been trained on stroke symptoms while in the police academy and ignored the classic signs of a stroke that Rhines exhibited, including noticeable, one-sided facial drooping, difficulty speaking, and loss of control of her right leg and arm, Donnelly said. Dashcam footage showed Rhines repeatedly requested help and told Albuja: “I think I’m having a heart attack,” according to court briefs.
The trooper instead hauled Rhines to the state police’s Somerville barracks and shackled her to a bench in a holding cell there, delaying medical care for hours, Donnelly said. The delay led to a brain bleed and left Rhines unable to communicate and in need of lifelong caretaking, he added.
Officers also learn at the academy that even people suspected of crimes or those who get arrested are entitled to medical treatment, Donnelly added. Besides getting quicker stroke care, taking Rhines to the hospital 10 minutes away would have proved or disproved Albuja’s suspicions of intoxication, he said.
Donnelly told the judges that an emergency room physician who testified at trial said: “Every day of the week, I’m an emergency room doctor, and police bring in people and ask me, are they drunk or are they sick?”
That argument seemed persuasive to Judge Jack Sabatino, one of the judges on the panel.
“If the concern of the officer was the preservation of evidence because of the dissipation of blood alcohol in the body, if the plaintiff had gotten immediate attention at a hospital, they could have done a blood draw, right? That would be probably the most reliable and most efficient way to preserve the evidence. Taking her to the hospital did not foreclose the preservation of evidence, right?” Sabatino asked the state’s attorney.
“It did not, Your Honor,” Long acknowledged.
Donnelly urged the panel to uphold the jury’s verdict, warning a new trial risked higher damages. The jury initially announced a $19.1 million verdict but reduced it, recognizing that Albuja did not cause Rhines’ stroke and attributing just 60% of her injury to the trooper’s conduct.
Long asked the judges to toss the verdict, order a new trial, or reduce damages.
If they decide a new trial is warranted, he said, they should require more thorough jury instructions about immunity as well as the differences between pain and suffering and emotional distress. Jurors had awarded Rhines $3 million for pain and suffering, and another $3.6 million for emotional distress. If they uphold the verdict, they should either reduce those damages or order a new trial just on damages, Long said.
“They need to be advised to not duplicate for the same harm twice,” Long said. “That’s a very uncontroversial statement in the law. And then here, it’s just so obvious that pain and suffering and emotional distress have a tendency in the human mind to sound similar and overlap.”
Monday’s arguments at the Richard J. Hughes Justice Complex in Trenton were the second time the state tried to overturn the verdict. The trial judge rejected the state’s bid for a new trial or reduction in damages in April 2025. It’s unclear how soon the appellate panel will issue a ruling.
The case has the potential to reshape whether police officers who err on the job get held accountable in New Jersey.
Cops here and around the country accused of brutality or blunders have long relied on immunity, a controversial legal doctrine social justice advocates have tried to restrict or abolish, to dodge civil or criminal liability.
Immunity is meant to empower officers to act decisively without worrying a mistake will incite a lawsuit — as long as they act in good faith and follow the law.
“We’re trying to take into account the confusing and often complicated situations that police officers and often public employees generally find themselves in, but police officers specifically, where signs can point multiple different ways and a determination has to be made on what the officer sees, saw, and believed,” Long said.
Immunity also protects taxpayers from unpredictable, crushing verdicts, Albuja’s attorneys had further argued in court briefs.
But critics contend it has allowed inept and violent cops to trample people’s civil rights with impunity, depriving victims of accountability.

name: National
title: Americans increasingly see crime declining, but fears of scams persist, survey finds
description: Americans are increasingly optimistic about the nation’s crime trends, with perceptions of rising crime hovering near historic lows even as nearly half the country still believes crime is getting worse, according to a new Gallup poll. Forty-six percent of U.S. adults say crime has increased nationally over the past year, down sharply from 77% in […]
text:
Members of the New York Police Department bomb squad and agents with the FBI conduct a criminal investigation in New York City. Americans’ perceptions of rising crime are near historic lows, according to a new Gallup poll, even as concerns about financial scams and identity theft persist. (Photo by Ryan Murphy/Getty Images)Americans are increasingly optimistic about the nation’s crime trends, with perceptions of rising crime hovering near historic lows even as nearly half the country still believes crime is getting worse, according to a new Gallup poll.
Forty-six percent of U.S. adults say crime has increased nationally over the past year, down sharply from 77% in 2023 and little changed from 49% last year. The figure has been lower only once since Gallup began tracking national perceptions in 1989.
Americans are even less likely to believe crime is rising in their own communities. About a third, 33%, say local crime has increased over the past year, among the lowest readings in more than five decades of polling.
The findings, based on an Oct. 1-19 survey, come as federal crime statistics show substantial declines in violence across the country.
States, cities move to ban cryptocurrency kiosks as scams mount

National crime data released earlier this year by the FBI showed violent crime fell 9.3% in 2025 from the previous year, the largest annual drop since the agency began tracking national estimates in 1936. The murder rate also plunged 18.5% to 4.1 killings per 100,000 people, tying its lowest recorded level in nearly 90 years. The rate matches those recorded in 1955 and 1956.
The decline extends beyond crimes reported to police. Preliminary findings from the federal Bureau of Justice Statistics’ National Crime Victimization Survey, which captures nonfatal crimes whether or not they were reported to law enforcement, showed that violent victimization, excluding simple assault, fell 25% in 2025. Aggravated assaults dropped 31%, while robberies declined 27%.
Still, Americans’ perceptions of crime have not entirely caught up with those trends.
The divide between national and local perceptions has persisted for decades, with Americans consistently more likely to believe crime is increasing across the country than to think it’s rising in their own neighborhoods.
That gap has narrowed considerably in recent years. In 2022, a record 56% of Americans said crime was rising locally, compared with 33% today.
Political differences also have diminished. Just two years ago, Republicans and Democrats were sharply divided over whether national crime was increasing. Those differences narrowed last year, and Republicans’ perceptions of rising national crime fell another 15 percentage points in the latest survey.
The poll also highlights a shift in what Americans fear most: Financial crimes continue to generate considerably more concern than violent offenses.
Seven in 10 Americans say they worry at least occasionally about becoming victims of identity theft, while 55% worry about being tricked by scammers into sending money or providing access to their financial accounts. Those were the only two offenses among 10 surveyed that worried a majority of respondents.
Violent, property crime victimization rates fell in 2025, federal data shows

By comparison, 41% worry about having their vehicle stolen or broken into, while the same share worry about a school-age child being physically harmed at school. About 37% fear a home burglary, and 22% worry about being murdered.
Concerns also vary considerably by age, income and gender.
Older Americans are particularly worried about financial crimes. Among adults 55 and older, 77% express concern about identity theft, compared with 52% of adults younger than 35.
Younger adults, meanwhile, report greater concern about most violent crimes. Women are also more likely than men to worry about all eight nonfinancial crimes surveyed, including sexual assault, which worries 40% of women compared with 13% of men.
Lower-income Americans consistently express greater concern about violent crime than higher-income adults. Nearly a third of adults earning less than $50,000 annually worry about being murdered, compared with 13% of those earning at least $100,000.
Although fears surrounding many crimes have eased from their recent peaks in 2022 and 2023, concerns about hate crimes, school violence and identity theft remain elevated. Worry about sexual assault also increased over the past year.
The findings underscore a persistent disconnect between improving national crime statistics and Americans’ concerns about their personal safety, particularly as financial fraud and certain forms of violence continue to weigh heavily on the public.
Stateline reporter Amanda Watford can be reached at awatford@stateline.org.

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Top Indiana lawmakers agree affordability is a top issue, but no agreement yet on action
description: Cost of living concerns were a top reason why Indiana voters made a big swing toward Democrats with this fall’s election.
text:
Indiana Senate Democratic leader Shelli Yoder, second from left, speaks alongside, from left, House Democratic leader Phil GiaQuinta, House Speaker-elect Ben Smaltz, Senate President Pro Tem-elect Chris Garten and Indiana Chamber of Commerce President Vanessa Green Sinders during a chamber-sponsored legislative preview event on Monday, Nov. 16, 2026. (Photo by Tom Davies/Indiana Capital Chronicle)Cost of living concerns were a top reason why Indiana voters made a big swing toward Democrats with this fall’s election. Just how the Republicans who still control the General Assembly respond will be a big question for the 2027 legislative session.
GOP and Democratic legislative leaders speaking during an Indiana Chamber of Commerce event Monday shared affordability as a major topic — without consensus on specific steps for the state to take.
For instance, Senate Democratic leader Shelli Yoder of Bloomington said “a good place to start” would be repealing the state 7% sales tax on residential utility bills.
Indiana House Speaker-elect Ben Smaltz speaks with reporters on Monday, Nov. 16, 2026. (Photo by Tom Davies/Indiana Capital Chronicle)
Republican House Speaker-elect Ben Smaltz of Auburn, however, immediately pointed to a projected $700 million loss of state tax revenue that would result.
“If we do that, do taxes somewhere else go up?” Smaltz said. “That’s the unintended consequence.”
Legislators meet Tuesday for their Organization Day session, during which Republicans are set to install Smaltz as the new House speaker and Sen. Chris Garten of Charlestown in the Senate’s top position as president pro tem. They will then return in January for their session lasting until late April.
After an election campaign in which many Democratic candidates targeted worries over large data center projects, House Democratic leader Phil GiaQuinta of Fort Wayne said his caucus would push to end the utility sales tax exemption that data centers now can receive.
GiaQuinta described such a step as a matter of fairness if families must continue paying the 7% sales tax on their utility bills.
“If we’re looking for more revenue, then you can end the sales tax exemption for data centers,” he said.
Cost of living by far top worry in poll
Results of a mid-October poll conducted for the Indiana Chamber show that cost of living was the top issue for 44% of the state’s voters — up from 29% a year ago. 
The next highest concern among voters was taxes and government spending at 12%.
Republican Gov. Mike Braun has tried to be aggressive on such affordability concerns, with his 2025 push for a rollback of homeowner property taxes that wasn’t embraced by GOP lawmakers and his overhaul of the Indiana Utility Regulatory Commission that sets electricity rates for most homes and businesses.
Garten acknowledged the clamor among voters for action on cost of living matters.
“One of the things we highlighted at almost every doorstep that I was on is property taxes, gas, fuel costs and utility costs,” he said. “These are real issues, these are real kitchen table issues.”
This month’s election results were the worst for Indiana Republicans in decades as Democrats won the secretary of state and state comptroller races, along with gaining 16 Indiana House seats and five state Senate seats.
Those give Republicans reduced majorities of 54-46 in the House and 35-15 in the Senate.
Top Senate Democrat “encouraged” by Republican response
Yoder argued that Republicans had ignored affordability issues for many years and “two weeks ago Tuesday, Hoosiers finally said, ‘Enough.’”
She told reporters after Tuesday’s event that she was glad Republicans were responding.
“Whether it’s healthcare affordability, childcare access and affordability, utility bills and those electric bills affordability, these are pains that Hoosiers are feeling each and every week,” Yoder said. “We’ll have to see how it actually falls into place. But we’re encouraged that we are hearing this from our Republican counterparts.”
Smaltz on Monday named leaders of the 21 House committees for the upcoming session, including 15 new chairs of those panels.
“I’ve given them all the same charge about affordability and how I want them looking at policy decisions through the lens of the people back home, the people whose doors that we are knocking on,” he said.

name: VTDigger
title: State help for flood survivors was disorganized and slow to arrive. For some, it never came.
description:
“A lot of folks simply were out of luck.” 
Read the story on VTDigger here:  State help for flood survivors was disorganized and slow to arrive. For some, it never came..
text:
This story is part of The Coming Storm, a yearlong investigation by VTDigger, in partnership with FRONTLINE (PBS), into Vermont’s ability to help communities recover from natural disasters.


VERMONT — In November 2025, almost a year and a half after deadly floods hit communities across northern Vermont, state disaster case managers scrambled to contact almost 1,700 households. Their program was running behind schedule, and their window to help people was closing.
“I know it’s been 17 months since the disaster, but our goal is to make sure everyone gets the support they need,” workers were supposed to tell survivors, according to a call script. 
State disaster case managers help survivors get as much federal aid and other funding as possible to pay for home repairs and relocation costs. But by the time Vermont’s program reached most people, recovery resources were dwindling. 
“A lot of folks simply were out of luck by the time we came in,” said Charlotte Hackett, one of four former state employees who spoke to VTDigger about the program. 
Charlotte Hackett worked as an emergency management support specialist for the Agency of Human Services until her contract with the state ended in September 2026. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger
Similar problems had come up before. 
A year-long VTDigger investigation found that Vermont’s programs aimed at helping the most vulnerable flood survivors failed to provide many with timely assistance. Following severe floods in 2023, the state’s case management program was slow to reach people and struggled to coordinate with community-based recovery groups – delaying much-needed assistance. After floods came again one year later, officials tried to fix earlier missteps and took a different approach, but the problems worsened.   
The first challenge was figuring out how to reach storm survivors. In 2025, Vermont’s disaster recovery leaders did not use a key federal data set to locate them — for 10 months.
Although more than 2,000 households applied for aid from the Federal Emergency Management Agency in 2024, state case managers helped 70, Vermont officials said. The program would have likely helped more survivors if officials had been better prepared and acted more quickly, according to interviews with former employees and documents reviewed by VTDigger. 
Poor communication from the state left community-led recovery groups confused, frustrated and overwhelmed, according to interviews with recovery groups and a state “after-action” report obtained by VTDigger through a public records request.  The report was not publicly distributed, but was shared among state government officials in December 2025.  
VTDigger’s findings are also based on emails between Vermont officials, and interviews with current and former state employees, emergency management experts and storm survivors. 

Read more of The Coming Storm series in partnership with FRONTLINE (PBS)

The problems with Vermont’s case management system come as climate change is bringing more frequent and intense rain to the state, and as President Donald Trump’s administration has reduced federal support for disasters, requiring states to manage more of the recovery. 
After the delays in 2023, state officials tried to help survivors faster when flooding returned in 2024, opting to use a different contractor, said Doug Farnham, Vermont’s governor-appointed chief recovery officer. But VTDigger found that the contractor didn’t speed up the process.
“Not one single Vermonter was turned away and not provided case management assistance” in 2024, Farnham said. He added that those who didn’t know about the program may not have received support. 
Many storm survivors told VTDigger they did not know how the state’s disaster recovery system worked, or which government agencies might offer help. 
After the storms, many relied on volunteers, donations and their savings. To pay for shelter and repairs, some took on new debt, went into foreclosure and took money out of retirement funds. Some lived in unsafe housing.
Jessica Farrar’s mobile home in Cavendish was pulled “off its piers” and partially “sunk into the water” after the 2023 flood, according to her FEMA aid application. 
Jessica and Aaron Farrar’s mobile home was “not safe to live in,” a FEMA’s housing inspector determined. She and her family stayed in the home which needed an estimated $60,000 in repairs — money they didn’t have. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger
“We did not have the money to pay rent to live somewhere else while we’re trying to fix our house,” Farrar said in September 2026. “We lived in our house even though it was deemed unsafe.”
FEMA aid covered a fraction of the repair costs. She wasn’t aware that more help was available from the state – and no state case managers contacted her, she said.
Another person in St. Johnsbury had to walk “a great distance” up the “mini mountain” to her home after her mile-long driveway had been washed out, according to an email exchange, which VTDigger obtained through a records request. She had four children, was “very pregnant” and couldn’t afford to pay the estimated $20,000 to $50,000 for repairs. She had missed the deadline to apply for FEMA aid. 
“I desperately need help,” she wrote in an email to state workers in July 2025, more than a year after the flood washed out her driveway. 
Sarah Henshaw, who leads a community recovery group in Lamoille County, said that before the floods, some families who had been “financially stable and able to pay their bills, and might have had a small savings or small retirement, and now are in debt by tens of thousands of dollars, living in a place that’s unsafe, and living right on the edge.”

ABOUT THE COMING STORM: For a year, VTDigger, in partnership with FRONTLINE (PBS), has reported on Vermont’s capacity to manage recovery from natural disasters. VTDigger obtained emails from state officials regarding assistance to flood survivors, reviewed state and federal disaster funding and risk-reduction plans, examined federal proposals to change the Federal Emergency Management Agency, and analyzed FEMA data on disaster aid, with assistance from Eric Sagara of Big Local News at Stanford University. VTDigger also interviewed flood survivors, frontline recovery workers, state and local officials, lawmakers, emergency management experts, scientists, and social services providers, among others, for this series.
A slow launch 
FEMA often funds case management programs after natural disasters so that states can pay the salaries of case managers and other administrators who work to help survivors recover.
When the 2023 flood hit, Vermont’s Agency of Human Services hadn’t run such a program since Tropical Storm Irene in 2011, which meant few employees had program experience, according to Jason Gosselin, Emergency Management Director for the state’s Agency of Human Services.
In 2023, FEMA provided Vermont $3.3 million, and the state contracted with Capstone Community Action, a nonprofit social service agency, to run the program. But it took eight months for the program to start helping survivors, said Liz Scharf, who helped lead case management at Capstone. Due to the organization’s low pay scale, they “hired less experienced staff who needed more training and supervision,” she said.
Capstone “could not launch quickly enough to meet early survivor needs,” according to the state’s after-action report.
Capstone used FEMA data to find survivors, but – due to confidentiality rules – case managers could not share that information with local volunteers already on the ground, said Sue Minter, who led Capstone at the time. (Minter’s husband, David Goodman, is a columnist for VTDigger.) It was “extremely, extremely frustrating — and enraging in some cases to other organizations.”
“Unclear roles, turf friction, inconsistent referrals, and uneven partner capacity” led to “fragmented and uncoordinated long-term recovery efforts,” after the 2023 flood, according to the report. The delays “left communities relying on informal or ad hoc networks.”
More than 6,000 households applied for FEMA aid after the 2023 floods, which were among the most destructive in Vermont’s history. By the time the program closed, it had opened 404 cases and secured more than $550,000 for survivors. 
Sue Minter, the former executive director of Capstone Community Action, speaks at a press conference in Barre in March 2020. Minter led the nonprofit when it provided case management services to flood survivors after the 2023 flood. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger
Capstone estimated it spent nearly $1.9 million in FEMA funding and, unable to fill all of its open case manager positions, sent the remaining $1.4 million back to the federal agency. The program secured more than $550,000 for survivors.
When another round of deadly flooding hit the state exactly one year later, the state approached Capstone about running another program, and Capstone said “they did not believe they had the capacity,” Farnham said. 
After the July 2024 floods, while state leaders pushed to reach survivors faster, the program was slower from the beginning. FEMA approved funding on January 24, 2025, seven months after the flood, and case managers didn’t reach survivors for months.
Then, the state hired Guidehouse, a for-profit global consulting firm that Farnham said had helped Vermont run more than 300 programs, including during the coronavirus pandemic. The firm had for years contracted with other states such as New York to manage federal disaster grants. 
Guidehouse subcontracted with the New England Annual Conference of the United Methodist Church, which hired case managers. The program was called Disaster Recovery – A United Methodist Ministries, or DRUMM.
The state realized Guidehouse was charging more than it had expected. FEMA warned Vermont that too much of its funding was going to the contractor instead of services for survivors. 
In response, Farnham and his team met with Guidehouse to discuss adjustments “so that we can get more money to disaster survivors,” he told lawmakers in a November 2025 hearing.
Even so, Hackett, the former state employee, said she felt that more of the resources the state spent on Guidehouse could have been used to help storm survivors. 
Guidehouse did not respond to multiple requests for comment. 
A looming deadline
One of the 2024 program’s biggest challenges was finding the survivors who needed help.
Farnham said that the state had raised awareness about the case management program through “broad-based communications” such as press conferences and community events, through community recovery groups and through contacting people who called a 2-1-1 hotline to report damage.
But many survivors did not know about the hotline, according to the after-action report. Many of those who did reach the line did not know that they also had to apply to FEMA to get aid –  and, if rejected, to appeal. 
FEMA also provides states a list of disaster survivors who file for federal aid, and state officials had access to that list. Federal rules limit access to prevent widely sharing individuals’ personal information.  
Doug Farnham, Vermont’s chief recovery officer, said that, of the storm survivors who requested help from the state, “not one single Vermonter was turned away and not provided case management assistance.” Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger
State officials decided to rely on 2-1-1 data and “not utilize the [FEMA data] as the primary source of data for outreach,” said Gosselin, Emergency Management Director for the Vermont Agency of Human Services.
Ultimately, those damage reports missed many Vermonters who needed help. 
After the 2024 flood, FEMA had authorized three people working on the program to see its survivor data: two state employees and the executive director of DRUMM, which was conducting the outreach. In the fall of 2025, DRUMM’s director took medical retirement. The state could not authorize another worker to access the data until the federal government shutdown ended in November, Gosselin said.
But, in an email, a FEMA spokesperson told VTDigger that Vermont could have authorized up to five people to “ensure continuous access” to its list. 
“FEMA wants these services delivered,” said Hackett, the former state employee. “That’s why they granted the award.” 
Hackett said it was frustrating that state officials didn’t try harder to use the FEMA information. Their approach, she said, was, “‘Well, we can’t use what you’ve given us because you’re so unhelpful, and we’re just going to make our own tool.’” 
Meanwhile, many Vermonters who had waited more than a year for help faced dire situations. 
In September 2024, the state’s recovery office intervened when they learned that a 72-year-old disabled veteran, whose home was flooded in 2023 and 2024, had been “sleeping in a construction trailer with no running water, without power, has no way to cook or refrigerate food items,”  according to an email from Kristen Gadbois, who worked for the state’s recovery office.  “Essentially, he has been homeless for over a year,” she wrote. 
Finally, in November, 2025, case managers gained access to FEMA’s data. State officials used the list as a back-up “just to make sure we didn’t miss anybody,” Gosselin said.
They saw that around 1,700 households who had applied for FEMA aid were not on the 2-1-1  list and still needed to be contacted.
Meanwhile a FEMA deadline loomed. Survivors who had been denied aid would need to appeal no later than February 21, 2026. 
Case managers kicked into overdrive through a massive outreach to make people aware of state support and getting applicants to file FEMA appeals before the deadline.
Farnham called that outreach “redundant,” and said it was “another layer at the end to try to make sure we helped as many people as possible.” 
“We had been communicating constantly over the course of that 17 months,” he said. “So to say that we haven’t contacted those households — did we pick up the phone and call every one of them individually? No, but you can’t have that direct communication be the only way you get the word out, right?”
But one former employee said that, without the November outreach, the program would not have been able to contact many survivors. It was the only reason the state’s program opened most of its cases, they said.
The former employee spoke on condition of anonymity due to concerns about retribution. 
‘I cannot compromise my integrity’
By design, case management programs take a long time to start up. By the time they’re active, much of the work is focused on people, often with low incomes, who are stuck, and “do not have the capacity to start on their own repairs,” Scharf said.  
In 2025, case managers rushed to reach those people. 
“We will be triaging our outreach efforts,” Misty Grassley, executive director of the case management program, wrote in an email, which VTDigger obtained through a public records request. 
Survivors with “critical needs” were to be assigned case managers immediately. These people were “lacking a safe, sanitary, and secure environment — for example, if the structure is unstable, there is no heat, the survivor is disabled, and/or they are exposed to mold and have compromised immune systems,” Grassley wrote in the email. Others could wait as long as 4 to 6 weeks before they heard from a case manager again.

Read more of The Coming Storm series in partnership with FRONTLINE (PBS)

Case managers “reached up to 800 households during the holidays,” Gosselin said. 
Kurt Thoma, who was a construction coordinator for DRUMM, helped storm survivors access resources they were not aware existed. One of those survivors was in a “dire” situation, “and without immediate foundation repairs, a portion of her home would have collapsed,” Thoma wrote in a text message.
He helped her appeal her FEMA claim and apply for assistance from the Vermont Community Foundation. She received a total of $50,000, enough “to repair her damaged foundation and save her home” he said.  
VTDigger could not independently verify those details. 
In total, after the scramble to reach people, case managers secured about $673,000 in financial support from FEMA and philanthropic funds for 70 households — more than Capstone had secured for the 404 households it helped.
But Allissa Vigil, a former emergency management support specialist in the state’s Agency of Human Services, was frustrated that the program didn’t accomplish more. She resigned on February 4, 2026, pointing to the program’s leadership – “internal conditions rather than external factors,” she wrote in a resignation letter. 
She wrote, “My first and foremost priority and loyalty is to the community, and I cannot compromise my integrity any longer.”
‘Exhausted and literally dirty’
In its outreach, the state relied heavily on volunteers and community groups, who had fanned across Vermont to help survivors long before the state launched its case management programs.
Vermont officials say these community efforts are a key part of the state’s support network. 
In 2023, Orleans County resident Meghan Wayland quickly realized few storm survivors were reporting their flood damage. Without adequate reporting, the county might not qualify for a disaster declaration – which meant residents would not be able to apply for assistance from FEMA.  
After floodwaters recede, damage can be harder to find, said Wayland. Often, it was “in people’s basements, which are literally underground. So then, the disaster is living underground, hidden away. It’s behind a door. Someone has to go in and look.”
Wayland drove long distances to knock on doors, documenting damage and encouraging people to report it. After Orleans County received its disaster declaration, FEMA officials sat down with Wayland at breakfast to persuade them to start a nonprofit “long term recovery group” (LTRG). Wayland showed up “exhausted and literally dirty,” they said, and ultimately agreed.
After flooding in 2024, Prem Linskey noticed that many of his neighbors were “living in homes that, landslides are creeping up, erosion’s creeping up, foundation’s cracking,” he started an LTRG that served Richmond, where he lived, and two neighboring towns. There was “such a big need,” he said.
Prem Linskey, a Richmond resident, noticed that many of his neighbors were struggling after the flood, living in homes where “landslides are creeping up, erosion’s creeping up” and foundations are cracking. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger
As the deadline to appeal for FEMA aid loomed, he received frantic emails from state case managers, and became increasingly worried. “These are people in my community that aren’t going to get their appeals in on time,” Linskey remembered thinking.
Alongside the state, long term recovery groups also have case managers, but the groups are created and run by community members.5 Some serve a single town while others serve multiple counties. Some areas don’t have one, which means not every Vermonter can access their support.
The state does not typically fund LTRGs. The Vermont Community Foundation, which manages much of the state’s philanthropic disaster aid, is a major source of funding. (VCF is also a financial supporter of VTDigger.) Many LTRG members are volunteers who also work full-time jobs.
As state case managers prepared to contact 1,700 households in November 2025, they requested help from LTRGs.
In November 2025, Mike Dacey, the head of an LTRG in Waterbury, told state officials in an email, which VTDigger reviewed, that his group could handle a large number of cases, but requested that the state pay for the work “associated with this increased case load.”
Gosselin responded that the state didn’t have money to pay recovery groups.45 The state’s case managers would handle all of the cases if the recovery groups didn’t have capacity, he said.
But in the background, case managers were overwhelmed. Between November and the February FEMA appeals deadline, they made several attempts to contact each of the 1,700 households.
Recovery groups had asked the state for money before, including after the 2023 floods. One recovery group leader told lawmakers survivors were receiving “slow, chaotic support” due to “a severe lack of state support and resources.”
If a region “can be served by an LTRG, it should be,” and the case management program should fill the gaps, said Farnham, the state’s chief recovery officer. He said that ongoing state funding was possible but “not super likely.” Since the floods in 2023, LTRGs have handled hundreds of cases.
Before the program ended in October 2026, case managers reached out to 2,222 households and opened 99 cases, according to Ashley Roy, public information officer with the Vermont Agency of Human Services. About one-third were unresponsive or withdrew from the program after their case work began, and therefore they “received limited assistance,” Roy said.  
In its application to FEMA, the state proposed 11 full-time service positions, but Guidehouse staffed seven through its subcontractor, including three fewer case managers. Over the course of the program, the state paid about $475,000 for Guidehouse, Farnham told VTDigger, and DRUMM salaries cost $872,000. 
By March 2026, the state had phased out Guidehouse and taken over the administration of the case management program, Farnham said. 
In the end, the state did not use $1 million of the $2.9 million that FEMA provided Vermont to operate the case management program after the 2024 flood. It plans to return those funds to the federal government, according to state officials. 
A FEMA spokesperson told VTDigger: “FEMA worked closely with our state partners to ensure all program requirements were met before the grant successfully concluded.”
‘The kindness of strangers’
When Farrar, the storm survivor in Cavendish, opened a letter from FEMA in September 2023, she couldn’t believe what she saw. 
FEMA’s housing inspector verified that her mobile home was “not safe to live in.” She and her family needed more than $25,000 to make repairs — money they didn’t have. 
But FEMA had approved just $5,319 in aid. 

“The amount of money you got is based on the damage FEMA’s housing inspector saw,” FEMA’s letter states. “This money is meant to help you make your home safe, sanitary, and functional. It is not meant to fully restore your home to its pre-disaster condition.”
The town had also told the Farrar family that, in order to stay on their property, they would need to raise their home out of the floodplain, which could cost tens of thousands of dollars on top of the other repair bills. Farrar wasn’t aware of any funding that could help them.
“The federal government was like a joke in all this,” she said. “Like, to give us $5,000 when we’re looking at almost $60,000 worth of damage  — to give us $5,000, it’s kind of a slap in the face.”
The United States uses a “limited intervention” recovery model, which means the federal government is “intentionally limiting how involved it is in individual and household recovery,” said Samantha Montano, associate professor of emergency management at Massachusetts Maritime Academy.
Disaster survivors often expect robust support, she said, but most federal and state policies are meant to fill in gaps after people use their insurance, savings and local charities to rebuild.
But the total amount of money that survivors get after a disaster — from sources like insurance and FEMA — “very often does not add up to be enough to cover your expenses related to recovery,” Montano said. In 2025, almost half of adults in the U.S. in 2025 did not have enough savings to cover three months of expenses in an emergency.
“Our recovery system in the U.S. does not make sense,” Montano said. “It does not work.”
Survivors and experts say this system has left people financially strained.  Some lose their financial footing in the months and years after a disaster, according to emergency management experts. 
“Just yesterday, I spoke to three families that reached out to us for support,” Henshaw, with the recovery group in Lamoille County, told lawmakers in April 2024, nine months after the first round of flooding in Vermont. “To date, all three families have either maxed out credit cards or significantly tapped into their household savings,” she said.
She noted that mold damage had caused one of the families to develop “persistent coughs,” one had a failed septic, and the other had contaminated fuel in their oil tanks. 
“There are dozens more like this throughout Lamoille,” she said. 
Some of the communities hardest-hit by the floods were among the state’s most financially challenged. In 2023 and 2024, floods affected more than a dozen mobile home parks across the state, destroying nearly all of the homes in some. Minter saw lines at Capstone’s food shelf grow, she said. 
After Hurricane Helene in 2024, disaster aid often didn’t arrive when survivors needed it most, and their financial hardships snowballed, said Andrew Rumbach, a senior fellow at the Urban Institute studying disaster recovery.
In 2019, a different set of researchers studied the impacts of disasters on more than 25,000 survivors and found that natural disasters have substantial negative impacts on “credit scores, debt in collections, bankruptcy, credit card debt, and mortgage delinquency and foreclosures,” and that financial strain worsened over time. 
Survivors in the study struggled more following medium-sized disasters, which researchers suggested may reflect less recovery funding for such events.
After flash floods in July 2024 eroded the foundation on Susan Grimaldi’s house in Plainfield, she had to abandon her home of 48 years. She had paid off her mortgage and had been enjoying her career as a pastel painter. One storm suddenly pushed her “into a place of need,” she said. “This is not typical for me.”


Susan Grimaldi had lived in her home for 48 years and had paid off her mortgage when the 2024 flood eroded her foundation and left the house uninhabitable. She fell “into a place of need,” she said. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger


“I was in my stride when all this occurred, at the one of the peaks of my whole life,” Susan Grimaldi said. “And then I’m down to feeling like nothing and nowhere, and who am I? Totally dependent on the kindness of strangers.”


Grimaldi applied for a FEMA buyout, and a town-appointed buyout coordinator helped her navigate her application. In the meantime, she couldn’t afford housing. She did not have a case manager from the state or local support to help her secure more aid.
An acquaintance offered an apartment for a discounted rent. While she was waiting to move in, she stayed in temporary housing, where, on her first night, she fell and broke her arm. She took out a loan to pay for her living expenses. 
“I was in my stride when all this occurred, at one of the peaks of my whole life,” she said. “And then I’m down to feeling like nothing and nowhere, and who am I? Totally dependent on the kindness of strangers.”
In September 2026, after more than two years of waiting, she learned that FEMA had approved her buyout application which brought “disbelief, then relief” she said. But it could take another year before she gets the money.

 
Video by Riley Robinson and Ben Braun for VTDigger

The coming storm
In October, state researchers with the University of Vermont published a report showing that climate change is accelerating. Compared to rainfall in 1900, the state now has 40% more days of heavy rain – defined as more than one inch in 24 hours – each year. 
FEMA officials say that states must be prepared to take on more disaster recovery responsibilities, including the costs.
Vermont officials say they’re ready for the future. 
“We’ve got experience under our belt now, when it comes to individual assistance recovery,” Gosselin said. In Vermont, Gosselin said, state officials “know what they want, based on their lessons learned.”
The state is working to ensure that its case management program is deployed more quickly after future storms, Farnham said. Officials are working with FEMA on “what we hope would be a pre-approved application template” for the next case management program, which would “dramatically shorten the approval timeline,” he said.
They are also creating a new master document that would guide the state’s approach to individual recovery, said Gosselin.
“A big lesson learned is the need for a recovery plan to help out households,” Gosselin said. “That plan will include things like coordinating with the volunteer efforts, coordinating with volunteer recovery groups.”
Farnham said the state would continue to use FEMA’s survivor data as a back-up and prioritize the data from the state’s 2-1-1 system. People on FEMA’s list have already signed up to work with the government, he said, but “there’s a whole other population that we’re constantly trying to reach that isn’t coming forward but still needs help.”
Former employees stressed that the state would need to do much more to reach storm victims.
Minter recommended that the state have a pre-arranged agreement with case managers who could be deployed as soon as flooding hits so that “volunteers don’t have to be depended on.” 
Wayland said long term recovery groups are asking the state for more support while preparing to go it alone, “understanding that the state apparatus may fail.”
“We could train each other to repair roofs. We can find windows on the side of the road and replace windows. We can scrounge and scrounge and scrounge, and we’re gonna have to,” Wayland said. 
“But I’m worried about a future in which we have, again, the same level, or greater, of catastrophic disaster. When will there be nothing left to scrounge? When will the disaster overwhelm our capacity to scrounge?”

title: Lendozia Edwards named interim Providence school superintendent
description: Providence Public Schools will hold a press conference Thursday to introduce its new interim superintendent. The Providence School Board appointed Lendozia Edwards to replace outgoing Superintendent Javier Montañez in an interim capacity during a Saturday morning meeting. She currently serves as chief of schools for Rhode Island’s largest school district. Di[...]
text:
Lendozia Edwards, chief of schools for Providence Public Schools, will become the district’s interim superintendent on Thursday, Nov. 19, 2026. (Photo courtesy of Providence Public Schools)Providence Public Schools will hold a press conference Thursday to introduce its new interim superintendent.
The Providence School Board appointed Lendozia Edwards to replace outgoing Superintendent Javier Montañez in an interim capacity during a Saturday morning meeting. She currently serves as chief of schools for Rhode Island’s largest school district.
District spokesperson Alex Torres-Perez said in an email Monday that Edwards will be the first Black woman to lead the capital city’s school district, which enrolled just under 20,000 students across 37 schools, according to state education data for the 2025-2026 academic year. 
Edwards’ interim term will last through June 30, 2028, School Board President Ty’Relle Stephens said in an email Monday.
The School Board met Saturday in executive session to discuss and interview a total of three candidates to replace Montañez, who announced his resignation Oct. 30 and will have his last day as superintendent on Wednesday. Stephens had previously said the board would prioritize suitable internal candidates in its search for Montañez’s replacement. 
The change in superintendents comes less than five months after Providence resumed local control of its schools after a nearly seven-year-long state intervention. 
The board voted 9-0 to confirm Edwards’ appointment, with one member absent, according to Stephens.
Edwards’ compensation is still being negotiated and discussed by the School Board, Torres-Perez said.
A former math teacher in Nashville, Tennessee, Edwards worked administrative roles in that city’s school system before leaving to become chief of academics and schools for Cambridge Public Schools in Massachusetts. She arrived in the Providence school system in 2024 as a transformation officer for DelSesto Middle School and Hope High School. She helped both schools improve enough to exit a roster of state-designated, chronically underperforming schools.
Edwards holds six academic degrees, including a doctorate in education from Tennessee State University. 
The time and location of the press conference Thursday were unavailable Monday afternoon.

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: Pennsylvania pitches plan for U.S. Space Academy with $285 million state investment
description: The new school, eventually enrolling up to 4,000 students, would be the nation’s sixth service academy and the second in Pennsylvania. The U.S. Army War College is in Carlisle, Cumberland County.
text:
A campus-level view of U.S.Space Academy at Southfield, the proposed main campus for residential, academic and athletic life at Pittsburgh International Airport.
(AI-assisted visualization courtesy of 
Penn State / Cocoziello Institute of Real Estate Innovation)Southwestern Pennsylvania could become the home of the United States Space Academy under a proposal Gov. Josh Shapiro and U.S Sen. Dave McCormick announced Monday. 
The pitch, which includes 300 acres of public land adjacent to Pittsburgh International Airport and a $285 million investment by the commonwealth, is in response to an executive order by President Donald Trump and a request for proposals by NASA, the U.S. space agency.
The new school, eventually enrolling up to 4,000 students, would be the nation’s sixth service academy. The U.S. Army War College is in Carlisle, Cumberland County.
Trump signed the order in August stating space is a critical domain for national security, economic growth, scientific discovery and technological innovation. It continued that the United States must train the next generation of astronauts, scientists, engineers and warfighters to ensure they’re capable of advancing American interests in space. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“The Commonwealth of Pennsylvania powered the first industrial revolution nearly 200 years ago and made the arsenal of democracy the most powerful manufacturing base in the world. Pennsylvania is now uniquely positioned to welcome the United States Space Academy – building off our robust space industry and world-class research universities,” Shapiro said in a statement. 
Shapiro added that Pennsylvania’s application to host the space academy is backed by a bipartisan team of leaders. It includes support from Penn State University, the Keystone Space Collaborative and Pittsburgh International Airport. 
The commonwealth also included the Bellwether District in Philadelphia – the former site of the Philadelphia Energy Solutions oil refinery – as an alternative site. 
“Pennsylvania has the talent, technology, and industrial strength to help America win the race for space dominance,” McCormick said. “Bringing the U.S. Space Academy to Pittsburgh would build on those strengths, create new opportunities for Pennsylvanians, and train the next generation of leaders who will ensure America remains the world’s leader in space.”
Students would learn under a curriculum led by Penn State and six other research universities across the commonwealth. Research and instruction would center on artificial intelligence, robotics, life sciences, advanced manufacturing and other space-related areas. Carnegie Mellon University and University of Pittsburgh both have research and teaching programs focusing on space engineering, AI and robotics.
Penn State President Neeli Bendapudi moderated a discussion between U.S. Sen. Dave McCormick, Gov. Josh Shapiro and two defense contractor executives Wednesday, July 15, 2026, at the U.S. Army War College in Carlisle, Cumberland County. (Photo by Peter Hall/Capital-Star)
“Working in collaboration with research institutions across Pennsylvania, we can provide the framework needed to train the next generation of astronauts, scientists, engineers, operators, entrepreneurs, and civil servants,” said Penn State President Neeli Bendapudi “Our proposed curriculum would provide students with critical hands-on experience and the skills they need to meet the rapidly changing workforce needs.”
As the federal government sought proposals for the new academy, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth recently announced an effort to strip civilian influences from the nation’s military curricula. 
In March, Hegseth ordered a 90-day review of the six senior service colleges including the war colleges of the Army, Navy, Air Force and Marines and the National Defense University and the National War College. It resulted in a memorandum outlining directives to rid the colleges of “relics of 19th century academia” and better prepare officers for modern warfare. 
“In the profession of arms, nostalgia is fatal,” he said. “When our war college graduates walk across the stage and take command, their minds cannot be anchored on the strategic consensus of a vanished world.”
A new campus
Pennsylvania’s proposal would site the new campus on 300 acres of public land in the Southfield Business Park beside Pittsburgh International Airport. 
The academy would break ground in 2027 and could formally open for 1,200 students in fall 2031.
The Shapiro administration said the commonwealth would benefit from billions of dollars in combined public and private investment that could bring thousands of new jobs.
The state’s $285 million investment would include $30 million for site preparation, $11 million for water infrastructure upgrades, and $45 million for regional transportation improvements and a commitment to raise a $200 million private endowment.
As the new academy site is renovated and developed, the first class of 300 students would be taught at the former Pittsburgh Technical College in North Fayette Township in Allegheny County, a few miles from the airport. The college, which closed in 2024, has housing for nearly 400 students. 
Pittsburgh International Airport Feb. 22, 2026. (Photo by John Beale/Pennsylvania Capital-Star)
Upon completion of the space academy campus, the former technical college would become an “innovation district” with residences for faculty and students’ families, additional laboratory and environmental testing space, classrooms and space for expansion.
Pittsburgh International Airport already has a military presence with the 171st Air Refueling Wing of the Pennsylvania Air National Guard and the Air Force Reserve 911th Airlift Wing sharing the airfield with commercial airline operations. 
“Our airport is known around the world as an innovation leader. Coupled with our abundant real estate options and proximity to two military bases on-site, this proposal presents a compelling opportunity to develop a transformational campus,” said Pittsburgh International Airport CEO Christina Cassotis.
Pennsylvania’s space economy generated $8.6 billion in economic activity supporting 556 businesses in the space supply chain, according to the Shapiro administration. The Pittsburgh region is home to 126 of those businesses.
“This established industrial and innovation base gives the Academy immediate access to the companies, technologies, specialized manufacturing capabilities, and research partnerships needed to educate the next generation of space leaders — and to translate their work into American economic strength, technological advantage, and national security,” the administration said in a release.
Allegheny County Executive Sara Inamorato noted the academy would bring new jobs, significant investment and opportunities for residents and businesses.
​​“Allegheny County has a proud history of building what’s next, and the United States Space Academy represents an incredible opportunity to carry that legacy forward,” she said.
