title: La Corte Suprema de Estados Unidos rechaza el intento de Trump de imponer políticas de DEI a los investigadores de la UC
description: La Corte Suprema de Estados Unidos rechazó la apelación del gobierno de Trump contra las decisiones de tribunales inferiores que le ordenaban restituir aproximadamente mil millones de dólares en subvenciones para investigación de la Universidad de California (UC). Los investigadores de la UC alegaron que se violaron sus derechos de la Primera Enmienda porque[...]
text:
This article is also available in English. Read it here.
La Corte Suprema de Estados Unidos rechazó la solicitud de la Casa Blanca para que el máximo tribunal revisara un caso que obligó a la administración Trump a devolver cientos de subvenciones de investigación a académicos de la Universidad de California.
El tribunal emitió la decisión el lunes. Ningún magistrado presentó un escrito explicando la decisión, lo cual es habitual.
 Los abogados del Departamento de Justicia de Estados Unidos argumentaron que las agencias federales tenían derecho a rescindir las subvenciones porque contravenían las órdenes ejecutivas de la administración Trump sobre la retirada de fondos a las iniciativas denominadas de Diversidad, Equidad e Inclusión, además de la investigación sobre los efectos del calentamiento global.
 Sin embargo, los abogados de los investigadores de la UC describieron ese razonamiento como peligroso para la ciencia y para los derechos constitucionales de los académicos. «Lo que comienza como un daño material —pérdida de dinero, personal, estudiantes de posgrado y posdoctorales— se convierte rápidamente en un daño simbólico: la imposibilidad de publicar investigaciones e influir en el debate público. Esto constituye una violación flagrante de la Primera Enmienda», escribieron los abogados de los investigadores de la UC en un escrito presentado ante el Tribunal Supremo.
 El caso se conoce como Thakur contra Trump y se refiere a subvenciones para la historia de Estados Unidos, la investigación de enfermedades y la biología, entre muchos otros temas. Entre enero y julio del año pasado, la Casa Blanca canceló más de 900 millones de dólares en subvenciones a investigadores de la UC, incluyendo casi 600 millones solo en la UCLA. Casi todas esas subvenciones fueron restablecidas después de que un juez de primera instancia ordenara a las agencias federales que las restituyeran en varias decisiones judiciales. Tras la apelación del gobierno federal, el Tribunal de Apelaciones del Noveno Circuito ratificó esas decisiones , dictaminando que la Casa Blanca probablemente violó los derechos de la Primera Enmienda de los investigadores. Según informó previamente CalMatters, las agencias suspendieron la financiación de proyectos de investigación mediante búsquedas de palabras clave en las solicitudes de subvención que incluían términos como “diversidad” o “cambio climático”. El Departamento de Energía recortó las subvenciones específicamente a los estados que votaron por Kamala Harris en lugar de Trump en 2024.
 Las subvenciones otorgadas por los Institutos Nacionales de la Salud también exigían que los académicos investigaran una muestra diversa de estadounidenses. Cuando la agencia canceló en abril del año pasado una subvención de 36 millones de dólares sobre demencia, dirigida por un profesor de la UC Davis, por centrarse en la diversidad, CalMatters informó que la primera administración Trump exigió que las solicitudes de subvención se centraran en la diversidad. Los Institutos Nacionales de la Salud restablecieron la subvención poco después de que CalMatters publicara su artículo.
 Algunos de los proyectos de investigación que la Fundación Nacional de Ciencias canceló no tenían nada que ver con iniciativas de diversidad y equidad, según escribieron los abogados de los investigadores. Afirman que la fundación se centró en subvenciones que incluían la palabra “diversidad” al describir un enfoque científico. Entre estos proyectos se encontraban aquellos con títulos como “Efectos de la diversidad foliar en la diversidad de insectos colonizadores acuáticos” y “Revelando la vasta diversidad dentro del mutualismo leguminosa-rizobio”.
 Claudia Polsky, abogada de los investigadores de la UC, afirmó que la decisión de la Corte Suprema beneficia a casos similares en todo el país. Los abogados de otros investigadores cuyas subvenciones fueron canceladas por el gobierno federal también argumentan que la Casa Blanca violó sus derechos amparados por la Primera Enmienda. Estos abogados pueden señalar que el Tribunal de Apelaciones del Noveno Circuito dio la razón a los investigadores de la UC y que la Corte Suprema rechazó la impugnación de la Casa Blanca. Esos tribunales “no están obligados técnicamente por nada. Pero creo que les resultará bastante convincente”, dijo Polsky. No cree que la Casa Blanca intente apelar de nuevo, ya que los magistrados no mostraron disidencia en su rechazo. Añadió que esta decisión beneficia directamente a los profesores de Cal State que demandaron a la administración Trump el mes pasado por la cancelación de las subvenciones de la Fundación Nacional de Ciencias . Los abogados de los investigadores de la UC volverán a comparecer el martes ante un tribunal inferior para argumentar que la cancelación de las subvenciones del Departamento de Energía por parte de la administración Trump también fue ilegal. Técnicamente, ese caso no guarda relación con la decisión de la Corte Suprema de hoy. 
Disputa legal
 Una de las principales controversias del caso radica en determinar cuándo el gobierno federal puede cancelar la financiación de las subvenciones. Los abogados de los investigadores argumentaron que, una vez otorgada una subvención a académicos —independientemente de la administración que la haya concedido—, se les debería permitir completar su investigación, incluso si la administración actual considera que dicha investigación supone un despilfarro del dinero de los contribuyentes.
 Pero el Departamento de Justicia insistió en que el gobierno federal puede cancelar subvenciones ya aprobadas. Según la agencia, esto no constituye una violación de la Primera Enmienda, ya que la Casa Blanca no impide que los investigadores busquen financiación privada para llevar a cabo sus investigaciones. Los investigadores de la UC no infringieron ninguna norma establecida por el Congreso en la forma en que llevaron a cabo su investigación y cumplieron con las directrices detalladas sobre cómo utilizar los fondos federales, según afirmaron las agencias federales en declaraciones firmadas este verano.
 Pero para la administración Trump, eso no importaba. Las agencias cancelaron las subvenciones de todos modos porque ya no se ajustaban a las directrices del presidente. Los abogados de los investigadores escribieron que el precedente legal esgrimido por la Casa Blanca acabaría con la estabilidad de la investigación federal en ciencia y humanidades. Argumentaron que cualquier proyecto financiado durante varios años que se extienda hasta el mandato de un nuevo presidente estadounidense sería susceptible de cancelación anticipada. La ciencia no puede funcionar bajo ese tipo de arbitrariedad, sostuvieron los abogados de los investigadores.
 Una jueza de primera instancia, designada por Biden, coincidió con esta opinión al ordenar a las agencias que restituyeran las subvenciones. «Se enfrentan a déficits de financiación inesperados, probablemente tendrán que despedir personal y sufrirán daños a su carrera y reputación si no pueden completar sus proyectos. Además, deberán dedicar tiempo a buscar financiación alternativa, un proceso laborioso con pocas probabilidades de éxito», escribió la jueza Rita F. Lin, del Tribunal de Distrito de los Estados Unidos para el Distrito Norte de California. El Departamento de Justicia representó específicamente a varias agencias federales, entre ellas el Departamento de Defensa, el Departamento de Transporte, la Fundación Nacional para las Humanidades, los Institutos Nacionales de Salud y la Fundación Nacional de Ciencias. Los abogados llegaron a un acuerdo con la Agencia de Protección Ambiental por cuestiones similares este año. 
 ¿Puede la Casa Blanca cancelar subvenciones ya aprobadas?
 Los abogados del Departamento de Justicia argumentaron que, siempre y cuando la administración no obligue a los investigadores a adoptar los puntos de vista de la Casa Blanca en sus asuntos privados, sus derechos no se ven violados. Los abogados de los investigadores criticaron duramente esa lógica. La Casa Blanca “no puede señalar ningún caso” en el que un tribunal federal “haya dictaminado que el Presidente y las agencias federales puedan rescindir subvenciones otorgadas mediante un proceso competitivo basado en el mérito, en función del punto de vista percibido de la investigación”, escribieron en su escrito legal instando a la Corte Suprema a rechazar el caso.
 El equipo legal de los investigadores escribió que la Casa Blanca está ignorando los procedimientos establecidos por el Congreso para la cancelación de subvenciones. Los abogados de los investigadores señalaron que el Congreso incluyó disposiciones en las leyes que rigen las agencias de investigación para fomentar la investigación centrada en mujeres, personas de color y personas con discapacidad, incluso en la Fundación Nacional de Ciencias. Unas disposiciones similares rigen el Fondo Nacional para las Humanidades, como la de otorgar “especial atención a los académicos y a las instituciones educativas y culturales que tradicionalmente han estado subrepresentados”.

name: National
title: New World screwworm spreading rapidly across Southern states
description: A deadly flesh-eating parasite that can plague livestock, wildlife and pets continues to spread across the American Southwest. Officials detected the arrival of the New World screwworm in June — the first time in decades the pest had been seen in the United States. Since then, detections have spiked, with 139 recorded cases across three […]
text:
A pinned specimen of a full-grown New World screwworm fly is shown in this image. Federal and state officials are grappling with a worsening infestation from the flesh-eating parasite that threatens livestock, pets and wildlife. (Photo courtesy of Michael Miller/Texas A&M AgriLife)A deadly flesh-eating parasite that can plague livestock, wildlife and pets continues to spread across the American Southwest.
Officials detected the arrival of the New World screwworm in June — the first time in decades the pest had been seen in the United States. Since then, detections have spiked, with 139 recorded cases across three states. While fewer than 10 total cases were recorded in August and September, the U.S. Department of Agriculture has already confirmed 53 cases this month.
“We got a bunch more cases all of a sudden,” said David Anderson, professor and extension economist in livestock and food product marketing at Texas A&M University.
Rising infections have pushed state leaders to designate certain outbreak areas across Texas, New Mexico and Arizona, where animal movement is being restricted. 
The movement of pets and livestock is restricted in all or parts of 31 Texas counties as officials there are tracking 77 sites with at least one confirmed case.
Contrary to its name, the screwworm grows into an adult fly about the size of a common housefly. The name screwworm refers to the larvae (maggots) that burrow into open wounds, feeding as they go “like a screw being driven into wood,” according to USDA.
The pest could threaten beef and dairy cattle — potentially exacerbating high prices for consumers. But the screwworm can also infect people, wildlife and pets. That’s pushed states to recommend or require certain monitoring of pet movements.
What you need to know about the flesh-eating New World screwworm

California, for instance, requires all warm-blooded animals coming from an infested zone to have a pretravel inspection, a veterinary certification and an entry permit into the state. In Texas, adoptions for thousands of dogs and cats were put on hold in August as most states restricted movement of animals from areas with screwworm infestations. 
“It’s thrown a wrench into things, for small rescues as well as the bigger shelters,” Mia Bendixsen, executive director of the Texas Humane Legislation Network, told The Associated Press. 
Earlier this month, the New Mexico Livestock Board broadened its screwworm tracking to regional infestation zones as more cases were confirmed across southern parts of the state. Those zones demarcate where ranchers must receive state authorization before moving cattle.
“We are working closely with our state and federal partners to investigate these cases, increase surveillance and monitor for additional infestations,” New Mexico State Veterinarian Samantha Holeck said in an October statement, according to Source New Mexico.
Screwworm maggots burrow into the flesh of living animals through wounds as small as a tick bite or in body openings such as the eyes or nose. That means ranchers must keep close watch over newborn calves with exposed umbilical cords and may need to rethink branding and tagging operations that provide an entry for the pests. 
While the flies could prove deadly to herds, USDA says they do not create food safety risks.
But a worsening infestation could impact beef prices, which are already near record high prices. 
In August, federal officials began a phased reopening of Southern ports for cattle imports from Mexico, which had been barred because of the screwworm infestation. That should slowly help rebuild the domestic cattle supply chain and eventually offer some relief for consumers, said Anderson, of Texas A&M.
Much of southern New Mexico a designated screwworm ‘infested zone’ as USDA reopens cattle imports

Anderson expects consumers could see some relief in prices next year. But grocery shoppers shouldn’t expect a return to the rock-bottom beef prices they enjoyed five to 10 years ago.
“Because there’s so many other costs, not only producing and processing the animals, but transportation, labor — everything is higher,” he said.
The screwworm can infect humans, but so far no domestic cases have been reported in people, according to the federal Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Mexico and Central American nations have reported more than 2,850 cases in people, according to CDC tracking. 
To eradicate the pests, the federal government plans to breed sterile male flies and then release them into areas with established populations. The sterilized males will mate with females, which will then lay unfertilized eggs. With females mating only once in their lifespan, officials say this method progressively reduces and eliminates the fly population.
USDA is constructing a $750 million sterile fly facility in Southern Texas that aims to produce up to 300 million sterile flies per week when it opens next year. The agency has also invested in sterile fly facilities in Mexico and Panama.
Last week, the federal government began the process of hiring 228 people for the new Texas facility.
“Protecting U.S. livestock and wildlife from New World Screwworm is a national security priority, and this new facility will drastically boost the availability of sterile flies – our most successful offensive capability to drive these serious pests away from our border,” Secretary of Agriculture Brooke Rollins said in a news release about the hiring.
Stateline reporter Kevin Hardy can be reached at khardy@stateline.org.

name: California
title: Departamento de Seguros de California revela accidentalmente que otro juez se quejó de mala conducta interna
description: El Departamento responde a la demanda del juez despedido, calificando las acusaciones de "atroces". Al hacerlo, reveló que un juez en funciones también presentó quejas ante el Colegio de Abogados del Estado.
text:
This article is also available in English. Read it here.
El Departamento de Seguros de California cambió de rumbo el viernes y optó por hablar sobre una demanda presentada por un ex juez administrativo contra el comisionado Ricardo Lara y otros, en la que se les acusa de aprobar ilegalmente aumentos de tarifas.
 Al hacerlo, el departamento parece haber revelado inadvertidamente que un juez administrativo en funciones, Karl-Frederic Seligman, también presentó quejas sobre mala conducta por parte de abogados del departamento.
Tal como informó CalMatters, la jueza administrativa Kristin Rosi demandó a Lara y a su exasesora especial Lucy Wang a finales de septiembre, alegando que la despidieron en represalia el año pasado después de que ella dictaminara en 2024 que estaban aprobando indebidamente las solicitudes de las compañías de seguros para aumentar las primas de sus clientes.
 La Proposición 103, la ley aprobada por los votantes en 1988 que rige los seguros en el estado, exige que el Departamento de Seguros celebre audiencias cuando una aseguradora solicita un aumento de tarifas del 7% o más si un miembro del público se opone a través del llamado proceso de intervención.
 Según la demanda que Rosi presentó ante el Tribunal Superior del Condado de Alameda, sus decisiones determinaron que los demandados se habían negado a celebrar audiencias obligatorias, se habían basado en reglamentos no autorizados y habían eludido las normas que exigen transparencia en los acuerdos.
 Rosi alega que Lara, Wang y otros empleados del departamento, aún sin identificar, intentaron socavar la autoridad de los jueces administrativos tras esas decisiones. Esto incluía pedirle a la jueza que modificara sus fallos o que dictara sentencias de cierta manera, según consta en la demanda.
 “Si bien nuestra política es no hacer comentarios sobre litigios pendientes, la gravedad de estas acusaciones manifiestamente falsas y las inexactitudes flagrantes exigen una respuesta”, dijo Gabriel Sánchez, portavoz del departamento, en un correo electrónico enviado a CalMatters.
 Sánchez afirmó que el departamento se defenderá “enérgicamente”: “En todo momento, el comisionado Lara y el personal del departamento actuaron de manera apropiada, legal y dentro del marco de la Proposición 103, vigente desde hace décadas, para proteger a los consumidores y garantizar la rendición de cuentas en sus operaciones”.
 El año pasado, Rosi presentó denuncias ante el Colegio de Abogados del Estado contra Wang y otros tres abogados del departamento. Las denuncias, que no son públicas pero fueron obtenidas por CalMatters, alegan en detalle reiteradas violaciones de la ley, incluyendo reuniones que, según el juez, deberían haber incluido a todas las partes involucradas en las audiencias sobre tarifas, incluidas las compañías de seguros y los intervinientes.
 Sánchez afirmó que el juez “malinterpretó… los procedimientos vigentes de la Proposición 103”, y que el Colegio de Abogados del Estado archivó esas denuncias y no halló irregularidades. Envió a CalMatters una carta de un investigador del Colegio de Abogados del Estado, fechada el 14 de julio, que declaraba el asunto cerrado. Dicha carta indicaba: “El Colegio de Abogados del Estado ha concluido la investigación de las alegaciones de mala conducta profesional presentadas por la Honorable Kristin L. Rosi y el Honorable Fredric J. Seligman”.
 Al parecer, no existen informes previos de que Seligman también haya presentado quejas ante el Colegio de Abogados del Estado. Es la única persona que figura como juez administrativo en el sitio web del departamento. Su personal no respondió de inmediato a la solicitud de entrevista de CalMatters.
 Wendy Musell, abogada de Rosi, dijo que su clienta apeló la decisión del Colegio de Abogados del Estado de archivar las denuncias.
 “Según tengo entendido, el Colegio de Abogados del Estado aún tiene jurisdicción y el asunto sigue en apelación”, dijo.
 Rosi había sido jueza de derecho administrativo en la Oficina de Audiencias Administrativas del departamento desde 2007. Fue nombrada jueza presidenta en 2016. En enero de 2025, el departamento la suspendió de sus funciones; su puesto se anunció como vacante en julio de 2025; y recibió la confirmación del departamento de que había sido despedida en noviembre de 2025, según su demanda.
 Rosi demandó a Lara, a Wang y a otros empleados no identificados en su calidad de funcionarios del Departamento de Seguros, por lo que el Departamento de Justicia estatal los representa en la demanda.
 El segundo mandato de Lara como comisionada finaliza en enero. Wang dejó el departamento a finales de 2025 y ahora trabaja para un bufete de abogados que representa al sector asegurador.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: Assembly panel approves changes to NJ rulemaking process
description: Changes hailed by business groups would increase public comment periods. Detractors warned the changes would empower interest groups.
text:
The legislation would expand public comment periods and notification requirements, but detractors warned it would give interest groups greater input over regulatory processes that seldom draw attention from the public. (Photo by Hal Brown for New Jersey Monitor)An Assembly panel on Monday approved legislation that would extend timelines for state agencies to adopt regulations, require the automatic award of attorney fees to groups or individuals who successfully challenge some rules, and expand public hearing requirements in the rulemaking process.
Business groups hailed the bill, arguing it would lend new transparency to the state’s rulemaking process, but progressive and environmental groups opposed it, warning that, despite support for some transparency provisions, the bill would expand the power and influence of special interest groups stung by two recent major regulatory defeats.
“This bill would have insidious consequences. It would render agencies less able to enact their legislative mandates to protect the residents of New Jersey, and it’s clearly an extension of earlier efforts to reduce the agencies’ ability to effectively make rules, and it would ensure that a small, outspoken minority can slow down the process,” said Alex Ambrose, a senior policy analyst for New Jersey Policy Perspective.
The bill would amend the Administrative Procedure Act, the state law governing how agencies can enact regulations, to increase the length of rulemaking public comment periods from 60 days to 90, require regulators formally flag a rule proposal in the state register to at least 30 days before it’s issued, and extend the notice agencies must give before they adopt, amend, or repeal a rule to 60 days.
It would command the Office of Administrative Law to build a database containing all pending and proposed regulations plus all non-confidential data and other information used to formulate the proposed rule and mandate public hearings on any rule that draws at least 50 commenters or would result in at least $50 million of increased spending by governments, businesses, or individuals.
The legislation would also require regulators to publish all public comments submitted on each rule, less any confidential information, rather than the comment summaries agencies include at present, and that they calculate the expected economic impact of every rule proposal on the state government, local and county governments, businesses, and residents.
Detractors warned that while some provisions would boost transparency, others would extend a rulemaking process that can already take years to yield new regulations.
“Again and again, there are parts of this legislation that are duplicative, that are going to slow down the process, that give undue influence to folks that are reading the New Jersey Register and have more of kind of an inside leg than folks at the average,” said Doug O’Malley, state director of Environment New Jersey.
The rulemaking process draws little interest from laypeople, O’Malley said, and the changes made by the bill would only empower interest groups
Business groups argued the changes made by the bill would boost transparency in rulemaking and would result in better regulations going on the books.
“We want to ensure that this rule, whatever rule is proposed — even if it’s not in our favor —  has thoroughly went through all the objections, understand the issues, and is properly drafted, and we believe this legislation would help us get there,” said Ray Cantor, deputy chief government affairs officer for the New Jersey Business and Industry Association.
The move to amend the Administrative Procedure Act follows two major regulatory defeats for business groups.
Those groups opposed rules codifying in regulation decades of case law governing a test that determines whether a worker is an employee or an independent contractor that went into effect last month.
And they fought against strict new flood rules former Gov. Phil Murphy adopted on the final day of his term. Gov. Mikie Sherrill has delayed the implementation of those rules to explore further changes.
“That’s a prime example of why this legislation is necessary. The Murphy administration failed to listen to stakeholder engagement that was presented during that entire time,” said Jeff Kolakowski, CEO of the New Jersey Builders Association, which represents residential real estate developers.
Detractors warned over one final provision that mandates the awarding of attorney fees to individuals or groups who successfully challenge in court regulations that an agency head adopts after rejecting or modifying an administrative law judge’s recommendation on the same.
The bill’s opponents warned the provision would encourage litigation against the state, creating a cottage industry to challenge its regulations.
With its Assembly committee hearing in the rearview and no appropriation in its text, the bill is ready to go to the lower chamber’s floor. It still needs to clear a hearing before the Senate State Government, Wagering, Tourism and Historic Preservation Committee to advance in the upper chamber.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Medical cannabis regulatory amendments forwarded to Nebraska AG without changes
description: LINCOLN — Proposed amendments to Nebraska’s regulations for medical cannabis establishments will proceed as-is to Attorney General Mike Hilgers for legal review despite all four of the state’s licensed cultivators urging changes around testing availability and fees. The Nebraska Medical Cannabis Commission voted unanimously Monday to forward the amendments t[...]
text:
The Nebraska Medical Cannabis Commission listens to a representative of one of the commission's four licensed cultivators during a meeting on Oct. 19, 2026, at the State Office Building in Lincoln. Commissioners seated, from left: Bud Synhorst of Lincoln, Jim Elworth of Nebraska City, Lorelle Mueting of Gretna (interim chair) and former District Judge J. Michael Coffey of Omaha. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)LINCOLN — Proposed amendments to Nebraska’s regulations for medical cannabis establishments will proceed as-is to Attorney General Mike Hilgers for legal review despite all four of the state’s licensed cultivators urging changes around testing availability and fees.
The Nebraska Medical Cannabis Commission voted unanimously Monday to forward the amendments to the Nebraska AG’s Office for constitutional review. The state’s licensed cultivators sent a joint letter in October asking the commission to consider changes.
Dustin Krajewski of Meadowlark Medicinals LLC, former state Sen. Kent Rogert of KRL Med LLC, Pat Thomas of MahāMotā Cultivation Co. and Robert Wagner of Midwest Cultivators Group signed the letter.
If Hilgers signs off on the constitutionality of the amendments, the proposal will head to Gov. Jim Pillen for approval. If he signs, the amendments would take effect five days later.
Power of the commission
The Legislature did not authorize the commission to assess fees until April, and the commission had already been working to finalize a prior set of regulations. The commission is refusing to grant more licenses until it can assess fees for future licenses. 
Commissioners on the Nebraska Medical Cannabis Commission during an April 13, 2026, meeting. From left, Commissioners Bud Synhorst of Lincoln, Jim Elworth of Nebraska City, Lorelle Mueting of Gretna (interim chair) and J. Michael Coffey of Omaha. All but Mueting also serve on the Nebraska Liquor Control Commission. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
A MahāMotā representative said in October that the company was on track to harvest this year but saw no path to how testing facilities could legally receive, possess or test their plant.
“We request an update to the current proposed regulations that provide clarification of the licensing or authorization process, who may transport samples to a laboratory, how transportation and manifest requirements apply to those transfers and whether out-of-state laboratories may be used,” the cultivators said in their letter.
Under the voter-approved laws in 2024, regulatory power over “registered cannabis establishments” for the possession, manufacture, distribution, delivery and dispensing of medical cannabis is “vested exclusively” in the voter-created commission.
A registered cannabis establishment is defined as a private entity licensed to possess, manufacture, distribute, deliver or dispense cannabis for medical purposes. 
Unless the Legislature changes that definition to include testing, the commission has no authority to grant in-state private facilities legal possession of marijuana.
Proposed regulatory amendments
Interim Commission Chair Lorelle Mueting had told the MahāMotā representative last month that the company had assured the commission that cannabis could be safely stored for up to two years. The commission last week clarified that it wasn’t estimating a two-year timeline before testing would be available.
At the same time, the commission offered no new estimate for when testing will be available.
Nebraska Attorney General Mike Hilgers, left, and Gov. Jim Pillen. Sept. 14, 2026. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
The latest commission amendments offer a few distinct changes from current regulations, the largest of which is proposed fees for applicants — a $5,000 application fee, annual license and renewal fees based on type (between $10,000 and $28,500), a $1,500 relocation fee and a $13,000 fee for participation in the state’s seed-to-sale inventory tracking system. Dispensaries would also need to pay a $250 fee to license a new product, plus a $100 renewal fee. 
Currently, there are no fees under the program. Sales taxes are currently prohibited by law.
The latest amendments would also merge transporter licenses with product manufacturers, so transportation would be an optional certification.
Other notable changes:

Removing a label that would list medical cannabis as a “Schedule I” controlled substance. In May, the federal government downgraded state-licensed medical cannabis from a Schedule I drug to a Schedule III drug.
Allowing disenrollment of healthcare practitioners who voluntarily choose to participate in the program if the practitioner fails to maintain a medical license in good standing.
Requiring healthcare practitioners to attest when an in-person appointment occurs before they issue a recommendation for medical cannabis. 
Attesting whether a provider knows whether a patient is pregnant before recommending medical cannabis. If the provider in the future learns a patient is pregnant, they must alert the commission.

State lawmakers hosted a series of three public forums in eastern Nebraska on medical cannabis, including one in Lincoln on May 5, 2025. From left, State Sens. Rick Holdcroft of Bellevue, Jane Raybould of Lincoln, Tom Brandt of Plymouth, John Cavanaugh of Omaha, George Dungan of Lincoln, Myron Dorn of Adams, Danielle Conrad of Lincoln, Jana Hughes of Seward, Margo Juarez of Omaha and Merv Riepe of Ralston. State Sens. Ben Hansen of Blair, Machaela Cavanaugh of Omaha and Terrell McKinney of Omaha attended earlier forums. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Current regulatory requirements
The current medical cannabis regulations call for the state to:

Establish a “Recommending Health Care Practitioner” directory and require patients who want to access Nebraska-licensed dispensaries to go through one of the in-state providers.
Cap cultivators at no more than 1,250 flowering plants at one time.
Restrict purchases of medical cannabis to 5 ounces of medical cannabis in 30 days, of which no more than 5 grams can be delta-9 tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) from the same dispensary. Delta-9 THC is the part of cannabis most associated with a “high.”
Allow no more than 12 medical cannabis dispensaries statewide, arranged by judicial district. That would mean one dispensary each in Douglas County (584,526 residents), Lancaster County (322,608 residents), Sarpy/Cass counties (217,202 residents) and Buffalo/Hall counties (112,979 residents), according to 2020 census data.
Prohibit the sale of smoking or vaping products and edibles of any kind.

Under current state law, possession of up to 5 ounces of medical cannabis is permitted with the written recommendation of any healthcare practitioner.
When asked last week whether the commission would support legislative changes ahead of the 2027 session, which begins Jan. 6, a commission spokesperson told the Nebraska Examiner that the commission “continues to evaluate the statutory and regulatory steps necessary to fully implement Nebraska’s medical cannabis program.”
The commission’s next meeting is scheduled for Dec. 14.

title: Bird flu detected in Oklahoma dairy herd
description: OKLAHOMA CITY — A case of the bird flu was detected by federal health inspectors in an Oklahoma dairy herd, according to the state agriculture department.  The U.S. Department of Agriculture’s Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service confirmed the case of Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza, but officials have not released the location of the infected […]
text:
Dairy cows and black birds. (Dusty Pixel photography via Getty Images)OKLAHOMA CITY — A case of the bird flu was detected by federal health inspectors in an Oklahoma dairy herd, according to the state agriculture department. 
The U.S. Department of Agriculture’s Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service confirmed the case of Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza, but officials have not released the location of the infected dairy herd.
The virus, which is highly contagious and most commonly found in wild birds, can also spread to poultry and dairy cattle, and in some rare cases has been detected in humans. 
There is currently no concern about the safety of pasteurized milk and dairy products, according to a news release from the Oklahoma Department of Agriculture, Food and Forestry. The commercial milk supply remains safe because of federal animal health requirements and pasteurization. 
Dairy farmers who suspect cases of the viral disease should contact the state agriculture department immediately. It has published a series of biosecurity recommendations to limit the spread of the illness. 
Signs of the avian influenza include decline in feed intake, decreased milk yield, changes in milk color and consistency, dehydration and fevers, according to the news release. 
The last confirmed, positive case of avian influenza in Oklahoma was Jan. 8 in Wagoner County.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Minnesota AG allows Allina Health acquisition by California-based Sutter Health
description: The Upper Midwest health giant Allina Health is set to be acquired by Sutter Health, a far larger California system, after the nonprofit health systems signed a 10-year oversight agreement with the Minnesota Attorney General’s Office. The consolidation, first announced in March, is set to take place in January. It will create a combined $26 […]
text:
Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison speaks at a press conference alongside Sutter Health CEO Warner Thomas and Allina Health CEO Lisa Shannon at Allina's Bandana Square Clinic in St. Paul, Minn., Monday Nov. 16, 2026. (Photo by Alyssa Chen/Minnesota Reformer)The Upper Midwest health giant Allina Health is set to be acquired by Sutter Health, a far larger California system, after the nonprofit health systems signed a 10-year oversight agreement with the Minnesota Attorney General’s Office.
The consolidation, first announced in March, is set to take place in January. It will create a combined $26 billion system with 39 hospitals serving more than 5 million patients in California, Minnesota and Wisconsin. Under the combined system, Allina would maintain its Minneapolis headquarters and become the Upper Midwest Division of Sutter Health, with Allina CEO Lisa Shannon remaining in leadership of the division.
The joining reflects a broader trend of health care consolidation — hospitals and clinics combining into sprawling health systems. In Minnesota this year, consolidation transactions are being proposed at what Erin Conti of the Minnesota Attorney General’s Office called a “breakneck pace” during a state Senate committee hearing.
Substantial evidence has shown that healthcare consolidation has led to higher prices, mainly because larger health systems have more power when negotiating their prices with insurers. Evidence on the effects on quality of care is mixed “at best,” according to a brief from KFF, a health policy research organization.
The Minnesota Attorney General’s Office was bestowed with expanded regulatory powers over healthcare mergers by the Legislature in 2023. It’s now able to analyze and sue to block hospital mergers if they are against the public’s interest — for example if they increase healthcare costs for patients.
“After this thorough review, we have concluded that the integration of Allina and Sutter has met the public interest standard and Minnesota’s health care transaction law,” Attorney General Keith Ellison said at a Monday press conference at Allina Health’s Bandana Square clinic in St. Paul.
At the press conference, Shannon said that challenges in the healthcare landscape — rising input costs, reduced reimbursement for care and widening gaps in the safety net — have led to financial losses for the health system, though Allina officials previously told the Star Tribune that the merger was not a financial rescue.
The signed oversight agreement binds Sutter to maintain Allina Health’s core services for five years, which refers to primary care, family medicine and internal medicine; mental health; cardiovascular services; emergency room services; ICU services; and stroke services.
Sutter committed $2.5 billion to complete Allina’s overhaul of its Abbott Northwestern campus; modernize Allina’s IT systems; and build out an outpatient care network, among other capital investments.
The agreement, summarized on the AG’s website, also includes labor protections, including a ban on noncompetes reflecting state law; and explicit investments into workforce training and rural healthcare.
The agreement does not include explicit guardrails to limit price growth, which is the central concern of many health economists when it comes to hospital consolidation, though Minnesota state law forbids health systems from entering into a transaction that substantially lessens competition.
Sutter, the fourth biggest health system in California by number of staffed patient beds, has previously been accused of driving up costs for Californians through anti-competitive behavior in two lawsuits brought by unions, employers, individuals and California’s attorney general. Sutter denied wrongdoing in the lawsuits’ settlements.
The Minnesota Attorney General’s Office gave the thumbs up to the acquisition of North Memorial Health by South Dakota-based Sanford Health under another 10-year oversight agreement, and is currently in the process of reviewing a proposed merger between HealthPartners and Essentia, both Minnesota-based health systems.
This is a developing story and will be updated.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: Federal grand jury indicts WV Auditor Mark Hunt, others in alleged property stealing scheme
description: A federal grand jury Monday handed up a multi-count indictment against Hunt and Charleston-area lawyer Robert L. Johns related to nine tax delinquent deeds Hunt signed for Johns.
text:
West Virginia Auditor Mark Hunt, a Republican elected in 2024, is under scrutiny for personally signing tax deeds for a friend. (Photo by Perry Bennett/West Virginia Legislative Photography)What state Auditor Mark Hunt called a “tempest in a teapot” has turned into a federal indictment. 
A federal grand jury Monday handed up a multi-count indictment against Hunt and Charleston-area lawyer Robert L. Johns related to nine tax delinquent deeds Hunt signed for Johns. 
Hunt, 66, of Charleston, told West Virginia Watch that Johns was a longtime friend and downplayed any legal issues associated with the transfers. 
U.S. Attorney Moore Capito’s office announced the indictments in a news release Monday, stating that signing the deeds amounted to theft. 
“As a result of the scheme, the defendants stole the nine properties from their lawful owners, the indictments allege,” the office wrote.
The grand jury also issued indictments against employees in Hunt’s office, including Deputy Chief of Staff David Cole, 57, of Charleston, who a West Virginia Watch investigation revealed was running a car lot with Hunt. Federal authorities say Cole and another member of staff, Frederic Caudill, 59, of Charleston, helped create the deeds. 
Caudill is also charged with lying to the feds during an October 2026 interview. 
Maria Hoffman, of Hurricane, was also indicted for time card fraud, after federal authorities said she charged state work hours to do work at Hunt’s private practice. 
“These counts further allege that Hunt, and Cole also frequently worked with Hoffman on Fridays at the law firm during state business hours,” the Attorney General’s Office said. 
Hunt, a Republican, has served as the state auditor since 2025. He is an attorney with Mark A. Hunt & Associates PLLC, where he has continued to practice law while working as a state official.
In late October, Brad McElhinny of WV MetroNews reported that the Auditor’s Office was served a federal grand jury subpoena. 
Hunt said last week that he didn’t know the subject of that investigation.
Before the federal indictment announcement, lawmakers on both sides of the aisle already called on Hunt to resign due to his handling of property deeds for Johns. 
The Federal Bureau of Investigation and the West Virginia Commission on Special Investigations investigated the case.

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: DesJarlais concedes Tennessee 4th Congressional District to Democrat Victoria Broderick
description: Almost two weeks after polls closed in the Nov. 3 midterm elections, Democrat Victoria Broderick has won Tennessee’s 4th Congressional District. Broderick defeated eight-term Republican U.S. Rep. Scott DeJarlais, giving Democrats their only U.S. House win in Tennessee during this election cycle. “I am incredibly grateful to the people of Tennessee’s 4th Dist[...]
text:
Democrat House candidate Victoria Broderick beat incumbent GOP Rep. Scott DesJarlais in Tennessee's 4th Congressional District Tuesday (Photo: Courtesy of Tennessee Democratic Party)Almost two weeks after polls closed in the Nov. 3 midterm elections, Democrat Victoria Broderick has won Tennessee’s 4th Congressional District.
Broderick defeated eight-term Republican U.S. Rep. Scott DeJarlais, giving Democrats their only U.S. House win in Tennessee during this election cycle.
“I am incredibly grateful to the people of Tennessee’s 4th District for putting their faith in me,” said Broderick in a statement. “It’s an honor to have earned your trust, and I don’t take the responsibility of representing our communities lightly.”
After Election Day, Broderick held a 285-vote lead over DeJarlais, with around 700 provisional ballots outstanding, leading to a drawn-out process to count them.
DesJarlais conceded Monday afternoon after provisional ballots counted in Nashville showed Broderick expanding her narrow lead.
Republican U.S. Rep. Scott DesJarlais conceded Tennessee’s 4th Congressional District on Nov. 16, 2026, after provisional ballots were counted and make Democrat Victoria Broderick’s win official. (Photo by J. Holly McCall/Tennessee Lookout)
“I have personally reached out to Ms. Broderick to offer my congratulations and support on this new undertaking,” DesJarlais said in a statement. “I am proud of the standard our office has set in terms of representing the values, interests, and needs of our district.”
The Associated Press had not officially declared Broderick the winner as of 1:15 p.m. Monday.
The District 4 race flew below the radar, as other Tennessee congressional races gained more national attention following a redrawing of the state’s U.S. House map in the spring.
National organizations, including the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee and a PAC funded by Illinois Gov. J.B. Pritzker, poured millions of dollars into candidates running in Tennessee’s 5th and 9th congressional districts, while Broderick raised less than $100,000.
Democratic candidates in the 5th and 9th narrowly lost their races.
Erin Covey, the head of the Cook Political Report’s U.S. House ratings, said President Donald Trump won the 4th district by 24% in 2024, making Broderick’s win the largest congressional district flip of the 2026 cycle.
Broderick, the former chair of the Lincoln County Democratic Party, ran against DesJarlais in 2024, earning 27% of the vote to DesJarlais’s 70%. But the district was drawn differently from the one she ultimately won.
During the May redistricting, Republicans redrew the state’s U.S. House map in hopes of flipping the last Democratic-held seat in Memphis.
Republicans held an unusual mid-cycle redistricting in the wake of the U.S. Supreme Court ruling in Louisiana v. Callais that scrapped key portions of the 1965 Voting Rights Act, chiefly one requiring states with a history of racially motivated voter suppression and discrimination to carve out majority minority congressional districts.
The new U.S. House map moved southeast Nashville into the 4th district and combined it with all of Rutherford County. Over 80% of Broderick’s total votes came from Davidson and Rutherford Counties.
In the Nov. 3 election, DesJarlais won nine of the district’s 11 counties, which are largely rural. Broderick beat DesJarlais in Rutherford County by a few hundred votes and ran up the vote tally in Nashville-Davidson County, defeating DesJarlais by a nearly three-to-one margin.
“Whether you voted for me or not, I want you to know that I will be your representative,” Broderick said in her statement. “I look forward to listening and doing the work you’ve entrusted me to do. Thank you for giving me this opportunity. I’m ready to get to work.”
Broderick defeated four other candidates in the August Democratic primary, including Metro Nashville Councilmember Mike Cortese.
Broderick is a tech support worker and member of the Tennessee Democratic Party executive committee who campaigned on affordability. She described herself as “a working-class mom from rural Tennessee” and said she was in the race “because we deserve better than being treated like an afterthought.”
She lives in Lincoln County with her husband and two sons.
DesJarlais, a physician, was elected to Congress in 2010 as part of the Tea Party wave, defeating incumbent Democrat Lincoln Davis.
He maintained his seat despite close elections, including the 2014 Republican primary in which he defeated then-state Sen. Jim Tracy by 38 votes.
Allegations of spousal abuse trailed DesJarlais in his first campaign and later, reports he pressured one of his patients, with whom he was having an affair, to have an abortion after he impregnated her.
He was a member of the ultra-conservative U.S. House Freedom Caucus and received an A-plus rating from Susan B. Anthony Pro-Life America, an anti-abortion group.

name: Virginia Mercury
title: FAA ground stop disrupts 532 flights at 4 Virginia airports
description: A combined total of 532 flights from four major Virginia airports — Reagan National, Washington Dulles, Richmond, and Norfolk — were affected by the nationwide ground stop on Friday, disrupting travelers for eight hours before it was lifted. Transportation officials said the ground stop, issued by the Federal Aviation Administration, followed an equipment fa[...]
text:
A plane flying overhead toward Dulles International Airport in Northern Virginia. (Photo by Nathaniel Cline/Virginia Mercury)A combined total of 532 flights from four major Virginia airports — Reagan National, Washington Dulles, Richmond, and Norfolk — were affected by the nationwide ground stop on Friday, disrupting travelers for eight hours before it was lifted.
FAA grounds all US flights due to air traffic control issue

Transportation officials said the ground stop, issued by the Federal Aviation Administration, followed an equipment failure at a facility in El Dorado, Arkansas. There, an obsolete 2011 router flooded the FAA network with data during maintenance work. The work is part of a larger plan to modernize the country’s air traffic control infrastructure. 
U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the incident is still being investigated as travelers recover and consider future travel, most notably for Thanksgiving next week. 
At a White House press briefing on Friday, Duffy was asked directly whether the FAA disruption would affect students returning home and other Thanksgiving travelers.
“I think we’re going to be back up and operational as we come into the … to the heat of travel during Thanksgiving,” said Duffy.
Still, he acknowledged that it would take time to recover from Friday’s disruption.
 “I believe that it’s going to take us some time to get back to capacity,” he added.
Gov. Abigail Spanberger, who was in Denver, Colorado, at the time of the ground stop, said in a post on social media Friday that her administration was monitoring the situation, which caused “significant” delays and cancellations at airports.
“The commonwealth is working to get answers and will update Virginians as we learn more,” Spanberger said.
Duffy, whom Congress confirmed as transportation secretary in January 2025, said over the weekend that it is safe to fly.
He also emphasized that the FAA’s air traffic control operations system remains intact, denied any evidence of a cyberattack, and urged Congress to distribute over $50 billion to the agency immediately to modernize neglected aviation infrastructure.
Duffy said the administration will not end its partnership with legacy contractor L3Harris, which owns the communication network the FAA uses.
L3Harris was conducting maintenance work and replacing aging copper wiring with fiber when the router malfunctioned, prompting the decision to stop all flights. 
In a statement, L3Harris said “safety and reliability” are the company’s highest priorities. The company said that, with its telecommunications partners and the FAA, it has completed more than 70% of the planned airspace communications conversion from legacy copper wires to a fiber optic system. 
“We are supporting the FAA in its investigation to understand the conditions that led to the Nov. 13 ground stop of our nation’s air travel,” the company stated. “L3Harris takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travelers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously.”
Last year, Congress allocated $12.5 billion through H.R.1, the new law President Donald Trump dubbed the “One Big Beautiful Bill” , to modernize the country’s aviation infrastructure.
Duffy said the $50 billion Trump’s administration is requesting from Congress will replace aging hardware, software and air traffic control towers.
“Give us the resources to build a state-of-the-art air traffic control system,” Duffy said on Friday. “Let’s not do a patchwork fix to a system that’s critical for every single family.” 
AAA reports that 81.5 million people will be traveling for Thanksgiving on Nov. 26, which is slightly down from a year ago. Flyers remain steady at 5.9 million.
