name: Michigan Advance
title: MEA looks to Benson, new Democratic majority for help addressing student behavior
description: Michigan’s largest teachers’ union will be looking to the incoming Democratic legislative majority and the state’s new governor to help educators find solutions to poor student behavior in the classroom, which the Michigan Education Association said could be addressed through a potential mix of pilot programs, appropriations and other solutions identified du[...]
text:
(Stock photo/Getty Images)Michigan’s largest teachers’ union will be looking to the incoming Democratic legislative majority and the state’s new governor to help educators find solutions to poor student behavior in the classroom, which the Michigan Education Association said could be addressed through a potential mix of pilot programs, appropriations and other solutions identified during a recent news conference.
Last week, the MEA presented new data from a survey of more than 4,000 members involved in preK-12 education, conducted Aug. 12-21, 2026. The MEA found that members continue to face challenges with student behavior and that almost all of the respondents surveyed reported at least one negative student behavior experience within the last year. The share of members concerned about student violence toward other students or employees has also risen, the data notes.
Of the key findings, almost half of members surveyed experienced aggressive physical contact with a student. Chronic absenteeism, verbal outbursts, the destruction of teacher or school property, and aggressive threats made by students all weighed in as predominant negative student behavior issues. Between 50% and 83% of those surveyed noted those issues as the most experienced concerns.
Although less frequently reported, more than 32% of respondents said they had experienced aggressive physical contact with a student, evacuations because of unsafe behavior or serious concerns about being physically injured by a student.
Erik Edoff, the MEA’s senior executive director, told reporters during a virtual press call that every student deserves a safe place to learn and that rang true of teachers and educators who spend a great deal of time each day with students.
Michigan needs more behavioral health professionals.

“Michigan educators are increasingly concerned about disruptive and sometimes dangerous behaviors among some of our students, these behaviors threaten both those students’ success and the success of their classmates, as well,” Edoff said. “They’re also forcing too many great educators out of a profession they love, at a time when we need to attract and retain the best and brightest to work in our neighborhood schools and keep our kids successful.”
Edoff added that teachers and school support staff are seeing disruptions among students of all ages and in all kinds of school settings from school buses and classrooms to front offices and school sporting events.
MEA has also said that the contributing factors to newly concerning student behavior issues included mental health challenges, constant access to smartphones and technology and overexposure to social media. Factor in cuts to recreational and recess time, along with a lack of support from communities and families, and the problem becomes more pronounced.
Edoff said MEA is committed to working with its members to address the issue, but he noted that it would also take some serious conversations and work with policymakers to assist them.
“It’s clear from both the surveys and the stories we’ve heard that educators need more resources from policymakers and support from administrators and families,” Edoff said. “Our public schools continue to struggle with inadequate and inequitable funding that leaves classrooms overcrowded and without enough trained quality educators to meet students’ very individualized needs. We must properly fund our neighborhood schools, so we have enough quality educators to help each and every student.”
The Michigan Legislature, through the past two years of divided government and in the previous legislative trifecta years of 2023-24 — when both the state House and Senate and the governor’s office were under Democratic control — has prioritized preK-12 education and made investments in things like school lunches and expanded mental health programs.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
MEA will have a new set of leaders to help them chart a path forward on student behavior in January. The Democrats expanded their majority in the state Senate while also flipping the House after it was in Republican control over the past two years. Gov.-elect Jocelyn Benson is set to hit the ground running after her inauguration early next year. Democrats have by and large made expanding education funding, and more specifically giving it an equitable funding model, during the past few budget cycles.
Michigan Advance asked Edoff if the MEA had a specific appropriation request in mind, and possibly a specific percentage increase over the last few budget years that might help them in their efforts to curb poor behavior.
Edoff said that although it was true that the Legislature had improved on preK-12 funding year over year, money that has helped with the situation, funding over the long road has not kept up with inflation and has not kept up with how schools were funded in the past.
“A large percentage of the funding that we have received is taken up by additional categoricals that go to programs and other things that not all districts benefit from, and healthcare costs,” Edoff said. “Healthcare costs for employees of districts, both our members and other types of jobs, have gone up so dramatically and have eaten into many of the costs or many of the dollars that have flowed in in recent years.”
Doug Pratt, MEA’s director of public affairs, also said that the state must remain conscious that every district is in a different financial situation in terms of what has been invested. State funding becomes strained when you look at different district staffing levels and their ability to recruit through shortages.
“From a global standpoint, we don’t really break this out into a, ‘We need X million dollars to do this,’” Pratt said. “It is a district by district situation. We do need to make sure, overall, that we’re better and more equitably funding public education to catch back up to where we were even 25 years ago, when you adjust for inflation.”
Deb Lotan, executive director of the Avondale/Rochester Education Association, added that intermediate school districts used to have center-based programs, and she said that those no longer exist for the most part in Michigan. Those programs — which gave structured specialized support to students outside the traditional education setting — were situated in students’ home schools, and required more support and additional funding.
“I can’t say that there’s a magic number when it comes to that, but talking to colleagues, there are districts in the state of Michigan that do not have dedicated social workers, like not even a social worker for a district,” Lotan said. “So they have to rely on support from the ISD or outside entities, and that’s important because, as I said at the beginning, social workers don’t have a caseload number. And if you have a district that doesn’t have the financial means to be able to provide a social worker in their district, it costs money.”

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico’s ‘insurer of last resort’ to make all enrollees reapply, director says
description: Roughly 8,000 New Mexico homeowners covered through the state’s “insurer of last resort” will receive notices next year that their policies aren’t being renewed, an official overseeing the high-risk pool announced Friday at a housing conference in Las Vegas.
text:
New Mexican homeowners who receive coverage from the Fair Access to Insurance Requirements Plan will receive notices of non-renewal sometime in 2027, the plan’s executive director announced Nov. 14, 2026, at the Rural Housing Summit in Las Vegas. (Photo by Patrick Lohmann/Source NM)Roughly 8,000 New Mexico homeowners covered through the state’s “insurer of last resort” will receive notices next year that their policies aren’t being renewed, an official overseeing the high-risk pool announced Friday at a housing conference in Las Vegas.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Analisa Sisneros, executive director of the state’s Fair Access to Insurance Requirements Plan, told attendees at the Rural Housing Summit that the plan’s administrators are updating the plan’s software and, in doing so, will issue non-renewal notices to all homeowners who are covered through the policy. 
All policyholders will be able to reapply for the FAIR Plan, Sisneros said, but only after they try again to receive coverage in the regular insurance market. The software update presents an opportunity for a “clean slate” that will help ensure the plan is available to those who most need it for years to come, she said.
The FAIR Plan offers homeowners insurance to those who face challenges getting policies in the private market due to increasingly expensive natural disasters and other factors. While the plan is supposed to provide temporary coverage and serve as the “insurer of last resort,” Sisneros said that some FAIR plan enrollees have been on the plan since the 1990s.
All policyholders will be able to reapply for the FAIR Plan, Sisneros said, but only after they try again to receive coverage in the regular insurance market. The software update presents an opportunity for a “clean slate” that will help ensure the plan is available to those who most need it for years to come, she said.
Analisa Sisneros, second from left, executive director of New Mexican Fair Access to Insurance Requirements Plan, announced Nov. 14, 2026, at the Rural Housing Summit in Las Vegas that homeowners who receive coverage from the Fair Access to Insurance Requirements Plan will receive notices of non-renewal sometime in 2027. (Photo by Patrick Lohmann/Source NM)
The notice of non-renewal, expected sometime next year, will “highly encourage” enrollees to seek coverage elsewhere, Sisneros said.
“But if that is not an option for you, you are more than welcome to come back to the FAIR Plan,” she said Friday. 
The FAIR Plan has seen steadily increasing enrollment in recent years, as well as scrutiny from state lawmakers concerned the plan isn’t adequate or solvent. A spike in private insurers opting not to renew policies across the state has heightened the plan’s importance. 
Homeowners in wildfire-prone counties, in particular, are increasingly turning to the FAIR Plan for coverage, state officials said recently. They’re joining homeowners in areas prone to damaging hail and high winds, such as southeast New Mexico. 
Faced with that trend, Sisneros said Friday that canceling everyone’s policies, at least temporarily, will make sure the plan remains available for those who truly need it. 
“The reimagined FAIR Plan is bringing it into the times and making sure we know what we’re ensuring and that we are not taking on business that in the long term can mess with the FAIR Plan solvency,” she said. “We want to make sure we remain around for years to come.”
Sisneros did not respond to Source NM’s phone call seeking further comment Monday. 
Rep. Anita Gonzales (D-Las Vegas), who convened the homeowners insurance panel where Sisneros made the announcement, told Source NM after the summit Friday that she expects a “lot of kickback” from policyholders who will have to submit new paperwork to apply or potentially see higher premiums as a result of the update. 
But she also said she understands the FAIR Plan administrators’ reasoning.
“I don’t think they’re necessarily trying to kick anybody off. It’s kind of like, ‘Let’s get you restarted,” she said. “This will require them to attempt to get on the market, and if they still get denied, they still have an opportunity to be on the FAIR Plan.”

name: California
title: U.S. Supreme Court rejects Trump’s effort to impose DEI policies on UC researchers
description: The U.S. Supreme Court denied the Trump administration’s appeal of lower court decisions ordering it to restore roughly a billion dollars in UC research grants. UC researchers said their First Amendment rights were violated because Trump cancelled the grants over DEI.
text:
In summary
The U.S. Supreme Court denied the Trump administration’s appeal of lower court decisions ordering it to restore roughly a billion dollars in UC research grants. UC researchers said their First Amendment rights were violated because Trump cancelled the grants over DEI. 


The U.S. Supreme Court rejected the White House’s bid to have the high court review a case that forced the Trump administration to return hundreds of research grants to academics at the University of California.
The court issued the decision today. No justice filed a brief explaining the decision, which is common. 
Lawyers for the U.S. Department of Justice argued that federal agencies had the right to terminate the grants because they ran afoul of the Trump administration’s executive orders on defunding so-called Diversity, Equity and Inclusion efforts, plus research on the effects of global warming. 
But attorneys for the UC researchers depicted that rationale as dangerous to science and to the academics’ constitutional rights. “What begins as material harm – loss of money, staff, graduate and post-doctoral students – quickly becomes expressive harm: the inability to publish research and affect public discourse. This is a quintessential First Amendment violation,” the lawyers for the UC researchers wrote in a legal brief to the high court.
The case is known as Thakur v. Trump and concerns grants on U.S. history, disease research and biology, among many others.Between January and July of last year the White House terminated more than $900 million in grants to UC researchers, including nearly $600 million at UCLA alone. Almost all of those grants were restored after a lower court judge ordered the federal agencies to restore them across multiple court decisions. After the federal government appealed, the 9th Circuit Court of Appeals upheld those decisions that said the White House likely violated the researchers’ First Amendment rights.Agencies terminated the grant funding of researchers through keyword searches of grant applications that used words such as “diversity” or “climate change,” CalMatters previously reported. The Department of Energy cut grants specifically to states that voted for Kamala Harris over Trump in 2024.
Grants issued by the National Institutes of Health also required academics to research a diverse pool of Americans. When the agency terminated a $36 million grant on dementia led by a UC Davis professor in April of last year for focusing on diversity, CalMatters reported that the first Trump administration required a focus on diversity in the grant applications. The National Institutes of Health restored the grant shortly after CalMatters ran its story. 
Some of the research projects the National Science Foundation terminated had nothing to do with diversity and equity initiatives, lawyers for the researchers wrote. They say the foundation targeted grants that included the word “diversity” in describing a scientific approach. Those included projects with titles such as the “Effects of Leaf Diversity on Aquatic Insect Colonizer Diversity” and “Revealing the Vast Diversity Within the Legume-Rhizobia Mutualism.”
Claudia Polsky, a lawyer for the UC researchers, said the Supreme Court’s decision is a boon to similar cases across the country. Lawyers for other researchers whose grants the federal government cancelled are also arguing that the White House violated their First Amendment rights. Those lawyers can point to the fact that the 9th Circuit Court of Appeals agreed with the UC researchers and the Supreme Court rejected the White House’s challenge. Those courts are “not technically bound by anything. But I think they will find it quite persuasive,” Polsky said. She doesn’t think the White House will attempt to appeal again, since the justices showed no dissent in their rejection.She added that this decision directly benefits Cal State professors who sued the Trump administration last month over the termination of National Science Foundation grants.The lawyers for the UC researchers will return to a lower court hearing Tuesday to argue that the Trump administration’s termination of Department of Energy grants were also illegal. That case is technically unrelated to today’s Supreme Court decision.
Legal dispute
A central dispute in the case is determining when the federal government can cancel grant funding. Lawyers for the researchers said that once a grant is awarded to academics — regardless of which administration issued it — the academics should be allowed to complete their research, even if the current administration views the research as a waste of taxpayer money. 
But the Department of Justice was adamant that the federal government can cancel already-funded grants. That’s not a First Amendment violation, the agency argued, because the White House isn’t preventing the researchers from seeking private funding to conduct their research. The UC researchers didn’t break any rules set by Congress in how they carried out their research and complied with detailed guidelines on how to use federal money, the federal agencies affirmed in signed statements this summer. 
But to the Trump administration, that didn’t matter. The agencies terminated the grants anyway because they no longer aligned with the president’s directives.Lawyers for the researchers wrote that the legal precedent argued by the White House would end stability for federal science and humanities research. They argued any project funded for multiple years that extends into the tenure of a new U.S. president would be susceptible to early cancellation. Science cannot operate under that kind of caprice, the lawyers for the researchers argued.
A lower court judge, appointed by Biden, agreed when ordering the agencies to restore the grants. “They face unexpected funding shortfalls, will likely have to lay off staff, and will experience career and reputational harm if they cannot complete their projects. They also must spend time seeking alternate funding, a time-consuming process with little chance of success,” wrote the judge, Rita F. Lin of the U.S. District Court for Northern California.The Department of Justice represented several federal agencies specifically, including the Department of Defense, the Department of Transportation, the National Endowment for the Humanities, the National Institutes of Health, and the National Science Foundation.The lawyers settled with the Environmental Protection Agency over similar issues this year.
Can the White House cancel grants already approved?
Department of Justice lawyers argued that as long as the administration isn’t forcing researchers to adopt the views of the White House in their private affairs, their rights aren’t violated. Lawyers for the researchers blasted that logic. The White House “can point to no case” in which any federal court “has held that the President and federal agencies may terminate grants awarded through a merit-driven competitive process based on the perceived viewpoint of the research,” they wrote in their legal brief urging the Supreme Court to reject the case. 
The legal team for the researchers wrote that the White House is disregarding the processes that Congress established for terminating existing grants. The lawyers for the researchers noted that Congress embedded language in the laws governing the research agencies to encourage research that focused on women, people of color and individuals with disabilities, including at the National Science Foundation. Similar language governs the National Endowment for the Humanities, such as giving “particular regard to scholars, and educational and cultural institutions, that have traditionally been underrepresented.”

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Work at Arkansas site linked to nationwide ground stop of flights
description: Work at a radio communications site in south Arkansas has been identified as a source of the problems that led federal officials to ground all flights in the United States for several hours last week. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy identified a “remote radio facility” in El Dorado where workers were deploying a new router as […]
text:
A plane prepares to land at Newark Liberty International Airport. (Photo by Dana DiFilippo/New Jersey Monitor)Work at a radio communications site in south Arkansas has been identified as a source of the problems that led federal officials to ground all flights in the United States for several hours last week.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy identified a “remote radio facility” in El Dorado where workers were deploying a new router as a source of the communications problems that led to the nationwide ground stop on Friday.
“There was an old fiber line that was going to be decommissioned by our telecom provider. We are moving over to fiber,” Duffy said on NBC’s “Meet the Press” on Sunday. “And what we saw when we turned this facility on was that the router we used was flooding the rest of our network with data.”
Duffy said he wants $50 billion to address the nation’s aging air traffic control system. Bryan Bedford, head of the Federal Aviation Administration, also stressed the importance of airspace modernization during a visit to Northwest Arkansas National Airport in March. 
The FAA identified the El Dorado site and a radar site in Amarillo, Texas as two potential sources of excessive data that flooded the nation’s air traffic control system.
L3Harris, the FAA’s network service provider, had been doing work at the El Dorado site, the agency said. The network stabilized after L3Harris blocked the two locations, and the broadcasting function on new routers was also disabled, the agency said.
“We are supporting the FAA in its investigation to understand the conditions that led to the Nov. 13 ground stop of our nation’s air travel,” L3Harris said Saturday in a statement on its website. “L3Harris takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travelers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously.”
Local officials took the national attention aimed at El Dorado in stride. The El Dorado-Union County Chamber of Commerce shared a link on its Facebook page to a Wall Street Journal article about the site’s role in the ground stop, along with a guide on how to pronounce the city’s name.
The correct pronunciation, the chamber said, is “El Duh Ray Duh.”
“And while we’re at it – tell the masses that our community is growing, we are adding jobs, your children can get their college tuition covered through the El Duh Ray Duh Promise, and we are home to Fortune 200 Retailer Murphy USA,” the chamber’s post said.

name: California
title: California is suing OpenAI over its ‘rogue’ AI agent hack
description: California Attorney General Rob Bonta sued OpenAI, saying its lack of safeguards led to the Hugging Face hack.
text:
In summary
California Attorney General Rob Bonta sued OpenAI, saying its lack of safeguards led to the Hugging Face hack.


California’s attorney general is suing OpenAI, saying a high-profile cybersecurity incident could have been avoided had the company installed proper safeguards.
In July 2026, OpenAI, the maker of ChatGPT, was evaluating internal research models when it discovered that its agents had compromised OpenAI systems and hacked their way into Hugging Face, an online platform where users can submit tools and data related to artificial intelligence.
The incident sparked public debate over the dangers of AI, with some calling the incident a landmark in the development of the tools. Commentators have long worried that incidents involving so-called “rogue” AI agents could damage critical infrastructure or compromise military weapon systems, and some pointed to the incident to demand greater government oversight of AI companies.
Attorney General Rob Bonta’s office announced an investigation into the hack in September. In the suit, filed today, Bonta said the Hugging Face incident “was entirely foreseeable” and the company should be held legally responsible for the incident.
“OpenAI’s actions escalated real-word cybersecurity risks, threatening the safety, health, and well-being of society,” Bonta said in a written statement announcing the suit. 
The attorney general’s office is asking a court to force OpenAI to change its business practices and pay civil penalties.
According to the state, the hack was the result of OpenAI operating dangerous models in a flawed testing environment. Its failure to adequately rein in its agents, the suit alleges, put the public at risk and violated California’s Unfair Competition Law, which is meant to stop companies from using unfair, unlawful, or fraudulent practices.
“The company knowingly tested a dangerous product without proper oversight or safety procedures and misled the public about it — this disregard for public safety violated California law,” Bonta said in the announcement.
In a press conference announcing the suit, Bonta said tools like OpenAI’s have “enormous potential” but “must be developed and designed safely.”
Bonta said the company failed to provide detailed information on dozens of other incidents as well.
“Without proper safeguards and monitoring, these models pose a danger to anything connected to the internet,” he said.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Avangrid’s gas utilities ask CT regulators to increase customer rates
description: Southern Connecticut Gas and Connecticut Natural Gas submitted a notice to PURA requesting a more-than 20% increase in revenue.
text:
Two of Connecticut’s largest natural gas utilities are asking state regulators to increase rates by a combined $256 million over a two-year period.
Attorneys for Southern Connecticut Gas and Connecticut Natural Gas submitted a notice to Connecticut’s Public Utility Regulatory Authority late last week laying out the proposed rate increase, which would represent a more-than 20% increase in revenue across both companies.
The two utilities — both of which are owned by Orange-based Avangrid — told the 5-member regulatory authority that the increases are needed in order to compensate the companies for current operating costs, customer assistance programs, future investments and expiring tax credits.
“CNG and SCG are committed to providing safe, reliable natural gas while keeping bills as affordable as possible,” Frank Reynolds, the president and CEO of both utilities, said in a press release. “Some of what we are addressing today reflects decisions and costs from prior years, while the rest is about what our system needs going forward. Our focus is on putting CNG and SCG on a path that supports continued investment, reliable service and the customers and communities we serve.”
Southern Connecticut Gas serves nearly 213,000 customers in 24 towns and cities located between Westport and Old Saybrook. And Connecticut Natural Gas serves nearly 190,000 customers in the Hartford region and Greenwich. 
In their notice to regulators, the companies noted that part of the proposed rate increase was beyond their control. They are requesting $54 million to cover ongoing customer assistance programs, which are available to low-income ratepayers. And they said they needed another $55 million to make up for expiring tax credits, the benefits of which were previously passed on to utility customers.
The rest of the rate increase, however, is meant to compensate the company for previous operating costs and investments made since 2023. The company is also asking to boost revenue for the company in order cover future investments in their natural gas systems.
“The proposed application therefore reflects two different needs: addressing costs and temporary measures from prior years that are now flowing into rates, and providing the resources necessary to operate and invest in the system going forward,” the utilities’ attorneys wrote. 
The company argued they need to make future investments across those systems in order to replace “non-state-of-the-art” gas mains and service lines. The companies’ lawyers also told regulators they needed to get ahead of “emerging capacity constraints” in parts of their distribution territory, including the gas mains in Granby, Canton, Simsbury and Avon.
The two companies are already facing pushback from the state’s Office of Consumer Counsel, which is responsible for representing utility customers in cases that go before PURA.
The last time Avangrid’s gas utilities asked to increase rates in 2023, the request resulted in a lengthy legal battle that ended with state regulators lowering customers bills.
That legal fight was resolved in September of this year — a fact that did not go unnoticed by the Office of Consumer Counsel.
Claire Coleman, the leader of that office, said the new rate request could increase the monthly bills for an average Connecticut Natural Gas customer by roughly 24% and an average Southern Connecticut Gas customer by 34%.  
“At a time when we are focused on addressing Connecticut’s energy affordability challenges, a request for a 34% increase over a two-year period is completely out of touch with the customers Avangrid serves,” Coleman said. “Connecticut families cannot afford this endless cycle of excessive rate requests and litigation. OCC will continue to oppose these inflated requests and fight to ensure only reasonable costs necessary to provide safe and reliable gas service are approved.”
The rate hike requests come on the heels of the midterm election, in which many voters cited the rising cost of living as one of their most important considerations. 
The attorneys for the two gas utilities acknowledged that reality in their filings with PURA. 
Company officials, they wrote, “recognize that any proposed increase in rates may be difficult for many households and businesses to handle, regardless of the merits of the factors driving the need for a rate increase.” 
The companies are “committed to working with PURA and other stakeholders to balance near-term customer assistance with the resources necessary to maintain safe, reliable and affordable service for customers over time,” they added.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Sen. Janice Weiner reelected to lead Iowa Senate Democrats
description: Iowa Senate Democrats announced Sunday they have reelected Sen. Janice Weiner of Iowa City to serve as Senate Democratic Leader.  Weiner was elected in to the Senate in 2022 and has been the minority leader since 2024, when she replaced former Sen. Pam Jochum.  Iowa’s legislature maintains a Republican majority in both the House and […]
text:
Sen. Janice Weiner, Senate Minority Leader, at a Planned Parenthood Advocates of Iowa and Planned Parenthood North Central States event Feb. 24, 2025. (Photo by Cami Koons/Iowa Capital Dispatch) Iowa Senate Democrats announced Sunday they have reelected Sen. Janice Weiner of Iowa City to serve as Senate Democratic Leader. 
Weiner was elected in to the Senate in 2022 and has been the minority leader since 2024, when she replaced former Sen. Pam Jochum. 
Iowa’s legislature maintains a Republican majority in both the House and Senate following the Nov. 3, 2026 election but with a smaller majority than previous years. 
Unofficial election results show Democrats have 18 seats in the Iowa Senate to Republicans’ 32 seats. The legislature will also be working with Democratic Gov.-elect Rob Sand who will replace Republican Gov. Kim Reynolds in January.

Weiner said she was “honored” to continue serving in the role. 
“I’m thankful for my colleagues’ trust and support,” Weiner said in a news release. “I welcome our new members and look forward to working with our talented and dedicated group to continue growing our caucus. And to echo Governor-elect Sand, Iowans voted for split government and they expect us to work together to deliver on the promise of a better Iowa for all.”
Senate Democrats maintained the rest of their leadership team from 2026 with Sen. Matt Blake, D-Urbandale, as Democratic whip, and Sens. Molly Donahue, D-Cedar Rapids, Renee Hardman, D-West Des Moines, Tom Townsend, D-Dubuque and Cindy Winckler D-Davenport, serving as assistant leaders. Sen. Catelin Drey of Sioux City will also serve as an assistant leader in 2027
House Democrats similarly voted last week to maintain 2026 leadership with Rep. Brian Meyer, D-Des Moines, serving as minority leader. 
Republican leadership in both the House and the Senate in the upcoming legislative session, which begins Jan. 11, 2027 will remain as: House Speaker Pat Grassley, House Majority Leader Bobby Kaufmann, Senate Majority Leader Mike Klimesh and Senate President Amy Sinclair.
Weiner said the election showed that Iowans’ priorities are for legislators to bring down costs, support public education, clean up water, lower cancer rates, bridge gaps in access to healthcare and tackle corruption.
“Our caucus is eager to get to work in this new, more balanced state government,” Weiner said.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: West Virginia National Guard honors killed service member with community service project
description: Seventy members of the West Virginia National Guard cleaned up the picturesque Kanawha Riverfront Monday in honor of specialist Sarah Beckstrom, who was killed last year during a security detail in Washington, D.C.
text:
Adjutant General James Seward and Gov. Patrick Morrisey speak to National Guard members Monday about a community service project commemorating Spc. Sarah Beckstrom, of Summersville, who was killed on a security detail in November 2025. (Photo by West Virginia National Guard)Seventy members of the West Virginia National Guard cleaned up the picturesque Kanawha Riverfront Monday in honor of specialist Sarah Beckstrom, who was killed last year during a security detail in Washington, D.C. 
The guard members assembled at the Gold Star Memorial at the Capitol Complex Monday morning to commemorate Beckstrom, of Summersville, who was shot and killed in November 2025 while she patrolled the streets of the nation’s capital. 
Staff Sgt. Andrew Wolfe was also shot in the attack, but has had a hard fought recovery. The shooter still awaits trial. 
Adjutant Gen. James Seward, of the West Virginia National Guard, said the idea of a commemorative service project was born from conversations had with Beckstrom’s parents. 
“She would be here, standing along with us,” Seward said. “This is what she would have wanted. She wouldn’t have wanted some big fancy memorial service, and so we’re doing this for Sarah today.” 
Guard members cleaned from Kanawha Boulevard to Magic Island Park in Charleston, West Virginia.
Gov. Patrick Morrisey said the community service project would be an example of how the guard helps people in West Virginia. 
“When the project’s finished, it’ll be cleaner and safer because of you,” Morrisey said. “It’s a great example of what partnerships with the guard look like. When the guard, the police, the state, the mayor’s office all come together — we want to have a community united in action, and I hope people across West Virginia take notice of it.” 
Seward said Beckstrom had a strong heart for community service and helping anyone in need — including feeding the homeless. 
“This is solely to honor Sgt. Sarah Beckstrom,” he said. “We love her. We miss her, and these mountaineers will continue to press on.”

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Tennessee governor picks former fed prison official, inmate to lead Correction Department
description: A former federal prison official who served time on a drug charge has been tabbed to lead the Tennessee Department of Correction. Gov.-elect Marsha Blackburn appointed Josh Smith, a former deputy director of the Federal Bureau of Prisons, as Correction Department commissioner, replacing Frank Strada, who resigned from office in October following a second bot[...]
text:
Gov.-elect Marsha Blackburn has named a former federal prison inmate and later, federal prison official, as her commissioner of the Tennessee Department Correction.
Photo of the Morgan County Correctional Complex. (Photo from Tennessee Department of Correction) A former federal prison official who served time on a drug charge has been tabbed to lead the Tennessee Department of Correction.
Gov.-elect Marsha Blackburn appointed Josh Smith, a former deputy director of the Federal Bureau of Prisons, as Correction Department commissioner, replacing Frank Strada, who resigned from office in October following a second botched execution on his watch in Tennessee.
Smith, who spent five years in federal prison on a drug trafficking charge before release in 2003, started a nonprofit agency to help ex-convicts change their lives and received a full pardon from President Donald Trump in 2021. He served on a committee appointed by Gov. Bill Lee to improve recidivism rates. 
“Josh Smith brings a distinctive combination of executive leadership, firsthand correctional experience, and an understanding of the challenges facing our prison system,” said Blackburn. “He has demonstrated the ability to lead large organizations, make difficult decisions, and tackle longstanding problems.”
Josh Smith, newly-appointed as Tennessee Commissioner of Correction by Gov.-elect Marsha Blackburn. (Photo from Office of Gov.-elect Marsha Blackburn)
Smith said in a release he will focus on institutional security, accountability, employee safety, effective community supervision, and preparing prisoners to become productive citizens when released. 
“I look forward to listening to employees, evaluating operations, and working with state leaders and public-safety partners to strengthen the department,” Smith said. 
The appointee did not mention problems with carrying out the death penalty in the release from Blackburn’s transition office.
Under Strada’s leadership, the Department of Correction had two failed executions this year, including the recent botched execution of Christa Pike, who survived two rounds of lethal injections before being hospitalized that night and, ultimately, released. Lee put executions on hold for the rest of 2026 and ordered a third-party investigation that could set the tone for Tennessee’s death penalty protocol, although Blackburn has said she wants to revert to electrocution via electric chair as the primary way to carry out the death penalty.
Senate Corrections Subcommittee members commended Blackburn for accepting their recommendation for the post.



Quotation







His work supporting correctional professionals, his federal leadership experience and his personal journey give him a valuable perspective on that mission.


– Sen. Ed Jackson, R-Jackson


Sen. Ed Jackson of Jackson, a key subcommittee member, said Smith understands that a strong
correctional system has to hold people accountable while preparing inmates for release. 
“His work supporting correctional professionals, his federal leadership experience and his personal journey give him a valuable perspective on that mission,” Jackson said.
Besides botched executions, Smith takes the position amid problems at the state’s Morgan County prison where a guard was stabbed to death after an inmate escaped from his cell by jimmying the door lock.
The state also has dealt with multiple problems at Trousdale Turner, a facility run by the state’s private contractor, CoreCivic, which has been under a civil rights investigation by the Department of Justice for multiple inmate deaths, staff shortages and other problems. 
In addition to Smith, Blackburn has appointed Todd Kaestner as commissioner of Finance and Administration, Commissioner Andy Holt to continue leading the Department of Agriculture, and Mark Ezell to remain as commissioner of Tourist Development.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: Foulkes demands ground stop on new contracts for quasi-public agency executives
description: Gov.-elect Helena Buonanno Foulkes is calling on the state’s quasi-public agencies to hold off on new or extended executive contracts and raises until she takes office in January. “These agencies exist to serve the public, and it’s time they were held to that standard,” Foulkes said in a statement Monday morning, calling the $2.1 million […]
text:
The Rhode Island Airport Corporation’s Board of Directors signed a three-year contract for CEO Iftikhar Ahmad last week that includes a maximum $2.1 million in pay and benefits for fiscal 2027. (Photo by Christopher Shea/Rhode Island Current)Gov.-elect Helena Buonanno Foulkes is calling on the state’s quasi-public agencies to hold off on new or extended executive contracts and raises until she takes office in January.
“These agencies exist to serve the public, and it’s time they were held to that standard,” Foulkes said in a statement Monday morning, calling the $2.1 million annual compensation package recently approved for Rhode Island Airport Corporation CEO Iftikhar Ahmad, “indefensible.”
The airport corporation’s board of directors on Nov. 12 signed a three-year contract for Ahmad that includes a maximum $2.1 million in pay and benefits for fiscal 2027. In addition to a nearly $688,000 base salary, Ahmad will also receive nearly $3.3 million in retention bonuses, divided into six payments over the next three years, plus retirement benefits and a 20% performance bonus, according to the contract, which is retroactive to Oct 13, 2026. The package, which is more than twice the $900,000 in pay and benefits Ahmad received in fiscal 2026 year, was first reported by NBC 10.
A resolution approved by the airport board Nov. 12 details the “significant accomplishments” achieved under Ahmad’s tenure, including an exponential financial turnaround and corresponding credit rating updates, along with expanded service, passengers and infrastructure improvements at Rhode Island T.F. Green International Airport.
“He has elevated every aspect of the airport and has worked tirelessly to achieve an unprecedented rate of growth over the past decade,” Jonathan N. Savage, board chair, said in a Nov. 12 statement.
Ahmad was hired as agency CEO in 2016. He was awarded a 9.2% pay raise and $97,000 performance bonus in September 2025. 
As one of 15 quasi-public state agencies, the airport corporation oversees six state airports — including the state’s main commercial airport in Warwick — with autonomy in financial, leadership and policy decisions. 
However, the seven unpaid members of its board of directors are appointed by the governor, with Senate confirmation. Savage, the airport board’s chairman, was first appointed by then-Gov. Lincoln Chafee in 2014. His current, four-year term expired in June 2025, according to the Department of State website. It is not uncommon for appointed board and commission members to continue serving past their term expiration if no replacement is named. 
Foulkes on Monday said she will order a full review of executive pay across all quasi-public state agencies, and appoint board members who “understand they answer to Rhode Islanders.”
A spokesperson for the airport corporation did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
In announcing the pay raise for Ahmad, the airport board said the payment was “paramount to maintain continuity” as major capital investments and expansion at the Warwick airport continue. 
Before inking a new contract, the board hired consulting firm Korn Ferry to study compensation packages for 25 comparable airport executives. 
A 10-slide Powerpoint presentation from Korn Ferry’s analysis, based on 2025 airport CEO compensation data, projects 2026 pay and benefits ranging from $472,279 to $1.2 million. The presentation does not identify pay by airport, though it categorizes each based on size (small, medium or large) and governance structure. Green is considered a small hub, though its scope is “closer to a medium hub authority,” the presentation states.
Among comparable small hubs, executive pay ranged from $509,723 to just over $1 million. Executives at medium hubs earned between $472,279 and $1.1 million, according to the consultant’s analysis.
Ahmad’s three-year, $3.28 million retention package puts him in the 95th percentile of comparable airport executive retention awards, according to Korn Ferry.
His salary and benefits, which are funded through airport revenues, not state taxpayer dollars, have been a topic of discussion on several recent public agendas for the airport board. And his existing contract expired Oct. 13.
However, Foulkes said the raise was “unjustified,” and indicative of a larger problem with transparency.
“Rhode Island’s quasi-public agencies are created by state law, governed by boards largely appointed by the Governor and confirmed by the Senate, and entrusted with assets and responsibilities that belong to the people of this state,” she said in a statement. “Yet too often they operate with too little transparency and too little accountability.”
Carlos Aramayo, president of UNITE Here Local 26, the union representing concession workers at Green airport, backed Foulkes’ criticism in a separate statement Monday. Aramayo contrasted Ahmad’s raise with the $4.19 to $8.19 hourly wages for airport food and beverage workers, who have gone more than 15 months without a contract.
Other quasi-public agencies include Rhode Island Commerce, Rhode Island Public Transit Authority, the Rhode Island Convention Center Authority and the Quonset Development Corporation. The latter, which governs development in Quonset Business Park in North Kingstown, approved a new compensation package for its managing director in September, according to meeting minutes. The fiscal 2027 contract was not immediately available, although the meeting minutes note a $314,357 base salary, with a 15% performance bonus plus a cost-of-living adjustment.
Jon Carvalho, a spokesperson for Foulkes’ transition team, did not immediately respond to questions, including the new administration’s take on recently-approved raises for other quasi-public agency leaders, and their appointed board members.
Ahmad’s new contract also includes 28 annual vacation days, with the option to be paid out for up to two weeks of unused vacation per year; eight personal days; and 192 hours of sick leave. He also receives a car for “unlimited use” with all operating and maintenance costs covered by the airport corporation.

name: VTDigger
title: Vermont Senate Democrats nominate Andrew Perchlik to be chamber’s next leader
description:
Since Democrats will control a supermajority of seats in the chamber, their choice for the president pro tempore post is likely to get the job. 
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Vermont Senate Democrats nominate Andrew Perchlik to be chamber’s next leader.
text:
Sen. Andrew Perchlik, D/P-Washington, chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee, listens as Rep. Robin Scheu, D-Middlebury, chair of the House Appropriations Committee, testifies before the committee at the Statehouse in Montpelier on Tuesday, Feb. 3, 2026. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger

MONTPELIER — The Vermont Senate’s incoming Democratic caucus chose Andrew Perchlik, a four-term senator from Washington County, as its nominee to be the chamber’s next president pro tempore Monday.
The full Senate will vote in a new president pro tem at the start of the upcoming legislative session in January. But since Democrats won control of a supermajority of seats in the chamber on Election Day, their choice for the top leadership post is likely to get the job, regardless of support or opposition from Republicans.
Perchlik, who lives in Marshfield, would succeed the chamber’s current pro tem, Sen. Phil Baruth, D/P-Chittenden Central, who did not run for reelection this fall.
The pro tem is the Senate’s political leader, who wields significant power over which bills come up for debate on the floor and which committees senators are assigned to. The role is similar to the speaker of the Vermont House.
Perchlik already has one of the Senate’s most powerful jobs: chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee, which writes the state budget. He was first elected to the chamber in 2018; this year, he finished third out of six candidates in the three-member Washington Senate district. Outside of the Legislature, Perchlik works as an energy program manager at the Vermont Department of Public Service.
This story will be updated.

name: Mississippi Today
title: 32 Americans named as Rhodes scholars have variety of interests, from space junk to art history
description: People walk around Oxford University's campus on Sept. 3, 2017, in Oxford, England.
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — A college senior who wants to clean up debris pollution in Earth’s orbit and a student who has researched AI use in healthcare are among the 32 Americans named as 2027 Rhodes scholars.
The winners, who were announced on Saturday, have a variety of interests, from bioelectronics to water scarcity to art history. They were chosen from 238 finalists who emerged from more than 1,000 candidates who received formal endorsements from their colleges and universities for the honor.
The students will attend the University of Oxford in England as part of the Rhodes scholar program, which awards more than 100 scholarships worldwide each year for students to pursue two to three years of graduate studies.
Two students are the first-ever Rhodes scholars from their schools — Prairie View A&M University in Texas and The Citadel — The Military College of South Carolina. Harvard University led the way with four 2027 Rhodes scholars, followed by Yale and Princeton with three each.
The winners include:
Evan Garrison Credit: Emily Grace McCall
Evan Garrison, of Webb City, Missouri, a senior at Mississippi State University majoring in aerospace engineering and mathematics. His research includes designing ways to detect objects in space, with an interest in cleaning up orbital debris known as “space junk.” He plans to study mathematical modeling, scientific computing and global governance and diplomacy at Oxford.
Asuka Koda, of New York City, a senior at Yale University majoring in mathematics and philosophy. She has researched AI adoption in healthcare and has been a health and science writer for CNN. She plans to study social science of the internet and international health and tropical medicine at Oxford.
Michael Bueker, from Wellesley, Massachusetts, a senior at Dartmouth College majoring in biomedical engineering. His research has focused on biodegradable, implantable neural stimulators and other ultrathin bioelectronic devices. He also grows giant pumpkins. At Oxford, he intends to study engineering science.
Elizabeth Koenck, of Aurora, Colorado, a senior at Georgetown University majoring in foreign service. Her research has examined water scarcity problems across the Middle East, North Africa and the Colorado River Basin. She plans to pursue degrees in migration studies and water science, policy and management at Oxford.
Sabrina Soriano, of Azusa, California, a senior at Yale University majoring in art history. Her research includes 19th-century French painting, with a focus on the relationship between art, religion and cultural identity. She plans to study history of art and visual culture and visual, material and museum anthropology at Oxford.
Named after British imperialist and benefactor Cecil John Rhodes, the scholarships were established at Oxford in 1903. The program has more than 8,000 alumni, many of whom have pursued careers in government, education, the arts and social justice.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Corporations are using Trump’s tariff refunds on bonuses rather than reimbursing consumers
description: Connecticut's Stanley Black & Decker is getting at least $298M in tariff refunds. It's going toward corporate bonuses, not repaying shoppers.
text:
This story was originally published by ProPublica, a nonprofit newsroom that investigates abuses of power. Sign up to receive their biggest stories as soon as they’re published.
When Stanley Black & Decker, one of the world’s largest tool companies, got hit with President Donald Trump’s tariffs last year, the firm made clear that it would be sharing the pain with its customers.
The Connecticut-based company raised prices again and again, moves its executives said were necessary because of the new fees on imports. 
Now, after the Supreme Court struck down Trump’s most sweeping tariffs earlier this year, the company is getting at least $298 million refunded. Instead of sharing that bounty with its customers, however, the firm has chosen different recipients: 
Its own leaders. 
The company is one of at least nine that have disclosed that they are using their refunds not to pay back the cash-strapped consumers who generally covered much of the tariff costs through higher prices, but to give bonuses, according to a ProPublica analysis of thousands of securities filings and earnings calls for publicly traded companies.
Other recognizable companies include the owners of discount department stores TJ Maxx and Marshalls and the golf equipment brand Titleist.
Dozens of other firms have said little about how they plan to use the money other than to characterize the windfall as the kind of earnings they use to determine executive bonuses.
The Trump administration has not publicly detailed which companies are getting the roughly $170 billion in refunds or how much they’ve asked for, and it has denied ProPublica’s requests for this information. But reporters found some of these details while reviewing the disclosures of thousands of publicly traded companies.
Some have described vague plans to pay the money forward by, for example, “returning tariff refunds to our members through pricing,” though they generally don’t say whether that involves price cuts or limiting future increases. Others are paying back businesses they sold products to because they had itemized receipts that detailed the tariff markups.
But consumers hoping for refunds appear to be largely out of luck. With the help of artificial intelligence, ProPublica identified companies that said they planned to refund customers with their tariff windfalls. Almost all of them deal with other businesses, not consumers. 
“Executive bonuses are probably the least just way to use this money because it wasn’t anything the executives did that they should be rewarded for. It was a government mistake that resulted in a refund,” said Gregory Germain, a corporate law professor at Syracuse University. “It really explains why it’s so important for the government, when they’re doing something like this, to think it through to make sure consumers don’t pay extra money and not get it back.”
The chain reaction that led to these bonuses began in the first months of Trump’s second term. In February 2025, Trump declared a national emergency over illegal drugs coming in across the border and unilaterally announced new tariffs on goods from the countries he deemed responsible: Canada, Mexico and China. 
Then, in April, he declared a second national emergency, this one over the U.S. trade deficit — the fact that the U.S. was importing more than it exported. Declaring it “Liberation Day,” Trump unveiled a poster in the Rose Garden detailing his most sweeping tariffs yet on goods from more than 100 countries.
Those tariffs remained in place, with some tweaks, until earlier this year when the Supreme Court struck them down, ruling that Trump had needed congressional approval to impose them. 
That left the federal government scrambling to figure out how to refund billions in duties it had collected over the prior year on more than 53 million imported shipments. U.S. Customs and Border Protection set up an online application system. But only the direct payers of the tariffs — called the “importers of record” — are eligible to apply, not the businesses and consumers who took a hit downstream. 
The New York Federal Reserve Bank, which analyzed the prices of a broad swath of goods, found that 26% of the tariff costs were eaten by American customers; a study from Harvard Business School put the estimate at 43%. One study estimated that Trump’s tariffs cost typical American households about $1,000 last year.
The administration and Congress have not placed constraints on how companies use the tariff refunds, though there have been calls to do so. After the Supreme Court ruling, a group of Democratic senators wrote to the president, asking if he would require companies to pass along part of their payments to consumers and assign penalties to those that did not. Doing otherwise, said Sens. Elizabeth Warren, Cory Booker and Peter Welch, would render the refunds “a giveaway to giant corporations that amounts to theft from the middle class.” 
Though Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has denied that the tariffs resulted in significantly higher prices, he has acknowledged the fundamental unfairness of only importers of record getting the refund. “I got a feeling the American people won’t see it,” he said in February at an Economic Club of Dallas event.
Bessent has made the argument that it’s the Democrats who challenged the tariffs in court, not the administration that imposed the tariffs, who are responsible for the transfer of wealth from American consumers to companies. 
“The Democratic attorney generals who filed a ridiculous lawsuit against this administration wanted the money to go back to the payer of record,” he said at a press conference. “If I hear another Democratic legislator make the inane remark, ‘The American people should get the money’ — the American people had the money in the U.S. Treasury and we were forced to give it back.”
In some cases, companies have said that they will be splitting at least some of their refund checks with their customers. ProPublica’s analysis shows these companies’ customers are generally other businesses, not average consumers. Among them is Varex Imaging Corp. in Utah, which sells X-ray imaging components for medical businesses and cargo screeners. Varex and firms like it have not elaborated on why they are passing along refunds, but trade experts suspect these business-to-business vendors have detailed contracts that itemize tariff costs.
Shipping companies, like UPS and FedEx, have set up online portals for customers seeking refunds. Though the firms are technically importers of record, they imported goods on behalf of businesses and individuals that paid them to ship products. The companies are itemizing how much customers paid in tariffs and reimbursing them.
A series of lawsuits are attempting to force companies that sell directly to consumers to share some of their refunds. Dozens of firms have been sued, including big-box stores Walmart and Target and apparel companies such as Nike and Lululemon. Apparel and leather costs were some of the hardest hit by Trump’s tariffs. Legal analysts have cast doubt on whether these lawsuits will succeed, though some trade experts have speculated that businesses that used the tariffs as cover to raise prices more than they needed to might settle to avoid embarrassing disclosures. 
One of the companies facing a lawsuit is Stanley Black & Decker, the toolmaker that ProPublica found was using some of its refund on bonuses. The named plaintiff is a Wisconsin resident who bought a handheld blower, an impact wrench, a hedge trimmer and other tools from the company last year, but the lawsuit seeks to represent thousands of other customers as well. 
“Unless restrained by this Court,” the complaint reads, the company “stands to recover the same tariff payments twice — once from consumers through tariff-inflated prices and again from the federal government through tariff refunds.”
On multiple occasions, the company has acknowledged publicly that it was raising prices because of the tariffs.
The month before the November 2024 election, as Trump was campaigning on dramatic new tariffs, the toolmaker’s then-CEO, Donald Allan Jr., told shareholders that Stanley Black & Decker was preparing for the possibility. “Obviously, coming out of the gate, there would be price increases associated with tariffs that we put into the market,” he said during an earnings call. Then, a few months after Trump unveiled his tariffs, Allan said his team was “remaining focused on executing our robust plan designed to mitigate tariffs” that he said included “targeted pricing actions to improve our gross margin.” Later that year, his successor as chief executive, Chris Nelson, described more price hikes: “We are implementing a second price increase during the fourth quarter to maintain our innovation and brand investments, given the pressures resulting from tariff-related cost increases.”
In its more recent disclosures, the company has been vague about how much of its refund was going to executives, simply saying that some of that gain “was partially offset by directly attributable costs for variable incentive compensation.” “Incentive compensation” is a term the toolmaker uses to describe bonuses. 
The company has not responded to the allegations in the lawsuit brought by the Wisconsin resident and did not answer ProPublica’s questions about who is getting paid the bonuses, how much they’re worth and whether customers should be reimbursed.
Securities experts who reviewed the disclosures for ProPublica said it appeared the windfall boosted the company’s profits, which factor into formulas that help determine bonus pay for executives and other employees.
“It wasn’t the executive that triggered that extra profit, so why should their compensation go up?” Germain, the corporate law professor said. “This is one of many examples where these formulas don’t do what they should do.”
The company’s leaders, securities experts said, could have given money back to consumers or lowered prices. Retail giant Burlington Stores, formerly known as Burlington Coat Factory, appears to have done just that. 
CEO Michael O’Sullivan recently said the company got $55 million in tariff refunds and “rather than taking a one-time boost to earnings” the company plans “to deliver even sharper values to our shoppers,” 
“Over the last few years, the rising cost of living has made life difficult for many customers,” O’Sullivan said, adding that the coming discounts meant investors should expect the “direct impact of tariff refunds to be neutral.” 
A company spokesperson confirmed to ProPublica that none of its tariff refund will be going to bonuses.
Not so for other companies.
Acushnet, the Massachusetts golf equipment company that includes the brand Titleist, disclosed an “incentive compensation expense of approximately $12.0 million” out of its refund. Acushnet declined to respond to questions from ProPublica.
TJX, the Massachusetts parent company of TJ Maxx and Marshalls, said it got back $331 million, but as a result, it “accrued incremental expenses of $112 million for year-end incentive compensation and discretionary bonuses for eligible Associates globally.”
The company declined to answer questions from ProPublica about how far down the chain of command the bonuses would go and how much of them would be reserved for top managers. “Given that this is an accrual, and we have not reached the end of our current fiscal year, we have not disclosed any breakout beyond this,” a spokesperson said. The company also declined to say whether it would lower prices or pay back customers with the rest of its refund, saying only that “the remaining amount will be used to support our future growth.” 
ProPublica’s examination of tariff refunds was limited to publicly traded companies, which are required to disclose detailed financial information. None of the companies that said they are using the money for bonuses have ever said they planned to refund customers. How private companies are using their refunds is unclear because they aren’t normally required to disclose such information. 
Nick Guest, an accounting professor at Cornell University who has studied executive compensation, said the argument for granting leaders bonuses based on the tariff refunds could go both ways. 
“If they were penalized for something out of their control,” he said, referring to earnings hits caused by Trump’s tariffs last year, rewarding them now “seems reasonable.”
“But you could say the same thing about customers. If they were penalized, then is it reasonable that they’re not getting rewarded now?” Guest asked. The companies, he said, are “not obligated to give refunds or reduce prices, but doing so could certainly build goodwill with customers.”

title: Flathead County Attorney named district court judge
description: Gov. Greg Gianforte appointed Travis Ahner to replace Flathead County District Court Judge Amy Eddy, who won the election to the Montana Supreme Court this month. text:
The Flathead County Courthouse, which houses the county's administrative offices, pictured on Dec. 31, 2024. (Micah Drew, Daily Montanan)Gov. Greg Gianforte appointed Travis Ahner to replace Flathead County District Court Judge Amy Eddy, who won the election to the Montana Supreme Court this month. Gianforte made the announcement Friday.
“Travis is an accomplished attorney who will bring his experience serving Flathead County to the bench,” Gianforte said in a statement. “As a native Montanan who has served his state and community for over a decade, I trust that he will apply the law in an objective and consistent manner.”
Ahner, a graduate of both Carroll College and the University of Oregon School of Law, will serve on the Eleventh Judicial District Court which cover’s Montana’s fourth most populous county. Ahner has served as Flathead County Attorney since 2018 and ran unopposed to retain that position in 2026.
The Flathead County Commissioners will appoint a replacement.
Montana Supreme Court Chief Justice Cory Swanson notified the governor on Aug. 25 of the vacancy on the court following Eddy and Flathead District Court Judge Dan Wilson both running for the same state Supreme Court seat.

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: State Superintendent Jill Underly requests $2.75 billion, new school funding system
description: Wisconsin State Superintendent Jill Underly is proposing that the state spend an additional $2.75 billion on Wisconsin’s schools and make major changes to the education funding formula to take the burden of paying for  schools off local property taxpayers. “It’s time to fix Wisconsin’s school funding formula,” Underly said in a two-minute video posted to […]
text:
“It's time to fix Wisconsin’s school funding formula,” Underly said in a two-minute video posted to social media Friday. Underly speaks to reporters after delivering her sixth State of Education address.  (Photo by Baylor Spears/Wisconsin Examiner)Wisconsin State Superintendent Jill Underly is proposing that the state spend an additional $2.75 billion on Wisconsin’s schools and make major changes to the education funding formula to take the burden of paying for  schools off local property taxpayers.
“It’s time to fix Wisconsin’s school funding formula,” Underly said in a two-minute video posted to social media Friday. “The era of operating referendums needs to come to an end. Our schools shouldn’t have to go back to their communities time and time again, asking property taxpayers for more money because of a broken school funding formula.” 
Wisconsin public schools have relied increasingly on property tax increases sought at the ballot box through referendum requests to meet an array of costs, including staff pay, course offering, electric and water bills.
According to a Wisconsin Policy Forum report published Friday, about 58% of 155 school referendum requests were approved in 2026 — a steep dropoff in approval rates during even-year elections. Typically, there is a higher rate of approvals during presidential and midterm election years, but this was the lowest approval rate in an even-year since 2010. 
The report also notes that a higher proportion of requests are operational rather than building capital requests. In previous years, there’s been about an even divide between the types of requests, but this year, about 80% of requests were for operations. The report concluded that the turn to operational referendums “signals the fiscal stress that some school districts are facing.” 
“It arises from multiple sources, including increased staffing to meet rising student needs, declining student enrollment, and a tight labor market and especially high inflation after the pandemic’s peak,” the report states. “State policy also has played a primary role.” 
Despite school districts’ needs, the approval rate for operational requests, 54%, was lower than the overall rate.
Underly is seeking to shift a larger portion of education costs to the state. 
Democratic state lawmakers and Gov.-elect David Crowley will write and approve the next state budget, but the process of drafting it starts with agencies putting forth their own proposals. 
Underly’s request for the 2027-29 budget includes a slate of changes to the way that schools are funded. 
Under her proposal, school districts would receive a significant increase to their school revenue limits, which cap the amount that districts can bring in through a combination of property taxes and state aid each year. There would be a boost of $1,108 per student in the first year of Underly’s budget and an additional $374 per student in the second year. 
The increases would be in addition to the $325 per student annual increases that school districts received through Gov. Tony Evers’ 400-year budget veto in the 2023 budget. The agency says that the increases are meant to help schools catch up with inflation. Inflationary increases to revenue limits were eliminated in 2009 during the recession, and since then, increases to revenue limits have been based on lawmakers’ appetite to provide them.
Underly’s proposal would once again tie future increases to the rate of inflation. 
The state’s special education reimbursement rate would be raised to 50% in the first year of the DPI  budget proposal and 60% in the second year. 
Another shift Underly proposed is making special education support a “sum sufficient” allocation, meaning that the state would guarantee a set reimbursement rate even if costs changed, as opposed to a “sum certain” allocation, where the state offers is a fixed amount of money that might or might not meet its projected rate of reimbursement, depending on costs.
Wisconsin Public Education Network Executive Director Heather DuBois Bourenane said in a statement that Underly’s proposal “takes a serious step toward addressing the root of the problem with Wisconsin’s unfair and inadequate funding formula.” 
“Wisconsin voters signaled last week that it’s time for Wisconsin to catch up to the rest of the nation and stop playing politics with school budgets while our kids and local taxpayers pay the price,” DuBois Bourenane said. 
Republicans have controlled of the state Legislature since Underly took office in 2021, and  often ignored her budget proposals and declined to invite her to make presentations to the legislative budget committee. 
Underly’s proposal this year could get more serious consideration from Crowley and Democrats who will be leading the budget writing process, but it will be in competition with a variety of other priorities and it’s unclear how much of Underly’s $2.75 billion proposal will make it into the final budget. 
The plan also seeks to help disadvantaged districts by shifting nearly $2 billion to Wisconsin’s equalization aid formula.
The equalization aid formula considers a number of factors including number of students, operational and debt service costs, and local property valuations. 
Equalization aid tends to provide districts with lower property wealth with more aid. Under the plan, districts that could potentially lose aid would be provided with a one-time payment.
The agency is also proposing that the state apply an additional 20% funding weight for economically disadvantaged students and English learners.
The Wisconsin Policy Forum report noted that “the same voter concerns about affordability widely seen as a major factor in sweeping Democrats into power appear to have played a material role in depressing referendum approval rates.”
DPI’s budget presentation asserts that the plan could be implemented without increasing the statewide property tax levy.
Affordability is a top priority for Crowley and incoming Democratic lawmakers. The state will enter 2027 with a $3 billion budget surplus, which could be tapped to address affordability  issues. It’s a much different financial position than in 2009, the last time Democrats had control of the state Senate, Assembly and governor’s office and the state had a $6 billion budget deficit.
Democrats have said that investing in schools could help bring down property taxes. Incoming Assembly Speaker Greta Neubauer has said that they want to stop the cycle of referendum requests to property taxpayers, make changes to the funding formula and provide free schools to help bring down families’ grocery costs.
“I think it’s possible that we will propose some changes in the school funding formula, but our No. 1 priority is to get kids and families the resources that they need,” Neubauer said. 
However, other Democrats, including incoming Senate Majority Leader Dianne Hesselbein, have discussed wanting to study potential changes to education funding and Gov.-elect Crowley has suggested he might appoint a blue ribbon commission to look at taxation.
In her video, Underly said the state does not need to study the issue further. 
“We don’t need to start from scratch. We don’t need another committee. We don’t need more rounds of studies or a series of proposals,” Underly said. “We know what needs to change, and we have the framework to do it. Now, we need state leaders to come together and put the solution into action.”

Shirley Lee SwensonDecember 30, 1936 – November 6, 2026Logan, UtahShared by: Schwab Mortuary & CrematoryShirley Lee Walker Swenson passed away peacefully at the age of 89 on November 6, 2026 in Logan, Utah. Born December 30, 1936 in Marvel, Colorado Shirley’s life was a testament to faith and family.
She met her loving sweetheart, Calvin in Afton, Wyoming, they married January 24, 1958. There were 10 children before they made their big move to BC, Canada in 1971, with 6 more arriving in the years following. Their posterity is hard to match, leaving this world with (including spouses) 29 children, 132 grand children, 150 great grandchildren, 9 great great grandchildren.
Anyone who knew Shirley knew of her many, many talents. She was a singer, dancer, pianist, seamstress, painter, Gardner, chef, baker, writer, crafter, researcher, and so much more and loved using her skills to add creative beauty to the world.
In the early 1990’s she put some of these skills to work in a new adventure, opening a craft shop/restaurant. It was an extra busy and exciting time in her life.
In 2013 she went on a senior service mission for the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-Day Saints, serving in the Family History Department in Salt Lake City, Utah. She loved it very much, combining her passions in faith and genealogy and enjoyed meeting new friends, learning new things, and having new experiences.
A life well lived and full of love, Shirley leaves behind an amazing legacy through her children: Jim (Argina), Anne (JT), Deborah (Don), Michael, Shane (Renee), Matt (Coreen), Weston, Sharon, Tamra (Mark), Amy (Nate), Josh (Corrine), Mindy (Jesse), Jeannie (Ron), Lisa (Scott), Lucy (Todd), and Kriket (Dion).
She will be deeply missed. Her memory will live on in the many who loved her and whose lives have been enriched by her warm and loving presence.








Lydia M. ThompsonOctober 9, 1944 – November 9, 2026Glenns Ferry, IdahoShared by: Vase Funeral HomeLydia M. Thompson, 82, a beloved wife, mother, and cherished member of the Glenns Ferry, Idaho, community, passed away peacefully on Monday, November 9, 2026 at the University of Utah Medical Center, Salt Lake City, Utah.
She was born October 9, 1944, in Wendell, Idaho, she lived a life full of love and service.
Educated in Nampa, Idaho, Lydia was a dedicated housewife who gave wholeheartedly to her family and community. She served two years on City Council in Glenns Ferry, Idaho, where she was also an active member of the Glenns Ferry Gem Team. Her kind heart led her to volunteer at the Glenns Ferry Food Bank and serve as an Emergency Medical Technician for the Glenns Ferry Ambulance Department.
Lydia found great joy in travel, especially to the family cabin in Silver City, Idaho. Her most treasured moments were those spent with her family and friends, particularly her grandchildren, whom she loved dearly.
Lydia is survived by her devoted husband, Glenn D. Thompson, and their loving daughter, Kelle Kathleen Grube and husband Mathew, all of Rock Springs, Wyoming. She also leaves behind her sister, Joyce Wariner of Draper, Utah; two treasured grandchildren, Echo Maxwell and husband Brandon and Jeremy Grube and wife Danielle; and six adored great-grandchildren, John Maxwell, Hayden Maxwell, Bayleigh Grube, Anastasia Grube, Camden Grube, and Easton Grube.
She was preceded in death by her parents, Arthur J. Shaw and Alta Shaw; her brother, James Shaw; her sister, Linda Vail; her maternal grandparents, John and Edith Johnson; and her paternal grandparents, John and Lydia Shaw.
Cremation will take place; a Private Family Service will be conducted at a later date.
Condolences and memories may be shared with the family at www.vasefuneralhomes.com
As we remember Lydia, may we carry forward her legacy of love, service, and generosity.
