name: West Virginia Watch
title: WV Supreme Court upholds admonishment of judge who spoke publicly about CPS understaffing
description: The West Virginia Supreme Court has decided to admonish a well-respected judge after he raised alarm bells publicly about a worrying shortage of Child Protective Services workers in his area.
text:
The West Virginia Supreme Court of Appeals upholds admonishment of Third Judiciary Circuit Court Judge Tim Sweeney after he raised issues about Child Protective Services shortages in his judicial district. (Photo courtesy of the West Virginia Supreme Court of Appeals)The West Virginia Supreme Court has decided to admonish a well-respected judge after he raised alarm bells publicly about a worrying shortage of Child Protective Services workers in his area.
Third Circuit Judge Tim Sweeney’s concerns about CPS staffing were legitimate, Supreme Court Chief Justice C. Haley Bunn wrote in a Nov. 12 opinion, but she said the judge’s actions were outside the bounds of rules governing judicial conduct. 
Justice C. Haley Bunn
“We readily acknowledge that Judge Sweeney has never been disciplined as a lawyer or judge despite many years of service. He was cooperative and forthright in this matter, and his misconduct was neither self-promoting nor dishonest,” Bunn wrote. “And while his motivations do not justify his actions, we find that an admonishment adequately deters similar misconduct in the future and is a proportionate sanction for Judge Sweeney’s conduct viewed in its totality.”
“That said, we have no doubt that Judge Sweeney had honorable motives and commendable concern for protection of the children in his circuit; this Court has expressed similar concern regarding understaffing,” the Chief Justice also wrote.
Last February, Sweeney ordered state health officials, including the former Human Services secretary, to report to the Ritchie County Courthouse and receive assignments as CPS workers. Sweeney said that local CPS workers were overworked and understaffed, leading to missed deadlines and treatment for children.
Sweeney contacted Ogden Newspapers reporter Steven Allen Adams about the issue, and Adams was the first to report on the order. Sweeney argued that he had an ethical duty to bring attention to the state’s CPS staffing crisis. 
The judge’s contact with a reporter over the matter landed him in hot water with the West Virginia Judicial Investigation Commission. The group admonished Sweeney, saying he violated five judicial conduct rules, including releasing judicial statements on pending and impending cases and admonished him. 
Sweeney objected to the commission’s admonishment, arguing that he spoke about systemic issues like CPS staffing, not confidential information about children’s cases. Human Services officials contacted Sweeney within hours of receiving the order and addressed staffing issues.
The state Supreme Court upheld the Judicial Investigation Commission’s admonishment. 
Justice Bunn, writing for the court, concluded that Sweeney committed seven total violations of the state Code of Judicial Conduct. 
“No part of a court’s charge to prioritize abuse and neglect proceedings includes the authority to use judicial powers and improper publicity to pressure the State to address an issue of its choosing and to its subjective satisfaction outside of a justiciable controversy,” Bunn wrote.
“While Judge Sweeney’s conduct happened to concern a matter that elicits universal agreement— the well-being of children — judges who stray so far outside their role such as to violate the Code are not immunized from discipline based on the popularity or success of their misconduct.”
Sweeney told Ogden Newspapers on Friday that he would accept his admonishment, but did not regret his actions regarding CPS understaffing. 
“Sometimes you just have to take a punch for the kids,” Sweeney said. “Abused and neglected children were helped and shortcomings were addressed. That was and continues to be my goal.”
Sweeney was also admonished for social media activity not related to the CPS staffing issues. Bunn said that Sweeney’s social media, which included sharing a fundraiser repost and law enforcement hiring posts, could create “an appearance of bias.” It called Sweeney’s impartiality into question, the Chief Justice wrote.

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Tennessee Gov.-elect Marsha Blackburn expected to prioritize closing of primaries
description: Tennessee Gov.-elect Marsha Blackburn will prioritize legislation to close primary elections in an effort to stop crossover voting, creating party conflict. The matter has caused in-fighting for years among Republicans who hold supermajorities in the state House and Senate and the governor’s office.  “Governor-elect Blackburn will work with the General Assem[...]
text:
Gov.-elect Marsha Blackburn will push to close partisan primaries, a spokesman for her office said. (Photo by John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)Tennessee Gov.-elect Marsha Blackburn will prioritize legislation to close primary elections in an effort to stop crossover voting, creating party conflict.
The matter has caused in-fighting for years among Republicans who hold supermajorities in the state House and Senate and the governor’s office. 
“Governor-elect Blackburn will work with the General Assembly to ensure that only Republicans vote in Republican primaries and, likewise, only Democrats vote in Democratic primaries. Closing primaries ensures that each party’s nominees reflect the values and principles of their respective parties,” Todd Rapp, spokesperson for Blackburn’s transition team, told the Lookout in response to questions.
Technically, primaries are supposed to be closed already, as voters are asked which party affiliation they’ll be voting with during primaries. But those are rarely, if ever, enforced.
Republican leaders have accused Democrats of voting in primaries to defeat certain candidates over the last couple of decades since the GOP gained control over the legislature as well as congressional seats.
But moderate Republicans believe restrictions could hurt the party and voter participation.



Quotation







I think it’s bad for democracy. We’re cutting people out from voting that are independents.


– Sen. Richard Briggs, R-Knoxville


Republican Sen. Richard Briggs of Knoxville, chairman of the State and Local Government Committee, told the Lookout he believes party registration could push independents out of the voting booth and put primaries in the hands of extremists on the left and right. Briggs said he understands that Blackburn is making it a priority but added that he expects “varied opinion” from lawmakers.
“I think it’s bad for democracy. We’re cutting people out from voting that are independents,” Briggs said.
Rep. Chris Todd, a Jackson Republican, said he has spoken with the Blackburn camp and understands it is a “priority” with the governor-elect.
“I’ve encouraged them to start with where we left off earlier this year with that bill,” which went through several revisions in working with the Secretary of State’s Office and Elections Administrator Mark Goins, Todd said.
Todd said he’s heard more “excitement” about the bill, and little, if any, “objection,” especially among Republicans. He said Democrats have told him the state needs the restriction.
Under current guidelines, Todd said, primary votes are relying on a person’s “emotional state” the day they enter the ballot box, whether they’re “pledging allegiance” to the party that day, which can change.
Federal lawsuit filed over new Tennessee law requiring polling places to warn voters against voting in the ‘wrong’ primary

Primaries are designed for private organizations, and for a voter to say, “I’m going to identify with the other side is less than genuine,” Todd said, “unless they have truly changed their mindset and literally agree with that party.” Trying to cross over and influence the outcome of an election “is not right, and I think everybody knows it’s not fair,” Todd said.
Gary Humble, founder of Tennessee Stands, an advocate for closing primaries, said he “couldn’t ever imagine any reason Marsha Blackburn would reach out” to him but said he heard her say  multiple times during her campaign that she supports closing primaries.
“I know Republicans across the state have wanted that, and the Tennessee Republican Party for quite a few years has wanted that, so let’s see if she’s actually going to do it,” said Humble, who serves on the Tennessee Stands board but is no longer involved in the group’s daily operations. 
A measure that would have required party registration died in the Senate State and Local Government Committee in 2025 when it failed to receive enough support to garner a vote. State Sen. Adam Lowe of Calhoun failed to drum up enough votes to pass it earlier this year.
Even though ultra-conservative groups have pushed for party registration and even measures for punishing those who cross over to vote, some Republicans want to keep primaries open to pick up votes when no Democrat is running against them in the general election.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: Who will be the NC Senate’s next leader and money man?
description: An election that only 50 North Carolinians will get to vote in will be hugely consequential for what happens in state government for the next two years.  Senate Republicans, who seem likely to hold onto a slim one-vote majority in 2027, will decide soon which person they’re going to nominate to lead the chamber next […]
text:
North Carolina Senate Leader Phil Berger. R-Rockingham, sits on the Senate floor during debate over a new Republican-led congressional map on Oct. 20, 2025. (Photo: Galen Bacharier/NC Newsline)An election that only 50 North Carolinians will get to vote in will be hugely consequential for what happens in state government for the next two years. 
Senate Republicans, who seem likely to hold onto a slim one-vote majority in 2027, will decide soon which person they’re going to nominate to lead the chamber next year. That nominee will go to a full Senate vote when the new legislative session starts next year. 
One of the Senate leader’s behind-the-scenes jobs is to raise money to help Republican state Senate candidates win elections. It’s not the Senate leader’s only role, of course. But it’s considered important. 
Outgoing Senate leader Phil Berger, R-Rockingham, has held the title and the power for 15 years. Berger lost his primary to Sam Page, who retired as Rockingham sheriff after 28 years in that post. 
‘The voters have spoken’: NC Sen. leader Phil Berger concedes to primary rival Sam Page

Here’s how much each of the Republican senators vying to lead the chamber contributed to the N.C. Senate Majority Fund political action committee, according to most recent campaign finance reports filed with the state Board of Elections. The fund, as the name says, is used to help Republican candidates for Senate. 

Sen. Brent Jackson of Sampson County raised $1.2 million and contributed $800,000 to the Senate Majority Fund. Jackson is president and CEO of a farming company and co-chairs the Senate budget committee. 
Sen. Todd Johnson of Union County raised about $862,500 for the election and contributed $335,000 to the GOP Senate fund. Johnson owns an insurance agency and is a co-chair of the Senate Commerce and Insurance Committee. 
Sen. Ralph Hise of Mitchell County raised $427,500 and contributed $310,120 to the PAC. Hise works at UNC-Asheville and is another Senate budget committee co-chair. 
Sen. Jim Burgin of Harnett County raised about $308,500 and gave $225,000 to the majority PAC. Burgin is president of an insurance company and is a co-chair of the Senate Health Committee. 

Berger raised about $3 million this year, but spent most of it on his own primary. 
In the last election cycle, through mid-October in 2024, Berger had raised nearly $3 million, and had given more than $2 million to the PAC.

name: WyoFile
title: Wyoming Boys’ School employee thought he had a ‘good relationship’ with former resident suing him for alleged abuse
description:
Another staff member's testimony painted a different picture of Chivers-King’s experience.
The post Wyoming Boys’ School employee thought he had a ‘good relationship’ with former resident suing him for alleged abuse appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
CASPER—Before Blaise Chivers-King sued him for alleged abuse at the Wyoming Boys’ School, employee Mike Nelson thought he had a positive connection with the former resident. 
“Up until the filing of this lawsuit, I would have sworn that I had a good relationship with Blaise,” Nelson said Friday in the trial spurred by Chivers-King’s lawsuit. Nelson, who worked as a risk management officer, a dorm director and a dorm supervisor when Chivers-King was at the school, testified that Chivers-King called him at home twice one Halloween when he was a resident. “I allowed staff to let Blaise call me direct at home” if they thought it would prevent him from escalating, Nelson said. Chivers-King also called Nelson twice after he had left the school, according to Nelson. 
Chivers-King is one of six former boys’ school residents who sued school staff in 2024. The school, which detains delinquent boys ages 12 to 21, is a 38-acre residential facility near Worland that’s overseen by the Wyoming Department of Family Services. Chivers-King, who spent time at the boys’ school between 2020 and 2022, alleged school staff violated his 14th Amendment rights by placing him in isolation, using excessive force and infringing on due process. He accused Nelson of unnecessarily placing him in isolation. 
Nelson’s testimony portraying Chivers-King’s time in isolation as humane was challenged by another staff member’s testimony who said the teenager’s condition degraded. Spotty record keeping also raised questions about just how much isolation Chivers-King experienced. 
A surveillance camera feed shows a solitary confinement room at the Wyoming Boys’ School in Worland. The room has a small black box over the toilet seat to protect student privacy. (Lauren Miller/Casper Star-Tribune)
A central piece of evidence Chivers-King’s attorneys have presented to the jury are logbook entries that record staff’s interactions with the former resident while he was confined on multiple occasions in cinderblock detention rooms at the state facility. 
Based on those entries, Chivers-King often interacted with other people for less than an hour a day and was only let out of the room to take a shower. Chivers-King’s attorneys showed the jury documents that outlined a schedule showing activities that a day in detention was supposed to include, such as school and reading assignments and physical exercise. They contrasted that with logbook entries, which didn’t reflect that Chivers-King engaged in those activities most days he was in detention, nor do they show that a mental health practitioner visited him when he was harming himself.
Nelson testified that the logbook “is incredibly incomplete” — some staff just noted that they checked Chivers-King, while others added more details. Regardless, he said that staff were “checking in with Blaise regularly, often,” including having conversations with him. “About as much as Blaise would allow, staff would be interacting with him.” 
Throughout the trial, Chivers-King’s attorneys have often brought up an incident in which Nelson made Chivers-King clean his own blood after the former resident had been banging his head against the wall in a detention room. “There’s an obvious biohazard present,” Nelson said when a defense attorney asked him why he made Chivers-King clean the blood. “It’s the safest way to clean a biohazard.” 
Robin McIntosh, a former boys’ school employee who worked at the facility from 2007 until March 2026, when he was put on administrative leave, painted a different picture of Chivers-King’s time in detention. 
McIntosh testified that staff confined Chivers-King alone in detention rooms “very frequently” and kept him there for far too long. “He would actively degrade the longer he was in there,” said McIntosh, who said in his deposition that he was put on administrative leave for encouraging another student to sue the school. “It was a good excuse to keep him in there because he wasn’t meeting expectations.” 
Defense attorneys suggested McIntosh may have been motivated to speak against the school because of conflicts with staff during his time at the facility. 
According to McIntosh, staff should have noted in the logbook when they opened the detention room door to visit Chivers-King and if a medical professional had visited him. McIntosh testified that staff would antagonize Chivers-King. “It was cultural,” he said. “Sometimes staff would make degrading comments to escalate a kid.” 
When an attorney for Chivers-King asked him why he agreed to be a witness, McIntosh said he “felt that it’s important to show what was happening inside the facility.” 
“What was going on inside the facility was greatly hidden from the public,” he said.

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: State Farm to pay $45M after Oklahoma insurance investigation
description: State Farm Fire and Casualty Co. will pay a $45 million settlement after a state insurance department investigation found it failed to properly pay roof damage claims by Oklahoma customers. The state’s incoming insurance commissioner, Republican Bob Sullivan, said he was still learning details on Friday but worried the settlement may take some flexibility ou[...]
text:
Oklahoma Insurance Commissioner Glen Mulready speaks at a press conference April 24, 2026 after surveying damage to an Enid neighborhood following a tornado. (Photo by Emma Murphy/Oklahoma Voice)State Farm Fire and Casualty Co. will pay a $45 million settlement after a state insurance department investigation found it failed to properly pay roof damage claims by Oklahoma customers.
The state’s incoming insurance commissioner, Republican Bob Sullivan, said he was still learning details on Friday but worried the settlement may take some flexibility out of any regulatory approach to State Farm under his administration.
The settlement calls for the Illinois-based insurance company, which has been the focus of hundreds of lawsuits, to let customers with wind and hail damage ask for an independent review if they had claims closed without payment from 2021 to 2025.
State Farm is Oklahoma’s top homeowners insurer, with more than 258,000 customers and $785.9 million in homeowners premiums in 2025. Its state market share in that category is more than 30%.

State Farm’s settlement includes at least $35 million for customer claims. The company will pay $10 million for new grants under the Insurance Department’s Strengthen Oklahoma Homes program. State Farm will also pay $2.86 million in fines and examination expenses.
The agency’s examination report said a review of claims showed the company closed some cases without notification or the paperwork. It also failed to settle claims where the damage was clear, the report found. The examination included reviews by professional engineering firms.

“In reviewing materials for this report, the examiners relied upon records provided by the company, inspection reports of storm damage to claimants’ roofs provided by the independent third-party engineer, and public court documents from litigation involving the company in the state of Oklahoma,” the report said.

The report noted that State Farm provided some documents as part of the discovery process in several ongoing lawsuits that examiners requested but did not provide during their examination.
The market examination comes after reporting by Oklahoma Watch showed the state was an outlier among surrounding states when it came to high homeowner premium costs. Newly unsealed internal company documents showed State Farm developed a playbook to lower its wind and hail claim costs in Texas that it then repeated in Oklahoma.
Insurance Commissioner Glen Mulready, a Republican who leaves office in January after two terms, said the agency’s examination and settlement bolsters consumer protection.
“We weren’t willing to simply take State Farm’s word for how these claims were handled,” Mulready said Friday in a written statement. “We took action that no other state has done in a traditional examination, putting independent engineers in the field to inspect roofs and help determine whether claims were handled appropriately.”
Mulready will be succeeded by Sullivan, who won the Nov. 3 general election with 59% of the vote.
Sullivan, in a phone interview Friday afternoon, said the settlement appeared to be good news for policyholders who have had their State Farm roof claims denied and haven’t filed their own lawsuits against the company. Still, he said the settlement agreement takes some regulatory flexibility off the table when it comes to dealing with State Farm.
“There’s a 12-month period where we’re not going to be opening market conduct examinations against State Farm as a result of this settlement agreement,” Sullivan said. “I’m not in love with it.”
Since he hasn’t yet taken office, Sullivan said he hasn’t been able to review the confidential materials that went into the final settlement with State Farm. Sullivan said he got word of the settlement from Mulready a few minutes before it was released Friday morning. He’ll be watching as details of the settlement get finalized, including how quickly a third-party administrator is appointed.
“Finding a third-party administrator that is disinterested from State Farm is a tall ask, so I’ll be following how that proceeds between now and January 11th,” Sullivan said.
In a written statement, State Farm said it disagreed with the conclusions in the market conduct exam. The company said it recorded $178.5 million in net underwriting losses in Oklahoma from 2021 to 2025.
“Over the past five years, State Farm has responded to more than 100,000 claims in Oklahoma,” the statement said. “A limited review of individual claims should not be mistaken for a complete picture of our overall claims-handling practices.”
State Farm said the financial commitments in the settlement were part of a negotiated resolution, not a punitive fine imposed after State Farm accepted the report’s conclusions.
Rep. Andy Fugate, D-Del City, has been among several lawmakers concernedabout the state’s insurance market. He said he was disappointed with the State Farm settlement because it doesn’t go far enough. Fugate questioned the timing of the settlement coming at the end of Mulready’s tenure and what it might mean for existing court cases and actions by the attorney general’s office.
“This settlement just forces State Farm to do what they should have been doing all along for their customers, many of whom have suffered great harm from State Farm’s harmful business practices,” Fugate said.
Homeowners who want their denied State Farms claims reviewed must respond to opt-in notices from the insurance company. Additional funds may be available beyond the initial $35 million in the settlement if demand exceeds that cap. More information about the program is on the Insurance Department’s website.
“If your roof claim was closed without payment during this period, don’t assume the decision was the final word,” Mulready said in his written statement. “This process gives eligible Oklahomans another chance to have their claims independently evaluated.”
The Legislature passed the Strengthen Oklahoma Homes Act under House Bill 3089 in 2024. The grant program provides eligible homeowners with up to $10,000 to help install fortified roofs. After starting as a pilot program in targeted ZIP codes, the program has helped fortify more than 500 roofs. Participants reported saving an average of $700 per year in their insurance premiums, according to the insurance department.
Oklahoma Watch, at oklahomawatch.org, is a nonprofit, nonpartisan news organization that covers public-policy issues facing the state.

name: Colorado Newsline
title: Defeated GOP Rep. Gabe Evans ditches Colorado battleground seat for safer 4th District in 2028
description: For the second time in three years, a Colorado Republican member of Congress on the outs in their district is fleeing for the safety of the state’s most GOP-leaning seat. U.S. Rep. Gabe Evans, a Fort Lupton Republican, announced Monday that he will seek election to Congress in 2028 — not in the 8th District, […]
text:
U.S. Rep. Gabe Evans, a Fort Lupton Republican, speaks at a press conference in August after he and U.S. Secretary of Agriculture Brooke Rollins held a roundtable with Colorado farmers and ranchers at Bobcat of the Rockies in Henderson, Colorado. (Photo by Lindsey Toomer/Colorado Newsline)For the second time in three years, a Colorado Republican member of Congress on the outs in their district is fleeing for the safety of the state’s most GOP-leaning seat.
U.S. Rep. Gabe Evans, a Fort Lupton Republican, announced Monday that he will seek election to Congress in 2028 — not in the 8th District, which he will represent until January after his midterm loss to Democratic challenger Manny Rutinel, but in the neighboring 4th District instead.
The announcement came less than 72 hours after The Associated Press called incumbent GOP Rep. Lauren Boebert’s loss in the 4th District Friday. Evans’ campaign did not address his motivations for the switch, or whether he plans to move to the 4th District, though it highlighted his childhood growing up within the district’s present-day boundaries. A spokesperson for Evans did not immediately respond to inquiries.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“I’m ready to keep fighting in the 4th District, where I grew up, and where my family has lived since 1976,” Evans said in a written statement. “I’m asking for the support of every family in this district who wants Colorado to stay Colorado.”
After three terms in Congress marked by political and personal controversies, Boebert said earlier this month that she would not seek reelection in two years if defeated in 2026. In the final tabulation of votes confirmed Friday, she lost to Democrat Eileen Laubacher by a margin of less than 1%.
Laubacher, a former Republican and retired Navy admiral who plans to join House Democrats’ centrist Blue Dog caucus, will be sworn in when the 120th Congress convenes on Jan. 3.
Evans’ flight to the 4th District resembles Boebert’s own district switch in late 2023, when, facing well-funded primary and general-election challengers after an unexpectedly close reelection fight in the 2022 midterms, she announced she would move across the state from the 3rd District to the 4th.
The U.S. Constitution only requires congressional representatives to live in the state, and not necessarily the district, they represent at the time of election. At the time of her switch, Boebert moved from her longtime home in Garfield County to the Front Range exurb of Windsor in the 4th District, which she called “the right move for me personally” after her divorce.
The 4th District, which includes Douglas County and extends across much of Colorado’s Eastern Plains, is Colorado’s most heavily Republican congressional district. President Donald Trump carried the district by more than 18 points in the 2024 election.
Evans, an Army veteran and former police officer, served one term in the state Legislature before launching his congressional bid for the 8th District in 2023. He narrowly defeated former Democratic Rep. Yadira Caraveo in the 2024 election.
A close ally of outgoing GOP House Speaker Mike Johnson, Evans did little over the last two years to distance himself from Trump and congressional Republicans’ agenda. Much of that agenda, including tariffs, the war in Iran and a mass-deportation program, proved deeply unpopular in the battleground 8th District, which includes parts of Denver’s northern suburbs and more rural areas in southern Weld County, and where 4 in 10 residents are Latino. Rutinel won in a relative landslide for the toss-up district, capturing 56% of the vote to Evans’ 41%.
The prospect of Boebert’s departure, meanwhile, in a district where the GOP will likely remain highly competitive for the foreseeable future, had already fueled speculation about the long list of Colorado Republicans who might seek to replace her.
Evans’ announcement, coming just 10 days after he conceded the 8th District race, may end that expected GOP cattle call before it’s even begun. Though otherwise scant on details of Evans’ reasoning behind the move, his campaign’s press release Monday rattled off a list of reasons why he’d be heavily favored in a 4th District primary contest, with “a head start in money, name recognition, and credibility before the field takes shape.”
“Gabe Evans will enter 2027 and the race for Colorado’s 4th Congressional District with $300,000 in campaign funds and name recognition that no first-time candidate in the district could match,” his campaign said. “Evans starts with name identification across the district’s population centers that would cost a new candidate millions of dollars and more than a year to build.”

name: VTDigger
title: Barre City Mayor Thom Lauzon dies
description:
Lauzon was elected earlier this year to his eighth term in office.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Barre City Mayor Thom Lauzon dies.
text:
Current Barre City Mayor Thomas Lauzon, center, spoke to members of the Senate Government Operations Committee in 2024 during his time as a Barre City Councilor. File photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger

Barre City Mayor Thom Lauzon died early Monday, Executive Office Manager Alberta Miller confirmed to VTDigger Monday morning. 
The Barre City Police Department received a call at 3:58 a.m. Monday, where officers responded to an “untimely death investigation,” Police Chief Braedon Vail said in an interview with VTDigger. 
“There were no suspicious circumstances,” he said. 
Lauzon was first elected mayor of Barre City in 2006 and held the office for 12 years before moving to the City Council in 2018. He returned to the mayor’s office in May 2024. 
He was reelected earlier this year, marking his eighth term as mayor, defeating challenger Bern Rose by 95 votes.
Lauzon grew up in Barre and graduated from Spaulding High School. A certified public accountant, he spent more than three decades at Salvador and Babic, an accounting firm in Barre, where he became senior partner. 
He and his wife, Karen, founded Metro Development in 2002, buying and rehabilitating commercial properties. They had two children, Alex and Miranda. As mayor, Lauzon also pushed for City Place, a downtown office development designed to bring about 200 state workers into the city center.
Lauzon was a Ward 1 city councilor when the July 2023 flood hit Barre. He later walked state lawmakers through the damage in the North End and pitched a plan to rebuild the neighborhood with multifamily housing and green space. 
Back in the mayor’s office when floodwaters rose again the following year, he declared a local state of emergency. Recovery remained a priority during his second stint as mayor. Last month, after the state rejected two earlier proposals, Barre secured $4.2 million for a scaled-back North End plan that included new housing and property buyouts.
This story will be updated.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Gov.-elect Cindy Holscher pledges to advocate for all Kansans: ‘I will work for you’
description: Democratic Kansas Gov.-elect Cindy Holscher offers postponed victory speech in extremely close race against Republican Ty Masterson.
text:
Gov.-elect Cindy Holscher talks to reporters at a Nov. 13, 2026, news conference at the Statehouse. She is accompanied by Lt. Gov.-elect KC Ohaebosim. Holscher is the narrow winner of the Nov. 3, 2026, election against Republican gubernatorial nominee Ty Masterson. (Photo by Sherman Smith/Kansas Reflector)TOPEKA — Counting and recounting of votes didn’t alter the outcome of the Kansas gubernatorial race, enabling Gov.-elect Cindy Holscher to personally offer thanks at the close of a campaign entwined with economic forces aggravating the cost of living.
“This election, it was never about Republicans versus Democrats,” Holscher said in a speech Friday at the Capitol in Topeka. “Throughout this campaign, I heard from Kansans across the state who want their leaders to put politics aside and work together for the good of the people.”
“It’s been about the families at the kitchen table with a stack of bills that keeps growing while their paycheck is stagnant,” she added. “It’s been about those farmers and ranchers watching the price of diesel rise and wondering if their farm is going to make it another year. It’s about the nurses pulling double shifts to get by, the teachers buying school supplies with their own money and the retirees trying to stay in the home where they raise their children.”
The Overland Park Democratic state senator, 57, survived a toss-up contest Nov. 3 to beat Republican Senate President Ty Masterson of Andover by less than 8,000 votes. Of 1.09 million votes counted in unofficial election results, Holscher earned 551,243 while Masterson received 543,842. She prevailed despite President Donald Trump repeatedly stumping for Masterson in a state with hundreds of thousands more registered Republicans than Democrats.
Holscher’s news conference at the Capitol was attended by Lt. Gov.-elect KC Ohaebosim, her immediate family and a handful of colleagues from the Kansas Legislature.
“Here’s my promise: Whether I earned your vote or not, I will work for you,” Holscher said. “We all know the challenges ahead of us. They’re real. But I’ve seen what Kansans can do when we pull together instead of pulling apart.”
Masterson, who remains president of the Kansas Senate, declined to concede until examination of late-arriving mail ballots and the required partial audit of ballots. He congratulated Holscher by telephone. Her victory coincided with the rare election of a Democrat to the U.S. Senate and the post of state attorney general. In addition, Democrats picked up 20 seats in the Kansas House.
“It looks like we will come up just short,” Masterson said. “It has been the honor of my life to carry the Republican banner for the state I love. This was a hard election for people who share our vision, here and across the country. But I believe in this state and in the people who live here, and that hasn’t changed.”
Masterson said Kansas retained the benefit of a Legislature led by Republicans. He said that GOP majority should concentrate on “the things that matter to them: property taxes, public safety, affordability and schools.”
The election of Holscher means the state will have its first Black lieutenant governor when Ohaebosim, a Wichita member of the Kansas House, formally takes the oath of office in January. Ohaebosim expressed gratitude to Holscher for placing her trust in him.
“I’m just very grateful,” Ohaebosim said. “I look forward to working to make sure that her policies are implemented to move the people of Kansas forward.”
Holscher expressed appreciation to Kansans who stepped forward to embrace her “people power” campaign.
“From Overland Park to Liberal, from Wichita to Kansas City to Manhattan, and every small town and city in between, I thank you. You gave what you could. You volunteered your evenings and weekends. You found five friends that you got to vote, and you proved that people power is more powerful than anything else,” she said.
Holscher, who follows two-term Democratic Gov. Laura Kelly, said economic issues confronting voters require the state government’s attention.
“Groceries, rent, utility bills, healthcare and property taxes keep climbing,” Holscher said. “Regular Kansans, they’re finding it harder and harder, and they’re getting left behind. It is time for that to change. As your governor, we’re going to lighten the load for Kansas families, and we’re going to work to cut your property taxes.”
“We’re going to work to make sure your schools are funded so every child gets access to solid public education, just like I got, and just like my kids got,” she added. “We’ll work to expand Medicaid, not because it’s a Democratic idea or a Republican idea, but because it’s a good idea for Kansas and it’s good for our people in our state.”
Holscher said her administration would strive to make state government work for Kansans rather than answer to billionaires, lobbyists and special interests with leverage to grab a seat at the table.
“I will work across the aisle to fully fund our schools, expand Medicaid and lower healthcare costs. I’ll work to cut property taxes with folks across the aisle and bring down the cost of living,” Holscher said.
“But make no mistake about this: I will always fight for Kansans, and I will not tolerate policies or politicians who try to impose laws that harm our state and our people. I will always fight for Kansans with an unmatched fierceness,” she said.
Holscher said details about the gubernatorial transition process would be forthcoming. That would include any special duty assigned to her lieutenant governor as well as appointment of cabinet officers to manage state agencies, she said.
The state Board of Canvassers must certify official results of the election by Dec. 1. Holscher would take the oath of office Jan. 11, weather permitting, on the south steps of the Capitol.

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: State Department conducts risk-limiting audit of the election
description: A key part of ensuring the integrity of Pennsylvania’s elections began Friday with a multi-colored set of 10-sided dice.
text:
Secretary of the Commonwealth Al Schmidt presides over the dice roll kicking off the risk-limiting audit of the 2026 election (captured from DOS livestream)A key part of ensuring the integrity of Pennsylvania’s elections began Friday with a multi-colored set of 10-sided dice.
Twenty of them were rolled by 10 State Department employees to generate a random 20-digit number. That number was then used to determine which batches of ballots from the recent election will undergo a manual audit.
That process is known as a risk-limiting audit and is one of several post-election safeguards employed in Pennsylvania to ensure election results are accurate. Chosen batches of ballots will be counted by hand, and the tally compared to the initial counts.
“We have the utmost confidence in [risk-limiting audits], which remain the gold standard of comprehensive election audits,” Secretary of the Commonwealth Al Schmidt said. “These audits provide a statistically sound, scientific method for confirming that the reported outcome of the election is accurate, and they are an integral part of our commitment to ensuring the integrity of Pennsylvania’s elections.”
Along with the risk-limiting audit, state law requires each county to perform a statistical recount. That’s where a random sample of 2% of all ballots, or 2,000 ballots — whichever number is fewer — is selected to audit.
Risk-limiting audits must be completed by Nov. 19, and counties must certify their results by Nov. 23.
“It’s important to remember in Pennsylvania we have multiple safeguards in place in addition to risk-limiting audits to ensure that our voting systems provide accurate results,” Schmidt said.

name: Honolulu Civil Beat
title: Clash Over Kauhale Pits Neighbor Against Neighbor In Waimānalo
description:
The planned village to house homeless people is an expansion of one started without permission during the pandemic that the state has since embraced — along with its founder — as a model to follow.
The post Clash Over Kauhale Pits Neighbor Against Neighbor In Waimānalo appeared first on Honolulu Civil Beat.
text:
(Jamm Aquino/Civil Beat/2026)
With the fluted black and green wall of the Koʻolau Range looming in the distance, Blanche McMillan sat at a table in the shade of a monkeypod tree surrounded by men and women who faced hard turns in life. 
She had gathered them to talk about how they found refuge, support and purpose in the Waimānalo village she created in 2020 — first for people who had been living along the highway through town, and then for others beyond the Windward Coast.
“Without her, everybody would be lost, I’d probably be dead,” said Richard Muraoka, 64. After his son died, he said he turned to drugs and was living in a Kapolei park when McMillan took him in three years ago. 
McMillan beamed.
“What I know in my heart is to take care of the poor,” she said. “I love my people.” Her people are Native Hawaiians, she said. But if there is room left over, others are welcome, too.
Today, 106 formerly homeless people live in the kauhale McMillan opened without official permission and named Hui Mahiʻai ʻĀina, which means the group farming the land. Most of the residents are Native Hawaiian, she said, and they must be clean and sober to live there. 
They pay $250 a month to live in 8×10 foot, timber-framed single-room dwellings with two windows. The newest arrivals live in tents. Mountain apple, ʻulu, avocado, ti, mangos and sweet potatoes sprout in a community garden. 
But the peaceful scene was clouded by an increasingly bitter dispute that has ruptured the Waimānalo community. It is playing out in often personal terms about a volatile mix of issues including housing homeless people in Waimānalo who are not from the community, placing more homeless facilities in an area that already has two emergency shelters, flooding and other safety concerns, as well as preserving and protecting cultural resources and Hawaiian land rights.

☀️ Get our free daily newsletter.
Read Civil Beat’s latest local updates before they hit the coconut wireless. Arrives daily at 7 a.m.







Sign me up!










To understand today’s conflict requires turning back in time, toward events that date back centuries, then tracing grievances from recent years through to the present. 
It revolves around what is happening on the 14-acre parcel where the current housing is located, which is owned by the stateʻs Department of Land and Natural Resources and borders Hawaiian homelands. The refuge McMillan built is to be relocated and expanded to the Makapuʻu side of the same property. 
There, the expansion — Hui Mahiʻai Village — is planned with water, sewer and electrical hookups that its forerunner doesn’t have. McMillan is to lead it and the current residents are to be joined by the dozens of additional homeless people she plans to welcome.

Waimānalo resident Mialisa Otis inspects a map of the proposed Hui Mahi’ai Village project in Waimānalo. (Jamm Aquino/Civil Beat/2026)

The project has set neighbors who have known each other since childhood against one another. Tensions have spread to streets nearby, including a human blockade of trucks headed to the work site. An October community meeting became so heated that police officers hovered to keep an eye on things.
Funded by public and philanthropic dollars, the expansion is a joint project of the state Office of Homelessness and Housing Solutions and the nonprofit aoi Foundation. In 2018, the foundation built a homeless village near Sand Island, Kahauiki, where about 700 people now live. The nonprofit’s development arm, Mahiʻai Development, was given a 65-year lease in February for the Waimānalo ​property.
Nearly everything about the new project is subject to debate, even basic facts, with no apparent common ground.
“If the emergency proclamation was not in place here, the community would not have let this happen.” Hiwahiwa Kaheaku-Rodenhurst, Waimānalo resident
Yet, to the dismay of opponents, it has been fast-tracked under Gov. Josh Green’s 2023 emergency proclamation on homelessness. That means the project legally leapfrogged certain initial zoning and permitting processes and environmental reviews so that work could proceed faster — although it must still meet health and other safety codes. 
“If the emergency proclamation was not in place here, the community would not have let this happen,” said Hiwahiwa Kaheaku-Rodenhurst, a  Waimānalo resident who is a leader of the opposition. 
For McMillan and her supporters, the kauhale expansion is a clear win-win. It will house more of the nearly 200 people who have been identified as homeless from Kāneʻohe to Kailua to Waimānalo, they say, and continue the work she has won plaudits for by creating a close-knit community of people whose lives are on the upswing as they recover from hard times.
“The goal really is to serve our community and get people off of the streets into a sustainable, healthy, stable home where they can jump off from into a new path,” said Jun Yang, director of the state’s homelessness office.
“The root cause of the opposition is they just don’t like homeless people.”Kalaninui Akau, Waimānalo resident
The project’s supporters maintain that at its core, the opposition is mostly a reluctance to have a kauhale nearby.
“The root cause of the opposition is they just don’t like homeless people,” said Kalaninui Akau, who grew up in Waimānalo, where more than half of residents are Native Hawaiian. Akau still lives there, and has produced promotional videos for McMillan — most for free — about Hui Mahiʻai ʻĀina. 
Others say it threatens a way of life.
“We grew up here, it was country,” said Cindy Parker, who was raised in the same house on ‘Oluʻolu Street where she raised her own family, on Hawaiian homestead land bordering the new kauhale property. 
Parker looked beyond her backyard to where she used to see monkeypod trees and koa haole, neighbors’ cows and sheep, owls at night. 
That all has been replaced by a bed of earth that raised the land about 13 feet to prepare for construction of the new housing project. 
Parker’s property flooded during the March Kona low storms, she said, because a retaining wall erected around parts of the site prevented water from draining toward the mountains as it used to. Portions of the wall have since been removed following discussions with the developer, but now Parker has other concerns, too: She has trouble breathing these days, which she blames on dust kicked up by backfill dirt being brought in.
“This is not,” she said, “what we want.”
The Land


Blanche McMillan sits under a tree at Hui Mahi’ai ʻĀina, the village she created in 2020 to house people living along Kalanianaʻole Highway in Waimānalo. (Jamm Aquino/Civil Beat/2026)


Waimānalo resident Tracey Parker backyard looks out on the plot of land where the Hui Mahi’ai Village is proposed. (Jamm Aquino/Civil Beat/2026)


Waimānalo resident Mialisa Otis, center, talks through the chain link fence with Carly Parker, left, and Cindy Parker. (Jamm Aquino/Civil Beat/2026)


On her phone, Mialisa Otis shows a photo of construction on the land where Hui Mahi’ai Village is being planned. (Jamm Aquino/Civil Beat/2026)


Heavy equipment has begun to grade the proposed Hui Mahi’ai Village plot, although neighbors have complained that some earth movement led to flooding. (Jamm Aquino/Civil Beat/2026)


Security cameras have been added to  the proposed Hui Mahi’ai Village plot. (Jamm Aquino/Civil Beat/2026)


The complicated history of land in Hawaiʻi looms large in the current clash.
After the Great Mahele of 1848, King Kamehameha III designated roughly 4,000 acres of the Waimānalo area’s Crown Lands, including where Hui Mahʻai Village is to be built behind what is now ‘Olu‘olu Street. Seized in the illegal 1893 overthrow of the Hawaiian Kingdom, all those lands were eventually transferred to the U.S. government. 
In 1959, when Hawaiʻi became a state, the land was transferred again, to the state Department of Land and Natural Resources, which still owns and manages it. Under the laws that governed Hawaiʻi’s admission as a state, public trust lands are to be used for “the betterment of the conditions of Native Hawaiians,” among other conditions.
That has shaped how many opponents view the kauhale project. When the facilitator of a contentious Oct. 6 community meeting suggested Hawai‘i’s fractured history through conquest and imperialism makes Native Hawaiians susceptible to division, one opponent called out: “It’s not about Hawaiians having a difference. It’s about how it all began.”
In more recent years, in 2015, the state land and resources department approved a community garden project on the property to be run by McMillan and a local nonprofit. 
That project sputtered, McMillan said. And in 2020, she switched tracks. 
With Covid advancing, and more than 350 people living alongside Kalanianaʻole Highway, she invited anyone who wanted to follow her to move onto the departmentʻs land, located behind her childhood home. She asked them to help her clear it of junk and brush and build homes for themselves. 
“The government, they said, ‘You have to stop.’ I said, ʻI ain’t stopping for you. I’m going to continue doing my work for the people.” Blanche McMillan, who founded Hui Mahiʻai ʻĀina
The land was zoned for agricultural uses and in a flood zone, so no building was allowed, but that proved no obstacle for McMillan. Within a few months, more than 30 people took up her invitation. 
“The government, they said, ‘You have to stop,’” she says today. “I said, ʻI ain’t stopping for you. I’m going to continue doing my work for the people. I don’t care what you say or what you do. I’m going to do it.’”
McMillan, 72, came from a family of 17 children, all raised in a small house next to the property where Hui Mahiʻai ʻĀina is now located. These days, when she’s not making the rounds of the village, she can often be found sitting in front of her childhood home with village residents. She watched her parents take care of hungry people in town and others who were lost, lonely and in need, she said, and became determined to follow their lead.
“I said, ‘One day I’m going to become what they were,’” said McMillan, who is universally referred to as Aunty Blanche. “Today that’s what I am. And when the pandemic happened, “I knew there was time for me to walk the talk and do the work.”
McMillan has a voice that needs no microphone, laughs quickly and rarely expresses doubt. She frequently cites God and love as her guides. In conversation, she often starts sentences with: “You know what, let me tell you something.”
There may be nobody in Waimānalo who doesn’t know her — including those who now find themselves questioning the wisdom of her plans.
“Aunty Blanche is a respected elder and has been for many years,” said Kimeona Kane, chair of the Waimānalo Neighborhood Board.
Kane believes the expansion project has strayed too far from McMillan’s original intent of helping people from Waimānalo. It has been forced onto the community, he said, causing “significant chaos.”
“There’s been a lot of generational and intergenerational infighting,” Kane said. “It’s been very harmful for the community because now we have polarizing positions where people are starting to attack personal beliefs and lots of other things are taking place.”
As McMiIlan’s village grew and became a fixture, though, government officials came around to her side. 
During his first state of the state speech in January 2023, Green signed his emergency proclamation on homelessness, officially launching the kauhale initiative. That month, an annual count found 6,223 people homeless in Hawaiʻi, the great majority on Oʻahu. 
In announcing the proclamation, Green singled out McMillan as a homeless advocate who was “showing that it takes the embrace of a village to help people find their way to a permanent home.”
“Business as usual won’t work anymore,” he said, “there is simply too much on the line to accept the status quo.”
‘No One Can Stop Her’


Resident Hi’i Spencer, right, shows a photo of her with her boyfriend Darien to Blanche McMillan outside her hale at the Hui Mahi’ai ʻĀina. (Jamm Aquino/Civil Beat/2026)


Resident Joey Santiago outside her hale at Hui Mahi’ai ʻĀina, built during the pandemic by and for homeless people. (Jamm Aquino/Civil Beat/2026)


Residents of the current Hui Mahi’ai ʻĀina share a common outdoor eating area. (Jamm Aquino/Civil Beat/2026)


Resident Kainoa Choy sits outside at Hui Mahi’ai ʻĀina, where some live in cottages and others in tents. (Jamm Aquino/Civil Beat/2026)


Cancer survivor Richard Muraoka reflects on his time living at Hui Mahi’ai ʻĀina, where he came after living in a Kapolei park. (Jamm Aquino/Civil Beat/2026)


Hui Mahi’ai ʻĀina resident Christine Felix talks to Blanche from inside her family home on the property. (Jamm Aquino/Civil Beat/2026)


By late 2024, the governor’s initiative had a full head of steam, with nearly 20 kauhale opened. The state’s homelessness office — then headed by Yang’s predecessor, John Mizuno — proposed building a bigger kauhale on the Waimānalo property in collaboration with aio Foundation.
The new kauhale would absorb Hui Mahʻai ʻĀina and house 188 people altogether, in 116 single, double and family units, and include a communal kitchen, health clinic, classrooms and a garden to also serve the larger community.
“I was very impressed with the model, but with this wahine as well. No one can stop her.” Dawn Chang, then executive director of DLNR
In a sign of how much favor McMillan had gained by then, she and the village she had skirted the law to create were held up as examples to follow.
“I was very impressed with the model, but with this wahine as well. No one can stop her,” Dawn Chang, then executive director of the Department of Land and Natural Resources, said at the October 2024 board meeting where the application for the expansion was unanimously approved.
It was made clear the project had blessings from the very top.
“The governor is in full support of this project, full support of Aunty Blanche,” Brandon Mitsuda, special assistant at the homelessness office, told the board members. “She is the model we follow, and anything Aunty Blanche needs, we help her.”
But the meeting also offered some of the first glimpses of the dissension to follow when Kane, of the Neighborhood Board, said the community hadn’t been properly involved in the process before that point.
“As much as we love and really appreciate what Aunty Blanche is doing, there has been very little to no community involvement with this new expansion,” he said.
Kane said he had told Mizuno that Waimānalo residents had not been adequately consulted and Mizuno had promised to pull it from the agenda. That didn’t happen, Kane said.
After first agreeing to discuss the matter, Mizuno declined to talk with Civil Beat.
At the 2024 meeting, board member Wesley “Kaiwi” Yoon asked Kane whether the project might face complications in the future: “Do you anticipate any hihia with this initiative going forward?”
Kane answered carefully. Some community concerns about the original village hadn’t been addressed, he said, and so the expansion was likely to face pushback of some sort despite a local desire for “supporting the need and effort to address the issue of homelessness in our community.” 
He said: “I anticipate that there will be some concerns shared in and around the area. However … there is still a beautiful love that Aunty Blanche has brought to this particular topic and issue within our community. So it’s hard to tell at this point what it’s going to look like.”
What It Looks Like
Waimānalo resident Hiwahiwa Kaheaku-Rodenhurst pauses at the entrance to a cave believed sacred to the Native Hawaiians. (Jamm Aquino/Civil Beat/2026)
Two years later, the opposition has crystallized. Foes have formed a nonprofit, Pono ʻOluʻolu, to fight the project. They have collected nearly 1,000 online signatures, and are seeking legal help to stop construction.
Tense encounters have played out on the streets around the site. Village residents who serve on McMillan’s security team have trailed opponents on ATVs as they walked nearby. Members of the team showed up to keep watch, stony-faced, as opponents gathered by the roadside this summer planning to block trucks from entering the property. 
Differences have spilled over at community meetings, too, where it’s clear opponents are tallying grievances and objections — among them an insistence that rules underlying the governor’s proclamation have not been followed.
A February 2024 archaeological inspection by a firm hired by Mahiʻai Development had uncovered some recent grading and clearing of the site, well before the Department of Land and Natural Resources approved the project. 
Likewise, they point out that in November 2025, months before the lease was approved this February, work started in earnest to clear and backfill the property with trucked-in dirt to elevate it above flood levels.
And they have called attention to a letter the state office of homelessness sent to Mahiʻai Development in August confirming the project was certified under the emergency proclamation. That proves, they claim, that the project had been proceeding illegally for months. 
Yang, however, said the letter was just a paperwork step since the project was already certified.
Opponents are also worried about the length of the 65-year lease. The proclamation’s terms include a condition that the property be used for homeless housing for at least 20 years  — which they say opens the door to more unwelcome types of development after year 20.
They say their concerns about flooding are not being fully addressed — the developer says they have been — and that the site’s cultural importance is being brushed aside.
“So all these kūpuna here — this is going to be an Otake Camp, you watch.”Gary Silva, Waimānalo resident
Pointing toward the kauhale site, Gary Silva compared what would happen there in a flood to a North Shore community extensively damaged in the March Kona low storms.
“We’re very low here, everybody is low compared to up there,” he said. “So all these kūpuna here — this is going to be an Otake Camp, you watch.”
Silva, who grew up in Waimānalo, owns a horse ranch that his uncles started about 65 years ago a quarter mile or so from where the kauhale is planned, just beyond ʻOluʻolu Street. It too flooded during the March storms. 
He helped build many of the villageʻs tiny homes when McMillan was getting started. Now he is dead set against its expansion.
As officialdom has come to favor McMillan, Silva said she has come to enjoy her new stature among government officials too much.
“She’s trying to get all this land from the governor so she can build herself up,” he said. “It doesn’t make me feel well.”
Besides flooding concerns, Silva said the expansion would disturb nearby cultural sites.
Chief among those, he said, is a cave called Ke Ana Luawai, just mauka of the project site. Surrounded by lāʻau lapaʻau — medicinal plants — the cave holds a freshwater spring that Silva said centuries ago sustained wounded Hawaiian warriors seeking respite from battle. 
“It’s super sacred ground,” Kaheaku-Rodenhurst agreed. “You do not desecrate it. You do not disrespect it.”


Waimānalo residents Onepookela Craig-Rodenhurst, Tracey Parker, Bernard Sampaga and Hiwahiwa Kaheaku-Rodenhurst marvel at a cave believed to be sacred to the Native Hawaiian people. (Jamm Aquino/Civil Beat/2026)


Waimānalo resident Mialisa Otis explores the Ke Ana Luawai cave, just mauka of the project site.  (Jamm Aquino/Civil Beat/2026)


Mialisa Otis holds seashells found inside the cave, which holds a fresh water spring thought to have sustained wounded Hawaiian warriors. (Jamm Aquino/Civil Beat/2026)


Waimānalo residents Bernard Sampaga, left, and Gary Silva examine an ancient Hawaiian petroglyph on a rock wall. (Jamm Aquino/Civil Beat/2026)


“It’s super sacred ground. You do not desecrate it. You do not disrespect it.”Hiwahiwa Kaheaku-Rodenhurst
Kaheaku-Rodenhurst and her husband, Onepookela Craig-Rodenhurst, both Hawaiian sovereignty activists, were asked by Pono ʻOluʻolu to help fight the project and are forming another nonprofit, Kupa’a o Waimānalo, to fund and spearhead legal action against the project.
“A lot of people are being woken up,” she said. 
Yang said he first learned about the cave at the Oct. 6 community meeting. “I am interested if these are something of significance, we’d love to be able to see if we can find a way to preserve them,” he said.
A report from ASM Affiliates, a California-based cultural resource management firm, said it had reviewed literature about the site and inspected three acres of its surface in February 2024. The report described the historic nature of the Waimānalo area as a landing site and occasional battleground for Hawaiians from neighbor islands, but said the firm had “identified no historic properties within the project area.” 
Opponents say that report is inadequate.
“It’s just the surface. They’re just kind of kicking rocks around,” said Mialisa Otis, who lives on Waimānaloʻs backroads and has led efforts to block trucks carrying backfill from entering the property.
The letter Yang’s office sent to Mahiʻai Development in August confirming certification of the project under the proclamation noted that the state’s historic preservation department requested ongoing archaeological monitoring at the site because it does not have enough information to determine what might be below the ground’s surface. 
An archaeologist monitor has been on site, Yang said, and has submitted a report that the state is now reviewing.
How It Was ʻFramed’
Waimānalo resident Bernard Sampaga goes over a property map of ʻOluʻolu Street, which borders the planned Hui Mahiʻai Village parcel, with resident Tracey Parker in the driveway of her Waimānalo home. (Jamm Aquino/Civil Beat/2026)
As the fight over the kauhale continues, Kane’s 2024 comments to the Department of Land and Natural Resources board about a lack of consultation have grown into wider complaints that the community has been largely ignored.
Opponents acknowledge that just two of them turned up at a Nov. 13, 2024 meeting at Hui Mahiʻai ʻĀina, a month after the application to develop a kauhale on the land was approved. But they say a second meeting, held on the property right before the Nov. 15, 2025 groundbreaking, came too late in the process for any real input to be gathered.
“It was in the news. Nothing. No comment. Nobody was upset. No one was saying, ‘Oh, why is this project here?’”Rep. Lisa Marten, whose district includes Waimānalo
Supporters of the project cite the lack of major opposition at those meetings as evidence that opposition has been drummed up only more recently.
“It was a large event,” said Rep. Lisa Marten, whose district includes Waimānalo, referring to the 2025 meeting. “It was in the news. Nothing. No comment. Nobody was upset. No one was saying, ‘Oh, why is this project here?’”
Marten emphasized that she did not initiate the project, although she does support it and attended the groundbreaking. She said she has spent hours batting down incorrect information from both sides in the dispute, including McMillan’s statement to HNN that she wants to house up to 1,000 people and opponents’ social media posts showing condominium towers on the site. 
Opponents name Marten among the officials who have stymied their input. At a March meeting this year on the property to discuss neighbors’ concerns about flooding, drainage and security, Otis said Marten told people like her who don’t live on ‘Olu‘olu Street that they couldn’t participate. 
Marten remembered things differently. 
Otis invited her to the March meeting about the flooding at the Parker residence, along with other issues, Marten said. She then initiated another meeting the following month to address those concerns and invited immediate neighbors and the project’s engineer and developer to it. She said Otis and others arrived uninvited at that meeting, but stayed and participated.
“I wanted to immediately figure out solutions to those solvable problems,” Marten said. “I didn’t want it to be about other people’s issues with the project that were not directly impacted by those drainage and security issues.” 
The meeting led to the installation of security fences between the kauhale site and neighboring properties in response to worries that future kauhale residents would enter neighbors’ yards uninvited, and the engineer agreed to new drainage measures, Marten said.
During another meeting later that month, at Waimānalo Beach Park, Otis said McMillan tried to overwhelm opponents by bringing along a crowd of more than 60 Hui Mahiʻai ʻĀina residents. 
Marten, who is chair of the House Committee on Human Services and Homelessness, said that it was only when the opposition broadened the scope of its complaints — from flooding and security to issues about encroaching on Hawaiian homelands and cultural and environmental concerns — that the pushback really grew.
“It became a social media thing with just a lot of propaganda and misinformation,” she said. “That’s when a lot of people across the community who don’t even live nearby, even in other communities who don’t even live in Waimānalo, became very concerned about it because it was framed as taking away Hawaiian rights.”
She added that she believes community members have unrealistic expectations about how much they can shape such projects.
“The community wishes they could choose what happens with every plot of land,” Marten said. “But they don’t get to.”
An Apology

The Koʻolau Mountains tower over some of the hale built by and for homeless people during the pandemic at Hui Mahi’ai ʻĀina. (Jamm Aquino/Civil Beat/2026)

On Oct. 6, the showdown reached the Waimānalo Hawaiian Homestead Association hālau, a pitch-roofed pavilion open to the air on all sides where gatherings are more often for large celebrations — of events such as weddings, birthdays or graduations — that mark people coming together rather than being driven apart.
With the meeting about to get underway, McMillan stood before a crowd spilling outside, and said she was sorry.
“If I have done anything wrong, I apologize,” she said. Many in the audience applauded. 
McMillan didn’t explain why at the time, but later made it clear that her apology was not because she had done anything wrong.
“The Lord had told me forgive the people, what they’re doing to us, to all of us in Waimānalo,” she said. “So I needed to let the whole Waimānalo community know who I was. And I made sure that I forgive each and every one of them.” 
Sponsored by Green’s office, the meeting had been promoted as a town hall to answer questions about the project. Officials were there to describe Hui Mahiʻai Village, including Yang, representing the state office of homelessness, and Duane Kurisu, a prominent businessman who is president of aio Foundation and leader of Mahiʻai Development.
Opponents were there in force, too, including Parker, Otis and Kaheaku-Rodenhurst.
Kumu Hinaleimoana Wong, a longtime community leader asked by the governor’s office to facilitate the meeting, opened it with a pule. But the effort to start off on a peaceful note failed.
A group in the audience erupted as Wong finished, holding signs that read, “Betrayers,” “Shame” and “Judas,” and “Pilau,” “Kapulu,” and “Haumia Nui,” or corrupt, desecrating and filthy. 
Craig-Rodenhurst began chanting in a staccato kepakepa style to convey, he later said, his ancestors’ argument against violating sacred land — and to call for it to be preserved.
“If more development happens, the more of our history gets lost and then everything is just in the books,” he said later.
After the outburst subsided, Wong — an artist, educator and political and cultural activist — tried to explain her role as a neutral facilitator. There was more loud applause. But as Wong, at the time a candidate for Oʻahu resident trustee for the Office of Hawaiian Affairs, continued, someone else shouted, “Are you Hawaiian with us, or are you Hawaiian with them?” 
“Let’s be clear,” Wong responded. “No matter how any kanaka feels. Support. No support. That’s not who I’m being tonight. I came because even when you talk any kine to me, I’m still gonna tell you I love you.”
At one point, a clearly frustrated Kurisu told the naysayers: “You know what? I’m not kanaka. But we’re building it for you.” Shouts of both derision and support greeted his statement.
Nearly three hours later, as officials tried to bring the meeting to a close, the vice chair of the Waimānalo Neighborhood Board raised the specter of historic land rights. 
“The land … is, in fact, Crown lands and it’s deemed Crown lands because of our kingdom,” Kūʻikeokalani Kamakea-Ohelo said.
Would it, he asked, be transferred back to the Department of Hawaiian Homelands in the future so “we can ensure that kānaka are taken care of in compliance with 1959 Admissions Act?”
His question was met with scattered applause, but nobody answered it.
“The divide can be made smaller by reminding ourselves we come from the same set of genealogies. We’re the survivors.”Kumu Hinaleimoana Wong, longtime community leader
As people started to stand, gather in new groups and disperse, Wong tried to close the night on a hopeful chord, circling back to the experiences Native Hawaiians have faced and share.
“The divide can be made smaller by reminding ourselves we come from the same set of genealogies. We’re the survivors. We’re all the survivors after the collision with foreigners,” she said. “We’re the ones that never succumb to the diseases. And we’re still hanging on despite all of the injustices to the community. 
“So I ask all of you, no matter where you stood tonight: Please aloha one another.”

Tracey Parker, right, embraces Mialisa Otis at Parker’s residence just outside the proposed Hui Mahi’ai Village plot in Waimānalo. (Jamm Aquino/Civil Beat/2026)

Later she said she understood the oppositionʻs anger.
“Anything encroaching upon what little is left, anytime you have anything that’s going to serve beyond Hawaiian interests in a community that has endured and survived historical and generational trauma,” she said, “this is the reaction that you’re going to get.” 
McMillan is tired of the controversy.
“What the governor says, it goes. It doesn’t matter,” she said. “He’s doing the right thing. He’s taking care of the people.”
Those opposed to Hui Mahiʻai Village have judged without knowledge what she does and what it will be, she said.
“It makes me sick because we’re Hawaiian. And it’s unreal what they do. But you know what? I don’t pay attention. I just do what I have to do,” she said. “You should put your two hands together and your mouth and your brains into this property and help me out.”
Work on the project has stopped in recent weeks while Honolulu’s permitting department and the state’s office of historical preservation review plans submitted by the kauhale’s developers, including the report of the archaeologist required to monitor the site. 
It’s a normal part of the timeline, Yang said, unlikely to lead to a lengthy delay. “We’re just waiting on these next steps as we work through the process,” he said.
“When my friends talk to me, what they tell me is, ‘You guys going lose. You’re going up against millionaires and the state.’” Cindy Parker, who lives near the proposed kauhale property. 
Kane, the Neighborhood Board president, said he believes only legal action could slow or halt the project. 
“Not even being able to take a pause right on this and just help figure it out, that has been crazy to me,” he said.
The opposition is nonetheless digging in, flooding social media with posts making their case, researching the land’s history, preparing to take to the streets again if necessary. 
They remain undaunted by the odds.
“When my friends talk to me, what they tell me is, ‘You guys going lose. You’re going up against millionaires and the state,’” Parker said, referring to Kurisu, who heads the development company. “What I always tell everybody that tells me that is, ‘Well, we’re going to give it our best shot and we’re going to do our damnedest to stop it.’”

title: Why Are We Trying To Get Rid Of Maui’s Police Chief?
description:
John Pelletier has listened, earned trust, made changes and proved himself. That's good leadership.
The post Why Are We Trying To Get Rid Of Maui’s Police Chief? appeared first on Honolulu Civil Beat.
text:
No, really. Why?
We needed a change in the Maui Police Department. We needed someone with the qualifications, experience, and willingness to make that change.
And we got John Pelletier.
He earned the position through an open, measurable process. He was selected for his qualifications alone. No relationships. Just skills.
His plan was to change the authoritarian system of policing we knew to community-led policing. That is what he meant when he talked about 21st-century policing. He had a plan, implemented it, used metrics to evaluate its progress, and adjusted based on what those metrics showed.
That’s the bare minimum we should expect from accountable leadership.
But we made him work for us without a hint of care.



Ideas showcases stories, opinion and analysis about Hawaiʻi, from the state’s sharpest thinkers, to stretch our collective thinking about a problem or an issue. Email news@civilbeat.org to submit an idea or an essay.


Read More

We did not care if we were dismissive, purposefully ignorant, hypercritical, or unkind because we believed he deserved it. Because he wasn’t one of us. He wasn’t from here. And he was police.
For the first few years, I refused to like him. I stayed very critical of him.
And I understand why others would, too.
Maui Police Chief John Pelletier says he believes he was put on leave because of what he says are investigations into corruption in the mayor’s office.  (Cammy Clark/Civil Beat/2024)
Our fundamental cultural flaw here is: If I don’t know your auntie or the high school you went to, you don’t belong here.
You don’t belong here. That’s heavy.
Nā Kānaka are still reeling from the grief and loss of what once was and are picking up the broken pieces of that identity. I feel that so deeply.
I’m not kanaka. My cultural pottery may be different, but the motions of searching for the scattered pieces of who we once were and trying to put them back into something even close to what once was, under the conditions we’ve been left in, are painfully familiar.
That pain doesn’t go away just because it started generations ago. That wound heals slowly because of what we face every day.
As if I can blame anyone for not accepting change?
I understand the desire to protect yourself. To refuse to engage with a system that has given you so many reasons not to trust it.
It took me years to do anything different. To see a person behind a uniform.
The world of policing is weird.
So many rules and so much structure. Sameness. It feels unnatural. They’re not robots.
They’re people.
People who flow between the rigidity of the law and the complexity of humanity, trying not to break either one. That’s a weird world to exist in.
The thing is, we have really good people at MPD who decided to become police officers.
They could have been veterinarians or professors or pitmasters or kumu hula or chicken farmers, but for whatever reason, life led them to policing in Maui County.
Being led by some … outsider.
It is hard to lead humans. Even harder when they don’t inherently trust you.
No one in Maui County who had suffered an injustice was going to inherently trust John Pelletier. He was going to have to do the work to prove himself.
And he did.
One of the first things Chief Pelletier did was create the MPD Multicultural Advisory Counsel. I am a founding member.
Instead of closing the door on the toughest critics of MPD, John invited us in.So, we yelled at him in his own office.
I refused to give him compliments or praise. I often reminded him in our MMAC meetings that it was not my job to praise him. It was my job to hold him accountable (fairly).
I tested him. I forced him into uncomfortable spaces to see if he could handle them.
But he was patient. He listened. He learned. He made changes.
That’s good leadership.
It took me five years to let my guard down. And these are not my stolen lands. I’ve never been incarcerated. I’ve never had a mental health crisis that required first responders. I’ve never been unhoused. I am economically stable. I am free.
It still took me five years.
We need every bit of knowledge and skill we can get.
The resistance is not lost on me.
But should we keep doing this?
We are in an environmental crisis.
We need every bit of knowledge and skill we can get.
We need to manage the resources we have. All of them. Including the people.
Chief John Pelletier is a resource. His experience, his ability to manage complex organizations during a crisis, his willingness to learn — for us.
Have we been squandering a resource?
From every book I’ve read and every story I’ve been told about Hawaiian leadership, one thing has been clear to me.
Nā Aliʻi were smart.
They knew how to manage resources. They knew how to incorporate new technologies.
They understood consequences. They knew how to be open to change and how to cleverly utilize it to benefit everyone.
Which brings me back to: Why are we doing this?
Maybe the why is that we are being taught something right now.
Maybe we are being taught that good resource management isn’t just knowing how to use a resource.
Maybe it’s having the wisdom to recognize one in the first place.
